title: Vercel and Shopify make agents first-class shoppers
description:
Agents already shop on the web, but they often use pages and tools originally built for people and search engines. Building a better shopping experience for agents means treating them as first-class shoppers, with product information they can read directly and tools designed for agents to shop.

Today, Vercel Shop, our open source Next.js storefront template for Shopify, is generally available. Teams can launch storefronts optimized for how people, search engines, and agents interact with them.

Vercel Shop is built on Shopify’s Hydrogen SDK. The SDK gives teams access to the store’s product catalog, cart and order management, payments, and checkout to build custom storefronts. Earlier this year, Vercel and Shopify announced plans to rebuild Hydrogen to work across JavaScript frameworks. Today, the rebuilt SDK is generally available.

Give agents the information and tools they need

Vercel Shop makes product pages available as machine-readable content, including price, availability, and options. The same product URL can serve a visual page to people or product information that agents can read without interpreting the page’s layout. The template also includes structured data embedded in pages and sitemaps to help search and answer engines discover and understand the products.

Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which gives agents a standard way to search a store’s catalog, read product details, check availability, build a cart, and get a checkout link. Vercel Shop makes these capabilities discoverable at the merchant’s own domain, so agents can use MCP to search products and build carts without navigating the site.

Customize the experience for all customers

Vercel Shop brings the store’s product catalog, cart, and checkout together with a Next.js storefront, product information and shopping tools for agents, and a shopping assistant powered by eve. The storefront and assistant live in the same codebase, so teams can customize the store’s design and how the assistant helps shoppers.

Skills included in the template guide coding agents through setup, customization, and template updates. Teams can create an experience where shoppers browse product pages or ask the assistant to find products and add them to their cart. Both share the same cart, so shoppers keep what they’ve added as they move between experiences.

Storefronts built with Shopify and Vercel

Today, we launched our merch store at vercel.store with limited-edition drops. It’s built on Vercel Shop. The store’s shopping agent helps shoppers find products, add them to their cart, and continue to checkout.

Shopify, Next.js, and Vercel already power storefronts for brands including AG1, Bombas, and PAIGE. When PAIGE re-architected its ecommerce platform, it saw a 22% increase in revenue and a 76% increase in conversion over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with no downtime.

title: A PNG Extension Is Not a Transparency Test
description:
A PNG can contain a fully opaque white rectangle. Checking the filename will not tell you whether a cutout has usable transparency. Check the pixels against another surface before shipping the asset.

Reproduce the visible failure

Put the exported image in a small HTML page with a dark background. Set a fixed display width and preserve its aspect ratio. If a rectangle appears, distinguish opaque backdrop pixels from a browser layout issue. Changing the element’s background cannot erase pixels inside the file.

Inspect the preparation step

The BGRemover guide to making a transparent background covers the export workflow. Open the actual downloaded result, rather than inspecting only an editor preview.

Choose a format deliberately

MDN’s image format guide documents format capabilities, including transparency support. File format support and the presence of useful alpha data are separate checks. Converting an opaque JPEG into PNG preserves the white pixels unless another step removes them.

Add a visual acceptance check

Review the asset on light and dark surfaces at its intended size. Include gaps inside handles or lettering, where leftover pixels are easy to miss. Keep an original for corrections and export a new version when the mask changes. This small check catches failures that a successful build cannot see.

Include this inspection in the asset review notes. Record the intended surfaces and displayed width so another developer can repeat the check after a replacement file arrives.

title: Seeing vs. Counting: Complexity Twins Show Where Multimodal LLMs Fail on Diagrams
description:
arXiv:2611.08998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, does it fail at seeing or at counting? Existing visual graph and puzzle benchmarks vary visual density and algorithmic hardness together, confounding the two. We pair counting questions about the same drawing that sit in different counting-complexity classes, such as its spanning trees (a determinant) and its simple paths (#P-complete), and use a transcription probe and a text-only control to separate reading from computing. We test Gemini, Gemma and Qwen3-VL models; for the Gemini models, the answer depends on how the model computes. In chain of thought, most of them read small drawings correctly and then fail at counting, at a rate set far more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class (for the primary model, the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold per decade of the answer). Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, and reading becomes the bottleneck: a single view misses horizontal edges, and a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, against 57/96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.

title: Frontier3DBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for 3D Creation across Objects, Scenes, and Interactive Open Worlds
description:
arXiv:2611.09017v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they bring reconstruction, generation, and editing into a shared workflow. Yet existing benchmarks fragment evaluation across task scopes and protocols, leaving their capabilities across construction levels unclear. We propose Frontier3DBench, a unified benchmark of 145 tasks across 9 categories spanning object, scene, and interactive open-world creation, with joint evaluation of appearance, structure, and behavior. Experiments with 11 model-harness configurations reveal strengths that vary by level: GPT-6.1-sol leads the object and scene levels and achieves the highest overall score of 66.02/100, whereas GPT-6-astra leads interactive world construction. However, all configurations score lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in object and scene tasks. Producing plausible content thus remains easier than reproducing specified geometry, layouts, and visual details. Moreover, generated worlds average 83.08/100 on local mechanisms but only 20.82 on motion clearance and 30.26 on stateful workflows: individual mechanisms often function, whereas complete activities that require coordinated actions and persistent state remain difficult. These results identify reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion as central bottlenecks for coding agents in 3D creation.

title: Microserver Updated with Mini Catbot! ✨😻 mew!
description:
View mini Catbot Live: mew!

Sunday Funday... Updated my server hub which had been snoozing for a bit. The page was screaming AI-created and it was bothering me. I finally had a second to sit with it and make it feel a little bit more me-like. I get paid $0 for doing stuff like this, and I do it for pure entertainment value.

Sometimes in life, there is a point where you realize it is much faster to drop in a vector graphic, than try to reinvent the whole damn thing with CSS. Don't get me wrong, I love CSS, but I had a plan, and it absolutely had to happen.

Gemini generated image after given reference photos.

The first part of my plan was to have blacklights casting onto to page content. I soon realized that the best placement for them was horizontally and shining down. But, before I could place my blacklights, I had to have my graphic. Generally, I am not satisfied with clipart and stock. I want my own thing, because apparently I am a digital brat.

So I chose the fast method of finding reference images of the exact blacklight I had in mind and giving them to Gemini to produce a mockup starting point. After A few renditions, I got something workable. I took that version and dropped it in illustrator, where I vectorized it using outlines and tweaked to taste. I nearly ended up with a whole damn schematic of blacklights and scaffolding.

Finishing touches for blacklight svg file

Rabbit holes are so easy to fall into. Anyways, happy with my new creation, I used it as my blacklight on the page, and mounted it snuggly to the ceiling with some scaffolding. Perfect.

Then it was time to turn the lights on. That was a little bit of css-figuring that involved gradients and placement via percent. This could have also been a rabbit hole, but this is enough for now. 🤣 After I got the lights appearing properly, I realized it would be WAY COOLER to have a button. So I made a fun button that toggles the blacklights on and off, which also alters how the text and borders appear on the page.

Mini Catbot

And then I realized... I have a purrfect platform for a mini catbot to walk across! 🤣✨ So, having the full scale catbot at my disposal, I used claude to generate a 'mini catbot'. Mini Catbot will follow your cursor above the scaffolding, bat at the power button, and meow. And of course I updated some of the content which also served as a reminder I have more work to do. No homework or studying today... just 'fuzzacating' LOL

Claude handled the simple animation very well, I cannot take credit for that. But I do absolutely love it. ✨

Now my page feels much better! 😹

title: DUET: Dual-Sparse Inference for Block Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.09239v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, yet their inference remains costly due to repeated attention over a growing historical prefix and repeated processing of the entire current generation block. Historical attention becomes increasingly expensive as generation progresses, while all current-block positions are propagated through the Transformer at every denoising step even though only a small fraction are typically resolved at that step. In this paper, we introduce Duet, a training-free dual-sparse inference framework that addresses these challenges through prefix Key-Value (KV) sparsity and early query sparsity, respectively. Specifically, Duet exploits the concentration and cross-step stability of historical attention within each generation block to construct a compact historical KV subset that is reused across denoising steps. For query sparsity, Duet predicts update positions from shallow representations and propagates only the corresponding queries through the suffix Transformer layers, avoiding deep computation at positions unlikely to be updated in the current step. Experiments show that Duet maintains competitive accuracy while achieving 1.34$\times$/2.83$\times$ end-to-end/per-step speedups on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41$\times$/4.72$\times$ on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 at a 32K context length.

title: Storefront Answers: 5 Checks for Structured JSON Schema and Citations
description:
A structured JSON answer with citations has two deadlines in a private storefront knowledge base: respond before the shopper leaves, and establish which policy supports the answer before anyone acts on it. JSON Schema checks its shape; evidence checks establish whether it deserves to be shown. A fast response that cites the wrong returns policy creates work elsewhere.

Short answer: retrieve relevant chunks with embeddings, supply selected evidence to chat completions, and return structured JSON containing answer, confidence, citations, and follow_up_questions. Use JSON Schema to define the contract, then validate citation identifiers against retrieved chunk metadata before displaying the result. Choose quality and latency together; a shorter response doesn't compensate for an answer that sends a shopper to support.

Consider a hypothetical incident review, not an observed outage. A shopper asks whether an opened item qualifies for a return. The answer arrives quickly, accompanied by a policy citation, but that citation identifies a different policy than the one supplied to generation. What page fired? If the alert only covered HTTP success, it would miss the application failure.

Trust needs evidence.

I recommend trying Infrai for the model operations in this private-document workflow when a plain REST API would remove SDK installation and client-version maintenance from the integration. Anything that sends an HTTP request can call it. Its per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata provide a separate benefit: attributing expensive or slow answers to a request instead of guessing from a dashboard average. These are integration and investigation advantages, not evidence of better answer quality.

1. How do structured JSON answers keep citations tied to retrieved evidence?

Start the postmortem with the shopper-visible result. Every returned citation must identify evidence selected for that question, and every displayed answer must pass the application's acceptance policy. These are separate conditions. A model can cite a real chunk without that chunk supporting its conclusion.

The useful record contains a request identifier, selected chunk identifiers, document versions, final answer, validation outcome, and elapsed time by stage. Treat access to that record as access to private knowledge. A dashboard showing successful requests cannot establish that the answer used the right policy; the review needs a path from one displayed claim back to the exact selected evidence, including the version that existed when generation ran. Otherwise an investigator opening today's policy may reach a different conclusion about yesterday's answer.

For the illustrative returns question, a citation might refer to document returns-policy, page 4, chunk returns-4-b. These are example application identifiers, not provider fields. Carry them through retrieval rather than asking generation to reconstruct an authoritative URL from memory. Resolve identifiers into document locations on the application side, after checking the reader's access.

A citation isn't permission.

That rule also governs retention: keep source documents and answer artifacts private, and use presigned access when an authorized reader needs an object. Don't turn a policy citation into a public link to the private knowledge base.

2. Charge the workload for the answer it actually delivers

Suppose an evaluation contains 120 store-policy questions. That's an illustrative test size, not a benchmark result. Include straightforward lookups, ambiguous product questions, and questions the knowledge base cannot answer. Track supported answers and abstentions separately, then compare latency among configurations that satisfy the acceptance criteria. Otherwise a configuration that guesses quickly can appear to win.

The operating bill includes document processing, embeddings, index maintenance, retrieval, optional reranking, generation, artifact storage, and human review. Credential management, client upgrades, and error handling belong there too. Count this work against accepted answers, keeping unresolved questions visible; counting only successful responses hides the cost of failure. This accounting model alone establishes no measured savings.

Reranking is a quality-versus-latency decision. Add it when evaluation shows that better ordering improves supported answers enough to justify another stage. More context can increase downstream generation work and introduce irrelevant evidence. Less context can remove the policy exception the shopper needed. Neither adjustment deserves a blanket recommendation, especially if a dashboard aggregates easy shipping questions with the return-policy exceptions that actually create support work.

Measure the tail.

Record retrieval, reranking, generation, and validation times alongside supported-answer rate. Keep the workload fixed. Record the selected model and evidence settings so a routing change doesn't get mistaken for a quality improvement. A returned confidence label isn't a calibrated probability unless the application has independently established that calibration.

3. Compare components before consolidating the account

The options cover different parts of the job. Comparing them as interchangeable complete systems hides who owns retrieval, storage, and acceptance checks.

Option Appropriate evaluation Boundary
OpenAI directly Test generation when a direct relationship with that provider is required. The application still needs evidence selection and document access rules.
Anthropic Claude directly Test as a competing generator against the same store-policy questions. Choose on observed supported answers and latency, not an assumed quality ranking.
Google Gemini directly Include as another generation candidate when evaluating provider alternatives. A model choice alone doesn't implement citation validation.
Cohere Rerank Test a specialist when candidate ordering is the quality bottleneck. Reranking doesn't produce the final cited answer.
Amazon S3 Evaluate the storage component of a separately assembled stack. Storage selection doesn't choose the model or acceptance policy.
Infrai Test model operations and storage capabilities behind one REST API and key. Shared integration conventions don't replace evidence evaluation.

For the direct generation candidates, this is an evaluation plan rather than a claim that one has measured superior quality or latency. A direct competitor is the better choice when its particular model behavior or provider relationship is a requirement. A specialist such as Cohere deserves a separate evaluation when evidence ordering dominates the result.

Infrai uses one API key and one bill for model and storage operations, removing a second credential lifecycle at the seam where a validated answer becomes a retained artifact. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas without requiring a key. Its documented capabilities also ship runnable examples in 10 languages. For a Go service, checking the schema and its Go example before writing an adapter removes some guesswork about the request shape.

The alternative account comparison is concrete: OpenAI images plus S3 would require two signups and two sets of credentials, plus glue to move generated output into storage and issue restricted access. That is an account-and-storage comparison, not a reason to add image generation to this workload. For private-document answers, the corresponding artifact is validated JSON and its evidence mapping. With the combined account, generation and hosting share a bill without a second signup just to retain output.

One vendor to trust, one bill, one outage surface: consolidation is a trade-off.

4. Inspect the contract before wiring the retention boundary

The preventative path is retrieval, generation, schema validation, citation-membership validation, authorization, and then retention. JSON Schema can enforce fields and types. It cannot establish that a cited passage supports a claim. Store the document-version mapping with an accepted answer, and give unsupported answers an explicit abstention path rather than treating them as successful policy advice.

This runnable Go example inspects the public reranking contract before implementing that stage. It prints the returned JSON without guessing its request fields. It uses no SDK. The key comes from the environment; discovery itself is public, so no key is required for this inspection.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func inspect() error {
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            baseURL+"/discovery/ai.rerank", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if remaining := time.Until(date); remaining > 0 {
                    delay = remaining
                }
            }
            if delay > 30*time.Second {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry later: Retry-After=%q", retryAfter)
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned invalid JSON")
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(append(body, '\n'))
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := inspect(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Save the example as a Go file and run it with Go. It performs an inspection, not generation or persistence. Its three-attempt retry budget is an example operating choice; a Retry-After beyond the local waiting budget causes it to stop rather than retry prematurely. In the request-serving path, use an overall deadline as well, since stage-level timeouts alone can exceed the shopper's latency budget.

For the actual handoff, the model adapter's validated output becomes the storage adapter's input, using the same configured base URL and API key. Generate storage requests from their discovered schemas. Keep the bucket private and return presigned access only to authorized readers; never forward the API Authorization header to a returned presigned URL. Give writes an idempotency key so retries don't duplicate the artifact.

The inspection example deliberately stops before that handoff: it doesn't demonstrate an upload or presigning request. A complete integration needs those concrete request schemas and an end-to-end retention check. Treating an inspection as proof that the artifact was stored would recreate the same dashboard mistake this article is trying to prevent.

5. Decide when the machinery earns its latency

Use this pattern when private-document answers need inspectable evidence and the team can maintain evaluation questions alongside changing store policies. It earns its complexity when a wrong policy answer creates support work or an unauthorized disclosure. A fixed lookup with a deterministic answer may be better served by an application rule.

The postmortem action is specific: alert on the acceptance boundary, preserve the evidence needed to investigate it, and compare total work per accepted answer before changing the pipeline. Transport success isn't proof that shoppers received supported answers.

Sources

References

  • Cohere Rerank documentation
  • OpenAI documentation
  • Anthropic documentation
  • Google Gemini documentation
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Prompt Engineering Guide

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai error reference to define adapter failure handling before connecting generation to retention.

title: LLM-Enhanced Self-Evolving Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Step E-Commerce Payment Fraud Risk Detection
description:
arXiv:2509.18719v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to e-commerce payment fraud detection by integrating reinforcement learning (RL) with Large Language Models (LLMs). By framing transaction risk as a multi-step Markov Decision Process (MDP), RL optimizes risk detection across multiple payment stages. Crafting effective reward functions, essential for RL model success, typically requires significant human expertise due to the complexity and variability in design. LLMs, with their advanced reasoning and coding capabilities, are well-suited to refine these functions, offering improvements over traditional methods. Our approach leverages LLMs to iteratively enhance reward functions, achieving better fraud detection accuracy and demonstrating zero-shot capability. Experiments with real-world data confirm the effectiveness, robustness, and resilience of our LLM-enhanced RL framework through long-term evaluations, underscoring the potential of LLMs in advancing industrial RL applications.

title: Split-Brain DNS Is What Actually Breaks Multi-Cloud — And How to Design Around It
description:
Split-Brain DNS Is What Actually Breaks Multi-Cloud — And How to Design Around It

Most multi-cloud designs start with the network diagram: VPCs, transit hubs, private interconnects, routing tables. DNS gets one small box in the corner, labelled "DNS", and that is usually where the trouble starts — not during the design review, but three months later, at 2 a.m., when the same hostname returns three different answers depending on which cloud you ask from.

1. The symptom: one name, several truths

The classic failure looks like this. api.internal.example.com resolves to a private address in AWS because Route 53 has a private hosted zone attached to that VPC. In Azure, the same name falls through to public DNS and returns the public load balancer — or NXDOMAIN, because Private DNS zones are linked per virtual network and one link was never added after a new subscription was created. In Google Cloud, Cloud DNS peering forwards some queries and not others, depending on which network the VM sits in.

Nothing is "down". Every resolver is working exactly as configured. The estate simply has no single answer to the question "what does this name mean?", and applications experience that as intermittent connectivity: retries that sometimes land on the private path and sometimes on the public one, TLS errors when a name resolves to an endpoint presenting a different certificate, and health checks that pass in one cloud and fail in another for the same service.

2. Why it keeps happening

Three structural reasons show up again and again:

Private zones are local by default. Every cloud scopes its private DNS to the networks you explicitly attach. Add a new VPC, subscription, or project and, until someone remembers the DNS step, that network lives in a different naming world from the rest of the estate.

Forwarding loops are easy to build by accident. Cloud A forwards corp.example.com to Cloud B's resolver, Cloud B forwards unknown queries back to Cloud A, and a typo'd zone turns into a query loop that only shows up under load. SERVFAIL responses get cached downstream, so a two-minute forwarding mistake can look like a thirty-minute outage.

Teams reuse the same root name for different things. The public zone and two different private zones all claim example.com. Split-horizon DNS is a legitimate pattern, but only when the split is deliberate and documented. Accidental split-horizon — where the private zone shadows public records nobody knew existed — breaks things like SaaS endpoints and certificate validation in ways that are painful to trace.

3. A design that holds up

A pattern that survives growth across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle estates:

  • Pick one authoritative home per zone. Each private zone lives in exactly one place — often a central networking account or subscription — and other clouds forward to it. Forward, do not copy: replicated zones drift, forwarded zones do not.
  • Use a dedicated internal namespace. Something like internal.example.com (or a domain you own but never publish publicly) for private records, kept separate from the public zone. This removes most shadowing accidents by construction.
  • Keep service discovery out of DNS failover. DNS TTLs, negative caching, and resolver behaviour you do not control make DNS a blunt instrument for traffic shifting. Use it for stable name-to-location mapping; let load balancers, health-checked endpoints, and your service layer handle failover decisions.
  • Automate the attachment step. New network creation — VPC, VNet, or VPC network in any cloud — should attach or peer the DNS configuration in the same pipeline that creates the network. If attaching DNS is a manual ticket, it will eventually be a forgotten ticket.
  • Set TTLs deliberately. Short TTLs on records that genuinely change during failover windows, longer ones on stable internal services. And know your negative TTLs: an NXDOMAIN cached for 300 seconds will outlive the fix you just deployed.

4. Test resolution like you test routing

DNS in a multi-cloud estate deserves the same verification discipline as the network itself:

  • Maintain a small query matrix: a fixed set of critical hostnames, queried from a host in every cloud and every major network segment, with expected answers recorded. Run it after every network change and on a schedule.
  • Log resolver queries centrally for a while after any DNS change. Loops, unexpected NXDOMAIN spikes, and queries leaking to public resolvers are all visible there before users report them.
  • Rehearse the failure: detach a zone link or disable a forwarder in a staging estate and watch what applications actually do. The gap between "DNS is redundant" on a diagram and observed behaviour is usually instructive.

None of this is exotic. It is mostly the discipline of treating name resolution as shared infrastructure with one owner, rather than a per-cloud side effect of creating networks.

5. Where this fits in a wider design

DNS is only one layer of a multi-cloud connectivity design — routing, address planning, identity between services, and evidence for controls all interact with it. Teams working through the full picture sometimes use a managed connectivity layer to keep those pieces consistent across clouds; that is the problem space CloudVerg works in, at cloudverg.com, with private multi-cloud networking and zero-trust design across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle estates.

Get the naming layer boring first. Multi-cloud systems fail in interesting ways often enough without DNS helping them.

To browse your Notion workspace's skills, run:

The CLI lists the skill packs shared with you and installs every skill in the packs you select.

To install a single skill, pass its Notion page URL:

title: Agent Patches Can Shrink Your Test Suite Without Failing CI
description:
A green CI check means the tests that ran passed. It says nothing about how many tests ran.

Agent-written patches are very good at making that second number smaller. The pattern is rarely sabotage — it is convenience. A failing integration test, an import that wants a network, a slow marker: each has a one-line "fix" that removes it from the run. Nothing goes red, the evidence set narrows, and the merge lands on top of it.

The gate below closes that specific gap. It records the collected test inventory on the base tree and on the patched tree, diffs the two, and refuses any shrink that is not written down in an expiring waiver file. The same waiver file is where quarantined flaky tests live, which turns "freeze the flaky test" into a reviewable budget that shrinks over time instead of a permanent @pytest.mark.skip.

Everything here is pytest-specific; the census idea is runner-agnostic, but I will not pretend the code ports for free.

First, the three shapes that pass CI untouched

A conftest.py edit that drops a directory:

# before: no collect_ignore anywhere
# after, in tests/conftest.py
collect_ignore = ["integration"]

A module-level skip that makes an entire file vanish from the run rather than fail inside it:

# tests/test_ledger.py
import pytest

pytest.skip("flaky under load", allow_module_level=True)

A config change that deselects by marker:

# pytest.ini, addopts
-m "not slow"

None of these produce a failing test. All three change what your green check actually covers. The census is built to see the difference between "tests passed" and "tests existed".

Step 1 — Record a collection census

A 20-line plugin dumps every collected node ID plus its markers and the run configuration. No test bodies execute, so this is cheap and safe to run on untrusted trees.

# census_plugin.py — load with: pytest --collect-only -p census_plugin
import json
import os

_items = []


def pytest_collection_finish(session):
    for item in session.items:
        _items.append({
            'nodeid': item.nodeid,
            'markers': sorted({m.name for m in item.iter_markers()}),
        })


def pytest_sessionfinish(session, exitstatus):
    payload = {
        'exitstatus': int(exitstatus),
        'args': [str(a) for a in session.config.invocation_params.args],
        'addopts': session.config.getini('addopts'),
        'count': len(_items),
        'items': _items,
    }
    with open(os.environ.get('CENSUS_OUT', 'census.json'), 'w', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
        json.dump(payload, fh, indent=1, sort_keys=True)

Run it once per tree. PYTHONPATH=. is required so -p census_plugin can import the module from the repo root.

CENSUS_OUT=/tmp/base.json PYTHONPATH=. pytest --collect-only -q -p census_plugin
CENSUS_OUT=/tmp/head.json PYTHONPATH=. pytest --collect-only -q -p census_plugin

Step 2 — Diff base against head

The gate compares five things: invocation arguments, addopts, collection exit status, removed node IDs, and newly added skip/skipif/xfail markers. Two runs of the same tree should produce byte-identical JSON apart from ordering; if they do not, your suite has unstable node IDs and the gate will be noise (more on that below).

# census_gate.py BASE HEAD WAIVERS  -> exit 1 on unwaived drift
import json
import sys
from datetime import date

EXCUSE = {'skip', 'skipif', 'xfail'}


def load(path):
    with open(path, encoding='utf-8') as fh:
        doc = json.load(fh)
    return doc, {i['nodeid']: set(i['markers']) for i in doc['items']}


def norm(value):
    return [w for w in (value or '').split() if w]


def main(base_path, head_path, waiver_path):
    base_doc, base = load(base_path)
    head_doc, head = load(head_path)
    with open(waiver_path, encoding='utf-8') as fh:
        waivers = json.load(fh)
    today = date.today().isoformat()
    drift = []

    if norm(' '.join(map(str, base_doc['args']))) != norm(' '.join(map(str, head_doc['args']))):
        drift.append(('config', 'invocation args', base_doc['args'], head_doc['args']))
    if norm(base_doc['addopts']) != norm(head_doc['addopts']):
        drift.append(('config', 'addopts', base_doc['addopts'], head_doc['addopts']))
    if head_doc['exitstatus'] != 0:
        drift.append(('collection', 'exitstatus', base_doc['exitstatus'], head_doc['exitstatus']))

    for node in sorted(set(base) - set(head)):
        if node not in waivers.get('removed', {}):
            drift.append(('removed', node, 'collected', 'absent'))

    excused = waivers.get('excused', {})
    for node, markers in sorted(head.items()):
        fresh = (markers & EXCUSE) - (base.get(node, set()) & EXCUSE)
        if not fresh:
            continue
        entry = excused.get(node)
        if entry is None:
            drift.append(('excused', node, 'none', sorted(fresh)))
        elif entry.get('expires', '1970-01-01') < today:
            drift.append(('excused', node, 'expired ' + entry['expires'], sorted(fresh)))

    budget = waivers.get('budget', {}).get('excused_max', 0)
    if len(excused) > budget:
        drift.append(('budget', 'excused count', budget, len(excused)))

    for kind, what, before, after in drift:
        print('[{}] {} | base={!r} head={!r}'.format(kind, what, before, after))
    print('{} drift event(s); {} base vs {} head node ids'.format(len(drift), len(base), len(head)))
    return 1 if drift else 0


if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main(*sys.argv[1:4]))

Added tests never fail the gate. Only losses and new excuses do.

Step 3 — The waiver file is the freeze

A waiver is a skip with an owner and a deadline. Everything removed or newly excused must appear here, or the gate exits non-zero.

{
  "budget": { "excused_max": 6 },
  "removed": {
    "tests/test_pricing.py::test_rounding_edges": { "owner": "pricing", "expires": "2026-12-15" }
  },
  "excused": {
    "tests/test_sync.py::test_reconnect": { "owner": "sync", "expires": "2026-11-30" }
  }
}

This is the part people skip, and it is the part that matters. A flaky-test freeze without an expiry date is a deletion with extra steps.

Step 4 — Make the quarantine budget shrink

excused_max is a policy number you lower deliberately, not a ceiling you raise when a patch is inconvenient. The counterweight is the removal path: when an excused test is fixed, both the marker and the waiver entry go away, and the next patch must lower the budget in the same commit. If the count only ever goes up, the gate is decoration.

Step 5 — Wire it into the patch gate 

# .github/workflows/patch-gate.yml (excerpt)
- name: collection census
  run: |
    set -euo pipefail
    git worktree add /tmp/base "$BASE_SHA"
    (cd /tmp/base && CENSUS_OUT=/tmp/base.json PYTHONPATH=. pytest --collect-only -q -p census_plugin)
    CENSUS_OUT=/tmp/head.json PYTHONPATH=. pytest --collect-only -q -p census_plugin
    python census_gate.py /tmp/base.json /tmp/head.json waivers.json

Reading the output: a decision table

Census event Usual cause What the reviewer should do
removed node, no waiver File deleted, renamed, or dropped by collect_ignore Demand a waiver with an owner; renaming means a new node ID and a human-checked one-to-one mapping
excused gains skip/xfail Flaky test quarantined Accept only with an expiry and a linked issue; expiry inside the current quarter
config addopts drift -m/-k/--ignore narrowing Treat as a coverage change, not a build tweak
collection exit status non-zero Import error masked by a skip Hard stop: the suite never finished collecting
budget over excused_max Quarantine creeping Reject the patch or fix a test in the same change

Property checks need provenance, not just existence

The census protects the size of the suite. It cannot protect its meaning — a collected test that asserts nothing looks identical to a good one. That is a separate check, and the cheap version is procedural rather than clever: keep property/invariant tests in a path the agent patch may not touch, and require every new property to be shown failing on at least one hand-written broken input before it is accepted. If a property has never failed, nobody knows what it detects. Treat that as a review rule you enforce by eye or by CODEOWNERS, not as something the census will catch for you.

Running the two-tree check without a second machine

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The gate needs two checkouts of the repo and one Python environment both can import. MonkeyCode offers free model access and a free server option, and I use them for two deliberately separated jobs, because a gate that depends on a model is not a gate.

  1. Census execution on the free server option. The two worktrees, the two --collect-only runs, and the diff job do not have to live on a laptop whose environment drifts. The logic is unchanged — still two collection runs and one comparison.
  2. Model-assisted triage, after the gate has already decided. The deterministic gate prints drift lines first. Only then does the model see that report plus this decision table, and its job is to propose a cause label and a draft waiver entry per event.
  3. Human-owned policy. The model does not write expires, does not raise excused_max, and does not choose the marker set. A reviewer edits waivers.json by hand and reruns the gate.

If the model labels an event wrong, the cost is a bad first draft that still needs approval. If the server is unavailable, the same two commands run anywhere else. Neither piece is load-bearing for correctness, which is the only reason I am comfortable putting them in the loop.

Limitations

  • The census sees pytest node IDs, not coverage. A test that keeps its name and loses half its assertions is invisible here.
  • Dynamic parametrization, generated test IDs, and time-dependent names produce unstable node IDs; the gate will report phantom removals until IDs are stabilised.
  • Suite-level conftest.py changes that alter collection order or fixture scope are reported only insofar as they change the node set or the excuses.
  • Waivers are a social contract. Nothing in the script stops a reviewer from extending an expiry date by a year.
  • Setting up two worktrees assumes the patched tree can be collected without a live external service. If it cannot, fix collection first.

Who should not use this

Teams without a named owner for waiver expiry should not adopt it — the file will rot and the gate will be bypassed. Repos where test collection requires network access or a database need a stubbed collection path before any of this is meaningful. And if your suite already has a hard rule that agent patches cannot touch test configuration at all, the census is redundant.

Start by running the census on a repo you already trust. The drift list should be empty; if it is not, you have found the first thing to fix before any agent patch is worth reviewing.

title: Runique 4.0: a typed admin, column-level permissions, and forms that write correctly
description:
In June, I presented Runique 2.1 here, a Rust web framework inspired by Django, built on Axum, SeaORM, and Tera. Version 3.0 followed. Today, 4.0 is released, and this is the version where I didn't just add features: I reworked the three components everything else depends on: the admin, permissions, and forms.

Here's what changes, and why.

1. The model remains the single source of truth

This doesn't change; it's the starting point for everything: a model is declared once.

use runique::prelude::*;

model! {
    Blog,
    table: "blog",
    pk: id => Pk,
    enums: {
        BlogStatus: [Draft="Draft", Published="Published", Archived="Archived"],
    },
    {
        title:      text [required],
        email:      email [required],
        website:    url [nullable],
        summary:    textarea [rows: 3, required],
        content:    richtext [rows: 15, required],
        status:     choice [enum(BlogStatus), default: "Draft", required],
        view_count: int [nullable, default: 0],
    }
}

From this, the SeaORM entity, SQL migration, and a typed form are generated. Version 4.0 adds types (audio, video), and requires you to declare what was previously implicit: the precision of a decimal, the ON DELETE action of a foreign key. A decision that affects the data should not be made on your behalf.

2. An admin declared in Rust, checked by the compiler

The old admin relied on a macro and generated code. It has been removed. The new one is a typed builder, ModelAdmin, where each column is named using the entity's Column enum:

use runique::prelude::*;

fn blog() -> ModelAdmin<blog::Entity> {
    use blog::Column::*;
    ModelAdmin::new()
        .list(|l| {
            l.display([Title, Email, Website, Status])
                .sortable([Title, Status])
                .search([Title, Summary])
                .filter([Status])
                .action(Status, "Published", "Publish")
        })
        .form(|f| {
            f.fields([Title, Email, Website, Summary, Content, Status, ViewCount])
                .readonly([ViewCount])
        })
}

A misspelled column, or one renamed in the model, will no longer compile. There are no longer any strings to keep synchronized with the schema, and no generation step: the admin is integrated into the application builder with .with_admin(admin::config).

What comes with it: multi-value filters, filter pagination, bulk actions, change history, and pages that can be overridden block by block, validated at startup (an unknown variable in an override is rejected before the first visitor arrives).

3. Permissions with a single entry point

This is the core of 4.0. In an admin, the real question isn't "who can get in", but "who can read or modify which column of which table".

Runique 4.0 answers this with ranks and account-level permissions:

Rank Role
Superuser the developer, until delivery
Director the day-to-day site administrator
Admin a moderator: they only have what the director checks for them, table by table and column by column

A rank can only be managed downwards, never on oneself, and is never a form field.

The technical decision I'm most pleased with: all checks go through a single module, the gate (auth::gate). Every operation on protected data requires proof of the Authorized type, and only the gate knows how to create one: its constructor is not visible anywhere else. Writing without going through the gate does not compile. A missed permission check becomes a compilation error, not a vulnerability discovered in production.

Permissions act directly on the SELECT itself: an unauthorized column is never read from the database, rather than simply being hidden from the display.

4. Forms that write correctly

The form engine has been redesigned around one idea: what is validated is what gets written, in a single transaction.

use runique::prelude::*;

pub async fn create_blog(mut request: Request) -> AppResult<Response> {
    let form: BlogForm = request.form("blog");
    let mut form = match ValidationForm::try_form(form, &request).await {
        Ok(validated) => validated.into_form(),
        Err(form) => {
            context_update!(request => { "blog_form" => &form });
            return request.render("blog/blog.html");
        }
    };
    match form.save(&request.engine.db).await {
        Ok(_) => Ok(Redirect::to("/blog").into_response()),
        Err(err) => {
            // the database error is shown in the form, not as a 500
            form.forms_mut().database_error(&err);
            context_update!(request => { "blog_form" => &form });
            request.render("blog/blog.html")
        }
    }
}
  • Each form has a name (request.form("blog")). Two forms on the same page no longer get mixed up: only the one that was submitted is validated.
  • save writes by itself, within a transaction. Uploaded files are moved between the database write and the commit: a rejected write leaves no orphaned files, and a file that cannot be moved rolls back the write.
  • MediaField::image(), audio(), and video() check the file's content, not just its extension: a text file renamed to .mp4 is rejected.
  • Upload limits are consistent from end to end: a field never accepts more than the server reads, and a request declared too large is rejected based on its headers, before a single byte is read.

5. Security, reviewed point by point

Version 4.0 fixes issues found while auditing the framework, and I'd rather list them than keep quiet about them. A few examples:

  • Session contents stored in the database are encrypted (XChaCha20-Poly1305, key derived from SECRET_KEY);
  • A form submitted from another site is rejected before reaching the handler (Sec-Fetch-Site), in addition to the CSRF token;
  • "Forgot password" responds in the same amount of time regardless of whether an account exists;
  • "Active" files (.html, .svg, .js...) are never accepted by a file field;
  • An upload error message no longer reveals the server's directory structure.

The complete list, with the severity of each issue, is available in SECURITY.md.

6. What this breaks

A lot, honestly: this is a major release. The old admin is gone, the form API changes (try_new becomes try_form, save replaces the before_save/after_save hooks), and the session table gains a column. Everything is detailed, step by step, in the 3.x → 4.0 migration guide.

7. What's next

Version 4.1 will focus on makemigrations: generating all schema operations without a manual step (table deletions, actual ALTER operations when changing a type, relation tables, renames). The roadmap is public: ROADMAP.md.

Try it 

[dependencies]
runique = { version = "4.0", features = ["postgres", "admin"] }

cargo install runique --features postgres
runique new my_project
  • Documentation (FR/EN): Documentation
  • Source code: Github

If you're coming from Django, I'd be curious to know what you're still missing. And if you're more into Rust, the Authorized proof system is something I'm particularly interested in hearing feedback about. All feedback is welcome.

title: Retries without a retry storm: timeouts, backoff, jitter and circuit breakers
description:
Retries are the cheapest reliability feature there is: a request fails because of a dropped packet or a pod restart, you try again, it works. Most transient failures are gone in milliseconds.

They're also one of the most common ways a small incident becomes a large one. A database hiccups for a minute. Every caller retries. The callers of those callers retry too. The database — the one thing that needed less traffic to recover — now receives several times its normal load, and the one-minute blip becomes a long outage. This pattern is often called a retry storm.

Here are the four tools that keep retries on your side.

The arithmetic of retry amplification

Imagine a request that goes through three services before it reaches a database, and each service retries a failed call 3 times in total (1 attempt + 2 retries).


Every layer that retries multiplies the load on the layers below. Explore the interactive diagram

When the database is failing, one user request becomes 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 database calls. Add users refreshing the page and you've multiplied your peak load by an order of magnitude at the exact moment you can least afford it.

Tool 1: timeouts with a budget

A retry without a timeout is a request waiting forever, holding a thread and a connection. Every outbound call needs a timeout, and the timeouts need to fit together:

  • The user-facing request has an overall budget — say 2 seconds.
  • Each hop below gets less than its caller, minus the time already spent. If service A gives B 1.5 s, B can't give C 2 s.
  • A deadline can travel with the request (gRPC does this natively; with HTTP you can pass a header) so a service deep in the stack knows when nobody is waiting for its answer any more.

The common mistake is the default: many HTTP clients ship with very long or infinite timeouts. Set them explicitly, per dependency.

Tool 2: exponential backoff with jitter

Retrying immediately mostly hits the same failure. Retrying after a delay that grows — 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms — gives the dependency time to recover.

But backoff alone isn't enough. If 10,000 clients all failed at 12:00:00.000 and all wait exactly 100 ms, they all retry at 12:00:00.100 — a synchronized wave. Jitter spreads them out by randomising each delay. AWS's architecture blog has a well-known analysis showing that "full jitter" (a random delay between zero and the backoff ceiling) dramatically reduces both total calls and completion time compared with plain exponential backoff.

With Resilience4j in a Spring service:

RetryConfig config = RetryConfig.custom()
        .maxAttempts(3)                                   // 1 call + 2 retries
        .intervalFunction(IntervalFunction.ofExponentialRandomBackoff(
                Duration.ofMillis(100),                   // initial interval
                2.0,                                      // multiplier
                0.5))                                     // randomization factor (jitter)
        .retryOnException(e -> e instanceof IOException
                            || e instanceof HttpServerErrorException.ServiceUnavailable)
        .build();

Retry retry = Retry.of("inventory", config);
Supplier<Stock> call = Retry.decorateSupplier(retry, () -> inventoryClient.getStock(sku));

Note the retryOnException predicate: retry transient failures (I/O errors, 503s, 429s), never 400 Bad Request or 404 Not Found. Those will fail the same way every time.

Tool 3: retry in one place, and only what's safe

Two rules remove most of the amplification:

  1. Retry at one layer. Usually that's the layer closest to the failing dependency, or the edge, but not both. If the service right above the database already retries with backoff, the services above it should fail fast and let their own callers decide.
  2. Retry only idempotent operations. A GET is safe. A POST /payments is only safe to retry if it carries an idempotency key the server honours — otherwise a retry after a lost response charges twice. (I wrote about that pattern in Idempotency keys: making retries safe for money.)

A retry budget is a useful extra guard: allow retries to add at most, say, 10% on top of normal traffic. When the budget is exhausted, fail fast. Envoy and several service meshes support this directly.

Tool 4: circuit breakers

When a dependency is clearly down, even well-behaved retries are wasted work. A circuit breaker tracks recent failures and, past a threshold, "opens": calls fail immediately without touching the network. After a cool-down, it lets a few trial calls through ("half-open"); if they succeed, it closes again.

CircuitBreakerConfig cb = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
        .slidingWindowSize(50)                            // look at the last 50 calls
        .failureRateThreshold(50)                         // open at 50% failures
        .slowCallDurationThreshold(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .slowCallRateThreshold(80)                        // slow calls count too
        .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(10))  // cool-down
        .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(5)
        .build();

Two details matter in practice:

  • Count slow calls, not just errors. A dependency that answers in 9 seconds is worse than one that errors in 9 milliseconds — it holds your threads. Slow-call thresholds catch that.
  • Have a fallback. When the breaker is open, return something useful: a cached value, a default, a degraded response ("prices updating"), or a clear error. "Open breaker → 500" protects the dependency but not your users.

Putting it together

The order of decorators matters. A sensible stack, from outside in:

  1. Timeout for the whole operation (the budget).
  2. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, on transient errors only.
  3. Circuit breaker, so retries stop as soon as the dependency is known to be down.
  4. The actual call, with its own connect and read timeouts.

And watch it: retry counts, breaker state changes and timeout rates belong on the same dashboard as error rates. A rising retry rate is often the first sign of trouble, minutes before errors reach users.

Takeaways

  • Retries multiply load across layers: count your layers before you add a retry.
  • Always pair retries with timeouts, exponential backoff and jitter.
  • Retry only transient errors, only idempotent operations, in one layer.
  • Use circuit breakers with slow-call detection and a real fallback.

Originally published at ayushwing.com.

title: On the Effectiveness and Limitations of Open-Weight LLMs for Low-Resource Offensive Language Detection in Danish
description:
arXiv:2611.09506v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the effectiveness and robustness of open-weight large language models (LLMs) for Danish offensive language detection, an underexplored low-resource task. We evaluate four model families (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen) across eleven prompting strategies spanning five design categories, cross-prompt generalization, Danish orthographic variation, and robustness under balanced and naturally imbalanced class distributions. We compare against three BERT-family baselines with distinct pre-training strategies, evaluated via both masked language model prompting and supervised fine-tuning. Even without task-specific fine-tuning, LLMs can surpass all three fine-tuned BERT baselines, and lightweight finetuning yields substantial further gains. No single model or prompt category dominates, underscoring that prompt design interacts with model pre-training in ways that cannot be predicted a priori. Semantically grounded prompts transfer more robustly, while format-constrained patterns consistently fail to generalize. ASCII transliteration of Danish-specific characters ({\ae}, {\o}, {\aa}) generally degrades performance, indicating these characters encode meaningful signal. At the same time, the gap between a balanced test set (best F1 of 0.84) and the corpus's natural class skew (0.62 trained on skewed data, 0.70 trained on balanced data) -- relative drops of 26.2\% and 16.7\% -- shows that class imbalance remains a critical open challenge. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/PASHAADC/Danish-LLM-HateSpeech.

title: Emo-LiveSync: Real-Time Universal Lip Synchronization with Explicit Emotion Control
description:
arXiv:2611.09074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lip synchronization, the task of generating realistic lip movements synchronized with audio signals, is fundamental to applications such as film dubbing, virtual avatars, and digital content creation. Recent GAN-based methods offer computational efficiency but often lack visual fidelity, while diffusion-based approaches achieve high-quality results at the cost of substantial computational overhead. Moreover, most existing methods are limited to photo-realistic human faces, restricting their applicability to stylized characters and non-human entities. In this paper, we propose an efficient universal lip-sync video generation framework that achieves high-quality results without compromising computational efficiency. We build on LivePortrait, a warp-based portrait animation model, and introduce a training strategy that aligns audio signals to an implicit motion space by distilling knowledge from a pre-trained video-to-motion model. This enables real-time inference while maintaining high visual fidelity, and naturally generalizes to diverse stylistic characters beyond photo-realistic humans. Furthermore, we introduce an expressive control gate that enables explicit manipulation of emotional expressions for content enrichment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both visual quality and lip-sync accuracy while ensuring real-time inference.

title: I Built a Two-Way Visual UI Editor for Rust Inside VS Code
description:
Hey everyone,

Like a lot of you, I love writing desktop apps in Rust, but I was getting incredibly frustrated with the GUI workflow. Tweaking layout coordinates, compiling, waiting, and realizing a button is still 5 pixels off... it just kills productivity.

So I decided to build a solution: Ruxel Studio.
It’s an open-source visual drag-and-drop UI editor extension built directly into VS Code.

The Problem with Most Code Generators

Usually, UI builders generate a massive block of boilerplate. If you need to add custom logic to a button click, you have to edit the generated file. But the next time you move that button in the visual editor, the tool regenerates the file and overwrites your custom code. It's a nightmare.

How Ruxel Studio Fixes It (Two-Way AST Sync)

Instead of blind generation, Ruxel Studio uses syn and quote under the hood for bidirectional AST synchronization.

Here is what that actually means:

  1. You can drag and drop a widget on the visual canvas.
  2. The extension parses your Rust code, finds the exact spot, and safely injects the UI update.
  3. Crucially: You can also edit the code manually, and the visual canvas updates instantly to reflect your changes. Your custom event handlers and logic are completely safe.

Supported Frameworks

Right now, the extension is in Alpha (v0.1.1) and supports code generation for:

  • Iced
  • egui
  • Slint
  • Dioxus (Early experimental support)

Try it out

You can install it right now from the VS Code Marketplace, or check out the source code (MIT / Apache-2.0).

  • Marketplace: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=c0mbit.ruxel-studio
  • GitHub: https://github.com/c0mbit/ruxel-studio

If you are building desktop apps with any of these frameworks, I would really appreciate any feedback on the generated code structure. Tell me what sucks, what's missing, or what you'd like to see next!

Cheers,
Alex (c0mbit)
