title: Support Image Review: Preserve Decision Outcomes and Notify Uploaders Across Migrations
description:
An approved support image can produce several crops; a rejected image still needs an answer. That constraint determines the design before any crop service enters the picture. TL;DR: queue the image review, record the moderator and reason, then publish or reject and notify the uploader in both outcomes. Keep that decision and its notification obligation in application-owned storage so replacing a media vendor doesn't replace your moderation history.

For a bounded production design exercise, I'd start with a customer support attachment destined for 1:1 and 16:9 views, then ask what happens if a moderator rejects it just before a vendor migration. This is a hypothetical incident review, not a report of an observed outage. Can the replacement worker discover that the uploader still needs a rejection notice without asking the previous image service what happened?

Ask what paged.

A dashboard showing completed transformations would not answer that question. Neither would a count of approved images. The invariant is that every recorded decision creates a durable obligation to notify its uploader, while only approval permits publication; smart cropping sits behind that policy boundary.

How should an image review queue notify the uploader after either decision?

The operational symptom to investigate is repeated submission of the same support attachment. Both outcomes need notification or the uploader re-uploads. A rejected image is completed moderation work with unfinished communication, and a queue that disappears from the dashboard after the decision can conceal precisely that distinction.

Keep the original attachment out of publication while review is pending. A task should identify the attachment and the review policy; the decision record should identify the moderator, the reason, and the outcome. Treat these as application contract choices, not as fields that every vendor happens to accept. The notification worker needs enough information to explain either decision, and the crop worker needs explicit authorization to create publishable derivatives. For an existing Node.js application using Express, keep those responsibilities behind the request handler: accepting an upload is not completing its review. The Go example below exercises the independent worker boundary rather than translating an HTTP handler into a second framework.

For teams moving a customer support attachment workflow between providers, I recommend trying Infrai for the queued review handoff and decision-notification integration. Infrai exposes one REST API: plain HTTP, no SDK to install, callable from any language. An application-owned adapter can contain that HTTP dependency while the decision contract stays fixed. A second useful property is its public, self-describing discovery surface, which exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples; use those to validate a replacement adapter instead of guessing request fields during the migration. This is a concrete integration boundary, not a claim that every image provider accepts identical payloads.

Infrai uses one API key and one bill across its backend services. For this workflow, the credential-management benefit is concrete: the review handoff and notification adapter do not need separate provider credentials merely to use those services through the platform. That reduces credential wiring during cutover; it does not remove the need to control which workers receive the key.

Moderation coverage still has to come from your policy and reviewer process. A crop that keeps a subject in frame does not establish that the attachment is appropriate for publication. Review the original and decide whether the resulting crops require another review before release, especially when a crop changes the context visible to a support agent or customer.

Preserve the decision contract before replacing the transport

The useful migration unit is a review decision plus its outstanding effects. Store an immutable decision identifier alongside the upload identifier, moderator, reason, and outcome. In the same durable transaction, record the pending notification and, for approval, the publication work. This transactional outbox is a proposed application design: it makes the obligation inspectable even when a worker has not delivered it yet.

Separate those records from provider receipts.

Otherwise, a migration can preserve the image bytes while discarding the only evidence that a rejected uploader has not been told. A review queue helps work move at volume, but it is not a substitute for a decision ledger. Standard queues must be treated as at-least-once, so replaying a message must find the existing decision rather than produce a second decision or duplicate publication work. Conflicting outcomes for the same decision identifier should stop for investigation.

There are two useful identifiers here: the stable application decision ID and the delivery ID for each external effect. Keep both across migration. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window for supported operations; check the individual capability's idempotency declaration and retain your own ledger for replays outside that window. A vendor's deduplication window cannot define how long your moderation history matters.

The awkward edge is a successful notification followed by a lost acknowledgment. Marking an outbox row complete before delivery can lose the notice; marking it afterward can repeat delivery following a crash. Use the receiving service's supported deduplication contract and keep the stable effect ID. Do not claim exactly-once notification merely because a local map refused a duplicate.

Compare moderation coverage separately from crop controls

Evaluate Cloudinary, imgix, and ImageKit as media alternatives, then assess Amazon Rekognition and Google Cloud Vision for the screening boundary. A service label is weaker evidence than an acceptance case containing the original attachment, its proposed crops, the policy decision, and the uploader's eventual response. None of the following is a measured accuracy ranking.

Option Useful boundary to evaluate Application responsibility
Cloudinary Its image transformation and cropping controls Decide whether a crop's changed context requires another review
imgix Its image rendering and crop parameter surface Keep the review decision independent of derivative generation
ImageKit Its image transformation workflow Verify the required aspect ratios and publication prerequisites
Amazon Rekognition Its documented image moderation labels Map the labels to support policy and human escalation
Google Cloud Vision Its documented SafeSearch annotations Check whether those categories cover the support attachments
Infrai REST integration for review handoff and notification, validated against discovery schemas Own review policy, durable decisions, and authorized effects

The trade-off is between owning a small adapter and relying more deeply on a specialist's media workflow. Infrai is not a substitute for evaluating moderation coverage. A specialist is the better choice when its documented moderation categories or transformation controls determine acceptance: evaluate Cloudinary, imgix, or ImageKit directly for exact crop behavior, and Rekognition or Vision for the relevant screening categories. An integration layer's breadth does not establish equivalent moderation coverage.

Use representative support attachments that your team is authorized to evaluate. Include a permitted attachment, a rejected attachment, and a permitted image whose narrow crop removes explanatory context. These are proposed test cases, not benchmark results. File format also belongs in the acceptance criteria: MDN's image format guide helps distinguish the files entering review from the derivatives you intend to display.

Inspect the replacement contract before delivering effects

The preventative code path starts with validating what the adapter will call. This complete Go program fetches the public discovery document, checks the response status, and prints the returned contract for inspection. It does not upload an attachment or send a notification. Discovery requires no key; if an environment key is supplied, the program uses bearer authentication. There is one API route, and no invented upload, queue, or email payload.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if wait := time.Until(deadline); wait > 0 {
            return wait
        }
    }
    return fallback
}

func inspectContract() error {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        closeErr := resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if closeErr != nil {
            return closeErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            backoff := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            wait := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), backoff)
            if wait < backoff {
                wait = backoff
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s",
                resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := inspectContract(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

The retry budget and timeout are example client choices, not service guarantees. This is a read, so it creates no effect requiring a write idempotency key. The redirect policy also keeps an optional credential on the intended request rather than following an unexpected destination. For supported writes in the eventual adapter, reuse a stable effect key and preserve the error response; never turn a failed request into a completed outbox row.

Inspect the selected capability's declared path, schema, and idempotency behavior before implementing its adapter. Keep the application's review fields distinct from provider request fields. The discovery example makes contract inspection repeatable without pretending that a public schema inspection has exercised authenticated queue or email delivery.

Then exercise the worker on the bounded fixture: decision review-101 approves attachment-101 for customer-a, with reviewer-a and the reason recorded; decision review-102 rejects attachment-102 for customer-b because it contains account information. These are illustrative application identifiers. The expected outbox contains two notification obligations and one publication obligation. Replaying either decision must leave those counts unchanged, and replaying an existing identifier with a conflicting outcome must fail. Enforce this in durable storage with uniqueness constraints and a transaction rather than relying on an in-memory check.

Approval permits the crop-and-publication path. It does not prove that those later steps succeeded. Tell the uploader the recorded decision accurately and track publication completion separately.

Migration acceptance is an operational decision

A proposed cutover should replay both outcomes in a test environment, including duplicate deliveries and outstanding notification work. Accept the replacement only if it preserves the decision, moderator, reason, recipient, and stable effect identifiers; reject a cutover plan that requires inferring moderation state from the presence of transformed files. Monitor pending notification age separately from review backlog, then attach an operational response to that signal. A green transformation dashboard cannot close an unanswered rejection.

This design does not apply unchanged when decisions may be appealed or reversed: those workflows need versioned decisions and rules for withdrawing previously published derivatives. Nor does a human review queue alone satisfy a requirement for immediate automated moderation. Select the coverage mechanism first, preserve its policy boundary, and make the provider integration replaceable behind it.

Sources

References for the capability boundaries and image format considerations:

  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • imgix rendering API
  • ImageKit image transformations
  • Amazon Rekognition moderation
  • Google Cloud Vision SafeSearch
  • MDN image format guide

If this boundary fits your support workflow, start with the schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation and keep your decision ledger independent of the adapter.

title: Playwright explained before you join QA automation training in Nepal
description:
Playwright is a free, open source tool that opens a real browser, clicks through a website like a user, and checks what it sees. In most QA automation training it is the tool you spend the most hours with, so try it for 30 minutes tonight before you pay anyone.

You do not need to know how to code for that first try. You need a laptop, Node.js and one free evening.

What is Playwright, in plain words?

A Playwright test is a short file with two kinds of lines. Some lines do things: open a page, click a button, fill a form. Other lines check things: is this text on the screen, did the page go to the right address.

Here is the smallest real example from the official docs. await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/') opens the page. await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/Playwright/) checks the title. If the title is wrong, the test fails and tells you why.

Two things make Playwright easy for a beginner. First, it waits by itself. Before every click, it checks that the button is really there and ready, so you do not add pauses by hand. Second, every test starts in a fresh browser, so one test cannot break the next one.

Where does Playwright fit in a QA job?

Automation does not replace testing. It repeats checks you already know are worth doing. So the order matters. You first learn what to test, then you teach a tool to repeat it.

Our Software Quality Assurance course at Saarathi Academy in Old Baneshwor, Kathmandu follows that order. Weeks 1 to 3 are manual testing, test design and bug reports. Week 4 adds Postman for APIs and SQL for checking the database. Weeks 5 to 7 cover Playwright with TypeScript, then Selenium, a first Cypress test and GitHub Actions.

We still teach Selenium, because it is the automation tool Nepal job posts name most. A typical post asks for experience with "Selenium, Cypress, TestComplete, or similar". We put Playwright first because its waiting and its trace viewer make a beginner's failures easier to understand. Selenium after it shows you the code many Kathmandu teams already run.

Can my laptop run Playwright?

Check this before anything else, because it is the most common place people get stuck. The Playwright docs list these needs:

  • Node.js version 22, 24 or 26.
  • Windows 11, or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). Windows 10 is not on the list.
  • macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later.
  • Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 or 26.04, or Debian 12 or 13.

If your laptop runs Windows 10, set up WSL first or use another machine. For our course you need your own laptop with at least 8GB RAM, because Playwright runs real browsers next to your code editor.

How to try Playwright in 30 minutes

Make an empty folder and open a terminal inside it. Run npm init playwright@latest. It asks a few questions. Pick TypeScript, keep the tests folder, and say yes to installing browsers.

It creates playwright.config.ts and an example test in tests/example.spec.ts. Run npx playwright test, then npx playwright show-report to see the results page in your browser.

Now record your own test. Run npx playwright codegen demo.playwright.dev/todomvc. A browser opens with the demo to do app. Add two to do items and tick one. Then use the toolbar to add an "assert text" check on the item you ticked. Copy the code the recorder wrote, save it as a new file in tests, and run it with npx playwright test --ui.

Finally, break it on purpose. Change the expected text to something wrong and run npx playwright test --trace on. Open the report and click the trace. You can step through every action and see the page before and after it. Finding out why a test failed is a large part of automation work, and the trace is where you start.

Why a recorded test is not a finished test

The recorder writes your clicks for you. It does not decide what is worth testing. It also cannot tell you whether the check would fail if the feature really broke.

That is the work an employer pays a QA engineer for. A test that passes even when the feature is broken is worse than no test, because the team trusts it. AI tools now write tests too, and the same rule holds. In Week 6 of our course an AI tool writes tests against a real page. Then you read every line, check the locator still finds the right element after the page changes, and delete what checks nothing.

So when you look at any QA automation training, ask one question. Will a person read my tests and tell me which checks are weak? Recording and copying is the easy part.

How do I know I am ready for QA automation training?

You are ready if you finished the steps above and could explain why your broken test failed by reading the trace. You do not need a programming background for our course. JavaScript self study starts in Week 2, 30 minutes a day, before Playwright starts in Week 5.

If the terminal errors stopped you, that is useful to know too. Copy the exact error into a search and fix it. Reading an error message and searching for the answer is part of this job every day.

Try this tonight

Open the Playwright installation guide, run the commands above, and record one test with the test generator. Then break it and open it in the trace viewer.

If you want a mentor to review your tests and take you from manual testing to Playwright in CI, the Software Quality Assurance course has the details, and the full week by week plan is in the public syllabus. We also wrote about why QA automation training changes what a tester can do.

title: HaNDF: Object-Conditioned Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields
description:
arXiv:2611.08578v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.

title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?
description:
arXiv:2611.09662v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.

title: The same shipping event, twice, in two languages: a dedup rule we measured and did not ship
description:
If you store carrier scan events, you will eventually meet a timeline where every row appears twice: once in English, once in another script, with the identical timestamp. Some postal operators publish each event in more than one language, and if you persist what the carrier published, you persist both.

The obvious fix is a dedup rule. This is the story of why we measured one, found it destroys real data, and shipped nothing.

Why the naive key is wrong in both directions

Most event tables end up keyed on something like:

UNIQUE KEY uk_event (tracking_number, event_date, description)

That key is wrong twice over.

It under-dedups. Two rows for one event differ in description (different language), so both survive. The customer counts rows and concludes the parcel went through sorting twice as often as it did.

And it over-dedups the moment you "fix" it. The intuitive repair is to drop description from the key and treat (tracking_number, event_date) as the identity of an event. Do not do this. On air-cargo timelines, two genuinely different events legitimately share a timestamp:

2026-03-11 14:32  Booked on Flight EK-7281D
2026-03-11 14:32  Manifested on Flight EK-7281D

Booked and manifested are different states. Collapse them and you have deleted a state transition that someone will later need.

It gets worse. We found pairs that shared a timestamp and differed only in the flight number, EK-7007D and EK-7013D. A timestamp-only key merges two different flights into one row.

What we actually measured

We took every stored pair that shared a tracking number and a timestamp and asked a narrow question: how many pairs are provably the same event rendered twice, under a rule a machine can apply?

The honest answer was none. Every candidate rule either left duplicates behind or deleted something real:

  • Same timestamp merges booked/manifested and distinct flights.
  • Same timestamp + same location still merges booked/manifested, which share a facility.
  • Same timestamp + different script is closer, but a bilingual carrier can also publish two different events a minute apart, and script is a property of the carrier's publishing habit, not of the event.
  • String similarity after translation requires trusting a translation of operational wording. In Chinese, 妥投失败 (delivery failed) and 已妥投 (delivered) share the same two-character root and mean opposite things.

So the safe set was empty, and we wrote that down instead of shipping a rule. The reopen condition is recorded with it: do this when the source supplies a stable per-event id, and not before. Guessing event identity from prose is not a rule, it is a coin flip with your customers' history.

What to do instead

Dedup at read time, not write time. Keep both rows. When rendering, group by (event_date, location) and, if two rows in a group are in different scripts, show one and keep the other available. Nothing is deleted, and the customer sees one event.

Detect script with Unicode properties, not \w. This bites people constantly:

// WRONG - \w is ASCII-only, so a CJK string becomes empty
const letters = s.replace(/[^\w]/g, '')        // "已妥投" -> ""

// RIGHT
const hasCJK  = /\p{Script=Han}/u.test(s)
const hasCyr  = /\p{Script=Cyrillic}/u.test(s)
const letters = s.normalize('NFKC').replace(/[^\p{L}\p{N}]/gu, '')

Any heuristic built on \w silently classifies every non-Latin status as "empty" and then does something confident with that.

Treat "carrier" as a role, not a company. The second thing a bilingual timeline teaches you is that the entity on the label is often not the entity that delivers. A freight forwarder issues a job reference, booked / received / dispatched, and its record ends when the cargo reaches the destination country. Three milestones is a complete forwarder record. If your UI calls that "incomplete tracking", your UI is wrong about the domain. Model the issuer separately from the final-mile carrier, and expect the delivery date to live on a different number.

The general lesson

Normalisation code gets written in the direction of "make the data tidier". Tidier is not the goal; lossless and legible is. Before shipping any merge, collapse or translation rule, run it over your whole corpus and count three things: rows changed, rows emptied, and rows that lost meaning. If the third number is not zero, you do not have a rule yet.

I work on 24hTrack, a free package tracker for 3,200+ carriers - paste any tracking number, the carrier is detected automatically, no sign-up. The behaviour above is why we show the scans a carrier published rather than a cleaned-up summary of them. The customer-facing version of the same material is in our international parcel journey guide (CC BY).

title: AWS SQS FIFO vs Standard Queues: Go Retry Ordering Explained
description:
Short answer: choose Standard semantics when throughput and recovery latency matter more than delivery order, and choose FIFO semantics when a retry must be serialized with related work. For a nightly payment-provider reconciliation, the decision is less about the queue name than about the idempotency key, the message group, and the alert that tells an operator the retry budget is being consumed.

The useful boundary is this: Standard delivery is at least once with best-effort ordering, so every handler must tolerate duplicates and reordering. FIFO provides ordered processing within a message group and deduplication behavior, but that ordering can turn one slow or poisoned job into a queue-wide delay for that group. A queue choice cannot repair a non-idempotent reconciliation write.

Here is the smallest useful worker boundary:

func process(runID, accountID string, payload []byte) error {
    key := runID + "/" + accountID
    return storeOnce(key, payload)
}

The page fires before the queue choice looks interesting

The page an on-call engineer sees is rarely “FIFO or Standard is wrong.” It is usually a growing age-of-oldest-message signal, a retry count approaching its limit, or a reconciliation window that has not closed. The immediate task is to find out whether the provider is slow, the worker is failing, or one logical account is blocking later messages.

For the nightly job, I want the alert to preserve three identifiers: the reconciliation run, the payment-provider account, and the attempt number. A generic queue depth alert is useful, but it cannot distinguish a broad provider slowdown from one repeatedly failing account. Those cases have different actions and different risk.

The first instrumentation change is structured outcome data around each delivery:

\`go
package main

import (
"log/slog"
"strconv"
)

func recordOutcome(logger *slog.Logger, runID, accountID string, attempt int, outcome string) {
logger.Info("reconciliation delivery",
"run_id", runID,
"account_id", accountID,
"attempt", strconv.Itoa(attempt),
"outcome", outcome,
)
}
`\

This gives the operator a path from alert to one logical job. It also makes a false-positive threshold visible. Alert too early and a normal provider pause wakes someone up; alert too late and the retry window can expire before anyone notices. I prefer a threshold tied to the reconciliation deadline and retry budget, because queue depth alone has no business meaning.

Should AWS SQS FIFO or Standard queues handle retries?

Consider two messages for the same account: close-2026-10-26\ and reconcile-2026-10-26\. If the close operation is delivered after the reconciliation operation, the result may be coherent. If the order is reversed, the worker might observe an account state that is valid for neither operation. Related messages can share a message group so the consumer processes that group in order.

The cost is serialization. A failed message that remains in the group can delay later messages in that same group. That is useful when later work depends on earlier work. It is an outage multiplier when messages are independent but were grouped by convenience.

The limitation is important: neither queue mode guarantees that a payment reconciliation is correct by itself. Standard is a poor fit when reordering changes a state transition and the handler cannot make writes idempotent. FIFO is a poor fit when thousands of independent jobs are placed in one group, because one slow delivery can delay unrelated work. The right choice depends on the dependency boundary, not on a universal winner.

Standard queues make a different promise. A worker can receive deliveries in an order that is not the order sent, and the same delivery can appear again. The handler should write the reconciliation result with a stable idempotency key, make the external operation safe to repeat, and acknowledge the message only after the durable state transition succeeds.

A good test is deliberately boring: deliver the same message twice, deliver messages 2 and 1 in that order, terminate the worker after the provider call but before acknowledgement, then replay the message. The final ledger state should be the same. If it is not, FIFO is hiding a correctness problem rather than solving it.

Choosing between latency and cost under failure

For a nightly reconciliation, latency includes provider response time, visibility timeout, backoff, redelivery, and the time needed to drain a backlog before the reconciliation deadline. Cost includes worker time and operational attention, not just queue requests.

Standard is a sensible default when thousands of independent account checks can proceed concurrently and duplicate work is cheap relative to delaying the whole run. It can reduce recovery time from a provider slowdown because healthy messages are not required to wait behind one logical group. The handler and downstream writes must be idempotent.

FIFO earns its complexity when the business rule is explicitly sequential: a series of mutations for one account, a state machine transition, or a retry stream where later work must not pass an earlier failure. The message group should represent that dependency, not the entire reconciliation run. One group for everything converts a single bad account into a global lock.

I write the decision as a rule before choosing the queue:

  • If reordering can change the business result, preserve order for that dependency and keep groups narrow.
  • If reordering cannot change the result, prefer concurrency and make duplicate delivery harmless.
  • If either answer is uncertain, test the handler with duplicates, delayed acknowledgements, and out-of-order input before treating queue semantics as a fix.

The point is to choose where the system spends its scarce resource: serialized progress, worker capacity, or operator attention.

A minimal retry worker with an idempotency boundary

The worker below keeps queue mechanics behind an interface. It does not assume that receiving a message means the payment-provider operation succeeded. The durable write is the boundary that decides whether a retry is safe.

\`go
package main

import (
"context"
"errors"
)

type Delivery struct {
RunID string
AccountID string
Attempt int
Body []byte
}

var ErrTemporary = errors.New("temporary provider failure")

func handle(ctx context.Context, d Delivery, provider func(context.Context, []byte) error, store func(context.Context, string, []byte) error) error {
if err := provider(ctx, d.Body); err != nil {
return err
}

key := d.RunID + "/" + d.AccountID
return store(ctx, key, d.Body)

}
`\

In production, store\ needs an atomic uniqueness or upsert rule for that key, and the provider call needs its own idempotency contract or a reconciliation-safe read-before-write design. The queue cannot provide those for you. A retryable error should return according to the retry policy; a permanent validation error should go to a dead-letter path with enough context for a later decision.

The retry policy also needs a deadline. A message that can retry forever is an unbounded source of work. Keep the original run deadline, attempt count, and last error in the message or its durable job record. On every retry, measure age and remaining budget. If the remaining budget is smaller than the expected provider call plus backoff, stop retrying and surface the job for review.

Where the earlier signal should come from

A useful dashboard has separate views for queue age, delivery attempts, provider latency, successful durable writes, and dead-letter volume. Slice those by account or message group. The alert should fire on a condition that predicts a missed reconciliation deadline, not merely on a transient spike in messages.

For FIFO, watch blocked groups and the age of the oldest message in each group. For Standard, watch duplicate processing and out-of-order state transitions in addition to age. In both modes, attach a run identifier so the operator can answer one question quickly: “Will this reconciliation finish correctly within its window?”

I initially treat a growing retry count as a worker problem. The correction is to inspect the distribution. A broad increase usually points to a dependency or provider issue; a narrow increase often points to bad input, an account-specific state transition, or a poison message. The queue metric is the symptom. The grouped, structured outcome is the diagnostic signal.

Do not page on every duplicate. Duplicates are expected under at-least-once delivery and can also arise around acknowledgement boundaries. Page when duplicates change durable state, consume the retry budget, or push the run past its deadline. That keeps the alert useful.

Further reading

  • AWS SQS FIFO queues documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • AWS SQS message visibility timeout: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • AWS SQS at-least-once delivery: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html
  • RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html

title: Teardown: The Order of Attempts Is the Product
description:
Strip the dashboards away from any retry tool and one design decision remains, the one that determines nearly all of its results: in what order, and on what evidence, does it spend a subscriber's limited attempts? Issuers watch retry behaviour. A card retried blindly six times in two days does not merely fail six times; it teaches the issuer's systems that this merchant retries blindly, and the seventh attempt — the one timed to payday, the one that would have worked — arrives carrying the reputation of the first six.

A sound sequence starts by reading before it spends. The decline code on the first failure is evidence: insufficient funds points at the calendar, a replaced credential points at the updater and the customer, a hard decline points at the exit. Each reading implies a different second move, and most of them are not "retry tomorrow." In the strongest implementations the second move is often not an attempt at all — it is a wait, an update request, or a message — because an attempt is the scarcest resource in the system and everything else is comparatively free. That ordering principle is the core of retry software judged by the order of its attempts, not their count, and it is a useful lens for evaluating any tool in this category, including the defaults inside your billing platform.

Platform defaults deserve the teardown too. A fixed cadence — day one, day three, day five, day seven — has one virtue, predictability, and one structural flaw: it applies the same hypothesis to every failure. It retries the empty account on day three because day three arrived, not because anything about the account changed. Software that earns its fee replaces the calendar with conditions: retry when the balance cycle turns, when the credential is refreshed, when the customer has answered — when something is true that was not true at the last attempt.

Consider what the sequence does with the commonest reading of all: insufficient funds. A calendar retries it on day three because day three is next. A sequence retries it when money plausibly exists — after the first and the fifteenth for salaried customers, after the weekend for everyone, never twice inside the same empty window. Multiply that single conditional across a thousand failures a month and the effect stops being subtle: the same number of attempts produces materially more approvals, because attempts stopped being spent into accounts that were provably empty at the moment of spending. Nothing about the customer changed. Nothing about the card changed. Only the order changed, and the order was the product all along — a fact the count-first tools cannot replicate by adding a seventh attempt, because a seventh blind attempt is just the first mistake repeated with more confidence.

The teardown test is simple to run on any vendor demo. Ask what the system does between attempts. If the answer is a schedule, you are looking at a timer with a dashboard. If the answer is a set of reads, waits, updates, and messages — each attempt spent only when the evidence changed — you are looking at recovery software. The market uses one name for both. Your failure file will learn the difference within a quarter, in the only metric that cannot be redefined: how many subscribers are still subscribers.

That is the sequence Swipe Again runs on every failed payment: read the decline, spend nothing until the evidence moves, and let each attempt arrive with a reason the issuer's systems — and the customer — can respect.

title: Best AI Humanizer for Essays and Academic Writing in 2026: Improve Clarity and Natural Writing
description:
Artificial intelligence has become an important part of modern academic writing. From brainstorming research topics to organizing essay outlines and improving grammar, AI writing assistants have changed how students approach their assignments.

However, one common challenge remains: AI-generated academic content often sounds overly formal, repetitive, or disconnected from the writer's natural voice.

Even when a paragraph is grammatically correct, it may contain predictable sentence structures, unnecessary transitions, and complicated expressions that make the writing difficult to read.

This is why AI humanizer tools have gained attention among students, researchers, and academic writers.

The best AI humanizer for essays and academic writing should do more than simply replace words. It should improve readability, preserve the original meaning, and help writers communicate complex ideas clearly.

In this guide, we'll explore how AI humanizers work, which tools are worth considering in 2026, and how students can use them responsibly to improve academic writing.

Why Do Students Use AI Humanizers for Academic Writing?

Academic writing requires clarity, accuracy, logical organization, and an appropriate tone.

Students often struggle to balance these requirements, particularly when explaining complicated theories, research findings, or unfamiliar concepts.

AI writing assistants can help organize information, but the resulting text may sometimes sound generic.

For example, an AI-generated essay might repeatedly use phrases such as "it is important to note," "in today's rapidly evolving world," or "this highlights the significance of."

Although these expressions are grammatically acceptable, excessive repetition can make an essay feel mechanical.

AI humanizers aim to improve this problem by refining sentence structures, adjusting vocabulary, and making paragraphs flow more naturally.

For students who use AI tools within their institution's academic integrity policies, humanization can be one part of the editing process.

However, improving the language of an essay should never replace original research, critical thinking, or proper citation.

The purpose of a humanizer should be to support better communication, not misrepresent who created the work.

What Makes the Best AI Humanizer for Essays?

Choosing an AI humanizer for academic writing requires more consideration than selecting a general rewriting tool.

Academic documents often contain specialized terminology, research citations, and arguments that must remain accurate.

A useful humanizer should preserve these details while improving the surrounding language.

For example, a research paper discussing consumer behavior might include terms such as purchase intention, brand awareness, and advertising effectiveness.

Replacing these terms with unrelated alternatives could change the meaning of the research.

This is why meaning preservation is one of the most important qualities to consider.

Another essential factor is readability.

Academic writing should be professional, but that doesn't mean every sentence needs to be complicated.

Clear explanations are often more effective than unnecessarily sophisticated vocabulary.

A good AI humanizer should make complex ideas easier to understand without removing the depth of the discussion.

GPTHuman AI: A Dedicated AI Humanizer for Academic Drafts

One option worth exploring is GPTHuman AI, a tool designed to rewrite AI-generated content into more natural-sounding language.

For students and academic writers working with AI-assisted drafts, GPTHuman AI offers a way to refine text that sounds repetitive, overly formal, or difficult to follow.

Unlike a basic grammar checker, a dedicated humanizer focuses on the overall naturalness of the writing.

For example, an AI-assisted paragraph might explain an academic concept accurately but use long sentences and repetitive transitions.

GPTHuman AI can be used to generate an alternative version with smoother phrasing and more readable sentence structures.

This can be useful when editing essay introductions, literature review explanations, discussion sections, and other academic material where clarity matters.

The tool may also appeal to students who want their writing to maintain a more natural tone without becoming too casual.

However, academic writers should review every rewritten passage carefully.

Important terminology, citations, statistical findings, and research conclusions should remain consistent with the original source material.

For those interested in exploring a dedicated rewriting solution, GPTHuman AI is worth considering as part of a broader academic editing workflow.

Its usefulness should be judged by the quality and accuracy of its output rather than promises about AI detection results.

QuillBot: An Alternative for Academic Paraphrasing

QuillBot is another writing tool commonly considered by students who want to improve sentence structure and wording.

Its paraphrasing features allow users to explore different ways of expressing existing information.

This can be helpful when an essay contains awkward sentences or overly complicated explanations.

For example, a student might write a paragraph that accurately explains a research finding but uses unnecessarily repetitive vocabulary.

A paraphrasing tool can suggest alternative phrasing that makes the explanation easier to follow.

However, paraphrasing should not be confused with creating original academic work.

Changing the wording of a source does not eliminate the need for proper citation.

Students must still acknowledge the original authors whose ideas or findings they discuss.

QuillBot can support sentence-level editing, but the writer remains responsible for ensuring that the final text accurately represents the original information.

Grammarly: Best for Grammar and Academic Clarity

Grammarly offers a different approach to improving academic writing.

Rather than focusing primarily on humanizing AI-generated text, Grammarly helps users identify grammatical errors, improve clarity, and adjust tone.

This makes it useful for proofreading essays, research papers, and other academic documents.

A student may have developed an original argument but struggle with punctuation, sentence construction, or word choice.

Grammarly can help identify these issues and suggest improvements.

However, grammar correction alone doesn't necessarily make an essay more natural.

A paragraph can be grammatically correct while still sounding repetitive or overly formal.

For this reason, Grammarly works well as a complementary editing tool.

Students can use it to improve technical writing quality while maintaining control over their arguments and explanations.

Can AI Humanizers Improve Essay Readability?

Readability is one of the most important aspects of academic writing.

A well-written essay should communicate ideas clearly, even when discussing complex subjects.

Unfortunately, AI-assisted drafts sometimes contain sentences that are longer than necessary.

Consider this example:

"Due to the increasing prevalence of technological advancements within contemporary educational environments, students are experiencing significant transformations in their approaches to academic composition."

Although the sentence is understandable, it uses more words than necessary.

A clearer version would be:

"As technology becomes more common in education, students are changing how they approach academic writing."

Both sentences communicate a similar idea, but the second version is easier to read.

This demonstrates why humanization should prioritize clarity rather than complexity.

An effective AI humanizer helps remove unnecessary wording while preserving the meaning of the original statement.

For academic writing, this can improve the overall reading experience and make arguments easier to follow.

AI Humanizer vs. Paraphrasing Tool for Research Papers

AI humanizers and paraphrasing tools share several similarities, but they are not always designed for the same purpose.

Paraphrasing tools primarily focus on expressing existing information using different words.

AI humanizers generally aim to improve the naturalness, tone, and flow of AI-assisted writing.

For example, a paraphrasing tool might restructure a sentence while keeping its formal style.

A humanizer might adjust the same sentence to make it sound more conversational and less repetitive.

However, these capabilities often overlap.

The distinction becomes especially important when working with academic documents.

Research papers require precise terminology and consistent explanations.

A rewriting tool that changes too much may accidentally alter the meaning of a theory, research finding, or statistical result.

Therefore, students should evaluate the output carefully instead of assuming that every rewritten version is an improvement.

Can AI Humanizers Help With Literature Reviews?

Literature reviews are among the most challenging sections of academic writing because they require students to examine multiple sources and explain how existing studies relate to one another.

A strong literature review does more than summarize individual articles.

It identifies patterns, evaluates findings, and explains how previous research connects to the current study.

AI-assisted writing can sometimes produce literature review paragraphs that sound repetitive or disconnected.

A humanizer may help improve transitions and sentence clarity.

For example, a paragraph might repeatedly begin with "According to the study" or "The researchers found that."

Rewriting these transitions can make the discussion easier to follow.

However, humanization cannot replace the analytical work required for a proper literature review.

Students must still read the original studies, verify the authors' conclusions, and accurately represent the evidence.

AI tools should never be trusted to invent citations or generate unsupported research findings.

The strongest literature reviews combine genuine source analysis with clear, carefully edited writing.

Can AI Humanizers Bypass Turnitin or GPTZero?

One of the most frequently asked questions about AI humanizers is whether they can prevent academic writing from being flagged by AI detection tools.

Platforms such as Turnitin and GPTZero use automated systems to identify patterns that may be associated with AI-generated text.

However, AI detection results are not definitive proof of authorship.

False positives and false negatives are possible, and different detection tools may classify the same passage differently.

Humanizing AI-generated text can change its wording and sentence structure, which may influence detection results.

However, no AI humanizer can reliably guarantee that rewritten content will receive a human-written classification.

More importantly, passing an AI detector does not automatically make a document academically acceptable.

Universities and educational institutions may have specific policies governing the use of generative AI.

Students should understand these requirements before using AI-assisted writing or rewriting tools.

The most responsible approach is to use humanization for legitimate editing purposes while maintaining transparency and academic integrity.

How AI Humanizers Can Support Better Essay Structure

Good academic writing requires more than clear sentences.

An effective essay also needs logical organization, smooth transitions, and consistent arguments.

For example, an essay introduction should establish the topic and explain the central argument.

The body paragraphs should develop that argument using relevant evidence and analysis.

The conclusion should summarize the main findings without introducing unrelated information.

AI humanizers can help improve individual passages, but they may not automatically fix deeper structural problems.

If an essay lacks a clear thesis statement or contains unsupported claims, rewriting the sentences won't solve those issues.

Students should first ensure that their ideas are logically organized.

Afterward, they can use editing tools to refine sentence flow and readability.

This approach produces more meaningful improvements than repeatedly rewriting an entire essay without evaluating its content.

Are Free AI Humanizers Good Enough for Academic Writing?

Free AI humanizers can be useful for students who want to experiment with rewriting tools before purchasing a subscription.

However, the quality and limitations of free services vary.

Some platforms restrict the number of words that can be processed, while others limit access to particular editing features.

Students should consider whether a tool can preserve academic terminology and maintain a professional tone.

A free tool that produces accurate, readable text may be sufficient for short assignments.

For longer research papers, writers may prefer tools that support more extensive editing workflows.

Regardless of pricing, the quality of the final output matters more than the number of features advertised.

A useful academic humanizer should make writing clearer without introducing factual errors or unnecessary complexity.

Why Manual Editing Still Matters in Academic Writing

Even advanced AI writing tools cannot fully replace the judgment of the original author.

Academic writing requires understanding the subject, evaluating evidence, and presenting arguments responsibly.

An automated rewriting system may improve sentence flow but misunderstand the importance of a particular term.

For example, a research paper might distinguish between consumer awareness and consumer behavior.

These concepts are related, but they are not interchangeable.

If a humanizer replaces one term with the other, it could change the meaning of the discussion.

This is why students should compare rewritten passages with their original drafts.

They should also verify quotations, citations, research findings, and technical terminology.

AI-assisted editing works best when the writer remains actively involved in the process.

Final Verdict: Which AI Humanizer Is Best for Essays in 2026?

The best AI humanizer for essays and academic writing depends on the writer's specific needs.

For students looking to improve the naturalness of AI-assisted drafts, GPTHuman AI is a dedicated option worth exploring.

Its focus on rewriting AI-generated content makes it relevant for improving sentence flow, readability, and tone.

Meanwhile, QuillBot offers paraphrasing capabilities, and Grammarly provides grammar correction and clarity suggestions.

Each tool serves a different purpose, and no single platform is guaranteed to produce the best result for every assignment.

The most important consideration is whether the rewritten text remains accurate, readable, and consistent with the writer's original ideas.

Academic writing should communicate knowledge clearly, not simply sound sophisticated.

Ultimately, the best results come from combining useful editing technology with independent research, critical thinking, and careful human review.

AI humanizers can improve how an essay is written, but the quality of the ideas, accuracy of the research, and integrity of the final work must always come from the writer.

title: Align3D: Image-Structure Co-Aligned 3D Scene Generation with Observability-Aware Fidelity-Preserving Guidance
description:
arXiv:2611.08861v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Align3D, an image-conditioned diffusion model that generates 3D indoor layouts that are both faithful to a single input photograph and physically plausible beyond the observed view. From the photograph we infer a confidence-calibrated scene graph and train a set-diffusion layout denoiser with image-structure co-alignment where confidence-weighted modality fusion balances image and scene-graph alignment using predicted confidences, while observability-aware fidelity-preserving guidance projects conflicting scene-quality gradients and reweighs them with an object-level confidence mask so under-observed degrees of freedom absorb physical priors without undoing the image-graph match. On 3D-FRONT, Align3D improves image-alignment and scene-quality metrics over recent baselines; once trained, it maps previously unseen photographs to layouts in a single feed-forward pass.

title: โค้ดเพิ่ม 400% แต่คุณไม่ได้เร็วขึ้น 400%: GitHub ชี้คอขวดใหม่อยู่ที่การรีวิว
description:
โดย Nokka (นก-กา) | 9 พฤศจิกายน 2026

บทความนี้เขียนโดย AI (deepseek-v4.1-flash · ผู้ให้บริการโมเดล: ollama-cloud) ผ่าน Hermes Agent ภายใต้การควบคุมและตรวจสอบคุณภาพโดยมนุษย์ - Nokka (นก-กา)

GitHub เปิดตัวเลขที่ทำให้ผมต้องหยุดอ่าน

ในเดือนตุลาคม 2026 GitHub มีคอมมิตมากกว่า 1.2 พันล้านครั้งในหนึ่งสัปดาห์ สูงกว่าปีที่แล้วกว่า 400 เปอร์เซ็นต์ และมากกว่าทั้งปี 2025 รวมกัน [1]

แต่บทความเดียวกันนั้นถามกลับว่า คุณรู้สึกว่างานมีประสิทธิผลขึ้น 400 เปอร์เซ็นต์หรือเปล่า

ลองถามตัวเองดูว่าใช่หรือไม่

ตัวเลขที่อธิบายความรู้สึกนั้น

สาเหตุอยู่ที่การศึกษาในบทความเดียวกัน

Faros AI พบว่าเมื่อทีมเปลี่ยนจากการใช้ AI น้อยไปเป็นการใช้ AI มาก pull request ใช้เวลาอยู่ในขั้นรีวิวนานขึ้น 441 เปอร์เซ็นต์ [1]

แปลว่าโค้ดถูกเขียนเร็วขึ้นจริง แต่ไปติดคอขวดที่คนต้องอ่านและอนุมัติ

คอขวดย้ายจากมือของคนเขียน ไปอยู่ที่ตาของคนรีวิว

สี่ขั้นที่ GitHub แนะนำ

บทความแบ่งงานออกเป็นสี่ขั้น และเสนอวิธีใช้เอเจนต์ในแต่ละขั้น [1]

1. Plan

รวบรวมบริบทที่กระจัดกระจาย ทั้งดีไซน์ในเครื่องมือหนึ่ง ข้อกำหนดในแชท และ pull request เก่า

ใช้ Copilot ใน Slack หรือ Teams เพื่อคุยกับทีม และให้มันร่างเป็น issue พร้อมเกณฑ์ยอมรับ

จากนั้นใช้ Plan Mode เปรียบเทียบแนวทางก่อนลงมือ [1]

2. Build

ทำงานหลายอย่างพร้อมกัน โดยไม่ต้องนั่งเฝ้าจอ

จุดที่ผมสนใจคือ session continuity ซึ่งทำให้เปิดเซสชันเดิมข้ามอุปกรณ์ได้

และ cloud sandbox ที่ให้งานรันต่อแม้ปิดแล็ปท็อป

3. Verify

ลดขนาดการเปลี่ยนแปลงให้รีวิวง่าย

GitHub แนะนำ stacked pull request เพื่อแยกงานที่พึ่งกันออกเป็นชิ้นเล็ก

พร้อมเครื่องมือตรวจคุณภาพก่อนถึงคน เช่น Code Quality, AI Scan, secret detection และ license compliance [1]

ในมุมมองของผม การให้เอเจนต์ช่วยรีวิวมีข้อจำกัดเรื่องขนาด

เวลาเอเจนต์อ่าน diff มันอ่านเป็น token และยิ่งบริบทใหญ่ ค่าใช้จ่ายกับเวลาก็ยิ่งสูงขึ้นตาม [2]

โมเดล Transformer ประมวลผล token ทั้งชุดผ่านชั้น attention และเลือกคำตอบด้วย probability ผ่าน softmax

แต่ละ token ถูกแปลงเป็น embedding vector ก่อนผ่านการคูณ matrix หลายชั้น ซึ่งเป็น linear algebra พื้นฐานของโมเดล

นี่คือเหตุผลที่ผมยังเชื่อว่า PR เล็กได้เปรียบเรื่องเวลาและค่าใช้จ่าย

4. Observe

เชื่อมข้อมูลจาก production กลับมาที่งานวิศวกรรม

ให้ Copilot ช่วยดูว่าคำขอไหนหรือลูกค้ากลุ่มไหนได้รับผลกระทบ แล้วร่าง issue พร้อมหลักฐานและ regression test

สิ่งที่ตัวเลข 441% บอกเรา

ถ้าคุณอ่านแค่ตัวเลข 400% คุณอาจคิดว่าทุกอย่างดีขึ้น

แต่ตัวเลข 441% บอกว่าคอขวดไม่ได้หายไป มันแค่ย้ายที่

และถ้าองค์กรยังใช้กระบวนการรีวิวแบบเดิม การเพิ่มความเร็วในการเขียนโค้ดจะทำให้คิวยาวขึ้น ไม่ใช่ส่งงานเร็วขึ้น

ตัวอย่างที่เห็นได้ในทีมจริง

สมมติทีมคุณมีนักพัฒนาห้าคน และใช้เอเจนต์เขียนโค้ดทุกวัน

ถ้าแต่ละคนเปิด pull request วันละสามใบ ทีมจะมี PR ใหม่สิบห้าใบต่อวัน

ถ้าคนรีวิวมีสองคนและใช้เวลาอ่าน PR ละครึ่งชั่วโมง ทั้งคู่ต้องใช้เวลารวมเจ็ดชั่วโมงครึ่งต่อวัน หรือคนละสามชั่วโมงสี่สิบห้านาที เพียงเพื่ออ่านโค้ด

นี่คือคณิตศาสตร์ง่าย ๆ ที่อธิบายว่าทำไม AI เร็วขึ้นแต่ทีมไม่เร็วขึ้น

สิ่งที่ทำได้ทันที

สามอย่างที่ผมคิดว่าคุ้มที่สุดสำหรับทีมไทย

1. จำกัดขนาด PR ไม่เกิน 400 บรรทัดที่เปลี่ยนแปลง ซึ่งเป็นเกณฑ์ที่ผมตั้งเอง ไม่ได้มาจาก GitHub
2. ให้เอเจนต์รันเช็กพื้นฐานก่อนเปิด PR ทุกครั้ง
3. แยกงานที่พึ่งกันเป็น stacked PR แทนการรวมเป็นก้อนเดียว

ทั้งสามข้อไม่ต้องซื้อเครื่องมือใหม่ แต่ต้องมีวินัยในทีม

ข้อควรระวัง

บทความนี้มาจาก GitHub ซึ่งขาย Copilot

ตัวเลขและกรณีศึกษาจึงควรอ่านโดยรู้ว่ามีส่วนได้ส่วนเสีย

แต่มันยังมีประโยชน์เพราะชี้จุดที่หลายทีมมองข้าม คือการรีวิวและงานหลัง deploy

ผมจะไม่ซื้อเครื่องมือเพิ่มเพราะบทความนี้ แต่จะเริ่มจากข้อหนึ่งคือลดขนาด PR

คำตอบของผม

AI ทำให้การเขียนโค้ดเร็วขึ้นจริง

แต่ความเร็วของทีมไม่ได้ขึ้นกับการเขียนโค้ดอย่างเดียว

มันขึ้นกับว่าคอขวดอยู่ที่ไหน และคุณขยับคอขวดนั้นหรือเปล่า

ถ้าคุณยังวัดความสำเร็จจากจำนวนบรรทัดหรือจำนวน commit คุณจะเห็นตัวเลขสวยขึ้นทุกเดือน โดยที่งานส่งถึงลูกค้าไม่เร็วขึ้นเลย

ก่อนจากกัน

ถ้าคุณกำลังวัดผลทีมด้วยจำนวน commit หรือจำนวนบรรทัด ลองเปลี่ยนไปวัดเวลาที่ PR รอรีวิวดู

ตัวเลขนั้นจะบอกความจริงกว่าว่าคอขวดอยู่ที่ไหน

title: I asked a chat app for a CSS specificity cheat sheet, then checked every row against MDN
description:
I do marketing for HelloAI (https://tryhello.app), the app in this test. Insider test, not a neutral review. Short version: I asked for a CSS specificity cheat sheet, it produced an editable document, and every claim in it survived a check against MDN. Here is exactly what it gave me, and the check.

The prompt

Make me a CSS specificity cheat sheet with about 10 worked examples. For each example selector, show its specificity as a-b-c (ID, class, type) and one line on why. Include at least: a plain element selector, a class, an ID, an attribute selector, a pseudo-class like :hover, a :not() with an argument, a descendant selector, a combined selector like ul#nav li.active, an inline style case, and an !important case. End with a short "who wins" section for three conflicts.

The output

It opened an editable document (they call it Canvas) with this table:

Selector or case Specificity Why
p 0-0-1 One type selector
.note 0-1-0 One class selector
#header 1-0-0 One ID selector
[type="text"] 0-1-0 Attribute selectors count like classes
a:hover 0-1-1 :hover counts like a class, and a is a type
p:not(.muted) 0-1-1 :not() itself adds nothing; its .muted argument counts, along with p
main p 0-0-2 The descendant combinator adds nothing; the two type selectors count
ul#nav li.active 1-1-2 One ID, one class, and two type selectors
button.primary:hover 0-2-1 Two class-level selectors plus one type selector
Inline style="color: red" outside the a-b-c score Inline styles outrank normal author stylesheet rules
.notice { color: red !important; } selector is 0-1-0, plus important !important is not specificity; it changes cascade priority and beats normal declarations

Then three "who wins" conflicts:

  • p { color: blue } vs .note { color: green } - .note wins (0-1-0 beats 0-0-1)
  • #nav li vs ul#nav li.active - ul#nav li.active wins (1-1-2 beats 1-0-1)
  • p { color: blue !important } vs #main p { color: red } - the !important declaration wins despite the lower selector score

The MDN check

I verified each row against MDN's specificity page:

  • The column rules match: an ID column, a class column (classes, attribute selectors, pseudo-classes), and a type column (elements and pseudo-elements).
  • [type="text"] at 0-1-0: MDN uses [type="password"] as its own 0-1-0 example.
  • a:hover at 0-1-1: same shape as MDN's input:focus example.
  • The :not() row: :not() itself adds nothing; only its argument counts. Correct here.
  • The descendant combinator adds nothing. Correct.
  • The tie-break ("if specificity ties, the later rule wins, assuming the same cascade origin and importance") matches.
  • On inline styles, MDN also describes them as a hypothetical 1-0-0-0 when it extends the notation. The sheet kept them outside the a-b-c score instead and said why. Different presentation, same rules.

Wrong rows in this run: zero.

The honest limits

One run of one prompt, free plan, about 300 words of output. It says nothing about the next prompt or a harder one. The document is editable, which matters more than it sounds: I could have fixed a wrong row in place instead of re-prompting. This time there was nothing to fix.

Why I check generated references at all

Specificity is a topic where an almost-right cheat sheet quietly costs you an afternoon. Whatever tool you use, verify a reference before you trust it. This one happened to survive.

The app: https://tryhello.app (free plan, no card)

title: I built a log compressor you can grep without decompressing
description:
Logs pile up. You compress them to keep them, and then the one time you need an answer, you sit there while zgrep inflates gigabytes. The other option is a search cluster that indexes everything and ends up bigger than the logs.

I wanted something in between: archive-sized on disk, searchable in place, nothing to run. So I built logjar, a Rust library and single binary.

$ logjar pack -o hdfs.ljar HDFS.log        # 1.5 GiB -> 52 MiB
$ logjar grep -c "blk_-1608999687919862906 " hdfs.ljar
268                                        # 0.9s

The same search with gzip -dc | grep takes 7.9 seconds.

The idea: most of a log line was written by printf

Look at a line from Hadoop's HDFS log:

081109 203615 148 INFO dfs.DataNode$PacketResponder: Received block blk_-1608999687919862906 of size 91178 from /10.250.10.6

Most of that is fixed text from one print statement. Only a few values change. logjar splits each line into three parts:

timestamp:  081109 203615
template:   <int> INFO dfs.DataNode$PacketResponder: Received block <var> of size <int> from /<var>
variables:  148, blk_-1608999687919862906, 91178, 10.250.10.6

HDFS has 11.2 million lines but only 65 distinct templates. Each template is stored once. The variables go into columns grouped by template and slot, so all the block sizes sit together, then all the IP addresses. Values in one column look alike, and that's what zstd compresses best. Timestamps become deltas.

This idea isn't mine. It comes from two research systems, CLP (OSDI '21) and LogGrep (EuroSys '23). logjar is an independent implementation with its own file format and search method.

Compression

Measured on the LogHub datasets. Every row is checked to unpack byte for byte.

dataset xz -9 zstd -19 logjar
Zookeeper 29.6x 39.0x 165.3x
SSH 20.3x 24.6x 95.5x
Hadoop 38.1x 42.8x 93.5x
Apache 28.4x 28.8x 57.8x
HDFS (1.5 GiB) 16.5x 16.1x 28.8x
BGL 22.9x 21.7x 25.6x
OpenStack 16.1x 16.7x 20.4x

BGL is the weak one. Every line has a second timestamp with microseconds in the middle of the line, and logjar only parses timestamps at the start, so each of those ends up as a one-off dictionary entry.

Search without decompressing

This is the part I like most. Before decoding a single line, logjar proves which templates can't match.

The query compiles to a small automaton. logjar then runs that automaton over each template symbolically:

  • literal text is just its bytes
  • an <int> slot means "one or more characters from [-0-9]"
  • a <var> slot means "any of this segment's actual dictionary values"

If no accepting state is reachable, then no line using that template can match, so those lines are skipped. If every template in a segment is skipped, the segment's big data blocks are never decompressed at all.

For the block-id search above, 45 of 48 segments are skipped this way.

The check only ever over-approximates, so it can't hide a match. I test that directly on random templates, and end to end by comparing every search against a naive scan, using random globs, random regexes, time windows and appended data.

It works for regexes too, and timestamps are indexed:

logjar grep -E '(WARN|ERROR) .*timeout' app.ljar
logjar grep --after 2026-11-01 --before 2026-11-02T06:00 "disk full" app.ljar

With a one-hour time window, the HDFS search takes 0.04 seconds, because the footer index rules out 46 of 48 segments before anything is read.

Where it loses

Plain grep on the uncompressed file, already cached in memory, is faster for simple searches: 0.2s against logjar's 0.4-0.9s. It's a memchr over bytes already in RAM, and that will always win. That file also takes 28x the disk space. Against anything compressed, logjar is 10-20x faster, and the more selective the query, the bigger the gap.

The bugs the tests found

Two bugs surfaced before release, and both were found by comparing logjar against something I trust:

  1. Case-insensitive negated classes. With -i, [^a] still matched A, because I folded case after negating the class. A test that checks my regex engine against the regex crate on 120,000 random pattern/input pairs caught it on the first run.
  2. $ on Windows logs. On CRLF files, [0-9]$ matched nothing. Archives keep the \r (they're lossless), so the line never ended in a digit. Comparing match counts with GNU grep on a real Zookeeper log caught it. $ now matches before the \r, and the pruning logic mirrors that so it stays sound.

Neither would have shown up in hand-written tests.

Try it 

cargo install logjar

Prebuilt binaries for Windows, Linux (x64 and arm64) and macOS are on the releases page. The file format is documented in docs/FORMAT.md, and the pruning design is in docs/DESIGN.md.

It also works as a library:

let archive = Archive::open("app.ljar")?;
let q = Query::regex(r"after \d+ retries")?;
archive.search(&q, &[], |m| {
    println!("{}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&m.line));
    true
})?;

Known limits are listed in the README: no shared dictionary across segments, no schema-aware handling of JSON logs, and no index on variable values yet. If you have a log format it handles badly, I'd like to see it.
