title: Postman AI Complaint: Check What Your API Tools Can See
description:
Postman AI Plugins: Check What Your API Tools Can See

An API client can hold more of your business than you realize: saved requests, test responses, workspace access, and credentials used to connect other systems. If an AI feature appears inside that client, the useful question is not just whether it is installed. It is what the feature can read, what it can change, and whether you can verify either one.

A public complaint about Postman’s AI plugin raised that question, but the available account does not establish that customer data or credentials left Postman. Here’s exactly how I would check a small business integration without treating an allegation as a confirmed breach.

What the Postman complaint does—and does not—establish

The reported behavior warrants an access review, not a claim that Postman leaked your API data. The available account describes an attempted connection that failed authentication; it does not establish a completed transfer, identify every affected installation, or show that the sequence was reproduced on another machine.

Keep four questions separate:

Question What would answer it
Was a plugin installed? The plugin’s installation status on each relevant machine and coding agent
Could it authenticate? Its configured credentials and the account or workspace they belong to
What could it reach? The permissions of those credentials and the tools available to the agent
Did data leave? Relevant transfer records or other evidence of an actual completed request

A “yes” in the first row is not a “yes” in the last. Likewise, a failed connection attempt does not prove that every other route was unavailable. If you need to investigate a specific incident, preserve the relevant records and examine that environment rather than generalizing from a headline.

Postman’s current desktop-app documentation describes how to uninstall the Postman Coding Agent Plugin. It also discusses installation behavior, but current documentation cannot establish exactly what a particular user saw during an earlier installation. Treat it as guidance for checking your setup now, not a reconstruction of someone else’s.

For a small team, the practical response is narrower: identify the API tools you rely on, inspect the access attached to them, and reduce anything you cannot justify.

Map the access path, not just the plugin

An AI feature’s effective reach depends on the entire path from agent to plugin to credential to resource. Checking whether the plugin exists is useful, but it misses the permissions that determine what an authenticated request could do.

Consider a lead-follow-up workflow. A new inquiry arrives, your team looks up the lead in a CRM, and an integration prepares a reply. During development, an API client may hold a sample CRM request, a saved response, and a credential for testing. The business job might require reading one lead and creating a draft. A credential that can also export customer records or delete them would have more authority than that job needs.

That example is hypothetical; it is not a finding about the Postman complaint. It gives you a way to inspect your own system. Draw the path as plainly as possible:

Coding agent
    → Postman plugin or connected tool
    → authenticated Postman account or API key
    → accessible workspaces and resources
    → any separately connected business service

Do not collapse the last two lines. Access to a Postman workspace does not, by itself, describe what a CRM credential inside a request can do. Conversely, finding no usable CRM credential does not tell you whether an agent can read or change Postman resources.

Postman’s API key documentation says an API key can access Postman data for which its owner has permission. That makes the key owner’s accessible workspaces part of your review. Postman also says its MCP server enables AI agents to manage resources including workspaces, collections, specifications, mocks, and monitors. “AI access” is therefore too vague to put in an approval note. Name the connection and the resources it exposes.

For each connection, write down what you can establish from the actual account and permission screens. Mark everything else unknown. An unknown is not evidence of exposure, but it is not a permission you have verified either.

Check installation, credentials, and resource access separately

A reliable audit has three distinct passes: find where the plugin is installed, identify how each connection authenticates, and inspect what the authenticated account can access. Removing a plugin addresses installation; it does not automatically revoke an API key or another service’s credential.

Start with the machines and coding agents used to build or maintain the integration. Postman documents a plugin status command that shows which detected coding agents have the plugin installed. Use the command in the linked documentation rather than guessing its syntax or assuming that a check on one machine covers the whole team.

Next, examine authentication. Look at the account attached to any Postman API key used by the tool, then check the workspaces that account can reach. Separately inspect credentials saved for the CRM, inbox, billing platform, or other services involved in your workflow. A credential’s presence and its permissions are different findings: record both.

Finally, compare available access with the job the workflow performs:

Access to inspect Question to answer
Saved requests and examples Do they contain real customer information or internal details?
Postman workspaces Which workspaces can the authenticated owner access?
Connected-service credentials Which account is used, and what actions does it permit?
Agent tools Can the agent only inspect resources, or can it change them?
Revoke controls Which specific key, connection, or plugin would you disable?

If you decide the plugin should not remain installed, Postman documents a remove command for detected coding agents. Its desktop-app instructions give another path: Help > Postman CLI and Plugins > Uninstall Postman Coding Agent Plugin, followed by restarting coding agents. Check installation status again afterward.

Then review credentials as a separate task. If a key has broader access than the workflow needs, change or revoke it through the relevant service’s controls after checking what production jobs depend on it. Uninstalling the plugin does not prove that no data was transferred, and it should not be treated as a substitute for credential review.

Test one workflow with synthetic data

A controlled test tells you what your integration does with a specific input; it does not prove what happened in someone else’s Postman installation. Use fictional records, observe the resulting actions, and keep production customer data out of the test.

Start with one workflow rather than an inventory of every tool in the business. Lead follow-up is a good candidate because the desired outcome is easy to state: receive a fictional inquiry, look up or create the appropriate test record, and prepare a draft for review. Whether the system should send a message, update the CRM, or stop for approval must be decided before you run it.

Create a test record clearly marked as synthetic. The fields below are an illustration, not a schema you should paste into a live CRM:

test_lead:
  name: "Test Customer"
  company: "Fictional Example Company"
  inquiry: "Synthetic request for a product demonstration."
  contact_route: "controlled test inbox"

expected_behavior:
  crm: "read or update only the test record"
  email: "create a draft; do not send"
  exception: "ask for review if the lead cannot be matched"

Run the workflow through the same entry point your team normally uses, with a test environment or other controls appropriate to your setup. Watch the CRM record, the draft folder, any send activity, and the workflow’s own execution history. Record observed behavior beside expected behavior. If you cannot see whether a step ran, write “not observable” rather than “did not happen.”

Pay attention to the handoff. A system that creates a draft but silently fails to flag an unmatched lead is not finished just because it avoided sending an email. Equally, a workflow meant only to draft replies should not have permission to send them merely because that was easier to configure.

If an AI feature participates, ask which data it receives for this test and which tools it can invoke. Can it see only the fictional inquiry supplied to it, or can it browse unrelated workspaces? Can it propose an update for review, or execute one? Those are configuration questions to answer from the tool and account in front of you, not assumptions to make from the word “assistant.”

Keep an access record you can use during an incident

The useful output is a short record that names the connected account, readable information, permitted actions, and exact revocation path. If an integration breaks or a new AI feature requests access, that record lets you make a decision without rebuilding the permission map from memory.

Here is a format you can use for a single workflow. The values are illustrative; replace them with findings from your own permission screens:

workflow: "Lead follow-up"
tool: "API client and connected coding agent"
connected_account: "record the actual account owner"

can_read:
  - "list verified resources here"

can_act:
  - "list verified actions here"

credentials:
  - "name where each credential is managed; never paste its value"

revoke_at:
  plugin: "document the installation removal path"
  postman_key: "document the key management path"
  connected_service: "document that service's credential controls"

unknown:
  - "list anything not yet verified"

test_result:
  expected: "draft for review"
  observed: "record what the synthetic test did"

Store this record somewhere the person maintaining the integration can find it, but do not put secret values in it. Update it when you change the account, credential, plugin, or workflow behavior. The record is especially valuable for a small team: the person responding to a problem may not be the person who originally connected the tools.

Make the permission check part of the build

Access mapping and a synthetic end-to-end test can be part of delivering a workflow, not cleanup after the AI feature is switched on. A working lead-follow-up system has a defined trigger, the minimum actions needed to prepare the reply, and a visible review or exception path. The Postman complaint is a reason to check those boundaries in your own tools—not evidence that your data has already left them.

Want more like this?

I’m Lazar Milićević, a senior engineer focused on practical AI automation for solopreneurs and small teams.

description:
API Gateway

Feature

Call Google Cloud APIs from streaming gateways

Streaming gateways can now call Google Cloud APIs such as aiplatform.googleapis.com. A gateway with an effectiveStreamingMode of EFFECTIVE_STREAMING_MODE_ENABLED authenticates to backends whose host ends in .googleapis.com or .vertexai.goog with an access token for the gateway's service account. Other backends still receive an ID token. An existing streaming gateway switches when API Gateway next rolls out a gateway update, or immediately when you update it to a new API config.

title: Subresource Integrity & CDN Script Pinning: Catching Silent Payload Swaps
description:
Your checkout page loads one script tag from a public CDN. You reviewed that library two years ago. Since then the file at that URL may have changed a dozen times, or the domain itself may have changed owners, and your page would happily execute whatever came back. In June 2024 that is exactly what happened to sites embedding polyfill.io: the domain changed hands and started serving injected code to some visitors. No deploy on their side, no diff in their repo, no alert.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command, attribute and header myself. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET, and I build PixelValut, a set of browser-side developer tools. This is Part 3 of the series Client Trust & Agent Hijack Defense. Part 1 covered prompt injection in fetched docs and Part 2 covered tool-calling attack surfaces. Both were about content you did not write steering your software. A third-party script is the most direct form of that problem: it runs with your page's full privileges.

📚 Series Roadmap — Client Trust & Agent Hijack Defense

  • Part 1: Prompt Injection via Docs Your Tools Fetch
  • Part 2: WebMCP & Tool-Calling Attack Surfaces
  • Part 3 (This Post): Subresource Integrity & CDN Script Pinning: Catching Silent Payload Swaps
  • Part 4: CSP, Trusted Types & Residual XSS: Reading Reports Like a Forensics Log
  • Part 5: Extension & npm Postinstall Forensics: Homoglyphs, Base64 & Unexpected Network
  • Part 6: Browser Secrets That Leak: Tokens, Storage Quotas & Exfil Paths

Related earlier posts: Deobfuscating Malicious npm & Browser Payloads · Subdomain Takeover & Dangling DNS Reconnaissance · Zero-Trust Reverse Proxy Hardening in Nginx

How does Subresource Integrity stop a swapped CDN script?

Direct answer: Subresource Integrity adds a cryptographic hash of the exact file you reviewed to the integrity attribute of a script or stylesheet tag. The browser hashes the downloaded bytes and refuses to execute them if they do not match. Pin exact versions, use SHA-384, add crossorigin="anonymous", and monitor the URL so you learn about swaps before users do.

What SRI actually checks

An SRI-protected tag looks like this:

<script
  src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/dayjs@1.11.13/dayjs.min.js"
  integrity="sha384-DpVxUeeBWjUvUV1czyIHJAjh+jYUZFu2lLakbdua5vbwOrBGi1UgaKCHjTC+x3Ky"
  crossorigin="anonymous"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer"></script>

The rules that matter in practice:

  • Algorithms: browsers accept sha256, sha384 and sha512. SHA-384 is the common default and what most CDNs publish.
  • Format: the value is algo- plus the base64 encoding of the raw binary digest. A hex digest will never match.
  • Multiple hashes: you can list several values separated by spaces. The browser picks the strongest algorithm present and accepts the file if it matches any hash of that algorithm. This is how you allow a planned upgrade window.
  • Encoding: the hash covers the response body after content decoding, so gzip or Brotli at the CDN does not break it.
  • Failure: on mismatch the resource is blocked, the element's error event fires, and the console logs an integrity error. Nothing is reported to your server unless you add that yourself.

Generating hashes correctly

Always hash the exact bytes the CDN serves, not a file you built locally and assume is identical.

# Hash the file the CDN actually serves
curl -sSL "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/dayjs@1.11.13/dayjs.min.js" -o dayjs.min.js
echo "sha384-$(openssl dgst -sha384 -binary dayjs.min.js | openssl base64 -A)"

# Same thing with shasum + xxd (handy on macOS)
echo "sha384-$(shasum -b -a 384 dayjs.min.js | awk '{print $1}' | xxd -r -p | base64)"

# Self-hosted bundle produced by your build
for f in dist/assets/*.js; do
  printf '%s sha384-%s\n' "$f" "$(openssl dgst -sha384 -binary "$f" | openssl base64 -A)"
done

The -binary flag is the detail people miss. Without it, openssl dgst prints a hex string, and base64-encoding that text gives a value that looks valid but never matches. If you are checking a hash quickly in the browser, the PixelValut hash generator supports SHA-384 and SHA-512; just make sure you compare base64 output of the digest, not hex.

The crossorigin attribute is not optional

For a cross-origin script, the browser can only verify integrity if the response is fetched in CORS mode. That means two things must be true:

  1. The tag has crossorigin="anonymous" (or use-credentials, which you almost never want for a public CDN).
  2. The CDN responds with an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that permits your origin, usually *.

If either is missing, the integrity check fails and the script is blocked, even when the hash is correct. Major public CDNs such as jsDelivr, cdnjs and unpkg send the header. A private bucket or a misconfigured asset domain often does not. Check the response headers before you ship:

curl -sI -H "Origin: https://shop.example" \
  "https://assets.example-cdn.com/widget/2.4.1/widget.min.js" \
  | grep -iE '^(HTTP|access-control-allow-origin|content-type|cache-control|etag)'

For a quick visual check of status codes, redirects and headers from a browser tab, the HTTP status checker shows the redirect chain too. Redirects matter: an asset URL that suddenly 301s to a different host is an early sign that something upstream changed.

Pinning: SRI only works on immutable URLs

SRI and floating versions do not mix. If the URL is /npm/lib@latest or /lib/3/lib.js, the bytes will change on the next release, the hash will stop matching, and your feature breaks. Teams then delete the integrity attribute "temporarily" and never put it back.

URL style Example Safe with SRI? Notes
Exact version lib@4.2.1/dist/lib.min.js ✅ The normal target for SRI
Major/minor range lib@4/dist/lib.min.js ❌ Breaks on every release
latest tag lib@latest ❌ Never pin a hash to this
Content-hashed self-hosted /assets/app.3f9a1c.js ✅ Ideal; generate hashes at build
Vendor SDK that must stay live payment or analytics loaders ⚠️ Vendor changes it on purpose; SRI not possible
User-agent varied responses some font or polyfill services ❌ Different bytes per browser cannot share one hash

The last two rows are the uncomfortable ones. Some vendors, payment SDKs included, explicitly tell you to load their script from their domain without self-hosting, because they push security fixes to it. You cannot SRI those. For them, the controls are a tight Content Security Policy that allows only that exact host, keeping them off pages that do not need them, and isolating them in a sandboxed iframe where the integration allows it.

The require-sri-for trap

Older articles recommend a CSP directive called require-sri-for script style to force every script to carry an integrity attribute. Do not rely on it. It lived in a draft spec, was only ever available behind flags, and has been removed from the specification and from browsers. A policy containing it is simply ignored for that directive.

The newer mechanism is the Integrity-Policy response header (with an Integrity-Policy-Report-Only variant), which lets you require integrity metadata for scripts and send violation reports. Support has landed in recent Chromium releases; check current browser support before depending on it, and keep the report-only form running first:

Integrity-Policy-Report-Only: blocked-destinations=(script), endpoints=(integrity-endpoint)
Reporting-Endpoints: integrity-endpoint="https://shop.example/reports/integrity"

Reporting failures yourself

Because SRI failures are silent to your backend, add a tiny beacon on the elements you care about:

<script>
  function sriFail(el) {
    navigator.sendBeacon('/reports/sri', JSON.stringify({
      src: el.src || el.href, page: location.pathname, ts: Date.now()
    }));
  }
</script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/dayjs@1.11.13/dayjs.min.js"
        integrity="sha384-DpVxUeeBWjUvUV1czyIHJAjh+jYUZFu2lLakbdua5vbwOrBGi1UgaKCHjTC+x3Ky"
        crossorigin="anonymous"
        onerror="sriFail(this)"></script>

The error event also fires for network failures, so treat a spike as "investigate," not "confirmed attack." For scripts you insert dynamically, set script.integrity and script.crossOrigin = 'anonymous' before appending the element.

Monitoring the URL, not just the page

SRI protects users at load time. You also want to know when the upstream file changes, before a user's browser blocks it. A scheduled job that refetches each pinned URL and compares the digest is enough:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# sri-watch.sh: lines in pins.txt look like "URL sha384-HASH"
set -euo pipefail
while read -r url expected; do
  actual="sha384-$(curl -fsSL "$url" | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl base64 -A)"
  [[ "$actual" == "$expected" ]] || echo "MISMATCH $url expected=$expected got=$actual"
done < pins.txt

Run it from CI or a cron job and alert on any MISMATCH line. An exact-version file on a reputable CDN should never change. If it does, that is a security event, not a cache quirk.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] Every third-party <script> and <link rel="stylesheet"> is inventoried with its owner.
  • [ ] All CDN URLs pin an exact version, never latest or a range.
  • [ ] Each pinned tag has integrity="sha384-..." generated from the served bytes.
  • [ ] Each cross-origin tag has crossorigin="anonymous" and the CDN returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • [ ] Build output gets integrity attributes automatically (bundler plugin or post-build script).
  • [ ] No policy depends on require-sri-for.
  • [ ] Scripts that cannot use SRI are restricted by CSP host allowlists and kept off sensitive pages.
  • [ ] SRI load failures beacon to a reporting endpoint.
  • [ ] A scheduled job re-hashes pinned URLs and alerts on mismatch.
  • [ ] Asset hosts are checked for unexpected redirects and expiring domains.

FAQ

Is SHA-256 good enough for SRI?

It is cryptographically fine. SHA-384 is the conventional default and what most CDNs publish, so using it avoids confusion.

Does SRI work for images, fonts or fetch requests?

In practice browsers enforce it on scripts and stylesheets (and modulepreload links). fetch() accepts an integrity option too. Images and fonts are not covered.

Will SRI break when the CDN recompresses files?

No. The hash is computed over the decoded body, so transfer encoding changes do not matter. Minifier or content changes do.

What about ES modules loaded with import?

Top-level module scripts take integrity like classic scripts. Statically imported dependencies can be pinned through the integrity section of an import map in browsers that support it.

Should I self-host instead of using a CDN?

Self-hosting with content-hashed filenames removes the third-party trust problem for those files. You still want SRI if assets are served from a separate domain or CDN you do not fully control.

Can an attacker who controls the CDN also change my integrity attribute?

Not unless they also control your HTML. That separation is the whole point: the hash lives in markup you serve.

Next in this series, Part 4 covers CSP, Trusted Types and residual XSS, and how to read violation reports like a forensics log.

title: Designing Fault-Tolerant API Through Idempotency
description:
So imagine I’m reading your post. I click Like, the heart turns red, and the request times out. My frontend’s retry logic sends it again.

This time, the success reply arrives. The heart turns grey.
I know I liked your post. But your code apparently has other plans because its not FAULT TOLERANT.

Fault tolerance is an application’s ability to keep working correctly when part of the system fails. Retrying can help us recover from a temporary connection failure, but our API has to handle the second attempt safely.

For database writes, there’s a catch. Saving the change and delivering the HTTP response are separate steps. The connection can drop after the database commits, leaving the client unsure whether the write succeeded.

Let’s follow that click through MongoDB and PostgreSQL on Neon, then make the retry safe in both.

One click became two requests

Our endpoint is POST /posts/42/toggle-like. It reverses the current state. If my like exists, remove it. Otherwise, create it.

Here’s how one click manages to do both.

  1. The API saves my like.
  2. The connection drops before the success reply reaches my browser.
  3. The browser retries.
  4. The API finds the like and removes it. This reply arrives successfully.

The first write succeeded. Only its reply was lost.

The retry recovered from the connection failure, but it also reversed the user’s action. Making this endpoint fault tolerant means handling both parts correctly.

Our like can live in a MongoDB document or a PostgreSQL row on Neon. Either database will execute a fresh request to remove it. Our API told it to toggle, and it followed the instruction.

Could we wrap the toggle in a transaction?

Yes. A transaction groups database changes so they all commit together or all roll back. That’s atomicity. MongoDB supports transactions across documents on replica sets and sharded clusters. Neon supports PostgreSQL transactions. MongoDB transactions · PostgreSQL transactions

In our example, though, the first transaction already committed before the reply disappeared. The retry starts a new transaction and reverses the like.

Both transactions succeed. I’ve now unliked your post with excellent data integrity.

A row lock also ends when its transaction finishes, leaving the later retry free to make another change. PostgreSQL row locks

We need to change what repeating the request does.

Make the request say what I mean

Instead of asking the API to toggle, ask it to make sure my like exists.

The first request creates it. The retry finds it and leaves it there.

That’s idempotency; repeating the request has the same intended effect as sending it once. The responses can differ while the intended effect stays the same.

We can use PUT /posts/42/like to ensure the like exists. For an unlike, DELETE /posts/42/like ensures the like is absent.

The handler’s database operation must implement that promise. Changing the HTTP verb alone leaves the original toggle behaviour in place.

MongoDB can create a missing like with an upsert. PostgreSQL on Neon can use INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. Both need a unique rule for the user-and-post pair so simultaneous requests also produce one like.

Implementation examples

MongoDB

Create the unique index once. Then use the upsert in the request handler, taking userId from the signed-in session.

// One-time setup
await likes.createIndex(
  { postId: 1, userId: 1 },
  { unique: true }
);

// In the PUT handler
await likes.updateOne(
  { postId, userId },
  { $setOnInsert: { likedAt: new Date() } },
  { upsert: true }
);

An existing like keeps its original timestamp. MongoDB unique indexes · $setOnInsert

PostgreSQL on Neon

Give the likes table a primary key on (post_id, user_id), then run this parameterised query.

INSERT INTO likes (post_id, user_id)
VALUES ($1, $2)
ON CONFLICT (post_id, user_id) DO NOTHING;

The retry finds the existing pair and leaves it alone. PostgreSQL ON CONFLICT

If you keep a separate like counter, increase it only when a new like was inserted, in the same transaction.

What if I need to keep the toggle endpoint?

The PUT approach above repeats the same desired state. If we keep POST /posts/42/toggle-like, we need a way to recognise that a particular action already happened.

Give each deliberate click an idempotency key. This key identifies one action across all its retries. The client reuses it when retrying and generates a new key for a new deliberate click.

In one transaction, claim the key under a unique constraint scoped to the user and endpoint, apply the toggle, and save its result. When the same key comes back, return the saved result.

Now test the exact failure. Let the write succeed, drop its HTTP reply, and retry. There should still be one like when you refresh.

Whether the like lives in MongoDB or Neon, both attempts now leave us with the result we wanted. One click. One like.

So if I liked your post. The heart should stay red 😂.
_I hope this helps you and can guide in making your code _

Thanks for reading 👍

title: Designing Evolvable Kafka Event Architectures: Schema Evolution Without Breaking Consumers
description:
Project Context:

This is Issue #13 of my ongoing implementation series for a Kafka-based distributed telemetry ingestion platform.

The complete implementation and future iterations can be tracked here: Repository.

This issue focuses on schema evolution, version-aware event processing, and designing stable event contracts for changing telemetry requirements.

While building this Kafka-based distributed telemetry ingestion platform, I reached a point where the problem was no longer about moving data from one place to another.

The pipeline already had the fundamental flow:

Sensor Producers → Kafka Topics → Consumers → Processing Layer → Persistence Layer → Database

The challenge was:

How do we evolve telemetry events when the data model itself changes over time?

Imagine a sensor device today sends:

  • Temperature
  • Humidity
  • Timestamp

Tomorrow, a newer generation of the device sends:

  • Temperature
  • Humidity
  • Timestamp
  • Battery Level

Current file structure:

Figure 1: Current telemetry package structure showing the organization of domain models, versioned event contracts, processing services, Kafka consumers, and persistence components.

The easiest approach is to keep modifying one event class and keep adding fields. But that creates a growing contract:

telemetry/domain/TelemetryEvent.java:

Initial telemetry event model before introducing version-specific representations. The model started accumulating fields that belonged only to certain device versions.

Over time, the original event becomes tightly coupled to every future requirement.

Older versions start carrying fields they never understood, and every new change risks affecting existing consumers.

The question became:

How do we allow event versions to evolve independently while keeping the processing pipeline stable?

Figure 2: The initial single-event approach where new requirements continuously expand the telemetry model, increasing coupling between event versions and consumers.

The first design decision was to separate telemetry versions.

Instead of one expanding model, I introduced:

TelemetryEventV1 -> Temperature + Humidity

telemetry/domain/event/TelemetryEventV1.java:

TelemetryEventV1 implementation representing the first telemetry schema version with only the common sensor fields defined by the VersionedTelemetryEvent contract.

TelemetryEventV2 -> Temperature + Humidity + Battery Level

telemetry/domain/event/TelemetryEventV2.java:

TelemetryEventV2 implementation extending the telemetry schema with battery support through BatteryAwareTelemetryEvent while maintaining the common VersionedTelemetryEvent contract.

Now the versions could evolve independently. But this introduced another question:

Who decides which version of the event should be created?

The answer was a dedicated version mapping layer.

The flow became:

Figure 3: Version-specific telemetry models allowing each event version to evolve independently while keeping version selection centralized through TelemetryEventVersionMapper.

The mapper correctly identified the version and created the corresponding event object.

telemetry/service/TelemetryEventVersionMapper.java:

TelemetryEventVersionMapper centralizing version selection and transformation logic to convert incoming telemetry events into their corresponding version-specific implementations.

Then I encountered a Java type system problem.

Initially, the mapper returned:

Object

This was because both versions were objects. The mapping worked. But the consumer received only:

Object event;

At that point, Java only knew:

"This is an Object."

It did not know whether it was:

TelemetryEventV1
TelemetryEventV2

The version information was lost at the contract level and the consumer could not safely access version-specific behavior.

This led to introducing a common contract:

VersionedTelemetryEvent

Now both event versions implemented the same interface. The flow evolved into:

Figure 4: Common event contract introduced through VersionedTelemetryEvent, allowing multiple telemetry versions to share a stable abstraction while preserving their version-specific fields.

The consumer no longer cared about the exact implementation. It only depended on the contract. This was the first application of the *Dependency Inversion Principle: *

High-level processing logic depended on an abstraction rather than concrete event classes.

telemetry/domain/event/VersionedTelemetryEvent.java:

VersionedTelemetryEvent defining the stable contract shared across all telemetry event versions while keeping version-specific capabilities outside the core interface.

But another design question appeared. If the processor receives:

VersionedTelemetryEvent event;

what happens when V2 has:

getBatteryLevel()

but V1 does not?

Should battery become part of the common interface? Something like:

interface VersionedTelemetryEvent {
getTemperature();
getHumidity();
getBatteryLevel();
}

That would solve V2, but it would force V1 to support functionality it does not have. The contract would become polluted.

The solution was capability-based design.

Instead of making every telemetry event support every possible feature:

VersionedTelemetryEvent -> BatteryAwareTelemetryEvent -> LocationAwareTelemetryEvent -> FirmwareAwareTelemetryEvent

Only events that support a capability implement it. So:

TelemetryEventV1 -> VersionedTelemetryEvent TelemetryEventV2 -> VersionedTelemetryEvent + BatteryAwareTelemetryEvent

telemetry/domain/event/capability/BatteryAwareTelemetryEvent.java:

BatteryAwareTelemetryEvent capability interface isolating battery-specific behavior so only telemetry versions supporting battery data implement this additional contract.

telemetry/domain/event/capability/LocationAwareTelemetryEvent.java:

LocationAwareTelemetryEvent capability interface designed to support future location-enabled telemetry versions without modifying the core event contract.

Now the processor can handle optional capabilities safely:

telemetry/service/TelemetryEventProcessor.java:

TelemetryEventProcessor consuming the common VersionedTelemetryEvent contract, transforming events into persistence records, and handling optional capabilities through capability-based interfaces.

This followed the** Interface Segregation Principle:**
Classes should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use.

The next responsibility boundary was processing.

The event object should not directly become a database entity.

So the final flow became:

Figure 5: Final telemetry processing flow separating event version handling, business transformation, and persistence responsibilities across independent layers.

The processor became responsible for transformation. The persistence layer became responsible only for persistence.

This followed the Single Responsibility Principle:

- Mapper handles version selection.
- Processor handles transformation.
- Persistence handles storage.

Each component has one clear reason to change.

Final Consumer Service - TelemetryConsumerService.java:

TelemetryConsumerService orchestrating the version-aware Kafka consumption flow by mapping incoming events, processing versioned telemetry contracts, and delegating persistence responsibilities.

The final architecture allowed:

- New telemetry versions without modifying existing ones.
- Optional capabilities without bloating the base interface.
- Cleaner separation between ingestion, processing, and storage.

The important realization was:
Schema evolution is not solved by adding a version number.
The real challenge is designing the boundaries correctly:

- What belongs to every event?
- What belongs to a specific version?
- What should become a capability?
- Which layer should know about version details?

One more architectural gap became clear during this process.

The consumer side is now version-aware:

Kafka Event -> Version Mapper -> Versioned Processing

But the producer side is still using the generic event contract.

The complete evolution will eventually become:

_Producer -> Versioned Event DTO -> Kafka -> Versioned Consumer -> Processing -> Persistence_

That introduces the next design area:

  • Polymorphic Kafka serialization
  • Producer-side versioned DTOs
  • Event envelope design
  • Schema compatibility strategies

The most valuable part of this implementation was not creating multiple event classes.

It was learning that good architecture often comes from repeatedly asking:

"Does this responsibility really belong here?"

Every uncomfortable question exposed a better boundary.

I would love to hear your thoughts and perspectives on designing evolvable event-driven systems. How do you approach schema evolution in Kafka-based architectures? What patterns or trade-offs have worked well in your production systems?

Open to discussions, feedback, and different architectural viewpoints.

Thank you.

title: AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay
description:
arXiv:2611.08755v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.

title: Grounding-Aware Judge Reward Reinforcement Learning for Out-of-Domain Face Anti-Spoofing
description:
arXiv:2611.09047v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Face Anti-Spoofing (FAS) must distinguish genuine faces from presentation attacks. A unified Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) is an attractive solution: it detects physical attacks (print, replay, mask) in one model and produces interpretable forensic evidence via Chain-of-Thought (CoT). A central obstacle to post-training such a model with reinforcement learning is that FAS reasoning has no rule-verifiable ground truth: only the binary verdict is checkable, while the reasoning chain cannot be verified by any hand-crafted rule. Optimizing the verdict alone is therefore a sparse, hackable signal. The model can reach the correct answer through a shortcut such as a false-rejection bias, which does not generalize. We address this with a grounding-aware judge reward. A 32B vision-language judge scores each reasoning chain against the image on evidence anchoring, logical coherence, and domain knowledge, turning the image itself into the verification signal. The reward is applied in a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) stage after CoT supervised fine-tuning. It is the judge, rather than the RL objective, that supplies the process supervision a verdict-only reward cannot. Our study starts from a model that already performs well In-Domain (ID) after CoT-based supervised fine-tuning and asks how to improve its Out-of-Domain (OOD) generalization. We find that grounding-aware rewards are an effective means to that end. We validate the method on OOD generalization, where the reward reduces ACER on two physical benchmarks (LCC-FASD 0.288 to 0.273, MSU-MFSD 0.431 to 0.409) while preserving ID accuracy (CelebA-Spoof 0.033 to 0.035). Against ResNet-50/101 and CLIP-ViT-B/16 baselines, the MLLM dominates ID and matches or surpasses the strongest baseline OOD. To our knowledge this is the first use of LLM-as-judge process supervision for FAS.

title: RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers
description:
arXiv:2611.09597v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) extends RL with verifiable rewards to open-ended tasks by scoring each response against query-specific rubrics. Under group-relative optimization, however, a rubric that every sampled response fails (unreachable) or passes (saturated) gives all responses the same outcome and no learning signal; in Qwen3-4B medical training, 60.88% of query-rubric observations are inactive. We find that the two states lack different supervision: stating an unreachable rubric in the prompt raises its satisfaction from 1.13% to 91.25%, whereas responses that all pass a saturated rubric still differ in quality. We therefore propose RuACT (Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers), which assigns each inactive rubric the role that supplies what it lacks. Rubric as Teacher uses unreachable rubrics as privileged information for reward-gated on-policy self-distillation, and Rubric as Critic decomposes saturated rubrics into child rubrics that separate current responses while sharing the parent's weight. RuACT outperforms GRPO, rubric reweighting, and rubric-guided exploration on all four medical and scientific benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and achieves the best average with Qwen3-1.7B. On initially unreachable rubrics, unguided recovery rises from 35.02% to 42.86%, while child refinement improves reward-quality alignment on independent rollouts from 57.74% to 60.77%. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/RuACT.

title: How browser encryption actually works in a private notepad
description:
How browser encryption actually works in a private notepad

Disclosure: I built the notepad this article is about — Outsmart Notes. It comes up once, at the end, because the encryption design below is the one I shipped.

Most notes apps encrypt your notes "in transit and at rest", which sounds thorough until you ask the obvious question: at rest where, and who holds the key? If the server holds the key, the server can read your notes. The encryption protects you from everyone except the people running the service — which is exactly the party a private notepad should protect you from.

There is a stricter design: encrypt in the browser, with a key the server never sees. Here is how that actually works, and where it breaks.

1. The key never leaves the device

The vault is locked with a password you choose. That password is never sent to the server. Instead, the browser runs it through PBKDF2 — 100,000 iterations — to derive an encryption key. The iteration count is the point: it makes guessing the password expensive, even for someone who gets hold of the encrypted data.

The derived key lives in browser memory while the vault is open. It is never written to disk, never put in a cookie, and never sent in a request. When you close the vault, it is gone. Forget the password and there is no recovery — that is not a missing feature, it is the guarantee. A vault the operator can open for you is a vault the operator can open.

2. AES-GCM does two jobs at once

The cipher is AES-GCM with a 256-bit key. It encrypts the note and, in the same operation, produces an authentication tag — a short value that proves the ciphertext has not been tampered with. If a single byte changes, decryption fails loudly instead of silently returning corrupted text.

That matters because an attacker who can modify stored data is a realistic threat model for a web app: a compromised server, a malicious extension, a bad sync. Encryption without authentication would let tampered notes decrypt into garbage you might trust. GCM makes tampering detectable, not just unreadable.

3. Sharing without sharing the key with the server

Encrypted sharing has a harder problem: how do you send someone an encrypted note without giving the server the key? The answer is the URL hash. The encryption key travels in the fragment after the # in the link — and browsers never send the fragment to the server. The server stores the ciphertext and serves the page; the recipient's browser reads the key from the hash, fetches the ciphertext, and decrypts locally.

The server sees an opaque blob and a request for a page. It cannot decrypt the note, because it never receives the key. The trade-off is real too: anyone with the link has the key, so a shared link is only as private as the channel you send it through. Treat it like a password, not a permalink.

4. Local-first is the other half of private

Encryption is only half the design. The other half is where notes live by default: in the browser, in IndexedDB, on your device. Notes are stored locally first and synced only when you choose to. That means the ordinary case — writing, reading, searching your own notes — involves no server at all.

Local-first also changes the failure modes. There is no account to breach for notes that were never uploaded, and no outage that locks you out of your own writing. The cost is the same as the vault's: the device is now part of the trust boundary. Clear browser data and local-only notes go with it, so export matters — JSON or plain text, on your terms.

5. What this design does not protect you from

Honest limits, because a privacy claim that hides them is worse than no claim:

  • It does not protect you from your own device. Malware, a compromised browser, or someone looking over your shoulder bypasses encryption entirely.
  • It does not protect you from a weak password. PBKDF2 slows guessing; it cannot save "password123".
  • It does not make shared links private. The key is in the link, so the link is the secret.
  • It does not hide metadata. The server can still see that you use the service, when, and how much data you store — just not what it says.

A notepad that is honest about those limits is more trustworthy than one that claims "military-grade encryption" and stops there.

The test that matters

Ask any notes app three questions: who holds the key, where does decryption happen, and what happens if I forget my password? If the answers are "we do", "on our servers", and "we can reset it for you", your notes are encrypted against everyone except the company itself. If the answers are "only you", "in your browser", and "nothing — there is no recovery", the privacy claim is real, and the inconvenience is the price.

The notepad I built from these lessons is Outsmart Notes — https://outsmartnotes.com — and those three questions are the ones I would ask of any tool before trusting it with a private note.

title: Serving CJK Web Fonts Without Killing Performance: A Practical Guide
description:
If you have ever tried to use a real Chinese, Japanese, or Korean typeface on the web, you already know the problem: a single CJK font file can be 5–15 MB. A Latin font might be 30–80 KB. Ship the CJK file the naive way and your page weight explodes, your Largest Contentful Paint tanks, and visitors on mobile leave before the text even renders.

The good news is that CJK fonts are very solvable — you just cannot treat them like Latin fonts. Here is the approach that works in production.

Why CJK fonts are so large

A Latin font needs a few hundred glyphs. A usable Simplified Chinese font needs 7,000+ common characters, and a full-coverage one can contain 20,000–30,000 glyphs. File size scales with glyph count, so no amount of compression alone will make a full CJK font small. WOFF2 helps (typically 30–40% smaller than TTF), but a 10 MB TTF still becomes a 6–7 MB WOFF2. You have to reduce which glyphs each visitor downloads, not just compress the file.

1. Split by unicode-range

The single most effective technique is font slicing: split one large font into 50–100 small subset files, each covering a contiguous unicode-range, and declare them all under one font-family in CSS.

@font-face {
  font-family: 'My CJK';
  src: url('/fonts/cjk-010.woff2') format('woff2');
  unicode-range: U+4E00-4FFF;
  font-display: swap;
}
@font-face {
  font-family: 'My CJK';
  src: url('/fonts/cjk-011.woff2') format('woff2');
  unicode-range: U+5000-5FFF;
  font-display: swap;
}

The browser is smart here: it only downloads the slices that contain characters actually used on the current page. A typical article page might trigger 8–15 slices at 30–60 KB each instead of one 6 MB file. Tools like cn-font-split and Google Fonts' own text-subsetting pipeline automate the slicing.

2. Always pair with a strong system fallback stack

Never let CJK text block on a web font. Use font-display: swap and a fallback stack that looks decent on every platform:

body {
  font-family: 'My CJK', 'PingFang SC', 'Hiragino Sans GB',
    'Microsoft YaHei', 'Noto Sans SC', sans-serif;
}

On most Chinese users' devices, PingFang (Apple) or Microsoft YaHei (Windows) will render instantly while the web font slices load in. If the web font never arrives, the page is still perfectly readable — this is progressive enhancement, not failure.

3. Subset for your actual content when you can

If large parts of your site are static — a landing page headline, a logo lockup, navigation labels — generate a tiny custom subset containing only those characters. A 200-character headline subset is often under 10 KB and can even be inlined as a data URI or preloaded. Reserve the full sliced font for user-generated or long-form content where you cannot predict the characters.

4. Preload sparingly, cache aggressively

Do not preload a whole CJK font. At most, preload the one or two slices covering your headline characters. For the rest, rely on long-lived caching: font files never change under a given URL, so serve them with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable and version the filename when you update the typeface. Repeat visits then cost almost zero font bytes.

5. Check the licence before you split or self-host

Not every free-to-download font is free to subset, modify, or self-host. Open licences like SIL Open Font License 1.1 generally allow subsetting and web embedding, but some freeware licences restrict redistribution of modified files — and a sliced font is a redistributed modified file. Before you ship, read the licence for modification and embedding clauses. If you are browsing downloadable Chinese fonts on a library like FontHubs, check each family's licence field first, and prefer OFL-licensed families for sliced self-hosting.

A quick checklist

  • Convert to WOFF2, then slice by unicode-range — compression alone is not enough
  • Use font-display: swap plus a native CJK fallback stack
  • Subset static headlines down to the exact characters used
  • Preload at most 1–2 slices; cache font files immutably for a year
  • Verify the licence allows subsetting and self-hosting

Done this way, a site can offer a distinctive CJK typeface at a real cost of a few hundred kilobytes per page — comparable to a hero image — instead of a multi-megabyte penalty. The typeface stops being a performance excuse and becomes a design choice you can actually afford.

title: Three Tauri bugs I found by not trusting a green build
description:
TL;DR 🧵 Last week I wrote about one Tauri bug. Someone in the comments told me to check the updater manifest, not just the files it points at. That one nudge turned one bug into three, and my pipeline into something I actually trust. Short version: a green build tells you the toolchain didn't crash. That's it. That's the whole lesson.

I maintain StackerPulse, a small Rust + Tauri v2 desktop app for Stacker News. If you build for macOS universal, bug 1 will find you eventually.

🍎 Bug 1: every binary but the main one gets left behind

My app crate has two binaries: the app, and a little secret scanner I ship as a CLI.

[[bin]]
name = "stacker-pulse"
path = "src/main.rs"

[[bin]]
name = "seedscan-cli"
path = "src/seedscan_cli.rs"
required-features = ["cli"]

Windows: fine. Linux: fine. macOS universal: the build dies at the bundling step.

Built application at: .../target/universal-apple-darwin/release/stacker-pulse
failed to bundle project: Failed to copy binary from
".../target/universal-apple-darwin/release/seedscan-cli": does not exist

Here's my favourite part. Both halves are doing exactly what they should.

Where What it does Correct?
desktop.rs, universal branch one lipo -create, main binary only ✅ yes, in isolation
get_binaries() returns every [[bin]] with required-features on ✅ yes
the bundler copies every binary from that list ✅ yes

Three correct behaviours, one broken build. The second binary is compiled for both architectures, never merged into the universal output directory, and then politely requested by name.

💡 Bug density tip: if Windows and Linux are green, this class of bug can hide in your repo for a long time. I only found it because I ship on three platforms from one workflow.

🎭 Bug 2: the CI that claps with no hands

So I fixed the workflow. Ran it again. Green. 🟢

The draft release had CLI archives, checksums, provenance attestations... and not a single installer. Not one. Zero.

tauri-action skips the upload when the release id it got is empty, and exits 0 while doing it. No warning, no red step, no "hey, I uploaded nothing". Just a green check and an empty release.

with:
  tagName: ${{ github.ref_name }}
  releaseName: "StackerPulse ${{ github.ref_name }}"

Two lines. Not a Tauri bug in the strict sense, more of a missing alarm on a door that opens silently.

🕵️ Bug 3: ten platforms in, two MSIs out

This is the one I'm actually proud of, and it exists because someone in the comments told me to check the manifest. So I did. I compared latest.json against the files that were really attached.

"platforms": {
  "windows-x86_64":      { "url": "..._x64_en-US.msi" },
  "windows-x86_64-msi":  { "url": "..._x64_ru-RU.msi" },
  "windows-x86_64-nsis": { "url": "..._x64-setup.exe" }
}

Notice the problem? I build two MSIs, one per language:

"windows": {
  "wix": { "language": ["en-US", "ru-RU"] },
  "nsis": { "languages": ["English", "Russian"] }
}

Two MSIs walk in. The manifest has one key per architecture. One MSI walks out. The Russian build overwrote the English one, and windows-x86_64 still points at English, so now two keys for the same architecture disagree about which language they serve.

Every installer is present. Every one is signed. Every asset check passes. And a Russian user on an MSI install gets an English app after the update, and probably never mentions it.

Nothing is broken and the result is still wrong. That's the failure mode that actually kills you.

🧟 What the three have in common

Each component does something reasonable alone. lipo merges a binary. The action uploads assets. The bundler writes one entry per artifact type.

The bug lives in the handover. In what one side assumes the other produced.

Which means "did the build succeed" is not a useful question. It's an answer to a question nobody asked.

🔍 Seven lines that replaced my optimism

None of these checks looks at build status.

# 1. the installers exist
gh release view "$TAG" --json assets -q '.assets[].name' | sort > actual.txt
diff -u expected.txt actual.txt

# 2. the manifest points at them
for p in windows-x86_64 linux-x86_64 darwin-aarch64 darwin-x86_64; do
  jq -e --arg p "$p" '.platforms[$p].url and .platforms[$p].signature' latest.json
done

# 3. and the manifest version matches the tag
jq -r '.version' latest.json | grep -qx "${TAG#v}"

The real version in the repo also checks that every download link is pinned to the tag. Draft releases hand out untagged-... URLs that die the instant you publish.

🛠 The fix, and two ways I almost made it worse

A patch for bug 1 appeared before I wrote mine. Reviewing it turned up something neither of us thought about:

// desktop.rs
let mut features = config_features;
features.extend(options.features);

Cargo gets both feature lists. get_binaries() filters on one. Enable a binary through build.features in tauri.conf.json and the merged set is smaller than what the bundler will ask for. Their patch fixes my repro and misses the next one. Classic.

And my own near-miss: my first plan was to rename the main binary inside the lipo loop, to honour main_binary_name. Then I read rename_app() and discovered it already renames it after lipo. My version would have made fs::rename hunt for a file that no longer existed. Ten minutes of reading the function I was about to duplicate. One broken release avoided.

tauri#16488 merges every binary from get_binaries(), config features merged in first, so both sides finally see the same list.

📊 How I verified it

I don't own a Mac. So the check runs in CI, on a real runner, against two refs of tauri-cli:

tauri-cli result
refs/heads/dev build fails, exit 1 🔴
refs/pull/16488/head build succeeds, seedscan-cli inside Contents/MacOS/ 🟢

A build that "passes" proves nothing. A build that fails without the patch and passes with it proves the patch does what it claims. Everything else is a wish.

🎁 What I'd pass on

A green build tells you the toolchain didn't crash. It says nothing about whether the artifact is correct, complete, or the thing you meant to ship.

The cheap version of catching that is seven lines of jq and gh release view. The expensive version is finding out from a user whose update quietly installed the wrong language, three months later, assuming they bother to tell you at all.

StackerPulse is a small Rust and Tauri app for Stacker News, MIT licensed. If you ship Tauri and build macOS universal, go count your binaries.

title: Testing Strategies: Unit, Integration, Mocking, and Test-Driven Development
description:
Software testing isn’t just about finding bugs—it’s about building confidence. A well-thought-out testing strategy helps ensure that applications work as expected, are maintainable, and can grow without breaking. Four important approaches to achieving this are unit testing, integration testing, mocking, and test-driven development (TDD). Let’s look at each one in detail and see how they work together.

1. Unit Testing: Building Blocks of Trust

What it is:

Unit testing means testing the smallest isolated piece of code—often a function, class, or module—to ensure it behaves correctly.

Benefits:
  • Catches bugs early in the development cycle
  • Makes refactoring safer
  • Encourages modular design
Example scenario:

If you write a function to calculate discounts, a unit test checks if it returns the correct discounted price given various inputs (e.g., regular customer vs. premium customer).

Unit tests are fast, simple, and should be run frequently during development.

2. Integration Testing: Ensuring the Pieces Fit

What it is:

Integration testing verifies how different modules or services interact with one another. Unlike unit tests, which focus on isolation, integration tests look at how the parts of a system behave as a group.

Benefits:
  • Validates communication between modules/components
  • Detects interface mismatches early
  • Ensures that combined behaviors match expectations
Example scenario:
  • After writing unit tests for both “payment service” and “order service,” an integration test checks whether a new order correctly triggers a payment transaction.
  • Integration tests are slower than unit tests but crucial for catching real-world issues.

3. Mocking: Controlling the Test Environment

What it is:

Mocking is about creating simulated versions of dependencies, such as databases, APIs, or external integrations, so that tests can run in controlled conditions.

Benefits:
  • Avoids reliance on external systems during tests (fewer failures due to network downtime)
  • Enables deterministic and fast feedback
  • Helps test edge cases that are difficult to reproduce with real systems
Example scenario:
  • When testing a service that fetches data from a weather API, you might mock the API call to return predictable responses instead of making live requests.
  • Mocking helps create confidence that code handles external dependencies correctly—even before those external services are available.

4. Test-Driven Development (TDD): Testing as Design

What it is:

TDD is a development practice where you write tests before writing the actual code. The typical cycle is:

  • Write a failing test (Red)
  • Write the minimum code to make it pass (Green)
  • Refactor the code while keeping the test passing (Refactor)
Benefits:
  • Encourages writing only the necessary code
  • Improves design by focusing on interfaces and responsibilities
  • Provides immediate feedback and a safety net for changes

Example scenario:

  • Before implementing a login function, you’d write a test: “Given the right username and password, user authentication should succeed.” You then implement just enough logic to make the test pass, refining further as more test cases are added.
  • TDD isn’t just about testing—it’s about shaping how the software is designed.

Final Thoughts

A solid software project typically uses all four approaches:

  • Unit tests keep functions and classes reliable.
  • Integration tests verify that modules cooperate correctly.
  • Mocks ensure external dependencies don’t block progress.
  • TDD provides discipline to write only the necessary, well-tested code.

By combining these techniques, development teams gain speed, resilience, and confidence. Automated tests become not just a safety net but a map of how the system is intended to behave.

Stay tuned for more insights as you continue your journey into the world of web development!

title: Java Collections and Generics
description:
1. Introduction

Java Collections and Generics are essential concepts for managing data efficiently.

Collections provide data structures to store, organize, and manipulate groups of objects.

Generics allow developers to write type-safe and reusable code by specifying the data type.

In Java + GenAI applications, they help manage prompts, AI responses, documents, and retrieved results.

2. What Is It?

Java Collections: A framework of interfaces and classes used to store and manipulate groups of objects, such as lists, sets, and maps.

Java Generics: A feature that allows classes, interfaces, and methods to work with specified data types while providing compile-time type safety.

3. Syntax / Example 

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class AICollectionExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> prompts = new ArrayList<>();

        prompts.add("Explain GenAI");
        prompts.add("Explain Machine Learning");

        for (String prompt : prompts) {
            System.out.println(prompt);
        }
    }
}

Output:

Explain GenAI
Explain Machine Learning

Here, List<String> uses generics to store only strings, while ArrayList provides the list implementation.

4. Practical Example

AI Chatbot Application

A Java chatbot can use a List<String> to store conversation messages and a Map<String, String> to associate prompt IDs with AI responses.

Collections make it easier to manage conversation history and retrieve information when needed.

5. Workflow and Hierarchy

Workflow

Receive Data → Store in Collections → Process Data → Retrieve Results → Send to AI Model

Collections Framework Hierarchy

Iterable
└── Collection
├── List → ArrayList, LinkedList
├── Set → HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet
└── Queue → PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque

Map (separate from Collection)
├── HashMap
├── LinkedHashMap
└── TreeMap

Generics Syntax

List<String> messages = new ArrayList<>();
Map<String, String> responses = new HashMap<>();

6. Key Takeaways

  1. Collections help manage groups of objects dynamically.
  2. Generics provide compile-time type safety.
  3. List maintains element order and allows duplicates.
  4. Set stores unique elements, while Map stores key-value pairs.
  5. Collections and generics improve code reusability and maintainability.

7. Conclusion

Java Collections and Generics simplify data management in modern applications. They help developers write reusable, type-safe, and maintainable code. In GenAI applications, they are useful for handling prompts, conversation history, and AI-generated responses.

Question: Which Java collection would you use to store an AI chatbot's conversation history?

title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection
description:
arXiv:2611.09014v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

title: Quand le jumeau numérique rencontre la réalité moléculaire : mon plongeon VR dans NexoPeek
description:
Quand le jumeau numérique rencontre la réalité moléculaire : mon plongeon VR dans NexoPeek

J’ai toujours détesté les slides PowerPoint qui vendent « la simulation temps réel » sans montrer le code. Le soir où j’ai ouvert le casque, la pièce sentait le café froid et le plastique neuf. Le projet : valider un circuit de signalisation MAP‑kinase avant la prochaine revue de design.

L’architecture de NexoPeek sépare le moteur de physique (C++ / CUDA) du front‑end WebXR (Three.js + React). Le pipeline de données passe par un bus gRPC qui stream les coordonnées atomiques à 90 fps. J’ai dû sharder le graphe de 1,2 M d’atomes en tiles de 64 k pour tenir dans la VRAM de ma RTX 3080 — un trade‑off classique entre granularité et latence.

// tile loader pseudo‑code
auto tile = loadTile(atoms, center, radius);
gpuUpload(tile.vertices, tile.indices);

Premier run : le taux de rafraîchissement chutait à 45 fps dès que j’activais les liaisons hydrogène. J’ai profité du profiler intégré (Chrome DevTools → Performance) pour repérer le goulot : le shader de calcul des forces recomposait les buffers à chaque frame. Passage à un compute‑shader persistant + double‑buffering a remonté le FPS à 88, stable même en mouvement libre.

Ce soir‑là, j’ai « touché » une phosphorylation en temps réel, vu le conformational change se propager comme une vague. Le sentiment n’était pas technique, c’était de la curiosité devenue tangible.

Si vous voulez transformer vos modèles statiques en expériences immersives, essayez le sandbox — vous y trouverez votre propre « aha » moment.

title: KLEAR: Knowledge-Matched LLM Evaluation in Korean across Application Requirements via Controlled Benchmark Transformation
description:
arXiv:2611.09223v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing Korean benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) evaluate performance across diverse knowledge domains, but their accuracy scores cannot distinguish whether incorrect responses arise from a lack of required knowledge or a failure to apply that knowledge correctly. Our analysis of existing Korean benchmarks reveals that most questions can be answered through factual recall alone, while those demanding greater application also differ in required knowledge, making it difficult to isolate application ability. To address this, we introduce KLEAR, a framework that constructs knowledge-matched contrasts by varying application demand while preserving the required knowledge. During construction, KLEAR identifies the knowledge underlying each source question as an explicit anchor bundle to guide generation of questions requiring more complex application. Generated candidates then undergo automated and human validation, with iterative revision based on evaluation feedback. Experiments demonstrate that the resulting knowledge-matched sets largely satisfy the intended constraints, enabling controlled evaluation across diverse LLMs. These evaluations reveal that increasing application demand exposes failures that persist even when the required knowledge is provided.

title: Pull Agoda hotel reviews with scores and sub-scores into a spreadsheet, in Python
description:
If you manage a hotel, run a reputation-management tool or analyse a city's hotel market, Agoda is one of the review sources you can't skip in Asia. A single hotel page there mixes two review pools: reviews from Agoda's own guests and reviews from Booking.com guests that Agoda republishes. Each pool has its own score, its own review count and its own six sub-scores (cleanliness, facilities, location, room comfort, service, value for money).

Reading that by hand works for one property. For a competitive set of 20 hotels, checked every morning, it doesn't. This post pulls the reviews and scores into a CSV in Python and shows a daily "new reviews only" setup.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built Agoda API, an Agoda reviews scraper. It's a paid tool (prices below).

What each row holds

One row per review, from the hotel's public Agoda review page:

  • source (Agoda or Booking.com), rating out of 10, rating_text, title, text, and for Booking.com-style reviews positives and negatives.
  • language, plus original_title and original_text when Agoda shows an English translation, so you keep the guest's own words.
  • review_date (the date the page shows), stay_month, nights, room_type, traveller_type (couple, solo, family, group, business).
  • reviewer_name and reviewer_country as Agoda displays them, helpful_votes, photos.
  • owner_response, owner_response_date and responder_name when the hotel replied.
  • The hotel on every row: hotel_name, star_rating, address, city, country, agoda_score, agoda_review_count, agoda_sub_scores, agoda_score_distribution, booking_score, booking_review_count, booking_sub_scores.

Hotels can be given as Agoda links (any language version), Agoda hotel IDs, or a hotel name with its city.

A competitive set in one run 

pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import defaultdict

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/agoda-reviews-scraper").call(
    run_input={
        "hotels": [
            "https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html",
            "Mandarin Oriental Bangkok",
            "Shangri-La Bangkok",
        ],
        "maxReviewsPerHotel": 300,
        "reviewsNewerThan": "90 days",
    }
)
reviews = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

fields = ["hotel_name", "source", "rating", "title", "text", "negatives", "traveller_type",
          "reviewer_country", "review_date", "owner_response"]
with open("reviews.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields, extrasaction="ignore")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(reviews)

hotels = {}
by_type = defaultdict(list)
for r in reviews:
    hotels[r["hotel_name"]] = r
    by_type[(r["hotel_name"], r["traveller_type"])].append(r["rating"])

for name, h in hotels.items():
    subs = h["agoda_sub_scores"] or {}
    print(f"{name}: Agoda {h['agoda_score']} ({h['agoda_review_count']} ratings), "
          f"Booking.com {h['booking_score']}; cleanliness {subs.get('Cleanliness')}, "
          f"value {subs.get('Value for money')}")
for (name, kind), ratings in sorted(by_type.items()):
    if kind and len(ratings) >= 5:
        print(f"  {name} / {kind}: {sum(ratings) / len(ratings):.1f} over {len(ratings)} reviews")

The hotel name in the second line is matched through Agoda's own search box; the run's status message says which property each name matched, so check it once and switch to the link if it picked the wrong one.

Ideas for the same data:

  • Complaint mining: "maxRating": 6, "sortBy": "lowest" gives the unhappy reviews first; feed negatives and text to an LLM and ask for recurring themes per hotel.
  • Reply rate: count rows with owner_response per hotel. It's a quick read on how actively each competitor manages its reviews.
  • Who stays where: group by traveller_type and reviewer_country to see which segments each hotel attracts and how each segment rates it.

New reviews every morning 

run_input = {
    "hotels": ["https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html", "..."],
    "maxReviewsPerHotel": 500,
    "onlyNewReviews": True,
    "trackingName": "my-compset-daily",
    "slackWebhookUrl": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/...",
}

With onlyNewReviews on, the first run returns the newest reviews up to your limit, and later runs with the same trackingName return only reviews newer than the ones you already have: reading newest first, each review source stops at the first review you already received. A daily run over 20 hotels takes seconds and bills $0.0003 per hotel plus the new reviews. Save the input as a task in the Apify Console, schedule it daily, and the Slack URL gets the count and the top 10.

Why this tool

  • $0.50 per 1,000 reviews ($0.40 on paid plans), cheaper than the leading tools.
  • Any number of hotels in one run, including by hotel name.
  • The original text next to the translation.
  • An only-new-reviews mode.
  • What it doesn't cover: room prices and availability.

Limits worth knowing

  • Rows exist only for written reviews. The review counts next to the scores include rating-only reviews, so they are higher than the number of rows.
  • Agoda's review service answers part of its requests with an empty page; the tool asks again before it decides a hotel has no more reviews, so long hotels take a little longer.
  • "Highest" and "lowest rated first" follow Agoda's own order page by page; sort the CSV if you need a strict order across both review sources.

The tool reads only what a logged-out visitor sees on Agoda's public review pages, never logs in, and returns reviewer names and countries exactly as Agoda shows them. Agoda's terms discourage automated access, so keep your use to analysing public reviews.
