title: Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection for Reasoning Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.09042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training smaller language models on reasoning solutions generated by a larger teacher model is the prevailing approach for transferring mathematical reasoning capabilities. However, the student tends to overfit the output distribution of the teacher and generalizes poorly when its own behavior at inference time deviates from the training data. Recent methods attempt to bridge this gap by incorporating error data, yet the corrective trajectories still reflect the reasoning patterns of the teacher, which the student cannot reliably reproduce, leaving the distribution mismatch largely unresolved. We propose a method, Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (FPRT), built on the insight that effective training data should be jointly determined by what the student fails on and what it can realistically learn. Our method first profiles the failure behavior of the student on each problem through repeated sampling, characterizing it in terms of error rate and error consistency to reveal qualitatively distinct failure modes. Each mode demands a fundamentally different training signal. The diagnosed mode then guides candidate generation from the teacher via distinct prompting strategies tailored to each failure type. Among the correct candidates, our method selects the one whose initial reasoning steps after the point of divergence are most reproducible by the student. These first corrective steps constitute the primary bottleneck, while the remaining steps follow an already corrected context and can therefore be continued more readily. This contrasts with standard reranking approaches, which score the trajectory as a whole and thereby dilute the signal at the critical reasoning transition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves the SOTA performance across the five benchmarks on both student backbones.

title: Website UX Audit on WordPress: From Heatmaps to a Client-Ready Report
description:
We build Opti-Behavior, the WordPress plugin discussed here. Originally published on optiuser.com.

A website UX audit is a structured check of how real visitors use a site: where they click, where they stop, which steps they abandon, and what to fix first. On WordPress you can run one with behavior data you already own, then hand the result to a client or your own team as a short PDF report that lists the problems found and what to do about each one. This guide shows the method step by step, with or without our plugin.

What a website UX audit should answer

An audit that ends with “the site could be better” is not useful. A good website UX audit answers four questions, in this order:

  • What happened? Traffic, sources, devices and the pages people really visit over a fixed period.

  • Where do visitors get stuck? Buttons nobody clicks, pages people leave fast, funnel steps where most of them quit.

  • What does it cost? How many visits each problem touches, so the list can be ranked.

  • What should we do now? One concrete action per problem, with the page where it happens.

Opinions about colours and fonts come last. Measured behavior comes first, because it tells you which problems are worth your client’s budget.

Step 1: Collect behavior data before you judge anything

Give the audit at least two to four weeks of real visits. Fewer visits means noisy figures: a page with 12 visits does not prove anything. Before you start, make sure that:

  • your own visits and your team’s are excluded (admin tracking off, office IP blocked);

  • bots and spam visits are filtered out of the figures;

  • a page cache does not block the tracking script (see heatmap not working after installing a cache plugin);

  • the key paths exist as funnels: product page → cart → checkout, or landing page → form → thank-you page.

In Opti-Behavior, each module collects one kind of data: Traffic, click heatmaps and funnels in the free plugin; session recordings, user journeys, error tracking and form analytics in Pro. Smart Insights then reads what the modules collected and turns it into a list of open problems.

Smart Insights with Opti-Behavior Pro active: the modules that collect (left), then the problems found. Free shows Analytics, Heatmaps and Funnels.

Step 2: Find the problems and rank them by cost

Go through the data with a fixed checklist, so every audit covers the same ground:

  • Pages that lose visitors: high bounce or exit on pages that should lead somewhere (pricing, product, contact).

  • Clicks that go nowhere: the click heatmap shows people clicking an image, a heading or a menu label that is not a link. See why a landing page is not converting for the usual causes.

  • Funnel drop-off: the step where most visitors quit, and on which device.

  • Content nobody reaches: the offer or the call to action sits below the point where most visitors stop scrolling.

  • Shop problems on WooCommerce: products viewed a lot but rarely added to cart (see add to cart rate).

Then rank. A broken button on a page with 2,000 visits a month matters more than an ugly footer on a page with 40. Smart Insights does this ranking for you: each open problem comes with the number of visits it touches, the page where it happens and a recommended action.

Step 3: Turn the findings into a UX audit report

Your client will not log in to WordPress to read heatmaps. They need a document. A useful UX audit report is short and always has the same structure:

  • Summary: the period, key traffic figures compared with the period before, and the three most costly problems.

  • One section per area: traffic and sources, most clicked elements, funnels, busiest times, shop, A/B tests.

  • Each problem as a card: what was found, where, and what to do.

  • Appendix: the detail of the most important pages.

Since version 1.10.1, Opti-Behavior builds this report from the same data, in Opti-Behavior › Reports:

  • Choose the period (last 7, 30 or 90 days, or two dates). The report compares it with the period before.

  • Or click Site report in the header of the Traffic or Smart Insights screen: the report opens with the period you were looking at.

  • The report opens in a new tab. Use your browser’s Print › Save as PDF to get the file to send.

  • It starts with a Summary (traffic tiles and the three most costly issues, each with Where and What to do), then one section for each part of the site that has data. A section with no data is left out.

Free: the short site report opens with a Summary, then the most costly issues, each with Where and What to do. Test site data, 22 Sep – 21 Oct 2026.

Free and Pro versions of the report

  • Free: the short site report described above.

  • Pro: the full site report, with a card for each of your most visited pages and per-page appendices (up to 10 pages), plus a report for one single page.

  • Pro, for agencies: the client’s name on the report (“Prepared for”) and sections you choose to hide from the client.

Pro: the Page X-Ray report of one page lists what to fix, most costly first, with why it matters, what to do and a button to the data behind it. Demo store data.

An optional “Made with Opti-Behavior” line can be added at the end of a report. It is off by default.

Step 4: Agree on the fixes, then check the result

The report is the start of the work, not the end. With your client:

  • Pick the two or three problems at the top of the list. Ignore the rest for now.

  • Write the fix next to each one: change the button text, make the image a link, shorten the form, move the offer above the fold.

  • Note the date of each change.

  • Run the same report again over the same length of period after the change, and compare the figures for the pages you touched.

  • When a fix is a matter of taste (two headlines, two layouts), test it with an A/B test instead of arguing about it.

Doing the audit again every month with the same report structure gives your client a clear before-and-after, and gives you a reason to talk about the next fixes.

A real audit: optiuser.com, October 2026

Here is the same method applied to our own site. Source: Opti-Behavior Smart Insights on optiuser.com, read on 31 October 2026, period 2 to 31 October 2026, spam traffic excluded. optiuser.com is a small site, so the numbers are small, and each finding says how much it can prove.

Finding 1: phone visitors click our buttons much less

In the button comparison (61 visits), visitors on mobile clicked a button in 49.2% of their visits, against 70.2% on desktop. The gap shows in conversion too: 4.9% for visits from phones, 9.6% for all visitors.

  • Where: site pages, on mobile.

  • Why it matters: a visitor who never clicks the main button never reaches the next step, whatever the quality of the page.

  • What to do: make the main button visible without scrolling on a phone.

  • Check: the mobile button click rate and the mobile conversion, 30 days after the change, over a period of the same length.

Finding 2: visitors stop at the URL field of our free heatmap tool

On our free heatmap generator, the field "Your page address" counted 30 visits and 26 field interactions over the period. The plugin’s own verdict on this row is a weak signal: look at recordings first.

  • Where: /heatmap-generator/, field "Your page address".

  • Why it matters: the tool only helps once a visitor has typed an address. A stop at this field is a stop before any result.

  • What to do: watch the recordings (Pro) of the visits that stop at the field before changing anything; then make typing optional with an example page.

  • Check: stops at the URL field and visits reaching a heatmap, 30 days after the change.

What this audit teaches

  • Split by device first. Our biggest gap was not a page but a device. Looking at all visitors together would have hidden it.

  • Write how strong the signal is. On the form row the plugin says the signal is weak. Writing that down stops a team from redesigning a page on a hunch: the next step is to look, not to change.

  • Two findings are enough. On a small site, two problems with a clear check are more useful than ten charts nobody acts on.

  • No result before the change. The "Check" line is written, the result is not. We will compare the same figures 30 days after each change. An audit that shows an "after" before the fix exists is inventing it.

The same two findings, as rows with an owner, a date and a check, are in our analytics report template. Copy it to write your own UX audit report.

FAQ

How long does a website UX audit take?

The data collection takes two to four weeks of normal traffic. Reading the data and writing the report takes a few hours by hand; with a generated report most of that time goes into choosing the fixes with the client.

Do I need session recordings for a UX audit?

No. Traffic, click heatmaps and funnels already show where visitors get stuck. Recordings (Pro) help you understand why, by watching a few of the visits behind a problem.

Is the PDF white-label?

No. The Pro agency options add your client’s name and hide the sections you choose, but the report still carries the Opti-Behavior footer.

Can I send the report every week automatically?

The site report is printed when you need it. The plugin also has scheduled e-mail reports, which send the key figures and the three most costly issues by e-mail.

What should a UX audit report include?

A summary with the period and the key figures, then one block per problem: where it happens, how many visits it touches, why it matters, what to do and the figure you will check after the fix. Three to five problems, the costliest first.

Try it on your own site

Install the free plugin, wait for a few weeks of visits, then open Opti-Behavior › Reports and print your first site report. The full report with per-page appendices, the Page X-Ray report and the agency options are in Pro.

Run a UX audit on your own WordPress site

title: Vom Nanomotor zum VR-Labor: Wie ein 2000 Jahre altes Prinzip meine Strukturbiologie-Arbeit veränderte
description:
Vom Nanomotor zum VR-Labor: Wie ein 2000 Jahre altes Prinzip meine Strukturbiologie-Arbeit veränderte

Als ich vor drei Jahren meine erste Cryo-EM-Session startete, fühlte sich der Datenfluss an wie ein undichter Schlauch: Terabytes roher Bilder, keine automatische Vorverarbeitung, und jede Rekonstruktion dauerte Tage. Ich erinnerte mich an das Archimedische Schraubenprinzip – ein 2000 Jahre altes Konzept, das Flüssigkeiten stetig und ohne Turbulenzen transportiert. Warum nicht die gleiche Idee auf den Datentransfer zwischen Detektor, GPU-Cluster und Speicher anwenden?

Ich baute eine leichte Pipeline in Rust, die Frame-Streams in fixen Chunk-Größen (256 MiB) pufferte, Backpressure über ein Ringbuffer regelte und mittels Zero-Copy‑MMAP direkt in den GPU‑Speicher schob. Benchmarks auf einem 8‑GPU‑Node zeigten: Durchsatz stieg von 1,2 GB/s auf 4,8 GB/s, Latenz fiel von 420 ms auf 78 ms pro Batch. Der Code blieb unter 1 kLOC, keine externen Message‑Queues nötig.

Der Durchbruch kam, als ich die Pipeline in ein Unity‑basiertes VR‑Labor einband. Forscher können jetzt in Echtzeit durch die 3D‑Rekonstruktion navigieren, Schnittstellen anpassen und Ergebnisse sofort annotieren – alles ohne die alte Wartezeit. Meine Promotion konnte ich so zwei Monate früher abgeben.

Im Nachhinein war das Profiling mit perf und Tracy der Schlüssel: ich sah, wie der Ringbuffer fast nie voll lief, während die GPU‑Kernels kontinuierlich gefüttert wurden. Ein kleiner Tweak – die Chunk‑Größe auf 512 MiB zu verdoppeln – brachte nochmal 12 % Durchsatzgewinn, ohne den Speicherbedarf zu sprengen. Seitdem nutze ich dieselbe Architektur für alle Streaming‑Workloads, von Einzelpartikel‑Analyse bis hin zu zeitaufgelösten Experimenten. Der Code lebt jetzt in einem offenen Repository, CI prüft bei jedem Push Latenz‑Regressionen, und die Community hat bereits zwei Forks für ARM‑basierte Edge‑Geräte erstellt.

Wenn du neugierig bist, wie alte Mechanik moderne Compute‑Architektur inspiriert, probier den Ansatz in deinem nächsten Projekt aus.

title: Building Windows Server MCP: Giving AI Agents Full Native Control Over Windows
description:
If you work with Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Windows environments, you've likely hit walls with legacy wrappers, frozen execution threads, and encoding errors.Today, I’m excited to share a major evolution of the open-source project Windows Server MCP—fully refactored, optimized, and now available directly on PyPI.

Repository: https://github.com/AstraxOf/windows-server-mcp

🚀 Quick Install
You can install the package directly via pip: pip install windows-server-mcp

⚠️ Fair Warning: Advanced Users OnlyThis tool provides total access and unrestricted control over the computer or server where it runs. It can execute raw PowerShell scripts, modify the Windows Registry, manage advanced processes, handle deep software audits, and—yes—delete files and folders if instructed by the model. Because of its high-privilege nature, it is strictly intended for advanced users, homelab enthusiasts, developers, and sysadmins who understand the security implications.

What’s New in This Version?This project is a complete refactor and evolution of the original windows-mcp-server repository (which was built on the legacy, standalone fastmcp package).

We updated the codebase to support the official mcp SDK (MCPServer), while maintaining backwards compatibility and fixing critical infrastructure bottlenecks.

Migration to Official MCPServer: Updated from legacy fastmcp to the current official mcp SDK structure (MCPServer / FastMCP helper), supporting both legacy setups and the latest protocol standards.

PowerShell Timeout & Deadlock Fixes: Fixed severe blocking issues where PowerShell subprocessing hung indefinitely and locked up the parent Python process.

We completely rebuilt the stream execution wrappers to enforce strict UTF-8 encodings and handle timeouts cleanly.

Massive Toolset Expansion: Added robust, modular tools for network diagnostics, hardware/driver maintenance, disk health, service management, security updates, and safe file operations.

Developer Experience: Restructured into a modular Python package architecture with a full test suite and an included VS Code extension.

Get Involved

If you want an AI agent that can actually manage your Windows machine or server under your direct supervision without crashing or hanging your threads, check out the repository.

I would love to hear your thoughts, see your pull requests, or receive any security feedback!

title: Study exposes limits of majority-vote labels in test-time learning
description:
Researchers analyse majority-vote pseudo-labels in test-time reinforcement learning, where models adapt to unlabeled data using self-generated labels. They decompose error into population-majority bias and finite-rollout variation, and propose a prompt-conditional distributional method to mitigate the latter during online DPO.

Why it matters

Test-time adaptation is attractive for unlabeled domains, but unreliable self-supervision could reinforce errors instead of improving models.

Analysis

Self-improvement methods will need explicit uncertainty handling rather than trusting majority votes.

title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
description:
Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.

We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.

Persisting state with a drive

Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:

Or from the Sandbox SDK:

In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.

The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.

Sharing state across sandboxes

Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately.

Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive.

Forking is generally available.

Get started

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans.

Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA.

title: Decoding spatial and semantic information from large-scale visual cortical activity for natural-movie reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.08887v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.

title: Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
description:
arXiv:2611.08506v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: How much of a neural population's measured dimensionality is the code, and how much is the act of measuring it? The slope of the participation ratio against subsample size is reported for cortical populations and for the layers of language models as a number that belongs to the system. It does not. One patch of eleven thousand mouse V1 neurons returns three slopes, 0.25 along random stimulus subsets, 0.31 along drift direction, 0.35 along neuron count, and only the middle one carries structure; the other two are the sampling floor.
  We split every exponent into that floor and a shift earned along a declared axis, and read the shift against two nulls: permuting the labels, and permuting them only among samples that share a nuisance. On V1 the direction-aligned shift clears the label null in eight of eight grating recordings, is positive in 32 of 32 animals in a second laboratory, and reads both sectors of the code's O(2) symmetry. The even sector sets how the ladder starts: it decides which order of adding classes climbs faster, predicts the opposite order in an equivariant network, and flows under coarse-graining by a closed-form factor that says what orientation columns do to mesoscale signals. The odd sector, carried by the direction-selective neurons, keeps the ladder climbing past half the classes. On language models the same split separates content inherited from the tokens from construction built with depth, on five architectures, and the second null shows that a grammaticality signal of twenty standard deviations is entirely carrier composition. With a floor and a declared axis, dimensionality scaling is an axis-resolved measurement, and where the axis follows a known symmetry it resolves the sector content of the code. The instrument, rung, trains no probe and reads any array or any Hugging Face model layer by layer (https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom).

title: ETL and ELT Explained: Choosing the Right Data Integration Method
description:
ETL and ELT are two common approaches to preparing data for analytics and reporting. Both move information from source systems to a destination, but they differ in when transformations happen. Understanding that difference helps teams select an architecture that fits their data platform, workload, and governance requirements.

How ETL works

ETL stands for extract, transform, and load. Data is collected from source systems, transformed in a processing layer, and then loaded into the target. Transformations may include standardising dates, converting currencies, removing duplicates, joining records, and applying business rules.

This approach can be useful when data must be cleaned or shaped before it enters the destination. It may also support environments where the target has limited processing capacity or where only approved, prepared data should be loaded.

How ELT works

ELT stands for extract, load, and transform. Data is extracted and loaded into the destination first. Transformations are then performed using the processing capabilities of that destination, often a modern cloud data warehouse or lakehouse.

ELT can make it easier to retain raw source data and create multiple transformed views for different teams. It can also take advantage of scalable cloud compute. However, it requires strong controls over raw data access, storage costs, and transformation logic.

Compare the requirements, not just the labels
ETL may be suitable when transformation must happen before loading, when source data needs strict filtering, or when the destination is not designed for raw data processing. ELT may be attractive when the destination can process large datasets efficiently and analysts need flexibility to build new models.

Some organisations use both methods. A sensitive dataset might be filtered before loading, while less restricted analytical data follows an ELT pattern. The best design is often a combination based on the needs of each data domain.

Pay attention to quality and governance

Neither ETL nor ELT automatically guarantees accurate information. Teams still need validation rules, data contracts, documentation, lineage, and monitoring. Business definitions should be consistent, and transformations should be tested when source schemas or reporting requirements change.

A comparison of data integration solutions should include support for both patterns, connector reliability, transformation tools, orchestration, security, and the ability to recover failed jobs. Also consider whether the platform can handle batch and incremental workloads without unnecessary complexity.

Make the choice through a pilot

Choose one representative dataset and test the full journey. Measure processing time, cost, data freshness, error handling, and the effort required to change a transformation. Include the people who will operate the pipeline after launch.

ETL and ELT are not competing goals. They are methods for moving and preparing information. A good architecture chooses the method that delivers trustworthy data with an acceptable level of cost, complexity, and operational risk.

title: How We Cut Maven & JUnit 5 Test Runs by 61% Across Apache Repos Without Missing Regressions
description:
How We Cut Maven & JUnit 5 Test Runs by 61% Across Apache Repos Without Missing Regressions

Most "predictive test selection" write-ups for Java come from vendors, and most of them give you a percentage with no way to check it. This one comes with the commit hashes. We replayed 800 consecutive commits from four open-source Java projects and counted what a dependency-based test selector would have run, what it would have skipped, and whether any skipped test would have caught a real bug.

The tool is blastradius, an Apache-2.0 test impact analysis plugin for Maven (and Gradle) with JUnit 5. The headline: 61.4% fewer test executions across the four replays, with 0 would-miss cases after the exclusions described below. The rest of this post is about what those two numbers do and do not mean.

The idea: record what tests actually load

Test impact analysis (TIA) answers one question on a pull request: which tests could be affected by this diff? Static guesses (package names, module graphs) are cheap but loose. Blastradius records ground truth instead:

  1. Track. On a base-branch build, a java.lang.instrument agent watches every class loaded while each test runs, and records which production classes each test really touched.
  2. Diff. On a change branch, it diffs the commit against the Git merge base, so only the PR's own changes count, not whatever landed on main after it diverged.
  3. Select. A test runs if one of its recorded dependencies changed, if it is new or modified, if an executed class reaches a changed class through one or two recorded static invocation edges, or if a non-source change (build files, resources) triggers the conservative "run everything" fallback.
  4. Gate. The selection narrows Surefire/Failsafe through the standard -Dtest= filter, so it keeps working with JaCoCo and custom argLine setups.

Missing or unusable baseline data always means a full run.

The experiment

For each project, the validation harness replays 200 consecutive commits, treating each commit as the change it introduced over the one before it. For every pair it asks the selector what it would run, then compares against ground truth. A would-miss is a test that caught a real regression or an injected mutant but that selection chose not to run. That is the failure that matters.

On the same window, the harness also runs bounded mutation validation: it injects synthetic faults into the head commit and checks whether the selected tests catch them.

Results: test executions skipped

Project Commit range Pairs (excluded) Would-miss Selected / full Skipped
apache/shenyu 69cd1d5 → 3a411e0 200 (0) 0 153,142 / 527,508 71.0%
apache/httpcomponents-client ef34bfa → 4dae8da 200 (12) 0 180,198 / 443,593 59.4%
jhy/jsoup b62e362 → 9d2241f 200 (10) 0 193,635 / 351,882 45.0%
apache/commons-io d403237 → ffd9dda 200 (12) 0 439,393 / 1,178,122 62.7%
Total 800 (34) 0 966,368 / 2,501,105 61.4%

The 61.4% is the aggregate: 966,368 selected executions out of 2,501,105 in the full suites. Note what it is: a count of test executions in a replay, not measured CI wall-clock time. Slow tests and fast tests count the same, and your savings will depend on where your slow tests sit.

Results: injected faults

Project Mutants (compilable) Caught by the full suite Killing tests selected
shenyu 872 (778) 339 943 / 943
httpcomponents-client 916 (916) 551 75,380 / 75,380
jsoup 940 (931) 606 53,300 / 53,300 (see below)
commons-io 901 (901) 850 30,637 / 31,648 (see below)

A "killing test" is one that passed on head, failed on the mutant, and stayed failed on confirmation. Those are the tests selection must not skip. Counts are per mutant, so a test that kills five mutants counts five times.

What we excluded, and what did not come out clean

A benchmark is only worth reading if the awkward parts are on the page. Here they are.

  • Excluded commit pairs (34 of 800). Pairs the harness could not measure count neither for nor against selection. In httpcomponents-client, 11 of 12 hit the build timeout on a slow multi-module rebuild and 1 hit a Surefire report containing an XML-illegal character (since fixed). In jsoup, all 10 exceeded the 40-minute mutation-build timeout. In commons-io, 11 hit the mutation-validation timeout and 1 failed to build under the harness.
  • Flaky tests were excluded from the verdict. HttpClientPluginConfigurationTest (shenyu) and TestTlsHandshakeTimeout#testTimeout (httpcomponents-client, flaky under parallel build load) were removed. Excluding the second is what brings httpcomponents-client's would-miss to 0.
  • commons-io had an unresolved case. A first recorded run showed a would-miss on URIOriginTest#testGetInputStream, a test parameterized on a live network fixture. A plain mvn clean test at that commit passed (6,376 tests, 0 failures), but the pair then failed to build under the harness and could not be root-caused. It is excluded, so the consolidated would-miss is 0, but that is "not a confirmed miss," not "proven clean."
  • commons-io skipped 3.2% of killing executions. 1,011 of 31,648 killing test executions were skipped, spread over 42 commit pairs on the diff-targeted or whole-tree-fallback path rather than dependency-match selection. Every one of the 850 killed mutants still had at least one killing test selected, so the gap is partial under-selection, not a blind spot. This figure is provisional.
  • jsoup exposed a real gap, which we then fixed. The first 200-pair run skipped 5,808 killing executions: 5,682 from 12 QueryParser mutations and 126 from two Normalizer mutations. jsoup's CSS selector engine is a string DSL, which is exactly where class-load tracking is weakest: a selector string reaches code that the test never loads directly. Adding a bounded two-hop static-invocation rule fixed it: targeted replays of all 14 mutation identities selected all 16,642 killing executions. Those were targeted replays, not a fresh full 200-pair rerun.

The lesson from jsoup generalizes. Reflection, string-dispatched APIs, generated code, and call paths deeper than two edges sit outside the evidence. If your project is built around selector engines, expression languages or query parsers, weigh that before adopting.

So, "without missing regressions"?

Within this window and these exclusions, blastradius had 0 would-miss cases across 800 commit pairs on four projects, and it selected a killing test for every mutant the full suites caught. That is the claim, and it is a measured one rather than a guarantee. We recommend running the full suite on a regular cadence (daily is the recommendation) as a safety net, so an occasional gap is caught within a day rather than never. Fast, sound-by-default selection on every build, backstopped by a full run, is the intended trust model.

Try it on your project

Add the plugin from Maven Central:

<plugin>
  <groupId>io.github.baokhang83.blastradius</groupId>
  <artifactId>blastradius-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>0.4.0</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <phase>process-test-classes</phase>
      <goals><goal>select</goal></goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
  <configuration>
    <baseRef>main</baseRef>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

On your base branch it tracks; on other branches it selects. For separate CI runners, persist and restore the .blastradius/ directory with your CI cache.

If you would rather check the mechanism against your own history before changing CI, the validator harness is the same shadow-mode tool that produced the numbers above: it replays your repository's commits, reports what would have been skipped, and flags would-miss cases without touching your build.

  • Repository: github.com/baokhang83/blastradius
  • Full methodology and footnotes: HISTORICAL_REPLAY_ANALYSIS.md
  • Maven guide: docs/maven-junit5-test-impact-analysis.md
  • Maturity and trust model: MATURITY.md

FAQ

What is test impact analysis (predictive test selection) for Java?

It is a way to run only the tests a change could affect, instead of the whole suite, on every pull request. Blastradius does it by recording which production classes each test loads on the base branch, then selecting the tests whose recorded dependencies overlap the diff.

How is this different from running tests by module or package?

Module and package filters guess from project structure. Blastradius uses classes actually loaded at runtime during each test, so a test in one module that exercises code in another is still selected when that code changes.

Does it work with JaCoCo and custom argLine settings?

Yes. Selection works through the standard Surefire/Failsafe -Dtest= filter, so it does not replace your test runner or conflict with JaCoCo or a custom argLine.

What happens when it cannot decide safely?

It runs everything. A missing or unusable baseline, or a non-source change such as a build file or resource, triggers the full-suite fallback. New and modified tests are always selected.

Do I still need to run the full suite?

Yes. Selection is sound by default, not guaranteed. We recommend a full-suite run on a regular cadence (daily) as a backstop, so any gap is caught within a day.

Does 61.4% fewer test executions mean 61.4% faster CI?

No. The figure counts test executions in a replay, not wall-clock time. Your speedup depends on where your slow tests fall, plus fixed costs such as compilation and startup. The tracking build on your base branch also runs the full suite once.

Where does it struggle?

Code reached only through string-dispatched APIs, reflection or generated code, or through call paths deeper than two recorded edges, sits outside the evidence. jsoup's selector engine exposed exactly this in the replay. Projects built around query parsers, expression languages or selector DSLs should weigh it.

Does it support Gradle and Kotlin?

Kotlin in the conventional src/main/kotlin and src/test/kotlin layout is supported, with a full-suite fallback for Kotlin inline functions. The Gradle plugin is in the repository, but at the time of writing it is not yet published to the Gradle Plugin Portal. The Maven plugin is on Maven Central.

Can I run it on separate CI runners?

Yes. Persist and restore the .blastradius/ directory with your CI cache. An S3-compatible shared index store is available as an option if that suits your runners better.

Can I check it against my own repository before adopting it?

Yes. The validator harness replays your own commit history in shadow mode, reports what would have been skipped, and flags would-miss cases without changing your build.

title: Shipment Updates: A Go Queue Solution for Retrying Failed Email Delivery Attempts
description:
The best place to retry a failed email delivery is a queue worker, not the daily report scheduler. Put one bounded delivery job per subscriber behind the schedule, retry transient failures with delay, and send exhausted jobs to a dead letter queue (DLQ). That keeps a slow provider from holding the report trigger open, while the worker owns the delivery latency and the application owns duplicate protection.

This is the boundary I would use for a property-management system that fans out a shipment update to many subscribers. It does add another state transition. The payoff is isolation: a provider outage becomes queued work with a visible stopping point instead of an open-ended loop inside the report job. The queue is a retry buffer, not a delivery ledger.

For this handoff, Infrai is a practical fit when the team wants queue publishing, consumption, and DLQ handling behind one REST surface. Its public discovery surface supplies schemas and runnable examples, so the worker can validate the contract before the integration grows.

Retries need a home.

Keep it boring.

What should the queue own?

The data flow should be small and explicit. A daily cron trigger enqueues a delivery record; a worker consumes it, calls the email provider, and acknowledges only after the provider result or a durable idempotent delivery record has been handled. A transient timeout or 5xx gets a delayed retry. A permanent address rejection goes to an application failure path. A message that exceeds its retry policy remains available for inspection and redrive in the DLQ.

Keep the report itself outside the message. Send a report reference, subscriber identifier, immutable shipment version, and a stable delivery key. The queue message body is limited to 256 KB, delayed delivery is limited to 7 days, and retention is at most 30 days; those are useful bounds for recovery, not a replacement for durable report storage.

The scheduler should trigger enqueueing rather than perform every email call. A cron execution has a 900-second limit. For a report or fan-out that can outlive that limit, the safe shape is cron trigger plus queue worker. This also separates three clocks: when the report is due, when a retry may run, and when a shipment update becomes too old to send.

The invariant is less glamorous than the queue choice: every attempt must be safe to repeat. Standard queues are at-least-once, and FIFO deduplication covers only a 5-minute window. Neither is a business-level duplicate guarantee. Derive an idempotency key from report_id/subscriber_id, persist the delivery state, and make the provider handoff or outbox transition idempotent before acknowledging the queue message. That means a worker can die after the provider accepts an email and before acknowledgement without turning the recovery path into a second shipment notice, provided the durable delivery transition uses the same key on the next attempt.

What is the best solution for retrying failed email delivery attempts?

I initially think of retries as a loop around the provider call because the code is close together. The operational boundary is wrong. When the provider slows down, the report job holds connections, the next schedule can overlap, and the operator has to distinguish delayed work from duplicate work.

Exponential backoff reduces pressure, but it does not isolate the dependency. A queue does. It gives the incident a finite place to stop: after the configured attempts, the DLQ records that the normal path ended. An operator can inspect the failure, correct address or credential data, and redrive eligible messages.

The enqueue call itself should also be explicit and retry-safe. This minimal Go request uses the verified publish route, an environment-provided key, a stable idempotency key, and a bounded response check. The request body must match the queue schema selected for the target queue; it is intentionally not an invented schema.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func publish(payload []byte, idempotencyKey string) error {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("queue publish failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }

        wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        } else if strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")) != "" {
            return fmt.Errorf("invalid Retry-After: %s", resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
        }
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("queue publish exhausted retries")
}

The same request, shown as a complete shell call for quick contract inspection, is still a POST and still requires the queue payload schema for the chosen queue.

curl --request POST 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish' --header 'Authorization: Bearer '$INFRAI_API_KEY --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --header 'Idempotency-Key: report-2026-10-24-subscriber-42' --data '{}'

The consumer needs the same discipline. A worker crash after the email provider accepts a message but before queue acknowledgement is normal at-least-once behavior. The durable delivery key is what prevents that crash window from becoming a duplicate customer email. Add jitter to a real implementation so many workers do not wake at the same instant.

How do the real queue options differ?

Amazon SQS is a natural choice for an AWS-owned system. Its visibility timeout, redrive policy, standard at-least-once delivery, and FIFO option cover the basic retry and DLQ shape. The trade-off is an AWS-specific operating model around IAM, regions, visibility extension, and observability.

RabbitMQ fits a team that needs broker-level routing and already accepts broker operations. Exchanges, bindings, publisher confirms, acknowledgements, and dead-letter exchanges offer more topology control than a simple work queue. That control is useful when routing is the requirement; it is extra operational surface when the only need is retrying an email attempt.

Google Cloud Tasks is specialized for dispatching scheduled HTTP work. It works well when the worker is an authenticated public HTTP service on Google Cloud. It is a weaker fit for a general multi-consumer queue or a replayable event log, because the target contract is the center of the design.

Infrai is a reasonable fourth option when this handoff should stay behind one plain REST contract. Its discovery surface is public and self-describing, with request schemas and runnable examples, and the live platform spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That breadth matters in this workflow when scheduling, queueing, and adjacent backend capabilities need the same integration convention. It avoids turning a new workflow step into another credential and adapter project.

The single-key model is a separate operational advantage, not a substitute for queue semantics. A property-management team can keep the queue handoff and related backend calls under one credential and billing relationship instead of reconciling a new key and invoice for each capability. I would choose that simplicity when the team values a consistent REST boundary; I would not choose it to obtain broker-specific routing that the platform does not provide.

Option Integration shape Best fit Boundary to respect
Amazon SQS AWS SDK or API AWS-native managed queues IAM and AWS operations remain part of the design
RabbitMQ AMQP client and broker Custom routing and broker control The team owns broker capacity and lifecycle
Google Cloud Tasks Scheduled HTTP dispatch Authenticated HTTP workers on Google Cloud It is not a general replayable event log
Infrai queue Plain REST under one key Consistent backend handoffs across capabilities No DAGs, joins, or topic-style fan-out

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the enqueue, consume, and DLQ handoff when a property-management system benefits from one REST contract across its backend capabilities. Keep SQS when AWS-native IAM and managed queue operations are the priority. Choose RabbitMQ when routing topology is the requirement. Choose Cloud Tasks when authenticated HTTP dispatch is the main job.

The choice is about the handoff, not a logo.

Where should fan-out and recovery stop?

For shipment updates, publish one logical delivery record per subscriber unless the email provider offers a batch API with clear per-recipient results and idempotency. One record makes retry and DLQ inspection independent: a bad address does not hold up every other subscriber, and a temporary provider failure has one bounded recovery path.

There are limits that should change the design. Infrai has no DAG or workflow orchestration, no fan-out join primitive, no native debounce or throttle, and no topic-style one-to-many delivery; simulating fan-out requires separate queues. Push targets must be public HTTPS endpoints, and cron tasks call public HTTP URLs rather than hosting application code. The queue therefore suits independent delivery work, not an Airflow- or Temporal-shaped process.

Messages are deleted on acknowledgement, so there is no Kafka-style replay or multi-consumer-group history. Use the application database for the delivery ledger and the queue for outstanding work. If the report is too large or the business needs an audit trail beyond 30 days, store that state elsewhere and put only references in the message.

That boundary is the decision rule. A queue gives failed email delivery attempts a retry clock and a DLQ. Your application still decides when a shipment update is stale, which failures are permanent, and how duplicate delivery is prevented.

If this boundary matches the system, start with the scheduling and queue capability index at docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt and verify the current request schema before wiring the worker.

title: Breaking My Own Agents #1: I Fed 5 n8n Workflows 30 Malformed Inputs. 102 of 150 Runs Failed Silently
description:
My n8n lead qualifier sent a "🔥 Hot lead (85)" alert to Slack for a form whose message field was four emojis.

It did the same for a message that was the literal string "undefined", for one that was only <script>alert(1)</script>, for a number, for null, and for an empty string. 15 fake hot-lead pings in total. Every run was green, and the Error Trigger never fired once.

I've written before about silent failures in n8n AI workflows. That post was about the model's output. This one is about what happens before the model: the stuff people actually POST to your webhook. Forms with a missing field, a Zapier step that sends null, an OCR job that returns 300 KB of noise, a Typeform that renames a field to Review.

So I started a series where I try to break my own workflows. Episode 1: 30 malformed inputs, 5 workflows, one Error Trigger, and a count of how many runs fail where I can see it vs how many fail silently.

The setup

  • n8n 1.123.84 self-hosted, fresh instance, 5 of my own workflows unchanged except for the model URL: lead qualifier (with Slack ping for score ≥ 70, pointed at a local mock), support FAQ, invoice extractor, meeting notes → action items, review reply.
  • Qwen 1.8B (Q4_K_M) in Ollama on CPU through its OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint, temperature 0.2, response_format: json_object, Ollama's default 4096-token context.
  • An Error Trigger workflow set as the error workflow on all 5. It posts every failure to a local receiver, so "loud" means "I'd have been alerted".
  • 30 payloads per workflow, built from one valid payload each:
    • 22 unusable ones that should never reach the model: empty body, {}, [], null, truncated JSON, main field missing / "" / whitespace / null / number / boolean / array / nested object, the strings "undefined" and "[object Object]", emoji only, zero-width characters only, ~300 KB of text, one 50,000-character token, the field name in the wrong case (Review), the payload double-wrapped in {"body": ...}, and a <script> tag with nothing else.
    • 1 edge case: valid text sent as text/plain.
    • 7 weird but valid ones that should still work: Arabic (RTL), Hindi, emoji mixed into real text, real text wrapped in HTML with a <script>, zero-width and control characters inside words, 300 junk extra fields, and {{ $env.HOME }} ${process.env.PATH} pasted into the text.

That's 150 runs per version, one round each. Every run got one of three labels:

  • Handled: unusable input rejected with an error the caller can see, or valid input processed correctly (I checked the actual answer: invoice total = 11,800, FAQ gives the 14-day refund rule, the meeting has its action items, and so on).
  • Loud: the execution failed and the Error Trigger fired.
  • Silent: green execution, but the output was built from garbage, or was wrong for a valid input.

The raw results: 102 of 150 silent

Raw workflows Runs
Handled correctly 37
Errored loudly (Error Trigger fired) 11
Failed silently (green) 102

The 22 unusable inputs are where it really shows: 95 of those 110 runs went green. n8n itself rejected exactly one kind of input, truncated JSON (HTTP 422 "Failed to parse request body", 5 runs). Every other kind of broken payload went straight to the LLM.

By workflow, it was the same story everywhere:

Workflow Silent Handled Loud
Lead qualifier 19 8 3
Support FAQ 22 6 2
Invoice extractor 20 8 2
Meeting notes 21 7 2
Review reply 20 8 2

What "silent" looked like

Not all silent failures are equally bad, so I split them. 46 of the 102 produced confident-looking output. The other 56 produced empty or "escalate" output, which looks harmless but is still a green run nobody gets told about.

The confident ones:

  • Lead qualifier, 19/19 silent runs confident. With the message missing, the model scored the rest of the form (company size, budget) and invented intent. For an empty message: "Priya Nair is a SaaS founder with 42 employees... Her interest in budgeting ($3,000/month) suggests she is looking for solutions." Score 85. Slack ping. For the emoji-only message it listed "The lead uses strong emojis in the message" as a reason. A completely empty body scored 45, and {} scored 50 ("warm").
  • Review reply, 20/20 confident. It wrote a polite public reply to every non-review. Emoji only: sentiment positive, rating_guess 5, "Thank you for your kind review! We're thrilled to hear that you enjoyed your experience at Cafe Mocha." The <script> review got topics ["script injection", "malicious code"] and a reply promising to "take steps to ensure similar issues do not occur in the future". If that goes to a Google review queue, it gets posted.
  • Meeting notes, 3. The transcript "undefined" produced invented action items: "Asha: Review and finalize the project timeline, due next week." Nobody said that.
  • Invoice extractor, 2. The worst single output in the test: invoice text that was only whitespace came back as a complete invoice. Vendor "ABC Corp", invoice INV-12345, dated 2023-01-15, subtotal 1,500, tax 300, total 1,800 USD, two line items, a GSTIN. None of it exists. The other one: the number 4521 sent as the invoice text came back as invoice_number: "4521".
  • Support FAQ, 2. Both were valid questions, and the answers were right, but the JSON was broken in a way nothing notices (more on that below).

The empty ones are the sneaky kind. The FAQ bot answered "I am not sure, a teammate will follow up shortly" with escalate: true on 19 unusable inputs, so a human gets a ticket with no question in it. The invoice extractor returned an all-null row 18 times, the kind of row that ends up in a Google Sheet. The meeting workflow returned "No summary provided" or a generic "Discussion on project progress and upcoming tasks." 18 times. None of them are dangerous on their own, but none of them told anyone the input was broken.

The 11 loud runs weren't as loud as I thought

The Error Trigger fired 11 times, always for the same reason: the prompt was bigger than the model's context window. The ~300 KB text and the 50k-character token (5 workflows each), plus the lead qualifier with 300 junk fields, because its Build Prompt does JSON.stringify(body) and sends every field to the model. Ollama answered 400 Bad request, the LLM node failed, and the alert arrived.

The webhook caller got HTTP 200 with an empty body in all 11.

That's because these workflows use "Respond to Webhook" and the execution died before reaching that node. So I got an alert, but whatever posted the form got a success code. If your form tool or Zapier step only checks the status code, it thinks everything's fine.

One bug I didn't plan to find

The FAQ checks were failing on valid questions too, even the baseline. The reason: in 8 of 31 raw FAQ runs, the 1.8B model returned the key " escalate", with a leading space. JSON-wise that's fine, so Parse Result passes it on, but $json.result.escalate is undefined. Any IF node that checks "escalate is true" will quietly treat those as "no handoff needed".

The fix: an Input Guard before the model

The rule I ended up with: the LLM should never be the first thing that looks at user input. A Code node goes right after the Webhook, checks the payload, cleans the text, and either passes a clean body on or routes to a "Reject 422" Respond node with the reasons.

Here's the Code node. The only thing that changes per workflow is SPEC (this one's for the review reply):

// Input Guard: runs right after the Webhook, before any LLM call.
const SPEC = { field: 'review', min: 3, max: 3000, optional: ['business', 'policy'] };
const problems = [];
const body = $json.body;
const ct = String(($json.headers || {})['content-type'] || '');
if (!ct.includes('application/json')) problems.push(`content-type must be application/json (got "${ct || 'none'}")`);
const isObj = body !== null && typeof body === 'object' && !Array.isArray(body);
if (!isObj) problems.push(`body must be a JSON object (got ${Array.isArray(body) ? 'array' : body === null ? 'null' : typeof body})`);
const b = isObj ? body : {};

// strip HTML, invisible/control characters, template syntax; collapse whitespace
const clean = s => String(s).normalize('NFC')
  .replace(/<(script|style)[^>]*>[\s\S]*?<\/\1>/gi, ' ')
  .replace(/<br\s*\/?>|<\/p>|<\/div>/gi, '\n')
  .replace(/<[^>]+>/g, ' ')
  .replace(/[\u0000-\u0008\u000B\u000C\u000E-\u001F\u007F\u00AD\u200B-\u200F\u202A-\u202E\u2060-\u2064\uFEFF]/g, '')
  .replace(/\{\{|\}\}|\$\{/g, '')
  .replace(/[ \t]+/g, ' ').replace(/\n\s*\n+/g, '\n').trim();

const out = {};
const v = b[SPEC.field];
if (v === undefined) {
  const near = Object.keys(b).find(k => k.toLowerCase() === SPEC.field.toLowerCase());
  problems.push(`missing field "${SPEC.field}"` + (near ? ` (found "${near}", field names are case-sensitive)` : ''));
} else if (typeof v !== 'string') {
  problems.push(`"${SPEC.field}" must be a string (got ${Array.isArray(v) ? 'array' : v === null ? 'null' : typeof v})`);
} else {
  const t = clean(v);
  const meaningful = (t.match(/[\p{L}\p{N}]/gu) || []).length;   // letters/digits in ANY script
  if (/^(undefined|null|nan|\[object object\])$/i.test(t)) problems.push(`"${SPEC.field}" is the literal string "${t}"`);
  else if (meaningful < SPEC.min) problems.push(`"${SPEC.field}" has ${meaningful} letters/digits after cleaning (min ${SPEC.min})`);
  if (t.length > SPEC.max) problems.push(`"${SPEC.field}" is ${t.length} chars after cleaning (max ${SPEC.max})`);
  if (/(\S{60,})/.test(t) && !/https?:\/\//.test(t)) problems.push(`"${SPEC.field}" contains a 60+ char unbroken token`);
  out[SPEC.field] = t;
}
// keep only the fields this workflow knows about, as short strings
for (const k of SPEC.optional) {
  const o = b[k];
  if (o === undefined || o === null) continue;
  if (typeof o !== 'string' && typeof o !== 'number') { problems.push(`"${k}" must be a string or number`); continue; }
  out[k] = clean(o).slice(0, 300);
}
const dropped = Object.keys(b).filter(k => k !== SPEC.field && !SPEC.optional.includes(k));
return [{ json: { body: out, guard: { ok: problems.length === 0, problems, dropped_fields: dropped.length } }, pairedItem: 0 }];

A few choices that mattered:

  • \p{L}\p{N} instead of [a-zA-Z]. Counting "meaningful characters" with a Latin regex would reject every Arabic and Hindi message. The Unicode classes count letters in any script, and they don't count emoji or zero-width spaces.
  • Whitelist, don't pass through. The output body only has the fields the workflow knows about. That's what fixed the lead qualifier's 300-junk-fields crash, since its prompt stringifies the whole body.
  • Limits are per workflow and based on the model: 1,000 characters for an FAQ question, 3,000 for a review, 4,000 for a lead message, 6,000 for invoices and transcripts. A 4096-token local model can't read 300 KB anyway, so it's better to say so with a 422 than with a context-overflow crash.
  • The fields stay named the same ($json.body.review), so the existing Build Prompt node works unchanged.

Then an IF node on {{ $json.guard.ok }} (boolean, is true). The true branch goes to the old Config node; the false branch goes to a Respond to Webhook node with Response Code 422 and this body:

{{ JSON.stringify({ rejected: true, problems: $json.guard.problems }) }}

That gives the caller a useful error instead of a fake success:

{"rejected":true,"problems":["missing field \"review\" (found \"Review\", field names are case-sensitive)"]}

I deliberately didn't send rejections to the Error Trigger. A bad form submission isn't an outage, and 22 types of junk paging me at 2 a.m. would make me mute the channel. The 422 goes back to whatever sent it.

And a strict parser after the model

I also replaced Parse Result. The original catches a JSON error and passes {error: ...} downstream as a normal item, which is a silent failure by design. The new one throws, so the execution fails and the Error Trigger fires:

// Strict parse: a bad model answer fails the execution, so the Error Trigger fires
const raw = ($json.choices?.[0]?.message?.content || '').trim()
  .replace(/^```
{% endraw %}
(?:json)?\s*/i, '').replace(/\s*
{% raw %}
```$/, '');
let o; try { o = JSON.parse(raw); } catch (e) { throw new Error('LLM returned non-JSON: ' + raw.slice(0, 200)); }
// per-workflow schema check, this one is the FAQ bot's
if (!(typeof o.answer === 'string' && o.answer.trim().length > 0 && typeof o.escalate === 'boolean'))
  throw new Error('LLM output failed schema check: ' + raw.slice(0, 200));
if (/<script|\{\{|\$\{/i.test(raw)) throw new Error('LLM output contains markup/template syntax');
return [{ json: { result: o }, pairedItem: 0 }];

The re-run: 145 of 150 handled

Same 30 inputs, same 5 workflows, same model:

Raw Guarded
Handled correctly 37 145
Errored loudly (Error Trigger fired) 11 1
Failed silently 102 4
...with confident-looking output 46 3
Unusable inputs that went green 95/110 0/110
Fake "Hot lead" Slack pings 15 0
Weird-but-valid inputs wrongly rejected n/a 0/35
  • All 110 unusable runs got a 422 with the reason: 105 from the guard and 5 from n8n's own JSON parser. Rejections took about 0.1 s and no LLM call. That's 105 model calls I don't pay for, on a hosted model.
  • All 35 weird-but-valid runs (Arabic, Hindi, emoji, HTML-wrapped, control characters, junk fields, template strings) got through the guard. The HTML-wrapped review got a normal reply with no <script> in it.
  • The text/plain request is rejected now. That's a choice: in the raw version, the lead qualifier happened to read the plain text, and the other four never saw it: three returned nothing useful, and the review bot replied to a review about "website speed" that nobody wrote.
  • The 1 loud run is the strict parser doing its job: the FAQ bot returned " escalate" again on the Hindi question, and this time I got an alert instead of a missing field.

The 4 it didn't fix

All 4 remaining silent runs are the meeting-notes workflow returning action_items: [] for a valid transcript (Hindi, HTML-wrapped, junk fields, template strings). My first thought was that the guard's cleaning broke the transcript. It didn't: I checked the execution data and the prompts were byte-for-byte identical to the raw version's.

So I sent the same valid transcript 6 more times to each version. Raw: empty action items in 1 of 6 runs. Guarded: 2 of 6. That's the 1.8B model, not the input. An input guard can't catch it, and my strict parser allows an empty array because some meetings really do have no action items. If I want that caught, it's an output check ("the transcript has 'I'll ... by Thursday' but action_items is empty"), and that's a different post.

What I'd tell anyone with a webhook-triggered AI workflow

  1. Your Error Trigger only sees crashes, and LLMs almost never crash. Give a model garbage and it writes a fluent answer. 95 of my 110 garbage runs were green. If you're counting on the Error Trigger as your safety net, it's covering about 10% of the problem.
  2. Guard the input before the model, in code. Type checks, a "meaningful characters" count that works for every script, length limits that match your model's context, and a field whitelist. It's one Code node and one IF.
  3. Reject loudly to the caller, not to yourself. A 422 with a reason fixes bad integrations faster than an alert channel nobody reads.
  4. Don't trust a 200. In Respond to Webhook mode, my workflows answered 200 with an empty body when they crashed. Make whatever calls the webhook treat an empty body as a failure. I haven't tested adding an error output on the LLM node to return a proper 5xx yet.
  5. Make your parser throw. catch (e) { out = { error } } turns every bad model answer into a silent failure.

The base lead qualifier and review reply workflows are in the free repo: github.com/arkintof/n8n-ai-agent-workflows (workflows/01-lead-qualifier.json and workflows/07-review-reply-agent.json). The guarded versions from this test are not in the repo yet, and neither are the FAQ, invoice and meeting workflows. Everything you need to add the guard is the code above: one Code node after the Webhook, an IF on guard.ok, a Respond node with code 422, and the stricter Parse Result.

Next in the series I go after the lead qualifier on purpose: fake budgets, injected scores, spam dressed up as a real lead.

What's the weirdest payload that's ever hit one of your webhooks, and did your workflow notice?

Written with AI assistance; workflow built and tested by me.

title: Database Transactions Are Lying to You: What Isolation Levels Actually Guarantee
description:
Two requests hit your database at the same time. One overwrites the other's work, and neither one errors. Here's why, and how to stop it.

Here's a scenario I've seen dozens of times.

A "buy now" button works perfectly in every manual test. One person clicks it, stock decrements by one, order gets created. Ships to production.

A few weeks later, a flash sale runs, and support tickets start coming in: customers charged for items that were actually out of stock. The inventory count went negative. Nobody's code has a bug you can point to. Every individual request did exactly what it was told.

The problem wasn't one request. It was two requests, reading the same stock count at the same instant, both deciding there was enough left, both writing "success."

This is what transaction isolation is supposed to prevent, and most developers wrap code in BEGIN/COMMIT assuming it fully does, without knowing which guarantees their isolation level actually makes.

This guide explains what a transaction really promises, the four standard isolation levels, and the concurrency bugs that slip through the cracks depending on which one you're using.

Let's make your writes actually safe under load.

What a Transaction Actually Guarantees

A transaction groups multiple operations so they succeed or fail as one unit. That's the "atomic" in ACID.

What it does not automatically guarantee is that your transaction is isolated from every other transaction running at the same time. That part is configurable, and the default varies by database.

BEGIN;
UPDATE inventory SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE product_id = 42;
INSERT INTO orders (product_id, user_id) VALUES (42, 7);
COMMIT;

This looks safe. It isn't, by itself. It only guarantees that within this transaction, both statements happen together. It says nothing about what a second, concurrent transaction running the exact same code is allowed to see or overwrite while this one is still in flight.

That's what isolation levels control.

The Core Problem: Two Transactions, One Row 

Time    Transaction A                Transaction B
----    -------------------------    -------------------------
t1      BEGIN
t2      SELECT stock FROM inventory
        WHERE id=42;  → stock = 1
t3                                   BEGIN
t4                                   SELECT stock FROM inventory
                                      WHERE id=42;  → stock = 1
t5      UPDATE stock = 0
t6      COMMIT
t7                                   UPDATE stock = 0
t8                                   COMMIT

Both transactions read stock = 1. Both decided it was safe to sell. Both committed. The final stock is 0, but two orders were created for one unit of inventory. Nothing errored.

This is a lost update, and it's the textbook example of what isolation levels exist to prevent.

The Four Standard Isolation Levels

The SQL standard defines four levels, each permitting fewer anomalies than the last, at the cost of more locking, more blocking, or more retries.

1. Read Uncommitted 

SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED;

The weakest level. A transaction can read data another transaction has written but not yet committed, including data that later gets rolled back. This is called a dirty read.

Transaction A: UPDATE balance SET amount = 1000 WHERE id = 1;  (not committed yet)
Transaction B: SELECT amount FROM balance WHERE id = 1;  → sees 1000
Transaction A: ROLLBACK;
-- Transaction B made a decision based on data that never existed

Almost nobody should use this in production. PostgreSQL doesn't even implement it as distinct from Read Committed. It's there for standards compliance only.

2. Read Committed 

SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;

The default in PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server. A transaction only ever sees data that has been committed: no dirty reads.

But it doesn't protect you from a non-repeatable read: if you query the same row twice in one transaction, another transaction's commit in between can change what you see the second time.

Transaction A: SELECT stock FROM inventory WHERE id=42;  → 1
Transaction B: UPDATE inventory SET stock=0 WHERE id=42; COMMIT;
Transaction A: SELECT stock FROM inventory WHERE id=42;  → 0
-- Same query, same transaction, different answer

3. Repeatable Read 

SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;

The default in MySQL/InnoDB. Once a transaction reads a row, it will see the same data for that row for the rest of the transaction, even if another transaction commits a change.

This fixes non-repeatable reads, but the standard still permits a phantom read: a query returning a set of rows can see new rows appear on a second run, even though individual rows you already read stay stable.

Transaction A: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status='pending';  → 5 rows
Transaction B: INSERT INTO orders (status) VALUES ('pending'); COMMIT;
Transaction A: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status='pending';  → 6 rows
-- A new row "phantom" appeared in the result set

(In practice, PostgreSQL's implementation of Repeatable Read is stricter than the SQL standard requires and also blocks phantom reads. But don't assume that behavior is portable to every database.)

4. Serializable 

SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;

The strongest level. Guarantees that the result of running transactions concurrently is identical to running them one after another in some order. No dirty reads, no non-repeatable reads, no phantoms, no lost updates.

The cost: the database has to detect conflicts and abort one of the transactions when it can't guarantee that ordering.

BEGIN;
-- ... transaction logic ...
COMMIT;
-- Sometimes returns:
-- ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update

Your application must be ready to catch this and retry.

Serializable isn't "safe and free." It's "safe, and sometimes it tells you to try again."

Quick Reference: What Each Level Prevents

The takeaway: your database's default isolation level is Read Committed in most systems, and Read Committed does not prevent the lost-update bug from the flash sale example. If you never explicitly thought about isolation, you're running at the level that permits it.

Common Isolation Problems

Problem 1: Assuming BEGIN/COMMIT alone prevents race conditions 

# Looks safe. Isn't, under Read Committed.
with transaction.atomic():
    product = Product.objects.get(id=42)
    if product.stock > 0:
        product.stock -= 1
        product.save()

Two concurrent requests can both fetch stock = 1, both pass the if, both decrement to 0, and both succeed. Wrapping code in a transaction guarantees atomicity of the write. It does not, by itself, guarantee the read-then-write is protected from another transaction doing the same thing in between.

Fix: use a row-level lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) to force serialization at the row.

with transaction.atomic():
    product = Product.objects.select_for_update().get(id=42)
    if product.stock > 0:
        product.stock -= 1
        product.save()

-- What select_for_update does under the hood:
SELECT * FROM products WHERE id=42 FOR UPDATE;
-- Second transaction's identical query now BLOCKS until this one commits

Problem 2: Using a lock when an atomic update would do

For simple counters, you often don't need a lock at all. You need to stop reading the value into application code in the first place.

# Race-prone: read, modify in Python, write
product.stock -= 1
product.save()

-- Race-free: the decrement happens entirely inside the database
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 42 AND stock > 0;

The second version pushes the read-modify-write into a single atomic statement the database executes as one operation. There's no window where two transactions can both see the same stale value. This is usually cheaper and simpler than a lock for pure counter updates.

Problem 3: Deadlocks from inconsistent lock ordering 

Transaction A: locks row 1, then tries to lock row 2
Transaction B: locks row 2, then tries to lock row 1
-- Both wait for each other forever

-- Transaction A
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;

-- Transaction B, running concurrently
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 2;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50 WHERE id = 1;

If A locks row 1 first and B locks row 2 first, each is now waiting on a row the other holds. The database detects this and kills one transaction with a deadlock error, but only after both have been stalled.

Fix: always acquire locks on multiple rows in a consistent order, e.g. always lock the lower ID first.

-- Both transactions now always touch id=1 before id=2
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE id = LEAST(:a, :b);
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + :amt WHERE id = GREATEST(:a, :b);

Problem 4: Long transactions holding locks under load 

with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.select_for_update().get(id=order_id)
    send_confirmation_email(order)   # slow network call, 2–3 seconds
    charge_payment(order)            # slow network call, 2–5 seconds
    order.status = 'confirmed'
    order.save()

The row lock from select_for_update is held for the entire transaction, including both slow external calls. Every other request trying to touch that order queues up behind it for as long as those network calls take.

Fix: keep locks held only as long as the database work itself takes. Do slow, unrelated I/O outside the transaction.

send_confirmation_email_async(order_id)   # queued, not inline
result = charge_payment(order)            # done before opening the lock

with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.select_for_update().get(id=order_id)
    order.status = 'confirmed' if result.success else 'failed'
    order.save()

Problem 5: Picking Serializable and not handling retries 

# Set isolation to Serializable, then treat it like it can't fail
with transaction.atomic(isolation_level='SERIALIZABLE'):
    transfer_funds(from_account, to_account, amount)

Serializable transactions can and will be aborted by the database whenever it can't guarantee a consistent ordering. This is expected, normal behavior, not an edge case.

Fix: wrap serializable transactions in a retry loop.

for attempt in range(3):
    try:
        with transaction.atomic(isolation_level='SERIALIZABLE'):
            transfer_funds(from_account, to_account, amount)
        break
    except SerializationError:
        if attempt == 2:
            raise
        continue

Choosing a Level for Your Use Case

Approach Use it for
Read Committed (the default, mostly) The majority of reads, and writes that don't depend on a prior read of the same row within the transaction. Most CRUD operations.
Row locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) at Read Committed The standard fix for read-then-write races on a specific row: inventory, balances, seat reservations. Cheaper and more predictable than jumping to Serializable.
Atomic SQL updates (SET x = x - 1 WHERE x > 0) The simplest, fastest option whenever the operation can be expressed as pure SQL without application logic between the read and the write.
Serializable Logic too complex for a single atomic statement or a simple row lock: multi-row invariants, complex financial transfers, anything where "occasionally retried" is an acceptable tradeoff for full correctness.

Checking What's Actually Happening 

-- PostgreSQL: see current isolation level
SHOW TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL;

-- PostgreSQL: see locks currently held and what's blocked on them
SELECT blocked_locks.pid AS blocked_pid,
       blocking_locks.pid AS blocking_pid,
       blocked_activity.query AS blocked_query
FROM pg_catalog.pg_locks blocked_locks
JOIN pg_catalog.pg_locks blocking_locks
  ON blocking_locks.locktype = blocked_locks.locktype
  AND blocking_locks.database IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocked_locks.database
  AND blocking_locks.relation IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocked_locks.relation
  AND blocking_locks.pid != blocked_locks.pid
JOIN pg_catalog.pg_stat_activity blocked_activity
  ON blocked_activity.pid = blocked_locks.pid
WHERE NOT blocked_locks.granted;

If you're seeing mysterious slow requests under concurrent load with no slow query in sight, checking for blocked locks is often more revealing than checking query plans.

The Bottom Line

Wrapping code in a transaction feels like it should make concurrency problems disappear. It doesn't. It only guarantees the specific things ACID promises, and by default, most databases run at a level that still allows two requests to read the same stale value and both act on it.

The flash-sale overselling bug isn't a bug in anyone's code; it's the predictable result of Read Committed doing exactly what it's documented to do.

Remember:

  • BEGIN/COMMIT guarantees atomicity, not isolation from concurrent reads. Those are separate guarantees.
  • Read Committed (most databases' default) still allows lost updates. Know your default, don't assume.
  • SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is usually the right fix for read-then-write races on a single row.
  • Atomic SQL updates (SET x = x - 1 WHERE x > 0) beat locks when the logic is simple enough to express in one statement.
  • Serializable transactions can fail on purpose. Your code needs a retry loop, not just a try/except that gives up.

The bug that only shows up during your highest-traffic moment (the flash sale, the ticket drop, the Black Friday spike) is usually a concurrency bug, not a capacity bug. Understanding isolation levels is how you catch it before that moment finds it for you.

Your Turn

Have you ever shipped a race condition that only showed up under real traffic? What gave it away? Tell me in the comments 👇

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.
