title: SaaS Reservation Holds: Dynamic Rate Limits Explained (and Why Queue Consumption Drifts)
description:
Short answer: choose a queue that exposes enough delivery state to build a feedback loop, then enforce the consumption limit in the workers. For an e-commerce reservation that expires after a fixed hold window, the queue is a transport and retry boundary; it is not the rate limiter.

Start with a modest worker concurrency, measure completion and failure rates, and change the allowance from observed demand. That keeps expiration work from competing blindly with checkout traffic. The important choice is latency versus cost: tighter expiry latency needs more continuously available capacity, while a cheaper design can tolerate a bounded sweep delay.

I start with three questions: how old may the oldest expiry message be, how much downstream capacity is reserved for it, and what happens when that capacity disappears? Those answers set the control interval and the ceiling more reliably than a queue feature checklist.

What fails when expiration is treated like a timer?

A reservation has two clocks. The business clock says that a hold is no longer valid after its fixed window. The delivery clock says when a worker gets around to marking it expired. Those clocks are related, but they are not the same thing.

A common first design scans a database, publishes every stale reservation, and lets workers consume as fast as possible. It looks efficient during a quiet test. During a promotion, the same scan can create a burst that consumes connection pools, competes with payment work, and produces a second burst when retries become eligible. The result is a reservation that is logically stale but operationally late. A 2-minute controller interval is a starting example, not a promise: the right interval depends on the hold window and the cost of each downstream call.

That is the boundary.

The opposite failure is subtler. A very small fixed consumer rate protects the rest of the system, but the backlog grows past the hold window. Increasing the rate forever is also wrong: the queue drains, but downstream dependencies see a short, sharp overload. A rate limit must respond to both backlog age and the capacity of the dependency being protected.

At-least-once delivery makes the data transition idempotent. A worker should attempt an update whose predicate still says the reservation is held and whose expiry timestamp has passed. If another delivery already changed it, the second attempt is a no-op. Acknowledging a message only after that durable result is recorded prevents a process restart from silently losing work.

Keep the retry path boring.

Which queue shape fits a dynamic limit?

Do not begin with a brand name. Begin with the state the scheduler needs to observe and control:

Requirement Queue capability to look for Why it matters
Bound worker pressure Explicit consumer concurrency or a pull operation The limiter needs a control point before work reaches the dependency
Detect late holds Approximate depth plus oldest-message age Count alone hides a small but old backlog
Recover transient failures Delayed retry or a separate retry schedule Immediate redelivery turns one failure into a tight loop
Isolate poison messages Dead-letter path with reason and attempt metadata A bad record must not block ordinary expiry work
Preserve correctness Acknowledgement after the database transition Delivery state must follow the business result

These capabilities can be implemented around many queue models. A pull-based queue makes the control loop explicit. A push-based queue can work when the worker has a local semaphore and the broker's prefetch or in-flight setting is bounded. A timer-oriented scheduler can also feed a queue, provided the queue remains the place where retries and backpressure are visible.

The selection rule is therefore operational: pick the simplest model that gives the team a bounded in-flight set, observable age, controlled retry behavior, and a quarantine path. A richer feature set is not automatically better. Every hidden retry or timeout is another state that has to appear in the runbook.

There is a real limitation here. A queue with weak age visibility is a poor fit when the business objective is tight expiry latency, even if it is inexpensive and easy to operate. A timer-heavy scheduler is a poor fit when the dependency needs fast backpressure and explicit retry inspection. In those cases, choose the model whose observability matches the objective; accepting more operational machinery is the trade-off for a tighter deadline.

How should the control loop change consumption?

Use a rate limiter as a governor, not as a promise about exact completion time. Recompute its allowance at a fixed cadence from signals such as oldest age, queue depth, downstream error rate, and available database capacity. Keep a floor so a quiet but stuck queue is still noticed, and keep a ceiling so a bad metric cannot unleash every worker.

For a small Go worker, the boundary can stay plain. The queue client is behind an interface; the limiter decides when the next receive is allowed; the handler owns idempotency and acknowledgement.

package expiry

import (
    "context"
    "time"
)

type Message struct {
    ReservationID string
    Attempt       int
}

type Queue interface {
    Receive(context.Context) (Message, error)
    Ack(context.Context, Message) error
    Retry(context.Context, Message, time.Duration) error
}

type Reservations interface {
    ExpireIfHeld(context.Context, string, time.Time) (bool, error)
}

type Limiter interface {
    Wait(context.Context) error
}

func Run(ctx context.Context, q Queue, store Reservations, limit Limiter, retryDelay time.Duration) error {
    for {
        if err := limit.Wait(ctx); err != nil {
            return err
        }

        msg, err := q.Receive(ctx)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }

        _, err = store.ExpireIfHeld(ctx, msg.ReservationID, time.Now().UTC())
        if err == nil {
            if err = q.Ack(ctx, msg); err == nil {
                continue
            }
        }

        if retryErr := q.Retry(ctx, msg, retryDelay); retryErr != nil {
            return retryErr
        }
    }
}

The example deliberately does not use queue depth as a direct worker count. Depth is a backlog signal, not a capacity measurement. A controller can raise the allowance when the oldest age approaches the service objective and downstream errors remain below their threshold. It should lower the allowance quickly on timeouts or database saturation, with a slower recovery to avoid oscillation. That choice trades freshness against load: raising the limit reduces expiry lag but increases the number of concurrent calls that can fail together.

The fixed hold window still needs a source of truth. Store the reservation expiry timestamp with the reservation, and make the conditional state transition authoritative. A message can arrive early, late, or twice. None of those delivery properties should change the business rule.

What should verification and rollback prove?

Test the failure modes, not only the happy path. The useful cases are a duplicate delivery, a worker restart after the database commit but before acknowledgement, a retry that arrives after the reservation was already released, and a dependency that returns errors while the backlog grows. Assert that each case leaves one valid business state and that the message eventually becomes acknowledged or quarantined.

For a deployment, canary the new limiter with a bounded worker set. Watch oldest-message age, expiry lag, in-flight messages, conditional-update outcomes, retry counts, dead-letter count, database saturation, and downstream error rate. A dashboard that shows only queue depth will miss the incident that matters: a short queue containing very old reservations.

Rollback should change the consumer configuration before it changes the data model. Lower concurrency, pause the expiry consumer, or restore the previous controller parameters while preserving the queue and its attempt metadata. Do not delete a backlog to make a graph look healthy. Once the dependency is stable, resume below the previous ceiling and let age, not panic, determine the next increase.

The practical decision is simple to state. Select the queue that makes in-flight work, age, retry state, and dead-letter state inspectable to the operators who will be paged. Put dynamic rate limiting at the worker boundary, make expiry idempotent, and choose the latency target before choosing how much always-on capacity to pay for.

References

  • RabbitMQ, “Dead Letter Exchanges”: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/dlx
  • RFC 6585, “Additional HTTP Status Codes” (429 Too Many Requests): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585
  • Martin Kleppmann, “Designing Data-Intensive Applications” companion resources: https://dataintensive.net/

title: AWS EC2 Pricing and Billing: The Meters Around the Instance-Hour
description:
Figure 1. Illustrative schematic. The instance-hour total is one meter, not the bill: storage, addresses, reservations and transfer are billed separately. Run your own numbers in the EC2 Compute Cost Calculator.

The instance-hour gets all the attention—and often accounts for only a fraction of the actual AWS EC2 invoice.

Below are the US East (us-east-1) Linux On-Demand rates for 13 common instance types (from the AWS price list published October 29, 2026) along with their 730-hour monthly cost, followed by the five billing meters the hourly price leaves out: the 60-second floor on short launches, attached EBS volumes on stopped instances, idle Elastic IPs, unused Capacity Reservations, and T-family Unlimited surplus credits.

Quick numbers from the worked model:

  • 10 × m5.large running all month (730 hours): $700.80 at $0.0960 per instance-hour.
  • 10,000 short jobs running 30 seconds each on m5.large: $16.00 for 83.33 hours of actual wall-clock work—because the 60-second minimum floor doubles the billed hours to 166.67.
  • An On-Demand Capacity Reservation for 20 m5.large instances with 12 in use: bills $560.64/month for the 8 idle slots nobody touched.

You can test your own fleet numbers locally in the EC2 Compute Cost Calculator (or read the full teardown on Buildopsy).

1. What the Hourly Rate Actually Buys

An On-Demand rate is a price for runtime, not for work done. AWS describes it as capacity by the hour or second with no long-term commitment, and it does not fall when the CPU sits idle. A ten-instance fleet that serves nothing for a month costs the same as one under load. Utilization changes how many instance-hours you need; it does not change the rate.

The same pricing page separates what the instance charge covers from what it does not: storage, addressing, load balancing, monitoring, and transfer are billed on their own meters.

Scope note: Rates move by Region, operating system, tenancy, purchase model, and instance family. The numbers below use one Region (us-east-1), one OS (Linux), and one purchase model (On-Demand) so every calculation can be checked.

2. Thirteen US East Rates to Anchor Against

These are Linux On-Demand rates for US East (N. Virginia), read from AWS's published EC2 pricing data (published October 29, 2026), covering burstable, general-purpose, compute-optimized, and memory-optimized shapes:

Instance type vCPU Memory USD per instance-hour Monthly at 730 h
t3.micro 2 1 GiB $0.0104 $7.59
t4g.small 2 2 GiB $0.0168 $12.26
t3.small 2 2 GiB $0.0208 $15.18
t4g.medium 2 4 GiB $0.0336 $24.53
t3.medium 2 4 GiB $0.0416 $30.37
c7g.large 2 4 GiB $0.0725 $52.93
c5.large 2 4 GiB $0.0850 $62.05
m5.large 2 8 GiB $0.0960 $70.08
m6i.large 2 8 GiB $0.0960 $70.08
r5.large 2 16 GiB $0.1260 $91.98
c5.xlarge 4 8 GiB $0.1700 $124.10
m5.xlarge 4 16 GiB $0.1920 $140.16
r5.xlarge 4 32 GiB $0.2520 $183.96

(The monthly column is rate × 730 hours, the mean month at 8,760 hours/year.)

Two rows are worth comparing side by side: c7g.large and c5.large both give 2 vCPU and 4 GiB, and the Graviton (c7g.large) option lists at $0.0725 against $0.0850—a difference of $9.13/month per instance, or $912.50/month across 100 instances for the same core and memory count.

3. The 60-Second Floor on Short Launches

Partial instance-hours bill by the second, which usually gets read as "a 30-second job costs 30 seconds." It does not.

The EC2 pricing page states a 60-second minimum, so any launch shorter than a minute bills a full 60 seconds. (SUSE Linux Enterprise Server is the single exception listed: those instances bill a full hour regardless.)

Take 10,000 short CI or batch jobs running 30 seconds each on m5.large:

  • Wall-clock runtime: 10,000 × 30 s = 300,000 s = 83.33 hours
  • Billed runtime at the 60-second floor: 10,000 × 60 s = 600,000 s = 166.67 hours
  • Billed cost: 166.67 × $0.0960 = $16.00 (instead of $8.00)

The floor is the economic argument for batching: launching once for 600 seconds bills 10 minutes, while launching twelve times for 30 seconds bills 12 minutes for 6 minutes of work.

4. What Keeps Billing After StopInstances

Stopping an EC2 instance ends the instance-hour charge, but several attached resources keep their own meters running:

  • Attached EBS volumes bill by provisioned GB-month whether the instance is running or stopped (in one-second increments with the same 60-second minimum).
  • Every in-use and idle Elastic IP address is charged.
  • Load balancers and CloudWatch bill on their own product pages.
  • Auto Scaling itself carries no separate fee—only the instances and monitoring it launches bill normally.

5. Capacity Reservations Bill the Slot, Not Just the Instance

An On-Demand Capacity Reservation is priced exactly like equivalent On-Demand usage. If the reservation is 100% utilized, you pay instance usage and nothing extra. If it is partially used, you pay for the unused portion too.

For 20 reserved m5.large instances with 12 running for a full 730-hour month:

  • Total reservation commitment: 20 × 730 × $0.0960 = $1,401.60
  • Used by running instances: 12 × 730 × $0.0960 = $840.96
  • Billed for idle capacity: 8 × 730 × $0.0960 = $560.64

6. Purchase Options and What "Up To" Means

AWS publishes headline discount ceilings rather than guaranteed rates:

  • Savings Plans: up to 72% off On-Demand in exchange for an hourly spend commitment.
  • Spot Instances: up to 90% off On-Demand in exchange for interruption risk.

At the published 72% ceiling, a $0.0960 m5.large would land at $0.0269/hour ($19.62 across 730 hours)—but that is a maximum ceiling illustration, and actual plan rates depend on term, payment option, and family scope.

7. Burstable Instances (T2 / T3 / T4g) and the Unlimited Credit Bill

T-family instances accumulate CPU credits while idle and spend them when bursting. In Unlimited mode, they can burst past their credit balance, and surplus credits bill per vCPU-hour regardless of instance size or purchase option:

  • T2 and T3 (Linux, RHEL, SLES): $0.05 per vCPU-hour
  • T4g (Linux, RHEL, SLES): $0.04 per vCPU-hour
  • T8i (Linux, RHEL, SLES): $0.06 per vCPU-hour
  • T2 and T3 (Windows / SQL Web): $0.096 per vCPU-hour
  • T8i (Windows / SQL Web): $0.1152 per vCPU-hour

8. Windows & SQL Licences: The Optimize CPUs Lever

Windows and SQL Server images bundle the licence into the hourly instance price. AWS exposes a lever here with no Linux equivalent: Optimize CPUs, which lowers the active vCPU count or disables hyper-threading while keeping the same instance RAM and network tier.

Published savings per vCPU-hour removed:

  • Windows Server: $0.046
  • Windows with SQL Enterprise: $0.421
  • SQL Standard: $0.166
  • SQL Web: $0.063

On an 8-vCPU m5.2xlarge, dropping active vCPUs from 8 to 4 saves 4 × 730 × $0.046 = $134.32/month on the Windows Server licence component alone.

9. Data Transfer Is Aggregated Across Services

Outbound internet transfer is aggregated across EC2, S3, Glacier, RDS, Redshift, SageMaker, SES, SimpleDB, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB, Storage Gateway, CloudShell, and CloudWatch Logs, with a 100 GB/month free outbound allowance across AWS services and Regions (except China and GovCloud). A terabyte leaving an EC2 load balancer and a terabyte leaving an S3 bucket climb the exact same tier ladder (see our S3 pricing teardown and CDN/egress model).

10. Run Your Own Numbers

An EC2 bill is a runtime meter surrounded by meters that do not care whether anything ran: a 60-second floor that doubles short launches, EBS volumes and Elastic IPs that outlive stopped instances, and Capacity Reservations that bill empty slots.

  • Interactive Calculator: EC2 Compute Cost Calculator (models instance-hours, the 60-second short-launch floor, and attached EBS in your browser)
  • Full Rate-Card Audit & FAQ: AWS EC2 Pricing and Billing: The Meters Around the Instance-Hour

Question for everyone running workloads on EC2: Which "non-instance" meter has surprised you most on a real AWS bill—forgotten EBS volumes on stopped instances, T-family Unlimited surplus credits, NAT Gateway / egress traffic, or idle Elastic IPs?

title: Who's Who in Our Tiny Desk AI Clip? Sliding Name Cards Into the Last Seconds With ffmpeg overlay (Python, Tested)
description:
Checked November 9, 2026 (12:00 CST, UTC+8) against the live pages linked below. I build tinydeskoutstanding.video, an independent studio that turns one to five photos into a 15-second vertical parody of the "Outstanding" Tiny Desk meme. The script was written for this post and tested on synthetic clips and solid-colour stand-in photos, not real faces.

Once a group clip of the Tiny Desk meme lands in a chat, the first reply is usually a question: "wait, who's on sax?" In the wide band shot the faces are small, and by the time people work out who is who, the clip has ended.

One fix that works well is a reveal: in the last few seconds, a card with each person's original photo and name slides in next to the band. This post builds that reveal with one ffmpeg filter graph, generated by about 80 lines of Python, plus a checker that proves the cards land where they should.

What the clip gives you

From the site's own pages:

  • Every clip is "15-second vertical video, 9:16", at 480p, 720p, 1080p or 4k, with newly generated sound (FAQ).
  • The stage has five faces: "lead, sax, keys, back left, and back right", and "a face you leave empty keeps the performer already in the scene" (band and guest slots).
  • The price doesn't change with the number of faces. Today a clip is $9.98 at 480p, $12.98 at 720p, $24.98 at 1080p or $39.98 at 4k (pricing).

So you get one to five cards to show, and a frame that may be anywhere from about 480 to 4k pixels wide. The script reads the real size with ffprobe and does not assume any of it.

The input: a tiny cast file 

{"reveal_at": 11.5,
 "cards": [
  {"spot": "lead", "name": "Maya", "photo": "maya.jpg"},
  {"spot": "sax", "name": "Jordan", "photo": "jordan.jpg"},
  {"spot": "back left", "name": "Biscuit", "photo": "biscuit.jpg"}
 ]}

reveal_at is in seconds. Pick it by watching your own clip: the cards should arrive after the joke has landed and before it ends. Use the same photos you uploaded to the studio, so people see the face that went into each spot.

The filter graph, one piece at a time

For each card:

  1. scale=...:force_original_aspect_ratio=increase,crop=... fills a 3:4 box with the photo and centres it, so a landscape photo is cropped, not squashed.
  2. pad adds a white border and a strip at the bottom; drawtext writes "Maya · lead" into the strip.
  3. overlay puts it on the video with an x expression that changes every frame: 
x = if(lt(t, start), W, max(W - w - margin, W - (t - start) * speed))

Before start, the card sits just off the right edge (x = W, invisible). After start, it moves left at speed pixels per second until it reaches its resting place, then max() holds it there. Each card starts 0.35 s after the previous one, which gives the staggered "one, two, three" feel. Overlays are chained, so the graph is [0:v][c0]overlay[v0]; [v0][c1]overlay[v1]; ....

Two details that bite:

  • Commas inside expressions must be escaped (\,) inside a filter graph, or ffmpeg reads them as filter separators.
  • eval=frame makes overlay re-evaluate x on every frame. Without it the card would be placed once and never move.

Cards start at a quarter of the frame width and shrink until the whole stack fits the height, so five cards on a 9:16 frame still fit.

The script 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Slide a 'who's who' card for each cast member into the last seconds of a clip.

usage: python3 reveal.py clip.mp4 cast.json out.mp4

cast.json: {"reveal_at": 11.5, "cards": [{"spot": "lead", "name": "Maya", "photo": "maya.jpg"}, ...]}
Cards stack down the right edge, each sliding in 0.35 s after the previous one.
Audio is copied untouched; video is re-encoded with libx264 (CRF 18).
"""
import json, os, shutil, subprocess, sys

FONTS = ["/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf",
         "/Library/Fonts/Arial Bold.ttf", "C:/Windows/Fonts/arialbd.ttf"]

def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0",
                          "-show_entries", "stream=width,height:format=duration",
                          "-of", "json", path], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    j = json.loads(out)
    return j["streams"][0]["width"], j["streams"][0]["height"], float(j["format"]["duration"])

def esc(text):  # drawtext text= escaping
    return text.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace(":", "\\:").replace("'", "\u2019")

def layout(W, H, n):
    """Card width, photo height, label height, gap, margin, top for n cards."""
    gap, margin = max(4, H // 120), max(6, W // 40)
    cw = W // 4                      # start at a quarter of the frame width
    while cw > 40:
        ph, label = cw * 4 // 3, max(14, cw // 7)
        top = (H - n * (ph + label) - (n - 1) * gap) // 2
        if top >= margin:
            return cw, ph, label, gap, margin, top
        cw -= 2                      # shrink until the stack fits
    sys.exit("frame too small for this many cards")

def build(W, H, dur, cast, font):
    t0 = float(cast["reveal_at"])
    cards = cast["cards"]
    if not 1 <= len(cards) <= 5:
        sys.exit("1 to 5 cards (the stage has five spots)")
    if not 0 < t0 < dur - 0.5:
        sys.exit(f"reveal_at must be inside the clip (duration {dur:.2f} s)")
    cw, ph, label, gap, margin, top = layout(W, H, len(cards))
    ch = ph + label
    parts, last = [], "[0:v]"
    for i, c in enumerate(cards):
        txt = f"{c['name']} \u00b7 {c['spot']}"
        card = (f"[{i+1}:v]scale={cw-4}:{ph-4}:force_original_aspect_ratio=increase,"
                f"crop={cw-4}:{ph-4},pad={cw}:{ch}:2:2:white")
        if font:
            card += (f",drawtext=fontfile='{font}':text='{esc(txt)}':fontsize={int(label*0.62)}:"
                     f"fontcolor=black:x=(w-tw)/2:y={ph}+({label}-th)/2")
        parts.append(card + f"[c{i}]")
        start = t0 + 0.35 * i
        x = f"if(lt(t\\,{start:.3f})\\,W\\,max(W-w-{margin}\\,W-(t-{start:.3f})*{W*3}))"
        y = top + i * (ch + gap)
        out = f"[v{i}]"
        parts.append(f"{last}[c{i}]overlay=x='{x}':y={y}:eval=frame{out}")
        last = out
    return ";".join(parts), last

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 4:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    clip, cast_path, out = sys.argv[1:]
    for tool in ("ffmpeg", "ffprobe"):
        if not shutil.which(tool):
            sys.exit(f"{tool} not found")
    cast = json.load(open(cast_path, encoding="utf-8"))
    base = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(cast_path))
    W, H, dur = probe(clip)
    font = next((f for f in FONTS if os.path.exists(f)), None)
    graph, last = build(W, H, dur, cast, font)
    cmd = ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", clip]
    for c in cast["cards"]:
        cmd += ["-i", os.path.join(base, c["photo"])]
    cmd += ["-filter_complex", graph, "-map", last, "-map", "0:a?",
            "-c:v", "libx264", "-crf", "18", "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", "-c:a", "copy",
            "-movflags", "+faststart", out]
    subprocess.run(cmd, check=True)
    print(f"wrote {out}: {len(cast['cards'])} cards from {cast['reveal_at']} s"
          + ("" if font else " (no font found, labels skipped)"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Audio is copied untouched (-c:a copy), so the generated sound is exactly what the studio delivered. The video has to be re-encoded, because you're drawing on it; CRF 18 keeps it close to the original.

If no font file is found, the cards still appear, just without names. Add your system's bold font to FONTS if you're on something other than Debian, macOS or Windows.

Testing it without real faces

A synthetic 15-second clip and three solid-colour "photos" make the check easy: if the red card is where Maya's card should be, the area there should average to Maya's red.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Synthetic stand-ins: a 15 s vertical 480x854 clip with a tone, and three
# solid-colour "photos". No real faces involved.
set -euo pipefail
ffmpeg -v error -y -f lavfi -i "testsrc2=size=480x854:rate=30:duration=15" \
  -f lavfi -i "sine=frequency=440:sample_rate=48000:duration=15" \
  -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -shortest clip.mp4
python3 - <<'PY'
from PIL import Image
for name, rgb in [("maya", (220, 40, 40)), ("jordan", (40, 160, 60)), ("biscuit", (40, 70, 220))]:
    Image.new("RGB", (600, 800), rgb).save(f"{name}.jpg", quality=95)
PY
cat > cast.json <<'JSON'
{"reveal_at": 11.5,
 "cards": [
  {"spot": "lead", "name": "Maya", "photo": "maya.jpg"},
  {"spot": "sax", "name": "Jordan", "photo": "jordan.jpg"},
  {"spot": "back left", "name": "Biscuit", "photo": "biscuit.jpg"}
 ]}
JSON
echo "made clip.mp4, 3 photos, cast.json"

The checker imports the same layout() the renderer uses, grabs one frame before the reveal and one at the end, and checks two things: before the reveal the output matches the source (nothing leaked in early), and at the end each card's photo area matches its photo's colour.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check reveal.py output: no card before reveal_at, every card in place at the end.

usage: python3 check_reveal.py clip.mp4 out.mp4 cast.json
Reads the average colour of each card's photo area from two frames.
"""
import json, os, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from reveal import layout  # same geometry as the renderer

def frame(path, t, W, H):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-ss", str(t), "-i", path, "-frames:v", "1",
                          "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8).reshape(H, W, 3).astype(int)

def main():
    clip, out, cast_path = sys.argv[1:4]
    cast = json.load(open(cast_path))
    base = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(cast_path))
    j = json.loads(subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
                                   "stream=width,height:format=duration", "-of", "json", out],
                                  capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout)
    W, H = j["streams"][0]["width"], j["streams"][0]["height"]
    dur = float(j["format"]["duration"])
    cw, ph, label, gap, margin, top = layout(W, H, len(cast["cards"]))
    ch = ph + label
    early_src = frame(clip, cast["reveal_at"] - 1, W, H)
    early_out = frame(out, cast["reveal_at"] - 1, W, H)
    late = frame(out, dur - 0.2, W, H)
    ok = True
    diff = np.abs(early_src - early_out).mean()
    print(f"before reveal: mean abs diff vs source {diff:.2f} (want < 3)")
    ok &= diff < 3
    for i, c in enumerate(cast["cards"]):
        want = np.array(Image.open(os.path.join(base, c["photo"])).convert("RGB")).reshape(-1, 3).mean(0)
        x0, y0 = W - margin - cw + 10, top + i * (ch + gap) + 10
        got = late[y0:y0 + ph - 20, x0:x0 + cw - 20].reshape(-1, 3).mean(0)
        err = np.abs(got - want).max()
        print(f"card {i} {c['name']:<8} expected {want.round()} got {got.round()} err {err:.1f}")
        ok &= err < 12
    print("PASS" if ok else "FAIL")
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Output on the box I tested on (ffmpeg 7.1, Python 3.13):

$ bash make_test_media.sh
made clip.mp4, 3 photos, cast.json
$ python3 reveal.py clip.mp4 cast.json out.mp4
wrote out.mp4: 3 cards from 11.5 s
$ python3 check_reveal.py clip.mp4 out.mp4 cast.json
before reveal: mean abs diff vs source 0.30 (want < 3)
card 0 Maya     expected [220.  40.  41.] got [220.  39.  41.] err 1.0
card 1 Jordan   expected [ 40. 160.  60.] got [ 38. 159.  59.] err 1.6
card 2 Biscuit  expected [ 40.  70. 220.] got [ 39.  69. 219.] err 1.1
PASS

I also ran it on a 1080x1920 test clip with all five spots filled and names containing a colon and an apostrophe ("Dr: Kim", "O'Neil"), which are the two characters that break drawtext most often. All five cards passed. The first version of the script failed that test with "too many cards for this frame height", which is why the card size now shrinks to fit.

Things to decide before you post

  • Ask again. Everyone in the clip agreed to be in it; a card with their real photo and name is a second, more personal step. The site's spots are for "one adult who agreed, or one pet" (band and guest slots), and the same courtesy applies to the reveal.
  • Nicknames are fine. The card text is whatever you put in name.
  • Keep it labelled as a parody. The sound is newly generated and "not the Gap Band recording, Charlie Wilson's performance or NPR audio" (FAQ).
  • Watch the clip first. Check the face in the band shot and the close-up before adding anything (check before posting). Cards draw attention to faces, including a face that came out wrong.

Variations

  • Cards on the left: swap the x expression to start at -w and stop at margin.
  • Fade instead of slide: keep x fixed and put format=rgba,fade=in:st=START:d=0.3:alpha=1 on each card.
  • Only the lead: one card, larger. Set the width to W // 2 in layout().

The full clip, the band and the scene come from the studio (tinydeskoutstanding.video); the reveal is a local edit you add afterwards, on your own machine, with your own photos.

title: Snowflake Just Made Business Ontology an AI Priority. Here’s What Comes Next.
description:
Enterprise AI needs to understand business concepts. But understanding what a customer is doesn't automatically reveal how customer data connects across systems.

Snowflake's recent emphasis on Business Ontology is an important signal. The conversation around enterprise AI is moving beyond better prompts and more capable models toward a harder problem: how do we give AI a dependable representation of the business?

I think that's the right direction.

But it raises a question that deserves just as much attention:

Once AI knows what a customer, contract, or revenue means, can it actually find how those concepts connect to the data inside the company?

That is where an elegant business model meets the messy reality of enterprise systems.

A customer exists in more than one system

Imagine a company with a CRM, an ERP system, and a billing platform.

The CRM stores account_id. The ERP uses customer_no. Billing has party_ref.

All three systems refer to customers, but the identifiers don't necessarily match. Some records represent legal entities; others represent sales accounts or billing relationships. A parent company may have several subsidiaries. An account may have changed identifiers during a migration.

Now someone asks:

Which customers generated the most revenue after contract adjustments last quarter?

A business ontology may define Customer, Contract, and Revenue, including the conceptual relationships among them. That's valuable. It can also define which revenue metric the organization recognizes.

But a conceptual relationship is not, by itself, a verified physical join.

The system still needs to establish which records correspond to the same entity, which tables bridge the relevant systems, and whether joining them changes the grain of the calculation.

Otherwise the AI may produce perfectly valid SQL that answers a subtly different question.

Business relationships and database relationships aren't interchangeable

This distinction is easy to overlook because both are called “relationships.”

A business model might say:

A customer signs contracts. Contracts generate invoices. Invoices may be settled through payments.

A physical database may instead contain:

crm_accounts
    |
account_mapping
    |
erp_contract_header
    |
contract_invoice_bridge
    |
billing_invoice
    |
payment_allocation

Some of those links may have foreign keys. Others may exist only in application code, historical SQL, naming conventions, or matching data values.

And the most direct-looking join may not be the correct one. Joining invoices directly to payments can multiply invoice amounts when a single invoice has multiple allocations.

Knowing the business relationship tells you what ought to connect. Discovering and validating the physical relationship tells you how the data can safely connect.

The two reinforce each other. Neither replaces the other.

Why reading the schema isn't enough

Many enterprise databases were not designed to explain themselves to AI.

Foreign keys may be missing because applications enforce relationships outside the database. Identifiers may have different names. Data migrations can leave legacy codes. A bridge table may be essential even though the user's question never mentions it.

An LLM can make an educated guess from column names and descriptions. But an educated guess is not relationship evidence.

A more defensible approach is to examine multiple signals:

  • Declared primary and foreign keys
  • Column naming and data types
  • Distinct-value overlap and inclusion ratios
  • Candidate bridge tables and join paths
  • Existing SQL and application usage, where available
  • Business confirmation for relationships that materially affect results

These signals help generate candidate relationships, not automatic guarantees. A high overlap ratio can be coincidental. A frequently used join can still be outdated or wrong.

The point is to move from “the model thinks these tables connect” to “here is the evidence for this proposed connection, and here is what remains to be validated.”

The missing step is connecting meaning to evidence

For natural-language analytics, I see three separate questions:

1. What does the user mean?

Does “revenue” mean booked, invoiced, collected, or recognized revenue? Which definition is approved?

2. Where does the corresponding data live?

Which tables and fields implement that definition across the organization's systems?

3. How can those data objects be combined correctly?

Which relationships and intermediate tables are required? What is the join cardinality? Will aggregation duplicate records?

The first is primarily a business-semantics problem. The second requires semantic-to-physical mapping. The third is a relationship-discovery and validation problem.

It is tempting to put all three into a prompt and ask the model to decide. But that turns enterprise-specific facts into model assumptions.

A better design treats business definitions and relationship evidence as governed inputs to query planning, with clarification when the evidence does not support a single interpretation.

Where Semora and IntaLink fit into this discussion

This is the distinction we have been exploring in our own work.

Semora focuses on enterprise business semantics: terms, semantic mappings, metrics, dimensions, ambiguity handling, and natural-language querying.

IntaLink focuses on discovering table- and field-level relationships, including candidates suggested by keys, field semantics, and actual value characteristics. Those relationship findings can be supplied to a query system as context.

In our architecture, Semora manages its own data connections and access. It maps the relevant data-source ID to IntaLink and calls its APIs for relationship information; IntaLink does not take over Semora's database credentials or query execution.

These are complementary capabilities, not a claim that we have built a complete enterprise ontology or solved every cross-system entity-matching and join-grain problem.

The broader architectural idea is simple:

Business semantics establish meaning. Relationship intelligence supplies evidence about how the underlying data connects.

When those two are brought together, AI has a stronger foundation than schema text alone.

What should come next?

If Business Ontology becomes a mainstream part of enterprise AI architecture, I think the next challenge is making it operational against imperfect, changing data environments.

That requires more than a diagram of entities and concepts.

It requires ways to:

Discover missing links. Find candidate physical relationships even when databases don't declare them.

Distinguish evidence from assumptions. Show whether a link comes from a constraint, observed data pattern, historical query, or human approval.

Validate the path, not just the edge. A set of individually plausible joins can still produce an incorrect aggregation.

Keep meaning and relationships aligned. When a business definition or physical schema changes, teams need to know what mappings and queries may be affected.

Know when to ask. If several customer identities or revenue definitions remain plausible, AI should not quietly choose one merely to produce an answer.

These are engineering and governance requirements, not features that any single ontology announcement automatically solves.

A practical test for enterprise AI buyers

When evaluating an ontology-enabled analytics system, I would ask it to answer one question across three real enterprise systems:

Which customers are most profitable after contracts, invoicing, and delivery costs?

Then I would ask:

  • Which definition of profitability did you use?
  • How did you reconcile customer identities across systems?
  • Which bridge tables and joins were necessary?
  • What evidence supports those joins?
  • How did you prevent duplicated amounts?
  • What would you do if two plausible mappings remained?

A system that can explain those choices—and admit when a choice is unresolved—is much more interesting than one that merely produces SQL quickly.

The bigger opportunity

Snowflake's attention to Business Ontology is another sign that the enterprise AI conversation is maturing. Organizations are recognizing that models need structured business meaning, not just access to raw data.

The next step, in my view, is to connect that meaning to the relationships hidden in operational databases.

Because defining what a customer means is not the same as finding that customer across CRM, ERP, and billing.

And defining revenue is not the same as proving that the tables used to calculate it are correctly connected.

Business Ontology gives AI a language for the enterprise. Relationship intelligence helps ground that language in the enterprise's actual data.

The most useful systems will need both.

title: One Space Broke the JSON-LD Headline on 62 Pages
description:
One of my page headings, Your <em>IP</em>, plainly, showed up in the JSON-LD as "Your IP , plainly". The same bug was in the structured data of 62 pages. On screen, every one of them looked right.

The site is MyIPScan, which I built. This post is about the bug class, how it happens, and a test that catches it.

TL;DR

  • If you derive a JSON-LD headline from heading HTML, inline tags like <em> can leave a space before punctuation: Your <em>IP</em>, plainly → Your IP , plainly.
  • Fix: delete inline tags without replacing them, and turn only block boundaries into spaces.
  • Catch it at build time: the JSON-LD headline must equal the visible heading's normalized text, and no generated text field may match / [,.;:!?)]/.

Why one space matters

JSON-LD is a copy of your page written for machines, and no human reads it. Google recommends JSON-LD for structured data when your setup allows it (Search Central intro), and its guidelines say: "Your structured data must be a true representation of the page content" (General Structured Data Guidelines).

The headline was still true, just sloppy. But a template stamps the same mistake onto every page it builds, and nothing on screen tells you. The visible heading was correct on all 62 pages.

Checking the page in a browser is real QA. For this bug it checked the wrong output.

Two explanations that don't fit

The source text. If the space were in the CMS, the visible heading would show it too. It didn't. A bug in the source shows up in both copies.

JSON escaping. JSON.stringify escapes quotes, backslashes and control characters. It does not add spaces.

That leaves the step that turns heading HTML into a string. I can't show you my original generator, but the output has the fingerprint of one specific mistake.

How this class of bug happens

The code below is an illustration of the bug class, not my generator. It reproduces the exact output, which is enough to reason about it.

A common way to strip HTML tags in JavaScript replaces every tag with a space, so that <p>one</p><p>two</p> doesn't become onetwo. Then it squeezes whitespace:

// Illustration: a naive stripper that turns every tag into a space
function naiveStrip(html) {
  return html.replace(/<[^>]*>/g, ' ').replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim();
}

naiveStrip('Your <em>IP</em>, plainly');
// "Your IP , plainly"

naiveStrip('What is my <em>IP address</em>?');
// "What is my IP address ?"

Step by step:

  1. Your <em>IP</em>, plainly
  2. Tags → spaces: Your IP , plainly (two spaces after "Your", one before the comma)
  3. Collapse whitespace: Your IP , plainly

The collapse hides half the damage. The double space after "Your" merges into one, so the result looks almost right. The space before the comma has nothing to merge with, so it stays.

The rule the stripper breaks: inline elements do not create word boundaries; block elements do. <em> sits inside a run of text. <p>, <li>, <h2> and <br> end one.

textContent and innerText

In a DOM, textContent "returns the concatenation of the textContent of every child node" (MDN), so <em> is harmless. It also includes <script> and <style> content, and it ignores <br>: in Chromium, Line one<br>line two gives "Line oneline two". innerText handles <br>, but for an element that isn't rendered, such as one in a detached tree, it returns the same as textContent (MDN). In a static build step with no browser, that is the case you are in.

The fix, as an illustration

For a heading, which is short and mostly inline, a small explicit function is enough. It deletes 26 inline tags and turns everything else into a space:

const INLINE = /<\/?(a|abbr|b|bdi|bdo|cite|code|data|dfn|em|i|kbd|mark|q|s|samp|small|span|strong|sub|sup|time|u|var|wbr)\b[^>]*>/gi;

function headingText(html) {
  return html
    .replace(INLINE, '')          // inline tags: no boundary
    .replace(/<br\s*\/?>/gi, ' ') // line break: boundary
    .replace(/<[^>]*>/g, ' ')     // any other tag: boundary
    .replace(/ /g, ' ')
    .replace(/\s+/g, ' ')
    .trim();
}

headingText('Your <em>IP</em>, plainly');        // "Your IP, plainly"
headingText('What is my <em>IP address</em>?');  // "What is my IP address?"
headingText('Line one<br>line two');             // "Line one line two"

The comments are real output from Node 22. This version decodes only  . If your headings contain & or ’, decode them properly (the test below shows a minimal decoder). If your build already has an HTML parser, use it instead of regex. The point is the boundary rule.

One design choice helps more than the function: build the visible heading and the JSON-LD headline from the same string, not from two code paths. Then they can't drift.

A Node test for the JSON-LD headline

The function fixes one build. A test keeps the next refactor from bringing the bug back. This one reads the built HTML, so it checks what a crawler fetches, not the template:

// jsonld.test.mjs  (run: node --test jsonld.test.mjs)
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { readFileSync, readdirSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';

const INLINE = /<\/?(a|abbr|b|bdi|bdo|cite|code|data|dfn|em|i|kbd|mark|q|s|samp|small|span|strong|sub|sup|time|u|var|wbr)\b[^>]*>/gi;
const ENT = { amp: '&', lt: '<', gt: '>', quot: '"', apos: "'", nbsp: ' ' };
const decode = (s) => s.replace(/&(#x[0-9a-f]+|#\d+|\w+);/gi, (m, e) =>
  e[0] !== '#' ? (ENT[e.toLowerCase()] ?? m)
  : String.fromCodePoint(e[1].toLowerCase() === 'x' ? parseInt(e.slice(2), 16) : +e.slice(1)));
const text = (html) => decode(html.replace(INLINE, '').replace(/<[^>]*>/g, ' '))
  .replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim();

function* pages(dir) {
  for (const e of readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true })) {
    const p = join(dir, e.name);
    if (e.isDirectory()) yield* pages(p);
    else if (e.name.endsWith('.html')) yield p;
  }
}

// every JSON-LD block, any attribute order
const blocks = (html) => [...html.matchAll(
  /<script\b[^>]*type=["']application\/ld\+json["'][^>]*>([\s\S]*?)<\/script>/gi
)].map((m) => JSON.parse(m[1]));

// walk objects, arrays and @graph; yield [key, string] for the fields we check
const FIELDS = new Set(['headline', 'name', 'description']);
function* fields(node) {
  if (Array.isArray(node)) for (const n of node) yield* fields(n);
  else if (node && typeof node === 'object') {
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(node)) {
      if (FIELDS.has(k) && typeof v === 'string') yield [k, v];
      else yield* fields(v);
    }
  }
}

const SPACE_BEFORE_PUNCT = / [,.;:!?)]/;

for (const file of pages(process.env.DIST ?? 'dist')) {
  test(file, () => {
    const html = readFileSync(file, 'utf8');
    const found = [...fields(blocks(html))];
    for (const [key, value] of found) {
      assert.doesNotMatch(value, SPACE_BEFORE_PUNCT, `${key}: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
    }
    const h1 = html.match(/<h1\b[^>]*>([\s\S]*?)<\/h1>/i);
    const headline = found.find(([k]) => k === 'headline');
    if (h1 && headline) assert.equal(headline[1], text(h1[1]));
  });
}

I ran it against four small fixture pages: a correct article, the broken headline, a page with &, ' and an @graph, and a FAQPage with no heading and a bad question name. Excerpt of the spec reporter output (node --test --test-reporter=spec, Node 22):

✖ dist/bad/index.html (2.665891ms)
✔ dist/entity/index.html (1.36117ms)
✖ dist/faq/index.html (1.048332ms)
✔ dist/good/index.html (0.35228ms)
...
  AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: headline: "Your IP , plainly"
...
  AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: name: "Can someone see my <em>IP</em> ?"

The two assertions catch different things:

  • Equality catches any drift between the visible heading and the headline, whatever the cause. The entity fixture passes because text() decodes & and ' before comparing.
  • The punctuation regex runs on every headline, name and description in every block, including @graph and nested FAQ questions. That covers pages with no heading to compare against.

The regex has false positives. I checked these in Node and all three match: Learn .NET in a weekend, Wait ... what, and French spacing like Bonjour !. Add exceptions if your copy has them.

Checking it by hand

Two free tools show you the parsed JSON-LD for a URL or a pasted snippet:

  • Google's Rich Results Test
  • The Schema Markup Validator

A stray space is valid Text, so there is nothing for them to flag. They show you the string, and you have to read it. That's why the automated test matters more than the manual check.

The rule

I built MyIPScan, a network privacy toolkit, and this bug sat in its structured data on 62 pages while every page looked fine.

Test the copy you don't look at. Visual QA only checks the page humans see.

title: Trajectory Forcing: Exploiting Diffusion Trajectories for Autoregressive Long Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.09096v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive (AR) modeling is arguably the only way to extend a fixed-length video diffusion model to longer or even streaming videos. However, existing AR diffusion methods use only the previously predicted chunk as context for the next, discarding the intermediate predictions that constitute the chunk's generation history. In contrast, conventional AR models such as LLMs condition on the entire history of preceding tokens. To this end, we propose Trajectory Forcing (TraF), an AR diffusion method that exploits the denoising trajectories of previous video chunks as context. TraF operates under two training regimes: (1) with ground-truth videos, where pseudo-trajectories are constructed from Gaussian interpolations and re-predicted by the model, and (2) with a teacher model, where real trajectories are obtained from the student's own denoising rollout. The first regime naturally provides a strong initialization for the second. On the 5-second VBench benchmark, TraF achieves a Total score of 85.15, outperforming Self Forcing (+0.84) and Causal Forcing (+1.11), with Quality and Semantic improving simultaneously. On 30-second generation---6$\times$ the training horizon---TraF achieves the highest overall quality among all compared methods.

title: Contextuality and Contradictions: Exploring Real-World Identifications of AI-Generated Writing
description:
arXiv:2611.08704v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI-generated content spreads into nearly every domain of human interaction, practices and discourses of AI detection, both formal and informal, have become an everyday part of how people interact with text and with each other. In this paper, we explore the real-world practices and discourses of AI identification that have emerged in response to a shifting discursive landscape where the human provenance of a text can no longer be taken for granted. We pair qualitative coding with computational analysis of lexical change, grounded in linguistic anthropological perspectives on language and communication, to investigate AI identifications among English Wikipedia editors and students. We find that these identifications draw on a diversity of evidentiary types, from discrete textual features and judgments about content to circular sense-making claims and presumptions about the author's moral character, and that they are contradictory, dynamic, and contextually dependent. In practice, what often motivates an AI identification is not the presence of any specific textual element, but pragmatic infelicity: a perceived mismatch between the elements present and those deemed appropriate within the text's particular context. Consequently, real-world identifications of AI-generated writing do not merely neutrally point out the perceived presence of "AI-like" features, but can be leveraged as a discursive resource to maintain and define sociolinguistic norms: what can be said in a given context, what is appropriate, and, ultimately, what is human. Further, the design and implementation of systems and tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property of text may therefore inherit, and enforce at scale, the norms of whichever contexts they were trained on.

title: Contact Form UX: Reduce Friction Without Losing Useful Requests
description:
A contact form succeeds when a visitor understands what is being requested, can correct mistakes, and receives a reliable confirmation. Reducing fields may remove friction, but it does not guarantee more completed submissions: a question can be necessary for the team to respond. Start with the user's goal, test the full journey, and measure confirmed outcomes.

Ask for a reason behind each field

Describe what the team does after a submission. If a written response is sufficient, an email address and message may be enough. A callback could require a phone number and an appropriate time. For every field, ask who uses the answer and whether it can be obtained later. Remove fields without a clear purpose and label optional information consistently.

For a consultation, a form might ask for a preferred contact method, the corresponding address or number, and a description of the question. A support form may need an order number instead. Agree on the minimum with the team handling requests: an excessively short form that triggers many follow-up questions can also frustrate users.

Explain labels, formats, and the next step

Use visible labels associated with their inputs. Placeholder text alone can disappear once someone types, leaving them uncertain about the field. Explain why sensitive information is needed: “Email address — we will send our reply here” is more informative than an unexplained input.

Show required formats near the field when truly necessary. Accept reasonable variations where possible and avoid rejecting valid data with an overly narrow custom rule. Validation and safe processing still belong on the server. Use a specific button label such as “Send question” rather than an ambiguous “OK.”

Before submission, explain who receives the request and what happens next. Give a response time only when the organization can reasonably meet it.

Make errors recoverable

An error should identify the field and tell the person what to fix. “Enter an email address in the form name@example.com” is more useful than “Invalid data.” Do not rely on color alone. Associate the message with the field and provide a clear summary when several fields need attention.

Preserve the other entered values. Losing a carefully written message after a validation error makes a retry much harder. If validation runs while someone is typing, avoid announcing an error before they have finished. Test that keyboard users and screen-reader users can find and understand the error.

For a network failure, say that the submission has not been confirmed, preserve the input, and offer an appropriate next action or alternative contact channel. Do not expose internal server details. A timeout is ambiguous: the server might have stored the request while the response was lost. Design duplicate protection and a way to check status rather than blindly claiming success.

Test mobile and keyboard access

Walk through the form without a mouse. Is focus visible? Does the order make sense? Can each control be operated, and are error messages discoverable? Check zoom and contrast as well. The W3C forms tutorial provides guidance on labels, instructions, and notifications.

On a phone, check field width, button placement, and whether labels remain visible. Appropriate input types and autocomplete attributes can help, but actual behavior varies between devices and browsers. Test real layouts rather than assuming the correct keyboard always appears.

For a modal form, verify focus management, a clear way to close the dialog, and a sensible return to the trigger. For an inline form, keep the purpose and context nearby. In both cases visitors should understand where their information is going.

Build trust without collecting unnecessary data

Explain the purpose of the data, who receives it, and where users can learn about processing. Applicable notices and consent depend on the purpose and context; review them with the person responsible for data handling. Avoid hiding optional marketing consent inside the core request.

Spam controls should address real risks without blocking legitimate users. Server-side rate limits, validation, and monitoring can form part of the solution. If an extra challenge is used, test an accessible alternative. For file uploads, define permitted types and size limits, safe storage, and server-side checks; a filename extension or browser validation alone is not enough.

Confirm the request, not just the click

Show a submitting state and prevent accidental repeated activation while a request is being processed. After confirmed storage, display a clear success message and the actual next step. Make the notification available to assistive technology.

Then check the operational side: did the submission reach the system of record, did the right team receive the notification, and is someone responsible for responding? A success animation cannot compensate for a lost request.

Measure the journey carefully

Define a denominator before comparing results. For example, completion rate can be confirmed submissions divided by started form attempts in the same period. Decide whether the unit is an attempt or a person and how events are deduplicated. A button click is not a confirmed submission.

Aggregate events such as form view, start, validation-error category, and confirmed submission. Do not send entered messages, passwords, or personal data to analytics. Account for consent settings and missing observations.

Compare similar traffic sources, devices, and periods. With few visits, a small number of submissions can move the percentage sharply. If the offer or advertising changed at the same time, avoid attributing the difference to one field. Where traffic permits, compare alternatives in a controlled way and check the quality of requests as well as their count.

A practical review

  1. Ask the receiving team why each field exists.
  2. Observe representative users on desktop and mobile.
  3. Test labels, errors, focus, and retained values using a keyboard.
  4. Simulate network failures and duplicate submissions on a test system.
  5. Verify data handling and delivery to the responsible team.
  6. Compare outcomes over a comparable period and revisit the remaining friction.

Start with one meaningful improvement, such as explaining a required phone number or preserving text after an error. Then test the entire path from opening the form to a confirmed request.

title: Pertulma Ultramarina: construyendo un directorio náutico bilingüe desde cero
description:
Entre el 7 y el 8 de noviembre estuve trabajando en Pertulma Ultramarina, un directorio náutico en español e inglés que reúne contenido sobre marinas, puertos deportivos, amarres y mantenimiento de embarcaciones.

Estas primeras jornadas tuvieron dos frentes: poner en marcha la infraestructura y ajustar la experiencia de navegación. Porque publicar una web es una cosa; conseguir que alguien entienda qué ofrece y encuentre por dónde empezar es otra.

Del dominio a una web en producción

El primer paso fue conectar el dominio, registrado en Namecheap, con Cloudflare y Netlify. Utilicé Aside Browser para trabajar sobre la configuración y dejar montada la base del sitio.

También quedó verificada la propiedad en Google Search Console y documentamos la configuración inicial de medición con GA4 y Google Tag Manager, apoyándonos en Claude Code.

Para orientar el contenido, seleccionamos una primera lista de 58 palabras clave en Ubersuggest, relacionadas con marinas, amarres, puertos deportivos y reparación de motores fueraborda.

No son 58 posiciones ganadas: son el punto de partida para investigar, organizar contenido y seguir su evolución.

Una portada que ayude a explorar

Buena parte de las iteraciones posteriores estuvo en la interfaz.

Uno de los ajustes fue simplificar el encabezado principal: Pertulma Ultramarina. La explicación del proyecto queda separada del nombre, en lugar de intentar meter toda la propuesta dentro de un título demasiado largo.

La portada actual incorpora:

  • Un buscador por puerto, ciudad o motor.
  • Un selector de categorías náuticas.
  • Accesos directos al directorio y a las guías.
  • Enlaces a ubicaciones como Cartagena, Miami y Palma de Mallorca.
  • Navegación hacia las secciones de información y contacto, con acceso a la versión en inglés.

La intención es ofrecer distintas formas de entrar al contenido: por ubicación, por servicio o por una consulta técnica.

Directorio y guías, conectados

El proyecto combina dos tipos de contenido: fichas de empresas y lugares, y artículos sobre temas náuticos.

La biblioteca ya muestra guías sobre puertos deportivos, alquiler de amarres, repuestos para motores fueraborda y mantenimiento. La idea es que el usuario pueda pasar de entender un problema a explorar servicios relacionados sin recorrer páginas desconectadas.

Qué hemos conseguido hasta ahora

El resultado tangible es una web publicada, con estructura bilingüe, contenido accesible y nuevas rutas de navegación desde la portada.

También observamos respuestas de Google que identificaban el proyecto como directorio náutico. Es una primera señal de descubrimiento, no una prueba de tráfico sostenido ni de posicionamiento consolidado.

Todavía queda trabajo de simplificación y revisión. El criterio para las siguientes iteraciones es concreto: que cada sección explique mejor su función y facilite el siguiente paso.

Puedes explorar la versión actual de Pertulma Ultramarina.

title: Vercel Daemons is now in public beta
description:
Vercel Daemons is now in public beta, allowing you to run long-running processes that pull and execute work from Vercel Queues, databases, or third-party systems without requiring an HTTP server:

  • Consumers using Vercel Queues poll mode, Celery, BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or Kafka.

  • Temporal or Cadence workers that long-poll their task queues.

  • Self-hosted CI runners for GitHub Actions, GitLab, or CircleCI that poll for jobs without requiring inbound connections.

Daemons run containers on Fluid compute and deploy alongside your app in the same project. Vercel builds your image and maintains the instance count you configure in each region, restarting instances that exit or crash.

Get started by packaging your application and dependencies in a Dockerfile or Containerfile, then adding a daemons entry to one configuration file at your project root. This example uses worker/Dockerfile to run one Celery worker in iad1 (Washington, D.C.):

Set any connection details your worker needs in your project's production environment variables, then deploy to production. Vercel starts the configured instances, and their output appears in your project's Logs. CPU and memory metrics are available with Observability Plus.

Learn more in the Vercel Daemons documentation and read the complete guide.

title: CoMET: Tracking the Shared Pose Error of Roadside Messages for Asynchronous Vehicle-Infrastructure Cooperative 3D Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.09121v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A roadside sensor can detect vehicles hidden from the ego vehicle, but a pose error shifts every detection in the same message. We study asynchronous vehicle-infrastructure cooperative 3D detection on V2X-Seq using only information available at decision time, without ground truth, future frames, or per-pair calibration offsets at inference. Objects seen by both sensors reveal the shared translation, but even at zero added delay, 38% of validation messages have no matched pair. We propose CoMET (Common-Mode Error Tracking), which estimates this translation over time. At each message arrival, CoMET matches vehicle and roadside detections, estimates the offset from mutually nearest pairs, and updates a Kalman filter for that sender. When no pair matches, the filter carries its estimate forward. The correction applies to all roadside boxes, including those unseen by the ego vehicle. The estimator has no learned parameters; a separate frozen head ranks the merged detections. Across four delays from 0 to 400 ms on 21 validation sequences, CoMET averages 66.63 bird's-eye-view AP at IoU 0.7, compared with 63.18 for the same late fusion using uncorrected online poses and 62.96 for the best intermediate-fusion baseline. Across five detectors from three architectures, CoMET gains 2.2 to 3.5 AP points over online poses and 0.3 to 0.6 over estimating the offset from the current message alone. We find that the benchmark uses a zero offset as a placeholder in 28% of validation messages and that its offset search reaches the boundary in 45% of the rest. These offsets affect the labels for objects seen only from the roadside. Under two alternative label references, CoMET improves on uncorrected online poses in every evaluated population. Retraining intermediate fusion with CoMET poses and corrected labels improves detection on all three architectures tested, with statistically significant gains on two.

title: LEF-JEPA: Denoising-Trained Latent Energy Fields for Spatial Representation Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.08989v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) that applies prediction supervision only at masked positions struggles to clearly capture object shapes and boundaries in its latent representations. We further observe that some existing methods improve spatial structure while also retaining rich variations in texture and color. However, preserving more low-level visual information does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action. This raises a key question: how can we strengthen the spatial structure in latent representations that supports prediction and action without over-encoding these details? We introduce LEF-JEPA, which learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and transfers this supervision to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint; the energy module is used only during pretraining and adds no inference overhead. To reduce the cost of energy optimization during pretraining, we further construct a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that allows low-energy-state search to be performed by specialized Ising solvers. On physical hardware, we validate the feasibility of achieving lower forward latency with fewer local updates. Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation protocol, both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in image classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.
