title: I Put Every School in Jordan Into One API: 2,601 Schools, 42 Directorates
description:
I build websites for a living, but the project I am proudest of is the platform for the Future Thinkers Club, a club for Jordanian school students who want to build things, read together, and start small projects. The platform lives at https://f-thinkers.vercel.app, and one of its most useful parts is something you never see on the homepage: a complete dataset of every school in Jordan.

The problem: students need to pick their school

When a student signs up, they pick their school. That sounds simple until you ask where the list comes from. Jordan has thousands of schools, grouped by governorate and then by directorate, the administrative areas the Ministry of Education uses. There was no tidy list I could just plug in, so I built one.

The dataset covers 12 governorates, 42 directorates, and 2,601 schools, ordered by the Ministry's official directorate structure. The API returns real data: ask for a directorate and you get its schools, ask for a governorate and you get its directorates.

How it fits into the platform

The platform itself is React on the frontend and Python on the backend, with Turso as the database. The schools data sits behind an API endpoint, so the signup form, the school directory, and anything else that needs a school list all read from the same source. One dataset, used everywhere, instead of a copy pasted into every page.

Getting the structure right mattered more than getting it fast. A school in the wrong directorate is worse than a missing school, because a student trusting the list would land in the wrong place. So the data follows the official structure: governorate, then directorate, then school.

What it enables

With the dataset in place, students from different schools across Jordan can find each other on the same platform, join the same club, and form teams across schools. A school list sounds like boring infrastructure, and it is. But it is the piece that makes everything else on the platform work: you cannot network students across schools if the platform does not know which schools exist.

The project is one of the 17 live builds on my portfolio at https://rayyans-showroom.vercel.app/projects/future-thinkers. If you are building anything that needs a real, structured dataset, my advice is simple: spend the time on the structure first. The features you build on top of it will be easy. The features you build on a messy dataset will not.

title: eSharp: Diffusion-based Sharp Monocular Metric Event-to-Depth Estimation
description:
arXiv:2611.08731v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Depth perception is fundamental for autonomous navigation, industrial inspection, and mixed-reality systems. It often operates under strict constraints on power and form factor. In such cases, monocular depth estimation (MDE) is often used. Even as recent advances continue to improve monocular depth quality, conventional frame-based MDE systems remain challenged by fast motion and high-dynamic-range scenes. This work introduces eSharp, an MDE framework that addresses these problems using an event camera. eSharp repurposes pretrained diffusion priors for event-only MDE and produces accurate metric depth with unparalleled sharpness on real data. Real-world event datasets provide only sparse LiDAR depth maps for ground-truth supervision, making dense prediction challenging. We address this limitation through cross-modal distillation, using LiDAR-calibrated dense pseudo-labels generated from a spatially co-registered frame camera to train eSharp. Experiments show that eSharp outperforms prior event-to-depth baselines in both metric-depth accuracy and spatial fidelity, establishing diffusion models as a promising foundation for event-driven 3D perception.

title: osFoundry, Codex को handoff प्रस्तावित करने के लिए एक tool और run शुरू करने के लिए अलग tool क्यों देता है?
description:
Sign in करने से पहले जब Codex CLI पहली बार osFoundry पर कोई session tool call करता है, तो उसे यह जवाब मिलता है:

POST /api/v1/external-mcp  {"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"propose_session_handoff","arguments":{}}}

HTTP/2 401
www-authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.osfoundry.io/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/api/v1/external-mcp",
                  error="invalid_token", error_description="Connect osFoundry to continue"

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{"isError":true,
 "content":[{"type":"text","text":"Authentication required"}], …}}

initialize और tools/list बिना token के जवाब देते हैं, यानी किसी के sign in करने से पहले ही client सभी 59 tools देख सकता है। इनमें से दो ऐसे लगते हैं जैसे एक ही काम करते हों:

{"name": "propose_session_handoff",
 "description": "Send a scoped task and context summary to the owner of an invited session. The owner must accept before a run is queued.",
 "required": ["session_type","session_id","goal","context_summary","requested_output","idempotency_key"],
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "openWorldHint": true, "destructiveHint": true},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:write"]}]}

{"name": "request_session_run",
 "description": "Queue a bounded goal for an agent, team, or loop session where this assistant is an invited runner. The osFoundry runtime executes the task when available.",
 "required": ["session_type","session_id","goal","idempotency_key"],
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "openWorldHint": false, "destructiveHint": true},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:run"]}]}

दोनों का नतीजा यही है कि कोई session काम करता है। इस post के बाकी हिस्से में बात है कि इन्हें अलग क्यों रखा गया है, हर एक पर कौन-सी सीमाएँ लगी हैं, और client side का एक Python rebuild जो इन सीमाओं को live schemas के against जाँचता है।

दोनों calls में फ़र्क क्या है?

हाँ कौन कहता है, और कब।

Handoff किसी इंसान से अभी पूछता है। Owner को notification मिलती है ("Codex CLI requests a handoff")। Session का Handoffs tab इसे "Outside assistant requests" (बाहरी assistants की requests) के नीचे दिखाता है, साथ में goal, एक खुलने वाला "Context and expected output" हिस्सा और लाइन "Up to N rounds on your agent runtime"। जब तक कोई Accept and run पर click नहीं करता, कुछ भी queue में नहीं जाता। Click होने पर web client {decision: "accept"} को /agent-sessions/{id}/external-handoffs/{handoff_id}/decision पर भेजता है, और toast में लिखा आता है "Handoff accepted and run queued"। Handoff की row pending से accepted, declined या cancelled में जाती है।

Run को पहले ही मंज़ूरी मिल चुकी होती है। Owner ने Connected tab में connection को Runner seat दी, और वही हाँ है। वहाँ का help text: "Invite it to a session as Contributor to post notes and propose handoffs, or Runner to also request runs. A handoff still needs the session owner's approval." Sign-in page पर run scope लिखा है "Run sessions where you grant a runner role"।

अगर आप दोनों को needs_approval flag वाले एक tool में मिला दें, तो caller तय करेगा कि किसी इंसान से पूछा जाए या नहीं। दो tools होने से यह फ़ैसला owner की तरफ़ रहता है, ऐसी दो जगहों पर जिन्हें caller छू नहीं सकता: OAuth scope (osfoundry:write बनाम osfoundry:run) और seat (Contributor बनाम Runner)। जिस Codex config में scopes के अंदर osfoundry:run नहीं है, वह Runner seat पर होते हुए भी run शुरू नहीं कर सकता।

Annotations भी इसी बँटवारे पर चलते हैं। propose_session_handoff में openWorldHint: true है, क्योंकि इसका output call के बाहर किसी इंसान तक पहुँचता है। request_session_run में openWorldHint: false है, क्योंकि यह सिर्फ़ उस session की queue को छूता है जिसने पहले से सहमति दी है। दोनों destructiveHint: true हैं, इसलिए Codex के default_tools_approval_mode = "writes" पर चलने वाला client दोनों में से किसी से भी पहले पूछता है।

Handoff में context summary ज़रूरी क्यों है?

क्योंकि कुछ भी चलने से पहले कोई इंसान उसे पढ़ता है। context_summary और requested_output handoff में ज़रूरी हैं और run में होते ही नहीं। Owner यह तय कर रहा है कि अपने session का runtime इस पर खर्च करे या नहीं, और सिर्फ़ "fix the export" से यह तय नहीं हो पाता। Runner के पास यह भरोसा पहले से है, इसलिए run को सिर्फ़ एक goal चाहिए।

Limits भी अलग हैं। Handoff का goal 5,000 characters पर रुकता है, साथ में 5,000 context के लिए और 1,000 requested output के लिए। Run का goal 10,000 तक जा सकता है। असल में run का goal ही context भी ले जाता है, क्योंकि उसके लिए कोई और field नहीं है।

Codex वापस क्या पढ़ सकता है?

Session में जितना है, उससे कम:

  • read_session_task_result: "the status and attributed runtime result for one task started by this connection"। किसी दूसरे connection का task id यहाँ काम नहीं आता।
  • read_session_mail: "notes addressed to this connection and notes it posted", हर page पर 1 से 20, पुराने notes के लिए before_id। "Internal agent analysis is excluded."
  • read_session_state: उस session का मौजूदा status और हाल के tasks, जिसमें connection जुड़ा है।
  • post_session_note: एक attributed note, जिसका जवाब agents "the returned external sender slug" के ज़रिए दे सकते हैं। यह "does not trigger an automatic run", इसलिए note के सहारे owner के click को bypass नहीं किया जा सकता।

Team session में ये notes Team mail में connection के display name और "outside assistant" label के साथ दिखते हैं।

Rebuild

इस Mac पर कोई codex binary install नहीं है, इसलिए client का काम handoff_sim.py (करीब 220 lines) करता है। यह तीन काम करता है:

  1. बिना token के live server को call करता है: initialize, tools/list और एक tools/call, हर एक 15 बार, और tool list save करता है।
  2. jsonschema (Draft 2020-12) से बारह argument cases को live inputSchemas के against validate करता है, ताकि सीमाओं के बारे में कुछ भी अंदाज़े से न हो।
  3. Seats, scopes, owner के फ़ैसलों और idempotency का एक छोटा in-memory model चलाता है। osFoundry का server code public नहीं है, इसलिए यह हिस्सा tool descriptions और handoffs दिखाने वाले web client के आधार पर दोबारा बनाया गया है। इसके responses model के हैं, server के नहीं। 
$ uv run --with tiktoken --with jsonschema python3 handoff_sim.py

Wire 

initialize             HTTP 200  median  566.3  p90  799.0
tools/list             HTTP 200  median  559.7  p90  937.7
tools/call (no token)  HTTP 401  median  482.6  p90  677.0

Milliseconds में, जापान में रखे इस Mac से CloudFront के KIX edge के रास्ते नापे गए, इसलिए ये numbers server से ज़्यादा route के बारे में बताते हैं। असली बात shape है। Discovery मुफ़्त है और इतनी तेज़ है कि हर Codex start पर चलाई जा सके। पहली असली call की कीमत एक 401 round trip है, और उस 401 में resource_metadata आता है, जिससे Codex बिना बताए OAuth server ढूँढ लेता है।

सात session tools पूरी list के 10,197 tokens में से 1,152 tokens हैं (11.3%, cl100k_base, इसलिए Codex के अपने tokenizer के लिए इसे अनुमान ही मानें)। enabled_tools में सिर्फ़ इन्हें रखने से prompt छोटा रहता है।

सीमाएँ

Tool Scope ज़रूरी fields Limits
propose_session_handoff write 6 goal 5,000, context 5,000, output 1,000, max_rounds 1–10
cancel_session_handoff write 1 सिर्फ़ handoff_id
request_session_run run 4 goal 10,000, max_rounds 1–10
read_session_state read 2 कोई नहीं
read_session_task_result read 3 कोई नहीं
read_session_mail read 2 limit 1–20
post_session_note write 5 subject 200, body 10,000

Live schemas के against बारह cases:

propose_session_handoff   6,000-char goal        REJECT maxLength: goal
request_session_run       6,000-char goal        ok
propose_session_handoff   no context_summary     REJECT required
propose_session_handoff   max_rounds omitted     ok
request_session_run       max_rounds 0           REJECT minimum: max_rounds
request_session_run       max_rounds 11          REJECT maximum: max_rounds
request_session_run       no idempotency_key     REJECT required
request_session_run       session_type 'room'    REJECT enum: session_type
request_session_run       extra field 'model'    REJECT additionalProperties
read_session_mail         limit 21               REJECT maximum: limit
post_session_note         201-char subject       REJECT maxLength: subject
cancel_session_handoff    only handoff_id        ok

इनमें से दो पर दोबारा नज़र डालनी चाहिए। वही 6,000 characters का goal run के तौर पर ठीक है और handoff के तौर पर बहुत लंबा। जो client एक लंबा prompt बनाकर जो भी tool उपलब्ध हो उसे भेज देता है, वह यहीं अटकेगा। और additionalProperties: false एक model field को लौटा देता है: caller session का model नहीं चुन सकता। Session अपनी settings पर ही चलता है।

max_rounds दोनों में optional है। Schemas कोई default नहीं बताते, इसलिए अगर यह number आपके लिए मायने रखता है, तो उसे भेजें।

Seats, cancel और accept (model) 

tool                      observer contributor runner
propose_session_handoff   -        yes         yes
cancel_session_handoff    -        yes         yes
request_session_run       -        -           yes
read_session_state        yes      yes         yes
read_session_task_result  yes      yes         yes
read_session_mail         yes      yes         yes
post_session_note         -        yes         yes
runner seat, token without osfoundry:run -> {'error': 'token lacks osfoundry:run'}

cancel while pending -> {'status': 'cancelled'}
owner clicks Accept after cancel -> cancelled
owner accepts -> accepted | cancel after -> {'error': 'already accepted'}
another connection reads that task -> {'error': 'not a task started by this connection'}

यह matrix Connected tab के help text को table में बदलकर बनाया गया है। दिलचस्प rule cancel window का है। cancel_session_handoff की description के मुताबिक यह "before its owner accepts it" काम करता है, यानी जो पहले हो, वही जीतता है। एक बार run queue में चला गया, तो उसे वापस लेना caller के हाथ में नहीं रहता। इसी वजह से cancel सिर्फ़ एक handoff_id लेता है: कोई state भेजनी नहीं है, बस एक pending row बंद करनी है।

खोए हुए responses

हर write में idempotency_key ज़रूरी है। इससे क्या मिलता है, यह देखने के लिए model 1,000 request_session_run calls भेजता है, 20% responses गिरा देता है (seed 7) और client को उसी key के साथ तीन बार तक retry करने देता है:

server honours idempotency_key=True  calls sent 1276  tasks queued 1000  duplicates 0
server honours idempotency_key=False calls sent 1276  tasks queued 1276  duplicates 276

किसी और के runtime पर 276 extra runs, ठीक इसी case के लिए key ज़रूरी रखी गई है। Timeout के बाद retry करने वाला हर client इससे टकराएगा, और जो run पहले ही शुरू हो चुका है, उसे आप दो बार नहीं चाहेंगे। Key को optional की जगह required रखने का मतलब है कि कोई client उसे भूल नहीं सकता।

पूरी script को Apple M1 पर 26.4 s wall-clock time लगा। लगभग सारा समय 45 network calls में गया, और user CPU time 0.37 s था।

अगर आप इसे खुद wire करें

  • "किसी इंसान से पूछना" और "पहले से मिली अनुमति पर काम करना" को दो scopes वाले दो tools में बाँटें, ताकि owner की पसंद token और seat में रहे, caller के set किए argument में नहीं।
  • जिन fields की इंसान को फ़ैसला लेने के लिए ज़रूरत है (context_summary, requested_output), उन्हें सिर्फ़ proposal पर ज़रूरी बनाएँ, और उनकी limit run के goal से कड़ी रखें।
  • Caller को सिर्फ़ तब तक cancel करने दें जब तक request pending है। Accept होने के बाद काम रोकना owner का काम है।
  • हर read-back को उसी तक सीमित रखें जो इस connection ने शुरू किया या जो इसे भेजा गया, और session का internal analysis उससे बाहर रखें।
  • हर write पर idempotency_key ज़रूरी बनाएँ, और repeat होने पर पहला result लौटाएँ।
  • Schema को additionalProperties: false से बंद करें, ताकि caller ऐसा model या tool list न घुसा सके जो session ने नहीं चुनी।

osFoundry के अपने agents steps के बीच काम कैसे आगे बढ़ाते हैं, यह handoffs page पर है। नीचे के protocol के लिए MCP glossary entry देखें।

title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
description:
arXiv:2611.08551v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, na\"ive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.

title: How to get the exact HEX code from any image (and turn it into a CSS or Tailwind palette)
description:
Every front-end developer has been there: a designer sends a screenshot instead of a Figma file, a client wants "the blue from our logo", or you're rebuilding a site and nobody remembers the brand colors. You need exact color codes, and you need them fast.

Here's the workflow I use, plus a few traps that make "the color from the image" less obvious than it sounds.

Why the color you pick is often wrong

Photos are noisy. Two neighbouring pixels on a wall that looks flat can differ by several shades because of JPEG compression, lighting and sensor noise. If you click one random pixel, you get a color, not the color a person would describe.

Two fixes:

  1. Average a small area. Sampling a 5×5 block (25 pixels) and averaging gives a much steadier value than a single pixel.
  2. Zoom before you click. Thin lines, text and logo edges are only a few pixels wide. A pixel-level magnifier stops you landing on the anti-aliased edge, which is a blend of two colors.

Which format should you copy?

The same color can be written several ways, and each has a job:

Format Example Use it for
HEX #1B8A8F CSS, Figma, Canva, brand guides
RGB rgb(27, 138, 143) Code, canvas, game engines
HSL hsl(183, 68%, 33%) Making a color lighter or darker in CSS
CMYK cmyk(81%, 3%, 0%, 44%) A starting point for print (confirm with a proof)
LAB lab(52, -27, -11) Comparing how different two colors look

For anything on screen, HEX is the default. HSL is underrated: once a brand color is in HSL, building hover and disabled states is just changing the lightness value:

:root {
  --brand: hsl(183 68% 33%);
  --brand-hover: hsl(183 68% 28%);
  --brand-muted: hsl(183 30% 85%);
}

From one color to a whole palette

Often you want the 5–8 main colors of an image, not a single pixel. Palette extraction groups similar pixels together (k-means clustering is the usual approach) and returns the center of each group. That gives you a palette that reflects what the image actually looks like, rather than the single most common pixel.

Once you have it, export it straight into your project instead of copying codes one by one:

// tailwind.config.js
module.exports = {
  theme: {
    extend: {
      colors: {
        brand: {
          1: '#879CAC',
          2: '#6A6C5B',
          3: '#283023',
          4: '#C6D0D4',
          5: '#297094',
        },
      },
    },
  },
};

Don't forget contrast

A color pulled from a photo looks great as an accent and often fails as text. Check it against WCAG before you ship: 4.5:1 for normal text (AA) and 3:1 for large text. A mid-tone teal like #2E7390 passes AA on white (5.29:1) but not on black (3.97:1), which surprises people.

The tool I use

I built ColorPickImage for exactly this workflow. You upload, paste (Ctrl+V) or drop an image, click with a pixel magnifier, and get HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV, CMYK and LAB with one click. It averages 1×1 up to 9×9 pixels and extracts a 4–12 color palette that exports as CSS variables, SCSS, Tailwind, JSON, PNG or SVG. It runs entirely in the browser, so client screenshots never leave your machine, and there's no sign-up.

In Chrome and Edge it can also pick colors from anywhere on your screen (other tabs, apps or videos) using the EyeDropper API, which is handy when the "image" is a live website.

Quick checklist

  • Zoom in before you click
  • Average 5×5 for photos, 1×1 for flat UI screenshots
  • Copy HEX for the web, convert to HSL for variants
  • Extract a palette rather than picking colors one by one
  • Check contrast before using a picked color for text

What's your workflow when someone sends you a screenshot instead of a design file?

title: I audited AI-built Supabase apps. These are the security bugs I keep finding
description:
Tools like Lovable, Bolt and Cursor can take you from idea to working app in a weekend. The demo works, the UI looks great, and you are ready to launch.

But "it works" and "it's safe to put real users on it" are not the same thing. I audit React + Supabase apps built with AI tools, and the same problems show up again and again. Here are the five that matter most, and how to check your own app in a few minutes.

1. Trusting IDs sent by the client

This is the most serious one. A server function receives something like notebook_id or order_id from the request, then reads or writes data with the service role key, which bypasses Row Level Security.

The function checks that the user is logged in, but not that the ID belongs to them. Any signed-in user can send someone else's ID and get their data.

Fix: before using an ID from the request, look it up with the caller's own session (so RLS applies), or check ownership explicitly.

2. Webhooks and callbacks that anyone can call

Payment webhooks and "job finished" callbacks often run without any secret check. Anyone who finds the URL can send fake payments or overwrite records.

Fix: verify the provider's signature, or require a long random token in the URL or a header.

3. RLS that is on, but not complete

RLS is enabled, but:

  • insert and update policies have no with check, so users can create rows for other users;
  • users can update their own profile, including the role column;
  • a view or a SECURITY DEFINER function quietly bypasses RLS.

Fix: read every policy, add with check, restrict updatable columns, and use security_invoker = true on views.

4. Data left in the browser

Persisted caches (React Query, Zustand, localStorage) keep customer data after logout. On a shared device, the next user sees it. And hard-coded seed data in src/ is shipped to every visitor, logged in or not.

Fix: clear caches on sign-out, and never put real data in the frontend source.

5. Mixing up public and secret keys

The Supabase anon / publishable key in your frontend is fine. It is designed to be public. The real problem is a service role key with a VITE_ prefix, or RLS that does not protect your tables.

The full checklist

I turned everything I check into a free checklist, with SQL queries you can run in the Supabase SQL editor:

👉 Lovable + Supabase Security Checklist

Only run these checks on apps you own or are authorized to test.

If you would rather have someone go through it for you, I offer audits and fixes for AI-built apps on Fiverr. Questions are welcome in the comments.

title: How to Find and Reclaim Unused Microsoft 365 Licences
description:
Short answer: build a report that flags possible waste, then have an administrator verify each account, workload, mailbox, group assignment and contract before changing anything. A disabled account or a long gap in sign-in activity is a reason to investigate, not automatic proof that a licence can be removed.

This report-first method helps teams find unused Microsoft 365 licences without disrupting work. It separates observable signals from decisions and keeps removal under human approval.

Start with evidence, not an automatic removal

A good licence assignment review starts with a dated inventory of users, account state, assigned products and service plans, assignment source, sign-in indicators, mailbox type and business owner. Microsoft Graph's licenseDetails endpoint returns details for licences assigned directly and through licensed-group membership. Its documentation identifies delegated LicenseAssignment.Read.All as the least privileged permission for that operation and says application permissions are not supported. This is a Microsoft API reference; administrators should confirm the current permission model and their approved reporting route before use.

Keep the extract limited to fields needed for the review, store it in an approved location and record when it was generated. A spreadsheet or read-only CSV report is enough to begin. Do not start by removing assignments or by treating a cost estimate as a realized saving.

Four signals worth reviewing

1. Disabled accounts that still have assignments

A disabled account with a paid product assigned is a strong prompt to ask whether the person has left, changed role, or still owns a service, workflow, mailbox or data. Check the account's owner and dependencies, group-based assignment rules, retention needs and any handover period. If the account is an emergency, service or shared workload identity, use the organization's specific policy instead of an employee rule.

2. Long gaps since sign-in

Microsoft 365 sign-in activity is one signal to review. Microsoft Entra's inactive-account guidance explains how sign-in activity can help investigate inactive accounts. It also stresses that an inactivity window depends on context. The documented lastSignInDateTime records an interactive sign-in attempt, which is not the same as proof of successful use. The page notes that displayed activity can take time to update; access to lastSuccessfulSignInDateTime has separate licensing and permission prerequisites.

Use a gap as a review threshold that your organization chooses. Check leave, seasonal patterns, non-interactive workloads and recent successful activity with the service owner. If the evidence is stale or missing, mark the candidate as uncertain rather than inactive.

3. Shared mailboxes

A shared mailbox licence needs its own review category. Microsoft's shared-mailbox guidance says a separate licence is not required in some situations, but lists exceptions tied to mailbox size, archiving, holds and advanced features. Verify the live mailbox configuration and current licensing terms before changing its assignment. A missing interactive sign-in is not a safe removal signal for a shared mailbox.

4. Duplicate or overlapping SKU assignments

Duplicate licence SKUs can look similar while providing different service plans, or the same entitlement can arrive by direct and group assignment. Compare the enabled services with the user's work, confirm the assignment source, and check whether a group rule will restore a removed licence. Label these rows "possible overlap" until an administrator and service owner verify the requirement.

Make the report useful to a reviewer

For each candidate, show the evidence and its date, why it was flagged, what remains unknown, the business or service owner, the next verification step and a status such as review, confirmed needed, approved to change or unresolved. Do not label a row "waste" just because an account is disabled or quiet. Keep the report separate from the action process: no automatic removal, no silent group changes and no unreviewed mailbox changes.

Before anyone acts, check dependent services, retention and legal holds, mailbox features, group membership and subscription commitments. The authorized administrator should make an approved change through the tenant's established process, document the decision and check that the user or service still works afterward. If a reviewer cannot establish the assignment's purpose, leave it in place until the right owner can decide.

Estimate savings carefully

Use the tenant's actual contract price, currency, renewal date and cancellation terms. A public list price may not match a negotiated rate, and a remaining commitment can mean that removing an assignment does not immediately reduce the bill. Keep confirmed changes separate from potential candidates, and state the assumptions behind any estimate.

A practical review checklist

  • Export a minimal, dated view of assignments and account signals.
  • Separate disabled users, long sign-in gaps, shared mailboxes and possible SKU overlap.
  • Confirm the signal with the account or service owner.
  • Check group assignments, enabled service plans, mailbox features and retention.
  • Verify actual contract and renewal terms before estimating savings.
  • Record approval before an authorized administrator changes anything.
  • Recheck the dependent service and assignment rule afterward.

Tools that help

The licence waste analyzer reviews a selected CSV locally in the browser. The Microsoft 365 licence cost calculator helps organize cost assumptions. Both are review aids: they do not connect to a tenant or remove licences.

Frequently asked questions

Does a disabled account always mean its licence is unused? No. Confirm its owner, services, group rules, retention requirements and any handover period first.

Does no recent sign-in prove a licence is not needed? No. Sign-in activity is a signal with timing and interpretation limits. Check with the owner and consider workload patterns.

Should a shared mailbox have its licence removed? Not without checking the mailbox's current size, archive, hold and feature requirements against Microsoft's current guidance.

Can duplicate products be removed automatically? This guide recommends human review. Similar names or overlapping assignments do not prove that an entitlement is redundant.

Originally published at cloudekhosting.com. Free Microsoft 365 and IT admin tools are at cloudekhosting.com/tools.

title: Discord Just Ditched Electron. Your App's 290MB Download Is a Choice
description:
Discord is dropping Electron and rebuilding its desktop app in Rust with GPUI. The news hit the Hacker News front page on November 7, and the replies split exactly the way you'd expect: one camp cheering, one camp saying "good luck rewriting everything," and a third camp quietly checking how big their own Electron app is.

The number that stuck with me: the Electron build of Discord reportedly sits around 290MB with two accounts signed in. Two hundred and ninety megabytes. For a chat app. An app whose core job is showing text messages and playing voice.

I keep thinking about that number, because it makes the whole argument in one figure. Desktop bloat is not a law of nature. It's a choice — one the industry made a decade ago, and one Discord has now decided to unmake.

Electron made sense in 2016. That's the honest part.

Credit where it's due, because the "Electron is trash" crowd likes to forget this: Electron let small teams ship a real desktop app with the people they already had. One codebase, web tech, Windows and Mac on day one. No hiring a C++ team. No maintaining three separate apps. For a startup trying to get a chat app into people's hands fast, that trade was obviously correct. Discord, Slack, VS Code — half the apps on your dock exist because Electron made them cheap to build.

And VS Code is the example Electron's defenders always reach for, because it's the best one. A fast, capable editor that happens to be Electron. It proves the framework isn't inherently slow. A good team can make it sing.

But "a good team can make it sing" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. For every VS Code there's a dozen apps that ship a whole Chromium browser to render a settings page. The 290MB figure isn't a bug in Electron. It's what happens when the easy path is also the heavy path, and nobody ever has a reason to take the hard one.

The bill came due

Here's the thing about trade-offs: they don't stay still. In 2016, shipping fast mattered more than anything, and a 290MB download was an acceptable price. In 2026, users have spent a decade watching chat apps eat RAM like it's free, and the patience is gone. Laptops haven't gotten 290MB more forgiving. The download is still 290MB. The startup is still slow. The memory usage is still the first thing people complain about in reviews.

Discord's move says the maths flipped. The cost of maintaining a native codebase in Rust is now lower than the cost of shipping a bloated app to millions of people who notice. That's not a technical argument, it's a business one — and it's the kind that actually moves companies. Nobody rewrites a working app for fun. They rewrite it when the old stack starts costing more than the rewrite.

Rust plus GPUI is a bet that the native route is viable again for teams that aren't Apple or Microsoft. GPUI is the UI framework behind Zed, the editor, and it's built for exactly this: fast, native rendering without dragging a browser along. If Discord pulls it off, every Electron app with a big user base is going to get the same question from its own team: what's our excuse?

So what does this mean if you ship desktop software?

Probably nothing, tomorrow. Electron isn't dying. There are thousands of Electron apps, most of them fine, most of their users happy enough. Discord leaving doesn't make your app worse.

But it does move the goalposts. "Everyone uses Electron" stops being a defence. When the biggest chat app on the planet decides the framework costs too much, the default answer to "why is our app 290MB?" gets harder. Not impossible — VS Code still exists, the one-codebase argument still exists — just harder. You need a better reason than "that's what everyone does."

And for users, it's good news regardless of whether the rewrite succeeds. Competition between approaches is what keeps software from settling into comfortable bloat. Electron got complacent because it won. A high-profile defection is the market working the way it's supposed to.

My prediction, for what it's worth: Discord's new app will be faster and smaller, the rewrite will take longer and hurt more than anyone admits publicly, and in two years some other big app will cite Discord as the reason it did the same thing. The 290MB download was never inevitable. It was a choice, made in 2016, that made sense at the time. The honest thing is admitting the time changed — and Discord just did.

title: Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Chinese spy

title: Towards Label-Efficient Geospatial Foundation Model Adaptation via Positive-Unlabeled Learning for Building Damage Mapping
description:
arXiv:2611.08561v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01, R03, R10 & How to Handle Them
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01, R03, R10 & How to Handle Them

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01, R03, R10 & How to Handle Them

When you're building a payout system, ACH returns are inevitable. A user's bank rejects the transfer, and your code needs to know why—and what to do next. The Nacha operating rules define 85 return codes (R01–R85), each signaling a specific failure reason. Understanding the most common ones is critical to building resilient payment flows.

The Most Common ACH Return Codes

R01: Insufficient Funds

What it means: The account doesn't have enough money to cover the debit.

When it fires: After the ODFI (your bank) has already sent the entry to the RDFI (recipient's bank). The recipient's bank checks the balance and rejects it.

Developer action:

  • Log the return with timestamp and amount.
  • Flag the payout as failed, not retryable (at least not immediately).
  • Notify the user: "Insufficient funds in your account."
  • Consider a retry after 2–5 days if your business logic allows (e.g., a payroll system might retry next cycle). 
{
  "return_code": "R01",
  "reason": "Insufficient Funds",
  "payout_id": "po_abc123",
  "amount_cents": 50000,
  "timestamp": "2025-01-15T14:32:00Z",
  "retryable": false,
  "next_action": "notify_user"
}

R03: No Account / Unable to Locate Account

What it means: The account number provided doesn't exist, or the routing number is invalid.

When it fires: During the RDFI's validation step, usually within 1–2 banking days.

Developer action:

  • This is a data quality issue. The user entered a wrong account or routing number.
  • Do not retry the same account.
  • Require the user to re-enter banking details.
  • Log for fraud detection if this happens repeatedly from the same user. 
if (returnCode === 'R03') {
  await updatePayoutStatus(payoutId, 'FAILED_INVALID_ACCOUNT');
  await notifyUser(userId, {
    title: 'Bank Details Invalid',
    message: 'We couldn\'t find an account matching the details you provided. Please verify your routing and account numbers.',
    action: 'UPDATE_BANK_INFO'
  });
}

R10: Unauthorized

What it means: The account holder (or their bank) says they didn't authorize this debit. Often a sign of fraud or a genuinely disputed transaction.

When it fires: Typically 2–5 days after the initial ACH entry posts, when the account holder disputes it.

Developer action:

  • Treat as a dispute. Respond within the Nacha dispute window (typically 10 days).
  • Do not retry without explicit user consent.
  • Flag for compliance review if you see multiple R10s from the same originating account.
  • Contact the user to confirm legitimacy. 
if (returnCode === 'R10') {
  await escalateToCompliance(payoutId, {
    reason: 'UNAUTHORIZED_DISPUTE',
    severity: 'HIGH'
  });
  await sendComplianceAlert({
    user_id: userId,
    payout_id: payoutId,
    message: 'Your bank has disputed this transfer. We need to verify this transaction with you.'
  });
}

Building Return Handling Into Your Payout Flow

When a return arrives, your system should:

  1. Receive the return file from your ACH processor (typically via SFTP or API webhook).
  2. Parse the return code using Nacha's official mapping.
  3. Classify the return as retryable, non-retryable, or requires-user-action.
  4. Update payout status in your database atomically.
  5. Trigger the appropriate workflow (retry, notify user, escalate, etc.). 
async function handleAchReturn(returnEntry) {
  const { payoutId, returnCode, amount } = returnEntry;

  const classification = classifyReturn(returnCode);

  if (classification === 'RETRYABLE') {
    await scheduleRetry(payoutId, { delayDays: 3 });
  } else if (classification === 'USER_ACTION_REQUIRED') {
    await notifyUserAndAwaitUpdate(payoutId);
  } else {
    await markPayoutFailed(payoutId, returnCode);
  }

  await logReturn(payoutId, returnCode, classification);
}

Key Takeaway

The Nacha R-code set is your map. R01, R03, and R10 account for roughly 40% of all

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: MCP Events support in Vercel Connect is now in public beta
description:
Vercel Connect now supports MCP Events in public beta, allowing your apps and agents to subscribe to webhook events from compatible MCP servers. Build agents for tasks like summarizing new messages, reviewing newly created issues, or responding to document feedback.

Connect creates subscriptions on the MCP server and renews them automatically as needed, verifying the server’s webhooks and forwarding events to your application using authenticated delivery.

You can use the Connect SDK to subscribe to MCP events:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 4OcwkT5TX5v1h28r0qLS1C At your delivery endpoint, use the SDK to verify that each delivery came from Connect before acknowledging receipt:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 2B5UlAEUePpGMQg3S2hD1L

You can also expose AI SDK event discovery and subscription APIs as agent tools, using Connect’s MCP Events adapter to manage subscriptions.

In eve, enabling events on an MCP connection gives agents tools to discover the server’s events and use Connect to create, inspect, or stop subscriptions.

Read the MCP Events docs and Vercel Connect quickstart for SDK setup and authentication.

title: I Replaced MongoDB with Turso Without Touching Roughly 1,250 Database Calls
description:
In October 2026, I moved the Future Thinkers Club platform off MongoDB and onto Turso. The interesting part is not the move itself. It is that the application code barely noticed: roughly 1,250 database calls stayed exactly as they were.

Why move at all

The platform runs on Vercel, on serverless functions. The native database driver path did not work there, so the fix was a pure-Python client that talks to Turso over HTTP. No native driver, no compiled dependency, just HTTP requests from Python. That one decision shaped the whole migration.

The adapter trick

Instead of rewriting every query in the app, I wrote a MongoDB-compatible adapter on top of Turso. The app keeps calling the same functions it always called, and the adapter translates them into Turso operations underneath. The interface stayed, the engine changed.

File storage moved the same way. Files used to live in GridFS; now they live in a single Turso table called fs_files, with a path, the file data as a BLOB, a content type, and metadata. The storage functions kept their exact signatures: save a file, read a file, delete a file. The rest of the app never knew anything changed.

The result

The migration went live with the health endpoint reporting the database up, and the platform kept working through the switch: logins, clubs, messages, book uploads, all on the new database. No data loss, no rewrite of the application, and no downtime for the students using it.

The lesson I took from it is one I now use on every project: when you need to change infrastructure, change it behind an interface you already own. If your app talks to a database through one adapter, you can swap the database. If it talks to MongoDB in 1,250 different places, you cannot.

The platform is live at https://f-thinkers.vercel.app, and it is one of the 17 projects on my portfolio at https://rayyans-showroom.vercel.app/projects/future-thinkers.

title: Extrapolation Matters: Sparse-Only Depth Completion Beyond LiDAR Coverage
description:
arXiv:2611.08782v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Extrapolation beyond LiDAR coverage is an important yet under-evaluated challenge of depth completion. In real camera--LiDAR systems, partial sensor overlap, occlusions, and limited field coverage often leave large image regions weakly observed or completely unobserved by LiDAR. Thus, we investigate depth completion in this beyond-coverage regime using only sparse supervision from raw single-sweep LiDAR, without dense depth labels, LiDAR accumulation, or pseudo-LiDAR generation. Our approach leverages a frozen monocular depth foundation model, lightweight per-frame alignment to sparse LiDAR geometry, and a refinement module that fuses the aligned prior with sparse LiDAR anchors to predict dense metric depth. To regularize learning under raw sparse supervision, we introduce a high-frequency normal-consistency loss defined as the image-space gradient of the per-pixel normal cosine discrepancy. This term penalizes spatial variation in scalar angular error; it does not directly match changes in neighboring normal vectors. We further introduce an evaluation protocol that explicitly separates LiDAR-supported and beyond-coverage regions, revealing extrapolative behavior that conventional depth-completion metrics can obscure. Our method achieves strong depth accuracy beyond LiDAR coverage while remaining competitive in LiDAR-covered regions, providing a practical way to deploy monocular foundation priors in multi-sensor systems.

title: ⚔️ Monolith vs Microservices – Real Experience Breakdown
description:
Nucleus, the backend behind this portfolio, is a useful real example for comparing deployment boundaries. It contains Blog, Course, Project, Finance, and other modules inside one Laravel application. The public Next.js website and mobile companion are separate clients, while Nucleus owns persistence and content rules.

This walkthrough uses that existing modular monolith to examine what a service extraction would change. The extraction example is a design exercise, not a claim that Nucleus's invoice or notification modules have already become independently deployed services. No performance improvement or traffic capacity is assumed.

Folders organize code; deployment and ownership define the boundary

A monolith is deployed as one backend application. It can still have well-defined modules, dependency rules, queues, and multiple web or worker processes. In Nucleus, ModulesServiceProvider discovers module routes, migrations, and commands within the same application. Those modules share Laravel's runtime and database authority.

This simplified structure captures the actual organization without suggesting that every internal class is a separate service:

app/Modules/
  Blog/
    Post/{Controllers, Requests, Repositories, Models, Jobs}
    PostCategory/
  Course/
  Project/
  Finance/
  Api/
    Portfolio/   # published content reads
    App/         # authenticated management endpoints

A monolith can keep domain code organized inside one application. The text example above shows Nucleus's module arrangement.

Microservices introduce independently deployable application boundaries. Each service owns its domain behavior and data contract. Other services use an API or events rather than directly writing its tables. A separate physical database server is one possible deployment choice; the important requirement is controlled ownership of data.

A conceptual service split. This figure is not a diagram of the deployed Nucleus system.

Separate applications do not automatically remove coupling. If all services require a coordinated release, share direct database writes, or make long chains of synchronous calls, their operation remains tightly connected. Microsoft's service-boundary guidance uses domain responsibilities, cohesion, consistency needs, and independent deployment to evaluate a split.

Follow one workflow before drawing new boxes

Consider a Nucleus blog edit. Validation checks the category and submitted fields. The repository updates the row and attachment state. An editor-body job can convert embedded images into stored files. Model events queue a webhook that expires the public portfolio's cached content.

The post belongs to a category through a foreign key that uses cascading deletion. Both records are currently managed by one database. Splitting categories into a different service would change that relationship: a remote category lookup cannot behave like an ordinary local foreign key or participate in the same SQL transaction.

Media creates another boundary. A database rollback does not reverse a file upload. Separating storage processing adds network outcomes and retries to that existing problem. Before extracting anything, list the invariants: a public article must have valid content, category changes must follow a deliberate deletion policy, and retries must not attach or delete the wrong files.

Scale a workload before assuming it needs a new service

If editor processing or PDF generation becomes slow, first measure the worker backlog, job duration, query time, and resource usage. A Laravel queue worker can be deployed and scaled separately from HTTP processes while using the same codebase. That changes execution capacity without requiring a new domain API.

Likewise, a modular monolith can run behind a load balancer. Shared session, cache, storage, and job configuration still need care. Microservices make scaling an individual service possible, but each service may bring its own datastore, deployment, monitoring, and incident handling. Independent scaling is a capability to use when a workload justifies it.

There is no reliable “five developers” or “high traffic” threshold that decides this architecture. Ask which workload is constrained and which team can own its full operation. A slow query remains a slow query after moving behind HTTP.

Compare the costs using concrete questions

Decision Module in one Laravel application Independent service
Changing a domain API Update callers and implementation in one release. Support deployed consumers and a compatibility window.
Saving related state Use a local transaction where the data shares a connection. Define messages, retries, and acceptable intermediate states.
Debugging a workflow Trace local calls and queued jobs. Correlate requests and messages across deployments.
Scaling background work Add or isolate workers for measured workloads. Scale the service and account for its dependencies.

Neither column guarantees faster development or higher availability. A small service with clear ownership may simplify a complex domain. Ten tiny services with unclear responsibility may make a simple change harder. The useful comparison is the cost of the workflow you actually have.

A hypothetical notification-service extraction

Suppose a notification workload needs an independent release cycle and operational owner. An initial contract might accept an event with a stable identity and explicit version. This is illustrative JSON, not an existing Nucleus endpoint:

{
  "event_id": "f3a8cdf4-0d42-467b-b186-50edb136cc50",
  "event_type": "content.published",
  "schema_version": 1,
  "content_id": 42,
  "occurred_at": "2026-10-11T09:00:00Z"
}

The publisher should durably record the event with the content change, then deliver it asynchronously. Otherwise, a process crash between the database commit and the HTTP call can lose the notification. A transactional outbox is one design option; it is additional infrastructure to implement and verify, not a property of ordinary event dispatch.

The consumer needs durable deduplication, bounded retries, and a delivery state. Receiving an event twice must not mean sending the same email twice. A provider timeout may leave the send result uncertain, which requires a deliberate recovery policy. Keep secrets and full recipient data out of broad event payloads.

Define what readers see when the notification service is unavailable. Content publication can succeed while delivery is pending if that is an accepted business rule. If every page request waits for notification service health, the extraction has added an unnecessary availability dependency.

Extract incrementally and keep a rollback path

Start by giving the module a small internal interface and stopping direct cross-module table writes. Add contract tests and observe calls. Then introduce an adapter that can route one workload to either the local implementation or the new service. Migrate a bounded set of operations and compare results before moving ownership.

Do not maintain two uncoordinated writers for the same records. Define when the new service becomes authoritative, how pending work is transferred, and how old consumers remain compatible. A rollback plan must account for data written since the cutover, not just the previous application binary.

For the current Nucleus architecture, modular boundaries, specific query improvements, and reliable queue processing are concrete improvements within the existing deployment. A future extraction should name a measured problem, an independent owner, and a contract that makes the added network boundary worthwhile.
