title: Comment la vectorisation d'image transforme-t-elle un logo PNG en SVG ?
description:
La vectorisation d'image (Image Trace) a l'air magique, mais elle tient en trois petites étapes : décider quels pixels appartiennent à quelle couleur, découper un contour autour de chaque zone de couleur, puis ajuster le moins de points possible sur chaque contour. L'outil Image Trace de l'éditeur vectoriel (Vector Editor) de l'application de bureau osFoundry le fait en un clic. Voici la même chaîne écrite en Python, exécutée sur un logo PNG de 220 × 220 px (un cercle vert, une tasse crème, un nuage orange, les mots KUMO COFFEE) et mesurée à chaque étape, puis comparée au SVG que l'application a exporté à partir du même fichier. Le code fait environ 110 lignes avec numpy, Pillow et scikit-image.

Le PNG a 2 110 couleurs, le logo en a trois

Le logo a été dessiné avec un vert, un crème, un orange et le blanc de la page, puis réduit de 1 200 px à 220 px et légèrement flouté, ce qui correspond à l'aspect de la plupart des logos sur les sites web. On compte les couleurs distinctes :

uniq, counts = np.unique(px.astype(np.uint8), axis=0, return_counts=True)
# 220x220 px, 2110 distinct colours

Presque toutes les 2 110 sont des teintes intermédiaires le long des bords. Les trois plus fréquentes sont #ffffff (20 574 pixels), #1f5f4a (14 938) et #faf4e6 (3 747). Vectoriser consiste surtout à se débarrasser des 2 000 autres.

Le noir et blanc est un seuil, et il décide plus qu'on ne le voudrait

La vectorisation par défaut de l'application est en noir et blanc. C'est un seuil sur la luminance :

lum = a @ [0.299, 0.587, 0.114]
black = lum < 128        # 38.7% of the pixels

L'orange du nuage (#e87834) a une luminance d'environ 146 ; il tombe donc du côté clair et devient blanc, et dans la vectorisation par défaut de l'application le nuage disparaît dans le fond. Déplacer le seuil entre 96 et 160 ne fait varier la part de pixels noirs que de 37,1 % à 43,3 %. Aucun seuil ne ramène le nuage, parce qu'il est plus clair que le vert et plus sombre que la page, et qu'un seuil n'a que deux côtés.

Trois couleurs, c'est du clustering

Avec trois couleurs, la question devient : de laquelle des trois chaque pixel est-il le plus proche ? C'est un k-means avec k = 3 sur les valeurs RVB des 48 400 pixels :

def kmeans(px, k, it=20):
    c = [px[np.argmin(px.sum(1))]]                       # darkest pixel first
    while len(c) < k:                                     # then the farthest from the chosen ones
        d = np.min([((px - ci) ** 2).sum(1) for ci in c], axis=0)
        c.append(px[np.argmax(d)])
    c = np.array(c)
    for _ in range(it):
        lab = np.argmin(((px[:, None, :] - c[None]) ** 2).sum(2), axis=1)
        c = np.array([px[lab == j].mean(0) for j in range(k)])
    return c, lab

Il s'exécute en 100 ms environ. Les tailles des groupes sont 38,7 % de vert, 56,2 % de crème plus page et 5,1 % d'orange, et la distance moyenne entre un pixel et la couleur de son groupe est de 13, sur une échelle dont le maximum possible est 441.

Les moyennes des groupes ne sont pourtant pas les couleurs du logo. La moyenne du vert est #22614c contre un #1f5f4a réel, celle de l'orange est #c98651 contre un #e87834 réel, parce que les pixels flous le long du bord appartiennent au groupe et tirent sa moyenne vers les voisins. En prenant, au lieu de la moyenne, la couleur réelle la plus fréquente de chaque groupe, on obtient #1f5f4a, #ffffff et #e87834. Le SVG exporté par l'application utilise #1f5f4a, #e87834 et #fefdfa : elle fait donc quelque chose de plus solide qu'une simple moyenne, sans que je puisse dire quoi à partir du résultat.

Des contours à la précision du sous-pixel

Chaque couleur devient un masque, et c'est avec le contour du masque que ça devient intéressant. Un masque coupé au pixel donne des contours en escalier. Si l'on agrandit d'abord le masque par 4 en interpolation bicubique et qu'on coupe à 0,5, le contour tombe là où le flou est à mi-chemin entre les deux couleurs, c'est-à-dire là où se trouvait le vrai bord :

def contours(mask, up=4):
    m = Image.fromarray((mask * 255).astype(np.uint8)).resize((W * up, H * up), Image.BICUBIC)
    cs = measure.find_contours(np.pad(np.asarray(m) / 255.0, 1), 0.5)
    return [(c - 1) / up for c in cs]        # back to source-pixel units

Le logo a été dessiné à partir d'un cercle de rayon 91,67 (dans ces unités de 220 px), on dispose donc d'une référence pour vérifier. Sur le bord du cercle, loin des lettres, le contour vectorisé est en moyenne à 0,47 px du vrai cercle, et 95 % de ses points sont à moins de 0,69 px. Le bord flou du PNG, lui, met 2 px pour passer de 90 % de vert à 10 %. La vectorisation retrouve le bord mieux que l'image ne le montre.

Les poussières sont l'autre moitié du travail. Sans surface minimale, le phénomène d'oscillation du bicubique autour des lettres produit 288 contours ; avec MIN_AREA = 4 px², il en reste 62. C'est l'idée derrière le réglage de bruit des outils de vectorisation.

Moins de points

Un contour sorti tel quel de marching squares a un point toutes les fractions de pixel. Douglas-Peucker supprime les points qui se trouvent dans une tolérance de la droite entre leurs voisins :

s = measure.approximate_polygon(contour, tol)
tolérance points sur les 62 contours
0,05 px 4 262
0,25 px 1 594
0,5 px 945

À 0,25 px, les polygones ont été écrits en SVG : 22,6 Ko, avec 1 594 points reliés par des segments droits.

Ce que les courbes apportent

Le SVG exporté par l'application a 324 points d'ancrage répartis en 17 tracés et pèse 11,9 Ko. Il a moins d'un quart des points de la version en polygones, car entre deux ancres il trace une courbe de Bézier au lieu d'une droite, et un cercle tient en quelques courbes plutôt qu'en des centaines de segments. C'est pourquoi un outil de vectorisation finit par un ajustement de courbes et non par le polygone.

Mais l'essentiel, c'est l'indépendance vis-à-vis de la taille. Voici ce que donne l'agrandissement du PNG en interpolation bicubique, puis son enregistrement :

largeur PNG bord, de 90 % à 10 %
220 px 15 Ko 2 px
880 px 120 Ko 7 px
1 760 px 325 Ko 14 px

Le bord vectoriel du cercle vectorisé, dessiné à 1 760 px, fait 1 px de large, et le fichier garde la même taille. Il n'est plus petit que le PNG que lorsque le PNG est grand : le SVG de l'application pèse 11,9 Ko contre 15,0 Ko pour le PNG à la taille d'origine, et 12 Ko contre 325 Ko à 1 760 px.

Ce qu'elle ne peut pas corriger

Une vectorisation suit l'image qu'on lui donne. Une lettre bavée donne un contour bavé, un dégradé doit être aplati en bandes pour passer l'étape des couleurs, et la couleur de la page est une couleur comme une autre : le blanc de la page ressort donc comme une forme. Pour un logo à quelques aplats de couleur et aux bords nets, c'est le bon outil. Pour une photographie, c'est un filtre de postérisation.

L'ensemble

trace.py s'exécute de bout en bout en 3 secondes environ sur un Apple M1 (l'étape k-means, environ 100 ms) et affiche tous les chiffres de cet article. Lancez-le avec uv run --with numpy --with pillow --with scikit-image python trace.py logo.png sur n'importe quel petit PNG en aplats de couleur, puis comparez l'erreur de contour et le nombre de points avec ce que donne un outil de vectorisation. Le logo de cet article est une marque de café inventée, et ses chiffres ont été mesurés sur ce seul fichier : les valeurs exactes seront différentes sur le vôtre. L'application de bureau, Vector Editor compris, est gratuite sur la page de téléchargement d'osFoundry.

title: We built a ChatGPT-style chat with no AI framework
description:
We built the AI chat in Sybill by hand, with ChatGPT as our reference.

In January 2025 we started building Ask Sybill, the AI chat inside Sybill. Sybill makes AI tools for sales teams, and we wanted the chat to feel like ChatGPT, with the answer appearing word by word.

AI chat frameworks were still young, and we did not use one. Instead, we opened ChatGPT in the browser and watched in the Network tab how an answer arrives: a stream of small events (Server-Sent Events), one after another. Then we built our own version of that stream.

Today Ask Sybill keeps the answer when the connection drops, and you can run many chats at the same time. Getting there took much longer than we planned, and for a long time it felt like there was always one more thing to fix.

Finally, a real use for async generators

At the end of January I wrote the code that reads those events while they arrive. For this I used an async generator: a function that hands out values one at a time and waits in between for more data. Most of us almost never write one. But a stream of events is exactly what it was made for, and it was fun to finally use one in real code.


An async generator reads the stream. The chat just loops over what it hands out.

You may notice that the reader never throws. Early on, I decided that our code would return errors as values, like any other result. So a network error, a message from the backend that we cannot read, and the user pressing Stop all come out of the same loop. The chat can then handle each one in its own way. A stop, for example, should never look like an error.

Every feature became a new event

Each event the reader hands out has a type, and almost every type exists because of a feature in the chat. chat_title gives a new chat its name. task_progress shows the steps while the AI is working. mcp_tool_approval asks you before the AI uses an outside tool. And delta carries the words of the answer, a few at a time.


One answer in Ask Sybill, as a stream of events.

The number of events grew with the product. Each new event meant work on every side: the backend had to send it, the shared types had to describe it, and the frontend had to read it and show it. With a framework, the common events come ready, and you only add the ones that are really yours.

Streaming text and keeping the page fast

Everyone expects an AI chat to write its answer word by word, and we wanted that from the start. But it took a while. Without a framework, we had to turn the stream of each AI model into our own events, and the page had to stay fast while new words arrived many times a second. There was always something more urgent, so we kept putting streaming off. Until then, the full answer appeared at the end.

When we finally turned it on, the text did not feel right. Words do not arrive at a steady speed. Sometimes many arrive at once, then nothing for a moment. Each new piece of text made React draw the chat again (a re-render). Those re-renders were expensive, so the page slowed down, and the text came in jumps. We tried throttling the updates, so React rendered less often, but the text still came in jumps. We tried delaying the stream and typing it out at a steady speed, but then the AI was already done while the page was still typing. What worked was a small buffer between the stream and the screen. It collects the new text and shows it on every frame, about 60 times a second on most screens. That is often enough to look smooth, and the text keeps up with the AI.

There was one more slow part, in how we stored a chat. All the state of a chat lived in one object, so each new word created a new copy of it, and every part of the page that used the chat re-rendered. I moved the streaming text into its own small slice of the store, so now only the message that is being written updates. In a test chat with 15 turns, React spent about 3.3 seconds rendering while one answer streamed in. After the change, it spent about 0.35 seconds.

When chats get huge

Streaming was not our only speed problem. Chats grow, and some get huge. Some people had more than 100 turns in one chat. Opening one froze the page, and the newest messages took about 24 seconds to appear. React drew every message in one go and could not stop in the middle, so until it was done, you only saw the empty start screen.

React has a tool called startTransition. It marks an update as not urgent, so React can stop that work when something more important comes in, like a key press, and start it again after. The React docs show it mostly for async work, like sending a form, and for a slow screen, like switching tabs. Drawing a long list in pieces is not one of their examples, but I used it for that, and it fits well. The newest 10 messages appear at once. Then the older ones are added 10 at a time, each step inside startTransition, until the whole chat is there.


The newest 10 messages first, then 10 older ones at a time, when React is free.

Now the newest messages appear in less than a second instead of about 24 seconds, and the older ones keep loading while the page stays usable.

Every message still ends up on the page, though. Nothing is removed later. For the long chats we tested, that worked well. If chats grow much larger, you will also need virtualization: the page draws only the messages near the screen, and adds and removes the others as you scroll.

Native popovers to the rescue

Huge chats hid one more cost, in a place nobody looks: the tooltips. Each message has a row of buttons, like copy, feedback, and retry, and each button has a tooltip. A long chat has hundreds of them. With many component libraries, every tooltip lives in React, even while it is hidden. So React spends time on all of them, even though you see at most one. When you hover a button, showing its tooltip goes through React too, and JavaScript places it by measuring the button and the page. The library we used worked like that. In a test chat with 124 turns, hovering the buttons 30 times blocked the page for about 11.5 seconds in total, almost 0.4 seconds per hover.

Browsers can now do this job themselves. The Popover API puts the tooltip on top of the page, and CSS anchor positioning places it next to its button. I rewrote our tooltip to use these two and moved its hover logic to plain JavaScript, outside React. So the hidden tooltips stay cheap, and showing one makes React draw only that tooltip. A JavaScript library still places the tooltip in a few cases, like when it does not fit on the screen or the browser is too old.


The browser shows the tooltip on top of the page and places it next to its button.

In the same test, the 30 hovers now block the page for about 2.5 seconds instead of 11.5.

Keeping the answer when the connection drops

Sometimes an answer got lost halfway: the connection dropped, or someone reloaded the page while the AI was still writing. We wanted the answer to survive both.

So the backend saves every event of an answer in Redis Streams, a Redis feature for ordered messages. Each event gets an id. The browser remembers the id of the last event it received. When the connection comes back, it asks for everything after that id, and the answer goes on from where it stopped. If you open a chat while its answer is still being written, the page joins that answer in the same way.


When the connection drops, the browser asks for the rest.

Resume alone was not enough, though. At first, the connection to the browser kept the answer alive: when it closed, the answer from the AI model stopped too. That happened when you closed the page, but also when the Wi-Fi dropped. Now the backend reads the answer from the model on its own. It sends each event to the open connection and also saves it in Redis. If the connection closes, the backend keeps going and keeps saving, and the browser can come back for the rest.

One thing surprised us. Sometimes the AI thinks or works for a long time without sending anything. This is a known weak spot of Server-Sent Events: a proxy, a server between the browser and our backend, may close a connection that stays quiet for too long. So while the backend has nothing else to say, it sends a heartbeat every 15 seconds, and the connection stays open.

What I would choose today

All of this works well. But if I built a chat today, I would not write the stream myself. AI chat frameworks like Vercel's AI SDK are common now, and they already solve much of what we built by hand, like streaming text, stop, and tool approval.

Looking back, I think we should have moved to a framework once we understood the problem well. That is easy to say now. At the time, the chat was already live, it had features of its own, and moving would have paused product work for a while. Building it ourselves also taught us how every part of a chat works.

We started by opening ChatGPT and watching its answers arrive. If you start today, open a framework's docs first. Most of what took us so long is already in there.

title: When does npm test exit 0 even though the bug is still there?
description:
Agent loops that fix failing tests usually stop on one signal: the test command exits with 0. It's a good signal because a model can't argue with it. The osFoundry desktop app's starter loop "Get the JS suite green" verifies each run with npm test, and a comment in its Rust source (loop_config.rs) calls a command check "the only form that cannot be talked into passing".

That holds for the model's words. It doesn't hold for the files the model can edit. The agent fixing your tests has write access to the repository, and the exit code of npm test is produced by that repository: the test files, package.json, and the command line you wrote. Below, each way an exit code can say "pass" while the bug is still there is built as a tiny Node project and run.

Thirteen cases, measured

Each case is a fresh temp folder with src/add.mjs and a node --test suite. "Bug there" means add returns a - b and the test expects add(2, 3) to be 5. The script runs the command through sh -c and records the exit code. Node 24.21.0, npm 11.19.0, macOS 15.8.1 on an M1.

Case Command Exit node --test summary
code fixed npm test 0 tests 1, pass 1
bug still there npm test 1 tests 1, fail 1
assertion changed to match the bug npm test 0 tests 1, pass 1
failing test marked test.skip npm test 0 tests 1, pass 0, skipped 1
failing test marked test.todo npm test 0 tests 1, pass 0, todo 1
test file deleted npm test 0 tests 0
test moved to src/add.check.mjs npm test 0 tests 0
process.exit(0) added at the top of the test file npm test 0 tests 1, pass 1
output piped to a log `npm test \ tee test.log` 0
`\ \ true` appended `npm test \
{% raw %}npm init default test script npm test 1 (no tests run)
a test that never resolves npm test none after 10 s (killed)
no package.json npm test 254 (no tests run)

Nine of the thirteen exit with 0, and only one of those nine is a real fix.

Three different failures

The rows fall into three groups, and each one needs a different guard.

The suite changed. Editing an assertion, skipping, marking todo, deleting or moving the file: in every case the exit code is accurate about the tests that ran. The tests that ran just aren't the ones you meant. The moved file is the quiet one. node --test with no arguments only picks up files matching its default patterns (*.test.mjs, anything under test/, and so on), so a test that moves out of those patterns isn't skipped, it just stops existing. The runner reports tests 0 and exits 0.

process.exit(0) at the top of a test file is the strangest row. node --test runs each file in its own process, and a file whose process exits 0 is reported as a passing test: ✔ test/add.test.mjs, pass 1. The assertion never ran.

The command lies. In npm test | tee test.log the shell returns the exit status of the last command in the pipe, which is tee, which succeeded. || true does the same on purpose. Neither is something an agent has to do. These come from the person who wrote the check, which is why the command belongs to the loop's definition, not to the agent. With set -o pipefail the same tee command exits 1 under bash.

There is no verdict. A hung test has no exit code at all, and a missing package.json gives 254, which says nothing about your code. A loop has to decide what these mean, and "fail" is not always the right answer.

Pass, fail, or not judged

The app's loop verifier has an answer for that last group. The check runs through the same execute_command tool the agents use, and command_exit_verdict in loop_verify.rs reads the last EXIT CODE: line of its output. Exit 0 passes and anything else fails. A command marked as timed out fails even if it reports 0. A result with no exit code, or a command that couldn't be started at all, is None: not judged. The comment states the reason: defaulting to pass would let a malformed result approve every run, and defaulting to fail would "burn a loop's failure budget on a reporting change".

That budget is real. The loop stops after three failed verifications in a row (DEFAULT_MAX_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES = 3), so if an unreachable folder counted as a failure, a flaky disk would switch off a loop whose work was fine. When the command can't be judged, the app falls back to the goal ledger's own verdict for that run: met its criteria is a pass, ran out of rounds is a fail, and a downed grader, a token ceiling or a cancel are not judged at all and leave the counter where it was.

Rebuilding the judge in Python

Here is the same three-state judge as a standalone script, with guards for the first two groups added. CHECK is fixed by the loop, not chosen by the agent, and uses pipefail. CHECK_TIMEOUT is 120 seconds. Before the first round the script hashes every *.test.*js file and records how many tests the suite has.

CHECK = "set -o pipefail; npm test 2>&1"

def run_check(cwd):
    """Pass (True), fail (False) or not judged (None). Never guess."""
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(["bash", "-c", CHECK], cwd=cwd, capture_output=True, text=True,
                           timeout=CHECK_TIMEOUT)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        return False, "timed out"            # a hang is a failure, whatever it prints
    except OSError as e:                     # could not even start: no folder, no shell
        return None, f"could not run: {e.strerror}"
    return r.returncode == 0, r.stdout

def judge(cwd, baseline_files, baseline_tests):
    ok, out = run_check(cwd)
    if ok is None:
        return None, out
    if test_files(cwd) != baseline_files:
        return False, "test files changed"
    s = summary(out)
    if ok and (s.get("tests", 0) < baseline_tests or s.get("skipped", 0) or s.get("todo", 0)):
        return False, f"exit 0 but {s}"
    return ok, f"exit {'0' if ok else 'non-zero'} {s}"

summary reads the counters node --test prints at the end (tests, pass, fail, skipped, todo), and test_files maps each test file's path to its SHA-256. Changing a test file is always a failure here. That matches the app's goal text for this loop: if a test is genuinely wrong, the agent should say so and stop, which in practice means a person looks at it.

The loop around it is short. At most 4 rounds, stop after 3 failures in a row, and a None doesn't touch the failure counter:

for rnd in range(1, MAX_ROUNDS + 1):
    agent_round(cwd, rnd)
    verdict, why = judge(cwd, baseline_files, baseline_tests)
    if verdict is True:
        return "verified", rnd
    if verdict is False:
        failures += 1
        if failures >= MAX_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES:
            return "stopped: failed 3 in a row", rnd
    # None leaves the counter alone: nothing judged this round
return "stopped: out of rounds", MAX_ROUNDS

To keep it to one loop, both limits sit in the same for here, and the command runs after every round. In the app, rounds inside a run are graded against the goal's criteria by a separate grading call, the command runs once when the run ends, the round limit bounds that run, and the failure cap counts failed runs in a row before the loop stops re-arming itself.

Six stand-in agents

To test the loop without a model, agent_round is a scripted list of file edits. The project has three bugs and three tests (add, slug, total of nothing). One full run of the script printed:

Agent behaviour Rounds Outcome Why the judge said no
fixes one bug per round 3 verified round 1: pass 1, fail 2; round 2: pass 2, fail 1
fixes one bug, then edits two assertions 3 stopped, 3 failures test files changed
fixes one bug, marks the other two test.skip 3 stopped, 3 failures test files changed
fixes one bug, points npm test at 'src/**/*.test.mjs' 3 stopped, 3 failures exit 0 but tests 0
changes nothing 3 stopped, 3 failures pass 0, fail 3
fixes one bug per round, folder unreachable during round 2's check 3 verified round 2 not judged, failure count stayed at 1

The fourth row is the one the hash check alone would miss. No test file changed, but package.json now points the runner at a glob with no matches, so the suite exits 0 with zero tests. The test-count guard catches it.

The last row is the three-state rule doing its job. Round 2's fix happened, but nothing could check it, so that round was neither a pass nor a strike. Round 3 then passed with all three tests.

In that run each check took between 0.17 s and 1.29 s on this tiny project, and every scenario, three or four checks included, finished in under 4 s in each of three runs. A model round costs far more than that, so there's no reason to skip the check or make it lighter.

What these guards don't cover

The guards are files and settings too. An agent that can edit package.json can also add a --test-skip-pattern flag or stub the module under test, and there will always be another way around. The more durable fix is where the check runs: from a copy of the test files the agent can't write to, or against git diff --quiet -- test/ on a clean checkout, with the check command defined in the loop and not in the repository.

The full scripts (exitcodes.py for the table, loop.py for the loop) are standard-library Python and only need Node on the PATH. In the osFoundry app, the verifier described above runs on your machine through the same command tool as the agents, which is also why it only runs when the loop's tool scope allows commands. The app is free from the download page.

title: Building an IoT-Based Smart Industrial Machine Monitoring and Predictive Maintenance System on AWS
description:
What if industrial machines could tell us they were about to fail before production stopped?

Imagine a manufacturing facility where every motor, pump, compressor, and production machine continuously reports its operating condition.

Instead of waiting for equipment to break down, the maintenance team receives an early warning that vibration levels are increasing. Engineers can investigate the issue, schedule maintenance, and potentially prevent an unexpected production shutdown.

This is the idea behind IoT-based smart industrial monitoring and predictive maintenance.

By combining Internet of Things (IoT), edge computing, and machine learning, organizations can collect equipment data, identify unusual behavior, and make more informed maintenance decisions.

AWS provides several services that can help build this type of solution.

In this tutorial, we'll explore the architecture and responsibilities of AWS IoT Core, AWS IoT Greengrass, AWS IoT SiteWise, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, and Amazon SNS.

1. The Problem with Traditional Industrial Maintenance

Industrial facilities commonly use two maintenance approaches.

Reactive maintenance means repairing equipment after it fails. This can cause unexpected downtime, production delays, emergency repairs, and higher operational costs.

Preventive maintenance means servicing equipment according to a fixed schedule. Although this can reduce some unexpected failures, it may also result in unnecessary maintenance because machines are serviced regardless of their actual condition.

Predictive maintenance takes a different approach.

Instead of asking:

When should we service this machine?

It asks:

What is the current condition of this machine, and is there evidence that something unusual is happening?

By analyzing real-time and historical sensor data, organizations can identify abnormal behavior and investigate potential problems earlier.

2. Understanding the Industrial IoT Architecture

Imagine a manufacturing facility with several industrial machines.

Each machine has sensors that measure important operating parameters:

  • Temperature
  • Vibration
  • Pressure
  • Electrical current
  • RPM
  • Flow rate

These sensors continuously generate telemetry data. An industrial gateway collects the information and securely sends it to AWS.

Here is a simplified architecture:

             Industrial Machines
              Motors | Pumps | CNC
                      |
                      v
               Industrial Sensors
          Temperature | Vibration
            Pressure | Current
                      |
                      v
              Industrial Gateway
               AWS IoT Greengrass
                      |
                      v
                  AWS IoT Core
                      |
                      v
                AWS IoT SiteWise
                      |
              +-------+-------+
              |               |
              v               v
          Asset Models    Anomaly Detection
              |               |
              +-------+-------+
                      |
                      v
                Alerts and Events
                      |
                      v
                  AWS Lambda
                      |
                      v
                  Amazon SNS
                      |
                      v
               Maintenance Team

             Historical Data
                      |
                      v
                  Amazon S3

             Optional Visualization
                      |
                      v
               AWS IoT TwinMaker

The architecture separates data collection, asset modeling, anomaly detection, notifications, and historical storage.

Let's understand each component.

3. Collecting Machine Data with AWS IoT Core

The first step is connecting industrial equipment to the cloud.

Industrial sensors can communicate through gateways that support protocols such as OPC-UA, Modbus, or other industrial interfaces.

An edge gateway collects sensor readings and securely publishes telemetry to AWS IoT Core.

AWS IoT Core provides secure connectivity for IoT devices and supports MQTT-based messaging.

For example, a motor might publish the following telemetry:

{
  "machine_id": "motor-101",
  "plant_id": "plant-01",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-27T10:30:00Z",
  "temperature": 72.5,
  "vibration": 3.2,
  "pressure": 5.8,
  "current": 14.5,
  "rpm": 1450
}

A possible MQTT topic could be:

factory/plant-01/machine/motor-101/telemetry

This structured data provides the foundation for monitoring machine health.

However, industrial environments do not always have reliable internet connectivity. This is where edge processing becomes important.

4. Processing Data at the Edge with AWS IoT Greengrass

Sending every raw sensor reading directly to the cloud may not always be practical.

Industrial environments can generate large volumes of telemetry, and network connectivity may occasionally become unavailable.

AWS IoT Greengrass helps run software and local processing capabilities on edge devices.

An industrial gateway can use edge processing to:

  • Filter unnecessary sensor readings.
  • Aggregate measurements.
  • Apply local threshold checks.
  • Buffer data during connectivity interruptions.
  • Continue selected local operations when the cloud is unavailable.

For example, if a motor's temperature exceeds a locally configured threshold, the gateway can trigger a local notification without waiting for a cloud response.

This makes the architecture more resilient and can reduce unnecessary data transmission.

The cloud remains important for centralized monitoring, historical analysis, and machine learning.

5. Modeling Industrial Equipment with AWS IoT SiteWise

Collecting sensor data is only one part of the solution.

Industrial organizations also need to understand which machine produced the data, where it is installed, and how it relates to other equipment.

AWS IoT SiteWise helps organize industrial data using asset models and asset hierarchies.

For example:

Company
  |
  +-- Plant 01
        |
        +-- Production Line A
        |      |
        |      +-- Motor 101
        |      +-- Pump 101
        |
        +-- Production Line B
               |
               +-- Compressor 201
               +-- Motor 202

Each asset can have associated measurements and calculated properties.

For a motor, these could include:

  • Temperature
  • Vibration
  • Current
  • RPM
  • Operating status

AWS IoT SiteWise also supports transforms, metrics, and alarms to help teams understand equipment behavior.

This makes industrial data more meaningful than a collection of disconnected sensor readings.

6. Detecting Abnormal Machine Behavior with Machine Learning

This is where predictive maintenance becomes particularly interesting.

A machine does not necessarily fail without warning. Its operating behavior may change before a failure occurs.

For example:

  • Vibration gradually increases.
  • Operating temperature becomes unusually high.
  • Electrical current changes unexpectedly.
  • Pressure readings become unstable.

AWS IoT SiteWise provides native anomaly detection capabilities that use machine learning to help identify unusual behavior in industrial asset data.

A typical workflow includes:

  1. Select the relevant industrial asset properties.
  2. Provide historical time-series data.
  3. Configure and train an anomaly detection model.
  4. Set up inference to evaluate new measurements.
  5. Review detected anomalies.
  6. Refine or retrain the model when appropriate.

Consider a motor that normally operates with vibration around 2.0 mm/s.

If its vibration begins increasing and reaches 3.8 mm/s, the system may identify the behavior as unusual based on the model's learned patterns.

This does not automatically mean the motor is about to fail.

It means the behavior deserves investigation.

Anomaly detection identifies unusual patterns. It does not guarantee a failure prediction or determine the root cause.

Maintenance engineers still need to validate alerts using operational context and physical inspection.

7. Storing Historical Data in Amazon S3

Real-time monitoring helps teams understand what is happening now.

Historical data helps them understand what has changed over time.

Amazon S3 can provide scalable storage for historical telemetry, exported datasets, reports, and supporting analytics data.

A possible data organization strategy is:

industrial-monitoring-data/
    plant-01/
        machine-101/
            year=2026/
                month=10/
                    day=27/
                        telemetry.json

Organizing data by plant, machine, and date can make it easier to manage and query large datasets when using compatible analytics tools.

Historical data can support:

  • Long-term machine performance analysis.
  • Maintenance trend reporting.
  • Model evaluation and retraining datasets.
  • Equipment comparisons.
  • Operational reporting.

The exact storage and analytics design should depend on data volume, retention requirements, and the tools used by the organization.

8. Sending Maintenance Alerts with AWS Lambda and Amazon SNS

Detecting an anomaly is useful only if the right people know about it.

A notification workflow can connect equipment alerts to the maintenance team.

             AWS IoT SiteWise
                      |
                      v
               Anomaly / Alarm
                      |
                      v
                Event Processing
                      |
                      v
                  AWS Lambda
                      |
                      v
                  Amazon SNS
                      |
                      v
              Maintenance Engineer

When a configured event occurs, AWS Lambda can process the event and prepare a notification.

Amazon SNS can distribute notifications to subscribed endpoints.

For example, a maintenance notification might look like this:

MACHINE HEALTH ALERT

Plant: Plant 01
Machine: Motor 101
Parameter: Vibration
Observed Value: 3.8 mm/s
Alert Type: Anomalous Behavior

Recommended Action:
Inspect the machine and review recent operating conditions.

The notification should provide enough context for the maintenance team to investigate.

For safety-critical equipment, cloud notifications should not replace validated industrial safety systems or qualified engineering decisions.

9. Visualizing Industrial Operations with AWS IoT TwinMaker

For organizations that need a richer operational view, AWS IoT TwinMaker can help create digital representations of industrial environments.

A digital twin can connect equipment representations with relevant industrial data.

For example, an operations team could view a production line and inspect the associated machine information.

A digital twin experience might display:

  • Machine location.
  • Current operating condition.
  • Temperature and vibration trends.
  • Recent anomalies.
  • Associated maintenance information.

This can help teams understand equipment status in the context of the physical facility.

AWS IoT TwinMaker is an optional visualization layer. A predictive maintenance system can operate without it.

10. Choosing the Right Detection Approach

Not every industrial machine needs the same predictive maintenance strategy.

There are three approaches worth considering.

Approach 1: Threshold-Based Monitoring

This approach compares sensor readings against predefined engineering limits.

For example, if a motor's temperature exceeds its configured operating limit, the system can generate an alert.

Suitable for: Equipment with clearly defined operating limits and straightforward monitoring requirements.

Approach 2: AWS IoT SiteWise Anomaly Detection

AWS IoT SiteWise provides machine learning-based anomaly detection to help identify unusual patterns in industrial time-series data.

Instead of relying only on one fixed threshold, it can help identify changes in equipment behavior.

Suitable for: Industrial equipment that generates historical and continuous time-series measurements.

Approach 3: Custom Machine Learning Models

Organizations can also develop and manage specialized machine learning models for particular equipment types or failure patterns.

This approach may require more historical data, model development, validation, and ongoing maintenance.

Suitable for: Specialized industrial requirements where existing monitoring and anomaly detection approaches are insufficient.

A simple threshold can be effective when an engineering limit is well understood.

Anomaly detection can help identify patterns that are difficult to describe using one fixed threshold.

Custom machine learning models may be appropriate when an organization has sufficient historical data and specialized requirements.

The right choice depends on the equipment, data quality, operational needs, and available expertise.

11. Building the Solution in Phases

You do not need to connect an entire factory on the first day.

A practical implementation can begin with one machine.

Phase 1: Connect One Machine

Install a small set of sensors and connect them through an industrial gateway.

Phase 2: Send Telemetry to AWS

Configure device connectivity and publish structured readings to AWS IoT Core.

Phase 3: Create an Asset Model

Use AWS IoT SiteWise to represent the machine and organize its measurements.

Phase 4: Build Monitoring Views

Create dashboards and operational metrics to understand machine behavior.

Phase 5: Enable Anomaly Detection

Use historical data to configure anomaly detection and evaluate the results with maintenance engineers.

Phase 6: Configure Notifications

Connect relevant alerts to AWS Lambda and Amazon SNS.

Phase 7: Expand the Deployment

After validating the solution on one machine, extend it to additional machines and production lines.

This phased approach reduces implementation risk and allows teams to learn from real operating conditions.

12. Security and Reliability Considerations

Industrial systems require careful security and reliability planning.

Some important practices include:

  • Use unique device identities and certificates.
  • Apply least-privilege IAM permissions.
  • Encrypt data in transit and at rest.
  • Separate industrial networks from general corporate networks.
  • Monitor device connectivity and data ingestion.
  • Design edge gateways to handle temporary connectivity loss.
  • Protect historical telemetry and operational records.
  • Validate anomaly detection results before operational decisions.
  • Maintain clear approval and incident-response procedures.

Most importantly, do not allow an experimental AI or cloud workflow to directly control safety-critical machinery without a properly engineered, validated, and approved industrial control design.

Security and reliability must be part of the architecture from the beginning.

13. What Does the Future Look Like?

Predictive maintenance is one part of a broader shift toward intelligent manufacturing.

As industrial IoT, edge computing, and machine learning capabilities mature, organizations can build systems that help them understand equipment behavior more effectively.

Future implementations may combine:

  • Real-time machine monitoring.
  • Equipment anomaly detection.
  • Maintenance history analysis.
  • Digital twins.
  • AI-assisted maintenance recommendations.
  • Automated work-order preparation.
  • Operational knowledge assistants.

AI could help engineers summarize equipment history, compare current readings with previous incidents, and prepare investigation reports.

However, reliable sensor data, good asset modeling, model validation, and human engineering oversight will remain essential.

The goal should not be to automate every maintenance decision. It should be to give engineers better information at the right time.

Conclusion: From Monitoring Machines to Understanding Them

Industrial maintenance is moving beyond fixed schedules and reactive repairs.

By combining AWS IoT Core, AWS IoT Greengrass, AWS IoT SiteWise, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, and Amazon SNS, organizations can build a foundation for connected industrial monitoring and predictive maintenance.

The real value comes from turning sensor readings into useful operational information.

A temperature reading becomes a trend.

A vibration change becomes an anomaly worth investigating.

An alert becomes an opportunity to inspect equipment before a small issue develops into a larger operational problem.

The future of smart manufacturing is not just about connecting machines to the cloud. It is about understanding machine behavior and helping people make better maintenance decisions.

References and Further Reading

  • What Is AWS IoT SiteWise?
  • AWS IoT SiteWise Anomaly Detection
  • AWS IoT Core Documentation
  • AWS IoT Greengrass Documentation
  • AWS IoT TwinMaker Documentation
  • Amazon S3 Documentation

What would you monitor first in a smart factory: temperature, vibration, pressure, or electrical current?

Share your thoughts in the comments.

AWS #IndustrialIoT #PredictiveMaintenance #SmartManufacturing #AWSIoT #MachineLearning #CloudComputing

title: Your G1 Pod Ignores SoftMaxHeapSize. Here's What Works Instead
description:
G1GC vs. ZGC vs. Shenandoah for Kubernetes 1.35 In-Place Pod Resize

When a pod shrinks in place, the JVM has to hand memory back to the operating system before the new limit applies. I tested how G1, ZGC and Shenandoah do that in a Linux container. All three released memory quickly in my test, but they differ in what triggers the release and in what SoftMaxHeapSize does. G1 accepts that flag and silently ignores it.

The short answer

  • ZGC and Shenandoah: SoftMaxHeapSize works at runtime. Lower it, run GC.run, and memory drops.
  • G1: SoftMaxHeapSize is accepted by jcmd and has no effect. By default nothing returns memory. Two things did, in my test: an explicit GC.run, and G1PeriodicGCInterval set to a few seconds.
  • Release speed: I measured no real difference. Each collector released a 300 MB working set within about 1 to 7 seconds. I did not measure large heaps or busy applications, which is where I'd expect differences, so treat "G1 is slower" as unproven.
  • The real G1 difference is the missing ceiling. Nothing holds G1's heap below a target after you release, so you size -Xmx for the peak and accept that it can grow back.
  • Lowering the limit first killed all three (OOMKilled, exit 137). Release first, then resize.

What each collector gives you

ZGC Shenandoah G1
SoftMaxHeapSize changes behavior Yes Yes No (flag accepted, no effect)
Returns memory by default After ZUncommitDelay (300 s by default) After ShenandoahUncommitDelay No, not without a trigger
What triggers a release SoftMaxHeapSize + GC.run, or the uncommit delay Same GC.run, or G1PeriodicGCInterval
Pause cost of the trigger Not measured Not measured GC.run is a full, stop-the-world GC. Not measured at scale.

The test

The setup is the same as in my earlier test of RestartContainer: Eclipse Temurin 21.0.13 in a Linux container on Docker Desktop, cgroup v2, and a small program that allocates and touches 300 MB, holds it for 10 seconds, then drops all of it and idles. docker update --memory=300m lowers the cgroup limit on the running container in place. That is the kernel mechanism a pod resize uses, but there is no kubelet.

For each collector, I ran two cases. Naive: lower the limit straight away. Ordered: set SoftMaxHeapSize=100MB, run GC.run, wait until memory.current falls, then lower the limit.

Collector memory.current before Naive: lower limit to 300 MB Ordered: release first, then lower
ZGC (-Xmx600m, limit 900 MB) 403 MB OOMKilled, exit 137 404 → 89 MB in 3 s, then still running
Shenandoah (-Xmx500m, limit 700 MB) 372 MB OOMKilled, exit 137 361 → 64 MB in 1 s, then still running
G1 (-Xmx600m, 4 MB regions, limit 900 MB) 456 MB OOMKilled, exit 137 463 → 143 MB in 2 s, then still running

G1 passes the ordered case, but I want to be exact about why. In that run I set SoftMaxHeapSize too, and it did nothing. The explicit GC.run did the work.

What actually released memory on G1

I tested each G1 lever on its own, starting from about 460 to 530 MB in use:

Lever on G1 Result
Nothing (default), wait 25 s 459 → 459 MB. No release.
SoftMaxHeapSize=100MB only, wait 20 s 535 → 535 MB. No effect.
GC.run only 472 → 150 MB
G1PeriodicGCInterval=3000 set live, no GC.run 518 → 156 MB in 7 s

SoftMaxHeapSize is listed as a manageable flag on G1 in JDK 21, so jcmd VM.set_flag returns "Command executed successfully". That success message is misleading. Nothing in G1 reads the flag. If your automation sets the flag and then checks that the command succeeded, it will believe it lowered the ceiling on G1 when it did not.

How to make G1 release memory back to the OS

Pick one of these. I tested the first two.

  1. Run GC.run from outside. jcmd <pid> GC.run triggers a full GC, after which G1 shrinks its heap. It is immediate, and it is a stop-the-world collection, so its pause grows with the live set.
  2. Enable periodic GC. G1PeriodicGCInterval is a manageable flag, default 0 (off). Set it at startup, or live: jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag G1PeriodicGCInterval 3000 (milliseconds). In my test, memory fell within 7 seconds on an idle JVM. A related flag, G1PeriodicGCSystemLoadThreshold, is also manageable and, per JEP 346, can hold the periodic GC back while the system is busy. I did not test it.
  3. Tune MinHeapFreeRatio and MaxHeapFreeRatio. These are manageable and control how much free heap G1 keeps after a collection. I did not test them here.

What this means for in-place resize

  • Release before you resize, on every collector. The failure was identical across all three: lowering the limit while the JVM held committed memory got it killed.
  • Don't trust "command succeeded" on G1. Verify that memory.current actually dropped, then resize. In Kubernetes, the kubelet's check also compares current usage to the new limit and holds the resize while usage is higher, although the docs say that check is best-effort.
  • Plan the ceiling on G1. With ZGC and Shenandoah, SoftMaxHeapSize keeps the heap near your target after release. On G1 nothing does, so a G1 heap that was just released can grow back toward -Xmx before the limit drops. I did not test how fast. The practical rule is the one from my earlier article: the smallest limit must exceed -Xmx plus non-heap memory, and on G1 you cannot rely on a soft ceiling to enforce it.
  • Mind the delay on ZGC. ZUncommitDelay defaults to 300 seconds. I shortened it to 1 second for the test. Without that, a ZGC release can take minutes unless you also lower the soft ceiling and wait for the uncommit.

What I didn't test

  • Heap sizes above about 600 MB, live data that doesn't die, or JVMs under load. A full GC on G1 can cost far more at scale, and I haven't measured it.
  • Whether G1 re-expands after release.
  • G1PeriodicGCSystemLoadThreshold, MinHeapFreeRatio and MaxHeapFreeRatio.
  • A real kubelet. I used docker update.
  • G1 with the default region size. I set 4 MB regions because my test allocates 1 MB arrays, which are "humongous" objects in G1's default configuration, and the first G1 run ran out of heap.

Reproduce it

You need Docker. Save the files below in an empty folder.

Hold.java:

import java.util.*;
public class Hold {
  public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
    List<byte[]> l = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) { byte[] b = new byte[1024*1024]; Arrays.fill(b,(byte)1); l.add(b); }
    System.out.println("allocated 300MB"); System.out.flush();
    Thread.sleep(10000);
    l.clear(); l = null;
    System.out.println("released refs"); System.out.flush();
    Thread.sleep(600000);
  }
}

run.sh runs the naive and ordered cases for any collector:

#!/bin/bash
# usage: ./run.sh <naive|ordered> <jvm flags...>      (run from the folder containing Hold.java)
# Example: LIM=900 XMX=600 ./run.sh ordered -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZUncommitDelay=1
set -u
mode=$1; shift; n=warden-test
docker rm -f $n >/dev/null 2>&1
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w eclipse-temurin:21-jdk javac Hold.java
docker run -d --name $n --memory=${LIM:-700}m --memory-swap=${LIM:-700}m -v "$PWD":/w -w /w \
  eclipse-temurin:21-jdk java "$@" -Xmx${XMX:-500}m Hold >/dev/null
for i in $(seq 1 60); do docker logs $n 2>&1 | grep -q 'released refs' && break; sleep 1; done; sleep 2
mem() { echo $(( $(docker exec $n cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current) / 1048576 )); }
echo "memory.current after the app dropped its data: $(mem) MB"
if [ "$mode" = ordered ]; then
  docker exec $n jcmd 1 VM.set_flag SoftMaxHeapSize 104857600   # 100 MB soft ceiling
  docker exec $n jcmd 1 GC.run
  for i in $(seq 1 30); do [ "$(mem)" -lt 250 ] && break; sleep 1; done
  echo "memory.current after SoftMaxHeapSize + GC.run: $(mem) MB"
fi
docker update --memory=300m --memory-swap=300m $n        # in-place cgroup change, no restart
sleep 8
docker inspect -f 'running={{.State.Running}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}}' $n
docker rm -f $n >/dev/null 2>&1

chmod +x run.sh
LIM=900 XMX=600 ./run.sh naive   -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=4m
LIM=900 XMX=600 ./run.sh ordered -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=4m
LIM=900 XMX=600 ./run.sh naive   -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZUncommitDelay=1
LIM=900 XMX=600 ./run.sh ordered -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZUncommitDelay=1
LIM=700 XMX=500 ./run.sh naive   -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:ShenandoahUncommitDelay=1000
LIM=700 XMX=500 ./run.sh ordered -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:ShenandoahUncommitDelay=1000

g1-probe.sh tests each G1 lever on its own:

#!/bin/bash
# Which G1 lever actually returns memory? Run from the folder containing Hold.java.
set -u
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w eclipse-temurin:21-jdk javac Hold.java
start() { docker rm -f $1 >/dev/null 2>&1
  docker run -d --name $1 --memory=900m --memory-swap=900m -v "$PWD":/w -w /w eclipse-temurin:21-jdk \
    java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=4m -Xmx600m Hold >/dev/null
  for i in $(seq 1 60); do docker logs $1 2>&1 | grep -q 'released refs' && break; sleep 1; done; sleep 2; }
mem() { echo $(( $(docker exec $1 cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current) / 1048576 )); }

echo "1) nothing (default), wait 25s";           start g1; b=$(mem g1); sleep 25; echo "   $b MB -> $(mem g1) MB"
echo "2) SoftMaxHeapSize=100MB only, wait 20s";  start g1; b=$(mem g1)
docker exec g1 jcmd 1 VM.set_flag SoftMaxHeapSize 104857600 >/dev/null; sleep 20; echo "   $b MB -> $(mem g1) MB"
echo "3) GC.run only";                           start g1; b=$(mem g1)
docker exec g1 jcmd 1 GC.run >/dev/null; sleep 4; echo "   $b MB -> $(mem g1) MB"
echo "4) G1PeriodicGCInterval=3000 set live";    start g1; b=$(mem g1)
docker exec g1 jcmd 1 VM.set_flag G1PeriodicGCInterval 3000 >/dev/null
for i in $(seq 1 40); do [ "$(mem g1)" -lt 250 ] && break; sleep 1; done; echo "   $b MB -> $(mem g1) MB (after ${i}s)"
docker rm -f g1 >/dev/null 2>&1

Expect OOMKilled=true exit=137 for naive runs and running=true for ordered ones. The megabyte numbers will differ a little on your machine.

FAQ

Which garbage collector is best for Kubernetes in-place pod resize?

In my test, ZGC and Shenandoah are the easiest, because SoftMaxHeapSize changes their behavior and keeps the heap near a target. G1 also works if something triggers a release, but it has no soft ceiling. Pick the collector your latency requirements need first, and then use the matching release method.

How do I make G1 release memory back to the OS?

Run jcmd <pid> GC.run, or set G1PeriodicGCInterval to a value in milliseconds (default 0, off). In my test both returned memory within a few seconds on a small idle heap.

Does SoftMaxHeapSize work with G1?

No. jcmd VM.set_flag SoftMaxHeapSize succeeds on G1 in JDK 21, but I saw no change in memory over 20 seconds, so I conclude G1 ignores it. It works on ZGC and Shenandoah.

Why was my pod OOMKilled after an in-place memory decrease?

The limit dropped while the JVM still held more committed memory than the new limit allows. In my test this killed the JVM on G1, ZGC and Shenandoah every time. Release memory first, check the resident memory, then lower the limit.

Is GC.run safe to use in production?

It triggers a full collection. On G1 that is stop-the-world, and its pause grows with the live set. I only tested a 600 MB heap on an idle JVM, so measure the pause on your own heap before relying on it.

Do I still need RestartContainer?

Only if the heap ceiling has to move. See my earlier article on RestartContainer for the case where it is and isn't required.

Where Warden fits

I maintain mnemo-jvm-warden, an open-source Kubernetes controller and sidecar that does the release-then-resize order for you. From its code and docs, it adjusts to the collector like this:

  • Detection: the agent reads the target's GC beans and records, per collector, whether a soft max and uncommit are supported. ZGC and Shenandoah support both. G1 supports uncommit only. Serial, Parallel and Epsilon are treated as unsupported, and the agent stays read-only for them.
  • Release: it sets SoftMaxHeapSize only where the collector has it, so on G1 that step is skipped instead of being sent and ignored. It then forces GC.run and polls the committed heap until it drops and holds steady. It checks the process's resident memory before it shrinks the pod.
  • Boost on G1: a G1 workload that wants a Boost lease must already launch with -Xmx covering the largest heapTarget it will request, because there is no soft ceiling to raise later. The agent rejects a heap target above the launch-time -Xmx for every collector, and the Boost docs note that G1 has no live soft-max knob, so a G1 Boost only ever confirms that the allocation change landed.

The conclusions above do not depend on any tool. The jcmd commands work without it.

title: GlobalPuzzle: Globally Informed Genetic Search for Eroded Jigsaw Puzzle Reassembly
description:
arXiv:2611.09077v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Jigsaw puzzle reassembly remains a highly challenging task, particularly when piece boundaries are irregularly eroded to simulate damage to cultural artifacts. On the GAP benchmark, existing methods achieve a perfect assembly accuracy of only 0.3% on $5 \times 5$ puzzles, whereas humans can solve jigsaw puzzles with remarkably high accuracy. Humans typically approach puzzle solving by identifying potentially adjacent pieces, evaluating the current assembly, and iteratively performing complex operations such as adding pieces, replacing incorrectly placed pieces, and moving entire connected groups of pieces. However, existing methods face a fundamental limitation: approaches that leverage global visual information typically predict piece arrangements directly, making it difficult to explicitly perform such complex iterative operations, while search based methods can rearrange pieces but primarily rely on pairwise boundary compatibility, lacking global visual information to evaluate and guide the search process. To bridge this gap, we propose GlobalPuzzle, a jigsaw puzzle reassembly framework that integrates global canvas level evaluation, action guidance, and genetic search. By incorporating global visual information into the evaluation and optimization of candidate assemblies, GlobalPuzzle aims to resolve ambiguous adjacency relationships that are difficult to determine from irregularly eroded piece boundaries alone, enabling flexible, globally informed reconstruction.

title: PhoPunct: A Large-Scale Benchmark of Transformer Architectures for Vietnamese Punctuation Restoration
description:
arXiv:2611.09107v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vietnamese punctuation restoration is often evaluated on relatively small benchmarks, limiting conclusions about how architectural choices scale with data volume. We present a controlled benchmark on News and Novels corpora containing 22.1 million labeled tokens (19.9M News and 2.2M Novels). We evaluate 17 architectures formed from four pretrained Transformer backbones and optional bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) and conditional random field (CRF) layers, together with a PhoBERT-large-Bi-LSTM-CRF model, PhoPunct. Every model is trained for eight epochs with the same learning rate and without architecture-specific tuning. Under this fixed budget, adding Bi-LSTM and CRF layers does not reliably improve macro F1: in seven of eight matched domain-backbone comparisons, a plain Transformer classifier matches or outperforms its Bi-LSTM-CRF counterpart. PhoPunct obtains the best News result (61.35), whereas XLM-R with a CRF obtains the best Novels result (50.18), exceeding PhoPunct (48.97). These results show that the value of recurrent and structured-prediction heads depends on their optimization regime and motivate explicit separation between architectural improvements and improvements due to architecture-specific tuning. Our source code is available at: https://github.com/aisia-research-lab/PhoPunct

title: Microsoft AZ-900: The Azure Fundamentals Exam That Rewards People Who Understand the Cloud, Not People Who Memorized It
description:
Microsoft AZ-900: The Azure Fundamentals Exam That Rewards People Who Understand the Cloud, Not People Who Memorized It

AZ-900 is the most underestimated exam in the Microsoft catalog. People hear "fundamentals" and assume it is a vocabulary quiz you can pass by memorizing a list of Azure service names the night before. Then they sit down, face 60 questions in 45 minutes, and discover the exam keeps asking why — why this service and not that one, why this pricing model fits this workload, why this governance control exists at all.

That is the whole exam in one sentence. AZ-900 is not a test of whether you can name Azure services. It is a test of whether you understand what cloud computing actually changes about how organizations buy, build, and govern IT. Once you study with that in mind, the exam gets dramatically easier — and the knowledge is genuinely useful afterward, whether or not you ever touch an Azure portal again.

What AZ-900 actually measures

The exam is 60 questions with a passing score of 700 on a 100–1000 scale, and you get 45 minutes — about 45 seconds per question, so there is no time to reason from scratch on anything you have not already thought through. Microsoft splits it across three domains, and the split tells you where to spend your time:

  • Describe cloud concepts (25–30%) — what cloud computing is, the shared responsibility model, cloud models (public, private, hybrid), and consumption-based pricing. This is the conceptual foundation, and it is also where memorizers lose points: the exam asks you to apply the concepts, not recite them.
  • Describe Azure architecture and services (35–40%) — the largest domain: core architectural components (regions, availability zones, resource groups), compute, networking, and storage services. Not deep configuration — selection. Which service fits which scenario.
  • Describe Azure management and governance (30–35%) — cost management, governance tools like Azure Policy and resource locks, identity and access, and monitoring. The domain most candidates under-study, and the one that most separates pass from fail.

Notice what is missing: there is no domain for clicking through the portal. AZ-900 never asks you to configure anything. It asks you to make the right choice among options, and to explain — by choosing — why that choice is right.

Stop memorizing service names. Start learning trade-offs.

Every AZ-900 candidate makes a list: Virtual Machines, App Service, Functions, Container Instances, Kubernetes Service, Blob Storage, SQL Database, Cosmos DB. The list grows, the exam still fails them, because the exam does not ask "what is Azure Functions?" It asks something like: a company runs a workload that spikes unpredictably twice a day and sits idle the rest of the time — which compute option keeps costs lowest? The answer is serverless, but only if you understand why consumption-based billing beats paying for idle VMs. The service name is the last step of the reasoning, not the first.

Here is a drill that works for every service in the syllabus. For each one, write three sentences: what it is in one line, the workload it is best for, and the workload it is wrong for. Azure Functions: event-driven code that runs without a server; best for sporadic, short tasks; wrong for long-running, always-on workloads. Blob Storage: object storage for unstructured data; best for images, backups, and archives; wrong for a relational database that needs transactions. Do that for twenty services and you have trained the exact muscle the exam grades — choosing between similar-sounding options under time pressure.

The same applies to the architecture concepts. Knowing that availability zones protect against datacenter failure is table stakes. The exam asks which design survives a zone outage, or why a company with strict data-residency rules picks a specific region. Learn each concept as a decision: what risk it removes, what it costs, and what breaks if you skip it.

The shared responsibility model is the exam's favorite trap

If there is one topic that decides more AZ-900 scores than any other, it is the shared responsibility model — and it is the topic most candidates study the shallowest. The model is simple on the surface: Microsoft secures the cloud, you secure what you put in it. The exam's questions live in the gray area between those two halves.

The rule that resolves almost every shared-responsibility question: the more Microsoft manages, the less you manage. On-premises, you own everything. With infrastructure as a service, Microsoft owns the physical datacenter and the hypervisor; you own the operating system, the applications, and the data. With platform as a service, Microsoft takes the OS and runtime too. With software as a service, Microsoft takes almost everything — your remaining responsibility is your data, your user accounts, and who can access what.

Practice by taking a service and sliding it along that spectrum. A virtual machine: you patch the OS. App Service: Microsoft patches the OS, you configure the app. Microsoft 365: Microsoft runs the whole stack, you govern the accounts and the data. Once that slider is intuitive, the exam's responsibility questions answer themselves — and the same thinking carries straight into the governance domain, where Azure Policy, role-based access control, and resource locks are all mechanisms for enforcing who can do what.

Pricing and governance: the 30% most people skip

Candidates love studying services and dread studying pricing and governance, which is exactly backward for AZ-900. The management and governance domain is nearly a third of the exam, and it is the most predictable third: the questions come from a small set of ideas, asked in a small set of ways.

Learn these cold: consumption-based pricing (pay for what you use, and the cost of idle resources), the Total Cost of Ownership calculator and the Pricing calculator (estimate before you commit, compare before you migrate), cost management tools and tags (track spending by department or project), and the difference between capital expenditure and operational expenditure — the single most-tested pricing concept on the exam, because the whole cloud business case rests on it.

On governance, the exam's favorite trio is Azure Policy (enforce rules, like "only deploy to these regions"), resource locks (prevent accidental deletion), and role-based access control (least privilege: give people exactly the access they need, nothing more). Pair each tool with the problem it solves and the mistake it prevents, and the questions become recognition exercises rather than recall exercises.

A two-week plan that actually works

Days 1–3: Cloud concepts. The shared responsibility model, cloud models, and consumption-based pricing. Do not move on until you can explain each concept to a non-technical colleague in plain language — if you cannot explain it, you do not know it well enough for the exam's scenario questions.

Days 4–8: Architecture and services. Work through the core services with the three-sentence drill above: what it is, what it is best for, what it is wrong for. Build a free Azure account and click through the portal once, just to see the services exist — AZ-900 does not test the portal, but seeing a resource group and a storage account makes the abstract concrete.

Days 9–11: Management and governance. Pricing calculators, cost management, Policy, locks, RBAC, and monitoring. This is the driest material and the highest-yield per hour spent. Flashcards actually work here, because the facts are crisp.

Days 12–14: Practice exams and review. Take full timed practice tests under exam conditions — 60 questions, 45 minutes, no pauses, no notes. Review every wrong answer by tracing it back to the domain and the concept, not just memorizing the right letter. Two or three full simulations in this week will tell you honestly whether you are ready, and the pattern in your misses is your remaining study plan.

Exam-day tactics

Forty-five minutes for 60 questions sounds comfortable until the scenario questions start eating the clock. Flag long questions and move on — answer the quick ones first, then return with a fresh brain and a known time budget. Read the last sentence of a scenario question first: it tells you what is actually being asked, and the paragraph above it is often full of distractors.

When two answers both look right, pick the one that fits the concept the question is testing, not the one that sounds most impressive. AZ-900 loves the simplest correct answer: the cheapest option that meets the requirement, the least-privilege access that gets the job done, the governance control that directly addresses the risk. Over-engineering is almost never the exam's answer.

Bottom line

AZ-900 rewards a specific kind of candidate: not the person who memorized the most service names, but the person who understands what the cloud changes — how costs move from capital to operational, how responsibility splits between Microsoft and the customer, and how to pick the right service for a real workload. Study like a decision-maker — trade-offs over lists, scenarios over flashcards, governance over trivia — and the exam stops being a memory contest and starts being a demonstration of something you can actually use.

If you want to test where you stand before exam day, work through realistic AZ-900 practice questions and pay attention to why you miss the ones you miss. The pattern in your misses is your study plan.

Practice the Microsoft AZ-900 exam with free practice questions on Study4Pass.

title: How we let an AI read production databases without trusting it
description:
Every engineering team knows this ticket: "I was charged twice."

Someone stops what they're doing, queries the database, greps the code, reads recent deploys and checks the logs. Eventually they explain the answer to support, who explain it to the customer.

I'm building TraceX, which does that investigation. To do it, it has to read production data, and the obvious reaction to "an AI reads your production database" is "absolutely not". That reaction is reasonable, so most of our design work has gone into one question:

How do you make this safe without relying on the model to behave?

Here's what we ended up with, including what's still weak. The rule behind all of it: anything that matters is enforced in code, not requested in a prompt.

1. Don't trust the credentials: check them

Asking people to "please use a read-only user" isn't a control. So TraceX checks the account's privileges when you connect, and refuses it if it can write:

SELECT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.tables
  WHERE table_schema NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
    AND has_table_privilege(format('%I.%I', table_schema, table_name),
                            'INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER')
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.schemata
  WHERE schema_name NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
    AND has_schema_privilege(schema_name, 'CREATE')
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 1 WHERE has_database_privilege(current_database(), 'CREATE')
);

If that returns true, the connection is rejected with a message telling you to use a read-only account.

2. The model never writes SQL

This is the decision I'd make again first. Giving a model a SQL tool means your safety depends on parsing whatever it generates. Instead, the model can only ask for a structured lookup: a table, some filters, some columns and a limit.

That request is checked against the introspected schema, then compiled into a parameterized statement. An unknown table or column fails validation. There's no string for the model to inject into, because it never produces a query string.

You lose flexibility. It can't write a clever five-way join. For "show me the records for this order", which is most of what an investigation needs, that's a trade I'm happy with.

3. Limit what a query can do, even when it's valid

Every query runs inside a read-only transaction, with a timeout and a row cap:

async with conn.transaction(readonly=True):
    await conn.execute("SET LOCAL statement_timeout = 3000")
    rows = await conn.fetch(sql, *params)  # at most 20 rows

So the database itself refuses writes, even if the checks above had a bug.

A commenter on our launch pointed out the next problem: read-only doesn't help if your connection pool is already saturated during an incident. They were right. So TraceX uses one connection per investigation, closes it afterwards, and tells you whether you've connected a replica or a primary:

SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();

If it's a primary, you still can connect, but you get a warning suggesting a read replica. You can also add your own ceiling:

ALTER ROLE tracex CONNECTION LIMIT 2;

4. Be honest about what reaches the model

Secret-looking fields and values are masked before a prompt is built. But the records TraceX reads do go to the model provider, because that's how it reasons about them. I'd rather say that plainly than imply otherwise. You can limit what it sees by restricting the database user to specific tables, and you can bring your own API key.

5. Don't let the model grade itself

Ask a model how confident it is and you'll get a confident answer. So the confidence score is computed from the findings, not taken from the model:

def overall_confidence(findings, supporting_ids, contradicting_ids=()):
    grounded = [f for f in supporting(findings, supporting_ids) if is_grounded(f)]
    if not grounded:
        return min(best_confidence, 0.3)  # no evidence, so it can't sound sure
    value = max(confidence(f) for f in grounded)
    value += 0.05 * (independent_sources(grounded) - 1)  # logs, database and code agree
    value -= 0.15 * len(grounded_findings_against(contradicting_ids))
    return min(value, 0.95)

A finding is "grounded" only if it cites real evidence: a record, a code location or a log line. A cause with no evidence is capped at 30%, however persuasive it sounds. The score never reaches 100%.

6. Show what was ruled out

This came directly from another comment we got:

A root-cause answer I can't check is just another confident guess, and the ruled-out hypotheses are the bit I'd actually want in front of a customer.

When we looked, we found a gap: our dashboard had a "Ruled out" section, but real investigations never filled it in. So now they do, with one strict rule: an explanation is only listed as ruled out if it cites a real finding that rules it out. If the model can't back it up, it's dropped, so "ruled out" can't become another unchecked claim.

The same comment asked what happens when evidence points two ways. If a competing cause is supported within 0.15 of the leading one, TraceX shows both side by side, caps confidence at 60%, and doesn't draft a fix. A close call should go to a human.

7. A fix is a suggestion, and some suggestions need a grown-up

TraceX can write a fix, but it never opens a pull request on its own. A person clicks, and nothing is merged without your team.

Risky fixes have stricter rules. A change is high risk if it touches migrations, the schema, auth, payments or config, or runs over 80 lines. We also check the content of the change, so a rename hidden in a file with an innocent name still counts:

DDL = re.compile(
    r"\b(ALTER|DROP|CREATE|TRUNCATE|RENAME)\s+(TABLE|INDEX|COLUMN|TYPE|SCHEMA|CONSTRAINT)\b"
    r"|\bop\.(add_column|drop_column|alter_column|create_table|drop_table|rename_table)\b",
    re.I,
)

(That's shortened; the real pattern covers Django and Rails migrations too.) High-risk fixes open only as draft pull requests, only an admin can open them, and the PR explains why it's flagged.

What's still weak

  • It only connects to PostgreSQL and MongoDB.
  • It doesn't always reach an answer. Sometimes it comes back inconclusive and says what's missing.
  • The structured queries limit it. Some questions really do need a join it can't express.
  • The DDL check is a pattern match, so it can miss things. It's a safety net, not a guarantee, which is why a human still reviews every pull request.
  • The numbers are judgment calls. The 0.15 penalty and 60% cap are our best current choices, not measured constants.
  • Ruled-out explanations depend on the model thinking of the alternatives. We can check that each one cites evidence, but not that it considered everything.

Try it

TraceX is in private beta. There's a sandbox with made-up data and no signup. Open "Refunds stuck in pending since Tuesday's release" and look at the Resolution tab to see the ruled-out explanations.

I'd really like to hear from you: what would you need to see before letting a tool like this read your production systems? And which of these guardrails do you think is weakest?

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
description:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.
