title: Un sang vieux de 115 millions d'années : ce que cela change pour quiconque lit des structures biologiques
description:
Un sang vieux de 115 millions d'années : ce que cela change pour quiconque lit des structures biologiques

Des chercheurs ont identifié des traces de sang ancien chimiquement confirmées à l'intérieur d'os de dinosaures vieux de 115 millions d'années. L'information, rapportée par ScienceDaily, bouscule une hypothèse confortable : celle selon laquelle les molécules biologiques ne résistent pas à l'échelle des temps géologiques. L'étude ne prétend pas avoir retrouvé de l'ADN intact ni de la matière vivante ; elle documente une préservation chimique inattendue, et ouvre des pistes sur la physiologie des dinosaures comme sur la recherche de vie ancienne ailleurs dans l'univers.

Pourquoi ce résultat concerne-t-il des gens qui ne travaillent ni en paléontologie ni en astrobiologie ?

Parce qu'il touche au cœur du métier structural : la persistance de l'information. Une protéine, une hème, un ligand, une carte de densité — tout cela n'est lisible que si l'on accepte de raisonner sur des signaux partiels. La découverte rappelle que la robustesse chimique est plus grande qu'on ne le pensait, et donc que l'interprétation d'une structure dégradée mérite autant de rigueur que celle d'une structure parfaite.

C'est précisément là que la représentation visuelle cesse d'être cosmétique. Une poche mal délimitée, une superposition d'homologues approximative, une distance interatomique mal lue : chacune de ces erreurs se paie en mois de travail.

NexoPeek est un laboratoire moléculaire en réalité virtuelle pour Meta Quest, développé par Seven Sportz. L'idée de départ est simple : arrêter de regarder une molécule aplatie sur un écran et marcher dedans, à l'échelle humaine.

Architecture de l'expérience

Deux pistes cohabitent dans un seul casque. La première est pédagogique : douze visites narrées réparties en six piliers — bases de la biotechnologie, fondements du vivant, voies et interactions, médicaments en action, technologies génétiques, biotech verte. On entre dans l'hémoglobine pour voir l'oxygène se fixer, on suit le glucose qui se décompose dans la glycolyse, on observe l'aspirine bloquer les enzymes COX, on regarde CRISPR-Cas9 éditer l'ADN. Toutes les visites tournent sur de vraies structures issues de la Protein Data Bank.

La seconde est un poste de travail scientifique. Une barre de recherche intelligente résout un nom de gène par cascades de mots-clés et synonymes UniProt à travers RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS-MODEL et PDBe, avec validation automatique du modèle chargé. Les fichiers locaux (.pdb, .cif, .mol2, .gro, .xyz, .dx, .xtc, .py) s'ouvrent directement, avec possibilité de superposer cartes de lignes de champ électrostatique, définitions de liaisons personnalisées et volumes de densité électronique.

Côté rendu, six préréglages Mol* dérivés des concepts MolViewSpec se cyclent en un geste : cartoon, ball-and-stick, spacefill CPK, surface moléculaire, carte B-factor, trace en tube.

Le banc d'analyse

C'est ici que la VR change la nature du raisonnement, pas seulement le confort.

À mains nues (ou avec les contrôleurs), on attrape, on met à l'échelle et on fait tourner la molécule. La prédiction de poches par IA met en évidence un site druggable lumineux — PrankWeb / P2Rank en cloud, ou le moteur hors ligne embarqué. Foldseek superpose un homologue pour évaluer la conservation fonctionnelle d'un domaine et tester des hypothèses de substitution médicamenteuse. L'inspecteur de ligands scanne les hétéro-composés, trace les réseaux de liaisons hydrogène et va chercher un ligand 3D dans PubChem. Sélectionner deux atomes à la gâchette donne la distance exacte en ångströms. Et les pastilles de résidus touchées dans la séquence projettent un halo 3D directement sur la structure.

Un point d'ingénierie mérite d'être souligné : le moteur de prédiction de poches existe en deux modes, cloud et hors ligne. Sur un bench de laboratoire sans réseau — ou sur un poste de terrain — l'analyse reste possible, simplement avec une latence et une couverture de modèles différentes. C'est un compromis classique entre fraîcheur des modèles et autonomie d'exécution, et il est ici explicite plutôt que caché.

Du cours à la découverte de médicaments

Un bouton Room View fait flotter la molécule dans votre vraie pièce, le menu mural restant opérable en mode passthrough. Un étudiant explore l'ATP, un enseignant explique CRISPR, un biologiste structural inspecte une poche de liaison — dans un seul casque, sans changement de contexte logiciel.

À savoir

NexoPeek est un logiciel éducatif et de visualisation pour la recherche. Ce n'est pas un dispositif médical : rien ici ne constitue un avis médical, un diagnostic ou un traitement. Les aides à l'analyse (prédiction de poches, alignement) soutiennent les pipelines scientifiques validés et le jugement professionnel — elles ne les remplacent pas. Vérifiez toute conclusion contre la littérature primaire et des méthodes validées.

Essayer NexoPeek sur Meta Quest : https://www.meta.com/experiences/nexopeek/1453797551140347/ — Step Inside the Molecule. Explore the Unseen World.

Source de l'actualité : https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261105224542.htm (ScienceDaily). Vérifiez les détails de l'étude auprès de la publication originale avant toute citation académique. Les informations sur les produits proviennent de la page officielle NexoPeek sur le Meta Quest Store ; les visuels évoqués ici sont des illustrations et non des captures de jeu officielles.

title: Lesson 9: Install Node.js and NPM inside a Docker Container
description:
Laravel Docker Lessons · Lesson 9

Add Node.js 22 and npm to Laravel Docker, install locked frontend packages, compile Vite assets and view a working Tailwind and JavaScript demo.

This written tutorial follows the actual lesson-9 source snapshot. The published Urdu video lesson is available alongside this written guide.

Continue from Lesson 8, or browse the complete blog.

This lesson adds Node.js 22 and npm to the existing PHP container, alongside Composer from Lesson 8. We use them to install this project's locked frontend dependencies and build its real Vite assets. PHP-FPM continues to serve Laravel; Node is a build tool in this example and is not a new application server.

Complete file checklist before running commands

The complete Dockerfile, updated Compose volume list, route, Blade page and JavaScript entry are shown below. The CSS entry and Vite configuration are inherited Laravel files, but their complete code is also included so the frontend demonstration can be recreated. Keep package.json and obtain the matching package-lock.json from this tag. Do not copy Windows node_modules into the container.

File Action from the previous lesson Exact source
Dockerfile Update the existing file; full code included View complete file
docker-compose.yaml Update the existing file; full code included View complete file
resources/js/app.js Update the existing file; full code included View complete file
resources/views/frontend-demo.blade.php Create this file; full code included View complete file
routes/web.php Update the existing file; full code included View complete file
.dockerignore Keep the inherited file; inspect the exact snapshot View complete file
package.json Keep the inherited file; inspect the exact snapshot View complete file
resources/css/app.css Keep the inherited file; inspect the exact snapshot View complete file
vite.config.js Keep the inherited file; inspect the exact snapshot View complete file
.docker/nginx/default.conf Keep the inherited file; inspect the exact snapshot View complete file

Use the committed lock files from the same tag. They are download/source links rather than abbreviated code samples: composer.lock, package-lock.json.

Recording preparation and follow-up checks

After renewing the anonymous node_modules volume, run npm ci again before npm run build. Stop any old Vite development server and remove its stale public/hot pointer before a build-mode recording. Open /frontend-demo and click its button to confirm JavaScript is loaded.

Before recording, follow the recording checklist and PowerShell preflight. Current main excludes generated bootstrap config cache and public/hot from Docker build context. For historical tags, clear old host config cache before rebuilding and renew PHP runtime volumes so earlier database settings are not reused.

Add Node and npm to the PHP image

The Dockerfile copies the Node executable and npm modules from node:22-bookworm-slim. It creates npm and npx symlinks and sets NPM_CONFIG_CACHE=/tmp/npm-cache for www-data. Both donor and PHP images use Debian/glibc; an Alpine/musl binary would not be interchangeable. A build-time version check verifies the copied tools run.

Node 22 meets Vite 7's Node requirement in this project. The exact frontend package versions come from package-lock.json. The official Node tag tracks updates within version 22; inspect node --version to see the resolved patch version.

Build and recreate PHP

Use a prepared .env and application key from earlier lessons, or follow Lesson 8's fresh-checkout bootstrap first.

docker compose build web
docker compose up -d --renew-anon-volumes db web nginx
docker compose exec web node --version
docker compose exec web npm --version
docker compose exec web npm ci
docker compose exec web npm run build
docker compose exec web php artisan migrate --force

npm ci installs the committed lock file without rewriting it. The separate anonymous /var/www/html/node_modules volume prevents host Windows modules from being reused inside Linux. It also keeps container dependencies out of the source checkout. After recreating with --renew-anon-volumes, rerun npm ci because that module volume is fresh.

The public/build output lives in the source bind mount, so the separate Nginx container sees and serves the generated files. node_modules is not a web asset directory and is not served. On a Linux host, make the bind-mounted source writable by the container's www-data user; do not solve permissions by making all project files world-writable.

View the actual Vite demo

Open http://localhost:8080/frontend-demo or use your configured application port. routes/web.php renders frontend-demo.blade.php, which uses Laravel's @vite(['resources/css/app.css', 'resources/js/app.js']) directive. The page is styled with the project's Tailwind/Vite pipeline, and a button proves the JavaScript module loaded.

The app's existing entry module adds an event listener for the demo button. It does not require a framework or another dependency. In the browser, clicking the button changes its text to JavaScript is working!.

Build mode versus development mode

This lesson uses npm run build: static versioned assets, no Vite development server, and no additional port. If you previously ran npm run dev, stop it and remove a stale public/hot file before viewing build output. Otherwise Laravel may try to load assets from that old development server.

docker compose exec web node -e "console.log(require('fs').existsSync('public/build/manifest.json'))"
docker compose exec web npm ls --depth=0
docker compose down

The first command should print true after a successful build. Missing-manifest errors mean the build has not completed or the output is not visible to PHP/Nginx. Stop without -v to retain named database data. This container includes developer tooling for teaching; a separate production image can later copy only built assets.

How the implementation fits together

Diagram of the implementation in the lesson-9 tag; this is not a production monitoring screenshot.

The working Vite Blade page

Actual browser verification with compiled Tailwind CSS and JavaScript.

Configuration and source code

The following files are read directly from this lesson’s Git tag. Later lessons add further capabilities; they do not change this snapshot.

Dockerfile 

FROM php:8.2-fpm

WORKDIR /var/www/html

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    libzip-dev \
    libpq-dev \
    unzip \
    && docker-php-ext-install zip pdo_mysql pdo_pgsql pcntl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN pecl install mongodb-1.21.2 \
    && docker-php-ext-enable mongodb

COPY --from=composer:2 /usr/bin/composer /usr/local/bin/composer
ENV COMPOSER_HOME=/tmp/composer

COPY --from=node:22-bookworm-slim /usr/local/bin/node /usr/local/bin/node
COPY --from=node:22-bookworm-slim /usr/local/lib/node_modules /usr/local/lib/node_modules
RUN ln -s ../lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js /usr/local/bin/npm \
    && ln -s ../lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npx-cli.js /usr/local/bin/npx \
    && node --version && npm --version
ENV NPM_CONFIG_CACHE=/tmp/npm-cache

COPY --chown=www-data:www-data . /var/www/html

RUN COMPOSER_ALLOW_SUPERUSER=1 composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader \
    && mkdir -p node_modules \
    && chown -R www-data:www-data vendor storage bootstrap/cache node_modules /tmp/composer \
    && chmod -R 775 storage bootstrap/cache

docker-compose.yaml 

x-laravel-environment: &laravel-environment
  DB_URL: ""
  DB_SOCKET: ""
  DB_CONNECTION: mysql
  DB_HOST: db
  DB_PORT: 3306
  DB_DATABASE: laravel_app
  DB_USERNAME: root
  DB_PASSWORD: root
  QUEUE_CONNECTION: database
  DB_QUEUE_RETRY_AFTER: 90

x-laravel-service: &laravel-service
  build:
    context: .
    dockerfile: Dockerfile
  image: my-laravel-app
  working_dir: /var/www/html
  user: "www-data"
  volumes:
    - .:/var/www/html
    - /var/www/html/vendor
    - /var/www/html/node_modules
    - /var/www/html/storage
    - /var/www/html/bootstrap/cache
  environment:
    <<: *laravel-environment
    SCHEDULER_DEMO_ENABLED: "false"
  depends_on:
    db:
      condition: service_healthy

services:
  web:
    <<: *laravel-service

  scheduler:
    <<: *laravel-service
    profiles: ["scheduler"]
    init: true
    command: ["php", "artisan", "schedule:work", "--no-interaction"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *laravel-environment
      CACHE_STORE: file
      SCHEDULER_DEMO_ENABLED: "true"

  worker:
    <<: *laravel-service
    profiles: ["queue"]
    init: true
    command: ["php", "artisan", "queue:work", "database", "--queue=emails", "--sleep=1", "--tries=3", "--timeout=30", "--max-time=3600", "--no-interaction"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    stop_grace_period: 45s

  nginx:
    image: nginx:latest
    ports:
      - "${APP_PORT:-8080}:80"
    volumes:
      - .:/var/www/html:ro
      - ./.docker/nginx/default.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - web

  db:
    image: mysql:8.0
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root
      MYSQL_DATABASE: laravel_app
    ports:
      - "${DB_FORWARD_PORT:-3308}:3306"
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/mysql
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "mysqladmin ping -h 127.0.0.1 -p\"$${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD}\" --silent"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 20
      start_period: 20s

volumes:
  dbdata:

package.json 

{
    "$schema": "https://www.schemastore.org/package.json",
    "private": true,
    "type": "module",
    "scripts": {
        "build": "vite build",
        "dev": "vite"
    },
    "devDependencies": {
        "@tailwindcss/vite": "^4.0.0",

        "laravel-vite-plugin": "^2.0.0",
        "tailwindcss": "^4.0.0",
        "vite": "^7.0.7"
    }
}

routes/web.php

use App\Http\Controllers\SchedulerDemoController;
use App\Mail\QueueDemoMail;
use App\Models\MongoNote;

Route::get('/queue-demo/mail-preview', fn () => new QueueDemoMail('Laravel Developer', 'preview-only'))
    ->name('queue-demo.mail-preview');

Route::view('/frontend-demo', 'frontend-demo')->name('frontend-demo');

resources/views/frontend-demo.blade.php

resources/css/app.css

@source '../../vendor/laravel/framework/src/Illuminate/Pagination/resources/views/*.blade.php';
@source '../../storage/framework/views/*.php';

Verification performed

The container ran Node.js 22.23.3 and npm 10.9.9. With a fresh www-data-owned node_modules volume, npm ci installed 91 packages and reported zero audit vulnerabilities at verification time. Vite 7.3.7 compiled 58 modules and produced a manifest, CSS and JavaScript. The Blade route returned HTTP 200, and a browser click changed the button to JavaScript is working!. The focused Blade test passed with three assertions.

title: VoluCompose: Constructing Compact Volumetric Visual Representations for Medical Image Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.08649v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at https://github.com/yezanting/VoluCompose.

title: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed
description:
arXiv:2611.09085v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hundreds of millions of Indians communicate with digital systems in romanized Latin characters -- typing "aap kaise hain" rather than native script -- yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. We demonstrate that automatic metrics (BGE-M3, BERTScore) systematically misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada generation. We evaluate four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on a 12-point rubric, whereas their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004. Two distinct model-specific failure modes emerge: Gemini produces script spillage (16.9% of Telugu responses leak native script), while Qwen collapses to English-only output (16.2% of Kannada responses). We introduce a failure-aware evaluation policy that assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses, and instruction collapses -- revealing failures metrics alone cannot detect. Our results show that evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle: semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.

title: Why Kubernetes In-Place Memory Resize Gets Stuck "In Progress" on JVM Pods
description:
You lowered a JVM pod's memory with an in-place resize, and the pod now shows PodResizeInProgress, an Error reason, and an old memory limit that never changes. The kubelet is not broken. It refuses to lower a memory limit below the container's current usage, and a JVM keeps its committed heap even after the objects in it are garbage. The resize completes as soon as the JVM gives the memory back, which I confirmed on a Kubernetes 1.35.8 cluster. Below are the real outputs, the fix, and how long it took.

The short answer

  • Cause: the kubelet will not apply a memory-limit decrease while the container's current usage is above the new limit. A JVM's usage stays high after garbage collection because it keeps the heap committed.
  • Symptom: condition PodResizeInProgress=True with reason Error. containerStatuses[].allocatedResources shows the new value, but containerStatuses[].resources still shows the old one.
  • It retries. The kubelet retried about every 11 to 15 seconds. The pod was not OOM-killed and did not restart. The check protected the JVM.
  • Fix: make the JVM release memory, then let the resize finish. Releasing after the patch finished the resize on the next retry (about 20 s in my run). Releasing before the patch finished it 2 seconds after the patch, and the error never appeared.
  • PodResizePending is a different problem. I saw it only when I asked for more memory than the node has (Infeasible).

What it looks like

I ran a JVM pod on a single-node kind cluster, Kubernetes v1.35.8. The pod has Guaranteed QoS with a 900Mi memory request and limit. The JVM (Temurin 21, ZGC, -Xmx600m) allocates 300 MB, holds it for 10 seconds, then drops all of it and idles. Inside the container, memory.current read 417 MB.

I shrank it to 300Mi through the resize subresource:

kubectl patch pod jvm --subresource resize -p \
  '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"app","resources":{"requests":{"memory":"300Mi"},"limits":{"memory":"300Mi"}}}]}}'

A few minutes later, kubectl get pod jvm -o yaml (trimmed) showed:

status:
  conditions:
  - message: 'cannot decrease memory limits: [attempting to set pod memory limit (314572800)
      below current usage (435347456), attempting to set container "app" memory limit
      (314572800) below current usage (435347456)]'
    observedGeneration: 2
    reason: Error
    status: "True"
    type: PodResizeInProgress
  containerStatuses:
  - name: app
    allocatedResources:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 300Mi        # what the kubelet accepted
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 900Mi      # what is actually applied
    restartCount: 0

At +10 s the condition was PodResizeInProgress=True with no reason. By +31 s the reason was Error. The cgroup never changed: memory.max stayed at 900 MB, and memory.current stayed at 417 MB for the whole minute I watched.

The events show a repeating error, and the kubelet log says why:

Normal   ResizeStarted   Pod resize started: {... "memory":"300Mi" ... "generation":2}
Warning  ResizeError     Pod resize error: {... "error":"cannot decrease memory limits: [attempting to set pod memory limit (314572800) below current usage (435347456) ...]"}
Warning  ResizeError     (repeats)

kubelet: "Allocated pod resize is not currently feasible" err="cannot decrease memory limits: ..."
kubelet: ... ResizePodInPlaceError ... (retries at 18:50:18, :33, :47, :58, 18:51:13, :25)

That matches what the Kubernetes docs say: before decreasing a container's memory limit, if memory usage exceeds the requested limit, the resize is skipped and the status remains in an "In Progress" state. They call this best-effort because usage can spike right after the check. What the docs don't show is the Error reason and the repeating ResizeError events, which look alarming but are the kubelet waiting.

Why a JVM does this

The kubelet compares the container's current memory usage with the new limit. A JVM's usage is dominated by committed heap, and the JVM does not return committed heap just because the objects in it are gone.

In my test the JVM sat idle for more than a minute with ZUncommitDelay=1 and gave nothing back. The likely reason is that no garbage-collection cycle ran after the data was dropped, so there was nothing to trigger an uncommit. I did not confirm that, and the behavior depends on the collector. Don't count on a JVM to release by itself.

PodResizeInProgress vs PodResizePending

Condition What it means What I saw
PodResizeInProgress The kubelet accepted the new resources and is applying them. With Error and "below current usage", the kubelet is retrying a memory decrease.
PodResizePending The resize can't be started yet. reason=Infeasible, message Node didn't have enough capacity: memory, requested: 68719476736, capacity: 8321712128, when I asked for 64Gi on an 8 GB node.

If you see Infeasible or Deferred, the problem is node capacity. If you see InProgress plus "below current usage", the problem is the container's own memory, and the fix is below.

The fix: release memory from inside the JVM

On ZGC, lower the soft ceiling and force a collection:

kubectl exec jvm -- jcmd 1 VM.set_flag SoftMaxHeapSize 104857600
kubectl exec jvm -- jcmd 1 GC.run

Releasing while the resize was pending. I ran the two commands against the stuck pod. memory.current fell from 417 MB to 96 MB. The kubelet applied the resize on its next retry, 20 seconds after I started the release. memory.max became 300 MB, restartCount stayed 0, the condition cleared, and a ResizeCompleted event appeared.

Releasing before the patch. I recreated the pod, released first (424 MB → 101 MB), then patched. The resize applied 2 seconds after the patch. For this pod, the events were ResizeStarted and ResizeCompleted only. The Error condition never appeared.

Releasing first is cleaner: no error condition, no wait for a retry. But if you are already stuck, you don't need to re-patch. Free the memory and the kubelet finishes the job.

When it stays stuck

The resize stays "In Progress" if the JVM can't get below the new limit:

  • Live data is bigger than the new limit. If the heap holds more live objects than the limit, I'd expect no collection to free enough, and the resize to stay pending. I didn't test this case. Pick a limit that fits.
  • The ceiling is fixed. -Xmx can't change on a running JVM. The new limit must be above -Xmx plus metaspace, code cache, thread stacks and direct buffers. If it isn't, you need a restart, which is what resizePolicy: RestartContainer is for.
  • Memory outside the heap. SoftMaxHeapSize only moves the heap. Native memory and direct buffers stay.

A debugging checklist 

# 1. Which condition? InProgress or Pending, and the reason
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[?(@.type=="PodResizeInProgress")]}{.reason}: {.message}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[?(@.type=="PodResizePending")]}{.reason}: {.message}{"\n"}{end}'

# 2. What is accepted vs actually applied
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='allocated={.status.containerStatuses[0].allocatedResources.memory} applied={.status.containerStatuses[0].resources.limits.memory}{"\n"}'

# 3. What the container is really using
kubectl exec <pod> -- sh -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max'

# 4. The events
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod>

If memory.current is above the new limit, the JVM is the thing to fix.

One gotcha from my own test: use the default strategic merge patch, as in the command above. With --type merge, the whole containers list is replaced, and the API server rejects it with "resource requests cannot be removed".

What I didn't test

  • Collectors other than ZGC in a cluster. I tested ZGC, Shenandoah and G1 in a container separately, in another article, but not through a kubelet.
  • A multi-container pod, or any version other than v1.35.8.
  • Whether the retry interval changes under load, or what happens if usage spikes right after the kubelet's check.
  • How long a release takes on a large heap under real traffic.

Reproduce it

You need Docker, kind and kubectl. Hold.java:

import java.util.*;
public class Hold {
  public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
    List<byte[]> l = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) { byte[] b = new byte[1024*1024]; Arrays.fill(b,(byte)1); l.add(b); }
    System.out.println("allocated 300MB"); System.out.flush();
    Thread.sleep(10000);
    l.clear(); l = null;
    System.out.println("released refs"); System.out.flush();
    Thread.sleep(600000);
  }
}

pod.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: jvm
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: eclipse-temurin:21-jdk
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    command: ["java","-XX:+UseZGC","-XX:ZUncommitDelay=1","-Xmx600m","/w/Hold.java"]
    volumeMounts: [{name: w, mountPath: /w}]
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 900Mi}
      limits:   {cpu: 500m, memory: 900Mi}
    resizePolicy:
    - {resourceName: memory, restartPolicy: NotRequired}
    - {resourceName: cpu, restartPolicy: NotRequired}
  volumes:
  - name: w
    configMap: {name: hold}

kind create cluster --name resize-test --image kindest/node:v1.35.8
kubectl create configmap hold --from-file=Hold.java
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/jvm --timeout=240s
# wait ~15 s until the JVM logs "released refs", then:
kubectl patch pod jvm --subresource resize -p \
  '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"app","resources":{"requests":{"memory":"300Mi"},"limits":{"memory":"300Mi"}}}]}}'
kubectl get pod jvm -o yaml        # PodResizeInProgress, reason Error
kubectl exec jvm -- jcmd 1 VM.set_flag SoftMaxHeapSize 104857600
kubectl exec jvm -- jcmd 1 GC.run  # the kubelet finishes on its next retry
kind delete cluster --name resize-test

The first image pull took about 90 seconds on my machine. The megabyte numbers will differ a little on yours.

FAQ

Why is my Kubernetes pod resize stuck in progress?

The kubelet will not lower a memory limit below the container's current usage, and it keeps retrying. Check kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml for PodResizeInProgress with a message saying "below current usage". Free memory inside the container and the resize finishes.

What is the difference between PodResizePending and PodResizeInProgress?

PodResizePending means the resize can't start yet. I saw it with reason=Infeasible when the request exceeded the node's capacity. PodResizeInProgress means the kubelet accepted the resize and is applying it. For a memory decrease it stays that way while usage is above the new limit.

Why won't the kubelet complete an in-place memory decrease for my Java pod?

A JVM keeps its committed heap after garbage collection, so the container's usage stays above the new limit. On ZGC or Shenandoah, lower SoftMaxHeapSize and run GC.run. On G1, use GC.run or G1PeriodicGCInterval.

Will the pod be OOM-killed while the resize is stuck?

Not in my test. The pod kept running at 900Mi, with 0 restarts, until I freed memory. The Kubernetes docs say the check is best-effort, with no guarantees.

Do I need to patch again after freeing memory?

No. The kubelet retries on its own. In my run it completed 20 seconds after I released memory, with no new patch.

How long does the kubelet take to apply the resize after the JVM releases memory?

20 seconds in the run where I released after the patch (the kubelet was retrying about every 11 to 15 seconds). If you release before the patch, it applied 2 seconds after.

Where Warden fits

I maintain mnemo-jvm-warden, an open-source Kubernetes controller and sidecar that does the release-then-resize order. The sidecar lowers the soft heap ceiling where the collector supports it, forces GC.run, and checks that the process's resident memory dropped. Only then does the resize reach the kubelet. That order is the second case in this article, where the error never appears. I haven't tested that exact path in the cluster in this article.

You don't need a tool for the fix: the two jcmd commands above work on their own.

title: PathXAI: Evidence-guided structured pathology reporting by transferable tissue segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.09117v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pathology reporting requires translating tissue observations across regions and slides into specific diagnoses and supporting morphological descriptions. However, the use of explicit tissue-composition measurements to guide H&E-based report generation remains underexplored. Thus, we developed PathXAI, which combines segmentation-derived tissue information with H&E images and optional domain knowledge to guide diagnostic reasoning, targeted reinspection and structured report writing. Its segmentation component exceeded baselines in mean Dice on internal and external tests. In automated report evaluation on 1,200 public and 151 private cases, PathXAI achieved higher agreement with reference diagnoses and documented morphology than the H&E-based comparators. On the public evaluation cohort, PathXAI-Report exceeded Qwen + H&E in cancer family match rate by 4.4 percentage points and in finding F1 by 5.7 percentage points. PathXAI generates evidence-linked reports with a self-hosted pretrained vision-language model, without updating its weights.

title: I Built an Interactive 3D Camera You Can Take Apart in Your Browser 📷
description:
I've been exploring Three.js and WebGL lately, experimenting with different ways to make websites more interactive.

One thing I really enjoy about 3D on the web is that you're not limited to displaying objects. You can actually let people interact with them, explore them, and understand how things work.

So I decided to build something around that idea.

Meet Camera Lab — an interactive 3D experience where you can explore a DSLR camera, take it apart, and see what's happening inside.

📷

What's interesting about it?

Instead of simply displaying a 3D camera that rotates, I wanted people to be able to explore the engineering behind it.

Here's what you can do:

  • 🔄 Rotate and explore: View the camera from different angles, zoom in, and inspect the details.
  • 🧩 Take it apart: Use the exploded-view slider to separate the camera's components and put everything back together.
  • 🔍 Explore 25 components: Click individual parts to learn more about them, including the lens, shutter, mirror, sensor, and internal electronics.
  • 👁️ X-ray mode: Look through the camera's exterior to see what's happening inside.
  • 🎯 Guided exploration: Follow a step-by-step tour showing how light travels through a DSLR camera.
  • 📸 Capture screenshots: Save a view of the 3D model directly from the experience.

One of my favourite parts is the exploded view. Seeing the different components separate and come back together makes the whole experience much more interesting.

🛠️ What did I build it with?

The main technologies behind the project are:

  • Three.js / WebGL — 3D rendering and interactions
  • React + TypeScript — Application structure and UI
  • GSAP — Animations and transitions
  • Tailwind CSS — Styling
  • Vite — Development and build tooling
  • Vercel — Deployment

The camera model is generated using procedural 3D geometry rather than relying on a downloaded camera model.

This made it possible to work with the components individually and create the interactive disassembly experience.

💡 Why I enjoyed building this

What interests me most about Three.js is how it opens up a different approach to web development.

A website doesn't always have to be a collection of pages, buttons, and forms.

Sometimes it can be an experience.

Projects like this make me want to keep exploring interactive product visualizations, 3D storytelling, and educational experiences on the web.

And honestly, there's still a lot I want to learn.

🚀 Give it a try!

I'd really appreciate some feedback from fellow developers, especially anyone working with Three.js, WebGL, or creative frontend development.

Live demo: https://the-camera.vercel.app/

GitHub: https://github.com/jude4/the-camera

💬 I'd love to hear your thoughts!

If you try it out, I'm curious:

  1. What's your favourite part of the experience?
  2. Is there anything you'd improve about the interactions or design?
  3. What other everyday objects would be interesting to explore this way in 3D?

I'm also thinking about what I could build next using Three.js.

Would love to hear your suggestions!

Thanks for checking it out! 🚀

title: UniRGBA: Unifying RGB and Alpha in Pretrained Video Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2611.09069v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have achieved remarkable photorealistic RGB synthesis, yet generating videos with a native alpha channel remains an open challenge. Existing approaches often rely on matting-style data and non-native RGBA designs, causing them to specialize in real-object scenes and to degrade severely on visual-effect content whose semi-transparency is spatially non-local and non-elliptical. We present UniRGBA, a unified framework whose key insight is that RGBA generation does not require a dedicated alpha encoder or complex latent-space restructuring---a minimal, targeted extension of the existing RGB pathway is sufficient. UniRGBA-VAE extends a causal video VAE to 4-channel RGBA via zero-initialized channel expansion, symmetric selective layer unfreezing (5% trainable), and a six-term progressive reconstruction loss anchored by a KL reference loss that prevents latent drift, followed by a two-stage schedule that introduces a lightweight GAN objective. We then apply standard DoRA to the pretrained DiT, reusing the unified 4-channel latent without any alpha-specific architectural changes. On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, UniRGBA substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA reconstruction while preserving RGB fidelity. For generation, UniRGBA outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA text-to-video tasks and matches or surpasses the original pretrained Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics, demonstrating that native alpha support can be integrated without compromising the underlying RGB prior or the model's architectural versatility.

title: ElevenLabs on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

The AI Gateway audio docs have examples across the ElevenLabs models. Browse all audio models on AI Gateway, and try ElevenLabs at 50% off until November 9th.

title: Vercel for Enterprise
description:
AI adoption in the enterprise is growing rapidly, and expanding beyond engineering users.

In the last three months, token usage by enterprise companies on AI Gateway has quadrupled, and OpenAI recently reported that from August 2025 to June 2026, non-developer Codex users grew 189x.

Our customers call these builders citizen developers. They know their part of the business better than anyone else, and with AI they can create the software they need to ship work faster and deliver better customer experiences.

Building has never been easier, but that also means that control and governance have never been harder. Employees are using AI tools whether they are approved or not, and if a citizen developer vibe codes a login page incorrectly, private data can reach the public internet.

Enterprise leaders have to figure out how to let everyone build, without giving up security or control.

Enterprise Apps and Agents

We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to solve these challenges at Vercel, and in June, we made it available to our customers. Enterprise Apps and Agents is a central control plane for governing every builder, app, agent, token, and dollar.

Today, we are expanding the platform:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) on AWS is generally available, giving you the full Vercel developer experience, while keeping compute and data inside your AWS boundary.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization through Vercel Connect is launching in public beta, giving agents the ability to access connected services on behalf of employees through your IdP.

A single control plane for governing enterprise AI

Enterprise Apps and Agents gives you a single deployment destination for both engineers and citizen developers, with central governance over access, providers, models, data retention, token budgets, integrations, and policies, managed through your existing IdP.

Vercel centralizes AI governance so that company policies can be applied consistently across control domains.

Control domain

Vercel controls

Deployment governance

Enterprise Managed Users and RBAC

Access governance

Vercel Passport, Deployment Protection, and Vercel Firewall

Integration and data governance

Vercel Connect and Enterprise-Managed Authorization

Model and token governance

AI Gateway, including US-only inference and budget controls

Apps and agents run on the same infrastructure that powers billions of production deployments, and Vercel gives you a single place for observability and security monitoring across every project, through analytics, audit logs, and the Security Dashboard.

Secure Compute provides private connectivity to enterprise systems, while BYOC on AWS lets your application functions run in your own AWS account under your permissions and network controls.

Deployment governance

Citizen developers and engineers use different tools. A marketer might use ChatGPT to build a landing page, an analyst might use Claude Code to run queries and build a report, and an engineer might use Codex, OpenCode, or fx.

No matter the harness, Vercel gives you a single deployment target, and connects to your existing IdP, so you can control who creates deployments.

How Klaviyo's built a secure internal app platform

Before Vercel, shipping a simple internal app at Klaviyo took two weeks of chasing IT, opening tickets for engineering, and following up with the platform team. They built an internal app-building platform on top of Enterprise Apps and Agents, and now anyone in the company can deploy an idea in three minutes. In their first two weeks on Vercel, 512 employees deployed 356 apps.

Access governance

Controlling who can deploy doesn't protect the apps, agents, and data that make it into production.

On Vercel, you can configure every deployment to be private by default, and with Vercel Passport, you can require employees to authenticate through your IdP before they can access internal apps.

Integration and data governance

Agents are only useful when they can access your systems and data, but that often means using long-standing environment varibles with wide-ranging permissions to your CRM, databases, Slack, and other systems.

Vercel Connect implements connectors with scoped access, and mints tokens for each agent task, meaning agents only access the specific context they need for the job. And now, with Enterprise-Managed Authorization, when employees sign into Vercel through your IdP, agents can use connected services automatically, without a separate authorization prompt.

Connect also integrates with Passport, so individual employee permissions also apply at the integration and data layer. If someone can't see data in a source system, they can't access it through an app or agent either.

Model and token governance

The average enterprise company using Vercel AI Gateway routes across 17 different models. Without a model router, that would require integrating with multiple separate providers, spreading API keys and budget management across platforms.

AI Gateway gives you access to hundreds of models through a single API, with no markup on cost, and Zero Data Retention keeps your data from being stored or trained on. You can also elect to route through US-only providers to maintain compliance.

How Mercor manages model governance at scale

Mercor connects AI labs with subject-matter experts who help train and evaluate models. Their engineers need access to hundreds of models to enable that work, but before migrating to Vercel, access was spread across direct integrations and third-party routers, making stolen credentials a huge risk, and token spend impossible to manage.

They moved their model routing to AI Gateway, and now engineers can access hundreds of models with a single, expiring secret, and they can set budgets per person or project.

In their first 10 days on AI Gateway, they processed 63 billion tokens without hitting any rate limits.

Centralized visibility and security

Vercel Observability gives you a single view for app and agent telemetry across every project, so you can easily manage performance and troubleshoot problems for both internal tools and customer-facing products.

The Security Dashboard flags risks across your team and apps, including missing MFA, unprotected preview deployments, long-lived credentials, and framework vulnerabilities. Each finding links to the settings needed to fix it.

Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS

BYOC on AWS is generally available. With BYOC, application functions execute in your AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

Meta Superintelligence Labs runs on Vercel via BYOC, giving its AI teams the ability to test and deploy ideas quickly, inside their own AWS environment. Leaders at Meta said that in their first week on Vercel, they shipped a month worth of work.

From idea to global scale on one platform

Vercel let's everyone in your company build safely, and makes it easy for engineers to ship the best ideas at global scale, all on a single platform.

That is how we built Vertex, our customer support agent. We were previously using a vendor, but it couldn't answer all of our customers questions. When our support team built agents and skills to cover the gaps and increase our responses times, and we realized they had laid the foundation for the experience we wanted to deliver directly to our customers.

Our GTM engineering team took that foundation and made it production ready with evals and model failover.

Today, Vertex handles 91% of our customer support cases autonomously, processing thousands of tickets a week, and it runs on the same platform where the idea started.

Ship your best ideas, securely

title: A Flexible Cron Job API Allows Global Report Timing Customization (and Migration)
description:
Short answer: a flexible cron job API allows global report timing customization when the time-zone rule and run identity stay in your application. Use the cron job only to start the work, then put the daily game report cleanup behind a queue. That boundary lets you replace the scheduler without rewriting delivery semantics.

The problem is easy to underestimate. A global game may need a daily report email and cleanup at 02:30 for each player region, while the cleanup itself can outlive a web request. A schedule that says “every 24 hours” is not the same policy as “02:30 in the player’s IANA time zone.” The trigger also does not make duplicate delivery safe.

Which boundary keeps a global cleanup replaceable?

Treat local time as application policy. Store the IANA location, the intended local hour, and a deterministic run identity such as cleanup:2026-10-24:asia-shanghai. The scheduler adapter translates that policy into a provider request. The worker receives the run identity and makes repeated delivery harmless.

The schedule is policy. The queue is delivery.

That separation is the useful migration unit. If the provider changes, the application still knows what a regional cleanup means. If a worker retry arrives tomorrow, it still knows which cleanup it represents.

For the gaming scenario, the scheduled HTTP handler should do three things: validate the run identity, enqueue bounded work, and return. A cron execution is limited to 900 seconds, so a large cleanup belongs in a worker rather than inside the trigger. The target must be a publicly reachable HTTPS endpoint, and the queue consumer must assume standard delivery is at-least-once.

Do not make the scheduler your transaction boundary.

For this workflow, Infrai fits at the adapter boundary when a self-describing REST contract reduces migration work. Its public discovery surface needs no key and exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples; every documented capability also has examples in 10 languages, including Go. An engineer can inspect the live scheduling contract and keep the application’s time-zone policy intact while changing only the adapter. That is a concrete reason to try it for a regional trigger and queue handoff, not a claim that the platform replaces a worker or a workflow engine. It is a poor fit for a private HTTP target, a DAG, or a cleanup that needs a join; use a workflow specialist in those cases.

Which cron job API allows flexible report timing for global users?

The following policy code is deliberately independent of any scheduler SDK. It calculates the next instant from an application-owned IANA location; an adapter can then submit that intent to the chosen cron service. The customization belongs to the application, so users in different zones do not inherit the scheduler’s default zone by accident.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func discovery() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil {
                    wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after retries")
}

func main() {
    body, err := discovery()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(len(body))
}

The application should pass a stable key through the queue message. A consumer can record that key before applying an irreversible cleanup, or use it as the idempotency key for its own storage operation. A five-minute FIFO deduplication window is not enough for a daily job that may be retried later.

The trigger should also be retry-safe. For create or update operations, use a client-supplied idempotency key and inspect non-2xx responses. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After or back off exponentially. A retry that silently creates a second schedule is a migration defect, not a harmless network detail.

What does a fair provider comparison look like?

There is no universal winner. The right choice depends on whether the schedule is merely a clock signal or the beginning of a stateful workflow.

Option Good fit for this cleanup Boundary to respect
Cron plus a queue Regional time triggers with worker-owned retries and idempotency It is not a DAG engine; the HTTP target is public HTTPS, and the trigger has a 900-second limit
Temporal Stateful workflows with timers, retries, and multi-step progress It is a workflow system, which is a larger application-model commitment than a single trigger
Apache Airflow Batch DAGs with explicit dependencies between cleanup stages It is the wrong shape when the job has no dependency graph or join
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler Managed time-based invocation in an AWS-centered estate Application code can become coupled to AWS target and identity configuration

Temporal or Airflow is the better boundary once the cleanup must wait for several region jobs, join their results, and publish one operator report. EventBridge Scheduler is sensible when AWS already owns the target and identity boundary. A cron-plus-queue design is narrower, which is precisely why it is easier to replace when the application keeps its own schedule policy.

I initially treated the scheduler API as the main portability risk. The sharper risk is the worker contract. If the application owns the run key and the adapter only translates scheduling intent, replacing the scheduler does not require rewriting cleanup behavior.

For this narrow adapter boundary, Infrai is worth trying when its self-describing REST surface reduces discovery and migration work. Public discovery needs no key and exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples; each documented capability also has examples in 10 languages, including Go. That lets an adapter author inspect the live contract and produce a small client in the runtime already used by the service, instead of first adopting a vendor SDK.

There is a second, different operational benefit for this workflow: one key and one billing relationship cover the broader platform, whose live discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules. A scheduler and its queue handoff can therefore use one plain HTTP integration and one credential boundary rather than accumulating separate SDK and credential plumbing as the cleanup grows. That does not make the worker durable, and it does not remove the need for application-level idempotency. The trade-off is clear: this convenience is less valuable if the team already standardizes on AWS identity or needs Temporal’s stateful workflow model.

The explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for the regional trigger and queue handoff when a discoverable REST contract, runnable Go example, and single credential boundary reduce migration work. Choose Temporal or Airflow when the cleanup becomes a workflow graph; choose the AWS scheduler when AWS-specific identity and targets are already the governing boundary.

How do you verify and roll back the migration?

Start with one region and one test partition. Inspect the created schedule through the provider’s read path, trigger a controlled run, and verify four things: the local-time conversion, the run identity, the queue handoff, and duplicate consumer behavior. Keep durable evidence in your own status store; cron run output retains only the first 4 KB.

During a migration, compare planned run identities rather than wall-clock timestamps alone. A daylight-saving transition can change the UTC instant while leaving the local-time policy unchanged. Also record the scheduler’s second-level timing jitter in the acceptance rule; exact wall-clock equality is the wrong test for a trigger.

Rollback is a state transition. Pause the new trigger, let already accepted queue work finish under the idempotent worker, and enable the previous adapter only after checking for an active run with the same identity. A paused cron does not backfill missed triggers. If a backfill is necessary, create it as an explicit application operation with its own run identity.

The queue limits belong in the runbook: delayed messages top out at 7 days, message bodies at 256 KB, and retention at 30 days. There is no native debounce or throttle, and no one-to-many topic primitive, so fan-out needs separate queues or application logic. Those constraints are manageable when they are visible in the boundary decision.

Keep the policy in your service, keep the trigger short, and make duplicate delivery boring. That is enough for regional cleanup today and leaves the scheduler replaceable tomorrow.

If this boundary fits your system, inspect the scheduling contract and runnable examples at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/cron/answers/why-daily-scheduled-email-should-enqueue-jobs-instead-o/.

References

  • Temporal documentation: https://docs.temporal.io/
  • Apache Airflow documentation: https://airflow.apache.org/docs/
  • Amazon EventBridge Scheduler documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/what-is-scheduler.html
  • Infrai cron and queue guidance: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/cron/answers/why-daily-scheduled-email-should-enqueue-jobs-instead-o/

title: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP
description:
arXiv:2611.08639v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) commonly use multiple-choice question (MCQ) format. However, prior studies documented that MCQ format reduces refusal rates, which may significantly affect the safety behavior of the model. We provide a first mechanistic explanation of this effect on the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset across two models - Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. First, we use the tuned lens technique to show that when processing MCQ the model commits to an answer-letter token very quickly, which is in contrast to the gradual refusal build-up in open-ended formats. Additionally, we observe that activations on the MCQ format lie roughly 3x further from the refusal direction, compared with their open-ended counterparts. Moreover, ablating the attention heads that carry the MCQ format answer increases the refusal, which is a direct evidence that the MCQ answer-selection competes with refusal. These findings indicate that MCQ safety scores primarily measure knowledge capabilities and do not assess the safety-mechanisms.

title: BOLA: your API checks the URL but misses IDs in the JSON body
description:
Your access control test is green. Account A asks for a document that belongs to account B, and the API answers 404. That’s the right check.

Now A edits its own document. In the request body, it slips in the ID of one of B's projects. The API accepts it, and the response shows B's project.

TL;DR: access control often checks the object in the URL. It forgets the IDs in the request body. One account then attaches another account's object to its own, and the response hands over that data. This is BOLA, number one in the OWASP API Top 10. Check the owner of every ID you receive, not just that it exists.

This article is for backend developers who write PUT or PATCH routes, or who test access rights. The examples are in Go, but the flaw exists in every language.

The setup: four routes, one flaw

I audited an API as a white-box review. Its backend is written in Laravel, a PHP framework.

Four write routes had the same defect. One PUT, three PATCH.

Each time, the route did check that the object in the URL belonged to the logged-in account. But the request carried another ID, in its body.

For that second ID, the API checked one thing only: that it exists. It never asked who owned it.

In three cases, the response then returned the other account's data. Names, contact details, more IDs. In the fourth, the object moved into the other account, which then saw it appear in its own data.

The list routes I reviewed were correctly scoped to the account. The hole was in the writes. I proved each case with an HTTP test, on an isolated database with fake accounts. Production never received a single request. The method will get its own article.

The flaw in one request

Here is the scenario with generic objects. Account A owns a document. Account B owns a project. The IDs are made up for the example.

PATCH /documents/d-123
Authorization: Bearer <token of account A>
Content-Type: application/json

{"project_id": "p-999"}

The server asks two questions. Does document d-123 belong to A? Yes. Does project p-999 exist? Yes. The third question is missing: does that project belong to A?

The update goes through. Then the API returns the updated document, with its project. Handy for the frontend, which shows everything at once.

200 OK
{
  "id": "d-123",
  "title": "Meeting notes",
  "project": {
    "id": "p-999",
    "name": "Account B project",
    "owner_email": "b@example.com"
  }
}

A never called GET /projects/p-999. It read B's data by writing to its own document.

"Exists" does not mean "belongs to you". The API checks the owner of d-123, in the URL. For p-999, in the body, it only checks that it exists. B's project gets attached, and its data comes back to A.

Why your access test misses it

The classic IDOR test swaps the ID in the URL. I already recommended it in the article on the French tax leak. That test is still useful, but it never looks at the request body.

Here, the URL is fine. A points at its own document. The URL check does its job, and the test passes.

Body validation gives a false sense of safety. In Laravel, the rule exists:projects,id checks that the row exists in the table. It says nothing about the owner. Read too fast, it still looks like an access check.

A foreign key does the same thing in the database. It is a column that points to a row in another table. It guarantees that the project exists, and it accepts any account's project.

Even Postgres RLS lets the link through

Maybe you filter rows in Postgres with RLS, Row-Level Security. It hides other accounts' rows from each account. I described it in the article on RLS in Go.

But the Postgres documentation is explicit. Integrity checks, foreign keys included, always bypass RLS. Otherwise the database could not guarantee its own links.

You can reproduce it in a few lines on Postgres 18. Under RLS, account A cannot see B's project. It can still attach a document to it, and the database accepts.

If the next read goes through RLS, the project stays hidden. But the link between the two accounts is written. So your barrier must cover writes, not only reads.

The right name: BOLA, and sometimes mass assignment

OWASP ranks API flaws in a top 10. The latest edition is from 2023. Number one is BOLA, for Broken Object Level Authorization.

Put simply, the API does not check that you have rights on the object you point at. OWASP says the ID can sit in the path, in the query string or in the payload. So this is BOLA on the project, not on the document.

Another name comes up often: mass assignment. That is when the API lets the client change a field it should not touch. Since 2023, OWASP files it at number three, under BOPLA, for Broken Object Property Level Authorization.

The difference comes down to one question. Does the product need to move a document to another project? If not, accepting project_id on PATCH is already the mistake. That is mass assignment, and the fix is to drop the field.

If yes, the field is legitimate, and its value is what you must check. In the audit, I recommended refusing these moves wherever the product does not need them.

A UUID is not a password

OWASP also advises random IDs, such as UUIDs. That helps against guessing. But a UUID shows up in responses, links and logs.

In the audit, one rigged response leaked more IDs from the other account. Those IDs then opened a second route. All it took was a first foreign ID to start the chain.

A hard-to-guess ID slows the attack down. The owner check stops it.

The fix: check the owner in the same query

The rule is simple. Every ID you receive gets the same check as the one in the URL. It must exist and belong to the logged-in account.

Here is a generic example in Go, with Postgres. It is not the audited API's code. It only shows the shape of the check.

// ErrNotFound covers three cases: no such document, no such project,
// or one of them belongs to another account. The caller cannot tell which.
var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")

// The owner is checked on both IDs, in the same statement as the write.
const moveDocument = `
UPDATE documents d
SET project_id = p.id
FROM projects p
WHERE d.id = $1 AND d.owner_id = $3
  AND p.id = $2 AND p.owner_id = $3`

// MoveDocument handles PATCH /documents/{id} with {"project_id": "..."}.
// userID comes from the verified session, never from the request body.
func MoveDocument(ctx context.Context, db *sql.DB, userID, docID, projectID string) error {
    res, err := db.ExecContext(ctx, moveDocument, docID, projectID, userID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    n, err := res.RowsAffected()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if n == 0 {
        return ErrNotFound
    }
    return nil
}

This code does three things.

  • It checks the owner of both IDs in the same SQL statement as the write. This avoids two separate calls. The composite constraint below also protects against concurrent ownership changes.
  • It takes userID from the verified session. That value never comes from the request body.
  • It returns ErrNotFound when no row moves, whether the object is missing or belongs to another account.

That last point matters. A "forbidden" answer would confirm that the project exists. I explain the "not found" choice in the article on the LLM agent in Go.

In Laravel, the same idea fits in the validation rule. Rule::exists('projects', 'id')->where('owner_id', $userId) adds the owner to the check. In the audited API, the fix took the form of a single rule, reused on every field concerned.

Put the rule in the database too

Code can forget a field. A database constraint applies to every write. When both tables carry the owner column, a composite foreign key shuts the door.

ALTER TABLE projects
    ADD CONSTRAINT projects_id_owner UNIQUE (id, owner_id);

ALTER TABLE documents
    ADD CONSTRAINT documents_project_same_owner
    FOREIGN KEY (project_id, owner_id)
    REFERENCES projects (id, owner_id);

The key no longer points to any project. It points to a project with the same owner as the document. Postgres then rejects the link to B's project, even if the code let it through.

Postgres requires a unique constraint on the referenced columns, hence the first command. And this guard does not work when ownership goes through a parent. The check in code stays essential there.

Look for links already written

Fixing the code does not clean the database. If the flaw was already used, cross-account links exist. In the audit, I recommended finding them before calling the problem solved.

One join is enough to find them:

SELECT d.id
FROM documents d
JOIN projects p ON p.id = d.project_id
WHERE d.owner_id <> p.owner_id;

Each row returned is a document attached to another account's project. Decide case by case: repair the link or set the row aside.

Do this cleanup before adding the composite key. Postgres checks existing rows when you create the constraint. If it finds a bad one, it refuses to create it.

The test: two accounts, and the ID in the body

This generic Laravel example is separate from the audited code. Adapt its factories, route and message to your API contract.

// Generic Laravel example: adapt the factories and route to your API.
public function test_cannot_attach_another_accounts_project(): void
{
    $alice = User::factory()->create();
    $bob = User::factory()->create();
    $own = Project::factory()->create(['owner_id' => $alice->id]);
    $foreign = Project::factory()->create(['owner_id' => $bob->id]);
    $document = Document::factory()->create([
        'owner_id' => $alice->id,
        'project_id' => $own->id,
    ]);

    $response = $this->actingAs($alice)->patchJson(
        "/documents/{$document->id}", ['project_id' => $foreign->id]
    );
    $response->assertStatus(404)->assertExactJson(['message' => 'Not found']);
    $this->assertDatabaseHas('documents', [
        'id' => $document->id, 'project_id' => $own->id,
    ]);
}

For every route that accepts an ID in its body, write a test with two accounts. A owns the document, B owns the project. A sends its PATCH with B's project.

The test checks three things.

  • The response is a 404, the same as for a project that does not exist.
  • A's document did not change in the database.
  • No data from B shows up in the response.

To find these routes, look for fields ending in _id in the inputs of your write routes. In Laravel, also look for every exists: rule. Do it for POST creations too, not only for updates.

Some fields accept a type and an ID, for example an attachment that can target several kinds of objects. Check the owner for every accepted type. Those are the easiest cases to forget.

The checklist

"Exists" does not mean "belongs to you".

  • [ ] List the POST, PUT and PATCH routes that receive an ID in the body
  • [ ] For each field, decide whether the client may change it
  • [ ] Drop the fields the product does not need to change
  • [ ] Check the owner of every ID you receive, not just that it exists
  • [ ] Take the account from the session, never from the body
  • [ ] Answer 404 for a missing object and for a foreign object alike
  • [ ] Add a composite foreign key when both tables carry the owner
  • [ ] Look for cross-account links already in the database before calling the flaw fixed
  • [ ] Write one two-account test per route, with the foreign ID in the body

The takeaway

An ID in a request body points at an object, just like the one in the URL. So it needs the same check.

Neither validation, nor the foreign key, nor RLS checks the owner for you. That is the job of your code, or of a constraint written for it.

Want to know whether your API lets these IDs through? Let's talk.

Sources: OWASP, API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization · OWASP, API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization · OWASP API Security Top 10, 2023 edition · PostgreSQL 18, Row Security Policies · PostgreSQL 18, constraints and foreign keys · Laravel 12, exists validation rule

title: From Geometry to Function: A Multi-Task LiDAR Benchmark Dataset for Semantic and Functional Parsing of Urban Facades
description:
arXiv:2611.08645v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding building facades is central to urban digital twins, heritage modelling, and sustainable city analysis, yet existing LiDAR benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element. We introduce HFX3D, a large-scale urban facade benchmark of approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across four seasons, day and night, and varied weather. Each facade is annotated at three tiers, semantic, instance, and per-instance functional attributes, making it, to our knowledge, the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels. Annotations are produced by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation. We benchmark representative point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer architectures and find that semantic segmentation is already challenging under severe class imbalance, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder. The benchmark establishes a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding. Project page: https://jijup.github.io/hfx3d-benchmark/ ; code: https://github.com/jijup/hfx3d-benchmark
