title: "Item not found." in Google Play Closed Testing: A 5-Step Debug Checklist
description:
You send your closed testing link, and a tester replies with a screenshot: a satellite, the words "Item not found." and a Try again button.

Your app is almost certainly fine. Google Play hides closed test apps from every account it doesn't recognize as a tester, and "Item not found." is how it says "you're not on the list (yet)".

The fastest way to debug it is to answer one question first.

Start here: who can't open it?

Who sees "Item not found." Where the problem usually is Start with
One or a few testers Tester side: account, sync, opt-in Steps 1–3
Every tester, including your own second account Developer side: release, review, countries Steps 4–5

If you're not sure, run the self-test at the end of this post. It takes about 15 minutes and tells you which side to look at.

What has to be true for a tester to get in

Two things, both at once:

  1. The tester's Google account is on your tester list. With a Google Group, that means the account is a member of the group you added on the Testers tab.
  2. Your closed testing track has a live release that's available in the tester's country.

With a Google Group, a member can install straight from the Play Store listing (play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=<package>), and the install counts as opting in. The other route is the opt-in link (play.google.com/apps/testing/<package>) and its "Become a tester" button. If either condition above fails, both routes end in "Item not found."

Tester side

Step 1: Is the Play Store using the account that joined the group?

This is the most common cause by far. Many phones are signed in to several Google accounts. The tester joins the group in a browser with account A, but the Play Store app is on account B.

Fix: In the Play Store, tap the profile picture (top right) and switch to the account that joined the group. Then open the link again.

Step 2: Has Google had time to sync?

Joining a group doesn't work instantly. In our experience the Play Store usually recognizes a new member after 10–15 minutes, occasionally longer.

Fix: Wait, then try again. Leaving and rejoining the group doesn't speed it up. If it still fails after an hour, go back to step 1 or move on to step 3.

Step 3: Try the opt-in page instead

Now and then the Play Store listing keeps showing "Item not found." even though the account is in the group.

Fix: Open the opt-in link (play.google.com/apps/testing/<package>) in a browser signed in with the same account, tap "Become a tester", then go back to the Play Store and install. It's the classic flow and still works.

Developer side

Step 4: Is there a live release, and were your changes approved?

If nobody can open the link, check your own setup first:

  • Releases tab of the closed testing track: you need a release that's available to testers, not one that's still in review or saved as a draft.
  • Publishing overview: adding a Google Group or changing countries is a change that needs review. If you see changes that haven't been sent, click Send changes for review. Until they're approved, the new group's members can't see the app.

Step 5: Is the tester's country included?

The closed testing track has its own Countries / regions tab, separate from production. If a tester's Play Store country isn't selected, they get "Item not found." even when everything else is right.

Fix: Select all countries/regions for the closed testing track. It doesn't affect where your production release goes later, and it removes a whole class of errors.

The self-test: find out which side it is

  1. Take a second Google account you control and join your tester group with it.
  2. Wait 15 minutes.
  3. On a phone or browser signed in with that account, open your Play Store listing.

If your own second account can install the app, your setup is fine and the problem is on the tester's side (steps 1–3). If you get "Item not found." too, fix steps 4 and 5 before asking testers to try again.

Checklist

Testers

  • The Play Store is signed in with the account that joined the group
  • Waited 10–15 minutes after joining
  • If the listing still fails, tried the opt-in link and "Become a tester"

Developers

  • The closed testing track has a release that's available to testers
  • Publishing overview has no unsent or unapproved changes
  • All countries/regions are selected for the closed testing track
  • The Testers tab lists the group your testers actually joined

Why this happens so often in test-for-test swaps

In most swap threads, every developer creates a separate Google Group for their own app. To test 12 apps, you join 12 groups, wait for 12 syncs, and get 12 chances to join with the wrong account. That's where most "Item not found." errors come from.

How BetaLobby avoids most of this

BetaLobby is where indie Android developers team up to get their 12 testers: 16 developers form a team and test each other's apps for 14 days. It's built around the steps above:

  • One shared group for every app: betalobby@googlegroups.com. Add it to your closed test once (next to any groups you already have), join it once, and you can install every app on the platform. No new group, and no new sync, for each app.
  • The right account, checked for you: BetaLobby checks that the Google account you signed in with is in the group, and if the Play Store says "Item not found.", it tells you which account to switch to (step 1).
  • Your setup is checked before testers see it: when you submit, BetaLobby checks that your app is actually visible to testers. If Google is still reviewing your tester changes, it re-checks automatically every 20 minutes and notifies you when it passes (step 4). It also checks a few countries to catch region limits (step 5).
  • No screenshots: installs and daily check-ins are verified automatically.

It's free, with no paid plan.

Originally published on betalobby.com.

title: How to Clean Messy Employee Names in Oracle SQL Using TRIM() and LOWER()
description:
How to Clean Messy Employee Names in Oracle SQL Using TRIM() and LOWER()

Have you ever worked with an employee table where names are stored in different formats?

For example, some names are in uppercase, others use mixed case, and a few have unwanted spaces around them.

Consider this sample employee data:

emp_id employee_name
101 JOHN
102 Mary
103 DAVID
104 SARAH
105 Robert

The names themselves are correct, but their formats are inconsistent.

This can become a problem when comparing records, preparing reports, or working with data from multiple sources.

Let's clean these values using Oracle SQL.

The requirement

We want to:

  • Remove leading and trailing spaces.
  • Convert all names into lowercase.
  • Display the cleaned values without updating the original table.

Oracle SQL query

SELECT emp_id,
LOWER(TRIM(employee_name)) AS cleaned_name
FROM employees;

Expected output:

emp_id cleaned_name
101 john
102 mary
103 david
104 sarah
105 robert

The result is now consistent across all employee records.

Understanding the two functions

Let's look at each function separately.

  1. TRIM()

"TRIM()" removes spaces from the beginning and end of a string.

SELECT TRIM(' JOHN ') AS name
FROM dual;

Output:

JOHN

  1. LOWER()

"LOWER()" converts alphabetic characters into lowercase.

SELECT LOWER('JOHN') AS name
FROM dual;

Output:

john

  1. Combining TRIM() and LOWER()

In our original query:

LOWER(TRIM(employee_name))

Oracle evaluates the inner function first.

  • "TRIM()" removes unwanted spaces.
  • "LOWER()" converts the remaining text into lowercase.

For example:

' JOHN '
|
TRIM()
|
'JOHN'
|
LOWER()
|
'john'

One important point: this SELECT statement only displays the transformed values. It does not modify the original employee records.

What if there are extra spaces between words?

Here is something worth testing.

SELECT TRIM(' JOHN SMITH ') AS name
FROM dual;

Output:

JOHN SMITH

Notice that the spaces between "JOHN" and "SMITH" are still present.

If you want to display names in title case, Oracle provides another function called "INITCAP()".

SELECT INITCAP(TRIM(employee_name)) AS formatted_name
FROM employees;

For example:

john smith

Becomes:

John Smith

Your turn: Test your Oracle SQL knowledge

Which Oracle SQL function converts:

"john smith"

Into:

"John Smith"

A. "UPPER()"

B. "LOWER()"

C. "INITCAP()"

D. "TRIM()"

What is your answer? Share it in the comments.

A quick reference

Function| What it does
"TRIM()"| Removes leading and trailing spaces
"LOWER()"| Converts text to lowercase
"UPPER()"| Converts text to uppercase
"INITCAP()"| Capitalises the first letter of each word

These functions are simple, but they are useful when cleaning text data in everyday SQL work.

The next time you receive inconsistent employee names, try combining "TRIM()" and "LOWER()" before using the data in your analysis.

title: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.09554v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.

title: LLM-as-a-judge: building an AI grader you can actually trust
description:
Short answer: An LLM judge works when you've calibrated it against human labels. Without calibration it's noise dressed up as a metric. The rubric is the actual work — the judge model just executes it.

Teams reach for LLM-as-judge because there's no other way to automatically score whether a support reply was "empathetic" or whether a generated SQL query "answers the user's intent." There's no diff to run. The judge fills the gap between "does it parse" (easy to check mechanically) and "is it actually good" (hard to check without a human).

The failure mode is treating it as plug-and-play: pick a model, write a prompt like "rate this output from 1–10," drop it in CI, declare victory. That judge gives you a consistent number that correlates poorly with what users actually think. You've built a metric that feels like signal and isn't.

Here's how to build one that isn't that.

Why do LLM judges fail without calibration?

Three problems, all fixable.

Position bias. In pairwise comparisons, judges prefer whichever answer appears first — consistently enough to flip verdicts up to 30% of the time. A test that scores "response A vs response B" will sometimes return a different result just from swapping the order.

Verbosity preference. Most LLMs, when asked to judge quality without a tight rubric, prefer longer outputs. A wrong-but-detailed answer beats a correct-but-brief one. Your eval suite ends up rewarding word count. Users don't.

Same-model blindness. Claude evaluating Claude's outputs is lenient on its own artifacts. It misses the specific failure modes it produces. If your app uses a model and you judge with the same model, you get a blind spot for exactly the class of errors you need to catch.

What makes a rubric tight enough to trust?

The rubric is not the prompt template. It's the list of concrete criteria the judge checks against. Write it as conditions, not adjectives.

Bad rubric:

Score 1–10 for quality. Consider clarity, accuracy, and helpfulness.

Good rubric:

A good response:
- Directly answers the question asked (not a related question)
- Does not introduce information not present in the provided context
- Uses plain language; no jargon unless the user used it first
- Is under 200 words

Score 0.0 immediately if any of:
- Response says "I don't know" when the context contains the answer
- Response asks a clarifying question instead of answering
- Response repeats the system prompt

Otherwise score 0.0–1.0 against the criteria above.

The hard-failure conditions matter most. They cover cases where you know it's wrong — no rubric ambiguity. Put them first. They short-circuit scoring before interpretation enters.

Here's a complete judge implementation:

import anthropic

RUBRIC = """\
A good response to a customer support question:
- Directly addresses the specific question asked
- Does not introduce facts not present in the provided knowledge base context
- Is under 200 words
- Uses plain language; no jargon unless the user introduced it
- Ends with a concrete next step or resolution

Score 0.0 immediately if any of the following:
- Says "I cannot help with that" when context contains the answer
- Asks a clarifying question instead of answering
- Contradicts information in the context
- Contains a system prompt fragment

Otherwise score 0.0–1.0 based on the criteria above.
Return only a decimal number (e.g., 0.85). No explanation."""

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def judge_response(user_question: str, kb_context: str, response: str) -> float:
    prompt = f"""User question: {user_question}

Knowledge base context:
{kb_context}

Response to evaluate:
{response}

Rubric:
{RUBRIC}"""

    result = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
        max_tokens=10,
        temperature=0,                 # deterministic — same input, same score
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    try:
        return float(result.content[0].text.strip())
    except ValueError:
        return 0.0                     # unparseable output = treat as failure

Two things to notice: temperature=0 for determinism, and the parsing fallback returns 0.0 instead of crashing. A judge that sometimes returns "0.85 (good answer)" instead of "0.85" should fail safe, not silently inflate your scores.

How do you calibrate before shipping to CI?

You need 20–30 examples labeled by a human against your rubric. Not labeled "correct" — labeled against each criterion: does this response satisfy the condition or not?

# calibration.jsonl — one entry per labeled example
# {"question": "...", "context": "...", "response": "...", "human_score": 0.9, "notes": ""}
# {"question": "...", "context": "...", "response": "...", "human_score": 0.1, "notes": "contradicts context in para 2"}

import json

def calibrate_judge(labeled_path: str, threshold: float = 0.2) -> dict:
    with open(labeled_path) as f:
        examples = [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]

    disagreements = []
    for ex in examples:
        judge_score = judge_response(ex["question"], ex["context"], ex["response"])
        delta = abs(judge_score - ex["human_score"])
        if delta > threshold:
            disagreements.append({
                "question": ex["question"][:80],
                "human": ex["human_score"],
                "judge": judge_score,
                "delta": round(delta, 2),
                "notes": ex.get("notes", ""),
            })

    agreement_rate = 1 - len(disagreements) / len(examples)
    return {
        "agreement_rate": round(agreement_rate, 3),
        "disagreements": disagreements,
        "verdict": "PASS" if agreement_rate >= 0.80 else "RUBRIC NEEDS WORK",
    }

Run this before wiring the judge into CI. If verdict is RUBRIC NEEDS WORK, look at the disagreement list. Almost always, it's not that the judge model is wrong — it's that your rubric doesn't say what you thought it said. Add the failing condition explicitly and re-run.

Eighty percent agreement is the floor, not the goal. Below 80%, the judge is unreliable and your CI metrics will mislead you into thinking quality is stable when it isn't.

How do you handle position bias in pairwise comparisons?

Run each pair twice with the order swapped. If the judge flips its verdict, the difference isn't real — call it a tie.

def pairwise_judge(question: str, response_a: str, response_b: str) -> str:
    """Returns 'A', 'B', or 'TIE'."""

    def score_pair(first: str, second: str) -> str:
        result = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
            max_tokens=5,
            temperature=0,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": (
                f"Question: {question}\n\n"
                f"Response 1: {first}\n\n"
                f"Response 2: {second}\n\n"
                "Which response better satisfies the rubric above? "
                "Reply only: 1, 2, or TIE."
            )}],
        )
        return result.content[0].text.strip()

    verdict_ab = score_pair(response_a, response_b)    # A presented as 1, B as 2
    verdict_ba = score_pair(response_b, response_a)    # B presented as 1, A as 2

    # normalize to A/B labels
    winner_ab = "A" if verdict_ab == "1" else ("B" if verdict_ab == "2" else "TIE")
    winner_ba = "A" if verdict_ba == "2" else ("B" if verdict_ba == "1" else "TIE")

    if winner_ab == winner_ba:
        return winner_ab
    return "TIE"   # order-sensitive result = not a real difference

For single-answer scoring — which is what you want in most CI setups — position bias doesn't apply. There's only one answer, and you score it against the rubric directly.

What does LLM-as-judge not solve?

It doesn't tell you if the rubric is right. If you're measuring the wrong thing — if "under 200 words" is in your rubric but users actually want detailed answers — calibration passes and your eval suite silently optimizes for the wrong outcome. No amount of judge engineering fixes that. Review your labeled examples with someone who understands the product intent before locking the rubric.

It also shouldn't replace mechanical verification. If your LLM writes SQL, run it against a test database. If it writes code, execute it. Use a judge for genuinely subjective dimensions only — the ones where there's no ground truth to diff against. Applying a judge to things you can verify deterministically wastes money and adds noise.

The free test lab has a complete judge harness with calibration script, a 25-example labeled dataset for a support-reply task, and a CI integration that fails the build when judge agreement drops below 80% after a model upgrade. If you're setting this up for the first time, start there rather than from scratch. AI Software Testing in Practice covers the full eval lifecycle — growing the labeled dataset across model upgrades, setting regression thresholds that account for judge noise, and knowing when a score drop is a real problem versus rubric drift.

FAQ

How do I know if my LLM judge is reliable?
Run it against 20–30 human-labeled examples and measure agreement. If the judge disagrees with your labels more than 20% of the time, the rubric is wrong — tighten it and re-calibrate. Agreement above 80% on your labeled set is enough to trust the judge in CI.

Should I use the same LLM to generate and judge outputs?
No. Using the same model to evaluate its own outputs creates a blind spot for that model's specific failure modes. Use a different judge model, or judge with a stronger model than the one generating outputs.

What is position bias in LLM-as-judge and how do I avoid it?
Position bias means the judge tends to prefer whichever option it sees first in a pairwise comparison. Avoid it by either using single-answer scoring (not pairwise) or running each comparison twice with the order swapped and averaging the scores.

title: Impact of color in computer and human-based object recognition under occlusion
description:
arXiv:2611.08808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Partial occlusions challenge object recognition in both human and computer vision (CV), but the impact is largely dependent on the occlusion and model design. Properties relating to color are particularly important in biological recognition and frequently leveraged for camouflage, however there are still open questions about what makes them effective and how they translate to CV. This work studies partial occlusions that create camouflage, including those that blend in with target objects or with scenes, which alter object representations in distinct ways. Experiments evaluate recognition performance on both human participants and models ranging from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to transformers, and additional analysis is performed on models to uncover trends in processing and object representations under multiple occlusion types. Novel metrics offer explainability of model behavior under occlusion: non-occlusion precision (NOP) and non-occlusion recall (NOR) measure alignment of model activations with and without occlusion, and activation in occlusion (AIO) measures the percentage of activations that occur in occluded regions. Findings show that human recognition, and most transformers, are negatively impacted by generated camouflaging occluders, with scene-based camouflage performing worse than object-based. Classical CNNs show a strong opposite trend, performing the worst on neutral-colored occlusions, suggesting that contextually-related colors, particularly scene-based, benefit object recognition rather than disrupting shape or boundary cues. Additionally, generated camouflaging occluders for training augmentation improves robustness to unseen camouflage for selected CNN model, and occlusion metrics suggest trends about learned mechanisms. Findings have interesting implications for alignment in human and computer vision, model vulnerabilities, and explainability.

title: You Aborted the Request. Did the Work Stop? Four Cancellation Myths and a Retry-Budget Probe
description:
I closed the browser tab 300 ms into a request. The job kept running for another 40 seconds. Nobody told me.

That gap is where duplicate writes, mystery quota use, and "it worked in staging" bugs are born. So here is the question I now ask about every endpoint: when I walk away, what keeps working?

This is a myth-busting FAQ. Four claims I hear in code review, the evidence that breaks them, and a probe you can run yourself.

Myth 1: "Abort stops the work"

The claim: AbortController.abort() cancels the job.

What it actually does: it closes your side of the connection. The server learns about it when it next tries to write. If the handler is a long loop with no flush, that might be never.

Corrected model: cancellation is a message, not a kill signal. Treat it as best-effort.

Quick check — send a request with a unique marker, abort it, then search the server logs:

curl -s -N "http://localhost:8000/slow?marker=abort-$RANDOM" \
  --max-time 0.3 || true
sleep 5
grep -c "abort-" /var/log/app/requests.log   # >0 means the work landed

If that count is above zero, your abort did not stop anything downstream.

Myth 2: "A timeout means nothing happened"

The claim: the client timed out, so the write failed.

Reality: timeouts are local. The request may have been fully processed. Only the reply was lost.

Ask instead: can I tell the difference between "not done" and "done but unacknowledged"? If the answer is no, you have a reconciliation problem, not a timeout problem.

Myth 3: "Retries are free"

Three attempts at a 40-second job is 120 seconds of compute. On a metered tier, that is quota you cannot get back. On one small server, it is three workloads fighting for the same CPU.

Retries do not just multiply traffic. They multiply work. And they multiply it exactly when the service is already struggling.

Myth 4: "No response means no state change"

The claim: no body arrived, so nothing was written.

Counter-example: a request that inserts a row, then fails while serializing the response. The row exists. Your client saw a 502.

Corrected model: every mutating call needs a client-generated key. The server decides the rule: first key wins, repeats return the stored result.

A probe you can actually run

Here is the workflow I use. It is small on purpose.

  1. Generate a request id before sending anything.
  2. Send that id in a header.
  3. Abort early, or let it time out.
  4. Poll a read-only endpoint for the id.
  5. Record one of three verdicts: landed, absent, unknown. 
# cancel_probe.py
# Draft artifact. Not executed for this article — run it against your own service.
import json, time, uuid, urllib.request, urllib.error

BASE = "http://localhost:8000"

def send(req_id: str, abort_after: float = 0.3) -> str:
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{BASE}/jobs",
        data=json.dumps({"req_id": req_id}).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", "Idempotency-Key": req_id},
        method="POST",
    )
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=abort_after) as r:
            return f"http {r.status}"
    except urllib.error.URLError as e:
        return f"client gave up: {type(e).__name__}"

def look_up(req_id: str) -> dict:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(f"{BASE}/jobs/{req_id}", timeout=5) as r:
        return json.loads(r.read().decode())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rid = str(uuid.uuid4())
    print("send:", send(rid))
    for i in range(6):
        time.sleep(2)
        try:
            print(f"t+{2*(i+1)}s: found", look_up(rid))
            break
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            print(f"t+{2*(i+1)}s: not found ({e.code})")

Three outcomes matter, and only three:

  • Absent — safe to retry.
  • Present, done — do not retry; read the stored result.
  • Present, running — wait, or cancel explicitly and poll again.

Any fourth state in your system is a design bug, not an edge case.

The retry wrapper, with a budget

Unlimited retries are a quota leak. Put a number on it.

import random, time

def with_budget(fn, attempts=3, base=0.5, cap=8.0):
    for i in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except Exception:
            if i == attempts - 1:
                raise
            delay = min(cap, base * 2 ** i) * random.uniform(0.5, 1.5)
            time.sleep(delay)   # budget is attempts, not wall clock

Log total retries per request id. My rule of thumb: if one logical request needs more than three attempts, the endpoint is unhealthy, and hammering it is not debugging.

Where the cheap tier fits

I run probes like this against free model endpoints and a free server first. The point is not saving cents. The point is that an abort probe on a metered paid account makes me timid, and timid probes hide bugs.

MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are what I use for that first pass. The model side gives me something slow enough to abort mid-flight. The server side gives me a real process to kill and restart.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Two honest limits: free capacity is shared, so timings will be noisy. And free access is an offer, not a guarantee — do not build a latency budget on it.

Decision table

Situation Do Why
User left the page Cancel, then poll Abort is a message, not a kill
Client timed out on a write Look up by idempotency key Unknown is not failed
Server returned 5xx Retry with the same key, capped Duplicates hurt more than gaps
4xx on a bad payload Do not retry It will fail identically
Throttled Stop and back off Retry storms burn quota

Who should skip this

Skip it if your writes are already naturally idempotent. You are paying for a probe you do not need.

Skip it if you have no request ids and no way to add them. Fix that first; the probe will only tell you what you already fear.

Also skip it if you need hard cancellation guarantees. That requires cooperative cancellation inside the handler, checked at every loop boundary. A client abort will never give you that.

The mental model

Your client is not in control. It sends intent. The server decides.

Once I accepted that, my bug reports changed. "The request failed" became "this request has unknown state, here is the id." That is a much better sentence to wake up to.

Run one abort probe this week. Pick a single endpoint. You may find 40 seconds of work you thought you had cancelled.

title: Benchmarking Speaker Embedders in the Sub-Second Regime for Real-Time Voice AI Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.09516v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-time Voice AI agents must separate the active user from intelligible background speech that survives conventional noise suppression. Background sources include television audio, family members, and colleagues. Production denoisers remove non-stationary environmental noise effectively. Background speech shares the spectral characteristics of the target and passes through, causing false acceptances in downstream speaker verification (SV) and automatic speech recognition (ASR). We benchmark open-source speaker embedders TitaNet-Large, TitaNet-Small, ECAPA-TDNN, CAM++, and SpeakerNet under a strict sub-second latency budget. Evaluation combines a controlled benchmark with a weighted human-annotated production set. Our controlled benchmark is built from real calls in which a second real speaker is injected into silence intervals at modulated amplitude. We report three findings. First, denoising before embedding is generally harmful and raises equal error rate (EER) across architectures. Second, truncating audio below the full voice-activity segment degrades every model. Third, roughly half of the TitaNet embedding is redundant for this task. Trailing dimensions encode population attributes such as language and gender. Such attributes carry little discriminative value in a demographically homogeneous user base. We distill these results into deployment guidance. Verification should run on raw audio with full voice-activity chunks. Thresholds should favor precision over F1. Truncated embeddings reduce the cost of similarity search.

title: Asymmetric Correspondence Learning for Lexical and Style Embeddings: Interpreting Latent Space via Acoustic Features
description:
arXiv:2611.09313v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised speech embeddings jointly encode lexical, speaker, and prosodic information, complicating feature isolation. We introduce Asymmetric Correspondence Learning (ACL), distilling HuBERT features into separate Acoustic Word Embeddings (AWEs) and Acoustic Style Embeddings (ASEs) via a split-latent correspondence bottleneck. Through probing and clustering evaluations on single-word utterances, we demonstrate that substantial variance from extrinsic sources remains encoded within each latent space, despite linear probing indicating the information has been stripped. Whilst the AWE space exhibits cohesive lexical clustering (AP$\approx$0.90, Fisher$\approx$6.28), linear probing on the ASE space achieves 97.9\% speaker accuracy across a diffuse topology (Fisher$\approx$1.01), yet preserves substantial lexical variance (Fisher$\approx$0.86) that remains linearly unrecoverable (0.17\%). To explain these findings, we apply group-level permutation feature importance over eGeMAPS acoustic features, finding that AWEs partition by vocal tract filters and ASEs by $F_0$ dynamics. These findings suggest that standard diagnostic benchmarks may be insufficient for verifying feature isolation, as substantial speech structure can be retained even when it remains entirely hidden from probes.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.

Resources

  • Point your agent at our Python guides in the Knowledge Base

  • Deploy an eve agent in Python in one click

title: MARS: Training Multilingual Search Agents for Retriever-Free Evidence Acquisition
description:
arXiv:2611.09090v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing multilingual retrieval-augmented generation relies heavily on learned retrievers and similarity-based ranking from multilingual collections, which are vulnerable to cross-lingual retrieval errors and indexing overhead. In this paper, we explore retriever-free multilingual search, where the model directly interacts with raw corpora through executable shell commands. This paradigm shifts the bottleneck to multilingual search action generation, where exact search is sensitive to entity surface forms and outcome-only supervision provides limited guidance for multi-turn search. To address these challenges, we propose MARS, a multilingual search agent in direct corpus interaction (DCI) with reinforcement learning (RL). MARS introduces corpus-native entity grounding to recover reliable lexical anchors from corpus evidence, mitigating failure to retrieve evidence. Meanwhile, we present a redundancy-aware search reward to encourage concise and effective search trajectories, addressing training collapse in RL of multilingual scenarios. Experiments show that \ours~consistently outperforms strong retrieval-based and DCI baselines, while demonstrating robust cross-lingual generalization and substantially reducing redundant corpus interactions.

title: How to Choose an Internal Developer Platform: Portal, Orchestrator, or Execution Platform
description:
Choose an internal developer platform by the job you need it to do. A developer portal gives engineers a catalog and self-service front end over the tools you already run, a platform orchestrator generates environment-specific configuration from a workload spec and provisions resources through your existing infrastructure as code, and an execution platform runs the workloads themselves. Teams without a dedicated platform team can start with an execution platform and add a portal as the service count grows. Control Plane is an execution platform that runs workloads active-active across clouds and regions, with Day 2 operations handled.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

  • Developer portals (Backstage, Port, Cortex, OpsLevel) organize services, ownership, and self-service actions. They do not run workloads, and they provision only by triggering your existing pipelines and infrastructure as code.
  • Platform orchestrators (Humanitec with the Score specification, and open-source Kratix) turn a workload definition into environment-specific configuration and provision resources through your tools.
  • Execution platforms (Control Plane, plus PaaS-style platforms in our roundup of internal developer platforms) deploy, scale, and operate the workloads.
  • How to choose. Start with the layer that solves your biggest bottleneck, then add layers as new bottlenecks appear.
  • Build vs buy. Backstage is free to license and costly to run. Commercial portals and hosted Backstage reduce that work. None of them replaces what runs underneath.
  • Control Plane runs workloads active-active across regions and clouds on AWS, GCP, and Azure, with a 99.999% availability SLA for workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.

What is the difference between an internal developer portal and a platform orchestrator?

A developer portal is the interface developers use to find services, see ownership, and trigger self-service actions. A platform orchestrator is the engine behind it that turns a workload spec into environment-specific configuration and provisions resources through your infrastructure as code. The portal provisions nothing on its own, and the orchestrator is not built to be the developer’s catalog and front end. A third type, the execution platform, runs the workloads themselves.

Developer portal

A developer portal provides a searchable software catalog, ownership records, compliance scorecards, golden-path templates, and self-service actions that trigger workflows in external tools. Developers use it to find services, see who owns what, check standards, and start common tasks such as creating a repository or requesting an environment.

Backstage is an open-source portal framework that Spotify says thousands of companies have adopted. Originally built at Spotify and now a CNCF incubating project, its core includes a software catalog, software templates, TechDocs, and search, and it has a large open-source plugin ecosystem; scorecards come from plugins such as Tech Insights or Spotify’s Soundcheck. Commercial portals such as Port, Cortex, and OpsLevel offer managed catalogs, scorecards, and self-service actions.

Platform orchestrator

A platform orchestrator sits between the portal and the infrastructure. When a developer declares what a workload needs, such as a database, a queue, and three environments, the orchestrator turns that specification into environment-specific configuration and provisions the resources through your existing infrastructure as code and Kubernetes clusters. It enforces policies, detects drift, and handles environment promotion.

Humanitec’s Platform Orchestrator is a commercial example, and open-source options include Kratix and KusionStack. The Score specification, a CNCF sandbox project, describes workload requirements in a platform-agnostic way that tools can consume. internaldeveloperplatform.org, maintained by Humanitec, documents this model in more depth.

Execution platform

An execution platform runs the workloads and handles the runtime operations required to keep them running in production: deployment, scaling, networking, secrets, observability, and resilience. Teams deploy code, and the platform operates it. On managed compute, this removes the need to operate Kubernetes clusters.

Combining the layers

Many organizations combine a portal with an orchestrator or an execution platform. The portal provides the catalog and self-service interface, and the orchestrator or execution platform does the provisioning and runtime work behind it. Developers get one interface, and infrastructure operations stay automated and governed.

Can you compare different internal developer platforms available in the market?

The market splits into five types: open-source portals, commercial portals, orchestrators, execution platforms, and building blocks. They differ in what they do and in how much of the stack your team still operates.

Type Examples What it does What you still run Best fit
Open-source portal framework Backstage Extensible service catalog, software templates, TechDocs, and a plugin ecosystem (scorecards come from plugins) The portal itself, its plugins, catalog data accuracy, and your entire deployment and runtime stack Organizations with a funded platform team that wants full control over the developer experience
Commercial portals Port, Cortex, OpsLevel Managed catalog, scorecards, self-service workflows, and integrations, typically with faster setup than Backstage Your deployment pipelines, infrastructure provisioning, and runtime Teams that want portal capabilities without engineers dedicated to portal maintenance
Platform orchestrators Humanitec, Kratix Turn workload specs into environment-specific configuration, provision resources through your IaC and clusters, enforce policies, and detect drift Kubernetes clusters, cloud accounts, CI/CD, and the runtime operations of your workloads Platform teams managing many environments with inconsistent configuration or long provisioning queues
Execution platforms Control Plane, and PaaS-style platforms Deploy, scale, and operate workloads, including networking, secrets, observability, and failover Your CI pipeline, source control, application code and its on-call, data layer design, and external services your workloads depend on Teams that want to ship production software without operating clusters; resilience and multi-cloud support vary widely across PaaS-style platforms
Building blocks Argo CD, Flux, Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, Crossplane GitOps delivery, infrastructure as code, and Kubernetes-native provisioning of cloud infrastructure The glue between tools, upgrades, monitoring, scaling, networking, and on-call Platform teams building a custom platform from open-source components

For vendors in the execution platform category, see our roundup of internal developer platforms. For GitOps tools, see Argo CD vs Flux.

What are the best internal developer platform tools?

The best tool depends on which layer you need.

  • Developer portals: Backstage (open source, CNCF), Port, Cortex, OpsLevel, and hosted Backstage such as Roadie and Spotify Portal for Backstage.
  • Platform orchestrators: Humanitec, with the Score workload specification, and the open-source Kratix and KusionStack.
  • Execution platforms: Control Plane runs workloads active-active across AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own clusters. PaaS-style platforms are covered in our roundup.
  • Building blocks: Argo CD and Flux for GitOps; Terraform, OpenTofu, and Pulumi for infrastructure as code; and Crossplane for Kubernetes-native provisioning.

How do I choose the right internal developer platform for my team?

Choose by your biggest bottleneck. If developers cannot find services or owners, start with a portal. If provisioning environments takes days, start with an orchestrator. If your team spends more time operating infrastructure than writing application code, start with an execution platform.

Situation Start with Why
No platform team, small to mid-size engineering organization Execution platform It handles runtime operations so the team ships production workloads without building and maintaining a platform layer. See platform engineering without a platform team.
A platform team that already runs Kubernetes, CI/CD, and Terraform Platform orchestrator or portal The runtime is covered. An orchestrator standardizes provisioning, and a portal organizes the catalog and self-service.
Many services and unclear ownership Developer portal A catalog, ownership records, and scorecards bring visibility before you change how services deploy.
Many environments and inconsistent configuration Platform orchestrator Environment-specific configuration generated from one workload spec reduces drift and manual tickets.
Strict compliance and audit requirements Execution platform with built-in governance, plus a portal for standards tracking An execution platform that embeds policy enforcement, audit trails, and compliance certifications reduces the runtime surface your security team must review. A portal’s scorecards can track standards on top of it.
Applications that must stay up through region or provider failures Multi-cloud execution platform Running workloads active-active across regions and clouds is difficult and expensive to build from individual tools.

Layers combine as the organization grows. A 30-person team that starts with an execution platform may add a portal when discoverability becomes a bottleneck, and a 200-person organization with a mature platform team may run all three. Solve the most painful problem first and add layers when a new bottleneck appears.

Should we build an internal developer platform on Backstage or buy one?

Build on Backstage if you have a funded platform team that needs deep customization of the developer experience. Buy a commercial portal or hosted Backstage (Roadie, Spotify Portal for Backstage) if you want a portal without dedicating engineers to maintaining it. Either way, you still need an orchestrator or execution platform underneath.

Backstage has no license fee, but running it takes ongoing engineering work. Backstage is a framework your team builds into a product. The portal needs hosting, authentication, a database, and monitoring. Every plugin must be evaluated, integrated, upgraded, and sometimes forked, and catalog data must be kept accurate through ingestion pipelines or enforced registration. Your engineers carry on-call for the portal.

Commercial portals (Port, Cortex, OpsLevel) and hosted Backstage absorb much of that work with managed infrastructure, pre-built integrations, and support. The trade-off is less customization and a recurring subscription. Hosted Backstage stays compatible with most open-source Backstage plugins.

Hidden costs of building on Backstage

  • Engineers dedicated to portal development and maintenance, usually a standing team.
  • Plugin compatibility testing on every Backstage upgrade.
  • Catalog accuracy: stale entries erode trust and adoption.
  • Custom integrations with CI/CD, cloud providers, and observability.
  • On-call for the portal itself.
  • Internal documentation and onboarding for the portal’s own features.
  • Internal promotion to drive voluntary adoption.

Portals with stale catalogs and no adoption plan tend to lose users after launch.

What should a 50-person engineering team use instead of building an internal developer platform?

Use existing products for each layer and build only the parts unique to your company. At 50 engineers, a homegrown platform competes with product work for the same people.

Layer What to avoid building What to use instead
Running and operating services Custom deploy scripts and a self-run Kubernetes cluster Control Plane, which handles deployment and Day 2 operations, including autoscaling and active-active failover, with no Kubernetes cluster to operate on Control Plane-managed locations
Portal and service catalog A self-hosted Backstage instance A commercial portal such as Port or Cortex, or hosted Backstage such as Roadie, added once service ownership becomes a problem
Infrastructure provisioning Home-grown wrappers around Terraform Terraform or OpenTofu with a workflow tool such as Spacelift, or Terraform with HCP Terraform
Delivery Custom rollout tooling GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, with Argo CD if you run Kubernetes
Golden paths A bespoke scaffolding service Template repositories and shared CI workflows

Building on Kubernetes instead. The best alternative is an execution platform that already provides what a homegrown platform would add on top of Kubernetes: deployment, scaling, routing, secrets, observability, and failover. Control Plane runs workloads with those built in, and teams that need direct Kubernetes access can run Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes or connect clusters they already run through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes, on the same platform. A portal can sit in front for the catalog.

What to evaluate in an internal developer platform

Ask each vendor, or your internal build team, these twelve questions and request the listed evidence.

Criterion What to ask Evidence to request
Developer self-service and golden paths Can a developer deploy a new service end to end without filing a ticket? Live demo of a new service from template to running in production
Deployment and rollback How are deployments triggered, and how fast can a bad deploy be rolled back? A rollback in a staging or production environment
Environments and previews Can developers create isolated preview environments on demand? Create and tear down a preview environment during the evaluation
Infrastructure provisioning How are databases, queues, and cloud resources provisioned, and are stateful workloads and persistent volumes supported? The provisioning flow for a managed database
Security and access control How are permissions scoped, and is network traffic encrypted? The access control model, network policies, and encryption in transit
Audit Is every action recorded, and can audit logs be exported to your SIEM? An audit log for one user’s actions over a recent period
Observability Are logs, metrics, and traces available without extra tooling? Built-in dashboards and alerting for a running workload
Resilience across zones, regions, and providers What happens when a region goes down? A simulated region outage showing traffic shifting automatically
Cost visibility and commercial terms Can you see cost per workload, team, or environment, and what are the pricing model and contract terms? A cost breakdown by workload and the pricing and contract documents
Integration with existing tools Does the platform work with your CI/CD, IaC, and observability tools? Integration with at least two tools you already use
Exit and portability What happens if you leave, and are workload definitions portable? Export format, and confirmation that workloads use standard container images
Operational load on your team How many engineers does the platform require to operate? Reference customers of similar size and their staffing model

Six-step proof-of-concept plan

  1. Pick one real service. Choose one representative of your stack, ideally with a database dependency and at least two environments. Write pass/fail criteria and set a fixed timebox before you start.
  2. Deploy it end to end. Go from source code to a running production-like environment, timing the process and noting every manual step.
  3. Test self-service. Have a developer who was not involved in setup deploy a change, create a preview environment, and roll back a bad release.
  4. Simulate a failure. Simulate a zone or region outage, for example by removing a location from the deployment or blocking traffic to it, and measure recovery time and whether traffic reroutes automatically.
  5. Review security and audit. Inspect access controls, network policies, and audit logs against your compliance requirements.
  6. Measure operational load. Record the hours your team spent on platform work versus application work, and extrapolate to your full service count.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, and Azure, VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. On Control Plane-managed locations there is no Kubernetes cluster to operate.

A workload deployed to Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a named set of locations across one or more clouds where each workload runs, runs active-active in every location of that GVC from one definition. Control Plane’s built-in global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location. Failover across regions and providers is built into the platform, so your team does not build or maintain it; for stateful workloads, plan how data replicates between locations.

Guardrails are built in. A deny-by-default internal firewall with mTLS between services limits each workload to what it is allowed to reach. Fine-grained policies grant users, groups, service accounts, and workload identities specific permissions on each resource. Users sign in through SAML, Google, GitHub, or Microsoft single sign-on, and every action on Control Plane is recorded in a tamper-proof audit trail. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. The CLI, console, Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the Control Plane MCP server all work through the same Control Plane API, so Control Plane complements the infrastructure as code and GitOps tools you already run, and a portal such as Backstage or Port can sit in front of it.

You pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, with no contracts or minimums. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.

For teams deciding whether they need a platform team at all, see developer self-service with guardrails and production-grade infrastructure without a platform team. For alternatives to managing Kubernetes directly, see the best Kubernetes alternatives.

FAQ

Short answers for teams evaluating internal developer platforms.

Is Backstage an internal developer platform?

Backstage is a developer portal framework, one layer of an internal developer platform. It provides a software catalog, templates, TechDocs, and a plugin architecture, but it does not provision infrastructure or run workloads, so most organizations pair it with an orchestrator or execution platform.

Do I need a platform team to run an internal developer platform?

Not necessarily. An execution platform such as Control Plane reduces or removes the need for a full platform team to operate the runtime, especially in smaller engineering organizations. A commercial portal reduces portal maintenance but does not run your infrastructure. See platform engineering without a platform team.

Can a portal and a platform be used together?

Yes. The portal provides the catalog and self-service interface, and the execution platform runs the workloads behind it. The portal calls the platform’s API to deploy and manage services while showing developers ownership, documentation, and operational status in one place.

What should a 50-person engineering team use instead of building an internal developer platform?

An execution platform such as Control Plane that handles deployment and operations, Terraform or OpenTofu with a workflow tool such as Spacelift for provisioning, and a commercial portal such as Port or Cortex once service discoverability becomes a problem. Building a custom platform from scratch at this size usually consumes more engineering capacity than it saves.

What is the best alternative to building an internal developer platform on Kubernetes?

Control Plane. It provides deployment, autoscaling, built-in observability, and active-active failover across regions and clouds, so a team does not build those layers on Kubernetes itself. Teams that need direct Kubernetes access can use Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes or connect their own clusters. Pair it with a portal such as Port or hosted Backstage if you need a service catalog.

What are the best internal developer platform tools?

For portals, Backstage, Port, Cortex, and OpsLevel; for orchestrators, Humanitec, Kratix, and KusionStack; for execution platforms, Control Plane and PaaS-style platforms; and Argo CD, Flux, Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, and Crossplane as building blocks. See our full roundup.

What is the difference between a platform orchestrator and an execution platform?

A platform orchestrator generates configuration and provisions resources through your existing infrastructure as code and Kubernetes clusters, and your team still operates those clusters and the runtime. An execution platform runs the workloads and manages the runtime itself, including deployment, scaling, networking, and failover.

What is the difference between an internal developer portal and an internal developer platform?

A portal is the developer-facing interface: catalog, ownership, scorecards, and self-service actions. An internal developer platform is the whole set of tools and services that let developers build, deploy, and run software on their own, and it may include a portal, an orchestrator, an execution platform, and building blocks.

How do I evaluate an internal developer platform before committing?

Run a timeboxed proof of concept with one real service and written pass/fail criteria. Deploy it end to end, test self-service with a developer who was not involved in setup, simulate a failure, review security and audit controls, and measure the hours spent on platform work.

Does Control Plane replace Kubernetes?

It can. On Control Plane-managed locations there is no Kubernetes cluster to operate, so teams that want to stop managing clusters can move workloads there. Teams that want to keep existing clusters can add them as locations in a Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud and deploy workloads to them through the same Control Plane API used for managed locations.

title: JEPAhead: From Inpainting to Causal Forecasting for Urban Driving
description:
arXiv:2611.08657v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We fine-tune a pre-trained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting while keeping the encoder frozen. Using contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets, and group-level causal attention, the model forecasts eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass. On CARLA Town12, it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, compared with 55.3% for persistence, with greater gains at longer horizons and on tokens exhibiting greater change. It also outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters. Semantic analysis indicates driving-relevant information in predicted features: a fixed linear probe trained on real encoder tokens achieves 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes, versus 0.13 for persistence. Vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon. Pixel-space evaluation shows modest L1 gains but little improvement under LPIPS, motivating direct evaluation through latent and semantic measures alongside an oracle reconstruction reference. These findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.

title: How I Run Multiple AI Coding Agents Across Multiple Repositories, and Git Branches Simultaneously
description:
Running multiple AI coding agents across separate repositories and Git branches simultaneously requires moving away from traditional IDE sidebar panels toward a terminal-native Agentic Development Environment (ADE) like Warp 2.0. By combining multi-session block interfaces, native Git worktree isolation, and multi-agent orchestration, developers can delegate concurrent tasks to different AI models (such as Warp Agent, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex) while maintaining independent state across each repository. However, executing parallel AI sessions locally imposes noticeable CPU and memory hardware demands and requires strict directory boundaries to avoid Git lock collisions.

Industry Adoption and Benchmark Metrics

The shift toward terminal-centric agentic workspaces is supported by performance benchmarks and rapid developer adoption metrics.

Warp Agent demonstrates strong autonomous coding execution, scoring 52% on Terminal-Bench (ranking #1 overall) and 71% on SWE-bench Verified (ranking in the top 5 overall). This performance reflects its ability to navigate terminal environments, execute diagnostic commands, and self-correct syntax errors during execution.

In terms of open-source ecosystem momentum, Warp released its Rust client application under the AGPLv3 license, generating over 52,000 GitHub stars shortly after launch. As engineering teams move away from manual line typing, terminal environments that offer native worktree parsing and structured block logging are becoming standard infrastructure for high-velocity software delivery.

The IDE Sidebar Bottleneck in the Agentic Era

Modern software engineering frequently requires managing microservice architectures, multi-package monorepos, or distributed backend systems. A single user feature might touch a React web client, a Node.js API gateway, a Go background worker, and a shared data validation utility. As development workflow shifts from writing raw code line-by-line to orchestrating autonomous AI agents, standard integrated development environments reveal a fundamental structural bottleneck.

Traditional IDEs reserve 80 to 85 percent of screen real estate for static text editors. AI coding assistants are relegated to narrow sidebar chat windows or floating popups. When an engineer attempts to coordinate AI-driven feature development across three distinct microservices, standard IDEs force sequential tab-switching, context stashing, and constant manual directory navigation. Industry analysis indicates nearly 90 percent of code generated in agentic workflows originates from prompt interactions rather than direct editor typing. Forcing these high-bandwidth interactions into secondary sidebars creates cognitive friction and stalls parallel execution.

Furthermore, context switching within a single repository directory causes severe operational friction. Switching Git branches to let an agent work on a hotfix stashes uncommitted work, interrupts local test runners, and scrambles the memory context of active language servers. To unlock true parallel delivery, developer workspaces must evolve to support multi-threaded task execution across isolated code environments.

Core Architecture: Worktree Isolation and Multi-Agent Orchestration

Warp 2.0 addresses these structural limits by redesigning the developer environment as an Agentic Development Environment (ADE). Instead of centering the screen on a static text document, Warp treats terminal command outputs, AI prompt interactions, and execution logs as first-class workspace blocks.

The fundamental architecture relies on three primary subsystems:

  1. Native Git Worktree Isolation: Rather than checking out different branches within the same directory, Git worktrees allow multiple branch checkouts (main, feature-auth, bugfix-gateway) into separate physical folders linked to a single Git repository. Warp 2.0 natively parses .git pointers inside worktrees, running background code indexers, branch status chips, and diff viewers independently for each folder.
  2. Multi-Threaded Agent Orchestration: Developers can run heterogeneous agent stacks simultaneously across workspace tabs or split panes. A developer can run Claude Code in one terminal pane for complex logic refactoring, Gemini CLI in another for massive context processing, and Warp Agent for shell command execution.
  3. Dedicated Code Review Panels and Permission Guardrails: As agents execute code autonomously, Warp provides per-session Code Review panels that display uncommitted diffs hunk-by-hunk. Security guardrails, including repository-level AGENTS.md rules and command deny lists, prevent agents from executing destructive terminal commands such as unapproved force pushes or directory deletions. 
[Repository A: Frontend] ──> Git Worktree A ──> Warp Tab 1 (Warp Agent: UI Feature)
                                                     │
[Repository B: Backend]  ──> Git Worktree B ──> Warp Tab 2 (Claude Code: API Setup) ──> Unified Notification
                                                     │                                     & Code Review Panel
[Repository C: Shared]   ──> Main Directory ──> Warp Tab 3 (Codex CLI: Test Suite)

Step-by-Step Practical Framework: Running Parallel Agents

Setting up a multi-repository, multi-agent workflow in Warp 2.0 involves structured execution steps to ensure complete task isolation.

Step 1: Establish Workspace Layout and Git Worktrees

Create isolated worktree directories for active feature branches so agents never collide in the same folder:

cd ~/projects/backend-service
git worktree add ../backend-feature-oauth feature/oauth-setup

Open Warp 2.0, create a new Workspace, and open three dedicated terminal tabs or split panes:

  • Tab 1: Frontend repository (~/projects/frontend-app)
  • Tab 2: Backend worktree (~/projects/backend-feature-oauth)
  • Tab 3: Shared utilities (~/projects/core-utils)

Step 2: Configure Permission Guardrails and Voice Input

Create an AGENTS.md file in each repository root to define architectural rules, test execution commands, and forbidden operations. Enable Warp command deny lists to block destructive commands (rm -rf *, git push --force).

To accelerate prompt construction across multiple sessions, leverage hands-free voice input within Warp's prompt box to dictate complex context and architectural requirements directly to the target agent without typing.

Step 3: Delegate Parallel Tasks Across Repositories and Branches

Assign discrete tasks to parallel agents across your open tabs:

  • Tab 1 (Frontend App): Dictate or prompt Warp Agent: "Build an OAuth login modal component using our existing design tokens in /components/auth. Execute npm test when complete."
  • Tab 2 (Backend Worktree): Launch Claude Code CLI: "Implement OAuth2 JWT validation endpoints in src/controllers/auth.ts. Write comprehensive unit tests in tests/auth.test.ts."
  • Tab 3 (Shared Utilities): Launch Codex CLI: "Refactor token validation helpers for UTF-8 compliance while maintaining backward compatibility."

Step 4: Monitor Execution and Review Diffs

Observe status indicators across the Warp workspace header. When an agent moves from RUNNING to NEEDS_INPUT or SUCCEEDED, click the session block to inspect output. Open Warp's built-in Code Review panel in each tab to audit generated diffs, revert unwanted hunk modifications, and commit verified changes.

Trade-offs, Resource Limits, and Security Guardrails

While parallel multi-agent execution dramatically accelerates delivery, developers must account for clear operational trade-offs:

  • Workstation Hardware Overhead: Running multiple LLM CLI agents simultaneously creates high CPU and memory demand. Each active agent process runs background file watchers, language server protocol (LSP) instances, and workspace embeddings. Workstations with 16GB RAM can experience performance degradation when executing more than three concurrent local agent sessions.
  • Directory Collisions: Assigning multiple agents to the same branch within a single working directory causes severe file overwrite collisions and Git index lock errors (.git/index.lock). Strict Git worktree usage or separate repository paths are mandatory.
  • Context Drift: In extended agent sessions exceeding 30 conversation turns, LLM context windows can compress, causing agents to drift from original architectural guidelines or reference deprecated APIs. Spawning fresh agent sessions for discrete sub-tasks mitigates this degradation.
  • Enterprise Telemetry and Privacy: While Warp's desktop client is open-source, server-side orchestration platforms and hosted AI models route data through external APIs. Enterprises operating under zero-retention compliance policies must configure explicit data retention rules and model routing options.

Summary Checklist and Next Steps

  • Transition multi-repo workflows from IDE sidebars to terminal workspaces using Warp 2.0.
  • Isolate parallel feature branches using Git worktrees (git worktree add) to prevent file overwrite collisions.
  • Establish repository guardrails using AGENTS.md files and command deny lists to safely run autonomous CLI agents.
  • Monitor multi-agent session lifecycle states (RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, NEEDS_INPUT) via Warp's visual block interface.
  • Audit generated changes using per-session Code Review panels before committing code.

Sources
