  • Warp Official Documentation: Git worktrees
  • Introducing Warp 2.0: Reimagining coding with the Agentic Development Environment
  • Managing Multiple AI Coding Agents in Warp Terminal: A Complete Guide
  • Warp Open-Source Client Repository

title: You're Probably Doing Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) Wrong
description:
The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern is crucial for securing modern applications, but it's widely misunderstood. In this video, we dive into the common pitfalls developers face when implementing BFFs. We break down why PKCE is not a replacement for a BFF, clarify the difference between a true BFF and a simple reverse proxy, and settle the debate on whether cookies are actually less secure than tokens. If you want to ensure your web apps are truly secure against XSS and token theft, this deep dive is for you.

What You'll Learn

  • Why PKCE protects authorization codes in transit, but doesn't secure token storage.
  • The critical distinction between a reverse proxy (token mediation) and a proper BFF.
  • The modern reality of HttpOnly cookies vs. localStorage tokens for XSS protection.
  • The security responsibilities you still have after implementing a BFF (like CSRF protection and session invalidation).
  • How to adopt the BFF pattern incrementally without rewriting your entire application.

Resources

  • Auth0 Blog Post: Things Developers Get Wrong About the Backend for Frontend Pattern
  • Checkout the Confused Developer Playlist for more videos like this.

title: We Moved to a Bigger Model to Debug the Test. Then We Went Back to the Smaller One.
description:
We Moved to a Bigger Model to Debug the Test. Then We Went Back to the Smaller One.

From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents (decide allow, deny, ask, rate-limit, or redact for every agent action, with shipped rule packs). Now on PyPI. This story is journal Groups 27, 29, and 30 of the v0.1.0 field test report.

AI disclosure: this article was drafted and edited with AI assistance. The field test, the defects, the fixes, and every number are real and linked below.

I did not move to a bigger model because I wanted to ship on a bigger model. I moved to a bigger model because I needed to answer a narrower question.

Was the 4-bit model actually the problem, or was my test harness lying to me?

That distinction mattered because the pinned field-test model was Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit, and I did not want to "fix" a harness bug by quietly upgrading the hardware bill. If the small model was genuinely too weak, I wanted to know that. If the harness was wrong, I wanted to fix the harness and come back to the pinned model.

That is exactly what happened.

The failure that looked like a model failure

The failing case was FT-FWK-SMOL, one of the live framework runs driven by scripts/run_field_agents.py. Ten agents in the case were green. One agent, sm-01, failed four of its five scenario rows.

Not randomly, either. Same four rows. Two runs in a row. Same failure shape: status=not-available called=False.

That is exactly the kind of pattern that makes a weak local model look guilty. The captured responses did not help. They showed the model narrating tool calls as prose instead of emitting them. I wrote the wrong diagnosis into my own report: deterministic tool-call hallucination on the small model.

At that point I had two choices. Keep arguing with the 4-bit model, or change one variable and see whether the failure survived.

Why the 9B run mattered

I switched to Qwen3.5-9B-MLX-4bit for one reason only: falsification.

If the stronger model passed, the small model was probably the issue. If the stronger model failed in the same way, then the model was not the issue at all.

The result was clean and brutal: the same four rows failed on the 9B model too.

That instantly changed the job. I was no longer trying to make the smaller model behave. I was trying to find the structural bug both models were faithfully exposing.

That is the part I wish more agent-eval writeups said out loud: a bigger model is sometimes most valuable as a debugging instrument. It is not always the fix. Sometimes it is the control in the experiment.

The bug the model upgrade revealed

The answer was in the captured pairs under field-test/v0.1.0/results/s16-frameworks/cases/FT-FWK-SMOL/.

My runner had built one agent carrying all five scenario tools:

scn_tools=[allow, audit, escalate, deny, adversarial]

Then it drove every scenario row through that one agent. So the model was free to call a different scenario's tool than the row under test. On the failing rows, that is exactly what it did. For example, a prompt naming scn_decision_allow_01 could trigger scn_adversarial_injection_01 instead.

The policy engine then made a correct decision about the wrong tool. My RecordingEngine keys decisions by (tool, action, env, data, agent), so when the test later looked for the decision tied to the row's tool, it found nothing. Result: not-available.

That meant the bigger model had done its job. It did not rescue the test. It proved the test was asking the wrong question.

Back to the smaller model

The fix was in the harness, not the model. _run_one now builds a fresh agent per scenario row, bound only to that row's tool. One row, one tool, one decision under test.

Then came the part I care about most: we went back to the pinned 4-bit model.

No quiet upgrade. No "it only works on the 9B." Back to the original box-local model, the one the benchmark chose for the sweep.

And it passed.

The results after the fix:

  • smolagents: 14/14 rows, 29 request/response pairs
  • CrewAI: 14/14 rows, 41 pairs, up from 10/14
  • pydantic-ai: 14/14 rows, 17 pairs, up from 9/14

All three flipped green on the pinned smaller model. The 9B model also verified 5/5 on sm-01, but it was no longer the point. The point was that the release did not need a stronger model. It needed a more honest harness.

What worked

  • Using the 9B model as a control, not a crutch. It answered the question I actually had.
  • Captured evidence over intuition. The pair files showed the wrong-tool picks. The logs never did.
  • Returning to the pinned model after the fix. That is what made the result usable for the actual release.

What did not work

  • My first instinct that a repeatable failure on a small model must be the small model.
  • One agent carrying five scenario tools. That setup tests tool choice, not policy correctness.
  • Treating a stronger model as the default answer before using it as a diagnostic step.

What I took away from this run is simple: if a failure survives a model upgrade, stop negotiating with the model and inspect the test. And if the bigger model helps you find the bug, go back to the smaller pinned one and prove the real workflow is green there.

More detail and evidence

  • The exact investigation: field test report, journal Groups 27, 29, and 30, including the wrong first diagnosis, the 9B falsification run, and the return to the pinned model.
  • The runner with the bug and the fix: scripts/run_field_agents.py and tests/field/agents/__init__.py.
  • The raw evidence: field-test/v0.1.0/results/s16-frameworks/cases/FT-FWK-SMOL/, plus the CREW and PAI result directories that flipped green on the same fix.
  • The benchmark and the model pin: scripts/fieldtest/omlx_bench.py, scripts/fieldtest/.env.example, and the benchmark section of the report.
  • The product: agentpolicy, pip install agentsec-agentpolicy, PyPI 0.1.0, part of the agentic-suite agent-security stack.

Have you ever upgraded the model just to isolate the bug, then gone back to the smaller one once you found it? That move saved this sweep, and I suspect it is underused.

title: Java: Write Once, Run Anywhere, But Consult Legal First
description:
In our previous installment, we explored Java's peculiar relationship with integer equality, collections that refuse to behave like collections, and the remarkable amount of engineering involved in concatenating two strings.

But those were merely quirks of the language.

The Java ecosystem is something else entirely.

Because somewhere along the way, Java stopped being just a programming language and became an entire civilization.

Complete with competing governments, religious disagreements, competing implementations, licensing disputes, and an astonishing number of products named after coffee.

If you think choosing a programming language should be the difficult part, Java has some news for you.

1. First, Let's Figure Out What Java Actually Is

This should be straightforward.

Java is a programming language.

Except Java is also commonly used to describe a runtime platform, a collection of libraries, a development kit, and an entire ecosystem of technologies that don't necessarily involve writing Java at all.

Let's meet the family.

Java: The programming language.

JVM: The Java Virtual Machine, which executes Java bytecode.

JRE: The Java Runtime Environment, traditionally the package needed to run Java applications.

JDK: The Java Development Kit, containing the compiler, runtime, and development tools.

OpenJDK: The open-source project providing a reference implementation of the Java platform and the foundation for many JDK distributions.

Simple enough.

Except the JVM isn't necessarily written by the same organization that distributes your JDK.

And a JDK doesn't have to use the same JVM implementation as another JDK.

And the JVM can execute programs written in languages other than Java.

And modern Java deployments often ship custom runtime images rather than requiring a separately installed JRE.

Already, we've managed to turn "install Java" into an architectural discussion.

But don't worry.

It gets better.

2. One JVM to Rule Them All. Except There Isn't One.

Java's original promise was revolutionary.

Write your program once. Compile it into bytecode. Run that bytecode anywhere a compatible JVM exists.

Which naturally raises an interesting question.

Whose JVM?

HotSpot: The Default Suspect

HotSpot is the familiar JVM implementation used by most mainstream OpenJDK distributions.

It's mature, highly optimized, and has spent decades becoming terrific at figuring out which parts of your code deserve special attention.

Its just-in-time compiler can optimize frequently executed code based on what actually happens at runtime.

This is one reason Java applications can perform impressively well despite running inside a virtual machine.

But HotSpot isn't the only game in town.

OpenJ9: Because One Virtual Machine Wasn't Enough

Eclipse OpenJ9 is an alternative JVM implementation with its own approaches to garbage collection, memory management, and compilation.

It's used in IBM Semeru Runtimes.

The interesting part is that OpenJ9 can run ordinary compatible Java applications.

Same language.

Same bytecode.

Different virtual machine implementation.

Depending on the workload, switching JVMs can change memory consumption, startup characteristics, garbage collection behavior, and performance.

Which means Java developers can spend hours tuning code, only to discover that changing the underlying JVM produces a bigger improvement.

Or makes everything worse.

Benchmark first. Celebrate later.

GraalVM: What if We Compiled the Whole Thing?

Then there's GraalVM.

GraalVM builds on HotSpot and provides the Graal compiler, an advanced just-in-time compiler written in Java.

Yes, Java has a compiler written in Java that helps Java run faster.

But GraalVM's especially interesting trick is Native Image.

Instead of running your application on a JVM at deployment time, you can compile it ahead of time into a native executable.

Potential advantages include faster startup and lower resource consumption.

Particularly attractive for certain cloud and serverless workloads.

Of course, ahead-of-time compilation brings different tradeoffs, including build complexity and restrictions around some forms of dynamic behavior.

So now Java can run on a JVM.

Or on a different JVM.

Or on a HotSpot-based runtime with a different optimizing compiler.

Or as a native executable that doesn't require a JVM at runtime.

Write once. Run anywhere. Spend three weeks deciding how.

3. Oracle Java Licensing: The Plot Twist Nobody Requested

For decades, Java was associated with Sun Microsystems.

Then Oracle acquired Sun in 2010.

And eventually, Java licensing became really interesting.

Not necessarily interesting in the fun programming-language sense.

More in the "why is procurement suddenly attending our architecture meetings?" sense.

Let's walk through the major developments.

2019: Wait, Java Isn't Free Anymore?

In April 2019, Oracle changed the licensing terms for certain Oracle Java SE releases and updates.

Some commercial production uses of newer Oracle JDK updates now required paid licensing where earlier terms had allowed broader use without a separate fee.

That created considerable confusion.

Because developers had spent years treating Java as something they could download, install, and run without thinking much about licensing.

Suddenly, organizations had to examine exactly which Java distribution they were using and under what terms.

But here's the important distinction:

Java the language did not suddenly become a paid product.

OpenJDK remained open source.

Alternative distributions remained available.

The licensing changes concerned specific Oracle-provided binaries and their terms.

Java itself hadn't disappeared behind a paywall.

Nevertheless, the confusion was understandable.

2021: Good News! It's Free Again. Sort Of.

Oracle introduced its No-Fee Terms and Conditions license, commonly abbreviated NFTC, with JDK 17.

This permitted free use, including commercial production use, for eligible Oracle JDK releases under those terms.

Excellent.

Problem solved?

Not exactly.

The free-use period for updates to an Oracle JDK long-term-support release doesn't necessarily last for that release's entire support lifetime.

Later updates can move to different licensing terms.

For example, Oracle JDK 21 updates through September 2026 were available under NFTC.

Beginning with the October 2026 update cycle, subsequent Oracle JDK 21 updates moved to the Oracle Technology Network licensing model, which doesn't grant the same unrestricted free commercial production rights.

Meanwhile, Oracle JDK 25 remains available under NFTC, with its own future transition schedule.

So if you're using Oracle JDK, you need to consider not only the Java version but also the specific update release and its license.

Because apparently version numbers weren't already complicated enough.

2023: How Many Employees Do You Have?

Then came Oracle's Java SE Universal Subscription.

Introduced in January 2023, this subscription moved to employee-based licensing.

Rather than simply counting installations or processors, the subscription model generally considers the size of the organization, according to its contractual employee definition.

That raised an obvious question.

What does the number of people working in accounting have to do with how many Java applications you're running?

Well, that's a question for the licensing department.

Oracle has since updated its pricing, including new small-business tiers introduced in October 2026. Its commercial offerings also include support, updates, and management capabilities.

And to be clear, organizations don't universally need an Oracle subscription to run Java commercially.

You can use appropriately licensed OpenJDK distributions.

But now the phrase "Which Java are we using?" can have financial consequences.

A programming language has successfully turned runtime selection into a procurement strategy.

Impressive, really.

4. Everyone Has Their Own Java

Thankfully, Java's open-source ecosystem provides plenty of alternatives.

You can choose from several OpenJDK-based distributions, including:

  • Eclipse Temurin, from the Adoptium project.
  • Amazon Corretto.
  • Azul Zulu.
  • Microsoft Build of OpenJDK.
  • BellSoft Liberica.
  • Red Hat builds of OpenJDK.
  • Oracle's own OpenJDK builds.

Most of these use HotSpot.

Some vendors offer additional runtime technologies or support arrangements.

And many are compatible implementations of essentially the same Java platform.

So why so many?

Different organizations provide different combinations of update schedules, supported platforms, packaging, long-term maintenance, commercial support, and optimization.

These differences can matter enormously for enterprises running thousands of applications.

But for developers trying to install Java on a new laptop, the experience can feel a little absurd.

You wanted a compiler.

Instead, you've been asked to evaluate a supply chain.

And then someone suggests SDKMAN! to manage all your JDK installations.

Which is genuinely useful.

But also rather funny.

We've created a tool to help manage the consequences of having so many tools.

5. The JVM Doesn't Actually Care Whether You Write Java

Here's where the ecosystem becomes much more interesting.

The JVM executes bytecode.

It doesn't particularly care which programming language produced that bytecode.

And developers have taken full advantage of that.

Kotlin: Java, but With Less Java

Kotlin was developed by JetBrains and has become particularly prominent in Android development.

It offers concise syntax, null-safety features, extension functions, and strong interoperability with Java.

You can call Java libraries from Kotlin.

You can call Kotlin code from Java.

You can even mix the two within the same project.

Kotlin also targets JavaScript, native platforms, and WebAssembly, so it isn't exclusively a JVM language.

But its JVM compatibility is a major reason for its success.

It offers developers a different language without requiring them to abandon the enormous Java library ecosystem.

Which is a polite way of saying:

"I like everything Java has built. I'd just rather not write so much Java."

Scala: What if Java Had a PhD?

Scala combines object-oriented and functional programming with a sophisticated type system.

It supports advanced abstraction, immutability, pattern matching, and a programming style very different from traditional Java.

It's also deeply connected to Apache Spark, which we'll get to shortly.

Scala can be extremely expressive.

It can also produce code that feels like a graduate thesis escaped into production.

The language is powerful enough to let you create abstractions that are beautiful, mathematically elegant, and almost completely incomprehensible to whoever maintains them next.

Groovy: Java After a Few Drinks

Groovy brings dynamic language features and scripting conveniences to the JVM.

It's closely associated with parts of the Java tooling world, particularly Gradle's traditional build-script DSL.

Groovy can use Java libraries and integrate with existing Java code.

Which means you can add a more flexible scripting language without leaving the ecosystem.

Clojure: For the Parentheses Enthusiast

Clojure brings a Lisp dialect and a functional programming philosophy to the JVM.

Immutable data structures.

Persistent collections.

Functions and sequences.

And parentheses.

Lots of parentheses.

Clojure demonstrates the JVM's flexibility particularly well.

You can write something that looks almost nothing like Java and still take advantage of Java's runtime and libraries.

The JVM has become a place where programming languages with wildly different philosophies agree to share the same infrastructure.

If only their developers could agree on indentation.

6. Apache: Where Java Became Infrastructure

Now let's leave ordinary applications behind.

Because Java's influence extends far beyond enterprise web development.

A remarkable amount of modern data infrastructure grew out of the Java and JVM ecosystem.

And much of it lives under the Apache Software Foundation.

Hadoop: The Elephant in the Data Center

Apache Hadoop helped popularize large-scale distributed data processing.

Its ecosystem included HDFS for distributed storage, MapReduce for processing, and YARN for resource management.

The appeal was simple.

Take large datasets.

Spread them across multiple machines.

Process them in parallel.

Make the system resilient when individual machines fail.

Simple in concept.

Considerably less simple when you're actually operating a cluster.

Suddenly your data pipeline has dozens of configuration files, services that need to discover each other, and an impressive collection of logs.

But Hadoop was enormously influential.

And it helped lay the foundations for much of the modern big-data world.

Spark: Python Developers, Meet Your JVM

Apache Spark emerged as a more flexible distributed processing engine.

Its core is closely tied to Scala and the JVM.

But Spark supports Java, Scala, Python, SQL, and, with some qualifications depending on version, R.

This creates a particularly entertaining situation.

A data scientist writes PySpark code in Python.

Spark coordinates distributed execution using its JVM-based engine, with Python worker processes involved where necessary.

So a Python application can be orchestrating work through a Java-based distributed computing platform without the developer writing a single line of Java.

Java has successfully infiltrated the Python ecosystem while allowing Python to take the credit.

To be fair, that's a pretty good arrangement for everyone involved.

Kafka: Everything Is an Event Now

Apache Kafka provides distributed event streaming.

Applications publish events.

Other applications consume them.

Events can be retained, replayed, and processed by multiple consumers.

Kafka became central to many event-driven architectures, data pipelines, and streaming systems.

It's powerful infrastructure.

It also has its own terminology, operational model, and configuration universe.

But there's one historical detail that deserves special attention.

Kafka spent more than a decade relying on another Apache project.

ZooKeeper.

7. ZooKeeper: Challenge Accepted

Distributed systems have a fundamental problem.

Several machines need to cooperate.

Machines fail.

Networks become unreliable.

Nodes disagree about who's responsible for what.

Someone needs to coordinate the chaos.

Enter Apache ZooKeeper.

ZooKeeper provides distributed coordination primitives for tasks such as naming, configuration management, synchronization, and leader election.

For years, Kafka used ZooKeeper to help manage cluster metadata and coordination.

Which meant that to run your distributed event streaming platform, you also needed a separate distributed coordination service.

You now had a cluster to manage your cluster.

And that cluster needed its own monitoring, configuration, and operational care.

At some point, the infrastructure diagram began to resemble a family tree drawn by someone with a grudge.

But here's the plot twist.

In March 2025, Apache Kafka 4.0 eliminated its ZooKeeper dependency entirely.

Kafka moved fully to KRaft, its own Raft-based metadata management architecture.

So after years of operating an additional distributed system to coordinate Kafka, the Kafka project finally said:

"Perhaps we could do this ourselves."

ZooKeeper itself remains a useful project for other distributed systems.

But Kafka's departure is a nice illustration of how the Java ecosystem evolves.

First, build a powerful framework.

Then build supporting infrastructure.

Then build infrastructure to manage that infrastructure.

Then spend several years simplifying the whole thing.

Progress!

And we haven't even discussed Apache Flink, HBase, Hive, or the wider collection of projects that helped turn Java into the plumbing of big data.

8. The Great Java IDE Wars

Surely, with all this complexity, at least the development environment is straightforward?

Of course not.

Java has an impressive history of competing IDEs.

And for a long time, choosing one was practically a declaration of personal identity.

NetBeans: The Old Guard

NetBeans has a long history, including years under Sun Microsystems and later Oracle.

It's now an Apache project.

It offers an integrated Java development experience with editors, debugging, refactoring, project tools, and GUI development capabilities.

For many developers, NetBeans was their introduction to serious Java programming.

A comfortable place to write code.

A reminder of a time when an IDE could feel like one reasonably coherent application rather than a marketplace for extensions.

Eclipse: Your IDE Is Also a Platform

Eclipse took a different approach.

Its plugin architecture allowed developers to extend the environment extensively.

Java Development Tools.

Refactoring.

Debugging.

Build integration.

Language support.

Application development frameworks.

And approximately seventeen different perspectives, views, and preferences screens.

Eclipse was enormously important to enterprise Java development.

It also introduced many developers to the experience of installing one plugin, discovering that it required three others, and then spending an afternoon resolving version compatibility.

Your IDE needed dependency management.

Which, in fairness, was excellent preparation for Java development.

IntelliJ IDEA: What if the IDE Actually Understood Your Code?

Then there's IntelliJ IDEA from JetBrains.

IntelliJ built a strong reputation around code analysis, refactoring, navigation, and developer productivity.

It also offers first-class support for Kotlin, which makes sense given that JetBrains created the language.

For many developers, IntelliJ became the preferred environment for modern Java development.

Although the perpetual debate over which IDE is best remains alive and well.

As with most religious disputes, empirical evidence is rarely invited to the discussion.

VS Code: Fine, Let's Make Everything an Extension

And naturally, Java development is also supported in Visual Studio Code.

Install the appropriate extensions, configure the JDK, set up your build system, and off you go.

Which means the Java IDE wars now include a lightweight editor that can be transformed into something resembling an IDE through plugins.

We've come full circle.

The IDE became a platform.

Then the editor became a platform.

And everyone continued arguing about keyboard shortcuts.

9. Maven, Gradle, and the Art of Building a Build System

Before we finish, we need to talk about building Java applications.

Because writing code is only half the battle.

The other half is convincing your dependencies to cooperate.

Maven: XML Will Save Us

Apache Maven brought standardized project structures, dependency management, and build lifecycles to Java.

It was a major improvement over manually downloading JAR files and assembling mysterious classpaths.

But Maven also embraced XML configuration.

A lot of XML configuration.

You could have a beautifully organized project whose build file was longer than some of its source files.

Still, Maven provided consistency.

And that's valuable.

Gradle: What if Our Build Files Were Programs?

Gradle offered a more programmable build system, supporting Groovy and Kotlin DSLs.

More flexibility.

More control.

Potentially less XML.

Naturally, this also meant build scripts could become arbitrarily sophisticated programs with their own bugs.

Because sometimes a build configuration isn't complicated enough until you can debug it.

Scala developers may also encounter sbt, adding another build tool to the mix.

And underneath much of this sits Maven Central and the wider ecosystem of artifact repositories, transitive dependencies, version conflicts, and the occasional library whose presence in your application nobody can explain.

Java didn't invent dependency hell.

But it certainly helped industrialize it.

10. And Then There's Enterprise Java

We could stop here.

But that would mean ignoring a particularly entertaining corner of the ecosystem.

Enterprise Java.

Java EE.

Jakarta EE.

Spring.

Spring Boot.

Hibernate.

Quarkus.

Micronaut.

And decades of arguments about dependency injection, annotations, XML configuration, and whether a sufficiently abstract factory should require another factory.

Java EE eventually moved from Oracle-led stewardship to the Eclipse Foundation, becoming Jakarta EE.

And because software history enjoys a good practical joke, the transition also involved moving many APIs from the javax.* namespace to jakarta.*.

Which sounds simple until you're migrating an application with years of dependencies.

Meanwhile, Spring built an enormous ecosystem around enterprise application development, and newer frameworks such as Quarkus and Micronaut pursued approaches tailored to modern cloud deployment.

All useful technologies.

All with their own philosophies.

All capable of inspiring passionate architectural disagreements.

At this point, the Java ecosystem contains enough competing approaches to solving enterprise application development that you could spend an entire career evaluating frameworks without ever deploying an application.

Although that might itself qualify as enterprise architecture.

Java's Greatest Strength Is Also Its Greatest Joke

After all this, it's tempting to conclude that the Java ecosystem is a confusing mess.

And in some ways, it is.

Multiple JVM implementations.

Numerous JDK distributions.

Oracle licensing policies that require careful attention.

Languages ranging from Kotlin to Clojure.

An enormous collection of Apache infrastructure projects.

Competing IDEs.

Competing build tools.

Competing application frameworks.

Competing opinions about nearly everything.

But here's the remarkable part.

Much of it actually works together.

A Kotlin application can consume Java libraries.

A Scala-based Spark engine can process workloads submitted through Python APIs.

A compatible Java application can move between different OpenJDK distributions.

A large Java codebase can survive decades of changes to operating systems, hardware, runtimes, tools, and deployment environments.

That's not a trivial achievement.

The JVM became one of the most successful common execution platforms in software history precisely because it allowed an extraordinary amount of innovation to happen around a relatively stable foundation.

And that flexibility created competition.

Competition created alternatives.

Alternatives created choices.

And choices created endless arguments.

Which brings us back to Java's famous promise.

Write once, run anywhere.

Thirty years later, we've added a few practical qualifications.

Write once.

Choose a JDK distribution.

Check the license.

Select a JVM.

Pick an IDE.

Choose a build tool.

Resolve your dependencies.

Decide which framework you believe in.

Configure your deployment environment.

And then...

Run anywhere.

title: I built a bridge so AI agents can order groceries in Hinglish, and can't order without your yes
description:
A friend in Varanasi types her grocery list like this:

do kilo aata aur 1 litre doodh

That is Hindi written in English letters (Hinglish). No search box on a seller's catalog understands it, and no AI agent today can take that sentence, find a nearby kirana store, and place the order safely.

So I built Haat (हाट, the village market): an open-source gateway that lets personal AI agents shop from sellers on ONDC, India's open commerce network, in the language people actually type, and never places an order without the person's explicit approval.

Live demo and docs | GitHub

The problem: two protocols that don't talk

  • Personal AI agents are starting to speak Poppy (the Personal Agent Protocol, announced by Sierra and Meta in October 2026).
  • Lakhs of Indian sellers already speak Beckn, the protocol under ONDC, with machine-readable catalogs and structured orders.

Small sellers will not implement a new protocol one by one. Without a bridge, they are invisible to the agents their customers use. Haat is that bridge: a Poppy "Company" on one side, an ONDC buyer app on the other.

When I searched on 1 November 2026, I found Poppy SDKs and separate ONDC MCP servers, but nothing connecting the two. That is a search result, not proof. If you know of related work, I would like to hear about it.

The end-to-end flow 

"do kilo aata aur 1 litre doodh"
  -> 2 x Whole Wheat Atta 1 kg, 1 x Toned Milk 1 L, Kashi Kirana Store
  -> "Total ₹197, pay on delivery. Approve?"
  -> yes
  -> order KKS-1001 (placed once)

Part 1: Parsing Hinglish without a model

I did not want an LLM deciding what ends up in a shopping basket. So the parser is rule-based and driven by data (a lexicon), and every step is testable.

The pipeline:

  1. Normalise the text. Digits of every Indian script (२ ২ ௨ ౨) become ASCII digits, and zero-width characters are removed.
  2. Split into items on separators (aur, and, और, commas, the danda ।).
  3. Read quantities: a digit or number word, then a unit.
  4. Drop stopwords ("mujhe", "chahiye").
  5. Match Latin-letter words through a phonetic key (ee becomes i, oo becomes u, dh becomes d). Words in Indian scripts are compared as written. The longest match wins.
  6. No match? Search the raw words as typed, so nothing is silently lost.

Two bugs the tests now pin:

  • Dropping a final vowel made makhana (fox nuts) equal makhan (butter). I removed that rule and added a regression test.
  • "do" means both "two" and "give". In "atta de do" it is the verb. A number word only counts if something follows it.

Coverage today is 130 grocery products in Hindi, Bhojpuri, Marathi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi and Odia, each in its own script and in Latin letters.

An honest caveat: only Hindi was written by hand. The other languages were drafted by a machine and have not been reviewed by native speakers. I say so in the docs and in the README. The tests prove the parser behaves consistently on the data, not that the words are right. This is the easiest place to contribute, and you don't need to write any TypeScript.

Part 2: The approval gate

The rule I would not compromise on: a language model never decides approvals. The person approves one exact revision of an order, through the protocol, and the model never sees tokens, keys, OTPs or full phone numbers.

Two details matter most:

At most once, even across restarts. An approved operation runs at most once. If the process dies mid-order and comes back, it must not order twice.

Unknown is not failed. If an action may have happened (a timeout, a connection reset, a 5xx with no NACK, a callback that never came), Haat throws OutcomeUnknownError and answers 503 Retry-After. It never says "failed". Telling a user "failed" when the order actually went through gets them to retry, and then they get two bags of atta. Only not_sent or rejected release the approval.

Seller URLs come from the registry, and prices come from the seller's own quote. Nothing the agent claims is trusted.

Verified, with numbers from real runs

  • 126 automated tests (unit and end-to-end over real HTTP), all passing, with lint and typecheck clean.
  • The official Personal Agent Protocol validator, run over real HTTPS: 99 checks passed, 0 failed, 0 warnings. The 22 skipped checks cover features Haat doesn't offer (MCP, browser join, Device and Mediated Sign-In).
  • No runtime dependencies. It uses Node 22.18+ running TypeScript directly, and node:sqlite for storage.

What it does not do (yet)

I would rather tell you than have you find out:

  • It works with a local mock network of ONDC-style sellers. It has not touched a real seller or real money.
  • A live ONDC connection needs a legal entity, whitelisting and ONDC's approval.
  • Sign-in codes need a real SMS provider.
  • It is not affiliated with ONDC, Sierra, Meta or the Personal Agent Protocol project.

Try it in one minute 

git clone https://github.com/techsaurabh-394/haat-gateway.git
cd haat-gateway
npm install
npm run demo

The demo asks you to approve the order in your terminal.

Help me with this

Haat is open source (MIT) and PRs are welcome. Most contributions need no TypeScript:

  • Review the machine-drafted Tamil, Bengali, Marathi or other language data
  • Teach the lexicon how your city spells pyaz
  • Add a domain pack or a mock seller from your neighbourhood
  • Improve the docs

Start with CONTRIBUTING.md and the good first issue label.

If you build agents, I would like to know how you handle the "unknown outcome" case. And if you speak one of those languages, tell me which words I got wrong.

Built by Saurabh Pathak, AI engineer and full-stack developer from Varanasi. GitHub | LinkedIn

title: Cloud Cost Governance at Scale: Policies, Automation, Savings Tracking, and Choosing VM Pricing Models
description:
Govern cloud cost at scale by making ownership and tagging mandatory, encoding cost rules as policy-as-code that runs in CI and against live accounts, automating the routine fixes (rightsizing, idle cleanup, schedules, commitment coverage), and reporting unit costs and savings per team and per deployment on a regular cadence. Choose on-demand, committed, and spot pricing per workload based on how steady and interruptible it is; Control Plane’s Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory for eligible workloads, and Control Plane bills for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, with no contracts or minimums, across AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own servers.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

  • Ownership and tagging. Every resource carries owner, application, environment, and cost-center tags from creation; without them there is no allocation or accountability.
  • Policy-as-code. Encode cost rules in tools such as Open Policy Agent and Cloud Custodian, run them in CI and against live accounts, and move from warnings to blocks as rules mature.
  • Automated remediation. Automate low-risk fixes such as schedules and idle cleanup; keep a human on rightsizing, commitments, and deletions that could hit live systems.
  • Savings tracking. Separate avoided cost from realized savings, normalize for growth, and report unit costs per request, customer, or environment.
  • Pricing models. Cover the steady baseline with commitments, run variable demand on demand, and move interruptible work to spot.
  • On Control Plane, Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory reservations from historical usage, billing follows what workloads reserve with no contracts or minimums, and one platform spans clouds and your own servers.

What is the most effective governance and automation approach for enforcing cloud cost optimization policies at scale?

The FinOps Foundation framework gives the operating model in three phases: Inform (make costs visible), Optimize (act on them), and Operate (build cost discipline into daily work). A central team sets standards, tag taxonomy, and reporting. Product teams own their budgets and optimization decisions. Automation handles the repetitive enforcement no central team can do by hand.

Ownership and mandatory tags

Tags turn a bill into accountable line items, so enforce them where resources are created.

  • AWS tag policies standardize tags across an organization, and service control policies can deny actions that lack required tags.
  • Azure Policy can deny resources missing required tags or add default values.
  • Google Cloud organization policies restrict allowed regions, services, and configurations, while labels and tags on projects and resources carry ownership; required labels need custom constraints or CI checks.

A minimum tag set is owner, application, environment, and cost center. Temporary resources should also carry an expiry date.

Policy-as-code

Cost rules written as code are testable, versioned, and enforceable at several points in the delivery pipeline.

  • Open Policy Agent (OPA) evaluates policies against infrastructure-as-code plans, Kubernetes admission requests, and APIs.
  • Cloud Custodian runs rules against live cloud accounts to catch drift and violations after deployment.
  • Infracost shows cost estimates on pull requests so engineers see the cost change before merging.

Enforce in stages: inform through dashboards, warn on deployments or approvals, block only clear violations such as a prohibited instance type in production, and auto-fix where risk is low, such as stopping an expired development environment.

Policy Where it runs Action
Required tags present CI (plan stage) Block merge if missing
Maximum VM size per environment CI and account Warn in development, block in production
Untagged resource older than seven days Account (scheduled scan) Notify owner, then quarantine
Budget threshold or forecast exceeded Account (provider budgets) Alert owner and FinOps team
Idle load balancer detected Account (scheduled scan) Notify owner, delete after owner approval
Non-production running after hours Runtime (scheduler) Stop automatically, allow self-service restart

Budgets and anomaly detection

Each provider ships budgets and anomaly alerts.

  • AWS Budgets and AWS Cost Anomaly Detection track actual and forecast spend and flag unusual patterns.
  • Azure Cost Management budgets alert on thresholds and can trigger automation.
  • Google Cloud budgets send alerts and can publish to Pub/Sub for programmatic responses.

Set budgets by account, business unit, product, and environment, each with a named owner, and alert on forecast overruns as well as actual spend so teams act before the period closes. When an anomaly fires, find the account, service, resource, and owner, confirm whether the change was intended, fix it if not, record the cause, and adjust the policy or threshold.

Which cost fixes should you automate?

Automation turns policies into controls, but only some fixes are safe to run without review.

Safe to automate:

  • Stopping development, staging, and preview environments outside working hours, with self-service restart.
  • Deleting unattached volumes, and snapshots outside retention policy, after a notice period to the owner.
  • Moving objects to cheaper storage tiers with lifecycle rules.
  • Adding default tags to untagged resources, or quarantining them.

Needs human review:

  • Rightsizing. Provider advisors (AWS Compute Optimizer, Azure Advisor, Google Cloud recommenders) suggest smaller instances, but averages can hide bursts.
  • Commitment purchases. Check utilization history, forecasts, migration plans, and break-even dates before committing.
  • Deleting idle databases or load balancers, only after owner approval, since they may be idle because of an incident or a paused launch.

Autoscaling sits between the two. It adjusts capacity continuously, while its minimums, maximums, and targets deserve periodic review. In Kubernetes, the gap between requested and used CPU and memory is often the largest waste, so track request utilization per namespace and adjust requests from usage percentiles.

Best solutions for tracking cost savings per deployment across multiple projects with dashboards and updates

Allocation. Tags and labels map resources to teams, products, and environments. Split shared costs, such as a shared cluster or database, by a usage measure like CPU-hours, requests, or storage. Separate accounts or projects per team simplify allocation, though shared platforms still need splitting.

Showback and chargeback. Showback reports costs to teams; chargeback bills them. Most organizations start with showback and move to chargeback once tagging and trust in the data mature.

Unit economics. Track cost per customer, per request, or per environment. For example, if total spend rises 20 percent while cost per request falls 15 percent, efficiency improved even though the bill grew.

Honest savings. Document a baseline period. Report avoided cost (spend that never happened) separately from realized savings (a lower bill), and normalize for traffic growth and architecture changes. For commitments, report coverage, utilization, effective savings rate, unused commitment cost, and break-even date.

Cost per deployment. Record deploy timestamps per service, then compare the service’s unit cost in equal windows before and after each release. In Kubernetes, allocate cost with OpenCost by a workload label that carries the release version.

Multi-cloud data. The FOCUS specification (FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification) defines a common billing schema across providers, which reduces the custom normalization multi-cloud dashboards need.

Metric Audience Cadence
Spend by team and environment FinOps team, leadership Weekly
Unit cost (per request, per customer) Engineering leads Weekly
Realized savings against baseline FinOps team, finance Monthly
Commitment utilization and coverage FinOps team Weekly
Cost change per release Engineering teams Each release
Anomaly alerts Resource owners As they fire
Idle resource inventory Engineering teams Weekly
Tag coverage (percent of spend allocated) FinOps team Weekly

What FinOps software options are available?

FinOps tools fall into four categories.

  • Native cloud tools. AWS Cost Explorer, Azure Cost Management, and Google Cloud billing reports give first-party visibility, budgets, and recommendations within one provider.
  • Open source. OpenCost, a CNCF incubating project, allocates Kubernetes costs by namespace, workload, and label and can add cloud costs from outside the cluster, without a commercial license.
  • Third-party FinOps platforms. Commercial platforms combine billing across providers, automate commitment management, and add reporting for large multi-cloud estates.
  • Pre-deployment estimation. Infracost and similar tools show cost changes on pull requests.

For a comparison of tools in each category, see the cloud cost optimization tools roundup.

How do I optimize cloud and hybrid deployments to reduce overall IT spend?

Place each workload where its cost profile fits, then remove duplication.

  • Match workload to venue. Steady, predictable workloads often cost less on committed capacity or owned hardware; bursty workloads benefit from cloud elasticity.
  • Watch data transfer. Egress between regions, between clouds, and to the internet, plus cross-zone traffic and NAT gateway processing charges, are the costs hybrid designs most often miss. Keep compute next to its data, cache close to users, and compress payloads.
  • Use owned hardware for steady load. Over a multi-year horizon, owned or colocated servers can cost less than on-demand cloud for stable demand, at the price of elasticity and operations work. See the cloud vs. on-premises vs. hybrid cost comparison.
  • Consolidate. Retire duplicate tools, clusters, and environments, and right-size per-core or per-VM licenses before renewal.

For tactics that lower an AWS bill without re-architecting, see cutting your AWS bill 30 percent.

What are the most cost effective cloud virtual machine providers and pricing models?

The cheapest model depends on how steady and interruptible each workload is.

Model AWS Azure Google Cloud Commitment Interruption risk Fits
On-demand On-Demand Instances Pay-as-you-go On-demand VMs None None New, short-lived, or spiky workloads
Resource commitment Reserved Instances Azure Reservations Resource-based committed use discounts 1 or 3 years, instance family or vCPU/memory quantity in a region None Steady workloads with stable instance types and regions
Spend commitment Savings Plans Azure savings plan for compute Compute flexible committed use discounts (spend-based) 1 or 3 years, hourly spend None Stable spend across instance families or regions
Automatic discount None None Sustained use discounts on older machine types (N1, N2, N2D, C2, M1, M2) None None VMs that run much of the month
Spot Spot Instances Azure Spot Virtual Machines Spot VMs None Reclaimable on short notice (AWS 2 minutes, Azure and Google Cloud 30 seconds) Batch, CI, analytics, development

Discounts vary by instance type, region, term, and payment option. AWS lists savings of up to 72 percent for Reserved Instances and up to 66 percent for Compute Savings Plans; check each provider’s pricing pages for current figures.

Rightsize first, then commit. Review 30 to 90 days of utilization, size the steady baseline, cover it with commitments, run the variable portion on demand, and move interruptible jobs to spot with retry and checkpointing. Ladder commitments with staggered purchases and expiry dates, and favor spend-based plans where instance families may change. Independent and bare-metal providers often price by flat monthly rates, which suit steady workloads that do not need elasticity.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a set of locations a workload runs across, and runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads on AWS, GCP, and Azure, on Kubernetes clusters you already run, and on your own machines turned into managed locations, including on premises.

Pay for what you reserve. Billing is for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, with no contracts or minimums. Capacity AI, Control Plane’s right-sizing of CPU and memory based on historical usage, sets that reservation between a minimum and maximum you choose. Control Plane also bills egress, storage, observability, dedicated load balancers, and GPUs, as listed on the pricing page. Capacity AI is not used for GPU workloads or for workloads that autoscale on CPU utilization or on multiple metrics.

Scale to zero. Serverless workloads scale to zero natively, and standard and stateful workloads can scale to zero through KEDA, enabled per GVC, so idle environments stop reserving capacity.

Redundancy without idle standby. A workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, so redundancy does not require an idle standby copy. See active-active vs. active-passive costs. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Those locations can be two regions of one cloud or locations on different providers.

Visibility. A Cost & Usage view shows spend per org and per resource with a projected total, a billing_viewer role gives read-only access, and a monthly spend alert goes to billing admins. Control Plane ships Terraform and Pulumi providers, so workloads sit in the same infrastructure-as-code review as everything else.

Operations. Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, Capacity AI right-sizing, built-in observability, and security, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate. Steady workloads can run on your own servers under the same management as cloud locations.

Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

FAQ

Short answers to common cost governance questions.

What is the most effective governance and automation approach for enforcing cloud cost optimization policies at scale?

Mandatory ownership tags enforced at creation, policy-as-code in CI and against live accounts, automated low-risk fixes, and staged enforcement that warns before it blocks, run under the FinOps Foundation’s Inform, Optimize, Operate model.

What are the best solutions for tracking cost savings per deployment across multiple projects with dashboards and updates?

Mark deploy times per service, compare unit cost in equal windows before and after each release, normalize billing data with the FOCUS specification, and report cost change at each release, unit costs weekly, and realized savings monthly.

What FinOps software options are available?

Native cloud cost tools, open-source OpenCost for Kubernetes allocation, and commercial multi-cloud FinOps platforms. The cost optimization tools roundup compares them.

How do I optimize cloud and hybrid deployments to reduce overall IT spend?

Put steady workloads on committed capacity or owned hardware, keep bursty ones elastic, keep compute next to its data to limit egress, and consolidate duplicate tools and clusters.

What are the most cost effective cloud virtual machine pricing models?

Commitments (Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, Azure Reservations and savings plans, Google committed use discounts) for the steady baseline, on-demand for variable demand, and spot for interruptible work. Rightsize before committing.

How does policy-as-code help control cloud costs?

It turns cost rules into versioned, testable checks that block expensive configurations in CI and catch drift in live accounts, reducing manual review for routine rules.

Which cost fixes are safe to automate?

Non-production schedules, cleanup of unattached volumes and old snapshots after notice, storage lifecycle rules, and tag enforcement. Rightsizing and commitments need human review, and idle databases or load balancers are deleted only after owner approval.

When should I use spot instances versus reserved capacity?

Spot for work that tolerates interruption, such as batch, CI, analytics, and development; reserved capacity or savings plans for steady production demand.

How should I structure cloud budgets across teams?

Set budgets per account, business unit, product, and environment, give each a named owner, and alert on forecast overruns as well as actual spend.

title: Routing NDIS Medication Events as Data: Reportable-Incident Rules, Awareness Clocks and a Competency Gate on the Roster
description:
Originally based on our article Medication management and NDIS compliance on rostery.com.au. This version is rewritten for developers and operations staff who maintain incident and medication workflows for a disability provider. It also corrects how the original describes when a medication error becomes reportable, covered in the first section.

Most medication software stops at the dose. A worker records what was given, the chart updates, a report shows adherence. That part is well understood, and we wrote about the record structure itself in an earlier post on designing a medication administration record for NDIS support.

This post is about what happens next: the moment a dose goes wrong, or a PRN is given for the wrong reason, or a worker who has never been trained on a participant's PEG tube is rostered on to give their evening medication. Those are routing problems. Something has to decide whether the event is reportable to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission, which clock applies, when the clock started, and whether the roster should have allowed the shift at all.

We'll build a small Python model for each of those decisions. It's deliberately plain: dataclasses, a few enums, pure functions you can test.

General information only, not legal or clinical advice. Rules were read on the NDIS Commission's website on 9 November 2026. Check the current Commission guidance before you rely on any of this in production.

The rule most systems get wrong

There's no "medication error" category in the NDIS reportable incidents list. A lot of policy templates, and our own original article, suggest one exists: an error that "results in, or is likely to result in, serious harm" is reportable. That's not how the Commission frames it.

The reportable incidents are defined by what happened to the person, not by the kind of mistake that caused it. A medication event becomes reportable only when it fits one of the listed incidents. For medication, three routes come up again and again:

  • Serious injury. The Commission's detailed guidance treats an injury needing hospital treatment, including a presentation to an emergency department, as a serious injury. A wrong dose that sends someone to ED is reportable on this route.
  • Neglect. A reckless act or a failure to act that results in, or could result in, death or significant harm, including failing to get someone medical care. A missed dose of a critical medication, left without follow-up, may sit here.
  • Unauthorised use of a restrictive practice. A PRN given mainly to change someone's behaviour, outside an authorisation and a behaviour support plan, is a chemical restraint used without authorisation.

Everything else, including most errors and every near miss, is internal. It still has to be recorded, reviewed and acted on, because the Practice Standards expect an incident management system that covers all incidents, not just the reportable ones.

So the first design decision is to keep two things apart: the medication event (what went wrong with the medication) and the incident route (what the Commission needs to hear about). One event can produce no routes, one route, or occasionally two.

Modelling the event

Start with the facts a worker can actually supply at the end of a shift. Avoid fields like is_reportable on the worker's form. That's a judgement for the office, and the form should collect the inputs to that judgement instead.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime
from enum import Enum

class EventKind(Enum):
    WRONG_DOSE = "wrong_dose"
    WRONG_TIME = "wrong_time"
    MISSED = "missed"
    WRONG_PERSON = "wrong_person"
    PRN_GIVEN = "prn_given"
    NEAR_MISS = "near_miss"

@dataclass
class MedicationEvent:
    participant_id: str
    medication_id: str
    kind: EventKind
    occurred_at: datetime
    recorded_by: str
    description: str
    # Facts that drive routing. Unknown is allowed: None means "not yet established".
    hospital_or_ed: bool | None = None
    harm_to_person: bool | None = None
    failure_to_act_risk: bool | None = None      # office judgement after review
    prn_primary_purpose_behaviour: bool | None = None
    prn_covered_by_authorisation: bool | None = None
    key_personnel_aware_at: datetime | None = None
    notes: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

Two choices in there are worth defending.

Tri-state booleans. None is not False. A worker writing up a wrong dose at 9pm doesn't know yet whether the person will end up in ED. If you default unknowns to False, your router will quietly decide "not reportable" for every fresh event. Treat None as "needs review" and surface it.

A separate awareness timestamp. The Commission's clocks run from when your key personnel become aware of the incident, not from when it happened. Those can be hours apart, or days apart if a worker sat on it. Store both. occurred_at belongs to the event; key_personnel_aware_at belongs to the organisation's response, and it should be set by whoever escalates, not inferred.

Routing as a pure function

The router takes an event and returns zero or more routes. No database calls, no side effects, so it can be tested exhaustively.

class Route(Enum):
    SERIOUS_INJURY = "serious_injury"
    NEGLECT = "neglect"
    UNAUTHORISED_RESTRICTIVE_PRACTICE = "urp_chemical_restraint"

@dataclass
class RoutingResult:
    routes: list[Route]
    needs_review: list[str]

def route(e: MedicationEvent) -> RoutingResult:
    routes, review = [], []

    if e.hospital_or_ed is None:
        review.append("Did the person need hospital or ED treatment?")
    elif e.hospital_or_ed:
        routes.append(Route.SERIOUS_INJURY)

    if e.kind in (EventKind.MISSED, EventKind.WRONG_TIME, EventKind.WRONG_DOSE):
        if e.failure_to_act_risk is None:
            review.append("Could the failure to act have caused significant harm?")
        elif e.failure_to_act_risk:
            routes.append(Route.NEGLECT)

    if e.kind is EventKind.PRN_GIVEN:
        if e.prn_primary_purpose_behaviour is None:
            review.append("Was the PRN given mainly to influence behaviour?")
        elif e.prn_primary_purpose_behaviour and not e.prn_covered_by_authorisation:
            routes.append(Route.UNAUTHORISED_RESTRICTIVE_PRACTICE)

    return RoutingResult(routes, review)

The neglect branch is the one you'll argue about with your clinical lead, and that's fine. Making failure_to_act_risk an explicit office judgement, recorded against a named reviewer, is better than burying a rule like "any missed anticonvulsant is neglect" in code. The code shouldn't pretend to make clinical calls. It should make sure someone does, and that the answer is written down.

The chemical restraint branch needs one more piece of context. Under the restrictive practices rules, chemical restraint is medication used for the primary purpose of influencing behaviour. Medication prescribed by a medical practitioner to treat a diagnosed mental disorder, physical illness or physical condition is excluded. That's why the PRN record needs a reason field with real options, not free text, and why prn_covered_by_authorisation should be looked up from the participant's authorisation records rather than ticked by the worker.

The clocks

Once you have routes, deadlines follow. The Commission's timeframes, read on 9 November 2026, with the 5-day report counted from awareness too:

Route First report 5-day report Final report
Serious injury 24-hour report Within 5 business days Within 60 business days, if the Commission asks for one
Neglect 24-hour report Within 5 business days Within 60 business days, if the Commission asks for one
Unauthorised restrictive practice, no harm None: the 5-day report is the only form Within 5 business days Within 60 business days, if the Commission asks for one
Unauthorised restrictive practice, person harmed 24-hour report Within 5 business days Within 60 business days, if the Commission asks for one

All of these count from when the provider became aware, not from when the event happened.

The 24-hour clock is wall-clock time. The others are business days, so you need a calendar. Keep public holidays in a table, not in code, and treat weekends and public holidays as non-business days.

from datetime import date, timedelta

def add_business_days(start: datetime, n: int, holidays: set[date]) -> datetime:
    d = start
    added = 0
    while added < n:
        d += timedelta(days=1)
        if d.weekday() < 5 and d.date() not in holidays:
            added += 1
    return d

def first_deadline(r: Route, e: MedicationEvent, holidays: set[date]) -> datetime | None:
    aware = e.key_personnel_aware_at
    if aware is None:
        return None  # escalate: nobody senior knows yet
    if r is Route.UNAUTHORISED_RESTRICTIVE_PRACTICE and not e.harm_to_person:
        return add_business_days(aware, 5, holidays)
    return aware + timedelta(hours=24)

def five_day_report_due(e: MedicationEvent, holidays: set[date]) -> datetime | None:
    # Applies to every route; for a URP with no harm it is the only report.
    if e.key_personnel_aware_at is None:
        return None
    return add_business_days(e.key_personnel_aware_at, 5, holidays)

Notice the URP branch checks harm_to_person, which is a different question from hospital_or_ed. A person can be harmed without going to hospital. If harm is None, the safe default is the shorter clock, and the code above gets that right only because not None is True. Make it explicit in your own version; implicit truthiness is exactly the kind of thing that breaks quietly in a refactor.

A few fixtures to pin it down:

def test_prn_for_behaviour_without_authorisation_routes_to_urp():
    e = make_event(kind=EventKind.PRN_GIVEN, prn_primary_purpose_behaviour=True,
                   prn_covered_by_authorisation=False, hospital_or_ed=False)
    assert route(e).routes == [Route.UNAUTHORISED_RESTRICTIVE_PRACTICE]

def test_wrong_dose_with_ed_visit_is_serious_injury_24h():
    e = make_event(kind=EventKind.WRONG_DOSE, hospital_or_ed=True,
                   failure_to_act_risk=False, key_personnel_aware_at=FRI_6PM)
    assert first_deadline(Route.SERIOUS_INJURY, e, HOLIDAYS) == SAT_6PM

def test_near_miss_has_no_route_but_stays_in_register():
    e = make_event(kind=EventKind.NEAR_MISS, hospital_or_ed=False)
    assert route(e).routes == []

That last test matters. A near miss with no route is still a row in the incident register. Never let "not reportable" mean "not recorded".

The competency gate: stopping the shift before the event

The cheapest medication incident is the one that never gets rostered. Two layers of training apply.

First, the core Practice Standard on management of medication expects medication to be accessed only by appropriately trained workers. That's a baseline for anyone who handles medicines.

Second, some medication tasks are high intensity supports in their own right. The High Intensity Daily Personal Activities module covers subcutaneous injections, enteral feeding (which includes medication through a tube) and complex bowel care (which can involve suppositories and enemas). Training for these has to be specific to the participant, and subcutaneous injections also need written or phone orders from the prescriber. Giving a tablet or applying a cream isn't a high intensity support under that module. Who may do it depends on state or territory rules and your own policy.

In data terms, that's a join between three tables: the participant's support needs, the qualifications those needs call for, and each worker's verified, unexpired qualifications. Participant-specific training is a qualification scoped to one participant.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Qualification:
    code: str                      # e.g. "MED_CORE", "SUBCUT_INJ"
    participant_id: str | None     # None = general; set = specific to one person
    expires: date | None

def missing_for_shift(worker_quals: list[Qualification], required: set[str],
                      participant_id: str, on: date) -> set[str]:
    have = {q.code for q in worker_quals
            if (q.expires is None or q.expires >= on)
            and (q.participant_id in (None, participant_id))}
    return required - have

Then decide what the scheduler does with a non-empty result. Blocking outright is tempting, but rosters have emergencies, and a hard block often leads to staff finding a workaround outside the system. A clear warning on save, recorded against the person who overrode it, is usually more honest. Whatever you choose, make the medication shift visibly different from an ordinary one so the coordinator can't miss it.

How it fits together in Rostery

We'll be specific about what our product does here, because routing logic is easy to over-claim.

In Rostery, the eMAR medication module records each dose with an outcome (given, refused, not available, held, or PRN not required), the carer's typed signature, a witness and running balance for S8 medicines, and an effectiveness review. Workers report incidents from the app with a type, priority and what happened, and the office manages each one in the incident register, where switches record whether it's NDIS reportable and whether it has been reported. Rostery doesn't lodge anything in the Commission's portal; that step stays with your key personnel.

On the roster side, SmartMatch links qualifications to participant support needs and ranks workers by how well their verified, unexpired qualifications cover them, and the scheduler warns when a worker is missing a qualification the participant's needs call for. The routing function in this post isn't a Rostery feature. It's a pattern you can apply in any system, including ours, by keeping the reportability decision with a named reviewer.

A short checklist for your own build

  • Keep medication events and incident routes as separate records.
  • Collect facts on the worker's form; make reportability an office decision.
  • Use tri-state answers and show unknowns as review tasks.
  • Store when key personnel became aware, separately from when it happened.
  • Count business days from a holiday table, and test the URP harm branch.
  • Record every event, including near misses, whether or not it's reportable.
  • Treat participant-specific training as a qualification scoped to one person.

If you want the floor-level version of this for team leaders, we wrote up what a shift supervisor checks before a medication round on our Blogger site.

Sources: NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission, Reportable incidents and Detailed guidance: Reportable incidents; NDIS Practice Standards, Core Module (Provision of supports environment: Management of medication) and High Intensity Daily Personal Activities module; NDIS Commission, High Intensity Support Skills Descriptors; NDIS (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018, section 6. Rostery feature pages read 9 November 2026.

Written by the Rostery team in Sydney. Rostery makes rostering, care and billing software for NDIS and aged care providers.

title: Three.js Exploded View: Explode a Real Multi-Part GLB (and What It Costs in Draw Calls)
description:
Originally published by Alicia Lu on 9 November 2026 at Digital Garden. Alicia is a 3D technical artist, TA and independent developer. Codex assisted with implementation, measurement and drafting.

A Three.js exploded view moves a GLB assembly apart by changing its part transforms. For this test, Codex built and exported a potted flower in Houdini 22.0.429 and ran it on Alicia’s RTX 5070 Ti desktop. The fixture has five assemblies: pot, soil, stalk, leaves and bloom.

The short answer. Give each movable part a name and a pivot, then save its rest position. The merged, 10-, 50- and 200-part GLBs all contain 30,848 triangles. They took 1, 10, 50 and 200 model draws on both backends. The raw renderer counts were 2, 11, 51 and 201 because an empty scene recorded one draw. From merged to 200 parts, WebGPU load to first GPU completion went from 89.7 to 116.2 ms. Point picking went in the other direction because the split created tighter bounds.

Export the parts and pivots from Houdini

The native scene uses a Geometry Stash SOP inside each OBJ mesh. Each part has a pivot at its local bounds center and is parented under a named assembly null. The merged control stores the same colored geometry under one mesh at the origin. The 10- and 50-part layouts group the same 200 source components in fewer meshes. The glTF 2.0 ROP exports the OBJ hierarchy, with one mesh primitive per part. A node extras dictionary stores the assembly name and component count. Three.js read both back from userData. SideFX glTF 2.0 ROP

All four native exports passed the glTF validator with zero errors and warnings. A separate audit matched every oriented triangle against the merged control and compared its world-space corners, normals and vertex colors. The largest component difference was 2.46 × 10⁻⁷. The saved HIP reopened with all four layouts and their geometry intact.

Flat traverse and a two-stage hierarchy

Flat explode moves each part away from the model center. The hierarchy path first moves the five parents apart. At slider value 0.5, the children still have their rest positions inside those groups. The second half moves each child away from its own group center. The two modes use different offsets to illustrate how they open. The flat view spreads parts along the plant’s overall shape, while the hierarchy view opens the five assemblies in stages.

Both methods compute positions from stored rest values. The test model sits under a rotated, nonuniformly scaled parent. To apply a displacement in world units, convert two points to the parent’s local space and subtract them. The resulting vector length accounts for parent scale. Three.js Object3D

function localOffset(node, point, worldOffset) {
  const start = node.parent.worldToLocal(point.clone());
  return node.parent.worldToLocal(point.clone().add(worldOffset)).sub(start);
}

// Hierarchy path after the local offsets have been prepared.
const groupT = Math.min(1, t * 2);
const partT = Math.max(0, t * 2 - 1);
for (const group of groups) {
  group.node.position.copy(group.rest).addScaledVector(group.delta, groupT);
}
for (const part of parts) {
  part.node.position.copy(part.rest).addScaledVector(part.child, partT);
}

Across 24 parted contexts, 960 out-and-back cycles returned to rest with zero measured drift. The largest world-position error in the displacement checks was 1.33 × 10⁻¹⁵ scene units. The two GIFs share a wider camera so the plant stays in frame at full separation. The timing runs use their own fixed camera.

Draw calls and first completion

Chrome and Three.js 0.186.1 ran at 1280 × 720, device pixel ratio 1. The WebGL2 path uses the WebGPU renderer’s WebGL backend on ANGLE/D3D11. Both selected NVIDIA hardware. Four fresh contexts per layout and backend loaded each GLB from localhost with cache disabled. Contexts shared a Chrome process and did not clear driver or OS caches.

These are medians in milliseconds. Asset-to-completion starts after renderer initialization and includes loading, scene setup, awaited compile and the first render with its work wait. WebGPU used the queue completion promise and WebGL2 used gl.finish(). This measures submitted work completion before display presentation.

Layout Backend Raw draws GLB MiB Fetch ms Parse ms Compile ms First render + wait ms Asset to completion ms
Merged WebGPU 2 0.965 5.6 2.4 60.9 20.7 89.7
10 parts WebGPU 11 0.977 5.2 3.4 61.5 20.7 91.5
50 parts WebGPU 51 1.027 5.2 4.9 64.6 21.0 96.4
200 parts WebGPU 201 1.215 5.9 9.8 71.2 30.0 116.2
Merged WebGL2 2 0.965 6.2 2.4 24.2 7.6 43.4
10 parts WebGL2 11 0.977 6.0 3.2 27.0 8.5 47.3
50 parts WebGL2 51 1.027 6.3 5.1 36.8 10.0 58.0
200 parts WebGL2 201 1.215 6.4 9.2 29.7 13.4 59.1

The 200-part asset cost about 26.6 ms more than the merged WebGPU median. The WebGL2 50-part runs ranged from 46.4 to 78.1 ms, which is wider than the difference between the 50- and 200-part medians. The file size, number of nodes and buffer layout all change with the split. The separate columns are medians from four runs and do not necessarily add up.

The harness reads renderer.info.render.drawCalls. Early pilots caught the empty-scene draw and a second issue: back-to-back render calls could accumulate statistics. The formal harness resets counters before each render and measures the empty scene after first completion. Three.js Info

200-part mode Raw draws WebGPU CPU submit ms WebGL2 CPU submit ms WebGPU / WebGL2 p95 rAF ms
Assembled 201 0.8 0.6 16.8 / 16.7
Flat 201 1.1 0.9 16.8 / 16.8
Hierarchy 201 1.0 0.9 16.8 / 16.8

CPU submit is elapsed time around the render call and counter reset. It excludes the per-frame transform update and GPU wait. Warm rAF intervals stayed near the refresh cadence. The assembly uses one opaque vertex-color material, no shadows and disabled frustum culling, so moving parts does not change the draw count.

Picking got cheaper as the mesh count rose

The harness times setFromCamera and intersectObjects on the same 49 rays. Each context ran 12 timed sweeps after three warm-up sweeps. Every sweep had 12 hits. The per-ray times are CPU measurements grouped by the renderer in use in that context. Picking uses an explicit mesh list and reuses its result array. Three.js Raycaster

Layout WebGPU µs/ray WebGL2 µs/ray Meshes reaching triangle loop per sweep Triangle loop entries per sweep
Merged 1,373.5 676.5 41 1,264,768
10 parts 234.7 117.3 59 208,192
50 parts 106.1 55.1 105 78,104
200 parts 65.3 30.6 130 37,952

An untimed CPU control counted entries after the built-in bounding tests in the same Three.js version. From 10 to 200 meshes, more candidates passed the bounds checks but many fewer triangles reached the inner loop. All 49 hit-or-miss outcomes matched. The largest difference in the nearest hit distance was below 0.000002 scene units. The result depends on the asset’s bounds and the ray distribution. Three.js r186 mesh raycasting source

Click to fade or hide

The live viewer picks on pointer release and ignores drags longer than five pixels. Fade assigns unselected meshes a shared translucent material at opacity 0.17. The selected mesh retains the opaque material. Hide makes the other meshes invisible and filters them out of the next pick. The camera stays fixed for the comparison.

Layout Fade / hide raw draws WebGPU fade / hide CPU submit ms WebGL2 fade / hide CPU submit ms Model triangles when hidden
10 parts 11 / 2 0.2 / 0.2 0.2 / 0.2 2,176
50 parts 51 / 2 0.4 / 0.2 0.3 / 0.1 2,176
200 parts 201 / 2 0.6 / 0.2 0.6 / 0.2 1,152

Fade kept the whole shape visible. Hide left one model draw plus the empty-scene draw. The hidden triangle count depends on the chosen part, whose grouping changes with the layout. The table shows warmed CPU submit medians. Transition completion samples are in the raw data. Some WebGL2 samples hit the timer floor, so they cannot support a more precise latency claim.

A separate browser interaction test moved the slider, changed the rendered canvas, picked a part, toggled hide and fade, and reset. A 300 ms idle window after each timed sequence logged zero further render calls in all 32 contexts. This counts submitted frames. GPU utilization and power were outside the test.

Reproduce the experiment

The bundle includes four native GLBs, the Houdini scene and generator, browser viewer, raw trials, chart sources, GIFs and the picking control. The formal set contains 32 contexts, 7,680 rAF intervals and 18,816 timed ray evaluations, including 14,112 on the three parted layouts. Pilot failures are separate from the formal data. Download the reproduction bundle or inspect the summary CSV.

The results cover one desktop, one browser version, one camera for timing and an untextured authored model. Mobile devices, production asset loading and batched alternatives are outside the measured scope. Related studies cover GLB loading and first frame and the forest draw budget with different fixtures.

By Alicia, a 3D technical artist, TA and independent developer. Codex assisted with implementation, measurement and drafting.

Questions

Can one merged GLB mesh explode?

A merged mesh has one object transform. Independent movement requires separate logical parts, such as separately transformed meshes or an explicit per-part representation. This study measured separate native GLB meshes.

Does every named part always add one draw?

Each mesh added one model draw in this one-primitive, one-material test. Extra materials, passes and batching change the count. The raw counter also recorded one draw in an empty scene.

Should click-to-isolate fade or hide other parts?

Fade keeps the surrounding assembly visible and retained all model draws here. Hide left one model draw for the selected mesh. Choose based on whether the rest of the assembly helps the reader.
