Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

  • Fixed an issue that affected connection stability and prevented calls from being accurately recorded as end-user hangups when callers hung up while waiting in a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing the queue service level field.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were disconnected when an agent finished their wrap-up following a queue transfer to a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls escalated from a virtual agent to a human agent reported inaccurate call-level queue and wait durations in reporting and data exports.

  • Fixed an issue where unrecorded voicemails incorrectly created Salesforce cases even when the Create CRM records for abandoned calls setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where activating a new language in the CCaaS portal caused the Languages & Messages page to crash or display an infinite loading spinner.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata files were duplicated across different day folders in external storage when re-uploads occurred after midnight.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became permanently stuck in a queued status without reaching a terminal state.

  • Fixed an issue where active agents were incorrectly signed out due to inactivity because the system didn't recognize activity outside the embedded call panel.

  • Fixed an issue where a permanent loading spinner appeared in the agent desktop top bar for instances with the email channel disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound keypad (DTMF) entries didn't reach the virtual agent during periods of stream instability or reconnection.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing required parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls involving a virtual agent didn't record an end time and duration when deflected to an overcapacity queue.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings weren't fetched or saved when CRM ticket creation failed.

  • Fixed an issue where after-hours phone deflections didn't appear in the Deflections dashboard if the outbound dial timed out or failed.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled phone number obfuscation caused degraded performance for live calls.

  • Fixed an issue where CRM ticket assignees weren't consistently updated following an agent's pickup of a chat.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became stuck in a queued state after a caller selected a callback during a cold transfer to a specific agent.

  • Fixed an issue where Smart Disposition suggestions weren't pre-selected on the wrap-up screen, causing the disposition field to remain empty after a call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were incorrectly routed to agents even when the minimum available agent floor wasn't met.

  • Fixed an issue where cold transfers to a direct agent extension didn't trigger overcapacity deflection, leaving callers on hold until they disconnected.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent replies were cut off or silenced when using bidirectional streaming with barge-in disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where JSON chat transcripts in external storage contained unredacted message text even when the setting to store unredacted transcripts was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where the Keep Waiting label in the overcapacity deflection screen displayed an inconsistent font style compared to other menu options.

title: Rethinking Data Selection as Distribution Matching on Semantic Manifolds
description:
arXiv:2611.08495v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.

title: AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs
description:
arXiv:2611.09094v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for creative tasks such as writing, design, and idea generation. For these uses, it matters whether a model's ideas depart from familiar examples or stay close to them. Novelty is one standard measure of creativity, and current creativity evaluations ask human experts or LLM judges to rate how novel an output is. However, these ratings have no fixed reference for what counts as novel (or, in other terms, departure from the familiar). Measuring this departure requires a task with known familiar defaults. The structured imagination task from cognitive psychology is such a task. In this creativity test, people imagine a creature from another planet. The departure from features of Earth animals, such as bilateral symmetry and legs as mode of locomotion, is used as measure of creativity. We introduce AlienBench, a benchmark that adapts the structured imagination task to language models. Models describe alien creatures, and a panel of three LLM judges extracts ten biological features from the description and labels them as either Earth-typical or a departure. The sum of feature departures is the score of a description, from 0 to 10. Each model describes alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing of the task and the planetary environment. Each model generates 30 descriptions per condition (180 in total), and its overall score is the mean across these descriptions. We evaluate 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight models. Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B). Interestingly, open-weight models score higher than proprietary models in this task (5.40 vs. 4.58). Under the baseline prompt, the models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. We release all prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores.

title: Compiling bounded server behavior into threshold networks with Netserve
description:
Netserve is an experiment in representing supported server behavior as neural-network weights. It is not an LLM answering HTTP requests, and the compiled protocol graphs do not learn online. A compiler turns bounded operations into exact threshold networks that a native Goose evaluator executes.

Try the no-signup playground | Repository

Where the network ends and the host begins

The graphs implement route recognition, static response generation and supported handlers. The host owns sockets, TLS, authentication, storage, deadlines and queue limits. Keeping that boundary explicit avoids treating cryptography or authorization as approximate model predictions.

A threshold neuron sums weighted inputs and a bias, then emits a bit according to whether the sum reaches zero. Boolean operations can be represented with these neurons and composed into exact circuits. Netserve supplies input bytes and state bits to a graph; its outputs describe response bytes and next-state bits. The supported language is restricted: this is not an arbitrary JavaScript-to-network compiler.

Three inspectable demos

A counter computes its next eight-bit state and JSON response, wrapping from 255 to zero. An echo graph preserves up to 64 UTF-8 bytes. A codec packs up to 32 characters from a 64-symbol alphabet into six bits per character, plus a length byte. Both encoding and decoding execute as networks. The sample shown in the demo goes from 30 to 24 bytes and restores exactly. Short inputs can grow, unsupported symbols are rejected, and this is not a learned universal compressor.

The browser uses a JavaScript threshold evaluator. The downloadable server uses native Goose. A parity test compares the browser evaluator with Goose across 359 cases, including counter wraparound. Platform CI builds and tests Windows x64, Linux x64, macOS ARM64 and macOS x64. The source includes the tests so the claims can be inspected and rerun.

Local protocol experiments

The local STUN/TURN experiment uses neural request recognition, protocol decisions and encoding, with host-enforced authentication and bounds. Its TURN peer policy permits only other live local relay allocations. A WebRTC test checks that both selected candidates are relay candidates and exchanges a message. This bounded local subset is not a production coturn replacement, a public relay, or an anonymity service.

What 90.32% measures

The project's 90.32% neural coverage is an equally weighted feature inventory, 28 neural units out of 31. It includes the default app routes and supported protocol/demo behaviors; secure host services, browser UI, build tools and historical experiments are excluded. Conventional HTTP framing, TURN attribute/peer parsing and response/inbound-channel assembly are counted as host behavior. This is not an independent certification or a measure of source code, runtime instructions, CPU work or memory. The complete inventory and measurement script are linked on the playground.

The interesting question is where exact compiled networks are useful enough to justify their overhead. Netserve does not establish a performance advantage over ordinary web servers. It provides a working, bounded experiment whose representation, host boundary and behavior can be examined.

Try the browser playground without signing in, or download a tested native package. Node.js 24+ is required for the server; setup instructions and local-security guidance are in BUILDING.md.

Downloads | Build instructions | Coverage inventory

title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
description:
For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.

Agentic infrastructure

Guillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself.

Agentic infrastructure has three parts:

  • Vercel is where you build and deploy your own apps and agents. We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale.

  • Vercel is where coding agents deploy that software. When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform.

  • Vercel itself is automated by agents. Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts.

Agentic Infrastructure is for developers

In his opening keynote, Guillermo pointed to claims that AI would replace developers, then used Vercel's own data to prove them wrong. In the last 12 months:

  • The number of developers on Vercel has grown 3x

  • The number of new projects developers ship has doubled

  • The number of their agent-triggered deployments has increased 28x

"We built Vercel for developers," he said, "because they are the difference between a world full of slop and a world full of software worth using."

Backends on Vercel

In the next keynote, Malte Ubl (CTO, Vercel) showed how frontends, APIs, backend services, containers, MCP servers, and background workers can all run on Vercel, with support for custom runtimes and system dependencies.

He then announced that Python is now generally available on Vercel. Run FastAPI, Flask, or Django with standard CPython, PyPI dependencies, uv, and pyproject.toml. With Vercel Services, your frontend and backend deploy together, with previews of the full app.

Malte also introduced Vercel Daemons, now in public beta, for continuously running background workers. Deploy your code or container image, set the number of instances, and Vercel keeps them running and replaces them if they fail. Bring Celery, Dramatiq, Temporal workers, or your existing worker processes.

Vercel is for shipping agents

Tomo Occhino (CPO, Vercel) walked through the Agent Stack and its latest updates. The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production.

  • Vercel Drives, now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace.

  • eve, our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard.

  • Vercel Connect is generally available, with more than 1,000 connectors. And MCP Events, now in public beta, lets agents respond to events from MCP servers. Connect handles subscriptions, renewals, and secure delivery.

  • AI Gateway now lets you set budgets for API keys, projects, individuals, and teams. You can also choose US-only inference to keep model processing in the United States, or enable Zero Data Retention so providers don’t retain your prompts or responses. He also introduced Vercel Token Pass, now in early access for Pro teams. Get $80 in GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 token credit for $30/month, with more models coming soon.

Vercel for enterprise

Jeanne Grosser (COO, Vercel) focused on what happens when everyone in a company can build. Engineers, marketers, analysts, and sellers need a common place to deploy, with controls over who can ship, who can access an app, which systems agents can use, and how much they can spend. Company building is now agent building.

Vercel for Enterprise brings those controls together, with two additions announced:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS is now generally available. Your application functions run in your own AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization for Vercel Connect launched in public beta. With supported services and your identity provider configured, agents can act on employees’ behalf without asking each person to authorize every connection separately.

Watch the full day of programming

Ship week in San Francisco

The rest of Ship SF brought more than 2,700 developers, founders, and technical leaders to the Palace of Fine Arts for talks, workshops, startup studio sessions, and agent labs.

Ship day sessions

  • Assaf Elovic from Ora showed how his team tests whether websites work for agents by sending real agents to sign up, integrate, and pay, then tracing every step. Ora built that fleet on eve and used Is-Agentic to score a live site.

  • Katelyn Lesse from Anthropic covered the work that starts after an agent is running: keeping it fast and improving its performance across thousands of production sessions with Claude Managed Agents on Vercel.

  • Prashant Ratanchandani from Meta Superintelligence Labs joined Tomo to discuss building products including Muse on Vercel.

  • Matt Lewis from Vercel and Mala Neti from Slack explained how we built v, our internal agent, around Vercel’s own data and working practices. Connect and Passport secure its access, and Slack gives employees a place to use it where their work already happens.

  • Max Peters from Adapta broke down the router behind Brazil’s largest generative AI platform. Built on AI Gateway, it serves 168 models through one integration, selects a model in under 200 milliseconds, and handles more than three million requests a day with automatic failover and per-user budgets.

  • Sarah Sachs from Notion and Malte Ubl discussed how AI is changing the software teams build and the context agents need to do useful work.

  • Olawale Oladehin from AWS walked through production patterns for agents on AWS and Vercel, from self-correcting agents to multi-agent orchestration, and how BYOC lets teams run application functions within their own AWS environment.

  • Philip Miseldine and Sophia Levens from SAP showed how SAP is using v0, eve, and json-render to build generative interfaces, with a focus on consistent design and government requirements.

  • Aaron Brown and Arty Vohmincevs from Mercor explained how hundreds of employees build internal tools without losing control of access or spending. Apps inherit a managed identity layer, while AI Gateway gives the team visibility into model usage and budgets.

  • Yury Izrailevsky from ClickHouse traced the company’s path from an open-source analytics database to a platform spanning observability, AI engineering, and managed Postgres. His focus was how open source earns developer trust and helps infrastructure expand into new workloads.

Panel: Fast AI

Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev, and Andrew Feldman, founder and CEO of Cerebras, joined Vercel for a discussion on model reliability, latency, and cost. The panel brought together the model and hardware sides of fast inference, from specialized models to wafer-scale chips.

Closing fireside with Tobi Lütke

Guillermo sat down with Tobi Lütke, CEO of Shopify, for "The Third Customer," a conversation about building for a world where agents research, compare, and buy products on people’s behalf.

Guillermo Rauch: What excites you about agentic commerce?

Tobi Lütke: It’s early, but the opportunity goes beyond handling purchases people already make. Think about project-based commerce: planning Halloween decorations for your house, or a 3D-printing project with your kids, then ordering everything to arrive before the weekend. Agents can help people follow through on things they otherwise wouldn’t have had time to do.

Guillermo Rauch: Where does that leave traditional storefronts?

Tobi Lütke: There’s still room for exceptional shopping experiences. A distinctive, thoughtful storefront can grow, just as a well-executed boutique can. The businesses that will struggle are the ones offering an undifferentiated experience. Quality and originality still matter.

Guillermo Rauch: How is AI changing engineering at Shopify?

Tobi Lütke: We now think of ourselves as verification engineers, building harnesses and acceptance tests that make changes verifiable. We’re rewriting our storefront renderer from Ruby to Rust, where we can compare the output byte for byte before switching over. We also celebrate simplification and code deletion. At a company hackathon, our internal Slack agent, River, topped the code-deletion leaderboard by a wide margin.

Guillermo Rauch: What should developers in this room go build?

Tobi Lütke: Explore the catalog APIs. They give you access to products from Shopify merchants, so you can build new commerce experiences without first recruiting both sides of a marketplace. Product discovery, recommendations, and curation are real business opportunities. People will pay for tools that help them find what they need.

Ship week San Francisco

Fast Forward hackathon

The day before Ship, Vercel and Meta hosted Fast Forward, with support from Shopify and Neon Postgres. Builders worked across three tracks: agents that keep working after you step away, multimodal apps, and immersive VR experiences.

Founder dinners, executive conversations, and Partner Day

Founders, partners, and enterprise leaders gathered throughout the week for dinners, Partner Day, and conversations on building with AI. The executive program focused on what happens when anyone with an idea can build, and how do you govern what ships.

Ship 2026 in London

Ship day keynotes

  • Tomo introduced the Agent Stack, bringing model access, durable execution, sandboxed compute, and messaging together for production agents.

  • Hedi launched Vercel Connect in public preview, giving agents scoped access to external tools and data without storing long-lived provider credentials in environment variables.

  • Shar demoed eve, our open-source agent framework. Each agent lives in a directory, with instructions in Markdown and tools in TypeScript. Durable execution, approvals, subagents, and evals are already wired in.

  • Jeanne introduced Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, including Vercel Passport in public beta for protecting internal apps with your identity provider, and Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS in private beta.

Ship week London

Our first Ship outside the U.S. ran five days of events leading into the keynote, and an ice cream truck spent the week working its way across the city.

Built in London hackathon

Two hundred builders shipped agents on Codex and Vercel in a hackathon with OpenAI. Three projects stood out. Stella hunts down unclaimed grants for London SMBs, Oscar is a co-pilot that sharpens your prompts before you send them to a model, and Phone Jail blocks distractions and roasts you when you reach for your phone anyway.

Media, Founder, VC, and CTO dinners

Reporters traded story ideas over a media dinner. Twelve founders talked through the future of AI in EMEA at a VC dinner. And a dozen CTOs from teams including Marks & Spencer and Currys went off the record on what it takes to build and scale agents in the enterprise.

Day Zero builder night

Day Zero, the day before the keynote, turned into a 400-person builder night. Enterprise teams Mentimeter, Okta, and MongoDB joined Vercel in a packed room alongside partners DeepMind, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

AI Social Club

A 160-deep waitlist formed for Malte's talk A New Stack for a New Era of Software, followed by Guillermo and Deliveroo's Will Shu's chat on building the agentic enterprise.

Ship day sessions

  • André Balleyguier from Anthropic showed Claude Managed Agents on Vercel, where Anthropic hosts the agent loop while every command the agent runs executes inside a Vercel Sandbox you own, keeping its filesystem, processes, and network egress in your environment.

  • Tomas Jansson from Currys/Elkjøp showed how his team evolved a Nordic retailer's ecommerce stack from storefronts toward shopping agents in three phases, anchored by a Next.js migration that cut time to first byte by 40%. The end state is one where customer intent replaces navigation.

  • Matan Kushner from Vercel broke down how Vertex, Vercel's support agent, now automates 91% of support tickets and saves 5,000 engineer-hours a month without degrading as its context grows.

  • Jas Sagoo and Sam Bellen from Auth0 made the case that getting an agent into production depends more on identity than on model quality. They demoed four standards-based identity patterns on the Vercel AI SDK, Token Vault, CIBA approvals, agents as first-class principals, and on-behalf-of delegation, so every action is scoped and traces back to a human decision instead of a shared API key.

  • Abhi Sivasailam from Vercel went deep into d0, Vercel's internal data agent built on eve, which runs analyses in a sandbox and now gets 45% of its questions from other agents, rather than people.

  • Romain Huet from OpenAI showed developers how to ship faster by delegating whole tasks to Codex Cloud Agents on Vercel, and made the case that as agents become users of your product, you design for agent experience with scoped API keys, markdown docs, and plugins.

  • Michał Pierzchała from Callstack demoed a QA agent that runs mobile apps on real devices, explores user flows on its own, and posts screenshots, recordings, and logs to pull requests on every PR.

  • Alex Holt from ElevenLabs paired the ElevenLabs Speech Engine with the AI SDK to build a voice agent that can reply in under a second, take interruptions mid-sentence, and switch language mid-conversation.

  • Malavika Balachandran Tadeusz from Vercel showed the mechanics of how software can ship itself, extending the agent loop past development into testing, observability, and experimentation with primitives like Vercel Flags and Skills.

Panel: Agents in production

Jeanne Grosser, COO of Vercel, moderated a panel on taking agentic workloads from prototype to production with some of the EU's top CTOs and AI leaders from frontier labs. A few highlights:

Arthur Viegers (Cursor): Autonomy should track risk, and the better an agent can assess the risk of a change, the more you can let it run on its own. Shopify and Amplitude already auto-review and merge 60-70% of low-risk PRs with no developer time, while a two-line change to authentication still goes to a human.

André Balleyguier (Anthropic): To decide what an agent can do on its own, judge each action by how reversible it is and how large its blast radius is, then contain it accordingly, for example inside a self-hosted sandbox. As you grant more autonomy, observability and evals become the things that keep it safe.

Ryan den Rooijen (Currys): The predicted death of stores never arrived, and Currys leads its markets by betting on humans. The open question for agentic commerce is which shopping journeys customers want an agent to handle and which they still want a person for.

Nicolas Le Pallec (AKQA): AI-native customer experience replaces navigation with intent. Reaching it takes three layers: a way to capture true customer intent, a brand brain that stores brand and product data for AI systems to retrieve, and generative UI that composes pages on the fly instead of serving static ones.

Fireside chat with Harry Stebbings

The day ended with a fireside chat between Guillermo and Harry Stebbings from 20VC. Below are excerpts from the lightning round at the end of the discussion.

Guillermo Rauch: What are the attributes of a founder you want to back?

Harry Stebbings: The profile has changed completely. It used to be a sales-led CEO who could fundraise and grow customers, where personality and sales carried the company. Now I want an engineering- and product-led founder.

Guillermo Rauch: Can you teach someone to become a voice for their industry?

Harry Stebbings: You can, but it's hard. You have to do it for six months straight. It's a muscle you build, and you have to commit to it every day and every hour.

Guillermo Rauch: When anyone can produce content and software, how do you stand out?

Harry Stebbings: You come up with a new format, a new intro, a new way to tell the story and shape the work. The content itself has shifted too. We used to do shows about leadership and hiring, and nobody cares about that anymore. What lands now is a founder and AI. Those are the two things.

Ship 2026 in Berlin

The Berlin event opened at the Old Mint, “Alte Münze”, where coins were once hammered by hand, before machine automation took over. It is also where the JavaScript logo was born, and where Guillermo Rauch (CEO) met Malte Ubl (CTO) for the first time at JSConf EU.

Software is moving the same way, from hand to machine, and Vercel is paving the way for building in the agentic era. Over 500 people gathered from across Germany to do just that at Ship 2026 in Berlin.

Ship day sessions

  • Suyog Rao from Vercel announced AI SDK 7. The AI SDK is now downloaded over 16 million times a week. Version 7 turns it into a toolkit for building and running agents that reason, call tools, run across many turns, and work across files and sandboxes, all behind one provider-agnostic interface with no lock-in.

  • Philip Miseldine from SAP showed how the company rebuilt its design system to be composable, so people and agents assemble interfaces from the same parts, with v0 running across its build, deliver, and decide stages.

  • Building with AI SDK 7 brought three speakers on stage. Lars Grammel, the primary engineer behind the update, went deep on the release, with the new harness layer and generation beyond text as the headline additions. Carsten Høyer from AKQA demoed the Starbucks ChatGPT app as a "generative store" that composes branded results from Starbucks' own products and visual identity, flipping the funnel so customers pull the brand into their conversation instead of visiting its site. Stephen Batifol from Black Forest Labs showed where the Flux image models fit in an agentic stack: sub-second generation and editing today, heading toward real-time generation and world models.

  • Arthur Viegers from Cursor showed how coding agents move from autocomplete to working across an entire codebase on their own.

Panel: CTOs on AI and growth

Chris Williams (Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, Vercel) moderated a CTO panel on building and scaling as the cost of creation trends toward zero. A few highlights:

Sven Rosemann (Flaconi): AI won't fix a broken business model, so the work is still operational excellence. He compares ecommerce to a decathlon, you win by being top-tier across every discipline at once. What's changing is discovery, which is moving into chat, so Flaconi is investing in the data foundation that makes its catalog retrievable by agents, betting that buying and checkout eventually happen there too.

Tjaž Silovsek (Astra AI): venture funding is no longer a prerequisite. For many ideas, you ship, find distribution, and iterate instead. Astra reached 10 million users and $25M ARR fully bootstrapped, with a small team kept fast by a stable foundation and agents given a lot of autonomy while kept as safe as possible.

DACH Partner Award

Vercel presented its first-ever DACH Partner Award to Valtech, for the exceptional impact and delivery, strategic thinking and team enablement it brought to clients. The presentation also thanked the event's sponsors: Auth0, Storyblok, Cursor, SAP, Accenture Song, Blazity, and JVM.

Ship 2026 in New York

Ship week New York

Ship NYC was the most in-demand of any stop yet with over 3,000 people registered. Founders, partners, leaders, and builders gathered for five days of hackathons, executive receptions, workshops, and more, with Ship day at the center.

Built in NYC

The week opened with Built in NYC, a hackathon co-hosted by Vercel and Anthropic alongside Sentry, Auth0, Resend, and Supabase. More than one hundred people joined us for an afternoon of building and demoing agents on Vercel.

VC, CTO, and VIP dinners

Jeanne DeWitt Grosser and Nick Bogaty gathered the leaders shaping AI-native development at a VIP reception. Founders traded notes on the future of agents over a VC dinner. At Per Se, Guillermo, Jeanne, Tom, and Malte took CTOs and CIOs for a closed-door conversation on where traditional architectures start to break in the agent era.

AI Social Club

AI executives and senior leaders assembled at Moss for a fireside chat led by Tom Occhino with William Anderson (CTO, Bloomberg Media), Jeremy Bunting (VP Engineering, Serhant), and Ali Patterson (Staff Design Program Manager, DoorDash). They discussed what's working, what's not, and where agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Ryan Coyne from SERHANT. walked through S.MPLE, a real estate agent built on Vercel that drove a 144% increase in commission income in its first full year.

  • Brandon Bloom from Brex gave its expense-audit agent a bash-only shell so it manages its own context instead of drowning in tool responses, cutting tool calls and token usage by 75%.

  • Ari Schapiro and Chris Sev from Auth0 demoed how to give an agent scoped, revocable power instead of a master key, with standards-based identity patterns like Token Vault and out-of-band human approval, live on the Vercel AI SDK.

  • Jenny Wang from Alta and Maxwell Osborne from PUBLIC SCHOOL NYC showed how Alta's AI styling app runs on Vercel, generating an avatar a second and 250M+ outfits so far. Together they built a custom version for PUBLIC SCHOOL's New York Fashion Week relaunch.

  • Charlton Roberts from FLORA showed three creative-production workflows running on Vercel Sandboxes. They collapsed 18 bespoke tools into two by letting the agent run and write its own code against the AI SDK.

  • Prasad Wangikar from Stripe broke down how to give agents spending power and capture agent-driven revenue using emerging protocols like MCP, UCP, and x402 for the machine-to-machine economy.

  • Shaown Nandi from AWS discussed how Vercel and AWS work together, with native AWS databases and OpenSearch available in the Marketplace and models through the AI Gateway, proven out by The Weather Company's 350M+ users.

Panel: Internal apps and agents in production

Jeanne moderated a panel on building and deploying internal agents with technical leaders on who should build, what governance looks like, and how teams can move from experiment to production. A few highlights:

Andy Martin (MJH Life Sciences): The way to win the shadow-IT battle is to constrain the stack and stay permissive inside it. His AI Accelerator trains non-engineers, marketers, and early-career staff to build internal apps on a deliberately tight stack of Claude Code, Vercel, and GitHub, with ephemeral preview deployments as the guardrail. As he put it, "If it becomes the Department of No, you will have people working around you."

Greg Chan (SERHANT): The cleanest way to structure agents is to mirror a human software team. Product-manager agents write requirements in Linear, engineering agents generate specs, and build-and-QA agents take it from there, so engineers become leads running multiple streams. To keep output safe, SERHANT runs evals for hallucination and compliance, including a custom model for Fair Housing Act rules.

Victor Oliveros (ZoomInfo): Embedding v0 inside your own product lets your customers build their own workflows. At ZoomInfo, 40,000+ of them do, turning the voice of the customer into a pull request. Agents analyze recorded calls and open PRs, so the product team decides what ships instead of synthesizing feedback. They pair Vercel's deployment guardrails with ZoomInfo's context-graph permissions, so each agent only touches data its user can see.

Fireside chat: Building agentic storefronts

Tom sat down with Vanessa Lee (VP of Product, Shopify) to discuss where commerce and software go next. Below are highlights:

Tom Occhino: Vercel and Shopify have shipped something new together. What is it?

Vanessa Lee: We boiled Hydrogen down to the parts of commerce that are genuinely hard (analytics, optimistic cart UI, variants) and made them work with any framework. So if you're on Next.js on Vercel, Shopify's commerce primitives now drop in, with an integration in the Vercel Marketplace. Read more here.

Tom Occhino: You also opened the Catalog API. What does it unlock?

Vanessa Lee: There's never been a good open product-search API. We have billions of products and millions of merchants, so we built one, the only widespread shopping API, made for commerce. It lets anyone embed shopping anywhere. Someone in my Toronto running group used v0 to build a site with a leaderboard and the weather, and the Catalog API surfaced products from nearby stores. Commerce stops being a destination and becomes part of what you build.

Tom Occhino: Shopify and Vercel both obsess over reducing friction. Why does that matter so much?

Vanessa Lee: Early on, Tobi's insight was that tools shape the market. The TAM was never limited by demand, it was limited by how hard the tools were to use. Make building easier and more people build. There's resourcefulness in the general population that's just untapped, and lowering the friction is what releases it.

Closing keynote with Ivan Zhao

We closed out Ship in New York with a conversation between Guillermo Rauch and Ivan Zhao (CEO, Notion). A few highlights:

Guillermo Rauch: You've started telling designers to design for the API first and the UI last. Why?

Ivan Zhao: Because your next customer isn't only a human, it's a human and an agent, and agents are blind. They don't see your interface, they read your semantics and your API. The most enduring software has always been a data structure anyway, the spreadsheet, or our block, a data structure that happens to have a UI. So design the structure and the meaning first, the interface last. A great tool for developers turns out to be a great tool for agents.

Guillermo Rauch: Vercel and Notion are both aggressively model-agnostic, Switzerland in the model wars. Why?

Ivan Zhao: The models leapfrog each other every few weeks, so picking a side is a losing game. We route automatically by the intelligence a task needs, frontier models for coding, smaller and faster ones for support and summarization. What excites me most is that as more use cases stop needing frontier intelligence, you can shape smaller models to your product and win back speed and cost. And speed creates discontinuities, a model five times faster can change the kind of interface you'd even design.

Guillermo Rauch: When a billion knowledge workers are agents, how does that reshape us?

Ivan Zhao: We can't fully see it, and that's the point. First-order effects are easy, the iPhone was an iPod plus a phone plus a browser. The second-order effects are the ones that surprise you, like what social media did to teenagers. We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us. With software that can think, the second-order effects are the ones we won't predict.

Guillermo Rauch: Taste or velocity, keep one.

Ivan Zhao: Taste. It's the distillation of wisdom from a lot of shots on goal.

Ship 2026 in Sydney

The Sydney event opened at Machine Hall, a 1930s electrical substation that ran the city's trams and wharves for half a century. Over 200 people gathered there to build for the agentic era at Ship Sydney.

Ship week Sydney

The week kicked off with the AI SYD meetup, where developers, AI engineers, and the Sydney technical community joined for an evening of lightning talks and networking. At the AI Social Club, senior leaders gathered at Shell House for a talk from Malte Ubl and a fireside with Suyog Rao and David Hyman (Founder, monō ai) on how agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Belen Garcia Fava and Vivek Katial from Heidi Health showed how their team ships fast in a regulated space with agents and Vercel, and made the case that trust is engineered, not granted.

  • Robin Yoong from Cursor created an eve agent by voice alone. Three models coded in parallel, and a spoken approval shipped it to Vercel.

  • Nonny Bell (Startup Manager APAC, Vercel) moderated a panel with Matthew Blode (AI Engineer, Linktree), Aarush Issar (GM AI Engineering, Auto & General Australia), and Leonardo Borges (Chief Engineer Gen AI, CommBank) on how their teams are adopting AI agents in production.

  • JJ Lecocq (Sales Director AUNZ, Vercel) led a discussion on how organizations are reshaping people, culture, and structure for AI.

Ship what's next

Thanks for joining us for Ship 2026 in London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco. We'll see you in May for Ship 2027.

title: MetricPose: Flexible 3D Human Pose Estimation with Depth and Geometric Cues
description:
arXiv:2611.08954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we present a 3D human pose estimator that predicts metrically accurate human joint positions in the camera coordinate frame. This task requires recovering the configuration of the body joints, scale, and metric camera-local placement. In monocular images, body size and camera distance are coupled through perspective projection and therefore cannot be determined uniquely from image alone. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining three complementary sources of information: learned RGB priors, direct depth measurements, and geometric constraints (e.g., ground contact) from the environment. We extend a pretrained full-body estimator with optional metric depth and geometry-processing modules that improve camera-distance estimation and depth-guided body refinement while preserving RGB-only operation. The resulting unified model supports RGB, RGB-Ground, and RGB-D using shared learned parameters. Unlike pelvis-relative error, camera-local error also measures placement relative to the camera. Compared with the existing foundation model SAM 3D Body, our methods with RGB, RGB-Ground, and RGB-D modes reduce camera-local joint-position error by 12.16%, 31.00% and 54.61% respectively.

title: Making a favicon from an SVG, measured: what breaks at 16 pixels
description:
Every favicon guide gives you the same list of files. I built the set from a real 716-byte logo to see the sizes, and found the one check most guides skip.

TL;DR: a square favicon.svg (with dark mode inside it), a favicon.ico with 16, 32 and 48 px images, a 180 px apple-touch-icon.png, two Android PNGs in a manifest, and four lines in <head>. Then look at it at 16 px.

The files, measured

File What uses it Bytes
favicon.svg Modern browsers, any size, dark mode 568 (377 gzipped)
favicon.ico Old browsers, tools that request /favicon.ico 2,574
apple-touch-icon.png iPhone and iPad home screen, 180 x 180 5,171
icon-192.png + icon-512.png Android home screen, via the manifest 20,196

1. Make the viewBox square

The logo had a 768 x 896 viewBox. Fitted to the drawing in the SVG Lab editor, the artboard came out 678 x 806. A favicon slot is square, so I set the viewBox to an 860 x 860 square around the mark and dropped the background rectangle.

2. Check it at 16 px

I had Chrome render the SVG at 16, 32 and 48 px. At 32 and 48 the bird is clear. At 16 the thin feather tips turn into grey specks. Nothing is wrong with the file: 16 pixels cannot hold a line that thin. If yours fails this check, use a bolder version of the mark.

3. Dark mode lives inside the SVG 

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="59 93 860 860">
  <style>
    path { fill: #111 }
    @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { path { fill: #f7f3ec } }
  </style>
  <path d="M 150 420 C 170 332 ... Z"/>
</svg>

Chromium draws SVG favicons in secure static mode, so no web fonts, linked images or scripts: keep everything in the file.

4. The ICO, with Pillow

Chrome rendered the PNGs; Pillow packed the small ones:

from PIL import Image
big = Image.open("fav-48.png")
big.save("favicon.ico", sizes=[(16, 16), (32, 32), (48, 48)],
         append_images=[Image.open("fav-16.png"), Image.open("fav-32.png")])

5. The head tags 

<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="32x32">
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
<link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">

Note sizes="32x32", not sizes="any". ChatGPT still gave me any on 7 November. The Evil Martians favicon guide switched to 32x32 in July 2023 to stop Chrome downloading both the ICO and the SVG.

Browser support: Chrome and Edge from 80, Firefox from 41, Safari from 26 (caniuse, 92.55 percent of browsers in use).

If you need the icon itself first, the SVG Lab MCP lets Claude, ChatGPT, Codex or Cursor draw icons as vector shapes through SVG Lab's Design Engine.

Full write-up with FAQ: https://svglab.app/blog/how-to-make-a-favicon-from-an-svg

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.

title: Compaction, decay and reinforcement in a two-tier conversational memory: a paired evaluation against retrieval-augmented generation
description:
arXiv:2611.09807v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A conversational agent that remembers has to decide what to keep. Retrieval-augmented generation keeps the transcript and searches it; the alternative is to compact each turn into atomic facts and search those. We compare the two on LoCoMo, with both arms answering all 1,985 questions in one window, against the same stores, with the same generator and judge, and both predictions on one row, which licenses McNemar's exact test on the 512 questions where they disagree.
  On the four categories comparable work reports, compaction scores 71.4 per cent against 64.6, a lead of 6.8 points (p = 5.5e-08) at 34 per cent fewer prompt tokens. On all five, including the adversarial set comparable work drops, the lead falls to 2.0 and stops being significant, because the baseline leads adversarial by 14.6.
  That loss has a structure. Our lead falls as the reference answer demands more source wording, 9.6 points ahead at one or two reference words and 3.1 behind past eight, with token overlap moving the same way, so the judge is not the cause. Compaction keeps what a fact asserts and discards how it was said, so it wins where the answer is a value and loses where it is a phrasing. We also report four negative results with their power calculations.

title: XMarkdown: Markdown charts, diagrams and math for AI reports
description:
Abstract

XMarkdown is an open-source Markdown renderer for documents that need charts, diagrams, equations, interactive controls, and validated SVG. The first MVP keeps familiar Markdown for prose and adds optional blocks for visual content. This article explains why I built it, how its shared Node/browser engine works, and what the initial measurements show. One complete demo used 208 source tokens against 1,219 for compact HTML/SVG; an extended streaming workload achieved a 5.48× improvement over repeatedly rendering growing prefixes. These results suggest a useful direction for AI-generated reports, with model generation and user studies still to come.

Try the live playground · Explore the GitHub repository · Install from npm

1. Why I started with Markdown

I like Markdown. I can read the source, edit a paragraph, and understand the document without opening a browser.

But I also want a report to contain a chart when a chart helps. Or a diagram when explaining a system through paragraphs becomes awkward. Seeing AI tools produce HTML artifacts for this kind of content made me wonder how much of that output really needed to be written again for each document.

A bar chart needs data and labels. Its author usually shouldn't have to decide the position of every tick mark or repeat the same SVG attributes. An AI generating the report has the same problem: it can spend a lot of its output describing rendering details that a library already knows how to produce.

That was the starting question for XMarkdown: could a document stay readable as Markdown while describing enough visual content for a renderer to do the rest?

I wanted the answer to include installation and real usage. The project now has a published npm package, a React component, and a live site with 18 examples, including capacity planning, release workflows, mathematical derivations, drawing, and a layered SVG architecture scene.

The site uses the actual XMarkdown engine. Its saved examples are rendered through the Node entry; edits run through the browser entry. Both share the same core.

2. Design: describe the content, reuse the rendering

XMarkdown uses markdown-it for ordinary Markdown. Headings, emphasis, lists, quotes, links, code fences, tables, and strikethrough keep their usual syntax.

The extensions are optional. A document can add an x-chart block for a chart or an x-diagram block for a directed graph. Those blocks contain data checked by the renderer before it produces the visual.

For example, this is a complete chart specification:

~~~x-chart
{
  "type": "bar",
  "title": "Requests per day",
  "description": "Monday 24; Tuesday 31; Wednesday 28.",
  "x": "day",
  "y": "requests",
  "data": [
    {"day": "Mon", "requests": 24},
    {"day": "Tue", "requests": 31},
    {"day": "Wed", "requests": 28}
  ]
}
~~~

The renderer supplies the SVG geometry, axes, and labels. A description also gives the document a textual explanation of the visual.

DEV displays these extensions as code. To see the graphics and interactions, paste them into the XMarkdown playground or use the package in your application.

This format has a cost: someone has to learn its schemas, and the host has to load a renderer. The benefit is that those schemas and rendering rules can be reused across documents.

Implementation matrix

Layer Existing processor What XMarkdown adds
Markdown markdown-it Extension rules, callouts, feature dispatch, checked links
Equations KaTeX Bounded input, lazy loading, MathML output, caching
Imported SVG saxes XML parser Allowed elements and attributes, local references, size limits
Charts and diagrams Custom JavaScript Data validation, geometry, SVG templates and labels
Controls and drawing Custom JavaScript Expression interpreter, native controls, shared widget runtime
Streaming Custom JavaScript Partial updates, bounded caching, final complete render

The implementation is JavaScript. Node, the browser API, and React share it. Other server languages can use a Node/HTTP bridge; separate Python, Go, or Rust parsers haven't shipped.

3. What the first MVP supports

Capability Current implementation Scope
Markdown prose Familiar Markdown plus tables and strikethrough Raw HTML is escaped; images currently display alt text
Callouts Notes, tips, warnings :::tip[Title] and related callouts
Charts SVG bar and line charts Up to 256 data rows
Diagrams Directed graphs with automatic placement Up to 32 nodes and 128 edges; basic routing
Mathematics Inline and display equations Supported TeX compiled by KaTeX into MathML
Calculated controls Ranges, numbers, toggles, selects, outputs Bounded expressions with arithmetic, comparisons and selected functions
Drawing SVG strokes, undo and clear Pointer interaction with stroke and point limits
SVG scenes Paths, groups, gradients, masks, clipping, patterns, symbols Validated static scene format
SVG imports Existing SVG markup inside an x-svg block Supported static subset, without linked resource fetching
Streaming Provisional previews and final rendering Bounded cache; a complete Markdown parse at completion
Integration Node, browser, React, TypeScript Next.js and Vue recipes; further adapters planned

The larger examples are where this becomes interesting. The architecture scene contains three layers, seven service cards, storage endpoints, curved connectors, reusable symbols, gradients, a grid pattern, masking, and clipping.

There is also a multi-input capacity model and a live React demo. They give a better picture of the renderer than a single chart does.

4. A complete React example

In an existing React 18+ project, install the package:

npm install xmarkdown-renderer

Use Node.js 22+ for the supported development/runtime setup. The current package version is 0.2.1, and TypeScript declarations are included.

Here is an editable report with prose, a chart, a diagram, an equation, and a live control:

import { useState } from 'react';
import { XMarkdown } from 'xmarkdown-renderer/react';
import 'xmarkdown-renderer/styles.css';

const initialSource = String.raw`# Service capacity report

Requests increased this week. **Here is the daily breakdown.**

~~~x-chart
{
  "type": "bar",
  "title": "Requests per day",
  "description": "Monday 24; Tuesday 31; Wednesday 28.",
  "x": "day",
  "y": "requests",
  "data": [
    {"day": "Mon", "requests": 24},
    {"day": "Tue", "requests": 31},
    {"day": "Wed", "requests": 28}
  ]
}
~~~

~~~x-diagram
{
  "title": "Request pipeline",
  "description": "Validate each request before storing it.",
  "nodes": [
    {"id": "validate", "label": "Validate"},
    {"id": "store", "label": "Store"}
  ],
  "edges": [["validate", "store"]]
}
~~~

For this queue model, stable arrival requires $\lambda < \mu$.

~~~x-widget
{
  "type": "controls",
  "title": "Try a different arrival rate",
  "description": "Compare arrival with a capacity of 100 requests/min.",
  "inputs": [
    {"id": "rate", "label": "Requests/min", "type": "range",
     "min": 0, "max": 180, "value": 80}
  ],
  "outputs": [
    {"id": "growth", "label": "Queue growth",
     "expr": "max(0, rate - 100)", "unit": "requests/min"}
  ]
}
~~~

:::tip[Try it]
Edit a chart value, or move the slider to test the capacity assumption.
:::
`;

export default function App() {
  const [source, setSource] = useState(initialSource);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  return (
    <main>
      <label htmlFor="report">Edit the report</label>
      <textarea
        id="report"
        rows={12}
        value={source}
        onChange={event => setSource(event.target.value)}
      />
      {error && <p role="alert">{error.message}</p>}
      <XMarkdown
        source={source}
        onError={setError}
        onDiagnostics={() => setError(null)}
      />
    </main>
  );
}

The ~~~ fences are standard Markdown and are convenient inside a JavaScript template literal. Backtick fences work as well. String.raw keeps the TeX backslashes intact.

The stylesheet supplies shared presentation for charts, diagrams, callouts, and widgets. Import it once in the application; document authors don't have to write CSS for each report. Hosts can override the theme or supply equivalent styles.

The browser parser prepares optional processors when needed. React mounts supported widget behavior automatically. For server rendering, the component can also accept a parsed document; the integration guide includes that path.

5. Evaluation method

The initial evaluation asks two different questions:

  1. How much author-written source does XMarkdown need compared with HTML/SVG for the supplied examples?
  2. How does parsing and rendering behave with ordinary documents, cached graphics, and growing streams?

For the source comparison, the repository contains 12 measured example pairs. The complete playground fixture is used for the main comparison. Its rendered body supplies literal HTML/SVG; a compact variant rounds numeric SVG attributes to 0.001 units while keeping the elements, labels, descriptions, and axes.

There is also an HTML baseline using shared graphics components. That baseline reuses the same validation and graphics renderer, so it tests how much of the saving comes from reusable components.

The tables below use the o200k_base tokenizer. The comparison artifacts also retain cl100k_base counts. Source has LF line endings. Shared runtimes and format instructions are excluded from the document-fragment counts; the separate format guide contains 383 o200k_base tokens.

Processing measurements ran locally on Windows with Node.js 22.22.0. The feature benchmark used seven timed trials with rotating condition order and warmups, reporting median time per document. An empty extension cache still had dependencies loaded. First-use observations include additional startup work and are reported separately in the benchmark.

These measurements were recorded for v0.2.0 on 8 November 2026 with markdown-it 14.3.3. The current 0.2.1 package uses markdown-it 15.0.3. Keeping the measurement version explicit makes the results reproducible.

6. Results: source size

The same complete document, five representations

Representation UTF-8 bytes Source tokens
XMarkdown 839 208
Literal HTML/SVG 3,610 1,259
Compact HTML/SVG 3,492 1,219
Standalone styled HTML 4,914 1,689
HTML with shared graphics components 1,044 261

For this fixture, XMarkdown used 82.9% fewer source tokens than compact HTML/SVG, and 20.3% fewer than shared-component HTML.

The component baseline is encouraging in its own way. It shows how much can be gained by moving repeated geometry into reusable software. Markdown then gives the surrounding prose a compact, familiar representation.

Results across the supplied examples

Example XMarkdown tokens Compact HTML tokens XMarkdown source reduction
Headings, emphasis and lists 20 42 52.4%
Comparison table 23 68 66.2%
Callout 19 47 59.6%
Chart with axes and labels 79 635 87.6%
Automatically placed pipeline 79 494 84.0%
Branching dependency graph 128 727 82.4%
Complete playground document 208 1,219 82.9%
Mathematical notation 14 75 81.3%
Queue what-if control 112 148 24.3%
Drawing application 52 317 83.6%
Complex vector scene 844 978 13.7%
Existing SVG import 225 219 -2.7%

The raw SVG import needs a fence around existing markup, so it uses slightly more source. A custom vector scene still has to describe its geometry. The largest reductions appear where a chart or graph can be described through data that the renderer understands.

These comparisons aren't measurements of an AI provider's billed usage or generation speed. Those require counting prompts, format examples, output, and repair turns in an actual model experiment. The source results give us a concrete starting point for that experiment.

Full source comparisons and paired examples

7. Results: parsing, caching and streaming

Early in the project, I asked for a parser that could be 50 times faster than a regular Markdown parser. Benchmarking helped turn that ambition into a more useful question: where can we avoid doing the same work again?

For a complete plain-prose document of 6,320 characters, bare markdown-it took 0.259 ms and XMarkdown took 0.268 ms. Adding document features has a processing cost. The current data doesn't support a general 50× parsing claim.

The extended workload shows where reuse can help:

Extended document workload Median parse + render time
Empty extension cache, dependencies loaded 0.652 ms
Extension cache disabled 0.508 ms
Repeated document with cached extensions 0.075 ms

In a separate streaming comparison, XMarkdown achieved 5.48× faster processing than repeatedly parsing and rendering the growing full prefix for that extended fixture.

Streaming emits provisional section updates and performs a complete parse at the end. The final pass keeps full-document Markdown semantics, including references. The bounded cache can reuse validated specifications and generated geometry, with SVG IDs rewritten for each placement.

The benchmark also includes cases where streaming helps less: the short math fixture measured 0.78× against repeated-prefix rendering. Document shape and chunking affect the result.

Browser layout, painting, network traffic, model generation, and total heap memory aren't part of these timing results. The next evaluation should measure the whole path from generated source to a usable document.

To reproduce the comparisons from a repository checkout with dependencies installed:

npm run compare
npm run bench:features

8. Complex SVG and the document boundary

I wanted the format to handle more than a few preset chart types. The MVP therefore has a structured SVG scene format and can import supported existing SVG markup.

Here is a small import that uses a gradient and a curved path:

~~~x-svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 180">
  <title>Capacity curve</title>
  <desc>A cubic curve drawn with a blue-to-green gradient.</desc>
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="capacity" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#38bdf8" />
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#a3e635" />
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>
  <path d="M20 140C110 0 290 0 380 140"
        fill="none" stroke="url(#capacity)" stroke-width="4" />
</svg>
~~~

The scene processor supports paths, groups, gradients, masks, clipping, patterns, markers, and reusable symbols. Both scene data and imported XML go through validation. Imports can need cleanup when an SVG editor adds unsupported metadata or styling.

Scripts, event handlers, external resources, foreignObject, filters, and animation are outside the current static SVG profile. Control expressions use a bounded interpreter without eval; authors can't add arbitrary JavaScript to a document.

Those choices give the format a defined document boundary. Validation still needs further fuzzing and independent security review. Applications handling hostile input should follow the security guide and apply isolation and resource budgets at the host level.

9. What this could change for AI products

The opportunity I see is a shared document layer for generated reports. A model could write the explanation and the data for supported visuals; the application could control presentation through a renderer it tests and maintains.

That could be useful for:

  • AI report builders that repeatedly generate prose alongside the same chart types.
  • Developer tools that explain request flows, dependencies, and architecture.
  • Internal analysis tools that put equations and what-if controls next to a written argument.
  • Education products that need editable explanations with mathematical notation and diagrams.

Teams at Anthropic working on Claude artifacts, and teams at OpenAI building AI interfaces, are audiences I'd like this proposal to reach. I'd also like to hear from developers building smaller AI products where document output is a daily integration problem. These are invitations to evaluate the approach; the project has no affiliation with either company.

For a company considering adoption, I'd start with a bounded report workflow that already uses supported chart and diagram types. Compare equivalent HTML/component output against XMarkdown, including:

  1. Total input and output tokens, with format instructions included.
  2. Valid-output rate and the number of repair turns.
  3. Generation, validation, rendering, and interaction latency.
  4. How accurately people understand and edit the result.

If those trials show consistent benefits, a compact document format with interoperable renderers could change how AI applications deliver rich explanations. That is the possibility worth building toward. XMarkdown is an installable first MVP that lets us start testing it now.

10. Where the project stands

The repository includes CI for Node 22 and 24, TypeScript declarations, tests, a changelog, and contribution and security policies. Node/browser integration checks and a live React application exercise the shared engine.

There is still work to do on graph routing, more chart types, a browser worker, accessibility coverage, and complete framework applications. Mermaid rendering, task-list checkboxes, and external-image handling are also future work. APIs and syntax can change before 1.0.

For a document containing only prose, I'd use regular Markdown. For unrestricted page layouts or custom applications, HTML and JavaScript remain the flexible option. XMarkdown is most useful when a report needs familiar text plus visual features that can be described and rendered consistently.

You can try it without cloning the project: npm install xmarkdown-renderer in your existing application, or open the playground.

If you try the renderer, an example that breaks, a missing chart type, or an awkward integration is useful feedback. Open an issue or contribute a change. If you'd like to follow the work, a star on the GitHub repository helps you keep track of it.

Source material

  • Repository and installation
  • Measured source comparisons
  • Feature benchmark methodology and results
  • Extension syntax and limits
  • Integration recipes
  • Evaluation plan
