title: What Is Next.js? Explained Simply for Beginners
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

Next.js is a free framework built on top of React that helps you build complete, fast and search engine friendly websites and web applications. React on its own is a library for building user interfaces, while Next.js adds the missing pieces around it, such as page routing, server rendering, data loading, image optimisation and even backend API routes. In short, React gives you the building blocks for the screen, and Next.js gives you the structure of the whole house. It was created by Vercel and is now one of the most popular ways to build React websites.

First, What Is React on Its Own?

React is a JavaScript library made by Meta. It lets you build a page from small reusable pieces called components. A button, a header, a product card and a full page can all be components. You write what the screen should look like, and React updates the screen efficiently when your data changes. Once this idea clicks, building interfaces starts to feel logical and even enjoyable.

However, React alone only solves one job, rendering the interface in the browser. It does not decide how pages are organised, how visitors move between them, how you appear on Google, or how your app talks to a database. With plain React, you must choose extra tools for almost everything else. That freedom suits experts, but for beginners it can feel like buying a car and being handed a box of parts. Next.js fills this gap with sensible defaults that already work together.

What Next.js Gives You That Plain React Does Not

File based routing is the first feature beginners notice. Your folders become your pages. Create a file inside the app folder and it becomes a route on your website, with no extra routing library to install or configure. To understand the details, read our guide on how routing works in Next.js once you have finished this introduction.

Search engine optimisation is another big win. Next.js can send fully rendered HTML to the browser, so search engines and social media previews can read your content straight away. With a plain client side React app, the first HTML is often almost empty and the content only appears after JavaScript runs, which can hurt indexing and make shared links look blank.

Next.js also includes built in image optimisation, so large photos are resized for each visitor's device instead of slowing everyone down. Its API routes let you write small backend endpoints inside the same project, so you can handle forms or fetch data securely without a separate server.

Your First Next.js App in Minutes

Getting started is refreshingly quick. You need Node.js installed on your computer, and then you run one command in your terminal. The setup tool asks a few simple questions. The defaults are fine for a first project, so you can happily accept them and let it work.

npx create-next-app@latest my-first-app
cd my-first-app
npm run dev

When the server starts, open http://localhost:3000 to see a starter page. It comes from a file in the app folder, usually called page.js or page.tsx. Saving an edit updates the browser almost instantly. The official Next.js documentation explains each convention clearly when you are ready to go deeper.

Here is a tiny first page component. It is just a React component that returns some markup, and Next.js turns it into a real web page for you.

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Hello from Next.js</h1>
      <p>This is my very first Next.js page.</p>
    </main>
  );
}

Notice there is no router setup, no server code and no configuration file to wrestle with. You wrote a component, saved the file, and the framework handled the rest.

The official Next.js documentation page on nextjs.org — the reference this guide follows.

Server Rendering and Static Pages, in Plain Words

These phrases sound intimidating, but the ideas are simple. Think of your website like a restaurant. With client side rendering, the visitor gets an empty plate and a recipe, and their browser does all the cooking. The result can be tasty, but there is a short wait and search engines mostly see the empty plate.

With server side rendering, often shortened to SSR, the kitchen prepares the dish for each order and sends a ready page to the visitor. This suits pages that change often or depend on the visitor, such as a dashboard or a personalised feed. The visitor sees content quickly, and search engines see real content too.

With static generation, often shortened to SSG, the kitchen prepares the dish once in advance and serves copies all day. This suits blog posts and documentation that do not change with every visit. Static pages are very fast and cheap to host.

Next.js lets you mix these approaches page by page. Your blog can be static and your account pages rendered on the server. Plain React normally renders everything in the browser unless you add extra tooling.

Next.js vs Plain React at a Glance

Feature Plain React Next.js
Routing You install and configure a router yourself Built in, based on your folder structure
First page load for SEO Often empty HTML, content loads with JavaScript Rendered HTML from the server or build
Backend code Needs a separate server project API routes inside the same project
Images You optimise and resize them yourself Automatic optimisation built in
Setup decisions Many choices before you write real code Sensible defaults from the start
Best for Small interactive tools and learning React itself Websites and full applications for real users

The table is not saying plain React is bad. React is the engine, and Next.js is the whole car built around that engine, with doors, lights and a dashboard already fitted. For a fuller side by side breakdown, see our comparison of React vs Next.js and their differences.

When Should You Use Next.js?

Choose Next.js for a real website that people find through search, share on social media, or use every day. Blogs, portfolios, company sites, shops, course platforms and dashboards all benefit from fast first loads, good SEO and tidy routing. It also suits projects needing a little backend logic, such as a contact form, without a second project to maintain.

Plain React can still be the better pick. If you are learning React itself, it keeps the picture small so you understand components, props and state without framework magic on top. For a tiny internal tool or quick prototype, the extra structure of Next.js may be more than you need.

A practical rule is this. If the content matters to Google or to first impressions, pick Next.js. If the app mostly lives behind a login and behaves like a private tool, either option can work well.

A Sensible Learning Order for Beginners

Do not try to learn everything at once, because that road leads straight to twelve open tabs and a headache. Start with basic HTML, CSS and JavaScript, since Next.js sits on top of all three. Then learn React fundamentals, including components, props, state and handling simple events. The lessons in React's official learning guide are an excellent, free place to build that foundation.

Once a small React app feels comfortable, rebuild that same app inside Next.js. You will notice the differences far more clearly than in theory. After that, learn file based routing, then data fetching, then server and client components. Build and deploy one small real project, such as a personal blog. Small finished steps beat grand unfinished plans every time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Next.js a replacement for React?

No. Next.js is built on top of React, so you still write React components inside it. It adds routing, rendering options and backend features around React rather than replacing it.

Is Next.js free to use?

Yes. Next.js is open source and free, and you can build commercial projects with it. Hosting can be free on small plans or paid as your traffic grows, depending on your provider.

Do I need to learn React before Next.js?

Yes, at least the basics. Understanding components, props and state first will make Next.js feel straightforward. Without that base, two new things happen at once and it can feel confusing.

Can Next.js handle backend work too?

Yes, for many common jobs. API routes let you handle forms, fetch data with secret keys and talk to a database from the same project. Very large backends may still deserve their own service.

Conclusion

Next.js takes React from a brilliant interface library to a complete way of building websites. It gives you routing, server rendering, static pages, image optimisation and small backend routes with sensible defaults, so beginners can focus on building instead of wiring tools together. Learn React first, then let Next.js carry the heavy structure for you. Your first project is only one command away.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python is now a first-class language and runtime on Vercel. Build APIs, full-stack applications, and AI agents with native Python SDKs and a shared development and deployment workflow for your Python backend and JavaScript frontend.

Python framework and runtime support

Vercel handles the infrastructure so you can focus on your application:

  • Automatic framework support: FastAPI, Flask, and Django applications are automatically recognized and configured, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the Vercel CDN.

  • Native Python runtime and tooling: Vercel runs CPython on Linux and supports uv and pyproject.toml for dependency management.

  • Compute for APIs and workers: Scale request-driven applications with Fluid compute and run long-running pull-based workloads with Vercel Daemons.

Native Python SDKs

Within your application, Python SDKs let you build agents, run untrusted code, and orchestrate durable workflows.

  • Sandbox: Give your application or agent an isolated Linux VM on demand.

  • AI SDK for Python (Beta): Generate or stream model responses and call tools. Get started with uv add ai.

  • Workflow SDK for Python (Beta): Persist execution state and retry failed workflow steps.

  • Queues (Beta): Send and receive messages for background work.

  • Connect: Obtain credentials for calling external APIs.

  • Blob: Upload and retrieve files in object storage.

Use the SDKs individually or combine them in the same Python application.

Your frontend and backend, together

For full-stack applications, Vercel Services allows you to deploy your frontend and backends together in one project, with shared previews and atomic deployments and rollbacks. Within that project, you can view logs by service and connect backends privately through service bindings.

For a frontend in frontend/ and a FastAPI app defined in backend/main.py, add this vercel.toml at the repository root.

Requests under /api/ reach matching FastAPI routes with the path unchanged, while other requests reach the frontend. Run both services locally with vercel dev, then deploy them together from the same repository.

Read the Python documentation to get started.

title: OmniLatent: Unified Latent for 3D Part Modeling
description:
arXiv:2611.09055v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the result sensitive to geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and limited part-level annotations. We present OmniLatent, a unified latent modeling framework for 3D part decomposition. Instead of predicting part labels in isolation, OmniLatent learns a shared latent space that jointly encodes geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, allowing data-rich geometric and visual priors to support data-scarce part learning. Given a single input image, the base model generates geometry, deformation, texture, and surface part IDs in one pass, producing a part-aware 3D asset without a separate segmentation stage. We further tune the pretrained model for two extensions: a point-prompt adapter that maps arbitrary 3D point prompts with binary part IDs into latent tokens for full segmentation, refinement, and part subdivision, and an amodal part completion model that completes partial surface masks into a coherent full-object decomposition through dynamic per-part token allocation, cross-attention to the given geometry latent, and alternating part-local and global attention. Extensive experiments show that OmniLatent produces semantically meaningful part segmentations with precise boundaries, supports interactive part editing, and completes partial part observations while preserving global object consistency.

title: Structuring Survey Histories for LLM Digital Twins: A Controlled Study of Background, Decision Procedure, and Evaluation Profiles
description:
arXiv:2611.08730v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based digital twins aim to predict how individuals would respond in new settings from representations of their prior responses. Existing evidence that compression of survey histories need not reduce predictive accuracy suggests that representation structure, rather than information volume alone, may be an important design choice. We study BDE, a fixed representation that organizes each respondent's survey history into Background, Decision procedure, and Evaluation. We evaluate it on Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025) by predicting each respondent's held-out answers on 17 tasks. In a paired evaluation with 100 respondents, a fully inferred BDE profile improves overall accuracy over the raw survey transcript by 1.27 percentage points (pp) on gpt-5.4-nano (p < 0.01) and 1.19 pp on gpt-5.4-mini (p < 0.001). Three analyses then examine the schema, extraction depth, and component composition. Against a length-matched free-form profile written from the same transcript by the same extractor, BDE improves pricing accuracy on both simulators (2.15 pp on nano, p < 0.01; 1.38 pp on mini, p < 0.05), while its overall advantage is significant only on nano (1.05 pp, p < 0.05). Allowing deeper inference during extraction yields no statistically significant gain on either simulator. By contrast, adding Evaluation to a Background--Decision procedure profile improves overall accuracy by 1.44 pp on nano (p < 0.001) and 1.22 pp on mini (p < 0.001). These results indicate that the advantage over raw transcripts is not explained by compression or length alone, and attribute it primarily to profile composition rather than deeper extraction.

title: How to plan an infrastructure task without losing your mind: a breakdown using an AWS deployment as an example
description:
The ticket fits on one line: "deploy a new web service to AWS and add jobs to deploy it." Inside that line are a network, containers, a database, secrets, a CDN, two workflows and dozens of small steps that an engineer usually keeps in their head. That works while nothing interrupts you. Then you join a call, come back, and can't remember whether you checked the security group. And when someone asks how long it will take, the honest answer is "a day or two."

I've been building IT infrastructure for about 15 years, and today I lead a DevOps team at a game studio. Tasks like "spin up a new service" or "change system X" land on my desk every week, and over the years I've settled into a fairly stable way of planning them. I tried to write that method down and then give it to an agent.

Part 1. How an engineer plans a task

The task

Let's take a concrete one:

Deploy a new web service to AWS. It has a React frontend and a Python backend, and requires PostgreSQL to run. The application repository is github.com/javdet/nib-demo-app. This should result in jobs in GitHub for deploying the infrastructure and the application.

Nothing unusual. Tasks like this come in all the time, and anyone who works with infrastructure has a rough idea of what's behind them. Let's walk through what happens in an engineer's head when this ticket arrives, step by step and slower than it happens in real life.

Step 1. Collect context

Before planning anything, the engineer answers three questions:

  1. What is the project? Who uses it, how critical it is, whether it has environments besides production.
  2. How does the current infrastructure work? Which AWS accounts exist, where the Terraform state lives, how the networks are laid out, what CI/CD is already there.
  3. What do we know about the products in the task? Here that's AWS, PostgreSQL and GitHub Actions: which AWS services fit, which Postgres version to use, how Actions will reach the cloud.

Some of the answers are already in their head. The rest they pull from git and the wiki: usually details of how the infrastructure is built and the company's internal rules for cloud, databases and CI/CD.


This step already shows the first problem, and we'll come back to it: a large part of the context isn't written down anywhere except in one person's head.

Step 2. Outline the stages

Once the context is collected, the task falls apart into large stages:

  1. Write infrastructure code for the AWS resources.
  2. Write the build and deploy workflows.
  3. Create the resources in AWS.
  4. Deploy the application.
  5. Check that everything works.

The stages depend on each other: you can't deploy the app before the cluster exists, and you can't create the cluster before the code exists. The dependencies matter more than the list itself, because they decide what can run in parallel and what can't.

Step 3. Break the stages into basic actions

Each stage is a set of simple actions you can do in one go:

  • edit a file;
  • run a CLI command;
  • make an API call;
  • change a setting in a UI.

For example, "create the resources in AWS" becomes a chain: create a bucket for the state, give GitHub Actions access to the account, run terraform plan, read the diff, run terraform apply, look at the outputs.

Step 4. Lean on rules and experience

To put the actions in the right order, the engineer relies on two things:

  1. Team rules. How we name resources, where we keep state, which tags are required, what we never do in production.
  2. Their own experience. They've done something similar before and remember where it hurt last time. ### Step 5. Build the plan: action, check, rollback

These pieces add up to a detailed plan. Usually it lives in the engineer's head, less often on paper. A good plan has three parts:

  • actions: what exactly we do;
  • checks before closing each stage: how to know the stage is really done, and not just "seems fine";
  • a rollback plan in case something goes wrong.


The Rollback column is the one people leave empty most often. Be honest: when did you last write a rollback plan before you needed it?

Step 6. Execute

Then the engineer walks the whole list: action, check, action, check. If a check fails, they roll back or fix the problem, and check again.
Tedious, right?

Where this process breaks

On paper it's a good process. In practice it breaks in three places.
1. The action list lives in your head, and items fall out of it. A call, an alert, a colleague asking you to look at their PR. An hour later you come back to the task and you're no longer sure whether you closed the database port to the internet. A plan in your head doesn't survive context switches, and you can't hand it to a colleague if you get sick in the middle of the task.

This happened to me when I was moving asset buckets from one cloud to another. I copied the data and set up access, but forgot to add CORS. It's a couple of lines of config, and it feels so obvious that it never makes it onto any list.

2. Checks get skipped. You want to save time: "the site opened, so it works." The fact that the database is reachable from the internet, or that backups aren't set up, comes up a month later. Checks are the first thing to go under a deadline, because skipping them doesn't break anything right away.

3. Nobody knows how big the task is. Ask "how long will it take?" and you hear "a day or two." That's not an estimate. Until the task is broken into actions, its size is invisible: to you, to your team lead, and to whoever filed the ticket.

All three have the same cause: the plan exists only in the head of the person doing the work, so you can't hand it over and you can't measure it.

What if an agent builds the plan?

So here's the natural question: what if an agent does the breakdown, the planning, the execution and the checks? The engineer still controls the stages, decides which steps to run, and accepts the final result.


That's why I built nib (Neuro Infrastructure Builder). It's a tool for infrastructure work: it splits a task into stages, writes concrete actions with checks for each stage, builds a rollback plan, and then either runs the steps itself or gives the operator detailed instructions.
Inside, nib follows the same logic as the engineer from Part 1. The work is split into modes, and each mode has its own role:


The context, rules and experience the engineer relies on exist in nib too: a knowledge base, rules and skills. In this post we only use the knowledge base. The rest is a topic for the next part.

Part 2. From git clone to a working site

Now let's run the same task through nib. The whole run is on video:

What you need

  • Docker;
  • an API key for an LLM provider. nib works with any OpenAI-compatible API, and the installer has presets for OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, Grok and Kimi;
  • an AWS account. I strongly recommend a separate sandbox account: the agent will need keys that can create resources;
  • a GitHub account and a fork of demo-app, if you want to repeat this exact task.

Installation

nib runs locally with Docker Compose or in Kubernetes with a Helm chart. The local option is enough to try it:

git clone https://github.com/javdet/nib.git
cd nib
make setup

make setup is an interactive script. It asks for the LLM provider, the model and the key (I use OpenRouter), then the name of your first project and, optionally, its environments, clouds and regions. You can skip those fields, but nib plans better with them, and you can add more projects later. Then the script generates tokens, writes .env and the config, and starts four containers: Postgres, the knowledge base server, the backend and the frontend.

At the end it prints the UI address (http://localhost:8080 by default; if the port is busy, it picks a free one) and an API token. You paste this token on the login screen. It's also saved in .env as NIB_API_TOKEN, so it's hard to lose.

Knowledge base: what to fill in for a new project

The first place to open after you log in is Knowledgebase. This is the "context" from step 1: everything the engineer knows about the company and the project, and the agent doesn't.

The Company Information card has the basic fields: company name and description, version control system and git base URL, git user, CI/CD system, issue tracker, wiki and team messenger. For our task the key ones are GitHub as the VCS and GitHub Actions as CI/CD, because they decide which workflows the agent will write.


You don't need to upload documents for a new project yet: there's nothing to describe. On a live project, this is where you put what usually sits in the wiki and in people's heads: the network diagram, naming conventions, where state lives, what's special about each environment. You can upload a Markdown document or ask the agent to generate one from a list of repositories.

When a plan finishes, nib writes a report and updates the knowledge base from it, so the next task starts with what the agent learned in the previous one.

Connecting GitHub, AWS and search over MCP

On its own, the agent can only think. To create a repository, look at AWS resources or find documentation, it needs tools. In nib they connect over MCP (Model Context Protocol). It's an open protocol: an LLM application gets a list of tools from an external server and calls them. One MCP server covers one system: GitHub, AWS, search.

If you don't know where to start, ask nib itself, for example: "How do I connect you to AWS over MCP?" Its answer is in the video.
This task needs three servers:

  • GitHub: the repository, PRs and workflows;
  • AWS: reading and creating resources in the account;
  • SearXNG: web search, so the agent can check current documentation instead of relying only on what the model already knows.

nib supports only the HTTP transport for MCP (streamable HTTP), so we run all three servers as containers on the same network as nib. Add them to docker-compose.yml.

GitHub MCP is the official server from GitHub:

github-mcp:
  image: ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  command:
    - http
    - --port=9082
  networks:
    - nib
aws-mcp:
  image: public.ecr.aws/awslabs-mcp/awslabs/aws-api-mcp-server:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  environment:
    AWS_API_MCP_TRANSPORT: "streamable-http"
    AWS_API_MCP_HOST: "0.0.0.0"
    AWS_API_MCP_PORT: "9081"
    AUTH_TYPE: "no-auth"
    AWS_REGION: "${AWS_REGION:-us-east-2}"
    AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS: "aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1"
    AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS: "aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1"
    READ_OPERATIONS_ONLY: "false"
    REQUIRE_MUTATION_CONSENT: "false"
    AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: "${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
    AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"
    AWS_SESSION_TOKEN: "${AWS_SESSION_TOKEN:-}"
  networks:
    - nib
searxng:
  image: docker.io/searxng/searxng:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  environment:
    SEARXNG_PORT: "9083"
    SEARXNG_BASE_URL: "http://searxng:9083/"
    SEARXNG_SECRET: "${SEARXNG_SECRET}"
  volumes:
    - ./searxng:/etc/searxng:rw
  networks:
    - nib

searxng-mcp:
  image: docker.io/isokoliuk/mcp-searxng:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  environment:
    SEARXNG_URL: "http://searxng:9083"
    SEARXNG_DEFAULT_RESPONSE_FORMAT: "json"
    SEARXNG_MAX_RESULT_CHARS: "500"
    SEARXNG_TIMEOUT_MS: "15000"
    MCP_HTTP_PORT: "9084"
    MCP_HTTP_HOST: "0.0.0.0"
    MCP_HTTP_STATELESS: "true"
  networks:
    - nib

The response format is an easy place to trip up. The MCP wrapper asks SearXNG for results in JSON, but by default SearXNG returns only HTML. The json format has to be enabled in searxng/settings.yml. The nib repository already ships this file with the right setting, which is why the volume is mounted from ./searxng.

Registering the servers in nib

Now nib needs to know where to find these servers. You edit the MCP config in Tools → Config (or through Tools → MCP Servers → Add):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "knowledge-base": {
      "url": "http://kb-mcp:8081/mcp"
    },
    "aws": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://aws-mcp:9081/mcp"
    },
    "searxng": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://searxng-mcp:9084/mcp"
    },
    "github": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://github-mcp:9082/",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}",
        "X-MCP-Toolsets": "all",
        "X-MCP-Readonly": "false"
      }
    }
  }
}


knowledge-base is the built-in knowledge base server, and it's already in the config after installation. We add the other three.

Note the ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in the header. Tokens never go into the config as plain text: nib fills them in from Variables → Secrets at request time. Each secret has a list of allowed hosts, so the GitHub token goes only to github-mcp and nowhere else.

So secrets live in two places, and it's easy to mix them up:

  • AWS keys are needed by the aws-mcp container itself, so they're in .env and reach the container as environment variables;
  • the GitHub token travels in the HTTP header of the request from nib to the MCP server, so it's in nib's secrets.

Checking the connection

After restarting the containers, open Tools → MCP Servers. For each server you can see the list of tools it exposes. If the list is empty or the server shows an error, the problem is in the network, the address or the token, and there's no point going further: an agent without tools plans blind.

In the video, the very first check fails: GitHub MCP returns an error. The container is up and the address is right, but the GITHUB_TOKEN secret doesn't exist yet, and without it the server returns nothing. We create the secret in Variables → Secrets, check again, and the tool list appears.

You create the token in your GitHub user settings, under Developer settings (github.com/settings/tokens). I used a classic token with the repo and workflow scopes. The second one is easy to miss: without it GitHub rejects pushes to .github/workflows/, and the agent can't commit its workflows.
In my case GitHub exposed a couple of dozen tools, SearXNG five, and AWS only two. That's expected. AWS API MCP Server gives the agent a generic AWS CLI call plus a helper that picks the right command, so all of AWS fits into two tools. GitHub is the opposite, with one tool per operation, and the next section deals with that.

Tool categories and a base set per mode

Three MCP servers give the agent a lot of tools. If you send all of them with every call, the model gets confused, the context grows, and you pay tokens for descriptions of tools this task will never use. Planning cloud resources doesn't need tools for logs and metrics. nib has two mechanisms for this.

Tool categories. Tools are grouped into categories (for example, everything about AWS, everything about git). During decomposition the agent decides which categories the task touches and gets access only to those. Each action in the plan gets an even narrower set: only the categories marked on that action. You don't have to sort the tools by hand. The Auto-fill with AI button on the Tool categories card does a first pass that you can then fix.

A base set for each mode. You can think of nib's modes as subagents: some break the task down, some work out the stages, some run actions. By default every mode gets every tool. In Tools → Included tools you can narrow this: modes that should only read and plan don't need tools that change things. The Distribute with AI button can only remove tools, so the read-only modes lose the tools that change things, and nothing extra gets added.

The first plan

Everything is ready, so we can plan. As a reminder, we're deploying demo-app, an online store for art supplies with a Python backend, a React frontend and a PostgreSQL database. Click New plan and paste the task from Part 1 as is.

From here, nib repeats what the engineer did in Part 1.

Collecting context. First the decompose agent asks clarifying questions, and for most of them it suggests answers you can pick with a click. It asked me two questions an engineer would ask whoever filed the ticket in the first five minutes:

  • How should the service be published? Is there a custom domain, or is the address that CloudFront generates enough? The answer decides whether DNS records and a TLS certificate show up in the plan.
  • How should the jobs run? Automatically on merge to the main branch, or manually? Really, this is a question about whether the infrastructure can change without a human.

I don't have a domain, so the site lives on the CloudFront address, and the jobs run automatically.


Stages and dependencies. After the answers, the agent shows a Summary (how it understood the task) and a DAG of the stages and the dependencies between them. A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a "what comes after what" diagram with no loops. Here you see for the first time what was implicit in the engineer's head: which stages can run in parallel and which ones block the rest. If you have no questions about the stages, move on to detailed planning.


Actions, checks, rollback. The Process plan here button starts planning. A separate agent works on each stage, in parallel with the others, and at the end the rollback plan is built. The whole thing took about two minutes. The result was four stages and a rollback plan:


Look at the last row: there are one and a half times more checks than actions. When the plan lives in your head, this is the part that shrinks first under a deadline.

Steps come in four types: run a CLI command, make an API request, work with code, or change something in a web UI. Each step has a detailed description of what to do, and if an action can cause downtime for a system that's already running, the plan warns about it separately.


This answers the third problem from Part 1. nib doesn't estimate in hours, but you see the amount of work before you start: four stages, ten steps, fifteen checks, and it's clear where you need code and where an API call is enough. You can take that to whoever asked "how long will it take," and the conversation will be more concrete than "a day or two."

Preparing access: the agent works over MCP

Each step has a run button, each stage has Execute all, and you can also start a step from the chat by asking the agent. A checkbox next to a step marks it as done, and you can leave a comment on any step. Only one action runs at a time. This is a deliberate limit, so that two agents don't change the same infrastructure in parallel.

The first stage is all API and CLI calls, so the agent ran it on its own, over MCP:

  1. Reconcile the GitHub Actions OIDC provider in AWS account: the OIDC provider that GitHub Actions will use to get access to AWS;
  2. Reconcile the remote Terraform state bucket for the prod stack: an S3 bucket for the Terraform state;
  3. Reconcile the infrastructure deployment role used by Terraform: the role Terraform uses to create resources;
  4. Reconcile the application deployment role for publishing and rolling out: a separate role for shipping the application;
  5. Create or reconcile the protected GitHub production environment: a protected production environment in the repository.

If you know Kubernetes, you know the word reconcile: bring the system to the desired state. If the resource doesn't exist, create it. If it exists but is configured differently, fix it. If it's already right, do nothing. A step like this is safe to run again, which helps if the plan stops halfway. The two separate roles are deliberate too: the role that ships the application has no reason to be able to create networks and databases.

After each step, the agent reports in the chat what it did. To make the demo clearer, I ran the stage checks myself: I opened the AWS console and made sure the OIDC provider was created, the bucket was there, and the environment had appeared in the repository. The agent can run the checks too; you just have to ask. Remember the OIDC provider check. We'll need it later.

Code: Terraform and workflows

In the second stage, API calls are no longer enough: we need to write Terraform and workflows. For steps like these, nib has an executor that runs a coding agent in a separate container. The agent clones the repository, makes the changes, commits, pushes and opens a pull request.

The first time you run a code step, nib sends you to the executor settings page (Tools → Executor). The executor has three options: off (the default), Local, which means containers on your machine through Docker, and Remote, which runs as Kubernetes Jobs. Local is enough to start: the agent runs right on your computer, and you can see the container logs in the UI.

Pick the agent type and the authentication method. The tokens we need aren't in the secrets list yet, so we create them:

  • CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN: the Claude Code subscription token, which you get from claude setup-token. You can use an Anthropic API key instead;
  • a GitHub token, so the agent can push its changes. It's the same one as for MCP.

You can keep the default agent image and model. Go back to the plan and run the step.

What the agent wrote

The PR has 20 files: two workflows, Terraform code in infra/terraform and an updated README. In short, here's the architecture:

  • CloudFront in front of everything: the frontend's static files come from a private S3 bucket, and /api/* requests go to an ALB;
  • the ALB accepts traffic only from the CloudFront managed prefix list, so you can't reach it directly from the internet;
  • the backend runs on ECS Fargate in private subnets and accepts traffic only from the ALB;
  • RDS PostgreSQL 16 sits in isolated subnets with no route to the internet. It's Multi-AZ, encrypted, with backups and deletion protection. Terraform generates the password and puts it straight into Secrets Manager;
  • GitHub Actions reach AWS over OIDC: the job assumes an IAM role and gets temporary credentials, so not a single long-lived AWS key is stored in GitHub. This is where the provider and the roles from the first stage come in.

And two workflows:

  • Deploy Infrastructure runs terraform plan and terraform apply. Apply runs only manually, with an explicit flag, in the production GitHub environment, where you can require approval. That's how the agent used my answer about running jobs;
  • Deploy Application builds the backend image, pushes it to ECR tagged with the commit, updates the ECS service, builds the frontend, uploads it to S3, invalidates the CloudFront cache and finally runs a smoke test against the CloudFront address.

Two decisions in this code are good examples of the "experience" from Part 1 that usually isn't written down anywhere.

The ECS service is created with desired_count = 0. When terraform apply runs, ECR doesn't have a single application image yet. If you ask for two tasks right away, ECS will keep trying to start an image that doesn't exist. So Terraform creates the service empty and ignores later changes to the image and the task count, and the deploy workflow publishes the first real image and scales the service to two. Without this detail, Terraform would undo the deploy on every run.

The cost is stated openly. A Multi-AZ database and a NAT gateway in every availability zone are a production setup, and they cost money even with no traffic. The agent put this in the README, next to the order in which to run the workflows. For a demo it's overkill, for production it's right, and it's a decision you should make on purpose instead of learning about it from the bill.

The changes look reasonable, so we merge the PR into the main branch.

First run, first failure

We run Deploy Infrastructure, and the first attempt fails.


This happens to experienced engineers too, so it's no big deal. Instead of reading the log myself, I show nib the error and ask it to figure it out. It finds the cause: the OIDC provider created in the first stage doesn't list all the thumbprints.

A thumbprint is a fingerprint of the identity provider's TLS certificate. AWS uses the list of thumbprints to verify that the token really came from GitHub. If the right thumbprint isn't on the list, AWS doesn't trust the token, and the job can't assume the role and get into the account.


We add the missing thumbprints and rerun the workflow. On the second try the infrastructure is created: the log shows the terraform plan and how many resources were created. We check that the database is ready and the load balancer is in place, and mark the steps as done.

Deploying the app: a second failure, then the site

We run Deploy Application, and it also fails the first time: the healthcheck doesn't pass. The deploy finished too quickly, and the app wasn't ready by the time of the check. This is expected, and the next step of the plan says exactly that: rerun the deploy. So we do.


On the second run the deploy passes and the smoke test is green. We open the CloudFront address and see the art-supply store, the service we set out to deploy.


We mark the remaining steps and click Finish. nib closes the plan, writes a report on the work done and updates the knowledge base. Next time a task about this project comes in, the agent will already know that it has a VPC, an ECS cluster and a database, and won't start from zero.

Wrapping up

We took an ordinary task: deploy a web service to AWS and set up GitHub jobs to deploy it. In two minutes nib split it into four stages with ten steps, fifteen checks and a rollback plan. The agent prepared AWS and GitHub access on its own over MCP, the executor wrote the Terraform and the workflows, and we worked through two failures on the way, the OIDC provider and the healthcheck, together with nib. At the end we opened the site and saw the store working.

Back to the three problems from Part 1:

  • Items don't get lost. The action list is written down in the plan. You can see it, hand it to a colleague and pick up where you left off.
  • Checks don't get skipped. They're written into every stage in advance, and the agent isn't tempted to save time on them. Still, the OIDC story showed that a check is only as useful as it is precise.
  • The size is visible before you start. You know how many stages and steps are ahead before the first command runs.

The decisions stay with you: you choose which steps to run, you read the PR, and you accept the result.

Even if you don't plan to use agents, try writing the plan for your next task in three columns: action, check, rollback. That alone solves the first problem and makes the second one much easier.

In Part 1 I said that an engineer relies on team rules and their own experience. You can give nib the same things. In the next post I'll show how to connect your own rules, skills and knowledge base, so the plans come out more accurate and closer to how your team works.

The repository is here: github.com/javdet/nib. Try it on a task of your own, and tell me in the comments: which infrastructure task would you trust to an agent first, and which one never?

title: Federated training performs as well as centralized for 3D Latent Diffusion for Diagnosis-Conditioned Brain MRI Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2611.08771v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative models of brain MRI are useful to understand brain conditions, and to enrich scarce and imbalanced neuroimaging data. However, training these models requires large, multi-site training sets, which is challenging. Federated learning (FL) allows for training deep learning models without sharing data. We show that training a 3D conditional latent model federatedly (where data is kept private at each site) performs similarly to centralized training (where all the data have been copied to a single site). We evaluate three metrics: conditional fidelity (how well generated MRIs perform in classification), diversity (how the generated images match the real data distribution, using MultiScale-SSIM), and realism (how close generated images are to real images, using Fr\'{e}chet Inception Distance). Our results show that federated training is a viable route to develop multi-site generative models of brain MRI.

title: Refer-CityFlow and M3Track: A Benchmark Dataset and Reference Framework for Language-Driven Multi-Target Multi-Camera Tracking
description:
arXiv:2611.08976v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Referring multi-object tracking enables users to specify targets through natural language, but existing Refer-MOT benchmarks primarily focus on single-camera settings. We formalize Referring Multi-Target Multi-Camera Tracking (Refer-MTMCT), where free-form queries specify identity-consistent trajectories to be recovered across a network of sequential, sparse-overlap cameras. We introduce Refer-CityFlow, a benchmark built on CityFlow's global cross-camera identity annotations and augmented with language queries requiring joint language grounding, cross-camera association, and spatio-temporal reasoning. Refer-CityFlow covers 96 videos from 40 roadside cameras with 660+ identity-consistent cross-camera trajectories, 4,362 trajectory-level descriptions, and 7,699 queries, including 1,699 real-user queries collected from 50 participants. Reference experiments on the four-camera Scenario 02 show that single-camera referring trackers reach 14.95-18.28 HOTA on real-user queries, while the evaluated cross-view method achieves about 0.05 HOTA in direct transfer. To establish reference performance, we provide M3Track, a modular multimodal reference framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent orchestrates interchangeable detection, tracking, and cross-camera association modules. M3Track reaches 44.10 HOTA and 65.40 IDF1 on the same real-user query set. The project repository is available at https://github.com/phuongnguyen194/Refer-CityFlow-and--M3Track.

title: GeoJeV: Unified Spatial Probability for Training-Free Efficient Evidence Acquisition in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
description:
arXiv:2611.08879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details but poses challenges for accurate and efficient multimodal understanding. Existing evidence acquisition methods selectively explore relevant image regions, yet largely rely on generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for intermediate search control. However, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) primarily aligns these models with human-preferred responses rather than explicitly optimizing region-level relevance judgments, while repeated autoregressive decoding introduces additional computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose GeoJeV, a training-free method that formulates evidence acquisition as spatial probability-driven decision making. At each evaluated region, a frozen JeV model produces a probability distribution over candidate regions. Specifically, Region Rank prioritizes candidate regions, Sparse Branch adaptively determines branching width through sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth based on branch sparsity and distribution concentration. By coordinating search priority, branching width, and refinement depth through a shared distribution, GeoJeV reduces reliance on RLHF-aligned generation and eliminates intermediate decoding. Experiments on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA achieve accuracies of 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32%, respectively. Across the three benchmarks, GeoJeV improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by +5.32pp with only 1.12 additional seconds per question, while achieving a 7.8-fold inference speedup over the recent method.

title: RTC Room Tokens Explained: 6 Identity and Permission Controls for Healthtech
description:
A patient-call notification is useful only if the intended clinician can join the intended room with the intended powers. Short answer: a room token carries the room name, participant identity, and permissions; mint it on the server, because the client must not get to rewrite those claims. Treat a permission change as a new-token event, not a UI toggle.

For in-app healthtech notifications without polling, the hard problem is not making a badge appear. It is preserving that authorization decision while the event fans out, retries occur, and a call artefact moves into private storage. I use six controls for that boundary. They are deliberately boring. Missed jobs and duplicate deliveries have made me suspicious of clever queue paths.

Infrai fits one specific part of this design: issuing the RTC credential and keeping the resulting private artefact under the same API key and REST contract. Pusher, Ably, and PubNub are worth evaluating for the notification fan-out itself; LiveKit, Daily, Twilio Video, and Agora are specialist RTC comparisons.

That's the map.

1. What Identity Does an RTC Room Token Carry?

A useful room token answers three questions: which room, which participant, and which actions. The room binds the credential to one call. Identity gives moderation and audit records a stable subject. Permissions decide what that subject may do.

Suppose a care coordinator receives an event for room consult-4821. The browser may display a Join button, but that button is not authority. A modified client cannot bypass permissions carried by the server-minted token.

Good.

Never mint this credential in the browser or mobile app. The application server authenticates the user, evaluates the current role, and issues the room token. Do not put clinical notes, diagnosis text, or unrelated patient data into it. None is needed to answer the three authorization questions.

2. Why can't the client change a participant's role?

Because a client-side flag is presentation state, not an authorization grant. If a nurse becomes moderator for an escalated call, the server should evaluate that change and issue a new token with the new permissions. The old token does not become stronger because the UI changed.

Identity is also the join point for operations. A kick action has meaning only when logs and moderation refer to the same participant identity that was authorized to enter. Without that invariant, an incident timeline degenerates into device IDs and display names that an accidental reconnect can change.

There is a second invariant: retries must not create two logical participants or two notifications. The fan-out transport may redeliver. Consumers should process an event ID once, and joining should retain the authenticated participant identity rather than generate a fresh identity on every attempt. Assume at-least-once delivery at the application edge. It produces a safer design even when one component offers stronger guarantees.

3. Carry one decision across notification fan-out

Push the in-app notification after the server has made the access decision, and include an opaque event ID plus the room reference the recipient needs. Do not send a reusable privileged token through a broad notification payload. Fetch or issue the room token at the authenticated join boundary.

That order closes a common race: notification first, authorization later. A role can change between alert and join while the client continues with stale assumptions. Server issuance turns the latest decision into the credential. If permissions change again, issue another token.

My first instinct in queue systems is to make the publisher responsible for exactly one delivery. That is the wrong place to spend confidence. Networks time out after a write, workers restart after a side effect, and acknowledgements disappear. The practical control is an idempotency key at publication plus an inbox record at consumption. Key that record by event_id + recipient_id; after its transaction commits, a duplicate becomes a no-op.

Consider the ugly sequence rather than the happy path. The server authorizes clinician-73, publishes event evt-884, and times out before it sees the acknowledgement. It publishes again. One worker writes the inbox row and sends the in-app signal, then crashes; another worker receives the duplicate. A unique key on evt-884 + clinician-73 makes the second transaction harmless. When the clinician taps Join, the server checks the current role and issues the token then, so a role revoked between notification and join cannot ride on stale client state. No promise of exactly-once transport is needed. The database invariant carries the load.

The contracts differ. The event says, "there is a call for you." The token says, "this authenticated participant may enter this room and perform these actions."

4. Join RTC to private storage under one trust boundary

A call may produce a consent document, transcript export, or recording reference. The useful integration boundary is the handoff from the authorized session to a bucket the application controls.

Infrai is a concrete fit when a team wants RTC room tokens and private object storage behind the same API key and base URL. Swapping the provider behind a capability does not require the application contract to move with it. Its public discovery response exposes each capability's method, path, request JSON Schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples, so a Go client can validate the live contract instead of copying an SDK-specific request type. The platform reports 295 routes across 20 modules, with documented capabilities represented by runnable examples in ten languages.

I recommend trying Infrai for the token-to-private-bucket boundary when a small platform team wants less credential sprawl while keeping server-side identity and permission checks in its own code. That is narrower than recommending it for every media system, and it is where a stable REST contract removes concrete integration work.

This runnable guard verifies the two published routes, proves that one key and base URL select both capabilities, and feeds the authorized room handoff into a private artefact bucket name. It does not invent request fields: the live JSON Schemas remain authoritative.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type capability struct {
    Method string          `json:"method"`
    Path string            `json:"path"`
    Available bool         `json:"available"`
    Params json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func discover(client *http.Client, id string) (capability, error) {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/discovery/"+id, nil)
    if err != nil { return capability{}, err }
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil { return capability{}, err }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        return capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery %s: %s", id, resp.Status)
    }
    var c capability
    err = json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&c)
    return c, err
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    rtc, err := discover(client, "rtc.token.issue")
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    storage, err := discover(client, "storage.bucket.create")
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    if !rtc.Available || rtc.Method != http.MethodPost || rtc.Path != "/v1/rtc/token/issue" {
        panic("RTC token contract changed or is unavailable")
    }
    if !storage.Available || storage.Method != http.MethodPost || storage.Path != "/v1/storage/bucket/create" {
        panic("storage contract changed or is unavailable")
    }
    room, participant := "consult-4821", "clinician-73"
    bucket := strings.ToLower(room + "-artefacts")
    auth := "Bearer " + key
    fmt.Printf("issue %s for %s, then create private bucket %s via %s\n",
        rtc.Path, participant, bucket, storage.Path)
    fmt.Printf("same base=%s same auth=%t schemas=%d/%d bytes\n",
        baseURL, strings.HasPrefix(auth, "Bearer ifr_"), len(rtc.Params), len(storage.Params))
}

Actual create calls generated from those schemas should use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, send an explicit POST, check every response status, and attach an idempotency key to writes. Storage stays private or signed-only. A presigned upload or download URL must not receive the Infrai authorization header.

One caveat deserves a plain sentence: consolidation means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface.

5. Compare credential friction before feature counts

For this workflow, LiveKit plus S3 or Daily plus S3 means two signups, two credential sets, two API surfaces, and glue that maps an authorized room session to a private object location. That separation may be desirable. It also has a cost.

Option Credential boundary Integration surface Better fit
Infrai RTC plus storage One key and base URL Plain REST and public discovery Stable capability contract and fewer secret rotations
LiveKit plus S3 Two signups and credential sets RTC tooling plus AWS storage APIs Specialist RTC with an existing AWS practice
Daily plus S3 Two signups and credential sets Call APIs plus AWS storage APIs Dedicated video product with accepted cross-service glue
Twilio Video plus object storage Separate media and storage credentials Video API plus chosen storage API Organization already standardized on Twilio operations
Agora plus object storage Separate media and storage credentials RTC surface plus chosen storage API Media-heavy product evaluating a specialist directly
Pusher plus RTC and storage providers At least three service boundaries Hosted channels plus separate media and storage APIs Teams already using Pusher Channels for app events
Ably plus RTC and storage providers At least three service boundaries Hosted messaging plus separate media and storage APIs Teams prioritizing Ably realtime messaging for fan-out
PubNub plus RTC and storage providers At least three service boundaries Event API plus separate media and storage APIs Teams with PubNub messaging expertise

Ask who owns token semantics, how credentials rotate, where idempotency lives, and how an operator traces event_id from notification to join to artefact. Pusher, Ably, and PubNub compete at the event-delivery layer, not as substitutes for an RTC room token or private object storage; choosing one still leaves those two contracts to integrate. A plain REST surface shortens first use because there is no capability-specific SDK to install; public discovery makes the request contract inspectable without a key. Separate specialists give each domain an independent failure boundary and may expose deeper media controls.

Choose the specialist when its media behavior is the requirement. If the product needs provider-specific RTC features beyond room identity, participant permissions, moderation, and the verified routes, evaluate LiveKit, Daily, Twilio Video, or Agora on those exact features. Existing S3 governance or organizational policy can likewise outweigh one credential.

6. Turn the invariant into a release checklist

Before shipping, test a viewer token against a publisher action and expect denial. Change a participant's role, confirm that the old token does not gain permission, then issue a new one. Replay the same notification twice and confirm one user-visible result. Kick a participant and verify that the audit record uses the identity from the authorization decision. Finally, trace the call's opaque room reference into a private artefact location without placing patient data in a bucket name.

Keep rollback dull. Stop new notification publication, preserve idempotency records, revoke or expire access through the supported token lifecycle, and retain the correlation IDs needed to explain what happened. Do not repair an authorization incident with client flags.

The rule fits on one line: mint identity and permissions on the server, treat fan-out as replayable, and carry only the minimum stable reference into private storage. If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect live discovery before writing a request.

Sources

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • LiveKit authentication and tokens
  • Daily meeting tokens
  • Twilio Video access tokens
  • Agora token authentication
  • Amazon S3 security best practices

title: yolow64: a Base64 codec for Rust that outruns the incumbents — extracted from PageSift
description:
While building PageSift (a Rust web-content engine for LLM pipelines), I kept hitting Base64 in places where throughput and allocation control actually matter: browser screenshots, MCP resources, proxy authentication. The codec that grew inside PageSift is now its own MIT-licensed library: yolow64.

  • Runtime-dispatched SIMD: AVX2 (with an assembly bulk decode loop on Linux x86-64), NEON on AArch64, scalar fallback; runtime detection is cached.
  • Zero runtime dependencies, std only, Rust 1.89+.
  • Slice / append / owned-output APIs, validation without decoding, streaming decode, and a one-shot data-URL builder.
  • Whitespace-tolerant mode ignores exactly space/tab/CR/LF in a single pass — built for MIME-style input.

Measured on an i7-10700 (same process, three full runs, medians of seven-round medians; full method, charts and raw CSVs in the repo):

  • Strict mode at 4 KiB–4 MiB: ~6.5–9× faster than the base64 crate, ~1.7–2.5× faster than base64-simd, encode and decode.
  • CRLF-tolerant decode: ~4× faster than base64-simd's forgiving_decode at the same sizes.
  • On the same machine it runs level with moego, the fastest Go implementation I measured.
  • Honest footnote: at ≤128 B inputs the three libraries trade wins — those differences are nanoseconds and noise-sensitive, and the repo's tables print them as-is. The whitespace modes also don't accept exactly the same inputs across libraries; the comparison covers valid padded CRLF inputs. 
[dependencies]
yolow64 = "0.1"

Repo: https://github.com/YOLOW92/yolow64 — benchmarks are reproducible from the included harness; corrections welcome.

title: Notes on generating QR codes for print: error correction, logo holes and quiet zones
description:
I work on sellphotos.online, where this was originally published.

Every event on sellphotos.online gets a QR code. Photographers print it on posters, notice boards and table cards, or put it on the last slide at a prize-giving. Guests scan it in poor light, at an angle, through glare on a laminated sheet. We generate the codes ourselves with the small uqr encoder, then draw them with our own code. These are the decisions that came out of that.

Pick the error correction level per medium

QR codes carry Reed-Solomon error correction at four levels. Roughly, these are the share of codewords that can be recovered:

level recoverable
L ~7%
M ~15%
Q ~25%
H ~30%

Higher levels need more modules for the same data, so at a fixed print size each module gets smaller. We use three levels, one for each place a code ends up:

  • M for codes read off a screen. These are the UPI and Pix payment codes on a buyer's order page. A screen is flat, lit and clean.
  • Q for printed event codes. Paper gets scuffed, laminate catches glare, and cheap printers blur edges.
  • H when a logo sits in the middle, because the logo hides modules on purpose.

For scale: a 35-character event link such as https://sellphotos.online/e/AbC1234 comes out as version 3 (29×29 modules) at M, version 4 (33×33) at Q and version 5 (37×37) at H.

The logo hole

Plenty of generators paste a logo over the finished code and count on error correction to cope. We clear a square of modules first and draw the logo inside it, with a little padding, so no dark modules peek out around a transparent logo:

// apps/web/app/lib/qr.ts
export const LOGO_RATIO = 0.24;

export function logoHole(matrix: QrMatrix, ratio = LOGO_RATIO): QrHole {
  let size = Math.max(3, Math.round(matrix.size * ratio));
  if (size % 2 !== matrix.size % 2) size += 1; // same parity: exactly centred
  const x = (matrix.size - size) / 2;
  return { x, y: x, size };
}

The parity line is easy to miss. A QR code's side is always odd (21 + 4 × (version − 1)), so an even-sized hole can't sit exactly in the middle. (size − hole) / 2 would land on a half module. Bumping the hole to the same parity keeps it centred on whole modules.

The hole is 24% of the side. At version 5 with H, that's a 9×9 hole in a 37×37 code: 81 of 1,369 modules, about 6%. H can recover about 30%, so most of that margin is left for scuffs, glare and print blur. That's an approximation, since modules map onto codewords unevenly and codewords are interleaved across blocks. Even so, a hole of a few percent behind a ~30% budget leaves real slack.

Also check where the function patterns are. At version 5, the only alignment pattern sits near the bottom-right corner, well clear of a hole spanning modules 14 to 22. From version 7 up, alignment patterns appear in the centre as well, so a long URL with a logo would put one under the logo. Short links matter here.

Quiet zone, and a caption that stays out of it

The standard (ISO/IEC 18004) asks for four light modules on every side, and we keep all four. Photographers can add the event title as a caption. It goes in its own band below the quiet zone, so the zone stays clear. Long titles are cut at 40 characters, and the font size comes from a rough width estimate (a bold sans is about 0.58 em per glyph), so we never measure text.

One path string, three outputs

The Share dialog shows a live preview and offers an SVG download, PNGs and a printable table card. They all come from one function that turns the matrix into SVG path data, in module units:

// square style (simplified): each row's dark runs become one rectangle
for (let y = 0; y < size; y++) {
  let x = 0;
  while (x < size) {
    if (!data[y][x]) { x++; continue; }
    let end = x;
    while (end < size && data[y][end]) end++;
    parts.push(`M${x + margin} ${y + margin}h${end - x}v1h-${end - x}z`);
    x = end;
  }
}

Merging runs keeps the path short. The rounded style draws data modules as dots of radius 0.48, slightly under half a module so they stay distinct. It draws the finder patterns as nested rounded squares and fills them with evenodd, which punches out their holes.

That one string feeds three renderers:

  • the React preview, as <path d={…}>
  • the SVG download, where the path goes into a standalone document on a white background
  • the PNG, drawn on a canvas with ctx.fill(new Path2D(d), "evenodd")

We never draw an SVG onto the canvas through an <img>. That keeps us clear of canvas tainting and of img-src rules for data: and blob: URLs, and because every output comes from the same geometry, they always match.

A few details on the PNG side:

  • Whole pixels per module. modulePx = Math.floor(width / side), and the code is centred in what's left over. A fractional module size blurs the edges between modules.
  • A size cap. The canvas stops at 4096 × 4096 pixels. The printable table card is A6 portrait at about 300 dpi (1240 × 1748 px).
  • Fonts first. A canvas doesn't wait for web fonts, so we await document.fonts.load(...) before drawing the caption. Otherwise the first download comes out in a fallback font.
  • The logo inside the SVG is embedded as a PNG data: URL, so the file stands alone when it goes to a print shop. It's re-encoded to PNG because design and print tools read PNG inside SVG, but not always WebP.

Colour

Photographers can pick a colour for the modules. We compute the WCAG contrast ratio against white and warn below 4.5. Our own note in the code puts the point where codes may stop scanning at about 3, so the warning fires with a margin to spare.

Keeping the encoder out of the client bundle

The encoder is small, but most visitors never need it, so we keep it out of the main bundle in two ways.

  1. Lazy loading for sellers. The Share dialog loads its QR tab on demand, so uqr ships only in that chunk.
  2. Server-only for buyers. The UPI payment code on a buyer's order page is built in the route's loader. React Router's client build drops loaders, and the QR module and uqr go with it. The browser receives a side length and a path string, and fills a Path2D: 
// apps/web/app/routes/buyer/order.tsx (simplified)
// Loader only: used in a component, this would ship the encoder to every buyer.
function upiHandoff(p: UpiPayment) {
  const uri = upiUri(p);
  const matrix = encodeQr(uri, "M"); // read off a screen
  return { uri, qr: { side: matrix.size + QUIET_ZONE * 2, path: qrModulePath(matrix) } };
}

The comment is there for the next person to touch that file. One import from a component would quietly put the encoder back into every buyer's download.

What we'd check before trusting a design

None of this replaces printing the thing. Before calling a style or logo size done, we'd print it at the size people will actually use, scan it from across a room with an older phone, and try it under a ceiling light reflecting off laminate. The numbers above say how much damage a code should survive. Testing on paper shows whether it does.

The code above lives in a photo-selling app. Each event's QR code opens a gallery where guests find their photos with a selfie. If you're curious what's at the other end of the scan, there's a sample gallery.

title: Insert Returning In JooqTemplate
description:
Using JooqTemplate requires no code generation and no XML configuration.

Add Dependency

gradle:

implementation 'net.sf.sprtool:sprtool-jooq:1.7.0'

maven:

<dependency>
    <groupId>net.sf.sprtool</groupId>
    <artifactId>sprtool-jooq</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

Inject JooqTemplate 

import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqTemplate;

@Autowired
private JooqTemplate jt;

Using JooqTemplate

Inserting with a Table Object

Pass a jOOQ Table object built with DSL.table(...) as the first argument; the behavior is exactly the same as passing the table name string — with a partial-field insert, unset fields are null, and an empty Map also inserts 1 record:

import org.jooq.Table;
import org.jooq.impl.DSL;

Table<?> productTable = DSL.table("product");

Map<String, Object> product = new HashMap<>();
product.put("name", "Bluetooth Headset");
product.put("category", "Electronics");
product.put("price", 299.00);

int result = jt.insert(productTable, product);
// result == 1

Passing a null Map throws NullPointerException / IllegalArgumentException; when the table does not exist, an exception is thrown and its message contains the table name.

insertReturningv: Insert and Return Specified Fields

insertReturningv(table, values, fieldName...) inserts one record and returns a jOOQ Record containing the specified fields. The typical scenario is getting the auto-increment primary key id:

import org.jooq.Record;

Map<String, Object> order = new HashMap<>();
order.put("order_no", "A20260002");
order.put("user_id", 1001);
order.put("amount", 698.00);

// Returns the two fields id and order_no
Record returned = jt.insertReturningv("order", order, "id", "order_no");

Integer id = returned.get("id", Integer.class);           // auto-increment id generated by the database
String orderNo = returned.get("order_no", String.class);

Returning Database-Generated Default Value Fields

The returned field list can include fields not assigned during the insert, such as create_time generated by database defaults:

Map<String, Object> product = new HashMap<>();
product.put("name", "Smart Band");
product.put("price", 199.00);

Record returned = jt.insertReturningv("product", product,
        "id", "name", "price", "create_time");

assertNotNull(returned.get("id", Integer.class));  // auto-increment primary key
assertNotNull(returned.get("create_time"));        // database default value

insertReturningv with a Table Object

The first argument also accepts a Table object:

Table<?> productTable = DSL.table("product");
Record returned = jt.insertReturningv(productTable, product, "id", "name");
String name = returned.get("name", String.class);

Without Specifying Return Fields

When no return fields are passed, the insert executes normally but the method returns null — be sure to pass "id" when you need the primary key:

Record returned = jt.insertReturningv("product", product);
// returned == null; the record was inserted but no return value is available

Edge Cases

  • The table named or corresponding to the Table object does not exist: throws an exception whose message contains the table name.
  • Returned fields are read by type via Record.get(fieldName, type), e.g. get("id", Integer.class).

title: How to Integrate WhatsApp Cloud API into Custom SaaS Platforms: A Step-by-Step Guide
description:
Introduction to WhatsApp Cloud API in Modern SaaS

Integrating direct messaging channels into multi-tenant software has evolved from a nice-to-have feature into a mission-critical infrastructure requirement. Whether you are building automated lead alerts, transactional notification engines, or conversational commerce pipelines, Meta's official WhatsApp Cloud API offers a direct, scalable conduit to your user base.

As a Senior Software Architect operating out of Kochi, I frequently help growing tech startups and MSMEs move away from fragile, third-party wrapper APIs to direct Meta Cloud API integrations. Doing this right requires deep technical discipline: handling asynchronous webhooks, implementing robust cryptographic signature validation, and managing rate limits without dropping outbound notifications.

Architectural Overview: The Event-Driven Pipeline

When scaling a SaaS platform that handles high volumes of WhatsApp messages, a direct synchronous call from your user action to the Meta Graph API is a recipe for failure. Network latency spikes or Meta rate-limiting (e.g., tier-based limits starting at 1,000 conversations/day) will block your core application threads.

A production-grade architecture relies on an asynchronous event-driven pattern:

  1. Outbound Trigger: Your core business logic (e.g., a subscription renewal alert or a CRM Software Development in Kerala pipeline status change) pushes a job onto a durable queue (e.g., Redis via BullMQ).
  2. Worker Isolation: Dedicated Node.js worker processes pop the job, format the WhatsApp payload, and execute the HTTP POST request to the Meta Graph API v20.0+ endpoint.
  3. Inbound Webhook Receiver: Meta posts incoming user replies and message status updates (sent, delivered, read) to your public-facing webhook endpoint.
  4. Signature Verification & Processing: Your webhook parser validates the X-Hub-Signature-256 header, acknowledges Meta with a 200 OK instantly, and dispatches the event payload to an internal event bus for state updates.

Step 1: Configuring the Node.js Webhook Receiver

Meta requires two distinct HTTP routes for webhook integration: a GET route for initial handshake verification and a POST route for real-time payload delivery. Below is a production-tested Express.js implementation incorporating HMAC SHA-256 signature verification.

import express, { Request, Response } from 'express';
import crypto from 'crypto';

const app = express();

// Raw body parsing is mandatory for cryptographic signature validation
app.use(express.json({
  verify: (req: Request & { rawBody?: Buffer }, res: Response, buf: Buffer) => {
    req.rawBody = buf;
  }
}));

const WEBHOOK_VERIFY_TOKEN = process.env.WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN;
const APP_SECRET = process.env.WHATSAPP_APP_SECRET || '';

// 1. Webhook Handshake Verification
app.get('/api/v1/webhooks/whatsapp', (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const mode = req.query['hub.mode'];
  const token = req.query['hub.verify_token'];
  const challenge = req.query['hub.challenge'];

  if (mode === 'subscribe' && token === WEBHOOK_VERIFY_TOKEN) {
    return res.status(200).send(challenge);
  }
  return res.sendStatus(403);
});

// 2. Inbound Event Payload Processor
app.post('/api/v1/webhooks/whatsapp', (req: Request & { rawBody?: Buffer }, res: Response) => {
  const signature = req.headers['x-hub-signature-256'] as string;

  if (!signature || !verifySignature(req.rawBody, signature, APP_SECRET)) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid signature' });
  }

  // Acknowledge Meta immediately to prevent webhook retries
  res.sendStatus(200);

  const body = req.body;
  if (body.object === 'whatsapp_business_account') {
    processWhatsAppEvents(body);
  }
});

function verifySignature(rawBody: Buffer | undefined, signature: string, secret: string): boolean {
  if (!rawBody) return false;
  const expectedHash = 'sha256=' + crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(rawBody).digest('hex');
  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(signature), Buffer.from(expectedHash));
}

async function processWhatsAppEvents(payload: any) {
  // Dispatch to event bus or queue (e.g., BullMQ)
  for (const entry of payload.entry) {
    for (const change of entry.changes) {
      if (change.field === 'messages') {
        const messages = change.value.messages;
        const statuses = change.value.statuses;

        if (messages) {
          // Handle incoming customer messages
          console.log('Received message:', messages[0]);
        }
        if (statuses) {
          // Handle delivery receipts (sent, delivered, read)
          console.log('Status update:', statuses[0]);
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

app.listen(4000, () => console.log('WhatsApp webhook engine active on port 4000'));

Step 2: Implementing Resilient Outbound Messaging Services

When transmitting template or session messages via the Meta Graph API, always handle transient network errors, HTTP 429 rate limits, and expired tokens gracefully. Here is an enterprise-grade service pattern written in TypeScript.

import axios, { AxiosInstance } from 'axios';

interface SendMessagePayload {
  messaging_product: 'whatsapp';
  to: string;
  type: 'text' | 'template';
  text?: { body: string };
  template?: {
    name: string;
    language: { code: string };
    components?: Array<any>;
  };
}

export class WhatsAppCloudService {
  private client: AxiosInstance;

  constructor(accessToken: string, phoneNumberId: string) {
    this.client = axios.create({
      baseURL: `https://graph.facebook.com/v20.0/${phoneNumberId}`,
      headers: {
        'Authorization': `Bearer ${accessToken}`,
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      },
      timeout: 10000,
    });
  }

  public async sendMessage(payload: SendMessagePayload): Promise<string> {
    try {
      const response = await this.client.post('/messages', payload);
      return response.data.messages[0].id;
    } catch (error: any) {
      const errorDetails = error.response?.data?.error || error.message;
      console.error('WhatsApp API dispatch failure:', JSON.stringify(errorDetails));

      // Implement custom exponential backoff or dead-letter queue routing here
      throw new Error(`WhatsApp Send Error: ${JSON.stringify(errorDetails)}`);
    }
  }
}

Architectural Best Practices for Production SaaS

  • Idempotency is Mandatory: Meta webhooks can occasionally deliver duplicate events due to network timeouts. Always store message IDs in your PostgreSQL or MongoDB instance with unique constraints to prevent duplicate processing.
  • Token Management: Never hardcode system user access tokens. Store them encrypted at rest within your multi-tenant database schema, paired with automated token rotation workflows.
  • Isolate Webhook Ingestion: Keep your webhook response loop under 200 milliseconds. Offload heavy database queries or AI-driven WhatsApp Automation in Kerala workflows to background workers immediately after validating the signature.
  • Local Infrastructure Considerations: If you are bootstrapping software initiatives or evaluating regional engineering budgets, understanding local market realities through a Freelance Software Developer in Kochi ensures you optimize your cloud infrastructure without incurring bloated agency overhead.

Summary & Fit Criteria

Integrating the WhatsApp Cloud API directly into your custom SaaS architecture eliminates third-party SaaS markup fees, grants you granular control over conversation data, and allows deep workflow customization.

This approach is ideal if:

  • You are scaling an existing SaaS platform requiring high-throughput, automated user notifications.
  • You operate a multi-tenant application needing strict data privacy and direct webhook ownership.

Consider alternative paths if:

  • You require a plug-and-play marketing inbox with zero developer involvement (though you sacrifice custom business logic integration).

He specializes in high-velocity Next.js 15 SaaS platforms, 60fps Flutter mobile applications, sub-10ms Node.js enterprise APIs, and production AI/RAG integrations.
