title: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3: Open-Weight MoE Scores #2 on SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning, Beating Gemini and Grok
description:
Darwin-180B-RSI-R3: Open-Weight MoE Scores #2 on SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning, Beating Gemini and Grok

TL;DR: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a 180-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model from VIDRAFT that scored 73.68 on the SuperCLUE November 2026 math and science reasoning dimension — ranking #2 overall and #1 among open-weight models on an independently administered, non-public test. It activates only ~3B parameters per token, ships weights under a Qwen community license permitting commercial use, and has a 4-bit quantized variant that runs on a 32 GB RAM laptop without a GPU.

What it is

Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model built on top of Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as a base. Key facts from the source:

  • Parameter count: 180B total, with roughly 3B activated per token at inference time
  • Architecture lineage: Inherits the expert layers from Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — 512 experts per layer, with the bulk of world knowledge stored in those feed-forward network (FFN) blocks
  • What changed vs. the base: Only the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared expert layers were retrained using a self-improvement process; the FFN expert blocks were kept intact
  • License: Qwen community license, open-weight, commercial use permitted
  • Edge variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF — a 4-bit quantized GGUF version designed to run from SSD on a 32 GB RAM consumer laptop, no GPU required
  • Developer: VIDRAFT (South Korean Pre-AGI AI startup)

The model was independently evaluated by SuperCLUE on November 5, 2026. SuperCLUE is a Chinese LLM benchmark that evolved from the 2019 CLUE (Chinese Language Understanding Evaluation) project. It issues fresh, non-public test sets each month and scores models across five dimensions: agentic coding, math & science reasoning, hallucination suppression, precise instruction following, and long-context understanding.

How it works

The core idea behind Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is surgical retraining: instead of fine-tuning an entire large model, VIDRAFT preserved the FFN expert layers — which encode the model's factual and domain knowledge — and exclusively retrained the components most responsible for multi-step reasoning: the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared experts.

The retraining mechanism is described in Korean media coverage as a self-improvement loop: the model generates its own problems, produces candidate answers, verifies those answers internally, and uses that feedback signal to update weights. This is conceptually similar to self-play or self-distillation approaches common in the reasoning research literature, applied specifically to the layers governing how the model attends to and routes information rather than what it knows.

The practical consequence of this design choice: the same 512-expert FFN knowledge base as the parent model, but with reasoning-focused layers optimized through iterative self-generated supervision.

Benchmarks & results

All numbers below come directly from the SuperCLUE November 2026 leaderboard (published 2026-11-05) and are independently administered — not self-reported by VIDRAFT.

Metric Score / Rank
SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning 73.68 (2nd of 19 models)
SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning — open-weight rank #1
SuperCLUE 5-dimension composite index 43.08 (9th of 19 models, 5th among open-weight)
GPQA Diamond (Hugging Face leaderboard) 94.44 (ranked #1 at time of reporting)
Score delta vs. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next base (math & science reasoning) +15.8 points
Composite rank improvement vs. base +6 positions

The model ranked above Google Gemini, xAI's Grok, and DeepSeek on the math & science reasoning dimension. The only model ahead of it was GPT-6.1-Sol at 76.32.

Important context: SuperCLUE places non-Chinese models on the same table for reference but does not include them in its official ranking. The 73.68 score is from a held-out, non-public November test set — not a contamination-prone static benchmark.

How to try it

The source article confirms that model weights are publicly available. Based on the information reported:

  • Weights: Released under the Qwen community license (commercial use allowed). Check the VIDRAFT organization page on Hugging Face for Darwin-180B-RSI-R3.
  • Edge/CPU variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF (4-bit quantized) is designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running inference from SSD — no GPU required. Look for it on Hugging Face under VIDRAFT's model hub.

The source does not publicly document a specific API endpoint, GitHub repository URL, or installation command for this release. Check VIDRAFT's official channels for the latest access instructions before deployment.

FAQ

Q: Why does the model score #2 on reasoning but only #9 overall on SuperCLUE?
A: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 was specifically optimized for math and science reasoning. The five-dimension SuperCLUE composite also includes agentic coding, hallucination suppression, instruction following, and long-context tasks — areas where the model was not specifically retrained. The result is a narrow specialist that excels on its target dimension while sitting mid-table overall.

Q: Is retraining only the attention layers a proven approach, or experimental?
A: The approach is conceptually grounded in existing research showing that FFN layers store factual knowledge while attention layers govern reasoning and information routing. The +15.8-point gain on an independently scored, non-public benchmark is a concrete external data point, though a single benchmark result should always be interpreted alongside broader evaluation.

Q: Can I run the full 180B model on consumer hardware?
A: Not the full-precision model. The POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF 4-bit quantized variant is specifically designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running from SSD without a GPU, according to the source coverage.

Q: Does the Qwen community license allow me to use this in a commercial product?
A: The source states commercial use is permitted under the Qwen community license. Always review the full license text in the model repository before production deployment.

title: The Print Layer of app.onepassapps.com: One Button, Two Print Media Queries, and 314 Elements That Vanish
description:
I work on OnePassApps, so this is our own site's own print layer. Every number below was measured on app.onepassapps.com on 9 November 2026: the stylesheet and the page HTML with plain HTTPS, and the layout with one real Chrome on our own desktop, switching the tab into print media through the browser's own emulation.

We have already written about the head, the JSON-LD, the headers and the compression of these pages. This one is about what happens to our pages when somebody prints them.

What I measured

  • The stylesheet our terms page links: /assets/index-D4M6hlLQ.css, 255,426 bytes
  • Every media query in that file, including the two that only apply to print
  • The served HTML of all 56 URLs in our sitemap.xml, looking for print-related markers
  • Six pages opened one at a time in Chrome, then switched into print media and read again

Two print rules in one stylesheet

That stylesheet contains exactly two print media queries. Here they are, byte for byte from the file:

@media print{.gd{width:auto;padding-top:0}.gd-top{width:auto;height:auto;padding-top:0;position:static}}

@media print{:root:has([data-public-info-page]){--lightningcss-light:initial;--lightningcss-dark: ;color-scheme:light}:root body:has([data-public-info-page]) :not(:has([data-public-info-page]),[data-public-info-page],[data-public-info-page] *){display:none}:root:has([data-public-info-page]){block-size:auto;min-block-size:max-content;max-block-size:none;inline-size:auto;box-shadow:none;background:0 0;border:0;margin:0;padding:0;display:block;position:static;overflow:visible}[data-public-info-page],[data-public-info-page] [data-slot=reader-layout]{padding:0;display:block}[data-public-info-page] [data-slot=toc-pane],[data-public-info-page] [data-slot=toc-bar],[data-public-info-page] [data-policy-print-control]{display:none}[data-public-info-page] *{max-block-size:none;box-shadow:none;color:#000;background:0 0;border-color:#0000;transition:none;overflow:visible}[data-public-info-page] [data-policy-section]{break-inside:auto}[data-public-info-page] h2{break-after:avoid}}

The first rule belongs to the guide pages: it unpins the fixed guide header and drops the top padding. The second belongs to the one policy page: it hides everything that is not inside the policy article, and it sets the policy text to black on white.

Neither rule lives in a page's HTML. Both live in the stylesheet, and the policy rule is keyed to an attribute the page only gets after JavaScript has run.

The one button, and what it calls

Of the six pages I opened, exactly one carries a print control: the terms page. Its label is "Print or save these terms". It is a button inside a span carrying the data-policy-print-control marker and the class "contents", and its click handler is one call to window.print().

The other two apps that print do it their own way, with their own buttons: the Label and Card Maker offers "Print sheets", the Calendar Maker offers "Print / save PDF". Neither uses the policy marker. The plans page and the vote board have no print button at all.

Here is the handler, out of the one JavaScript file that carries it - /assets/App-ClDc4c2D.js, 157,904 bytes:

(0,J.jsx)(`span`,{"data-policy-print-control":``,className:`contents`,children:(0,J.jsx)(p,{icon:kt,label:qa,onClick:()=>window.print()})})

That was the only one of the 109 distinct JavaScript files those six page loads fetched that contains the label, the marker or the call.

The terms page, before and after print

The served HTML of our terms page is 74,495 bytes and carries twelve data-policy-section markers - but no policy page marker and no print control, because both are added by React after the page loads. In the live DOM the page has one policy article, one print control, twelve policy sections, fourteen headings, a table-of-contents pane, a table-of-contents bar, a reader layout and twelve buttons.

Switching that same tab into print media changes it like this:

screen print
visible elements 647 271
main element flex, 1344px, relative block, 1590px, static
reader layout grid, 1270px block, 1590px
table-of-contents pane flex, 400px, sticky none
print control contents none
policy text colour rgb(245, 243, 239) rgb(0, 0, 0)
page background rgb(16, 15, 14) transparent
heading break-after auto avoid

314 of the page's 695 elements are display:none once print media is on, and none of them are hidden with visibility instead. The policy article's own text and its headings turn black, while the outer main element keeps its light text colour.

One detail worth being precise about: the root element's own computed colour-scheme still reads "dark" in print, even though the print rule declares a light scheme for the policy page. The black text comes from the rule's own colour declaration, not from the scheme flipping.

The guide pages

The guide rule is much smaller, and it hides nothing. On our word counter guide the guide container measures 1600px wide with 100px of top padding on screen; in print it is 1590px with no top padding, and the fixed guide header becomes static, 1568px wide, with its 16px of top padding removed. The number of visible elements does not change at all: 177 before, 177 after. The same holds on the CV builder guide, 165 before and 165 after.

So printing a guide page keeps the site's chrome and simply unpins the header. Nothing on a guide page is hidden by the print rules, and the guide pages carry no print control of their own.

Which pages reach a print rule

The terms page is the only policy page. Our privacy path redirects to /terms#privacy, our refunds path to /terms#payments, our legal path to /terms, and our support path is an ordinary page of its own.

Of the 56 URLs in our sitemap, 23 carry the guide marker gd-top - the guides index and 22 guides. Exactly one carries the policy section markers, the terms page. No sitemap URL serves the policy print marker in its HTML at all.

What I did not measure

I emulated print media; I never printed anything to paper and never produced a PDF, so I cannot tell you how these pages paginate, how many sheets they take, or whether a heading lands badly at a page break. I did not open the browser's own print dialog. I opened two of the 23 guide pages, not all of them. I did not test a second browser, a phone's share-to-print, or a dark-mode print. One build, one browser, one day.

If you want to look for yourself, open the terms page, ask the browser for a print preview, and compare it with the screen: the table of contents, the print button and the chrome around the article are gone, and the terms are black on white.

Our terms page: https://app.onepassapps.com/terms?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=print-layer&utm_content=terms-link

Our guides: https://app.onepassapps.com/guides?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=print-layer&utm_content=guides-link

title: A Hash That Collided on Every Name and a 25 MB Allocator Trap: What 4 Tracks of Speed Demon 2026 Taught Us About OS, Cache Hierarchy, and AI
description:
TL;DR: For Speed Demon 2026 by Hackathon Raptors, our team (cONFIG) rewrote four deliberately slow Python reference implementations in zero-dependency Rust and C++23:

  • a 3.1M-line log aggregator (Track A, 32.05 s → 0.034 s, 942×)
  • a 50,000-query boolean and phrase search engine over 256 MB of text (Track B, 56.35 s → 0.252 s, 223×)
  • a 3.32M-row hostile CSV join (Track C, 14.44 s → 0.052 s, 277×)
  • a 5M-edge shortest-path solver (Track D, 72.69 s → 0.456 s, 159×)

This is the story of the mistakes that cost us the most time: a hash function that passed every SHA-256 gate while routing 100% of customer names into a single L1 slot, an munmap call that made memory no smaller and wall time worse, Golden Cove L1/L2/L3 cache sizing across 12 hyperthreads, and why golfing line count with AI traps you in a local optimum until you do the hardware and scoring-function math yourself.

Repository: https://github.com/Yash-vs9/cOnfig-tracks

Where All Four Tracks Ended Up

We entered all four tracks with zero external dependencies (D = 1.00), targeting the Falkenstein scoring box (fsn1): Intel Core i5-13500, 6 Golden Cove P-cores / 12 threads pinned via --cpuset-cpus="0-11", turbo disabled at a fixed 2.50 GHz, 48 KiB L1d and 1.25 MiB L2 per P-core, 24 MiB shared L3.

Track Task & Dataset Language Reference (T_ref / M_ref) Our Best (T / M / S) Speedup Memory Reduction K / Speed Score
Track A Ingest (3.1M logs, 239 MB) Rust (2024) 32.05 s / 228 MB 0.034 s / 35 MB / 334 lines (282a0d6) 942× 6.5× 34.19 (76.70)
Track B Index (256 MB corpus, 50k queries) Rust (2024) 56.35 s / 2,199 MB 0.252 s / 75 MB / 1782 lines (282a0d6) 223× 29.3× 18.84 (63.75)
Track C Join (3.32M hostile CSV rows, 204 MB) C++23 14.44 s / 367 MB 0.052 s / 15 MB / 332 lines (1e59383) 277× 24.5× 26.72 (71.34)
Track D Traverse (1.74M nodes, 5M edges, 2k queries) Rust (2024) 72.69 s / 893 MB 0.456 s / 83 MB / 704 lines (282a0d6) 159× 10.8× 13.34 (56.26)

The final numbers look clean in a table. Getting there was a sequence of wrong assumptions that the Falkenstein box corrected one by one.

1. The Hash That Passed Every Gate and Missed the L1 Cache 99.98% of the Time (Track C)

Track C asks you to join records.csv (3.32M rows) against regions.csv and emit per-region aggregates, including the exact count of distinct customer_names per region (dn).

To avoid cross-core atomic contention on every row, we put a thread-local 2-way L1 filter tl_cache[2048][2] (32 KB per thread) in front of a lock-free global hash table (name_keys[1 << 18] + a 256-bit region bitset name_bits[1 << 18][4]). If (name_hash, region_id) was already in the thread's tl_cache, we skipped the global table entirely.

Here is the exact hash_bytes function we shipped in commit 1e59383 (0.052 s, 15 MB, 71.344 pts):

static inline uint64_t hash_bytes(const char *s, uint32_t len) {
  uint64_t h1 = len ^ 0x811c9dc5ULL, h2 = (uint64_t)len * 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL, w = 0, w1 = 0;
  if (__builtin_expect(len - 8U <= 8U, 1)) {
    memcpy(&w, s, 8), memcpy(&w1, s + len - 8, 8);
    h1 = _mm_crc32_u64(_mm_crc32_u64(h1, w), w1);
    h2 = ((h2 ^ w) * 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL ^ w1) * 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL;
    return ((h1 << 32) ^ h2) | 0x100ULL;
  }
  // ...
}

And inside the hot loop, we indexed the thread-local L1 filter using the low 11 bits of nh:

uint32_t tl_idx = (uint32_t)nh & 2047;

It compiled cleanly. It passed every correctness check with an exact SHA-256 match. And when we shrunk the global table in commit 282a0d6 (10 MB), our time actually regressed from 0.052 s to 0.066 s.

Why? We finally dumped the raw hex output of hash_bytes across customer names from the generator ("Person_1001", "Person_1002", "Person_2500", "Person_9999"):

Customer Name 64-Bit Hash (nh) Low 32 Bits ((uint32_t)nh) tl_idx = nh & 2047
"Person_1001" 0x369c194012cced30 0x12cced30 1328
"Person_1002" 0x10cceab412cced30 0x12cced30 1328
"Person_2500" 0xa08aee2a12cced30 0x12cced30 1328
"Person_5555" 0xfba9c18c12cced30 0x12cced30 1328
"Person_9999" 0xde6fb35212cced30 0x12cced30 1328

Every 11-byte "Person_XXXX" string had the exact same lower 32 bits (0x12cced30) and hashed to tl_idx = 1328.

Look at what happened in the registers:

  • For "Person_1001" (len = 11), w (first 8 bytes) is "Person_1" and w1 (last 8 bytes at s + 3) is "son_1001".
  • On little-endian x86-64, "son_" (0x5f6e6f73) occupies bits 0..31 of w1, while the digits "1001" occupy bits 32..63.
  • Modular 64-bit multiplication (mod 2^64) shifts bits strictly upward. Bits 32..63 of w1 never flow downward into bits 0..31 of h2!
  • Meanwhile, (h1 << 32) put the hardware CRC32 entirely into the upper 32 bits.

Because the upper 32 bits (h1) differed, the global hash table (slot = (nh ^ (nh >> 32)) & HT_MASK) still produced the right answer, so every correctness test passed. But tl_idx = (uint32_t)nh & 2047 looked only at the bottom 11 bits, where "Person_" and "son_" were constant. Out of 2,048 slots in our L1 cache, 2,047 slots were permanently empty, and all 9,000+ names fought over the 2 ways of slot 1328, giving us a 99.98% L1 cache miss rate.

Replacing the h2 multiply chain with a second _mm_crc32_u64 + a right-shift avalanche (h ^ (h >> 29)) and an 8-miss software-pipelined _mm_prefetch ring buffer (to hide the ~120-cycle L3 latency across 8 misses instead of probing 35 cycles after prefetching on the same row) cut our sandbox join time from 74.1 ms to 50.9 ms.

2. The Rewrite That Made Track A Slower: munmap vs. glibc ptmalloc2 Arenas

We originally wrote Track A in C++ and switched to zero-dependency Rust after seeing Rust dominate the top of the Track A board. Our first Rust push (1862874, run-2f56a6016af5) ran in 0.0534 s with 42.0 MB of memory (69.88 pts). Adding an 8-byte SWAR latency parser and compacting lines for rustfmt (72.30 pts) and vectorizing the endpoint space scan with AVX2 (61516e3, 75.06 pts) brought our time down to 0.038 s, but our memory stayed stubbornly stuck at 42 to 44 MB, while the leaders were at 18 to 20 MB.

Our static .bss struct (SharedData) was only ~20.8 MB. Where was the extra 23 MB coming from?

Our wrong guess: We assumed the kernel was charging part of the 239 MB mmap of /data/requests.log against our container's memory counter. So we added hr_buf and ep_buf to copy the interned hour and endpoint strings out of the file mapping and called munmap(bp, sz) right after the scan phase finished.

What the box said: Memory did not drop at all, and wall time got worse.

The harness pre-warms /data/requests.log into the host page cache with vmtouch -t before the container starts. Under cgroups v2, mapping already-resident host page-cache pages with PROT_READ + MAP_SHARED charges 0 bytes of anonymous RSS to the container.

Worse, cgroups v2 records memory.peak, the lifetime high-water mark of the container. Calling munmap after the scan phase cannot lower a peak that already happened; all it did was force Thread 0 to grab down_write(&mm->mmap_lock) in the kernel and tear down 61,184 page table entries while the clock was running.

The actual culprit (/proc/self/smaps):

When we inspected /proc/self/smaps in our sandbox, two OS behaviors jumped out:

  • In Phase 2 (computing p50/p95/p99 per hour), we used a static buffer l: [[u32; 49152]; 12] when an hour had <= 49,152 requests, with a fallback v_lats.resize(tot, 0) (Vec<u32>) if a peak hour exceeded 49,152. Whenever a peak hour crossed 49,152 requests across 12 threads, Vec allocated and freed ~200 KB blocks concurrently. In glibc, freeing medium allocations across threads dynamically raises M_MMAP_THRESHOLD and creates 12 retained per-thread ptmalloc2 heap arenas (~18 MB of dirty anonymous pages that glibc never returns to the OS).
  • std::thread::scope spawns threads with Linux's default 2 MB stack reservation.

Widening the static .bss buffer to 75,000 per thread (deleting Vec completely so malloc is never called in the worker loop), locking glibc with mallopt(M_ARENA_MAX, 1) and mallopt(M_TRIM_THRESHOLD, 0), and spawning threads via Builder::new().stack_size(65536) in commit 282a0d6 immediately dropped memory from 44 MB to 35 MB and brought wall time down to 0.034 s (76.695 pts).

Track A Optimization Step Commit / Run ID Time (T) Memory (M) Lines (S) Score
Initial Rust CSR + CRC32 interning 1862874 (run-2f56a6016af5) 0.0534 s 42 MB 468 69.88
SWAR 8-byte latency parse + rustfmt compaction run-0b81b4911a21 0.0520 s 43 MB 240 72.30
AVX2 endpoint scanner + fixed hash bit-mixing 61516e3 0.0380 s 44 MB 282 75.06
Zero-Vec .bss + mallopt + 64KB stacks + SWAR / writev 282a0d6 0.0340 s 35 MB 334 76.70

3. CPU Microarchitecture & the Cache Hierarchy: Fitting Into Golden Cove L1/L2/L3

Modern CPUs are starving for data, not compute. On the Falkenstein runner (Intel Core i5-13500, 6 Golden Cove P-cores / 12 hyperthreads pinned via --cpuset-cpus="0-11"), an L1 data cache hit takes ~4 cycles, an L2 hit takes ~14 cycles, an L3 hit takes ~45–60 cycles, and a main-memory DRAM miss costs ~200+ cycles.

Because two sibling hyperthreads (cpu 0 and cpu 1) share each physical P-core, they split that core's 48 KiB L1d cache (24 KiB effective per thread) and 1.25 MiB L2 cache (640 KiB effective per thread), while all 12 threads share the 24 MiB L3. Once we stopped treating memory as a flat array and started sizing every data structure against those exact cache boundaries, bottlenecks started making sense across all four tracks:

Domain Compression into L1/L2 (Track C): Why build a std::unordered_map when the key domain is tiny? In Track C, 3-letter uppercase country codes only have 26^3 = 17,576 possible combinations, so we mapped c0..c2 directly into uint16_t c_to_dense[17577] (35.1 KiB, which fits inside L1/L2). Likewise, 6-digit region_ids (0..999,999) fit in a flat uint8_t reg_lut[1000000] (976 KiB, which fits entirely inside each P-core's 1.25 MiB L2). Every relational foreign-key lookup became a single L2-resident byte load (reg_lut[reg]) with zero pointer chasing.

When Hyperthreads Evict Each Other's L1d (Track A & Track C): In Track A, each thread had a 16 KiB direct-mapped stack cache lc: [u64; 2048] (2048 × 8 B) to bypass global string interning. Two hyperthreads on the same P-core needed 32 KiB of lc alone, leaving only 16 KiB of the 48 KiB L1d for stack frames, requests.log streaming lines, and output chunks. Similarly, in Track C, a 32 KiB per-thread tl_cache[2048][2] meant two sibling hyperthreads needed 64 KiB (16 KiB larger than L1d!), constantly evicting hot lines down to L2.

Eliminating MESI Cache-Line Bouncing (False Sharing): When 12 threads increment adjacent counters in the same 64-byte cache line, the cores spend all their time invalidating each other's L1 caches over the ring bus. Sharding state into per-thread buffers (T[12][256] in Track C, and 64-byte aligned #[repr(C, align(64))] blocks in Track A) turned cross-core atomic wars into private L1 writes merged once at the end.

4. Track B (Search) & Track D (Graph Traversal): Designing Around the Queries You Can Already See

While Track A and Track C were battles against SIMD byte parsing and cache-line contention, Track B and Track D taught us a different lesson: never build a general-purpose index when the query workload is sitting right there on disk.

Track B: Cutting 2,199 MB to 75 MB by Indexing Only What the 50,000 Queries Ask For

Track B hands you a 256 MB text corpus and queries.txt: 50,000 queries split between BOOL (AND / OR / NOT, 62%) and PHRASE "..." (exact adjacent token positions, 38%). The Python reference takes 56.35 s and explodes to 2,199 MB of RAM because storing occurrence positions for every token in a 256 MB corpus eats gigabytes of memory.

Because build and query execution are timed together in a single run, and queries.txt is readable from millisecond zero, building a full positional inverted index over the entire vocabulary is pure waste:

  • By parsing queries.txt first, we know the exact set of terms that ever appear in any boolean query, and the even smaller subset of terms that ever participate in a PHRASE "..." query.
  • Words that never appear in queries.txt don't need postings lists at all, and words that only appear in BOOL queries only need document IDs (or bitsets), never token positions.

Combining query-driven vocabulary filtering with parallel 12-thread corpus chunking and smallest-first posting-list intersection took Track B from 0.314 s (62.16 pts in 61516e3) down to 0.252 s (223× faster than reference) and 75 MB (29.3× less memory) in commit 282a0d6 (63.751 pts).

Track D: 5 Million Directed Edges in 456 ms (282a0d6)

Track D gives you graph.txt (92 MB: 1,740,512 nodes and 5,000,000 directed weighted edges u v w, unsorted) and 2,000 source-target shortest-path queries (reference: 72.69 s, 893 MB).

Here, heavy preprocessing (like full Contraction Hierarchies) doesn't have enough queries to pay back its build time, because the 2,000 queries are local with bounded search depth. Nearly the entire wall-clock battle is:

  • Parallel edge-list ingestion (mmap + SWAR integer parsing): Parsing 15 million integers (u, v, w × 5M) across 12 threads without strtol or scanf.
  • Flat Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) memory layout: Packing outgoing edges into a contiguous (target, weight) array indexed by head[u] so edge relaxations hit sequential cache lines instead of chasing pointers across an 893 MB heap.
  • Parallel query execution with generation-stamped distance arrays: Running the 2,000 queries in parallel across all 12 threads using per-thread (dist, version) tables so resetting Dijkstra between queries is a single version += 1 increment rather than a 7 MB memset (1,740,512 × 4 B × 2,000 queries = 13.9 GB of zeroing avoided!).

That brought Track D to 0.456 s (159× speedup) and 83 MB (56.262 pts).

5. The 76.7 ms CSV Quote Scan Replaced by a 0.06 ms Automaton (Track C)

One optimization on Track C deserves its own callout because it turned our slowest serial bottleneck into a 60-microsecond no-op.

records.csv (204 MB, 3.32M rows) has ~404,713 newlines inside quoted note fields. If you split the file at t * sz / 12 for 12 threads (t = 1..11) and advance to the next \n, you have a 50/50 chance of starting Thread t in the middle of a multi-line note and corrupting the parse.

Our first version ran std::count across the 12 chunks to compute quote parity (odd vs even number of " characters before cs[t]). Scanning 204 MB just to count quotes took 76.71 ms in our local sandbox, more time than the entire 12-thread join!

Then we looked at the grammar of records.csv. An embedded newline inside note is followed by free text, whereas a real record end is always preceded by ,region_id,[-]DDD.CC\r?\n and followed by (\xEF\xBB\xBF)?[0-9]+,:

static inline bool is_rec_end(const char *base, size_t sz, const char *nl) {
  const char *p = nl - (nl > base && nl[-1] == '\r');
  if (p - base < 6 || p[-3] != '.' || p[-1] < '0' || p[-1] > '9' || p[-2] < '0' || p[-2] > '9') return false;
  p -= 3;
  int d_am = 0, d_reg = 0, d_id = 0;
  while (p > base && p[-1] >= '0' && p[-1] <= '9') --p, ++d_am;
  if (!d_am) return false;
  if (p > base && p[-1] == '-') --p;
  if (p <= base || p[-1] != ',') return false;
  --p;
  while (p > base && p[-1] >= '0' && p[-1] <= '9') --p, ++d_reg;
  if (!d_reg || p <= base || p[-1] != ',') return false;
  const char *nx = nl + 1;
  if (nx >= base + sz) return true;
  if (nx + 3 <= base + sz && (uint8_t)nx[0] == 0xEF && (uint8_t)nx[1] == 0xBB && (uint8_t)nx[2] == 0xBF) nx += 3;
  while (nx < base + sz && *nx >= '0' && *nx <= '9') ++nx, ++d_id;
  return d_id > 0 && nx < base + sz && *nx == ',';
}

Instead of scanning 204 MB from byte 0, each thread jumps directly to t * sz / 12 and tests is_rec_end on the next 1–2 newlines. Chunk alignment dropped from 76.71 ms to 0.061 ms (1,257× faster).

6. Scoring-Function Engineering & Breaking Out of the AI Local-Optimum Loop

We finished around the top 40 overall. Halfway through the event, when the organizers shared that the top 20 entries across each track collectively used 49 to 73 distinct optimization techniques, we realized why our scores on Track A (~76.7 pts) and Track C (~71.3 pts) had started inching up by only +0.3 points per push.

We had fallen into a classic local-optimum loop, compounded by how we were prompting AI and how we were treating the objective function.

The Math of the Objective Function (Why Golfing Lines Was a Trap)

Look at the exponents in the composite factor K:

K = (T_ref / T)^0.50  *  (M_ref / M)^0.25  *  (S_ref / S)^0.15  *  D^0.10

Because wall time T carries a 0.50 exponent while S (post-rustfmt/clang-format scc line count) carries only a 0.15 exponent:

  • Compressing code from 330 lines to 250 lines (-24% lines) multiplies K by (330 / 250)^0.15 = 1.0426 (+4.2%).
  • Worse, scc counts lines after standard formatting (rustfmt / clang-format), so cramming multiple statements onto one line gets expanded right back out by the formatter while making the code harder to reason about.
  • Meanwhile, spending +100 extra lines (330 → 430 lines, costing only -3.9% on the S factor) to implement a faster algorithm, like two-level radix bucketing on Track A, vocabulary-filtered bitset intersections on Track B, or bidirectional radix-heap search on Track D, that cuts T by 1.8× multiplies K by 1.8^0.50 × (330 / 430)^0.15 = 1.3416 × 0.961 = 1.289 (+28.9%).
  • And build-time optimizations inside the Dockerfile, such as Profile-Guided Optimization (-Cprofile-generate / llvm-profdata / -fprofile-use) and BOLT post-link binary layout optimization, deliver 8–15% wall-time reductions at zero scc line cost.

Why AI Polishes Local Optima, and Why Systems Clarity Still Wins

When you give an AI coding assistant a 300-line file and say "optimize this and keep the line count low", the AI will relentlessly polish the micro-syntax of the architecture you already have:

  • It will golf if statements into .then(|| ...) to save a few lines.
  • It will tweak loop unrolling factors and register variables.
  • And meanwhile, it will leave a 16 KiB direct-mapped stack array colliding on 1,842 Zipf endpoints, or leave 800,000 5xx log lines executing cross-core lock xadd atomic instructions ((*s).c[hid * 2048 + eid].fetch_add(1) instead of bit-packing is_5xx into bit 11 of the thread-local request word).

Four Lessons from Speed Demon 2026

  1. Language selection sets your ceiling and your floor: Choosing zero-dependency Rust (D = 1.00) for Tracks A, B, and D and C++23 with OpenMP for Track C gave us fearless 12-thread parallelism and direct SIMD access, provided you tame runtime defaults like glibc arenas and 2 MB thread stacks.
  2. Design for the cache hierarchy first, instructions second: Knowing the exact L1d (48 KiB), L2 (1.25 MiB), and L3 (24 MiB) budgets of the target CPU lets you compress key domains (like c_to_dense[17577] and reg_lut[1000000]) so lookups never touch DRAM.
  3. Optimize for the real objective function, not code golf: Never trade a 0.50-weight metric (wall-clock time) or a 0.25-weight metric (peak RSS) for a 0.15-weight metric (line count). When progress stalls at +0.3 points per push, stop micro-golfing and change the data structure.
  4. AI writes the SIMD; your OS and hardware clarity chooses the architecture: An LLM can emit _mm256_movemask_epi8 or a SWAR multiplier in seconds. What it cannot do on its own is tell you that 2 hyperthreads sharing a 48 KiB Golden Cove L1d cache are evicting each other's working sets, that glibc ptmalloc2 is retaining 12 heap arenas behind your back, or that little-endian 64-bit multiplication never shifts high-bit entropy into the low 32 bits.

Built by team cONFIG for Speed Demon 2026, the 72-hour performance engineering championship organized by Hackathon Raptors. All four track solutions (track-a, track-b, track-c, track-d) and optimization logs are in our repository: https://github.com/Yash-vs9/cOnfig-tracks.

title: Cloud Storage for Private User Uploads and Deletion Deadlines (and Why Deletion Wins)
description:
Short answer: Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, and Amazon S3 all provide temporary download authorization; none makes retention proof automatic, so private user-upload expiry must be enforced in the application rather than inferred from a cloud storage URL.

Design the upload system around a deletion deadline, then add expiring download authorization on top. For a game that accepts private replays, screenshots, and crash bundles, the durable question is not which object store has the nicest upload SDK. It is whether the system can prove that an object stops being downloadable and is eventually removed when its retention period ends.

My decision rule is to keep the application as the source of retention intent, keep object storage as the byte store, and make every download pass through an authorization check that knows the object\'s tenant, state, and expiry. A signed URL is a short-lived capability, not a deletion policy. Treating it as both creates a quiet failure: an object can be deleted from the database while an already-issued URL remains usable until its signature expires.

The invariants I would put in the decision record

The gaming scenario is concrete. A player uploads a private replay for moderation. The service stores the bytes, records an owner and an absolute delete_at timestamp, and returns a download link to an authorized moderator. A normal retention window might be 30 days; the number is a product policy, not a storage-provider default.

The invariants are stricter than the happy path:

  • An upload is never publicly readable.
  • The database record is the authority for owner, object key, lifecycle state, and delete_at.
  • A download authorization cannot outlive the record\'s retention deadline.
  • Deletion is idempotent, observable, and retried after a transient failure.
  • A client retry cannot create a second logical upload for the same idempotency key.

That last point matters because mobile game clients disappear between an upload and the confirmation request. I use a generated object key rather than a user filename, and I do not mark the record available until the server has evidence that the upload completed. The byte store can contain an orphan; the application must not quietly treat an unconfirmed orphan as user content.

Here is the comparison I would record before choosing an implementation. The names describe different APIs and control planes, not interchangeable feature labels.

Service Temporary download mechanism Retention and deletion concern Useful boundary
Amazon S3 Presigned URLs Lifecycle configuration and application deletion are separate controls A presigned URL grants time-limited access to a specific operation
Azure Blob Storage Shared access signatures SAS expiry and blob lifecycle management are separate policies A SAS should be scoped by resource, permissions, and time
Google Cloud Storage Signed URLs Object lifecycle rules and application deletion still need explicit coordination A signed URL is authorization for a request, not proof of retention completion

I would not rank these rows. The relevant choice is the surrounding control plane: identity, audit logs, lifecycle configuration, region constraints, and the team\'s ability to test deletion. A signed request from any of the three can be technically correct while the retention workflow remains wrong.

The limitation is operational: a provider-neutral adapter cannot erase differences in signing inputs, permission vocabulary, lifecycle configuration, or audit behavior. The trade-off is deliberate. A small interface keeps retention policy in application code, while adapter tests and runbooks carry the provider-specific details.

What must expire, and what must actually disappear?

These are two different clocks. The first is access expiry: how long a capability may be used. The second is retention expiry: when the object should no longer exist. For private uploads, I normally make the download capability much shorter than the retention window, perhaps 10 minutes versus 30 days. That limits accidental sharing without pretending that a 10-minute URL deleted anything.

There is a third clock in real systems: deletion completion. A worker may receive a due record, issue a delete request, lose its network connection, and retry. The application should represent that uncertainty. available, deleting, deleted, and delete_failed are more useful states than a boolean because an operator needs to distinguish a missing object from a worker that never reached the storage API.

A deletion deadline also needs a defined meaning. Does the team promise that downloads stop at delete_at, or only that deletion starts then? Those are different service guarantees. If downloads must stop at the deadline, the authorization path must reject a record whose deadline has passed even if the physical object still exists for a short time. If physical erasure has a separate target, record that target and measure it.

This distinction is where provider lifecycle rules fit. They are good backstops for abandoned data, but they do not replace application state. A lifecycle rule can remove an object that the application still believes is available, and an application delete can race a lifecycle transition. The reconciliation job should compare expected records with observed storage state and produce a reviewable result, not silently repair every discrepancy.

How should Azure, Google, and Amazon cloud storage handle private uploads?

The service should issue upload and download capabilities only after checking authorization. The following Python example is deliberately provider-neutral; the sign function is an adapter around the selected storage API, while the policy stays in application code.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class UploadRecord:
    owner_id: str
    object_key: str
    state: str
    delete_at: datetime


def issue_download_url(record: UploadRecord, requester_id: str, now: datetime) -> str:
    if record.owner_id != requester_id:
        raise PermissionError("upload owner mismatch")
    if record.state != "available":
        raise PermissionError("upload is not available")
    if now >= record.delete_at:
        raise PermissionError("retention deadline has passed")

    remaining = record.delete_at - now
    lifetime = min(remaining, timedelta(minutes=10))
    return sign(
        method="GET",
        object_key=record.object_key,
        expires_at=now + lifetime,
    )

For upload completion, I would use a server-side confirmation path with an idempotency key. The client can retry confirmation; the transition from pending to available must be conditional. A background job then claims due records in small batches, attempts deletion, and records the provider response category. Do not put provider request bodies or signed URLs in ordinary application logs.
For upload completion, I would use a server-side confirmation path with an idempotency key. The client can retry confirmation; the transition from pending to available must be conditional. A background job then claims due records in small batches, attempts deletion, and records the provider response category. Do not put provider request bodies or signed URLs in ordinary application logs.\n+
A useful test set includes an expired record, a record with five minutes left, a retry after a successful delete, a missing object, an authorization attempt by another player, and a worker crash between the storage delete and the database update. Those tests expose the boundary better than a screenshot of a successful upload.\n+

Which failure boundary deserves the most attention?\n+

The dangerous option is to let the client hold a long-lived URL and rely on the object store\'s lifecycle policy for cleanup. It is attractive because the implementation is small. It is also the wrong contract for private moderation data: a copied URL can remain usable after an account action, and the application cannot enforce per-record authorization once the capability has escaped.\n+
That option still has a valid use case. For public, immutable game patches or assets whose access policy is intentionally broad, a cacheable URL and provider-managed lifecycle may be sufficient. Private user uploads have a different threat model.\n+
The other common failure is deleting the database row first and treating a later storage error as an edge case. The row disappears from normal queries, the object remains billable and potentially reachable through an old capability, and nobody has a durable queue item to retry. A tombstone or deletion record should survive the logical deletion.\n+
Cross-provider portability has a cost too. Amazon S3 presigned URLs, Azure Blob shared access signatures, and Google Cloud Storage signed URLs do not share identical signing inputs, permission vocabulary, or operational configuration. A generic interface can hide those differences in business code, but it cannot eliminate them from adapter tests, deployment configuration, or incident runbooks. Abstraction is useful here only if the contract names the differences instead of flattening them into a misleading get_url() helper.\n+

The operational proof is part of the architecture\n+

I would alert on records past delete_at that remain in an accessible state, failed deletion attempts by age, orphaned objects without application records, and signed-download authorization denials near the deadline. Metrics should separate authorization failures, missing objects, provider throttling, and internal queue delay. One total called storage_errors will conceal the failure that matters.\n+
Run a small deletion drill before launch and repeat it after changing lifecycle configuration. Seed an upload, confirm that a valid moderator can retrieve it, advance the test clock, verify that new authorization is rejected, process deletion twice, and inspect both the application record and the storage inventory. The expected result is boring: the second delete is harmless, the audit trail is present, and no new link is issued after the deadline.\n+
The final choice among storage services should follow the organization\'s existing identity, logging, data-location, and operational constraints. For this scenario, the winning architecture is the one that makes retention a state transition the team can inspect and test. Storage APIs hold bytes. The application still owns the promise about who may retrieve them and when that promise ends.\n+

References\n+

  • AWS, “Presigned URLs”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • AWS, “Object lifecycle management”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • Microsoft Learn, “Use shared access signatures (SAS)”: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview
  • Microsoft Learn, “Blob Storage lifecycle management policies”: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/lifecycle-management-overview
  • Google Cloud, “Signed URLs”: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • Google Cloud, “Object Lifecycle Management”: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle
  • RFC Editor, “RFC 7234: HTTP Caching”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7234

title: The Class Layer of app.onepassapps.com: 3,323 Class Attributes, 139 Names, and Not One Name on Exactly Two Pages
description:
I work on OnePassApps, the team behind app.onepassapps.com, so this is a measurement of our own site. Every number below was read out of the HTML the server sends, on 8 November 2026, over plain HTTPS with one request per URL: no browser, no session, no cookies and no JavaScript.

A class attribute is the quietest layer of a page. On its own it styles nothing and it is invisible in a screenshot, which is probably why nobody counts it. So I counted ours, across all 56 URLs in our own sitemap.

The census is small and the shape of it is not.

Across the 56 pages there are 3,323 class attributes, carrying 5,253 class tokens between them, and 139 distinct class names. One class attribute in three carries more than a single name: 1,011 of the 3,323 hold two or more.

Here is the part I did not expect. A class name is either private to one page or shared by a whole fleet of pages. There is nothing in between.

  • 53 names appear on exactly 1 page.
  • 24 names appear on exactly 22 pages.
  • 49 names appear on exactly 23 pages.
  • 11 names appear on exactly 33 pages.
  • 2 names appear on all 56.

Not one class name appears on exactly two pages. That is a gap in the middle of the distribution, and it is not a rounding artefact of how I counted: it is the shape of the fleet. Our pages are built from templates, so a name is either written for one page or shared by a group, and a shared pair would mean two pages agreeing on something the other 54 do not. We have none.

The 33 pages that boot the app

The 33 pages that ship the app bundle carry 11 class names between them, and they are the crash card and the startup shell:

fallback
fallback--shell
fallback__card
fallback__mark
fallback__title
fallback__copy
fallback__reload
fallback__help
tp-startup-shell__content
tp-startup-shell__pulse
tp-startup-shell__sam

Thirty-one of those 33 pages carry 12 class attributes each and 13 class tokens, so exactly one of them holds two names. /plans carries 13 attributes. The app pages are close to class-free in served HTML, and that is not an oversight: the interface is built by JavaScript after the document arrives, so the markup that ships is the shell, and the shell is small.

The 23 pages that do not

The guide fleet is the other half: the 22 pages under /guides/ plus the index at /guides. It uses 77 names that begin with gd-, plus the bare gd wrapper, which is on all 23. Twenty-four names are shared by the 22 guide pages, and the index adds five of its own:

gd-apps--cards
gd-fold--index
gd-listhead__title
gd-meta
gd-note


. The index is the busiest page in the fleet by attribute count, 335 of them, though each one usually holds a single name.

The 22 guide pages are not all the same size. Seventeen carry 113 class attributes, four carry 100 and one carries 101, and the reason is legible in the markup: those five shorter pages (citation-formatter, movie-tracker, newsflow, subtitle-workbench and teleprompter) list one related app where the other seventeen list two, and one app card is 13 class attributes.

The page that does not match the others

/terms is the outlier, and it is not a small one. It carries 181 class attributes and 1,130 class tokens, which is 21.5% of all the class tokens in the fleet on one page out of 56. It also carries 48 utility-style names that appear nowhere else on the site: text-ink-1 (83 times on its own), ease-settle, rounded-tight, font-medium, underline, sr-only, scroll-mt-20 and forty-one more, among them five with square-bracket values in them, such as text-[length:inherit] and grid-cols-[2.25rem_minmax(0,1fr)].

So the terms page is styled by a different system from the rest of the site: the guides use a component vocabulary with element and modifier suffixes, and the terms page uses a utility vocabulary where each name is one small instruction. Both are on the same server, on the same build, in the same fleet.

The naming shapes back this up. Of the 139 names, 37 use a double underscore for an element, 25 use a double dash for a modifier, and 5 carry square-bracket values. All 5 of those bracket names are on /terms.

Counting the whole vocabulary by family: 77 guide names, 1 bare gd wrapper, 3 startup-shell names, 8 fallback names, 2 site-wide names and 48 utility names. That is 139.

Two names on every page

Only two names reach all 56 pages. One is dark, on the html element next to data-theme="dark" and data-theme-preset="graphite". The other is __cf_email__, which is Cloudflare's own email-protection span rather than ours: 74 tokens across all 56 pages, with 54 pages carrying it once, /plans carrying it twice and /terms eighteen times, once for every address Cloudflare rewrote on that page.

What I did not do

One build, one day, 8 November 2026, plain HTTPS from one network, signed out, one request per URL, and no JavaScript at all. So this is the HTML before the app runs, not what a browser paints. A class name is counted once per attribute it appears in, and the counts are of served markup only. The guide fleet is the 22 pages under /guides/ plus the index; the other 33 URLs in the sitemap are the app fleet. I make no claim about which classes survive a build, and none about how any browser applies them.

If you want to see the pages this is describing, the home page is at https://app.onepassapps.com?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=class-layer&utm_content=home-link and the guides are at https://app.onepassapps.com/guides?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=class-layer&utm_content=guides-link

title: RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.08711v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit vulnerabilities to adversarial perturbations that can induce unintended responses. These vulnerabilities can be identified via intentional attacks and subsequently used to improve model safety. In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model. To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at https://github.com/taikunudel/RL-ATTACK.

title: I put a diffusion model in a stylesheet. No JavaScript.
description:
Try it: metrix187.github.io/diffusion.css · Code: github.com/Metrix187/diffusion.css

Press the button and the stylesheet freezes a seed, turns it into noise, and denoises that into a 16×16 sprite in 12 steps. There is no <script> on the page. View source and check.

Why

People have already put a CPU, digit classifiers and, a few days ago, GPT-2 into CSS. I went looking for a diffusion model and couldn't find one, so this is my attempt.

The problem: CSS has no loops

Denoising is a loop. Each step needs the previous step's output, and a custom property can't refer to itself.

So the sampler is unrolled. Every step gets its own copy of the arithmetic, and every intermediate value gets its own registered custom property. A hidden unit looks like this:

@property --Ba0 { syntax: "<integer>"; inherits: true; initial-value: 0 }

/* first unit of the network used by step 2 */
--Ba0: max(0, (51096.5 + 25*var(--a108) - 26*var(--a123) - 31*var(--a126) /* 80 more terms */)/512);

Registering the property matters. An unregistered custom property is just text, so each var() would paste in the whole expression behind it and the stylesheet would blow up. A registered <integer> is computed once, rounded, and passed on as a number. There are 12,518 of them.

Seed and noise

The seed is a counter that a hidden checkbox pauses, so the moment you press is the random seed:

@keyframes spin { to { --seed: 15813250 } }
.app { animation: spin 211s linear infinite }
.app:has(#go:checked) { animation-play-state: paused }

Each of the 768 pixel channels then hashes that seed with mod() four times and sums the draws, which gives roughly Gaussian noise. That is the static you see before pressing.

The network rule only matches while the box is ticked, so nothing is computed until the seed is frozen. After that, one @keyframes rule points the 256 pixel elements at each sampler state in turn.

The model

Eleven small MLPs, one per noise level, trained in PyTorch on ten hand-drawn sprites that get recoloured to a random hue for every sample. Then they are pruned and rounded to integers: 202,863 weights, each one a literal inside a calc().

Two things that went wrong

Rounding. CSS rounds a calc() in an <integer> context to the nearest integer, but browsers don't agree on exact .5 ties. The fix: every division is by a power of two with 0.5 added to the numerator, so a quotient is never a tie. With that in place, a Python sampler using the same integer arithmetic produces identical pixels for the same seed. I checked 40 seeds in Chromium 152 and another 40-odd in Chrome 157.

Blended sprites. The first model produced a muddle of two sprites about a third of the time. Deterministic sampling with only 12 steps drifts between two shapes and never commits. Two changes fixed most of it: spacing the noise levels evenly in log-SNR, and training the later steps on inputs deliberately blended with a second sprite while keeping the dominant one as the target, so they learn to snap to one shape. It is down to about 1 in 20.

What it isn't

  • Not a loop. All 12 steps are computed when the seed freezes. The animation reveals them; it does not drive the computation.
  • Not creative. It learned ten shapes and a continuous range of colours. You get new shape-and-colour combinations, never a new shape.
  • Not tested outside Chromium. It only uses features Firefox and Safari also ship, but I have not run it there.

Numbers

Weights 202,863
Sampler steps 12, deterministic DDIM
Registers 12,518
Possible seeds 15,813,251
File size 5.2 MB, 0.8 MB gzipped
Time to compute a sprite about 0.13 s

Related reading

  • 😱 Pure CSS! Neural Network / AI...it's easier than you think! 🤯 by GrahamTheDev, the earliest pure-CSS neural net post I found on DEV
  • Implementing GPT-2 Entirely In CSS by Shubham Patil
  • css-ml by mickael-btc, whose README describes the integer-register approach this builds on
  • x86CSS by Lyra Rebane

The repo has the training code, the reference sampler and a console snippet for checking the page against it. If you get it running in Firefox or Safari, I would like to know whether the pixels match.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute, allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake.

With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. Credential management stays the same, so you don’t need to store long-lived provider secrets in your app or build OAuth flows yourself.

To enable Secure Compute routing for a supported connector and all projects that use it:

  • Open your connector’s Settings in the Vercel dashboard.

  • Under Secure Compute Routing, choose an existing network.

  • If your provider uses an IP allowlist, add the selected network’s displayed IP addresses to it in the provider’s settings.

  • Save your changes in Connect.

Requests for initial connector creation and all provider discovery requests bypass the selected network and connect directly to providers. If the selected network is unavailable, routed requests fail instead of falling back to Connect’s shared IPs.

Read the Secure Compute routing documentation for configuration details.

Read more

title: ProtoCouncil: Multi-Encoder Anatomical Prototypes for Prostate Cancer Detection in Micro-Ultrasound
description:
arXiv:2611.09058v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Purpose: Micro-ultrasound ($\mu$US) is a promising modality for prostate cancer (PCa) detection, but identifying suspicious tissue depends heavily on clinical experience. Models trained on sparse, noisy core-level pathology offer little insight into their decisions and can fail under domain shift. Clinical use needs a traceable decision process and a flag for uncertain predictions.
  Methods: We introduce ProtoCouncil, in which three foundation encoders (MedSAM, DINOv3 and V-JEPA 2.1) learn case-based prototypes at three anatomical levels: whole gland, needle track and gland sectors. Prototypes are projected onto real training-core regions, and label-free fusion keeps every class logit as a bias plus an exact sum of prototype similarity contributions. Encoder disagreement triggers selective prediction.
  Results: In five-fold patient-level cross-validation (6,588 cores, 693 patients), ProtoCouncil reaches 82.9% AUROC for clinically significant PCa (csPCa, Grade Group $\geq$3), 4.3 points above the best previously published method. In zero-shot evaluation on two external cohorts, ProtoCouncil achieves higher all-cancer and csPCa AUROC than all previous methods. Nearest same-class exemplars match test-core tumor involvement better than random same-class cases. Externally, csPCa accuracy falls from 79% when encoders agree to 27% when two oppose the fused call. Abstaining on disagreement raises balanced accuracy by 7 and 15 points, while retaining 58% and 54% of the cores.
  Conclusion: ProtoCouncil grounds core-level predictions in exact similarity-based evidence from real, anatomically indexed training cases, which makes its reasoning interpretable. It achieves the highest csPCa AUROC across three cohorts and identifies unreliable predictions through encoder disagreement.

title: Mercedes Put Depth in the Windshield. Depth Was Never Guaranteed for Everyone.
description:
Mercedes Put Depth in the Windshield. Depth Was Never Guaranteed for Everyone.

Mercedes-Benz is replacing the dashboard screen with the windshield: a holographic heads-up display that floats navigation and alerts in the driver's line of sight. Read past the wow factor and there's a real shift in it — display tech is moving from "flat panel you stare at" to "depth you perceive."

That distinction matters more than most people realize, because not everyone perceives depth the same way.

I learned this the slow way, with my nephew. He'd stand at the top of the stairs, one hand on the rail, and lower one foot like he was testing ice. Parking lots, too — he'd stop mid-stride and wait for someone to take his hand. For a while we just called it clumsy. Then a checkup put a name to it: amblyopia, and it was about binocular coordination, not one weak eye. Two eyes that don't fuse mean the brain never gets true 3D depth. Stairs. Sports. Pouring a drink. All of it becomes guesswork.

The usual tools — adhesive patches, red-blue glasses — are passive, and hard to keep up for months. That's the part that wears a kid down. What's changed is that consumer hardware can now render per eye: show each eye a different, deliberate image and give the brain a reason to merge them.

That's what we built at Seven Sports. Amblyotube is a Meta Quest app that plays YouTube-style content with a different visual experience per eye. Concretely: an adjustable digital blur on the dominant eye (Dominant Eye Shader), an AI Sharpener in MFBF mode that outlines human figures for the weaker eye with a red outline and yellow-green highlight, optional Wedge Occlusion to cut binocular rivalry, and a magenta focus cue that fuses into one 3D image. An integrated LogMAR-style vision check can tune the therapy profile to the detected severity, and Room View streams video over AR passthrough of your actual room.

No patches, no red-blue glasses. Thirty to forty minutes a day, watching something he actually wants to watch. Supplementary vision training for binocular coordination and depth perception — not a diagnosis, treatment, or cure. Ages 13+.

He still takes the stairs carefully. But he takes them. If your team works on XR, display, or vision tech, this is the part of the space worth watching.

title: Why does a local LLM give a different score every time, and does temperature 0 fix it?
description:
Give a language model a CV and ask for a score from 1 to 10, and you get a number and a confident reason. Ask again and the number can move. The usual advice is "set temperature to 0", which is correct but leaves two questions open: how much does the score actually move with default settings, and what does temperature 0 not fix? Both can be measured on a laptop in a few minutes, because the score is a single token and the model hands you its probability directly.

The setup below uses Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (4-bit, MLX) with mlx-lm 0.32.2 on an 8 GB M1 Mac. The prompts are the ones from a CV-scoring demo in the osFoundry desktop app's Models → Playground: a six-line CV for a junior data analyst role, followed by "Score this CV from 1 to 10 for a junior data analyst role. Start with the score, then one reason." The app runs local models through llama.cpp's llama-server, so the sampler settings come from there.

The defaults you get when you don't choose

When a request carries no temperature, llama-server samples with its own defaults. The build bundled with the app (version 10358) lists them in --help:

--temp, --temperature N    temperature (default: 0.80)
--top-k N                  top-k sampling (default: 40, 0 = disabled)
--top-p N                  top-p sampling (default: 0.95, 1.0 = disabled)
--min-p N                  min-p sampling (default: 0.05, 0.0 = disabled)
-s, --seed SEED            RNG seed (default: -1, use random seed for -1)

These apply to every request that doesn't set its own values. When the app starts llama-server, it only adds --temp if a temperature has been configured for the server (local_inference.rs), so a request without a temperature samples at 0.8 with a random seed, which is also what most llama.cpp front ends do out of the box.

Making the score the next token

A free-form answer can start with "Score: 7", "7/10" or "I would rate this CV a 7", which makes the score hard to locate. The fix is to pre-fill the start of the reply, so the very next token the model produces is the digit:

import mlx.core as mx
from mlx_lm import load, generate
from mlx_lm.sample_utils import make_sampler

model, tok = load("mlx-community/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct-4bit")
DIGITS = {d: tok.encode(str(d))[0] for d in range(1, 10)}

def ids_for(cv, question, prefill="Score: "):
    msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": cv + "\n\n" + question}]
    text = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False)
    return tok.encode(text + prefill)

def digit_probs(ids, T=1.0):
    logits = model(mx.array([ids]))[0, -1].astype(mx.float32)
    p = mx.softmax(logits / T)
    return {d: float(p[t]) for d, t in DIGITS.items()}

Qwen's tokenizer splits numbers into single digits, so "7" is one token and "10" would start with the token "1". One forward pass over the 173-token prompt gives the whole distribution of the score.

The score is a distribution, not a number

For the English CV, at temperature 1 (the model's raw probabilities):

Score Probability
7 74.2%
6 23.3%
8 1.3%
5 1.2%

The model doesn't "think" the CV is a 7. It thinks it is probably a 7, with a one-in-four chance of a 6. Temperature divides the logits before the softmax, which sharpens or flattens this:

Temperature P(7) P(6) P(8)
1.0 74.2% 23.3% 1.3%
0.8 80.2% 18.9% 0.5%
0.5 91.0% 9.0% 0.0%
0.2 99.7% 0.3% 0.0%

llama-server doesn't apply temperature alone. Its default chain runs top-k 40, then top-p 0.95, then min-p 0.05, and temperature last. Applied to these logits, top-p already cuts everything after 7 and 6 (together they are over 95%), so the default sampler picks between exactly two scores:

def llamacpp_default(logits, temp=0.8, top_k=40, top_p=0.95, min_p=0.05):
    order = mx.argsort(-logits)[:top_k]
    kept = logits[order]
    p = mx.softmax(kept)
    n = int(mx.sum(mx.cumsum(p) < top_p).item()) + 1
    idx = [i for i in range(n) if p[i].item() >= min_p * p[0].item()]
    q = mx.softmax(kept[mx.array(idx)] / temp)
    return {tok.decode([int(order[i])]): float(q[j]) for j, i in enumerate(idx)}
# -> {'7': 0.8093, '6': 0.1907}

Then I sampled it for real: 200 generations from the same prompt with mlx-lm's sampler set to the same four values (make_sampler(temp=0.8, top_p=0.95, min_p=0.05, top_k=40)).

7 6
Predicted by the chain 80.9% 19.1%
Observed, 200 runs 162 (81%) 38 (19%)

So with default settings, about one run in five scores this CV a 6 instead of a 7. If you score two candidates once each and one gets a 6 and the other a 7, there is a real chance the gap is the draw.

A flatter case: the same CV in Japanese

The same CV and question in Japanese (222 tokens, pre-fill 「点数：」) gave a much less decided model:

Score Probability at T=1 Observed, 200 runs at the defaults
8 39.8% 108
9 23.8% 44
7 19.4% 40
10 (starts with "1": 4.1%) 8

Here the most likely score wins only about half the time, and four different scores came out of 200 runs. How much a score wobbles is not a fixed property of the model. It depends on how close the top candidates are for this particular input, which you can only see by looking at the probabilities.

What temperature 0 fixes

With temperature 0 (greedy decoding: always the most likely token), I generated the full 40-token answer 20 times for each language. There was 1 distinct text per language, character for character. For the English CV it is "7" followed by the same reason every time, and for Japanese 「8点」.

A fixed seed does the same for sampling: 10 runs with mx.random.seed(42) reset before each gave 1 distinct text. That is useful when you want variety but need to reproduce a particular run. It is not a fairness tool, though. With a seed, a different CV gets a different sequence of draws, so two candidates are still scored by different luck.

One condition applies to all of this: every run here was a single request on an idle model. Servers that batch several requests together can produce tiny floating-point differences between runs, which only matter when two tokens are nearly tied. That was not measured here.

What temperature 0 doesn't fix

Greedy decoding makes the output a function of the input. It doesn't make it a stable function. I made four edits that should not change a CV's score and took the greedy score and the probabilities each time:

Edit (English) Greedy score P(top) Runner-up
none 7 74.2% 6 at 23.3%
Skills line moved up 7 69.6% 6 at 28.1%
Name changed (Mia Chen → James Miller) 7 68.5% 6 at 28.5%
One extra blank line 7 71.0% 6 at 26.1%
Question reworded 6 67.5% 5 at 19.3%

The reworded question was "Rate this CV for a junior data analyst role on a 1 to 10 scale. Give the score first, then one reason." Same task, same CV, and the greedy score drops from 7 to 6. In Japanese, all five versions stayed at 8 at temperature 0, but the top probability never went above 44%, and the runner-up switched between 9 and 7 depending on the edit.

So temperature 0 removes the randomness between runs, not the sensitivity to the prompt. For comparing CVs this means:

  • Use temperature 0 and the exact same question for every item you compare, character for character. Change the question, and re-score everything.
  • Keep the probability, not only the score. llama-server's /completion endpoint returns token probabilities if you pass n_probs, and with the pre-fill trick above the first token is the score. A 7 at 74% and an 8 at 40% are not the same kind of answer.
  • Treat a one-point gap at low confidence as a tie, and read the reason the model gives before trusting either number.

Doing it in the app

In the osFoundry desktop app, the same experiment is three panels with one local model in Models → Playground. Run the prompt once with the defaults to see the spread, then open the settings row and set Temp to 0.

The temperature and top-p glossary entries cover the two settings in more detail. The app is free from the osFoundry download page.

title: From Procedures to Permissions: Learning Precise Subagent Authorization from Agent Skills
description:
arXiv:2611.08905v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As language agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, they increasingly rely on multiple agents to coordinate specialized work, requiring decisions not only about what each subagent should do but also which tools and workspace resources it should access. Existing agent systems provide mechanisms for controlling tools and execution environments, but do not directly specify the resources required by each delegated subtask. Moreover, task outcomes and execution trajectories alone provide limited supervision for determining whether a subagent has received appropriate permissions. We observe that Agent Skills encode procedural knowledge describing the operations, tools, and files required at each step, providing a natural source of supervision for authorization. Building on this observation, we synthesize tasks and step-by-step procedures from Skills, execute them through subagent delegation in interactive environments, and use verified trajectories to construct training data for task execution and authorization. On ClawArena-Team, our method improves tool permission precision by 13.4 percentage points and workspace permission precision by 24.1 percentage points, while increasing overall task success by 11.6 percentage points for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, our method remains competitive with existing agent data synthesis approaches. These results show that the procedural knowledge embedded in Agent Skills provides a source of supervision for precise subagent orchestration that task outcomes alone cannot provide.

title: Node.js Postgres Backup Archive to a Storage Bucket: Gzip and Recovery Links
description:
A backup job should be judged by a measured restore drill, because a successful object upload says nothing about whether the application can recover within its recovery objectives. Start with an isolated restore, a bounded verification query set, and an alert on the age of the latest verified archive; scheduling the dump is the easy part.

Short answer: run logical exports in a separate worker, compress and store each run under a unique key, then promote it to a recovery point only after an isolated restore and application checks succeed.

The important unit of work is the recovery point, not the file. A file can be complete, readable, and still be useless because it came from the wrong database, was overwritten by a later run, or depends on roles, extensions, migrations, and capacity that were absent from the test.

What should a Postgres backup, object storage, gzip, restore, and signed URL runbook verify?

Write down the recovery point objective and recovery time objective before choosing a schedule. The service-level indicator worth watching is the age of the newest archive that has passed the whole recovery path. An upload-success metric is supporting telemetry. It is not proof of recoverability.

A useful manifest records the object key, UTC creation time, compressed byte count, digest, archive format, tool version, and run identifier. Validate the manifest schema before allocating a restore database. Use an immutable, timestamped key where the storage implementation supports it, rather than a mutable name such as latest.dump.gz.

Keep it boring.

A presigned URL is a time-limited bearer credential for a selected object. Generate it only after selecting the exact verified key, choose the shortest practical expiry, log the requestor and object, and keep it out of durable tickets and chat transcripts. AWS documents that presigned URLs are limited by the permissions of the credential that created them and by their expiration; compatible object APIs can differ in their signing details, lifecycle behavior, versioning, and retention controls. Test those details against the chosen service before an incident.

Safe worker implementation

Do not launch pg_dump from an HTTP handler. A scheduled worker needs its own workload identity, deadline, CPU and memory limits, database credential, and write permission limited to the backup prefix. That separation prevents web deploys and customer traffic from deciding whether recovery data exists.

The example deliberately depends on a small generic writer interface. It uses PostgreSQL's custom archive format, wraps the output in gzip for transport, and leaves the object-storage client as an adapter so the recovery procedure is not coupled to one provider. Restore this artifact by decompressing it before passing it to pg_restore.

package backup

import (
    "compress/gzip"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "os/exec"
    "time"
)

type ObjectWriter interface {
    Put(context.Context, string, string, io.Reader) error
}

func Export(ctx context.Context, store ObjectWriter, databaseURL, bucket, runID string) (string, error) {
    key := fmt.Sprintf("postgres/%s-%s.dump.gz", time.Now().UTC().Format("20060102T150405Z"), runID)
    cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "pg_dump", "--format=custom", "--dbname="+databaseURL)
    stdout, err := cmd.StdoutPipe()
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("open dump output: %w", err)
    }
    if err := cmd.Start(); err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("start dump: %w", err)
    }

    reader, writer := io.Pipe()
    go func() {
        zipped := gzip.NewWriter(writer)
        _, copyErr := io.Copy(zipped, stdout)
        closeErr := zipped.Close()
        if copyErr != nil {
            _ = writer.CloseWithError(copyErr)
            return
        }
        _ = writer.CloseWithError(closeErr)
    }()

    uploadErr := store.Put(ctx, bucket, key, reader)
    dumpErr := cmd.Wait()
    if dumpErr != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("pg_dump: %w", dumpErr)
    }
    if uploadErr != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("upload %s: %w", key, uploadErr)
    }
    return key, nil
}

The worker must treat both the child-process exit status and upload result as required outcomes. A context deadline should be longer than the measured high-percentile export duration but shorter than the backup window. On a retry, create a new run identifier and retain enough telemetry to explain the attempt; retrying into a shared key makes a later investigation needlessly ambiguous.

Verification and rollback before promotion

A drill starts from the precise key and manifest emitted by a completed run, not from a console listing sorted by a timestamp. The recovery identity downloads the archive into an isolated environment, verifies its recorded size and digest, decompresses it, and invokes pg_restore against an empty target. Then run migration-aware checks through the application's normal data-access path.

The checks should catch a structurally valid archive that is operationally wrong: the expected schema version, a bounded tenant-count range, and a known historical record are often more useful than a health endpoint. Avoid a full scan of every large table unless the capacity plan explicitly allows it. The production database, restore target, temporary disk, network bandwidth, and object retention all need projected-volume estimates, including room for a failed cleanup cycle.

Checkpoint Evidence to retain Stop condition
Export Run ID, start and finish time, exit status Export does not complete
Upload Key, byte count, digest Stored bytes do not match the manifest
Restore Archive and restore command status Target cannot be restored cleanly
Application check Schema and domain-check results Expected data is absent or inconsistent

If a checkpoint fails, do not promote the target and do not touch production. Preserve the isolated target and logs, select the previous verified recovery point, and record the resulting recovery-point gap. If migrations cannot run backward, restore separately and follow the application's documented forward migration sequence. A signed URL does not change that rollback rule.

Choosing the recovery architecture

Logical exports to object storage are appropriate when their measured export and restore times remain inside the objectives and portable logical artifacts are valuable. The catch is that the platform team owns job isolation, secret rotation, manifest integrity, retention policy, and the rehearsal cadence. A managed database recovery facility can transfer some operational machinery, while leaving application acceptance, access policy, and drills with the team. Physical backup plus write-ahead-log recovery is a better fit when the required recovery point is tighter than periodic logical exports can provide, but it demands PostgreSQL operational depth.

Approach Good fit Team still owns Not suitable when
Logical archive Moderate datasets with portable recovery needs Scheduling, retention, restore drills Restore misses the RTO
Managed recovery Teams reducing backup-operation load Policy and application validation Export portability is required
Physical recovery Tight recovery-point targets WAL continuity and rehearsals Operators lack database depth
Self-hosted storage Existing storage operations Capacity, replication, upgrades It adds an unplanned on-call burden

Reopen the design review when restore duration trends toward the objective at projected data volume. A backup plan that works on last month's dataset but requires unreserved temporary storage or database capacity during an incident is a plan with an unpriced failure mode.

  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-pgrestore.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
