title: DINO-Nucleus: Multi-Level Self-Supervised Features for Nucleus Instance Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.09133v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Nucleus instance segmentation and counting are essential for quantitative microscopy, enabling reliable analysis of cell populations, tissue organization, and disease-related changes. However, accurately separating touching nuclei remains difficult, and many existing approaches rely on complex models or sensitive post-processing procedures. We present DINO-Nucleus, a parameter-efficient framework that leverages multi-level self-supervised DINOv2 representations for nucleus instance segmentation and counting. The model jointly predicts nucleus regions, pixel-wise instance flows, and explicit nucleus centers, while a consistency objective encourages the predicted flows to converge toward their corresponding centers. Multi-level transformer features provide complementary spatial and semantic information, and the pretrained backbone is adapted using lightweight LoRA modules to reduce fine-tuning cost. Experimental results show that DINO-Nucleus achieves strong segmentation and counting performance with parameter-efficient backbone adaptation. These findings demonstrate that parameter-efficient adaptation of multi-level self-supervised features can provide an effective solution for nucleus instance segmentation in microscopy images.

title: Finite-sample Calibration Guarantees for Binary Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.09120v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning based segmentation models are frequently miscalibrated, producing for each pixel a label prediction whose associated confidence does not accurately reflect the true underlying probability. This limitation is particularly critical in high-stakes applications such as medical image segmentation. Although several calibration methods have been proposed, only a small subset of them provides theoretical guarantees on the calibration error, i.e., they do not typically ensure that, with high probability, the model exhibits a low calibration error. In this work, we develop a post-hoc calibration method for which formal calibration guarantees can be established. To achieve this, we derive from standard concentration inequalities an improved theoretical bound that explicitly accounts for the spatial dependence inherent in binary segmentation outputs. We empirically demonstrate that the proposed calibrator satisfies the derived guarantee and outperforms existing post-hoc calibration approaches.

title: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.09770v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.

title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
description:
arXiv:2610.42039v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? We audit six widely deployed LLMs from four providers on smoking cessation, a domain with codified clini- cal guidance and substantial public-health stakes, by putting the same four cessation questions to twelve user personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise, and smoking history, for a total of 2,880 responses. What the models say depends on who appears to be asking. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points, and in five of six models a persona presenting health- care expertise received fewer facts than a persona presenting none. We then evaluate one deployable intervention: a short system prompt specifying a factual floor, the set of core med- ical facts every user should receive when they are relevant, while leaving tone, vocabulary, and framing free to adapt. The prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in both magnitude and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another. Two cautions frame these results. Equal mention rates are not always the correct clinical target, because prescription cessation pharmacother- apy is not recommended for minors, so a defensible factual floor must be age-aware rather than uniform. And because our personas vary on several attributes at once, we report scenario- level differences rather than isolated effects of age or expertise. We release all 2,880 responses and the analysis code.

title: Are These Programmers Ripe Enough to Eat? Evaluating How LLMs Handle Lexical Knowledge Conflicts in Translation
description:
arXiv:2611.09785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: External lexical resources can help large language models (LLMs) translate texts in low-resource languages and specialized domains, but these resources may conflict with models' prior lexical knowledge. To isolate this conflict, we construct a controlled Mandarin-to-English translation task in which familiar source words are assigned new meanings within and across semantic categories. We treat these prompt-supplied meanings as contextual knowledge (CK) and systematically evaluate the effects of word frequency, sentence context, and prompt framing on the translated outputs. Across nine models, CK reliance is greater for less frequent source words and in sentence contexts that support the supplied meanings. Prompt framing can reduce CK reliance, but seven of nine models favor CK even when explicitly instructed to ignore the supplied meanings. Within model families, larger models are more likely than smaller models to utilize CK in their outputs. Three follow-up experiments further show that modal weakening lowers CK reliance, the effect of repetition depends on prompt layout, and the effect of reasoning varies across models. Overall, our controlled study reveals how CK reliance varies across conditions and models, motivating new methods to detect and evaluate lexical conflicts and guide models' lexical choices in LLM-based translation.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

The following AlloyDB AI functions and improvements are available in Preview:

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

Feature

Regular expression URL rewrites (regexRewrite) for route rules in URL maps are now generally available (GA) for Application Load Balancers. Direct access ports let you connect directly to a workstation port using the standard https://WORKSTATION_NAME.CLUSTER_ID.cloudworkstations.dev:PORT URL format instead of encoding the port as a prefix in the URL.

To set direct access ports, use the --direct-access-ports flag with the gcloud beta workstations clusters create and gcloud beta workstations clusters update commands—for example, --direct-access-ports=80,8080.

title: Two migrations collide: one loud failure, one silent one
description:
In the previous post I argued that migrations don't earn Git's protections by being made of files: two incompatible schema changes live in two separate migration files, so there is nothing to textually conflict, and both branches merge clean. The repository accepts the pair without comment.

That post ended with a claim: the collision is not resolved in the repo, so it must be resolved somewhere else — at apply time, per environment, inside the database. This post is that claim, run for real. What actually happens when the pair lands?

I ran the collisions on PostgreSQL 16 to find out. The answer comes in two flavors — one loud, one silent — and the silent one is worse.

None of what follows is an argument against migrations, or against the defensive idioms people write in them. Every tool below does exactly what it promises. The point is what those promises do and don't cover once two branches meet.

The loud collision: order decides which environment breaks

Branch A adds a column to users. Branch B renames users to accounts. Semantically incompatible; textually invisible to Git; both merged.

Each environment applies the migrations in whatever order they arrive — and the order can differ between environments, because branch merge order and migration timestamp order are two different clocks. So I built two databases and applied the pair in both orders:

-- env_one: add column, then rename
ALTER TABLE            ✓
ALTER TABLE            ✓

-- env_two: rename, then add column
ALTER TABLE            ✓
ERROR:  relation "users" does not exist

env_one is fine. env_two is broken — and its migration run has now halted partway, with everything after the failed file left unapplied.

Note what this means operationally: the same pair of migrations produces a healthy database in one environment and a failed deploy in another, decided by application order alone. If your staging environment happened to apply them in the survivable order, staging is green and the failure is waiting in production. The check that was supposed to catch this — running migrations in staging first — passed honestly and told you nothing.

Still, this is the good outcome. The error is loud, it names a relation, someone gets paged, the incident gets fixed. Postgres refused to do something incoherent. The failure mode below refuses nothing.

The silent collision: IF NOT EXISTS and a shared name

Defensive migrations are common: CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS, ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS. They make migrations re-runnable, and they feel like safety.

Now let two branches each add an index on users(email) — same obvious name, different definitions. Branch A indexes the raw column; branch B, written with case-insensitive lookup in mind, indexes lower(email):

-- migration A
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_users_email ON users (email);
-- migration B
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_users_email ON users (lower(email));

Apply both, in both orders, on two databases:

-- silent_one: A then B          -- silent_two: B then A
CREATE INDEX                     CREATE INDEX
NOTICE:  relation                NOTICE:  relation
  "idx_users_email"                "idx_users_email"
  already exists, skipping         already exists, skipping
CREATE INDEX                     CREATE INDEX

Every statement reports success. Exit code zero, four times. The migration history table in both databases now records both migrations as applied.

Here is what the two databases actually contain:

silent_one:  CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users USING btree (email)
silent_two:  CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users USING btree (lower(email))

Two environments, same applied-migration set, different schemas. No error, no failed deploy, no page. One environment will use the index for WHERE lower(email) = ... and the other will sequential-scan, which surfaces months later as "this query is slow only in production" — a symptom nobody will trace back to a merge.

IF NOT EXISTS checks the name. It knows nothing about the definition. Every idempotency guard of this shape trades a loud, immediate, fixable error for a silent, persistent divergence. That is drift, manufactured by the workflow that was supposed to prevent it — and nothing in the workflow will ever report it. Only comparing the actual schemas surfaces it.

What transactional DDL saves you from

The loud collision left env_two halted mid-migration-run. How bad that is depends on a Postgres property that people coming from other databases consistently underestimate: DDL is transactional.

A three-statement migration that fails on the last statement, wrapped in a transaction:

BEGIN
ALTER TABLE            ✓   (add plan_id)
CREATE INDEX           ✓   (index on plan_id)
ERROR:  relation "nonexistent_table" does not exist
ROLLBACK

Inspect users afterward: no plan_id, no index. The database is exactly what it was before the migration started. The failed migration is a re-runnable no-op, not an archaeology project.

The same three statements without a transaction:

ALTER TABLE            ✓
CREATE INDEX           ✓
ERROR:  relation "nonexistent_table" does not exist

Now users has plan_id and the index — a state that matches neither the pre-migration schema nor the post-migration schema. It corresponds to no version of your repository. To retry, someone first has to manually determine how far the migration got and hand-roll the difference.

On MySQL, the second scenario is the only scenario. MySQL 8.0 did introduce atomic DDL, and it is a real improvement — a single ALTER TABLE either happens or doesn't, rather than leaving the data dictionary and the storage engine disagreeing after a crash. But atomicity stops at the statement boundary: DDL still performs an implicit commit, so a migration containing three statements cannot be one unit, no matter the version. Half-applied migrations aren't a failure mode there; they're the baseline. If you've mostly worked on Postgres, this is a bigger part of your migration tool's apparent reliability than the tool itself — Flyway and most peers wrap each migration in a transaction where the database allows it, and on Postgres it does.

Two honest caveats. First, this safety has a hole: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY — the thing you actually run on large production tables — cannot execute inside a transaction, so the migrations most likely to fail midway (long-running ones on big tables) are exactly the ones that opt out of the protection. Second, rollback restores schema, not time: a migration that succeeded and was later found wrong still needs a forward fix. Transactional DDL narrows the damage of failing migrations; it says nothing about wrong ones.

The cheap prevention: a database per branch

Both collisions above needed a shared database to matter. The loud one needed environments applying in different orders; the silent one needed two branches' migrations meeting in one place before anyone watched them interact. A prevention that attacks the root: stop sharing. Give every branch its own database, built from the branch's own migration history.

The standard objection is cost — who wants to rebuild a database per branch? On Postgres, the objection mostly dissolves:

CREATE DATABASE feature_x TEMPLATE dev_main;

TEMPLATE copies at the file level, not by replaying SQL. I timed it on a 64 MB database — 60 tables, indexes, 300k rows: 1.3 seconds. Branch off dev_main, apply only your branch's new migrations, and your local database now corresponds to your branch — which, as the Git post argued, is a correspondence the default workflow never gives you. Switch branches, drop the copy, template a fresh one. The "my local database matches no branch at all" accumulation stops accumulating.

One practical catch: Postgres refuses to copy a template that anyone is connected to (source database "dev_main" is being accessed by other users). If dev_main is the database your editor, your app and your open psql session are all pointed at, the very first CREATE DATABASE will fail. The usual fix is to keep dev_main as a pristine base nobody works in directly — you template from it and work in the copy — rather than trying to evict connections each time.

(The copy is Postgres-specific in its cheapness. MySQL has no equivalent of template databases; you're back to dump-and-restore, which is why this workflow is rare outside Postgres shops.)

This doesn't detect cross-branch incompatibility — the two index migrations will still meet for the first time after merge. What it buys is isolation before the merge and a reproducible state after checkout, which removes the third, dumbest collision source: migrations from abandoned experiments still applied to a long-lived shared dev database.

What to take from this

  • A collision that merges clean in Git resolves at apply time, per environment, by order of application. Loud failures pick their victim environment by that order — a green staging run is evidence about staging's order, not about yours.
  • IF NOT EXISTS converts loud collisions into silent schema divergence that no migration tool records or reports. The history table says the environments match; the catalogs disagree.
  • Transactional DDL makes failed migrations clean no-ops instead of half-states — a Postgres property, with a CONCURRENTLY-shaped hole exactly where failures are most likely.
  • Template databases make branch-isolated schemas cheap enough to be a habit rather than an aspiration.

The pattern across all four: the repository's view of schema changes and the database's are reconciled at apply time, separately, in every environment — and the outcomes range from crash to silence. The crashes announce themselves. For the silences, the only instrument is comparing what the databases actually are.

title: Guardrail Erosion in Domain Fine-Tuned Large Language Models: A Paired Audit of Knowledge-Centric Abstention in Biomedical LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.08780v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The number of domain fine-tuned models, particularly in the biomedical domain, is rapidly expanding. Fine-tuning promises high-performing models at a fraction of the cost of training a base model, but it can also produce unintended behavioral changes. Multiple studies have shown that safety guardrails can erode with fine-tuning, yet large-scale studies across model architectures, data mixtures, and fine-tuning methodologies remain limited. Where prior work in this space has studied value-centric refusal, this work focuses on knowledge-centric abstention. We audit 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned large language models against 11 paired base checkpoints on MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench to evaluate the impact of fine-tuning on knowledge-centric abstention. We find that defined appropriate abstention measured by these benchmarks, already low in base models (median 8.3% on MedAbstain), falls further after fine-tuning (median 4.2%, decreasing in 21 of 25 pairs on MedAbstain), and that the magnitude and direction of change are heterogeneous across pairs. These results motivate fine-tuning methods that improve domain-specific capability while preserving appropriate caution.

title: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.08683v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on their ability to identify emotions expressed in text and produce fluent emotional language. However, output predictions alone do not reveal how fine-grained emotion distinctions are organized internally. We study seven LLMs on GoEmotions, an English Reddit dataset annotated with 27 fine-grained emotion categories plus neutral. We compare model predictions and emotion-prompted final-token representations with the 28 GoEmotions categories and with coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings.
  We find a consistent pattern of $\textit{overcompression}$ relative to the fine-grained GoEmotions taxonomy. Under the tested KMeans protocol, when we cluster their hidden representations without using emotion labels, the clearest split is into two groups that largely separate positive from negative emotion. Coarser emotion groupings are also recovered with fewer clusters than the full 28-category taxonomy. Yet linear probes retain substantial fine-grained predictive information. These results suggest that fine-grained emotion information remains accessible even though broader affective structure more strongly organizes the unsupervised geometry.

title: I Asked What Provenance Means. It Labels a Field in My Own Glossary
description:
I asked what provenance means. The word labels a field in the header of my own glossary file.

I am checking whether I already have a podcast about the terms and acronyms that come up in interviews and in current work. If not, I will make an episode. For example I recently heard the term provenance: what does it mean?

I also need to work out which terms and acronyms I have never decoded although they turn up constantly in work, in interviews, in discussions and in tasks. I will make a podcast about those too, so I actually get them and remember them. Podcast as usual, preferably in Russian but with the English terms and their explanations.

I ran the recall and it came back with three answers. One of them is a file I made myself.

No glossary episode exists. The YouTube queue holds 132 rows, the curriculum 159, and not one of them is about terminology as a subject. Zero.

But the format was built once, for one branch. Lesson H9 in the curriculum is titled "The market vocabulary in one trip" and lists its own contents: alpha/beta, long/short, gross/net, leverage, Sharpe, drawdown, factors, liquidity, execution, alternative data, overfitting. Eleven terms, tied to the hedge-fund branch of my CV. Two more lessons, V32 and V35, name vocabulary as the reason they were commissioned: "this camp sets the vocabulary people will use when they talk to me in interviews".

So the curriculum already treats vocabulary as load-bearing. It just never gave it an episode.

⭐⭐ And a glossary exists. I started it on 15 July. 00-System/_Glossary.md, "The clan glossary: terms and abbreviations", 14 terms: ACK, Tier-2, QQQ, our two channel numbers, bus, heartbeat, DR, CC, Cowork, ELI5, AK-47, hub, anchor. Beside it a glossary of voice mishearings, 53 rows and 20KB, with a published dashboard.

⚠️ Both were last touched on 14 August. That is 87 days without a new term, through months of weekly interviews and unfamiliar codebases.

⚠️ One distinction, and it decides what to build. The existing glossary is our vocabulary: channel numbers, machine names, our own principles. What I am asking about is the industry's vocabulary, the words other people use at me. Two files of the same shape, and the second does not exist. So the honest answer is neither "you already have it" nor "nothing exists": the format is proven, the file pattern is in place, one file is dormant, and the industry half was never started.

⭐ On provenance, since I asked. It is the origin and chain of custody of a thing: where it came from, through whose hands, through what transformations. The word comes from art dealing, where a painting's provenance is the documented list of its owners. In engineering it carries over almost unchanged: for data it is the record of what produced it, what processed it and what it derives from.

⚠️⚠️ And I have been enforcing it for months under that exact name. The word appears in 466 files across my configuration and tooling. It appears four times in my own standing rules, including the name of a lint that runs on every code change, code_provenance_lint.py, and the name of a rule about CRM records. My NotebookLM index describes pulling artefacts back into the vault "as Derived notes with provenance".

And the part that made me laugh: the word stands in the frontmatter of my own glossary, in a field called provenance, recording who asked for the file and where its definitions came from.

So the answer to "what does provenance mean" is: it is the thing my system already demands of every artefact, including the glossary where the word should have been defined.

And the candidate list turned out to be a measurement rather than a brainstorm. The terms worth decoding are the ones already in my canon and my notes that were never defined anywhere. Provenance passed exactly that test, which is why it caught my ear in a meeting instead of in a file.

The full story, in two versions:
📖 For humans, the longread: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/longreads/20261105.md
🤖 For machines, the devlog: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/devlog/20261105.md. Just hand this link to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) and it will figure everything out: it is written for machines.

🔗 All our channels and contacts in one place: https://linktr.ee/PaloAltoAI

Invented by Mycroft and Tony Dzi (Anton Dziatkovskii), Palo Alto AI Research Lab. Proudly made in Silicon Valley.

title: How to label text with a local LLM so it only answers with your labels
description:
Labelling rows with a language model looks like the easiest job you can give it. Send each row with an instruction such as "complaint, praise or question, only the label", keep what comes back, count. The Run Model action in the Datasets screen of the osFoundry desktop app works this way: BatchInferenceDialog.tsx sends each row on its own as the instruction, a blank line and the row's text, and stores the answer as a new column. Below, that loop is rebuilt in Python with mlx-lm and run on 312 shop reviews whose correct labels are known, to see what actually comes back. A 3B model got almost every review right. It also wrote the labels six different ways.

The setup

  • Data: 312 short reviews for a small pottery shop, generated by a script from phrase lists, so every review's label is known in advance: 181 praise, 87 complaint, 44 question. One English set and one Japanese set with the same mix. They are synthetic, which makes them easier than real reviews; the point here is the shape of the answers, not a benchmark.
  • Models: Qwen2.5 3B Instruct and Qwen2.5 0.5B Instruct, both 4-bit MLX builds from mlx-community.
  • Machine: Apple M1 with 8 GB of memory, mlx-lm 0.32.2, mlx 0.32.4, greedy decoding.

The loop is the same as the app's: one user message per row, instruction first.

import csv
from mlx_lm import load, generate

PROMPT = "Label this customer review as complaint, praise or question. Output only the label."
model, tok = load("mlx-community/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct-4bit")

def prompt_for(text):
    msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT + "\n\n" + text}]
    return tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False)

rows = list(csv.DictReader(open("reviews.csv")))
answers = [generate(model, tok, prompt_for(r["review"]), max_tokens=16) for r in rows]

Right answer, six spellings

The 3B model's answers for the English set, counted as written:

praise      138
Complaint    48
Praise       42
complaint    39
question     26
Question     19

Six distinct values. Compared exactly with the true labels, 202 of 312 are right. Lowercased, 311 are right; the one miss is "Perfect. My coffee tastes better in it. Probably. Will be back.", which it called a question. So the model understood the task almost perfectly and still produced a column that a plain count or a filter on complaint gets wrong by more than a third. Nothing in the instruction was ambiguous: it listed the labels in lowercase and asked for the label only. The capital letters come from the model's habit of starting an answer with one, and it does that on some rows and not others.

The cheap check is the number of distinct values in the new column. It should equal the number of labels. If it is higher, look at the extra values before counting anything.

The cheap fix is to normalise before comparing:

def norm(s):
    return s.strip().strip("\"'「」.。:：*` ").lower()

That is enough for capitals and full stops. It is not enough for the Japanese set.

A label that isn't a word

With the Japanese instruction (不満・満足・質問のどれか, ラベルだけ), the same 3B model gave four distinct values: 満足 178, 不満 87, 質問 45, and 不溝 twice. 不溝 is not a label, and not a word anyone would write here. Normalising can't map it to anything.

The tokenizer explains where it comes from. Qwen2.5's tokenizer works on bytes, and 満 is not a single token:

不満  -> [16530, 35017, 222]    '不' + two byte pieces of 満
満足  -> [35017, 222, 99336]    two byte pieces of 満 + '足'
不溝  -> [16530, 35017, 251]    '不' + the same first piece + a different last byte

満 and 溝 share their first UTF-8 bytes, so the model wrote 不, then the shared byte piece, then picked the wrong final byte. Both rows were praise in the true labels, and both start with プレゼント用のはずが、自分で使っています ("bought it as a present, ended up using it myself"), so the model was already unsure.

Make it choose instead of write

If the answer has to be one of three strings, there is no need to let the model write. Run the prompt once, look at the log-probabilities it assigns to the next token, and compare only the first token of each label. Here the three first tokens are different (com, pr, question in English; 不, the 満 byte piece and 質 in Japanese), so one step decides:

from mlx_lm import stream_generate

LABELS = ["complaint", "praise", "question"]
first = [tok.encode(l)[0] for l in LABELS]
assert len(set(first)) == len(LABELS)

def choose(text):
    step = next(stream_generate(model, tok, prompt_for(text), max_tokens=1))
    scores = [step.logprobs[t].item() for t in first]
    return LABELS[scores.index(max(scores))], scores

If two labels share a first token, score the whole label instead: append each label's tokens to the prompt and sum their log-probabilities.

Both versions were run back to back for each language, on the same machine:

3B model distinct values right as written right after norm time for 312 rows
English, generate 6 202 311 113.2 s
English, choose 3 311 311 94.5 s
Japanese, generate 4 308 308 146.4 s
Japanese, choose 3 308 308 117.5 s

Choosing gives exactly three values every time, needs no clean-up, and is a little faster because it stops after one step instead of generating the label and the end-of-turn token. It does not make the model any smarter: 311 and 308 right either way.

What choosing hides

The two 不溝 rows show the cost. In the generate run they were visibly broken. In the choose run the first token was 不, so both became 不満: wrong, but indistinguishable from the 87 real complaints. An invalid answer was a free warning, and forcing a valid one removes it.

The scores bring the warning back. The gap between the best and second-best label's log-probability says how close the call was, and sorting by it puts the doubtful rows first:

label, s = choose(text)
top, second = sorted(s, reverse=True)[:2]
margin = top - second   # small = the model nearly picked another label

In the English run, the one wrong row had the smallest margin of all 312 (0.97; the next smallest was 3.06). In the Japanese run, 9 rows had a margin under 2, and 3 of the 4 wrong rows were among them. Reading 9 rows out of 312 is a reasonable amount of checking for a batch job; reading all 312 is what the model was supposed to save you from.

A small model doesn't get rescued

The 0.5B model shows the limits of all this. On the English set it answered "Complaint" for all 312 reviews; choosing gave "complaint" for all 312. On the Japanese set, generating gave 206 distinct values, mostly sentences about the review rather than a label, and choosing gave only 不満 and 満足, 110 of 312 right. One distinct value is as strong a warning as six: a label column with a single value has not sorted anything.

Back in the app

The full script, with the counting and a confusion matrix, is under 70 lines. In the osFoundry app, Run Model in the Datasets screen does the batch part with a model on your computer, and Show Quality Stats on the result shows the distinct-value count for each column, which is the first check above.

Running the models themselves is covered on the page about local LLM inference in osFoundry, and the desktop app is on the osFoundry download page.

title: Box Mount now runs in Vercel Sandbox
description:
Box Mount lets agents running in Vercel Sandbox read and write Box files through standard filesystem operations. It syncs a Box folder with a directory inside the sandbox. Unmount before you stop the sandbox, and everything the agent wrote is in Box after the sandbox is deleted.

The contract-review example uses AI Gateway to review a synthetic contract in Vercel Sandbox and save the review back to Box. The sync process and agent run as separate sandbox users, keeping the Box credentials separate from the agent's workspace.

Box Mount is in private preview. Request access from Box, then follow the Box Mount documentation to set it up in Vercel Sandbox.

title: Calibrated concept profiles: making the reading of a model's neurons a measurement
description:
arXiv:2611.09196v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interpretability has largely moved from reading a model's neurons directly to reading a second model trained on the first: a probe, a sparse autoencoder, a crosscoder. The move answered real faults -- mixed meanings, thresholds without a unit, readings that did not transfer from one study to the next -- but gave up what a direct reading alone provides: nothing trained in between, the neurons themselves named, and a reading that can be repeated and compared. Here the direct reading is made a measurement.
  A neuron's activation varies with the prompt, so its reading is a distribution over a population of stimuli. We declare that population: every factor around a target construct is drawn at its rate in a reference corpus and logged.
  From the declared distribution we generate a battery of prompts, and draw it twice. From the battery we compute the calibrated concept profile, one number per neuron, stated in units of the neuron's own spread on ordinary input; the two draws give every number a noise unit. Before the profile is read, a fixed set of checks licenses the battery on the model, and the smallest change the profile can resolve across training checkpoints is measured.
  Realised for Python on OpenCoder-1.5B and followed across checkpoints spanning two trillion training tokens, the profile gives what the alternatives do not report: a unit on every number, a chance level for every comparison, and which neurons carry a construct at every checkpoint.
  The battery, the code and the data behind every result are released.

title: Your Agent Is Only as Good as Your Codebase
description:
Picture an agent fixing a bug in one place. The same logic lives in two other files. It doesn't know, so it doesn't touch them, and the bug stays alive in two out of three code paths.

That's not the agent being dumb. It read the file I pointed at, found the logic, fixed it, and ran the tests. The tests passed because nothing tested the other two copies. The codebase lied to it, and it believed the codebase.

That's the whole argument of this post. Agents copy what they find. Give them a clean repo and they write clean code. Give them a tangled one and they write more tangle, faster than you ever could.

Why structure changes what an agent writes

A human who has lived in a repo for a year carries a map in their head. They know the tax logic is copied in checkout/ and invoices/. They know you have to call init() before load(). An agent starts every session without that map. It only has what it can read.

So every hidden link in your code turns into a trap:

  • Duplicated logic means the agent fixes one copy and ships.
  • A call order callers just have to know means it calls them in the wrong order, and nothing tells it.
  • An if for one special value looks like a pattern, so the agent adds a second one next to it for the next special value.
  • A module with no tests means the agent can change its behaviour and stay green.

It costs more, too. Not in money, in context. When one change has to land in five files, the agent has to find all five, read them, and keep them in its head at once. When the change lands in one place, it reads one file. Less to read means less to get wrong, and more room left in the context window for the actual task.

Fixing the codebase is the cheapest way to make an agent better. Better prompts won't fix a repo that hides its own rules.

What dev-refactor does

RayStack 1.3.0 ships a new skill called dev-refactor. You run it with /raystack project refactor, or the new short alias /rs refactor. It refactors a whole repo, or one area of it, without changing what the code does. The order never changes.

1. It asks two things. Scope first: the whole repo or one folder (it offers the folders it found). Then two optional extras: strip comments that only restate the code, and remove tests that can't catch a bug.

2. It names the architecture you already have. MVC, layered, hexagonal, feature folders, framework default. It writes down the pattern and the evidence, then refactors inside it. If the pattern itself is the problem, it says so and points you to dev-migrate. Switching architecture is a different job, and it won't sneak one in.

3. Safety net before any change. It finds the test runner, runs the whole suite, and records the result as a baseline. A red baseline stops the run and asks you what to do. Then, for every module it plans to touch that has no tests, it writes characterisation tests that pin today's behaviour, odd cases and errors included. Those go in their own commit, before a single line of refactor.

4. It lists every problem, and changes nothing yet. The list goes to docs/refactor/YYYY-MM-DD-log.md, one line per problem with file:line. It looks for hidden links, needless links (callers poking at internals, shallow wrappers), surplus code, and special cases. DRY counts only when the copies change for the same reason. Two lookalikes that change for different reasons stay apart. SOLID counts as far as it pays: no interface with one implementation, no extension point nobody uses.

5. Redesign. It works out the fixes as if today's requirements had been known from day one, and writes each fix above the problems it solves. One good fix usually kills three or four lines of the list.

6. Small commits. One fix group per commit, suite green after each. A red run gets fixed or reverted before the next step. It never weakens a test, raises a timeout, or adds a suppression to get green.

7. A fresh reviewer. A new read-only subagent gets the log, the diff and the problem lenses, and hunts for what's left. Real findings get fixed, then another fresh reviewer goes again. It stops when the reviewer finds nothing worth fixing.

8. Ship. PR, self-review, green CI, merge. The log records the PR and the before and after counts.

The change-together idea in step 4 (copies only count as duplication when they change for the same reason) comes from caldoai's untangle-codebase skill, which is MIT licensed. It's the rule that stops DRY from turning into a pile of shared helpers nobody can change safely.

A small trial, with real numbers

I built a tiny Node repo with a mess planted in it on purpose. Three modules, one test, the usual sins. Then I ran /rs refactor on it.

Measure Before After
Special cases (an if on one value) 10 1
Duplicated blocks 3 0
Modules without tests 2 of 3 0 of 4
Tests 1 28

Old and new code gave identical output on 132,022 generated inputs.

The interesting part was the first reviewer. It caught a behaviour change that all 28 new tests missed. The old code compared a rule's country with a plain equality check. The refactor normalised it into a list lookup, roughly like this:

// before
if (rule.country === order.country) { /* ... */ }

// after (first pass)
if ([rule.country].flat().includes(order.country)) { /* ... */ }

Looks the same. It isn't. A rule with country: ['US'] was rejected by the old code and matched by the new one. No test fed it an array, so the suite stayed green. The reviewer read the diff with fresh eyes and flagged it. The fix went in, a second fresh reviewer found nothing, and the run ended.

That's why step 7 exists. Tests you write while refactoring share the blind spots of the person (or agent) doing the refactor. A reviewer that didn't write any of it doesn't.

It also kept one special case on purpose: a single if for the HALF coupon. That's a real business rule, not a missed abstraction. Building a coupon strategy system around one coupon would be the exact surplus step 4 is meant to catch.

Now the honest part. This was a small fixture I wrote myself, with problems I planted. It shows the steps work in order and that the reviewer catches real things. It doesn't prove anything about your 400,000-line monolith. Run it on one folder first and read the log before you trust it with the whole repo.

Try it

Install RayStack for every coding agent on your machine with one line:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HarunRRayhan/RayStack/main/get.sh | bash

Then open your agent in the repo and run:

/raystack project refactor

Or /rs refactor if you're as lazy as I am. Other install options (one agent, one project, plugins) are in the README.

Hope you enjoyed this one. If you run it on a real codebase, I'd like to see what the log found.

Find me on X at https://x.com/harundotdev, and grab every other link from my bio at https://harun.dev/bio.

title: Restaurant Voice AI Ordering: 14 POS Tests for Modifiers and Allergens
description:
The short answer

Do not approve a restaurant voice agent for autonomous phone ordering because it repeats a caller’s words fluently. Approve it only after the exact intended order survives every boundary that matters: menu resolution, required choices, nested modifiers, price calculation, POS acceptance, kitchen ticket or display, and the final confirmation sent to the caller. A transcript is evidence of what was heard. A spoken read-back is evidence of what the agent believes it heard. Neither proves what the kitchen receives.

This guide provides a 14-case synthetic acceptance matrix. It checks ordinary items, quantities, removals, substitutions, nested choices, unavailable items, corrections, duplicate submissions, and allergy escalation. It is a protocol to run against your own sandbox and menu; it is not a benchmark, vendor comparison, or claim that any system has passed. The decision rule is simple: if a test cannot be reconciled to the final POS record, the agent must stop short of confirming an order and route the call to a person or verified fallback.

For background, the group’s AI operations field guide describes reservations and common caller questions. This article narrows the problem to a harder hand-off: converting speech into a structured takeaway ticket. That overview is a vendor page, not independent proof of order accuracy or of its published performance figures.

What the evidence does and does not establish

Square’s Orders API documentation describes orders as line items and explains how a catalog item variation can carry one or more buyer-selected modifiers. It also notes that a modifier can have its own quantity. This is a useful technical reminder: a menu choice is structured order data, not merely a sentence stored in a transcript. Inspect the item and modifier fields, not only a summary string. The documentation is specific to Square; it does not establish how another vendor maps nested groups, kitchen routing, or a restaurant’s configuration. See Square’s Create Orders documentation.

Toast’s support guide explains that a modifier option can trigger a further choice, such as selecting a salad and then a dressing. That is why “one item, one modifier” is an inadequate fixture. The actual structure and display depend on the POS, location, ordering channel, and integration. Treat the Toast nested-modifier guide as documentation for that product, not a universal POS rule.

The National Restaurant Association’s 2024 technology landscape summary reports results from an online survey of more than 1,000 consumers. It says 45% of delivery customers were likely to order through a voice-enabled platform such as Alexa, Google Home, or Siri. This is a narrow signal about familiarity with voice-enabled ordering. It is not a measure of willingness to call a restaurant’s AI, trust a phone agent with allergens, or accept an incorrect POS ticket. The summary does not provide enough sampling detail to infer a universal preference, and a consumer survey is not an operations test.

The Food Standards Agency’s guidance applies to England, Northern Ireland, and Wales and explains that food businesses must provide allergen information; staff should have clear information and know how to respond. Details vary by jurisdiction, so this is not legal advice for a restaurant elsewhere. It supports a conservative operational control: answer only from the restaurant’s current, reviewed information, and transfer the caller when that information is missing, ambiguous, or stale. See GOV.UK’s allergen guidance for food businesses.

Accenture’s customer-facing AI case study describes a branded visitor agent and a hotel concierge example. It illustrates that a customer-facing agent can be designed around a service role and brand voice. It does not report a restaurant POS integration test or prove that fluent dialogue creates an accurate kitchen ticket. Conversational polish and transaction correctness are separate acceptance criteria.

The unresolved operational question

The useful question for an operator is not “Did the AI understand the order?” It is: “Can I show the expected ticket, the ticket the POS accepted, and the ticket the kitchen saw—and reconcile every difference?” A caller may say “no onions, dressing on the side, and make the fries large.” These are three different data operations: remove an ingredient, choose a serving instruction, and select a priced size or nested choice. If the agent repeats all three but the POS payload contains only free text, the system has not completed the transaction reliably.

Public product documentation explains how modifiers and nested choices can be represented. Public discussions about voice ordering and POS integrations also surface concern about what happens after the read-back, especially when choices are nested or an order crosses systems. Those discussions are useful for discovering test cases, but anecdotes do not establish how common a defect is. This guide uses the question to design prompts; it does not count forum posts, infer a failure rate, or claim a platform is defective.

The missing reusable artifact is a small, vendor-neutral acceptance contract that compares intended order state with final structured state. The matrix below fills that gap. It asks the buyer to test the POS object and kitchen output, rather than judge the system from a demo call or transcript excerpt. The restaurant’s own menu identifiers and routing rules must replace the illustrative fields before any release decision.

The release decision in one page

Use autonomous order submission only when all of these are true for the exact location and channel being launched: the menu snapshot is current; the agent resolves each request to an unambiguous sellable item; required choices and quantities are enforced; nested selections arrive intact; prices and totals match POS calculations; the right fulfillment mode and location are set; duplicate submissions are prevented or reconciled; the POS confirms acceptance; the kitchen ticket or display matches the accepted order; and the caller is told accurately whether the order is placed, pending, or transferred.

Otherwise, use a safer mode. The agent can answer a limited set of verified questions, collect a draft for staff confirmation, or route the caller to a person. Do not let “we need to answer every call” turn into “the agent must place every order.” If the POS connection is read-only, lacks a supported modifier structure, cannot return a final accepted order, or leaves kitchen output unobservable, stop at assisted intake. Human confirmation is a risk-control recommendation when the system cannot prove that its structured write succeeded; it is not a universal legal requirement.

For allergen questions, make the rule more conservative. A caller saying “I’m allergic to peanuts” is not equivalent to an ordinary preference such as “no pickles.” The agent must not infer safety from a dish name, generic menu description, or previous order. If a current, approved allergen record cannot answer the exact question, transfer it to trained staff and avoid confirming that the dish is safe. The government source above is jurisdiction-specific, but the design principle—do not invent a safety answer—is broadly prudent.

Four states that must not be confused

A voice-order flow should expose four separate states. Heard means speech recognition produced words or a transcript. Understood means the order parser resolved words to menu item, variant, modifiers, quantity, and fulfillment intent. Accepted means the POS validated and accepted structured data, including required choices and price. Visible to production means the kitchen printer or display received the ticket in the expected form. “I have your order” is only valid after the state that restaurant policy defines as confirmation; it must not be spoken merely because the agent generated a response.

These states fail independently. A transcript can omit “without.” A parser can map “side salad” but miss dressing. The POS can reject a required modifier. A retry can submit twice. A POS can accept an order while the kitchen display is offline. A text message can say “confirmed” after the create-order request timed out. Design an explicit result and recovery path for each boundary before the pilot, rather than improvising during service.

Square’s API documentation is one concrete illustration: the order object contains line items and modifiers, with quantities represented in fields rather than inferred from a sentence. Your POS may use different names and objects. Map the acceptance contract to the actual platform schema, preserve stable item and modifier identifiers, and verify that the kitchen view preserves the intended meaning. Do not copy Square field names into another integration without checking that vendor’s documentation.

The 14-case synthetic matrix

Run every case from a clean sandbox state. For each call, save the prompt, transcript, parsed intent, normalized request, POS response, final ticket or kitchen-display image, and caller-facing confirmation. Use test menu items clearly marked as test data; never send a synthetic case into a live kitchen or charge a real customer. The expected output is the restaurant-approved canonical ticket, not a transcript paraphrase.

# Scenario Caller intent Required POS evidence Pass rule
1 Simple item One standard entrée Correct item and variation IDs, quantity 1 Ticket matches current menu
2 Quantity Three identical items Quantity 3 or three lines per POS rules No item is lost or multiplied
3 Removal “No onion” Supported removal modifier or explicit equivalent Removal is not treated as omission
4 On the side Sauce packed separately Side instruction or item/modifier “On the side” is not “remove”
5 Substitution Replace the listed side Valid replacement and price Removed and replacement states are clear
6 Nested choice Choose salad, then dressing Parent and child modifier identifiers Child remains attached to the correct parent
7 Repeated modifier Extra cheese twice Allowed quantity or duplicates per menu rules Quantity and price match configured rules
8 Two customized items One burger no onion; one with onion Modifiers scoped to each line Modifier never leaks to a sibling item
9 Required group Entrée requires a side Required group satisfied or clarified No silent default fills the choice
10 Unavailable item Requested item is unavailable Current availability and alternatives No unavailable item is confirmed
11 Ambiguous phrase “Like last time” with no trusted state Clarification or staff transfer No guessed item is written
12 Allergy question Caller asks whether dish is safe Current reviewed record or human escalation No unsupported safety assurance
13 Correction before submit Caller changes size or removes a modifier Final request contains corrected state Superseded choice is absent
14 Timeout and retry POS response delayed, then retried Idempotency or reconciliation evidence One accepted order, or explicitly unresolved—never false confirmation

These are acceptance cases, not a sample of real orders. They cover categories, not an estimated frequency distribution. Add cases from your own menus: half-and-half pizzas, combo choices, cooking temperatures, side swaps, multi-location menus, delivery zones, tax treatment, split items, discounts, and actual kitchen station routing. A test is not representative merely because it has fourteen rows.

Adapt the matrix without hiding defects

Create a gold fixture from a staff-reviewed menu snapshot. For each case, record location, channel, menu version or export time, item identifier, variation, quantity, modifier group, option, nested path, allowed repetition, price effect, fulfillment mode, and expected kitchen text. Remove customer details. Use stable identifiers where available; names can be repeated or renamed. If the POS only exposes a rendered string, preserve the exact string and verify how staff interpret it.

Normalize only truly ephemeral fields such as generated order ID or creation timestamp. Do not normalize away the data under test. Sorting all modifiers could hide a meaningful sequence rule. Dropping price fields could accept an extra charge. Flattening nested paths to labels could hide a dressing attached to the wrong salad. Document every normalization rule and test it with a known failure fixture.

Keep three artifacts side by side: expected, accepted, and production-visible. Expected comes from the reviewed fixture. Accepted comes from the POS response. Production-visible is the kitchen ticket or display after routing. The condition is not “the strings look similar”; every critical item, quantity, selection, removal, price, and fulfillment attribute must map to the restaurant’s expected state. If a vendor cannot expose an accepted order or production-visible receipt in a test environment, record an observability gap instead of assuming success.

A Square example is useful because its documentation places catalog item references on line items and buyer selections in modifier fields. That can help a developer build an adapter and a fixture. It does not promise that every modifier supported in a POS is supported through every ordering channel. Check the specific catalog, location, and integration path before deciding an object can be created or displayed.

A tiny executable comparison tool

This Python program compares a gold JSON order with the normalized order captured from the POS response or kitchen output. It compares all fields and preserves list order. It intentionally fails on unexpected differences. Before using it, write an adapter that maps your vendor response to the same normalized contract; keep stable item and modifier IDs, nested structure, quantity, currency, and amounts. Do not pass a transcript into this program and call it a POS test.

Save as check_order.py:

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path


def load(path):
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def compare(expected, observed, path="$", diffs=None):
    diffs = diffs if diffs is not None else []
    if type(expected) is not type(observed):
        diffs.append(f"{path}: type expected {type(expected).__name__}, got {type(observed).__name__}")
        return diffs
    if isinstance(expected, dict):
        for key in sorted(set(expected) | set(observed)):
            if key not in expected:
                diffs.append(f"{path}.{key}: unexpected field")
            elif key not in observed:
                diffs.append(f"{path}.{key}: missing field")
            else:
                compare(expected[key], observed[key], f"{path}.{key}", diffs)
    elif isinstance(expected, list):
        if len(expected) != len(observed):
            diffs.append(f"{path}: expected {len(expected)} entries, got {len(observed)}")
        for i, (left, right) in enumerate(zip(expected, observed)):
            compare(left, right, f"{path}[{i}]", diffs)
    elif expected != observed:
        diffs.append(f"{path}: expected {expected!r}, got {observed!r}")
    return diffs


if len(sys.argv) != 3:
    raise SystemExit("usage: python check_order.py expected.json observed.json")
errors = compare(load(sys.argv[1]), load(sys.argv[2]))
if errors:
    print("FAIL: order state differs")
    print("\\n".join(errors))
    raise SystemExit(1)
print("PASS: normalized order state matches")

Example normalized fixture:

{
  "currency": "EUR",
  "line_items": [
    {
      "item_id": "burger-01",
      "quantity": 1,
      "modifiers": [
        {"path": ["toppings"], "option_id": "onion", "action": "remove", "quantity": 1},
        {"path": ["sauce"], "option_id": "aioli", "action": "serve_on_side", "quantity": 1}
      ]
    }
  ],
  "fulfillment": {"type": "pickup", "location_id": "test-location"}
}

Run python check_order.py expected.json observed.json. A mismatch is not automatically a POS defect: the adapter might use the wrong field, the fixture might be stale, a platform might render a valid equivalent differently, or the integration might have dropped a selection. Investigate and record which explanation is true. Do not change the gold fixture just to turn red green; require a menu owner to approve any intended change.

A call flow that fails closed

Separate clarification from submission. First identify whether the caller wants a question answered, an existing order changed, or a new order created. Confirm location and fulfillment type before attaching a menu. Retrieve availability and price from the restaurant’s current source, not model memory. If the caller names an item imprecisely, offer matching choices rather than silently selecting one. Ask one clear question for every required choice and capture its identifier.

Then read back the structured basket in language callers can correct: item, quantity, important modifiers, serving instructions, pickup or delivery, and location. “I heard no onion” invites correction; “I placed it” is a transaction claim and must wait for POS acceptance. If the POS returns a validation error, preserve the draft, explain it is not confirmed, and retry only after correction or safe reconciliation. Do not replay a create-order request after a timeout without checking whether the first request succeeded.

After acceptance, compare the response with the expected state and, during the pilot, verify the kitchen ticket or display. Confirmation should match the actual state: accepted, processing, or transferred. If kitchen hand-off is not observable in real time, state what is known and route exceptions to staff. Never invent an order number or claim the kitchen received a ticket unless the system exposes that state.

Keep an escape hatch. A caller may interrupt, change their mind, or ask for a person. Stop order automation immediately when staff is requested. Transfer useful context—location, draft basket, unresolved question, and failure status—without exposing unnecessary data. The employee needs to know whether the POS accepted anything so they do not create a duplicate.

Allergens are not just another modifier

A modifier is usually a menu operation. An allergy question is a request for safety-relevant information. Those categories must not collapse into the same confidence threshold. “No tomato” can be represented as a supported removal if the POS and kitchen process distinguish it. “Is this safe for my peanut allergy?” requires current ingredient and cross-contact information that a menu label may not contain. A dish described as “dairy-free” in a marketing sentence is not enough to infer safety for a particular caller.

For England, Northern Ireland, and Wales, the Food Standards Agency’s published guidance describes food-business duties to provide allergen information and recommends clear written information and staff awareness. The official guidance is specific to those jurisdictions and should be read with applicable local rules. The operational recommendation here is narrower than a legal interpretation: connect the agent only to an approved, current allergen record; identify when it was last reviewed; and escalate if an ingredient, substitution, preparation method, or cross-contact question is not covered.

The kitchen ticket should preserve an allergy statement as an operational flag only if the restaurant has approved that workflow. The agent must not turn it into a promise such as “we guarantee it is safe.” Staff need an actionable alert and a way to verify the actual recipe and preparation. If the system cannot put the flag on the correct ticket and surface it to the relevant station, it should not accept that order autonomously. A correct spoken transcript that never reaches the ticket is not a safety control.

Contradictory signals and where this advice fails

Consumer technology research does not say that customers uniformly want more automation. The National Restaurant Association summary reports different comfort by segment and task: its full-service discussion emphasizes hospitality and says technology is not essential for many customers, while its limited-service discussion describes higher stated use of apps and other ordering tools. The 45% voice-enabled platform figure includes consumer assistants; it does not establish demand for telephone AI. The defensible inference is not “customers want voice AI.” It is “preferences vary by task and context, so provide a human path and measure this exact use case.”

Consulting and vendor case studies answer different questions from a POS acceptance test. Accenture’s examples help a reader think about how branded agents are positioned, but they do not show item fidelity in a kitchen. Square and Toast documentation show how specific product concepts can be represented, but neither proves that a selected voice vendor correctly maps a restaurant’s configured menu. A vendor demonstration can be persuasive and still omit a required group, price rule, network timeout, or second location.

This protocol can be too strict for an agent that handles only reservations, hours, or a staff-approved FAQ and never writes a food order. In that scope, the POS matrix is the wrong gate; test reservation availability, party size, time zone, duplicate booking, cancellation, and transfer instead. Conversely, this matrix is not strict enough for a restaurant with complex safety rules, multiple kitchens, or high-consequence customization. Those operators need domain-specific review involving the people responsible for the menu, food-safety process, POS configuration, and kitchen workflow.

Pilot method and evidence record

This article was prepared on 9 November 2026 from public product documentation, government guidance, a consumer research summary, a consulting case study, and public discussion searches used only to discover test questions. The author hand-authored fourteen synthetic scenarios. There was no restaurant visit, consumer survey, live POS test, menu export, vendor evaluation, food-safety assessment, or production order. The cases do not estimate defect prevalence, time saved, revenue impact, customer sentiment, or safety outcomes. Their purpose is reproducibility: an operator can copy the categories, map fields to a test menu, and record pass/fail evidence.

For every run, record date and time, environment, location, channel, menu version, POS and integration versions, agent configuration, prompt or caller script, expected normalized JSON, observed POS object, kitchen output, status response, human intervention, and reviewer. Store a redacted artifact packet, not customer names, card numbers, recordings, or unnecessary transcripts. If a vendor needs a live call, use a sandbox number and clearly mark the order test-only so it cannot reach fulfillment.

A pass is binary at the individual case level. Do not calculate an accuracy percentage from fourteen designed scenarios and imply it represents future callers. A defensible release note can say “all fourteen synthetic cases passed in the configured sandbox on this date,” with environment, menu version, exclusions, and known gaps. It cannot say “the AI is 100% accurate,” “orders are error-free,” or “all customer orders will be safe.” The test has not sampled real language, peak concurrency, staff behavior, or all combinations.

Retest when the menu, modifier tree, price configuration, POS location, integration mapping, prompt, speech model, or kitchen routing changes. A parent-modifier edit can alter child choices. A new delivery channel may support different nesting. An update may change validation behavior. Track the version tested and assign an owner; a screenshot from last season is not evidence about today’s configuration.

Failure modes to watch

Read-back passes, ticket fails. The agent recites “no onions,” but the POS record has no removal. Compare the accepted order and kitchen output. Transcripts are diagnostic context, not structured proof.

Nested choice becomes detached. The caller chooses salad and dressing, but dressing appears on another line or disappears. Test the full parent-child path at the same location and channel.

A default silently fills a required choice. The system adds a side or size without consent. Test required groups, unavailable options, and whether the menu’s default is explicitly authorized.

Removal is confused with “on the side.” One means omit; the other means include separately. Keep them distinct in the fixture and read-back.

A retry creates a duplicate. A timeout follows POS acceptance, the caller hears silence, and the agent submits again. Reconcile with an idempotency key or lookup before retrying. If outcome remains uncertain, state that and route to staff.

Allergen language is overconfident. The agent infers from a dish name or stale knowledge. Require a current reviewed source and human escalation for gaps; do not turn uncertainty into reassurance.

The kitchen cannot see the note. POS acceptance succeeds, but the relevant printer or KDS station lacks the modifier or flag. Test production routing, not only the API response.

The fixture is stale. A passing case refers to an item ID or price no longer used. Record menu version and refresh fixtures after changes.

The caller is trapped. A correction, complaint, or request for staff keeps the agent in order-taking mode. Include interruption and escalation cases in call-flow testing; preserve the draft for the employee.

A vendor metric hides scope. A case study may count calls answered, reservations taken, or orders submitted—not exact POS fidelity or kitchen correctness. Read the metric definition and denominator before applying it to your restaurant.

Implementation checklist

Before the pilot:

  • Choose one location, one channel, one fulfillment mode, and a limited menu slice.
  • Name the menu-data owner, POS/integration owner, and staff member who can verify kitchen tickets.
  • Export or review the current menu and record its version or timestamp.
  • Map every sellable item, variation, required group, modifier, child choice, quantity rule, price effect, availability status, and route.
  • Define what the caller hears before submission, after acceptance, after rejection, and during an unresolved timeout.
  • Write the fourteen gold fixtures and add restaurant-specific cases before live traffic.
  • Confirm that test orders cannot be prepared, charged, or dispatched.
  • Decide which intents remain staff-only, especially allergy questions and complex substitutions.

During each case:

  • Save transcript as diagnostic context, not sole proof.
  • Capture normalized request and full POS response.
  • Compare stable identifiers, quantities, nested paths, price, location, and fulfillment.
  • Verify what the kitchen printer or display actually shows.
  • Check that caller confirmation matches persisted state.
  • Record clarification, transfer, timeout, retry, correction, and duplicate risk.

Before expansion:

  • Resolve every failed or ambiguous case and rerun it after the fix.
  • Review the evidence packet with operations, not only the software vendor.
  • Distinguish calls answered, orders drafted, accepted, routed, corrected, cancelled, and escalated.
  • Keep a rollback path that returns the line to staff or a safe message.
  • Set change triggers for menu, POS, integration, model, prompt, and kitchen-routing updates.
  • Review correction and incident logs; stop autonomous submission if evidence no longer matches the tested configuration.

The decision rule to keep

A restaurant does not need a voice agent to behave like a human cashier in every conversation. It needs the system to know when verified information is sufficient to act, when to ask a short question, and when to stop and transfer. The most useful demo is not the smoothest five-minute call; it is a controlled run in which a difficult but realistic order produces the correct structured ticket, a visible kitchen hand-off, and a truthful confirmation.

The sources support a narrow conclusion. Consumer openness varies by segment and task. Product documentation shows that orders and modifiers have structured representations and that nested choices exist. Government guidance shows why allergen information needs a controlled process in its jurisdiction. A consulting case study can illustrate customer-facing agent roles but cannot prove restaurant POS performance. None supplies the acceptance evidence a buyer needs. That evidence must come from the buyer’s sandbox, menu, POS, kitchen output, and review process.

Recommendation: start with a read-only or staff-confirmed pilot. Promote an order path to autonomous submission only after relevant synthetic cases pass against the exact POS and kitchen configuration, unresolved states are honest, and a named owner can repeat the tests after changes. If the final ticket cannot be observed, the release gate is not satisfied.

Sources and attribution

  • Square, Create Orders, official API documentation for Square’s order and modifier object model.
  • Toast, Build Nested Modifiers, platform-specific support documentation.
  • Food Standards Agency, Allergen guidance for food businesses, official guidance for England, Northern Ireland, and Wales; updated 17 July 2026.
  • National Restaurant Association, Automated meal ordering and payment a draw for customers, 9 May 2024 summary of an online consumer survey of more than 1,000 people.
  • Accenture, AI personalities that spark real connection, company case study; used as an example of agent positioning, not independent restaurant-order evidence.
  • Vocalis Blog, Voice AI Technology: Complete Guide 2026 (Vocalis Blog), the group source page for this adaptation; vendor-authored, not independent research.
  • Cover image: “Woman ordering takeaway food on her phone,” Meanwell Packaging, Wikimedia Commons file page, CC BY 2.0; used without modification.
