title: How to Evaluate a Neocloud for AI: CoreWeave vs Lambda vs Nebius vs AWS on Performance, Networking, Capacity, and Compliance
description:
A neocloud is worth adding to your stack when GPU price, availability, or interconnect performance for your workload beats what your hyperscaler offers by enough to cover the cost of running a second environment. Evaluate it on workload fit, networking, capacity and lead times, reliability, compliance, integration time, and total price. Control Plane lets teams add a neocloud GPU cluster as another location next to AWS, GCP, or Azure and run the same workloads across them from a single definition, which cuts integration time.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Core evaluation criteria:

  • Workload fit: Does the provider offer the GPU model, memory, and cluster topology your training or inference job needs?
  • Networking: Does the interconnect (InfiniBand, RoCE, or EFA) support your distributed training communication patterns?
  • Capacity and lead times: Can you get the GPUs you need, when you need them, at a commitment term that matches your planning horizon?
  • Reliability: What uptime SLA does the provider publish, and how fast does it replace failed GPUs?
  • Compliance: Does the provider hold the attestations your security team requires, and can it meet your data residency constraints?
  • Integration time: How long will it take your team to connect networking, identity, CI/CD, observability, and data pipelines to a new provider?

When a neocloud wins: You need large contiguous GPU clusters fast, your workload is sensitive to interconnect quality, or your hyperscaler cannot deliver capacity on your timeline.

When to stay on the hyperscaler: Your stack leans on its managed services, or you need only a few inference GPUs.

Integration time drivers: Private connectivity, identity federation, CI/CD changes, observability, images and drivers, and data movement. The more provider-specific glue your application uses, the longer integration takes.

How Control Plane fits: Teams can add a GPU cluster running on a neocloud as a location in Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a set of locations a workload runs across. Services then run across the hyperscaler and the neocloud from one definition, and GPU inference runs across GPU clusters on both, with no separate deployment pipeline, dashboards, or access controls per provider.

How do I evaluate whether a neocloud is worth adding to my stack?

Use this scorecard to structure your evaluation. For each criterion, ask the provider the listed question, compare the answer against what good looks like, and watch for the red flags.

Criterion What to ask the provider What good looks like Red flags
Workload fit (training, inference, fine-tuning; GPU models and memory) Which NVIDIA GPU families do you offer, and what is the maximum cluster size for a single training job? The provider offers the GPU generation your framework requires with enough scale for your largest job. Only older GPU generations available; no clear path to next-generation hardware.
Price and commitment terms What are your on-demand, reserved, and spot or preemptible rates? What is the minimum commitment? What are egress charges? Transparent pricing with flexible terms, low or zero egress fees, and per-minute or per-hour billing for on-demand. Long mandatory commitments with no early-exit clause; opaque or high egress fees.
Capacity and lead times How quickly can you provision a 64-node GPU cluster? Is capacity available now or contracted for a future date? Clear communication about current inventory, waitlists, and delivery dates. Vague timelines; capacity “subject to availability” with no commitment on provisioning.
Cluster networking (InfiniBand, RoCE, GPUDirect RDMA, topology) What interconnect fabric do you use between nodes, and at what bandwidth per GPU? What is the oversubscription ratio? Do you support GPUDirect RDMA? Can I control placement topology? InfiniBand or RoCE at the bandwidth your job needs (400 Gb/s per GPU is common on current clusters), a non-blocking (1:1) fabric, GPUDirect RDMA enabled, and topology-aware scheduling. Shared Ethernet fabric with no RDMA support; oversubscribed links; no topology guarantees.
Storage and data movement What parallel file system do you offer? How do I bulk-ingest datasets? Do you offer S3-compatible object storage? What does it cost to copy checkpoints to another cloud? A high-throughput parallel file system, checkpoint writes that do not stall training, and a bulk ingest path. NFS-only storage; checkpoint I/O is a known bottleneck; per-GB egress on checkpoint copies.
Reliability (SLA terms, status history) What is your uptime SLA? What does your status page history look like? A published SLA with service credits and a transparent incident history. No published SLA; status page is empty or hidden.
GPU health and replacement How do you burn in nodes before handover? Do you run active health checks such as DCGM diagnostics and NCCL tests? How fast do you replace a failed GPU or node, and do you credit the lost time? Burn-in and acceptance tests before handover, continuous health checks, automatic cordoning, and a written replacement window with credits. No acceptance testing; you find bad nodes yourself; replacement on a best-effort basis.
Support model What are your response times by severity? Is support 24/7? Do I get a named engineer and escalation to people who know the fabric? 24/7 support with severity-based response times, a named technical contact, and direct escalation for fabric and hardware issues. Ticket-only support; business hours only; no response-time commitment.
Compliance and data residency Which compliance attestations do you hold, and do they cover the data center operator as well as your own operations? Where are GPUs physically located? Do you sign BAAs? The attestations your security team requires, a HIPAA BAA where needed, and clear data residency documentation. No published attestations; unclear data residency; unwillingness to sign a BAA.
Managed Kubernetes, Slurm, and APIs Do you offer managed Kubernetes, managed Slurm, or both? What APIs and IaC integrations exist? CNCF-conformant managed Kubernetes and managed Slurm with GPU-aware scheduling, Terraform or Pulumi providers, and APIs for provisioning. One scheduler with no managed option; CLI-only management; no IaC support.
Integration with your existing cloud Can I set up private connectivity to my AWS, GCP, or Azure VPC? How does identity federation work? Private interconnect or VPN options, OIDC or SAML identity federation, and observability export to standard tools. Public internet only; no identity federation; proprietary monitoring with no export.
Exit cost What happens if I want to leave? Are there early termination fees? How do I get my data out? No lock-in beyond the commitment term, reasonable data export mechanisms, and standard formats for models and data. Punitive early termination fees; proprietary data formats; slow data export.

Worked scoring example

Assign each criterion a weight based on your organization’s priorities. The weights and scores here are illustrative; adapt them to your workload.

Criterion Weight Provider A score (1-5) Provider B score (1-5)
Workload fit 15% 5 4
Price and commitment terms 15% 3 4
Capacity and lead times 15% 4 3
Cluster networking 15% 5 3
Storage and data movement 5% 4 3
Reliability and GPU health 10% 4 2
Support model 5% 4 3
Compliance 10% 3 4
Managed Kubernetes, Slurm, and APIs 5% 4 3
Integration with existing cloud 3% 2 5
Exit cost 2% 4 3

Multiply each score by its weight and sum to get a composite. In this example, Provider A scores 3.99 and Provider B scores 3.36. A team doing multi-node distributed training will weight networking and capacity heavily. A team running single-GPU inference endpoints may weight integration and compliance higher.

CoreWeave vs Lambda vs Nebius vs AWS for GPU workloads

This table compares four providers across the dimensions buyers most often ask about, based on each provider’s own pages. No ranking is implied.

Dimension AWS CoreWeave Lambda Nebius
What it is Global hyperscaler with a broad cloud services portfolio, including GPU compute. GPU-specialized cloud provider focused on AI and HPC workloads. GPU cloud built for AI researchers and engineers. AI-focused cloud provider with infrastructure and managed AI platform services.
NVIDIA GPU families offered A broad range of EC2 GPU instances, including H100 (P5), H200 (P5e and P5en), and Blackwell GPUs (P6-B200, P6-B300, and P6e-GB200). H100, H200, and Blackwell-generation GPUs, per CoreWeave. H100, H200, B200, B300, and GB300 GPUs, per Lambda. H100, H200, and Blackwell-generation GPUs, per Nebius.
Cluster networking Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) for low-latency node-to-node communication, and EC2 UltraClusters for tightly coupled GPU placement. NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand, with GPUDirect RDMA. Quantum-2 InfiniBand for multi-node GPU clusters. InfiniBand fabrics for GPU clusters.
Managed Kubernetes Amazon EKS. CoreWeave Kubernetes Service (CKS). Managed Kubernetes on 1-Click Clusters. Managed Service for Kubernetes.
Managed Slurm AWS Parallel Computing Service (PCS) and SageMaker HyperPod. SUNK (Slurm on Kubernetes). Managed Slurm on 1-Click Clusters. Soperator (Slurm on Kubernetes).
Capacity model On-Demand, Spot, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, and EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML for reserved GPU access during defined windows. On-demand, spot, and reserved capacity. On-demand with per-minute billing, and reserved clusters. On-demand, preemptible, and committed capacity.
Breadth of surrounding services Hundreds of managed services: databases, analytics, ML platforms, event systems, identity, and networking. Focused on compute, storage, and networking for AI and HPC. Focused on GPU compute with integrated AI frameworks. AI platform services, including managed inference, storage, and developer tooling.
Published compliance attestations A broad set, including SOC 1, 2, and 3, ISO 27001, HIPAA eligibility, PCI DSS, and FedRAMP, per the AWS compliance programs page. SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 27017, and ISO 27018, per the CoreWeave trust center. SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, among others, per Lambda. SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and GDPR, per the Nebius trust center.

Attestations change, so confirm current scope on each provider’s page before you sign. For a broader survey of GPU cloud options, see the best GPU cloud providers in 2026.

How do performance and networking differ between hyperscalers and alternative AI infrastructure providers?

The differences show up most clearly in five areas: GPU interconnect, placement control, storage throughput, egress pricing, and latency to your existing data and users.

Interconnect between GPUs and nodes. Distributed training jobs spend a significant share of their time in collective operations (all-reduce, all-gather) that move gradients between GPUs across nodes. Inside a node, GPUs talk over NVLink and NVSwitch; the scale-out fabric carries traffic between nodes. Neoclouds commonly use InfiniBand fabrics with GPUDirect RDMA, which lets the network adapter read and write GPU memory directly, so data moves between GPUs on different nodes without passing through the CPU or host memory. Hyperscalers differ from one another. AWS uses its Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), an RDMA-style transport. Azure ND-series GPU VMs use InfiniBand. Google Cloud’s A3 Ultra and A4 machines use RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) with GPUDirect RDMA. Each can deliver high bandwidth; the right test is your own job at your target scale.

Placement and topology control. Training performance degrades when GPUs that communicate often sit far apart in the network topology. AWS addresses this with EC2 UltraClusters and placement groups. Neoclouds that build clusters only for GPU workloads often let you request nodes on the same leaf switches or rail group.

Storage throughput. Large training jobs read terabytes of data and write checkpoints frequently. Both hyperscalers and neoclouds offer high-throughput parallel storage, but the products and performance vary. Check whether checkpoint writes stall training and whether storage sustains throughput under concurrent access from many nodes.

Network egress pricing. Hyperscalers typically charge for data leaving their network. Some neoclouds advertise zero or low egress fees. This matters when you move training data in, ship model artifacts out, or serve inference results to users on another network.

Latency to your data and users. A neocloud region far from your databases or users adds latency to every call that crosses providers. Plan where data lives before you plan where GPUs run.

Inference is less sensitive for models that fit on one GPU. For those models, interconnect performance matters far less than for multi-node training, and the decision shifts toward availability, price, latency to your users, and integration effort. Models sharded across GPUs with tensor parallelism need NVLink within the node, and models served across nodes need the same fabric checks as training. For running inference across several providers, see how to run AI inference across multiple GPU clouds.

How do I evaluate capacity constraints and lead times when procuring GPUs?

GPU capacity is not interchangeable. The GPU model, cluster size, interconnect, and region all constrain what is available and when. Check these points before committing:

  • Current versus contracted capacity. Confirm whether the quoted capacity exists today or is a future commitment.
  • Cluster size limits. Find the largest contiguous cluster the provider can deliver. A 256-GPU cluster on a single InfiniBand fabric is a different product than 256 individual GPU VMs.
  • Delivery in tranches. Large reservations often arrive in batches, so get the delivery schedule in writing.
  • Reservation terms. Understand the minimum commitment, whether you pay for idle capacity, and what happens if you need to scale down early.
  • Preemption notice. On preemptible capacity, confirm the notice period and that your job can checkpoint and resume within it.
  • Hyperscaler quotas. GPU instances on AWS, GCP, and Azure need quota increases, and approval can take time.
  • Hardware generation roadmap. Ask whether the provider will offer next-generation GPUs when they ship, and what the migration path is.

Hyperscalers expose reserved capacity through structured programs. AWS offers EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, which reserve GPU instances for a defined time window. Google Cloud and Azure offer their own reservation mechanisms for GPU VMs.

The best defense against single-provider capacity risk is keeping workloads portable. If your training job runs in containers on Kubernetes with standard frameworks, you can move it between providers from one run to the next when capacity or pricing changes. For when to build your own GPU cluster versus renting, see the build vs rent GPUs break-even model. For a broader look at alternatives, see the best hyperscaler alternatives in 2026.

Which GPU hosting providers are best for developers and AI users who need compliance and privacy?

The best fit is the provider whose published attestations, regions, tenancy options, and key controls match your requirements. Hyperscalers hold the broadest compliance portfolios, and the leading neoclouds publish SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 attestations, with HIPAA coverage at some. Verify current scope on each provider’s trust page.

What factors determine GPU hosting versus private cloud for compliant AI workloads?

Check these dimensions before comparing price.

Attestations. SOC 2 Type II is the usual baseline for enterprise workloads, and some buyers also require ISO 27001. If you handle protected health information, you need a HIPAA business associate agreement. Many neoclouds run in colocation facilities, so ask whether an attestation covers the provider’s own operations, the data center operator, or both.

Data residency and region choice. Know where your GPUs physically sit. Under GDPR, confirm that training data and model weights stay within approved jurisdictions. Hyperscalers operate far more regions than any neocloud, though GPU instance types are available in only a subset of them, and neocloud regions vary by provider.

Tenancy. Dedicated, single-tenant hardware removes noisy-neighbor concerns and satisfies some rules that prohibit shared infrastructure. Several neoclouds offer bare-metal instances, and AWS offers dedicated hosts and bare-metal instances. Confirm whether “dedicated” means dedicated hardware or a dedicated VM on shared hardware.

Encryption and key control. Verify encryption at rest and in transit, and whether you can bring your own keys. AWS KMS and CloudHSM provide extensive key management. Neocloud key management varies, so confirm it directly.

Audit logging. Your compliance team needs records of who accessed what, and when. AWS CloudTrail is the usual reference point. Confirm that a neocloud offers equivalent audit logging that you can export to your SIEM.

When private cloud or your own GPUs make sense. If your data cannot leave your premises, or your compliance framework requires physical control over hardware, a private GPU cluster is the right answer. You then absorb the full operational burden: procurement, power and cooling, networking, patching, and hardware failures. On Control Plane, those servers can join as a location through the Generic provider in Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, so the Kubernetes layer is managed for you. For most organizations, a compliant cloud provider with the right attestations and contractual controls is more practical.

How long does it take to add a new cloud provider to an existing production app?

It depends on how much provider-specific glue your application uses. An application that calls Amazon SQS, DynamoDB, S3, and IAM through SDKs in every service takes much longer to run on a second provider than one built on Kubernetes-native APIs and portable storage interfaces.

The main drivers of integration time:

  • Networking and private connectivity. VPN tunnels or dedicated interconnects between your existing cloud VPC and the new provider, which often involve procurement, IP planning, and firewall changes.
  • Identity and secrets. Federating identity so workloads on the new provider can reach your existing cloud services without long-lived credentials. Each provider has its own IAM model.
  • CI/CD and IaC changes. Pipelines and Terraform configurations need to target the new provider, and a platform-specific deployment tool may require a second pipeline.
  • Images and drivers. CUDA, NCCL, and driver versions must match the new provider’s hosts, and large images must pull quickly from a registry near the new location.
  • DNS and traffic routing. Endpoints and load balancing must cover the new location.
  • Observability. Metrics, logs, and traces from the new provider must flow into your existing dashboards and alerting.
  • Data movement. Training data, model artifacts, and application state must be reachable from the new location through replication, caching, or new storage mounts.
  • Running a second set of tooling. Without a unifying layer, your team operates two sets of dashboards, access controls, and runbooks.

A platform layer that abstracts provider-specific details reduces each of these drivers. You define your workload once and deploy it to multiple locations instead of building bespoke integrations for every provider. For a walkthrough, see how to add a neocloud to AWS or GCP without running a second stack.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, and Azure and on Kubernetes clusters you already run, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds. VM workloads run on locations with KVM-capable nodes created with Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), a CNCF-certified Kubernetes service that runs worker nodes in your own cloud account or on your own servers while Control Plane operates the Kubernetes control plane.

You can add a GPU cluster you already run, including one on a neocloud, as a location through Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), Control Plane’s way to register an existing Kubernetes cluster. You create the location in Control Plane and apply its generated kubectl install command to the cluster, which deploys the Control Plane BYOK agent. You can also build a cluster from neocloud GPU servers with the Generic provider in MK8s, which joins Linux servers by running a join script on each one; its CPLN Platform add-on then installs the location. Workloads on those locations request the cluster’s GPUs by the Kubernetes resource name its nodes advertise. Control Plane’s pricing page lists NVIDIA GPUs from T4 to B200; GPU pricing on a neocloud location is set by that provider.

On Control Plane, every location in a GVC serves the same workload at once. You can serve inference from a GPU cluster in your AWS, GCP, or Azure account and a neocloud cluster together, with both added as locations, and each workload’s global endpoint routes requests to the nearest healthy location, so traffic moves to the remaining locations if one fails. This applies to inference and services; a distributed training job runs inside one provider’s GPU fabric.

Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity (UCI) lets workloads call AWS, GCP, and Azure services with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, which shortens the identity step of adding a provider.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. You never have to operate a Kubernetes cluster on Control Plane-managed locations. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Those locations can be on different providers, for example one AWS region and one neocloud location.

Control Plane ships its own Terraform and Pulumi providers, so it complements the infrastructure as code you already run. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

FAQ

These are the questions teams ask most often when deciding whether to add a neocloud.

Is a neocloud cheaper than AWS for GPUs?

It can be, depending on commitment terms, utilization, egress volume, and the surrounding services you use. A neocloud may offer a lower per-GPU-hour rate, but if you also need managed databases, queues, or global networking from AWS, the total cost comparison shifts. Compare total cost of ownership, including services, egress, and integration work.

Do neoclouds offer SLAs?

Some do. Published SLA terms vary by provider and product, and some neoclouds publish none by default. Read each SLA’s definition of downtime, the exclusions, and the remedies before you rely on it.

Can I run the same workload on a hyperscaler and a neocloud?

Yes for inference and services, if the workload is containerized and uses portable APIs. A single distributed training job stays inside one provider’s fabric, though the next run can start on a different provider. On Control Plane, a service deployed to a GVC that spans a hyperscaler region and a neocloud cluster runs active-active across both from one definition.

When should I stay on my hyperscaler for AI?

Stay when your workload depends heavily on its managed services, when your compliance requirements call for certifications a neocloud does not hold, when you need only a few GPUs for inference, or when integrating a second provider costs more than it saves.

What GPU networking technology should I look for in a neocloud?

For multi-node distributed training, look for InfiniBand or RoCE with GPUDirect RDMA and a non-blocking fabric. For models that fit on one GPU, standard Ethernet is usually enough. The interconnect matters most when a job runs frequent collective operations across many nodes.

How do I avoid vendor lock-in with a neocloud?

Run containerized workloads on Kubernetes, store data in portable formats, avoid provider-specific orchestration APIs where you can, and use a platform layer such as Control Plane, where one workload definition runs on any provider in your GVC, so changing providers does not mean rebuilding your deployment pipeline.

What compliance certifications should I require from a GPU cloud provider?

Start with SOC 2 Type II, add ISO 27001 if your buyers ask for it, and require a HIPAA BAA for protected health information. Government workloads may need FedRAMP authorization. Verify every certification on the provider’s own trust page.

How does Control Plane help me add a neocloud without a second stack?

You register your neocloud GPU cluster as a location and add it to your GVC next to AWS, GCP, or Azure regions, and your workload definition stays the same. The global endpoint, autoscaling, built-in observability, and access policies apply across every location, so adding a provider adds a location instead of a second toolchain.

What is the biggest operational risk of using a neocloud for production AI?

Concentration on a provider with a narrower service catalog and a shorter track record than a hyperscaler. At large scale, GPU and node failures are routine, so replacement speed decides how much training time you lose. Running services across more than one provider keeps a single provider’s issue from taking down your product.

Should I benchmark before committing to a neocloud?

Yes. Run your actual workload with the same model, dataset, and configuration you use in production, and measure training throughput, checkpoint time, network utilization, and tail latency. Run nccl-tests all-reduce at your target node count to check fabric bandwidth. Published specs do not always reflect performance under your access patterns.

To add a neocloud without running a second set of infrastructure, talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

title: YouTube sur Quest : la refonte immersive qui change la donne — et ce que ça implique pour l'entraînement visuel
description:
YouTube sur Quest : la refonte immersive qui change la donne — et ce que ça implique pour l'entraînement visuel

Selon UploadVR, Google travaillerait sur une refonte majeure de la vue immersive de YouTube sur Quest, pour rapprocher l'expérience de celle d'Android XR et de visionOS. Ce n'est pas une simple mise à jour d'interface : c'est le signe que le casque devient une plateforme de contenu à part entière, avec des heures d'usage réel.

Et des heures d'usage réel, pour certaines personnes, ça n'a rien d'anodin.

Pourquoi ce moment compte

Pour les personnes concernées par l'amblyopie (le « lazy eye »), la question n'a jamais été le manque d'exercices : c'est la régularité. Les patchs adhésifs, les lunettes rouge-bleu, les séances d'orthoptie à la maison tiennent rarement sur la durée. Ce qui tient, en revanche, c'est le contenu qu'on aime déjà regarder.

Si YouTube immersif devient une habitude dans le casque, alors l'entraînement visuel a enfin un véhicule quotidien. Pas un exercice de plus à caser dans une journée déjà pleine — une activité que l'on fait de toute façon, et qui devient le support d'autre chose.

Ce que fait Amblyotube

Amblyotube, développé par Seven Sports, est un logiciel récréatif et éducatif pour des exercices de coordination visuelle et d'attention en VR. L'application Meta Quest affiche une expérience visuelle différente pour chaque œil pendant que vous regardez du contenu de type YouTube.

Concrètement :

  • Vous choisissez l'œil concerné (gauche/droite) et un préréglage de sévérité (léger, modéré, sévère), ou vous lancez le test de vision LogMAR.
  • Vous lancez une vidéo dans une salle virtuelle ou en Room View (passthrough AR).
  • L'œil dominant reçoit un flou numérique ajustable (Dominant Eye Shader).
  • L'œil concerné bénéficie de l'AI Sharpener (MFBF), qui détecte les silhouettes humaines : contour rouge marqué, rehaussement jaune-vert, scintillement pulsé à rythme régulier.
  • Une occlusion en coin (wedge occlusion) peut masquer une partie de la vue de chaque œil, pour que chaque œil voie des portions uniques de la scène et réduire la rivalité binoculaire.
  • Un repère magenta dans l'œil concerné et un point gris neutre dans l'œil dominant se rejoignent en une seule image 3D cohérente — le cerveau apprend à fusionner les deux yeux et à traiter la vraie profondeur.

Ce que ça change, côté usage

Il faut distinguer deux choses : la news YouTube, qui relève du confort de visionnage, et l'usage thérapeutique, qui relève d'un tout autre cadre. Amblyotube ne dépend pas de la refonte YouTube pour fonctionner aujourd'hui — l'application lit du contenu vidéo dans son propre environnement. Mais si l'écosystème immersif de YouTube s'améliore, l'expérience de visionnage gagne en fluidité, en confort de lecture et en temps passé dans le casque. Et c'est précisément le temps passé qui compte.

Le cadre, sans exagération

30 à 40 minutes par jour recommandées, 1 heure maximum. 13 ans et plus. Amblyotube est un outil complémentaire d'entraînement visuel et d'assistance pour la coordination binoculaire et la perception de la profondeur : ce n'est ni un diagnostic, ni un traitement, ni une cure.

Ce qui rend la news YouTube intéressante, c'est justement qu'elle ne parle pas de santé. Elle parle d'un usage qui devient naturel. Et c'est souvent comme ça qu'une habitude de soin s'installe : pas par discipline, mais par plaisir.

Pourquoi ça compte pour l'écosystème VR

Vu d'un œil technique, cette refonte s'inscrit dans une tendance de fond : les plateformes de contenu vidéo cherchent à occuper l'espace immersif, pas seulement à s'y projeter. Android XR et visionOS ont montré que la vidéo 2D dans un environnement 3D n'est pas un gadget — c'est un usage massif, quotidien, mesurable en heures. Quest suit le mouvement.

Pour les développeurs d'applications VR, cela signifie une chose simple : le casque cesse d'être un objet de session courte et devient un écran de consommation longue durée. Et quand une plateforme passe de « sessions de 20 minutes » à « soirées entières », tout ce qui se greffe sur cet usage gagne en pertinence — y compris les outils qui demandent de la régularité plutôt que de l'intensité.

Découvrir Amblyotube sur le Meta Quest Store : https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: Reflection AI's Beam now available on AI Gateway for free
description:
Beam from Reflection AI, previously available in stealth as stealth/cat-jam, is now available on AI Gateway. Beam is free to use for a limited time during the launch period when serviced by Reflection AI.

Beam is an low latency US open-weight reasoning model for coding and agentic tasks, with weights released under Apache 2.0. Beam supports tool calling and structured outputs, with a 1M-token context window for code, documents, and conversation history. Reasoning effort is adjustable. Beam is designed for speed, activating only 23B of its 501B parameters per token and avoiding tokens a task doesn't need, so it tends to reach answers sooner than larger open models.

There are 2 ways to access Beam for free:

  • Using the standard model name (reflection/beam with provider reflection). When the free period ends, the model slug will automatically transfer over to pricing with no downtime.

  • Using the -free suffix to the standard name (reflection/beam-free). The model will stop serving when the free offer ends.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select reflection/beam or reflection/beam-free in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Beam in the model playground.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

title: Context Cancellation in Go: Propagating Deadlines Across Service Calls
description:
Here's a client method that looks like it was written by someone careful:

func (c *InventoryClient) Reserve(ctx context.Context, sku string, qty int) error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    return c.post(ctx, "/reserve", reserveReq{SKU: sku, Qty: qty})
}

It takes a ctx. It sets a timeout. It calls cancel. It compiles, and go vet has nothing to say about it. And it throws away every deadline the caller ever had. That first line overwrites the incoming ctx with a brand-new one rooted in context.Background(), so the 800ms budget your edge gateway gave this request is gone. From here on, this call has 5 seconds, no matter what.

That's the whole topic in one line. Go's context makes deadline propagation almost free, and "almost" is where the outages come from. This piece is about how a single timeout at the edge is supposed to cascade through every call it triggers, what the machinery actually does at each layer (in-process, over gRPC, over plain HTTP, through a proxy), and the specific places the chain snaps without anyone noticing.

If you want the broader resilience picture (retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads), that's covered in Designing for Partial Failure. This one goes deep on the deadline itself.

One clock for the whole call tree

The idea isn't Go-specific. Google's SRE book describes it in the chapter on cascading failures, and the wording is worth reading closely: "Rather than inventing a deadline when sending RPCs to backends, servers should employ deadline propagation." The tree of calls that fans out from one request should share one absolute deadline.

Their worked example: server A picks a 30-second deadline and spends 7 seconds before calling B, so the RPC to B carries 23 seconds. B spends 4 seconds before calling C, so C gets 19. Every hop inherits what's left, not a fresh number.

Then they show what happens without it. A calls B with a 10-second deadline. B takes 8 seconds to get going, then calls C with a hardcoded 20-second deadline instead of the 2 seconds it actually has. C pulls the request off its queue 5 seconds later and, in the book's words, "processes the request thinking it has 15 seconds to spare." Nobody's waiting for that answer. A gave up long ago. C is burning CPU, holding a connection, maybe taking locks, for a response that will be thrown on the floor.

That sounds like a waste problem. It's actually a capacity problem, and the same chapter has the numbers to prove it. Picture a frontend with 1,000 worker threads handling 1,000 QPS at 100ms each, so about 100 threads busy at any moment. Now 5% of requests start hanging until their deadline, and that deadline is 100 seconds. Those 50 QPS want 5,000 threads' worth of waiting. The frontend has 1,000. The book's arithmetic lands on the frontend serving 19.6% of requests, "resulting in an 80.4% error rate." A 5% backend problem became an 80% outage because the deadline was long and nobody short-circuited the doomed work.

So the goal is simple to state: one budget, set once at the edge, visible and shrinking at every hop. Let's see how much of that Go gives you for free.

What context actually does with a deadline

Some quick history, because it explains the API's shape. Sameer Ajmani introduced the context package in the July 2014 Go blog post "Go Concurrency Patterns: Context", and it lived at golang.org/x/net/context until Go 1.7 moved it into the standard library, with support wired into net, net/http, and os/exec. Go 1.8 added QueryContext, ExecContext, and friends to database/sql. Go 1.20 added cancellation causes (WithCancelCause, Cause), and Go 1.21 added WithoutCancel, AfterFunc, WithDeadlineCause, and WithTimeoutCause. We'll use most of those below.

Under the hood a deadline is just two things: a time you can read with ctx.Deadline(), and a Done() channel that closes when that time passes, when someone calls cancel, or when the parent's Done() closes, whichever comes first. Cancellation flows strictly downward. A child can't cancel its parent, and the parent's cancellation reaches every descendant.

Here's the part that surprises people. The docs for WithDeadline say the child's deadline is "adjusted to be no later than d", and more bluntly: "If the parent's deadline is already earlier than d, WithDeadline(parent, d) is semantically equivalent to parent." A child can shorten the budget. It can never extend it.

parent, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 100*time.Millisecond)
defer cancel()

child, cancelChild := context.WithTimeout(parent, 5*time.Second)
defer cancelChild()

pd, _ := parent.Deadline()
cd, _ := child.Deadline()
fmt.Println(cd.Equal(pd)) // true: the 5s asks for more than the parent has, so it's ignored

<-child.Done()
fmt.Println(child.Err()) // context deadline exceeded, after ~100ms

This changes how you should read per-call timeouts. A WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second) around a downstream call isn't a promise of 5 seconds. It's a cap: "at most 5 seconds, or whatever the caller has left, whichever is smaller." That's exactly the SRE book's advice to put "an upper bound for outgoing deadlines" on calls to noncritical backends. So hardcoded per-hop timeouts are fine in Go, as long as they're derived from the incoming ctx.

Which is why the opener is so nasty. The bug isn't the 5 seconds. It's context.Background(). The moment you root a new context there, the min-of-both rule has nothing to take the min of.

When the deadline hits, ctx.Err() returns context.DeadlineExceeded. When someone calls cancel (or the client hangs up), it returns context.Canceled. Keep those two apart in your logs and metrics. They mean different things: "we ran out of time" versus "nobody wants this anymore."

Across the wire, part 1: gRPC carries it for you

Inside a process, the deadline rides on a pointer. Between processes it has to become bytes on the wire, and this is where gRPC earns its keep.

The gRPC HTTP/2 protocol spec defines a grpc-timeout request header: a positive integer "of at most 8 digits" followed by a unit, H, M, S, m, u, or n (hours down to nanoseconds). If the header is missing, "a server should assume an infinite timeout."

Notice it's a timeout, not a deadline. The client sends "you have 1.5 seconds", not "finish by 14:03:07.250". The gRPC deadlines guide explains why: gRPC "converts the deadline to a timeout from which the already elapsed time is already deducted. This shields your system from any clock skew issues." Two machines don't have to agree on what time it is. They only have to agree on how long a second is.

You can see the mechanics in grpc-go's source (internal/transport/http2_client.go). When it builds the request headers, it does roughly this:

if dl, ok := ctx.Deadline(); ok {
    timeout := time.Until(dl)
    if timeout <= 0 {
        return nil, status.Error(codes.DeadlineExceeded, context.DeadlineExceeded.Error())
    }
    headerFields = append(headerFields, hpack.HeaderField{Name: "grpc-timeout", Value: grpcutil.EncodeDuration(timeout)})
}

Two details worth knowing. First, if your budget is already spent, grpc-go fails the call locally with DeadlineExceeded and never sends it, which is precisely the "don't start doomed work" behavior you want. Second, EncodeDuration picks the finest unit that fits in 8 digits. One and a half seconds is 1,500,000,000 nanoseconds, too many digits, so it goes out as 1500000u.

On the receiving side, grpc-go's server transport parses the header and wraps the stream's context with context.WithTimeout(ctx, timeout). So your handler's ctx already has the caller's remaining budget in it. The gRPC guide lists Go (and Java) among the languages where propagation is "enabled by default", but in Go, "by default" really means "if you pass the handler's ctx to the outgoing call":

func (s *checkoutServer) reserve(ctx context.Context, sku string, qty int32) error {
    if dl, ok := ctx.Deadline(); ok {
        slog.DebugContext(ctx, "reserving stock", "budget_left", time.Until(dl))
    }
    _, err := s.inventory.Reserve(ctx, &inventorypb.ReserveRequest{Sku: sku, Qty: qty})
    switch status.Code(err) {
    case codes.OK:
        return nil
    case codes.DeadlineExceeded:
        return fmt.Errorf("inventory: out of time budget: %w", err)
    default:
        return fmt.Errorf("inventory: %w", err)
    }
}

Pass ctx, and the inventory service receives a grpc-timeout equal to whatever the checkout service had left minus the time it already spent. Pass context.Background(), and inventory gets no header at all, which per the spec means infinite.

One thing gRPC can't do for you: stop your handler. The cancellation guide is explicit that "the gRPC library in general does not have a mechanism to interrupt the application-provided server handler." When the deadline passes, the server cancels the call, your ctx.Done() closes, and your code keeps running unless it looks. More on that in a minute.

Across the wire, part 2: plain HTTP carries nothing

If your services talk JSON over HTTP, here's the uncomfortable truth: there's no standard header for "this request has N milliseconds left". An IETF draft proposing a Request-Timeout header was written back in March 2011 and expired without becoming a standard. So http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, ...) bounds how long your client waits, and the transport abandons the request when ctx fires. But the server on the other end has no idea what your budget was. It will happily process the request for as long as its own settings allow.

Other ecosystems solved this by picking their own header. The Connect protocol sends Connect-Timeout-Ms (a positive integer of at most 10 digits). Envoy sets x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms on internal requests, documented as "the time in milliseconds the router expects the request to be completed" so the upstream "can make decisions based on the request timeout, e.g., early exit."

For your own HTTP services, you can do the same thing in about 30 lines. The header name below is our own convention, not a standard. Pick one and use it everywhere.

const timeoutHeader = "X-Request-Timeout-Ms" // our own convention, not a standard

// Server side: turn the incoming header back into a context deadline.
func DeadlineMiddleware(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if v := r.Header.Get(timeoutHeader); v != "" {
            if ms, err := strconv.ParseInt(v, 10, 64); err == nil && ms > 0 {
                ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), time.Duration(ms)*time.Millisecond)
                defer cancel()
                r = r.WithContext(ctx)
            }
        }
        next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
    })
}

// Client side: stamp the remaining budget on every outgoing request.
type deadlineTransport struct{ base http.RoundTripper }

func (t deadlineTransport) RoundTrip(req *http.Request) (*http.Response, error) {
    if dl, ok := req.Context().Deadline(); ok {
        remaining := time.Until(dl)
        if remaining <= 0 {
            return nil, context.DeadlineExceeded // don't even dial
        }
        req = req.Clone(req.Context()) // a RoundTripper must not mutate the caller's request
        ms := max(remaining.Milliseconds(), 1)
        req.Header.Set(timeoutHeader, strconv.FormatInt(ms, 10))
    }
    return t.base.RoundTrip(req)
}

var client = &http.Client{Transport: deadlineTransport{base: http.DefaultTransport}}

A few choices in there are deliberate:

  • Send a relative duration, not a timestamp. Same reason gRPC does: it sidesteps clock skew between hosts. An absolute X-Deadline: 2026-09-23T14:03:07.250Z only works if every box agrees on the time to the millisecond, and they don't.
  • Never let a tiny budget round down to "no header". connect-go used to skip Connect-Timeout-Ms entirely when less than a millisecond remained, and a missing header means infinite. The fix truncates to 1ms and sets the header "to avoid an unbounded call." Same trap here: Milliseconds() of 0.4ms is 0, and the middleware above ignores non-positive values, hence the max(..., 1).
  • Clone before setting the header. The http.RoundTripper contract says implementations shouldn't modify the request.
  • Only ever shrink. The middleware wraps r.Context(), so if the server has its own tighter limit, WithTimeout's min rule keeps it. A caller can't use the header to buy more time than the server is willing to give.

One more net/http detail that works in your favor: for incoming server requests, the docs say the context "is canceled when the client's connection closes, the request is canceled (with HTTP/2), or when the ServeHTTP method returns." So if the edge gateway gives up and hangs up, your handler's ctx fires too, and anything you passed it to (outgoing HTTP, gRPC, database/sql) gets cancelled with it. That's cancellation propagation, the SRE book's companion to deadline propagation, and you get it for free as long as you don't drop the ctx.

The proxy in the middle has its own opinion

Now put a service mesh or an API gateway between two gRPC services. The client sends grpc-timeout: 1500000u. What does the proxy do with it?

For Envoy, the answer is "probably not what you assume." The route configuration docs say that unless max_grpc_timeout is configured (it's deprecated now in favor of grpc_timeout_header_max under max_stream_duration), "the grpc-timeout header is not used and gRPC requests time out like any other requests using timeout." And that route timeout defaults to 15 seconds.

Think about what that means for the chain:

  • Your edge sets 800ms, the caller's context expires on time, and the caller gets DeadlineExceeded. Fine.
  • But the proxy's own timer is running at 15 seconds, not 800ms. The proxy itself enforces nothing tighter.
  • And if some intermediate service dropped its ctx, so no grpc-timeout went out at all, the proxy will still cut the call at 15 seconds. That's a deadline, just not yours. It'll look like propagation is "sort of working" in load tests.

Envoy also supports grpc_timeout_header_offset (formerly grpc_timeout_offset), which subtracts a fixed amount from the incoming grpc-timeout, so the proxy times out slightly before the client and can return a clean error instead of racing it. Whether you want that depends on your mesh; the point is that it's configuration you have to go and set, not something that happens by itself. If you run Istio, Linkerd, or a cloud load balancer, go read what its defaults are before assuming the header survives with meaning.

The five places the chain breaks

Put it all together and the failure modes are pretty specific. In rough order of how often I'd expect to find them in a codebase:

1. A fresh root context somewhere in the middle

The opener. It shows up in client libraries, in "helper" functions that don't take a ctx parameter, in code written before the caller had one, and in background goroutines that got a context.Background() because it was the only thing in scope. The fix is mechanical: every function that does I/O takes ctx context.Context as its first parameter (the context docs say exactly this) and derives from it. context.Background() belongs in main, in tests, and at the top of genuinely independent background jobs. Grepping for context.Background() and context.TODO() outside those places is one of the cheapest audits you can run.

2. Fan-out that doesn't share a context

A handler that calls pricing and stock in parallel should give both goroutines a context that dies when the request does, and ideally when either sibling fails. golang.org/x/sync/errgroup does both:

func productPage(ctx context.Context, sku string) (Quote, Stock, error) {
    var q Quote
    var s Stock
    g, gctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
    g.Go(func() (err error) { q, err = pricing.Quote(gctx, sku); return })
    g.Go(func() (err error) { s, err = stock.Level(gctx, sku); return })
    return q, s, g.Wait()
}

If pricing fails, gctx is cancelled and the stock call stops early. If the edge deadline hits, both stop. Hand-rolled go func() plus a sync.WaitGroup usually loses one of those two properties.

3. A handler that never looks at ctx

Cancellation in Go is cooperative. ctx.Done() closing doesn't stop anything by itself; it's a signal for code that checks. Anything that blocks on a context-aware call (HTTP, gRPC, QueryContext) checks for you. A CPU-bound loop doesn't:

func rank(ctx context.Context, rows []Row) ([]float64, error) {
    out := make([]float64, 0, len(rows))
    for i, row := range rows {
        if i%1000 == 0 { // checking every iteration is fine too; this just keeps it cheap
            if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
                return nil, err
            }
        }
        out = append(out, score(row))
    }
    return out, nil
}

The gRPC cancellation guide says it plainly: a long-lived handler "must periodically check if the RPC it is servicing has been cancelled and if it has, cease processing." And the SRE book has a smart exception: if the work is an expensive catch-up that checkpoints its progress, check the deadline after writing the checkpoint, so the work you already paid for isn't thrown away.

For blocking calls that don't take a context at all (a raw net.Conn, some older SDK), context.AfterFunc from Go 1.21 lets you wire one in. This is the pattern from the package's own examples, adapted:

func readWithContext(ctx context.Context, conn net.Conn, buf []byte) (int, error) {
    stopc := make(chan struct{})
    stop := context.AfterFunc(ctx, func() {
        conn.SetReadDeadline(time.Now()) // unblocks the Read below
        close(stopc)
    })
    n, err := conn.Read(buf)
    if !stop() {
        // The AfterFunc already ran: wait for it, then clear the deadline so the conn stays usable.
        <-stopc
        conn.SetReadDeadline(time.Time{})
        return n, ctx.Err()
    }
    return n, err
}

4. Retries that ignore the budget

A retry loop with exponential backoff and no awareness of the deadline is a slow way to fail. If you have 300ms left and your next backoff is 400ms, sleeping is pointless: you'll wake up to an expired context. Check the budget before you sleep, and sleep with a select so cancellation cuts it short:

func retry(ctx context.Context, attempts int, base time.Duration, op func(context.Context) error) error {
    var err error
    for i := range attempts {
        if err = op(ctx); err == nil {
            return nil
        }
        backoff := base << i
        if dl, ok := ctx.Deadline(); ok && time.Until(dl) < backoff {
            return fmt.Errorf("not enough budget left to retry: %w", err)
        }
        t := time.NewTimer(backoff)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            t.Stop()
            return context.Cause(ctx)
        case <-t.C:
        }
    }
    return err
}

This is simplified (no jitter, no retryable-error check; the partial-failure article covers those), but the budget check is the part people skip.

5. A hop that doesn't speak the protocol

Plain HTTP with no timeout header, a proxy that ignores grpc-timeout, a message queue in the middle. Every one of those is a place where the in-process deadline becomes a local timeout and the downstream side starts a fresh clock. Queues deserve a special mention: a message has no caller waiting on the other end in the same sense, so "propagating the deadline" there usually means putting an expiry timestamp in the message and having the consumer drop anything already stale. That's a different design, and a good reason not to pretend an async hop is part of the synchronous budget.

Leave yourself some room

Propagating the exact remaining budget has a subtle flaw: if the downstream service uses all of it, the response arrives at the same instant your own deadline fires. The gRPC deadlines post (by Google SRE Grainne Sheerin) notes that "both the client and server make their own independent and local determination about whether the remote procedure call (RPC) was successful", so a call can succeed on the server and still fail on the client. Then you have nothing left to log, map the error, or return a fallback.

The SRE book suggests reducing "the outgoing deadline a bit (e.g., a few hundred milliseconds) to account for network transit times and post-processing in the client." For an 800ms edge budget, a few hundred milliseconds is most of it, so scale that to your own numbers. The helper is tiny:

func withReserve(ctx context.Context, reserve time.Duration) (context.Context, context.CancelFunc) {
    dl, ok := ctx.Deadline()
    if !ok {
        return context.WithCancel(ctx)
    }
    return context.WithDeadline(ctx, dl.Add(-reserve))
}

Use it on outgoing calls where you have a meaningful fallback (a cached price, a degraded page section). If you don't have a fallback, the reserve buys you a clean error instead of a racing one, which is still worth something.

When work should outlive the request

Sometimes you want work to keep going after the caller leaves: an audit record, a cache fill, a webhook ack. The wrong fix is context.Background(), because it also throws away the request's values, like the trace ID your logs depend on. Go 1.21's context.WithoutCancel is the right tool. Per the docs, it returns a context that "is not canceled when parent is canceled" and "returns no Deadline or Err, and its Done channel is nil." Values survive, cancellation and deadline don't.

func handleRefund(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    evt := Event{ /* ... */ }
    detached := context.WithoutCancel(r.Context()) // keeps values (trace IDs), drops cancellation and deadline
    go func() {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(detached, 2*time.Second)
        defer cancel()
        if err := audit.Record(ctx, evt); err != nil {
            slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "audit write failed", "err", err)
        }
    }()
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
}

My strong opinion here: never use WithoutCancel without immediately wrapping it in a fresh WithTimeout. A detached context with no deadline is exactly the unbounded call this whole article is trying to eliminate, just moved into a goroutine where it's harder to see. And if the work really matters (money moved, an email must go out), a goroutine isn't durable anyway. That's an outbox or a queue, not a detached context.

Make the logs say which deadline fired

The last practical problem: when something fails with context deadline exceeded, which deadline was it? The edge's 800ms? A 200ms cap on the recommendations call? The proxy's 15 seconds (which would show up as a gRPC status, not a context error)? With a deep call tree, the bare error message tells you nothing.

Go 1.21's WithTimeoutCause and WithDeadlineCause let you attach a reason, and context.Cause reads it back. ctx.Err() still returns plain context.DeadlineExceeded, so existing errors.Is checks keep working:

var errCheckoutBudget = errors.New("checkout: 800ms edge budget exhausted")

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(r.Context(), 800*time.Millisecond, errCheckoutBudget)
defer cancel()

// ... later, after the deadline fires:
fmt.Println(ctx.Err())                                     // context deadline exceeded
fmt.Println(context.Cause(ctx))                            // checkout: 800ms edge budget exhausted
fmt.Println(errors.Is(ctx.Err(), context.DeadlineExceeded)) // true

Log context.Cause(ctx) wherever you log a context error. It costs one line per timeout you set, and it turns "something timed out somewhere" into a specific budget you can go and tune. Pair it with the budget_left debug log from the gRPC example and you can reconstruct how the budget was spent hop by hop.

What I'd actually do on Monday

If I inherited a Go service mesh and wanted to know whether edge timeouts really cascade, I wouldn't start by reading code. I'd send one request with a deliberately tiny budget (say 50ms) through the edge and look at the traces. Every span that runs longer than 50ms past the edge's start is a hop where the deadline didn't arrive. Then the fix list is usually short and boring: a context.Background() in a client wrapper, an HTTP hop without a timeout header, a proxy route without max_grpc_timeout, a CPU loop that never checks ctx.Err().

None of these are hard to fix. They're hard to see, because every one of them works perfectly on a good day. The edge timeout still fires, the user still gets a 504, and the only evidence that the chain is broken is a fleet of backends quietly finishing work nobody is waiting for. The SRE book's bimodal-latency example shows how that "quiet" turns into an 80% error rate on a bad day. Carry the ctx, everywhere, and make every hop honor what's left of it.

Originally published at andriiboyko.com.

title: Digital Approval Workflow: Checklist for Teams
description:
A Digital Approval Workflow means your team can efficiently review, approve, reject and track requests. Instead of leaving things to chance with a mix of emails, paper forms and chasing people for responses, you can easily manage your approvals, responsibilities and keep everything in order.

To make sure it runs smoothly, you'll need to think about your requirements, who is approving and what tools are best for the job.

A checklist will help your team plan, implement and manage your Digital Approval Workflow. 

1. Purpose
Before considering any software to use or the stages of your approval workflow, you'll want to know what you're trying to achieve. This will help you avoid any extra steps in your process and make sure your system is working well.

Checklist:

  • What tasks need to be approved?
  • What is the main aim of your approval? Are you looking to speed things up, improve accuracy or keep things compliant?
  • Who are the employees, managers and departments involved?
  • What are the common issues with your current approval process?
  • How will you know if it's successful?
  • What requests require extra attention?

For example, a marketing team may need approvals for blogs, adverts, social media and campaign budgets. Each request may need their own approval process.
Knowing the purpose and the people involved will help your team create a workflow that aligns with business needs. +1 eLearning Industry

2. Roles
Every approval workflow should clearly state who is submitting, reviewing and approving the request. This will avoid confusion and double checking.

Checklist:

  • Who is the owner of the process?
  • Who can submit approval requests?
  • Who will be reviewing and approving?
  • What roles do each person have within the process?
  • What level of access do they have to view, edit and approve documents?
  • Who are the backup approvers?

For example, a purchase request may be submitted by an employee, reviewed by the department manager and approved by the finance team. Everyone should know their role within the process.

3. Submit Requests
A Digital Approval Workflow should make it easy for employees to submit fully completed requests. Having standardized forms will also help avoid missing information.

Checklist:

  • Centralise where requests can be submitted.
  • Create standard forms for regular approvals.
  • Make sure there are all the necessary fields included. For example type of request, description, amount and deadline.
  • Mandatory fields should be included for essential information.
  • Include a place to attach relevant documents.
  • Include clear guidance on how to complete the form.
  • Clarify what will happen if the request is incomplete.

For example, a standardized purchase request may have fields for product name, quantity, estimated cost, supplier and reason for purchase. This will give the approver all the information they need to make a decision.

4. Approval Process
Depending on the request, you may need different people to approve. Some requests may only need one manager to approve whilst others may need finance, legal, compliance or senior management to review.

Checklist:

  • Map out the full approval process.
  • Decide if you'd like approvals to be sequential or parallel.
  • Set rules for approvals. Depending on the request, department, value or risk.
  • What requests require extra review?
  • Clearly state what happens if a request is rejected.
  • What rules do you have for exceptional requests?
  • Avoid any unnecessary approvals.

For example, a small expense may only need approval from the department manager. Whereas a large purchase may also need finance and senior management approval.

5. Choose the Right Digital Approval Tool
Ensure the platform you choose will meet your teams approval needs. It should be easy to use, secure, flexible and allow for future growth.

Checklist:

  • Is it easy to use?
  • Does it include the required approvals?
  • Can you customize the forms and rules?
  • Can users access it on mobile?
  • Is it secure?
  • Does it keep a record of approvals?
  • Can it integrate with other business tools?
  • Can it handle increased volumes of requests?
  • Compare the price, support and maintenance.

6. Set Timeframes, Alerts and Escalation
If people aren't aware they need to take action, approval requests can be delayed. By setting timeframes and alerts your team can ensure requests are moving along.

Checklist:

  • Set a timeframe for each approval.
  • Notify when a request has been submitted.
  • Notify approvers when they've been assigned.
  • Send reminders for pending approvals.
  • Set rules for escalating requests.
  • Have a backup approver.
  • Create a process for urgent requests.

For example, if a manager doesn't review a purchase request within 2 working days they may receive a reminder. If it still hasn't been approved it can be escalated.

7. Document Control
Many approval processes will include documents that will need editing. Without good version control, people could be reviewing old documents.

Checklist:

  • Store documents in one place.
  • Keep a record of different versions.
  • Show who has made changes and amendments.
  • Ensure reviewers have access to the most up to date version.
  • Record comments.
  • Limit editing.
  • Keep a history of approvals, rejections and amendments

8. Data Protection
Your Digital Approval Workflow may include financial information, employee information, contracts and other sensitive documents. You should ensure only those who need to have access and keep a record of important actions.

Checklist:

  • Secure logins and authentication.
  • Role based access.
  • Limit access to sensitive documents.
  • Keep a record of who submitted, reviewed and approved.
  • Keep a record of dates, decisions, comments and amendments.
  • Set rules for keeping and deleting documents.
  • Regularly check security and compliance.

Having a clear audit trail will help your organization understand how decisions have been made.

9. Integration
A Digital Approval Workflow will be more useful if it can integrate with the tools your employees are already using. This will help reduce double entry.

Checklist:

  • Identify what tools are currently being used.
  • Does the approval tool integrate with the tools you need?
  • Integrate with relevant document storage.
  • Consider integrating with finance, HR, procurement or project management software.
  • Reduce double entry.
  • Test that information is transferred correctly.
  • Identify who will deal with any integration issues.

10. Test Your Workflow
Testing your workflow will help you identify any missing steps, incorrect rules, access issues or other problems.

Checklist:

  • Test with sample approval requests.
  • Ensure requests go to the right approver.
  • Test approval, rejection and amendment options.
  • Test alerts.
  • Test escalation for overdue requests.
  • Ensure access is working.
  • Test document uploads and version history.
  • Test any unusual scenarios.
  • Get feedback from employees.

For example, you could test an incomplete purchase request to ensure the system highlights this and sends it back to the requester.

11. Training
Even if you have a great digital system in place, if your employees don't know how to use it, it won't be successful. Training will help your users follow the correct process.

Checklist:

  • Explain why a new workflow is being put in place.
  • Show how to submit and review requests.
  • Show approvers how to approve, reject or request amendments.
  • Explain timeframes and escalation.
  • Provide guidance on uploading documents and version control.
  • Provide support for common technical issues.
  • Get feedback.

The training should be practical and relevant to the role of the user. Requesters should know how to complete their requests with all the information whilst approvers should know how to review requests and record decisions.

12. Review Performance
Once you've launched your workflow you should regularly review how it is performing. This will help you identify any delays, recurring errors and ways to improve.

Checklist:

  • Track the average approval time.
  • Track the number of pending requests.
  • Review how many approvals are overdue and how often they're being escalated.
  • Identify any stages where requests tend to be delayed.
  • Track the number of rejections and resubmissions.
  • Get feedback from requesters and approvers.
  • Review any automation and integration issues.
  • Update approval rules if business needs change.

Some useful KPIs to track include how long approvals take, approval rate, number of pending requests and how many requests are sent back.
 
Examples of Digital Approval Workflows
The checklist can be tailored to different departments as each team will have different requests to approve.

Team Example Approval Process Key Considerations:

  • Marketing Draft content > Editor > Marketing Manager > Publish Version control, feedback and timeframes.
  • Finance Expense request > Department Manager > Finance team Budget limits, supporting documents and audit trail.
  • Human Resources Leave request > Reporting Manager > HR confirmation Employee records, permissions and timely alerts.
  • Procurement Purchase request > Department Head > Finance > Final approval Purchase limits, supplier details and authorization.
  • Legal Contract submission > Legal reviewer > Senior approval Confidentiality, document history and compliance.

For example, a marketing team may use a Digital Approval Workflow to submit a blog draft using a standardized form. The content will be reviewed by an editor, checked by the marketing manager and then the final approved version can be moved onto publication. If amendments are required it will be sent back to the writer with feedback.

Conclusion
A successful Digital Approval Workflow will need clear approval rules, roles, standardized forms, secure documents and reliable communications.

Heloixcan be seen as part of this wider approach to improving your digital processes. When planning your approval workflows you should first identify what your operational needs are and then look at what solutions would be best for your team. This should consider usability, flexibility, integration and visibility.

Using a checklist will help organizations plan for implementation, identify any potential issues and ensure everything is managed at every stage. Regular testing, training and monitoring will ensure your workflow remains effective as your business needs change.

Following a team checklist will help organizations reduce any unnecessary delays, increase accountability and create a more organized process.

References

  • The Ultimate Checklist for Setting Up a Remote Approval Workflow - eLearning Industry 
  • A Useful Workflow Approval Platform Checklist - Perivan 
  • How Do Teams Workflow Approvals Actually Work? A Step-by-Step Breakdown - ONES 
  • Digital Workflow Management Checklist for Shared Services - Neotechie

title: Agents draft. People decide.
description:
Many useful agents never act on their own. They prepare work, and a person decides what happens next. Teams sometimes see this pattern as a stepping stone, but it is often the right long-term design.

Design the review step deliberately. The reviewer should see:

  • the original request;
  • the agent's draft;
  • the sources it used.

They should be able to edit the draft as easily as approve it, so that reviewing is quicker than writing from scratch.

Record every action. The audit trail should show:

  • what the agent drafted;
  • what the reviewer changed;
  • who approved the result, and when.

This helps with quality, training and compliance.

Explain how roles change. When an agent takes on preparation, the role moves towards review, judgement and improvement. Be open about which tasks are moving and what each role gains in return.

Teach supervision as a skill. Reviewing AI output well is a learnable skill. It covers:

  • spotting unsupported statements;
  • checking tone;
  • knowing when to escalate.

It is worth training for.

Keep judgement where it belongs. Decisions that affect customers, colleagues or money stay with a named person, even when an agent does the preparation.

A short checklist:

  • Can a reviewer see the agent's sources alongside its draft?
  • Does your audit trail separate what the agent wrote from what a person changed?
  • Have the people affected been told how their role will change?

From the 2SD Technologies team (2sdtechnologies.com). Part 5 of "Don't just build agents".

title: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS): A Formal Mathematical Framework
description:
arXiv:2611.08778v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) operates on document pairs, returning a single scalar per comparison. In a multi-document setting where several sources may have contributed to one or more targets, pairwise STS cannot disentangle each source's marginal semantic contribution from their shared vocabulary. In this paper, Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is introduced as a conditional form of STS that computes similarity between two documents after eliminating semantic elements shared with a third via set-theoretic operations. SCS makes four contributions: 1) it introduces directionality, partitioning pairwise relations into lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) classes; 2) conditioning induces role-dependent asymmetry by extending the comparison domain from unordered pairs to ordered, conditioned triples of a target, a reference, and a conditioning document; 3) SCS introduces inter-document conditioning by subtracting shared content from a third document, complementing the intra-document conditioning in recent C-STS work; and 4) the set-theoretic decomposition achieves threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content, requiring no arbitrary similarity cutoff. Although developed for the $n \to 1$ configuration, the framework extends to $1 \to n$ via vertical role reversal and to $m \to n$ via independent composition of source- and target-side conditioning. With the established $1 \to 1$ case, these span the full spectrum of document cardinality. SCS scores should be interpreted ordinally, as rankings of marginal contributions rather than absolute measurements. The broader implication is that metric space axioms commonly assumed in similarity formalizations constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, and that extending the domain to conditioned triples can recover information that pairwise-symmetric comparisons suppress.
