title: Node.js SaaS Avatar Upload Reliability: Signed URLs or a Server Proxy?
description:
Node.js SaaS Avatar Upload Reliability: Signed URLs or a Server Proxy?

Short answer: for a beginner SaaS, choose the upload path that makes authorization, retries, and deletion observable before optimizing the number of network hops. A signed URL keeps large bytes away from Node.js and usually gives the application a better capacity envelope; a server proxy is the more controlled boundary when the application must inspect, transform, or sequence every byte. For a property-management product, that same decision should protect tenant backup snapshots, because an avatar upload is small but a restore can occupy the system for much longer.

The reliability question is easy to miss. A profile image that appears to upload successfully can still leave a database row pointing at an object that was never completed, while a retry can create a second object and a tenant restore can select the wrong snapshot. The URL style is secondary. The state and ownership model are what keep the system explainable.

Start with an object state, not a URL

I would model an upload as a short control-plane transaction followed by a data-plane transfer. The application authenticates the user, checks the tenant, allocates an opaque object key, and records a pending row. It then returns either a narrowly scoped signed URL or a proxy endpoint. Only after the object is verified does the application mark the row ready and make it the current avatar or an eligible backup snapshot.

That sequence gives retries somewhere safe to land. A lost response does not mean the client should invent a new identity; it should repeat an operation identified by an upload ID, and finalization should be idempotent. The signed URL is a temporary capability. It is not the avatar identity, and it should never be stored as one because it expires.

That is the contract.

For tenant backups, the restore API should accept a snapshot ID that the database has authorized, not a client-supplied storage path or “latest” prefix. A snapshot becomes selectable only in the ready state and only for its owning tenant. This is the invariant that matters when several tenants upload files at once.

Here is the policy boundary in Go. The storage adapter can be replaced in tests, while the application still owns tenant checks and state transitions.

package uploads

import "errors"

type Upload struct {
    ID       string
    TenantID string
    ObjectKey string
    State    string
}

func AuthorizeRestore(upload Upload, tenantID string) error {
    if upload.TenantID != tenantID {
        return errors.New("upload belongs to another tenant")
    }
    if upload.State != "ready" {
        return errors.New("upload is not ready for restore")
    }
    return nil
}

The code is deliberately unglamorous. A production implementation still needs to verify size and integrity metadata, serialize the pending-to-ready transition, and make repeated finalization return the same result. Those rules apply to an avatar even if its payload is only a few megabytes; they become more consequential when a property-management backup contains a large file and restore selection must be auditable.

How should a beginner Node.js SaaS handle signed URLs and server proxy uploads?

The two paths place different obligations on the application.

Decision area Signed storage URL Node.js server proxy
Byte path Client or worker transfers directly to private storage Every byte crosses the application tier
Application work Authorize, scope, record, verify, and finalize Authenticate, stream, inspect, possibly transform, and finalize
Main reliability risk Expiration, browser policy, or incomplete finalization Connections, backpressure, memory, and app-tier saturation
Best fit Large files or many concurrent transfers Small files or mandatory byte-level policy
Test that matters Permission scope and retry behavior Stream limits and capacity under concurrent load

The signed path is attractive only when the surrounding contract is explicit. The URL must be limited to the intended object and operation, the expiry must fit the expected transfer time, and the deployed browser origin must permit the request. A backend test is not proof that a browser upload will work. Test an expired capability, a retry after a completed write, an oversized body, and a finalization request that arrives twice.

The proxy path is easier to reason about when inspection is non-negotiable. It can enforce a single request policy and make the application the visible choke point, but that convenience consumes the same connection and egress budget needed for ordinary dashboard traffic. Streaming is required; buffering an entire backup in a Node.js process turns a file-size decision into a memory incident.

Short version: control belongs in the application, and bytes belong wherever the measured capacity envelope can carry them.

Reliability needs separate SLOs for control and data

“Upload latency” is too vague for a service that stores both avatars and tenant backups. Track authorization latency, time to durable object completion, finalization latency, restore completion time, active transfers, retry count, and the oldest queued restore. A restore request being accepted is a different SLO from the selected snapshot becoming usable.

Capacity planning should use the upper tail of file size and concurrency, not the average avatar. If ten large transfers hold connections open while a worker reads a selected backup, CPU can look healthy while request queues and restore latency grow. I would also treat a 413 response as a policy result to observe, not as proof that the storage path is unreliable: the declared limit, the actual object size, and the client retry behavior need to agree. The useful load test repeats that overlap across tenants: an upload completes, the client misses the response, finalization is retried, and a restore is selected during the pending window; then it repeats with a slow reader, an expired capability, and a process restart between writing the object and recording readiness. That sequence is long enough to expose the difference between a durable object and a durable application decision, which is why a green single-file test says very little about the property-management workload. Watch memory, open connections, queue depth, and bytes transferred together.

I would keep a decision record with the 95th and 99th percentile file sizes, concurrent-transfer target, retry budget, and restore-time objective. Your mileage may vary because a beginner SaaS may have little traffic today, but the measurement that resolves the uncertainty is straightforward: run the largest expected transfer beside normal authenticated requests and the restore workload. Don't turn a small early user count into a permanent assumption about file size.

Governance is where the upload design earns its keep

Private object storage does not decide which tenant may replace an avatar or restore a snapshot. The database should retain the tenant ID, object key, upload ID, state, integrity metadata, and audit timestamps. Object keys should be server-assigned and opaque enough that a user cannot choose another tenant's path. A cleanup process should remove abandoned pending objects without deleting a ready object still referenced by a current record.

Retention also needs an explicit rule. Backup lifecycle management can remove old snapshots, but the application must record the retention policy and protect a selected snapshot for the duration of a restore. Deletion should be observable and reviewable, especially where a property manager may need to explain which tenant data was restored and when.

For a downloaded restore artifact, set Content-Disposition deliberately. The HTTP header distinguishes inline display from attachment handling, and any filename should come from trusted snapshot metadata rather than a request parameter. Delivery policy and authorization are separate concerns.

When is a proxy the more reliable choice?

Choose a proxy when every byte must pass through validation or transformation, when the browser cannot safely receive a scoped capability, or when the team cannot yet test the signed path's origin, expiry, and retry behavior as one workflow. The catch is capacity: the proxy is not suitable when large-file throughput already consumes the application SLO budget or when restore traffic competes with interactive requests.

Choose a signed URL when the application can authorize the operation first, the storage policy can scope it to one object, and the team can finalize and verify the transfer idempotently. It is not a complete backup strategy. It does not replace restore drills, tenant authorization, retention rules, or an on-call runbook.

The practical rule is to keep the control-plane state in Node.js and move the byte path outward when large-file throughput is the limiting risk. Keep the proxy while its tested envelope covers the largest transfer burst and normal traffic with room for retries. Revisit the choice when the evidence changes, not when a new upload library becomes fashionable.

Sources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

title: Discord Swapped Electron for Rust. The 290MB Claim Needs a Caveat
description:
Stanislav Vishnevskiy posted a 15 second clip of two ThinkPads side by side, and the left side is the part that got me.

That's the Discord you and i have installed right now. Black window for about three seconds. Then a loading tip: "In the ancient days, Discord started as a browser-only app."

The joke writes itself. The app is still shipping a browser engine while telling you about its browser-only past.

The right side is the new client, codenamed Phoenix. It gets double clicked a second and a half later. Window fades in within a second.

By the time the Electron app finally shows its interface, the Rust client already has the friends list loaded.

The old app still says "There are no friends online at this time" while the new one is done.

The clip hit 2.3 million views. People asked if it was a tray launch.

Coral, who leads audio and video at Discord, said both were cold starts. Travis, who filmed it, pointed out that a tray launch would mean the friends list was already loaded.

Then came the number. 290.2MB of RAM. With two accounts signed in at once.

A Discord employee said in December 2025 that normal usage sits under 1GB, and the company tested auto restarting the app at 4GB. So 290MB is roughly 70% below the normal mark.

One reply called 290MB "still vile" for a chat app. Vishnevskiy answered: "Those 4k avatar decorations gotta render somewhere ;) but joking aside this client is actually running 2 accounts concurrently."

That reply is where i stopped scrolling and started taking notes.

What GPUI actually is

Most people guessed Tauri. Tauri uses Rust for app logic but builds the interface in HTML and CSS inside the system webview. Discord didn't do that.

They went with GPUI, the framework from the Zed editor team. It draws the interface on the GPU with no HTML at all. Rust handles memory without a garbage collector.

Tech What it is Role
Rust Systems language New client and shared code
GPUI Rust UI framework from Zed Draws the desktop app
Electron Chromium plus Node Current app, being removed
Tauri Rust plus system webview Not used

So the chat app stopped being a website wearing a coat.

The mobile apps drop React Native and share the same Rust core. The browser version keeps rendering HTML but moves its logic to WebAssembly. Web tech stays for the things that need it, like YouTube embeds and Activities.

The 290MB number is a screenshot

Here's what the headlines skip. That number came from Task Manager on a ThinkPad, not a benchmark. Discord hasn't published a like for like test of both clients.

And the 4GB figure was a restart threshold Discord set for itself, not typical usage. Normal was under 1GB. So "4GB to 290MB" compares a ceiling to an idle snapshot.

That's not a knock on the client. The thing genuinely looks fast in the clip. But the math in the headline is doing a lot of work.

i had Discord open the entire time i was reading about this. Activity Monitor said 1.4GB. i closed it and opened it again out of spite.

A cold start comparison is real evidence. A single Task Manager screenshot is a claim.

The real reason this is happening

i used to think the case for Electron was settled. One codebase, every platform, ship it. The cost of writing native UI three times was the whole argument.

A commenter on r/rust named its_lukebond put the shift better than any article did. GPUI maturing, plus AI writing most of the platform glue, is making that cost argument fall apart.

That's the story people are missing. Not the RAM. The price of not using Electron went down.

Which is also why this is bigger than Discord. If a company with a decade of React investment can walk away, the next one has less excuse.

The accessibility question

here's a question people always ask when a web stack gets dropped. What happens to screen readers?

On Hacker News, a legally blind user said per app UI zoom in the web stack made their life easier. Someone else pointed out that Windows apps had accessibility before computers had 25MB of RAM total.

Both true. Which is the annoying part.

But a developer who built on GPUI, zac_attack_ on Reddit, said the crate's README still had a broken 404 link for "Accessibility." He also hit rendering bugs and rough edges.

The framework's own docs couldn't find the accessibility page.

Discord's VP of Engineering says accessibility and security matter as much as performance. i want that to be true. i also want to see the commit history.

Where this gets messy

the first time i tried this kind of thing, it was a small tool, not a chat app with millions of people. Immediate mode UI gets harder as the tree grows.

A commenter, Grollicus2, worried about exactly that. Thousands of chat messages in one component tree, all needing diffing on every change.

That's the risk specific to Discord. Zed mostly renders editor panes. Discord renders a firehose.

And modded clients probably die. Disconsented pointed out that client mods like BetterDiscord and Vencord depend on the Electron shell.

Blocking already misbehaves with ghost notifications. A rewrite is a clean place to close that door.

A short detour about codenames

The build is called Phoenix. Which is a strange choice for a company that already rose from a browser.

Every big rewrite gets a codename like this. Phoenix, Nova, Atlas, something with a bird or a star. Nobody ships a rewrite called "Project Dave."

i once worked somewhere that named a migration after a Greek god. The migration failed twice and the name stopped being funny. Nobody says "Zeus is down" without sounding like they've lost it.

Phoenix is at least honest. It implies the old thing has to burn first.

Who should not care about this

If Discord runs fine on your machine, none of this changes your week. You will get the update eventually and it will feel slightly snappier. That's it.

The 290MB number also won't hold. As accessibility, features, and years of patches land, that figure creeps up.

Chrome used about 25MB per tab in 2010. It's often 500MB now. Every app gets heavier once real users show up.

And if you run a modded client, this is bad news dressed as good news. Performance you didn't ask for, at the cost of the thing you actually use.

Discord hasn't shipped a public date. Private testing starts soon, and the company says it's taking its time on stability and security. Believe that when the build is in your hands.

What i keep coming back to

The part that stuck with me wasn't the RAM. It was Vishnevskiy thanking Travis for "finding these janky old laptops."

ThinkPads with a Copilot key. Machines from 2024. He called them janky.

That's a person who has been staring at this problem for years, finally watching the old thing lose to the new thing on hardware he clearly doesn't respect. There's something honest in that.

i still have the Electron app installed. i'll probably keep it until the day it updates itself into something faster. And i'll open Task Manager that day, out of habit, and judge the number.

title: User Reminders in Node.js: How Cron Triggers Webhook Tasks Explained
description:
The least complex design is a cron trigger that calls a public webhook, waits for that webhook to enqueue the reminder work, and lets an idempotent worker perform delivery. Cron decides when an attempt starts; it does not prove that every subscriber received a shipment update.

How do I use cron to trigger webhook tasks for user reminders?

The page fires at 09:00, but the useful signal is not “cron ran.” It is closer to “the scheduled run produced no accepted queue message” or “the queue has stopped making progress.” An on-call engineer should see a schedule identifier, the attempt status, and a request ID. The payload should contain only the reminder facts needed by the worker, not a full student record.

Work backwards from that page. A publicly reachable cron URL invokes the webhook. The webhook validates the request, publishes one message per required subscriber, and returns a small success or failure status. The worker consumes each message, records a deduplication key such as shipment-update:shipment-1842:subscriber-77, and performs the delivery. If a runtime error occurs, log the failed attempt with the schedule, subscriber, and retry decision.

That is the short answer. A cron expression is a clock, not a delivery guarantee.

Start small.

For this boundary, Infrai is worth testing as the managed clock-to-queue leg: its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples before an API key is needed. That makes the handoff contract inspectable during the experiment; it does not move delivery idempotency out of your worker.

Start with the failure you can reproduce

Before choosing a scheduler, run the same experiment with a test shipment and a fixed subscriber set. Use 100 reminder messages, a schedule that fires once per minute, and a worker that deliberately fails every tenth message. Keep the payload below the queue’s 256 KB message limit. Record five things for each attempt: scheduled time, webhook response status, queue acceptance, worker outcome, and deduplication key.

The pass criteria are deliberately boring: every accepted message reaches a terminal outcome, failed deliveries are retried without creating a second reminder, and the execution log distinguishes success from failure. A run is a fail if a missed cron trigger is silently treated as delivered, if the webhook performs the long delivery inline, or if a retry creates duplicate notifications. Do not call the test a benchmark. It is a contract test for your recovery path.

A threshold has a cost. Alerting on one transient 5xx creates noise and trains the on-call engineer to ignore the page. Waiting until an entire reminder batch is late hides the problem. Start with an alert on a failed webhook or a queue with no successful consumer outcome for the expected interval, then tune it from observed test runs.

The boundary that matters: clock, handoff, worker

The cron task should do one short thing: invoke the public HTTP endpoint. A cron execution is limited to 900 seconds, so anything longer belongs behind the webhook. The worker owns retries and idempotency. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once; assume duplicate delivery even when the happy-path test never produces one.

The webhook should acknowledge only after the message has been accepted. Its response payload can be a minimal record such as status: accepted plus a request identifier. Keep the execution output small because run history retains only the first 4 KB. A paused cron does not replay missed triggers, and second-level timing has jitter, so the worker needs a business date or reminder ID rather than an assumption that every tick is exact.

No shortcut.

Here is the handoff boundary in Go. The in-memory map is a test seam; production needs a durable uniqueness constraint in the consumer’s database. The example also shows a complete, authenticated discovery call so the request contract can be inspected before the protected publish step is wired.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strings"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Reminder struct {
    ID           string `json:"id"`
    SubscriberID string `json:"subscriber_id"`
}

var seen = struct {
    sync.Mutex
    keys map[string]bool
}{keys: make(map[string]bool)}

func webhook(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
        http.Error(w, "method not allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
        return
    }
    var reminder Reminder
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&reminder); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "invalid payload", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }
    key := reminder.ID + ":" + reminder.SubscriberID

    seen.Lock()
    duplicate := seen.keys[key]
    seen.keys[key] = true
    seen.Unlock()
    if duplicate {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
        _, _ = w.Write([]byte(`{"status":"duplicate"}`))
        return
    }

    // Replace this log with a durable queue publish. Do not send inline.
    log.Printf("queued reminder key=%s", key)
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
    _, _ = w.Write([]byte(`{"status":"accepted"}`))
}

func discoverQueuePublish() error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    request, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish", nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        response, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := response.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := time.ParseDuration(retryAfter + "s"); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = seconds
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: %s: %s", response.Status, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limited after retries")
}

func main() {
    if strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")) == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    http.HandleFunc("/reminders", webhook)
    go func() { log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)) }()
    if err := discoverQueuePublish(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

The same discovery request, as a copyable shell call, is:

curl -X GET "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish" -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY"

The map disappears when the process restarts. In production, make the key unique in the consumer’s database or use the queue’s idempotency convention. A five-minute FIFO deduplication window is not a substitute for consumer idempotency, especially when a reminder can be retried later. The later POST /v1/queue/publish body should come from the returned schema rather than guessed fields; create or publish retries need a client-supplied idempotency key.

Which tool fits the delivery contract?

Node-cron is the smallest option when the application already owns a process and needs a timer that invokes its own handler. It has a small operational surface, but process restarts, multiple replicas, and public reachability become your responsibility. It is a clock, not durable queue storage.

BullMQ is a stronger fit when Redis is already part of the platform and the main requirement is delayed jobs with worker controls. It gives the team a queue-oriented programming model, while Redis availability and queue operations become part of the failure domain. The application still has to make the consumer idempotent.

Temporal is the better boundary for long-lived, stateful workflows, compensation, and explicit orchestration. That power has a corresponding operational and modeling cost. It is the wrong tool for a single periodic HTTP handoff whose work can be represented as a queue message.

Option Interface Best fit Main boundary
node-cron Node.js library One process already owns the timer Restarts, replicas, and endpoint exposure are yours
BullMQ Node.js and Redis Redis-backed delayed jobs and workers Redis and queue operations become part of the failure domain
Temporal SDK and workflow service Long-lived state and multi-step orchestration More workflow machinery than a single handoff needs
Infrai scheduling and queue REST, with public discovery A managed cron-to-queue experiment Public HTTP targets, bounded retention, and at-least-once consumers

An API scheduler such as Infrai sits between those choices for teams that want a managed cron-to-queue boundary over REST. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities, request schemas, response schemas, and runnable examples, so an engineer can inspect the scheduling or queue contract before installing an SDK. Every documented capability also has runnable examples in 10 languages, which shortens the path from a discovered schema to a small reproduction. The same surface exposes per-call request metadata, giving a useful handle for correlating a cron attempt with the webhook log.

There is a second advantage in a different dimension: Infrai has one key and one bill for 295 routes across 20 modules. One key and one bill reduce the credential rotation and billing reconciliation work that appears when the service later needs an adjacent backend capability; this does not change the delivery guarantee. The interface remains a plain REST boundary, so switching the worker’s queue implementation remains an explicit engineering decision rather than an SDK-wide rewrite.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the clock-to-queue part when you want a self-describing REST integration and a reproducible handoff test, while keeping reminder delivery and its idempotency record in your worker. Choose BullMQ when Redis is already your reliable queue boundary; choose Temporal when the reminder is one step in a real workflow.

There are hard limits, and this is where Infrai is the wrong choice. The main limitation is that cron tasks support public http_url targets, and push subscription targets must be public HTTPS endpoints; an internal-only webhook will not receive the call. Delayed messages are capped at 7 days, retention at 30 days, and acknowledged messages are deleted, so this is not Kafka-style replay with multiple consumer groups. There is no native debounce, throttle, or topic fan-out; use separate queues when that is the required shape. The trade-off is clear: choose Temporal for workflow joins or compensation, and choose BullMQ when Redis is already the durable boundary you operate.

Make the decision from the test

Run the 100-message test against each candidate with the same schedule, payload, injected failures, and subscriber set. Pass only if the candidate preserves the handoff contract, makes retries observable, and leaves no duplicate reminder after the worker is restarted. Record operational work as part of the result: how many components must be configured, who owns public endpoint security, and how a failed run is inspected.

The decision rule is simple. Select the least complex candidate that passes the recovery test and fits the longest job. If the work can finish behind a cron-triggered queue worker, a managed cron plus queue is enough. If the process needs durable workflow state or joins across branches, use a workflow engine instead. No scheduler can repair an ambiguous delivery contract.

Test the handoff twice: once with a normal response, and once with a retry. For the managed boundary, the next step is https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/cron/answers/why-daily-scheduled-email-should-enqueue-jobs-instead-o/.

Further reading

  • OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • node-cron documentation
  • Queue publish capability discovery

title: Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.09768v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language, bluntly or politely. We test whether such differences change how other agents judge and act, using the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realization. We rewrite only the realization, check that the game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. We vary linguistic range consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons; the largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is bald on-record regardless of role.

title: Look Closer, Align Better: Explicit Visual Attributes for Robust EEG-to-Image Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.09123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: EEG-to-image retrieval commonly aligns neural responses with representations from pretrained vision encoders. However, these representations may underrepresent fine-grained visual details needed to distinguish semantically similar images. To address this limitation, we first investigate the EEG decodability and complementary predictive value of explicit visual attributes, identifying visual cues that capture EEG-relevant information beyond pretrained representations. Building on these findings, we propose AttrEcho, a framework that enriches pretrained visual representations with complementary, spatially aligned visual attributes. Specifically, Region-Aligned Visual Attribute Fusion (RAVF) integrates EEG-relevant local visual attributes with spatially corresponding pretrained features through a learnable signed residual gate. We further employ Feature Token Aggregation (FTA), which learns dimension-specific weights across regions to aggregate refined visual features for contrastive alignment with EEG representations. Experiments on THINGS-EEG demonstrate that AttrEcho achieves 94.8% Top-1 and 99.7% Top-5 accuracy in intra-subject 200-way retrieval, while maintaining 82.1% Top-1 accuracy as the gallery expands to 1,600 images with same-concept distractors. AttrEcho also achieves 25.3% Top-1 and 53.0% Top-5 accuracy in inter-subject retrieval. These results highlight the importance of EEG-relevant visual attributes and spatially aligned fusion for fine-grained EEG-to-image retrieval.

title: Using an LLM to Tackle Difficult Cases in NER for Nepali Tweets
description:
arXiv:2611.08967v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Named entity recognition (NER) is challenging for social media data in a low-resource language. LLMs often lag behind pretrained language models (PLMs) in NER performance, but they show promise in handling cases that PLMs struggle with. Using a dataset of Nepali tweets, we split the test set into "easy" and "hard" cases using token probabilities from a fine-tuned pretrained language model (PLM). We then evaluate an LLM on the hard test cases using 16 different prompt configurations. We find that selecting examples based on semantic similarity and increasing the number of examples improves F1 score by almost 10 points from the baseline configuration. Although the LLM underperforms the PLM on the full and easy test sets, it surpasses the PLM on the hard test set, resulting in an improved score when the two models are combined.

title: Scalable Notification System — Architecture & Engineering Design
description:
Scalable Notification Platform

Proposed reference architecture • Private engineering design • Version 1.0

Open architecture canvas

01 — System Architecture (original Eraser diagram)

1. Requirements and design targets

Support multi-tenant email, SMS, mobile push and in-app notifications; OTP/security, transactional updates and opt-in campaigns; scheduling, localization, quiet hours, preferences, delivery tracking and cancellation.

Assumptions, not benchmarks: 10M logical notifications/day, 1.5 deliveries per notification, 15M channel deliveries/day. Average: 116 requests/s and 174 deliveries/s. A 20× burst requires approximately 3,500 deliveries/s before retries or extra device fanout. Actual traffic, budget, cloud, regions and providers remain open decisions.

Proposed SLOs: 99.95% monthly API availability for valid authorized traffic within agreed tenant limits; overload rejection within those limits counts as failure. p95 durable acceptance under 200ms. Critical queue age p99 under 5s when providers and quotas are healthy. Scheduled jobs become eligible within 60s of their due time. These targets require load validation. Provider acceptance latency and actual carrier/device delivery latency are separate metrics.

Critical, transactional and bulk traffic have separate queues and reserved worker capacity. Bulk traffic must not exhaust critical capacity.

2. Architecture and request flow

Initial AWS reference stack: stateless services on ECS, managed PostgreSQL, SQS standard queues, Redis, S3 archives, interchangeable email/SMS adapters, FCM/APNs and SSE/WebSocket gateways. Use managed services and a single active region spanning availability zones. Kafka becomes an option when long replay retention or many independent consumers justify its operational cost.

  1. Producers call authenticated ingress through WAF/API gateway. Validate payload, tenant scope, template, recipient, expiry and limits.
  2. In one PostgreSQL transaction, insert notification request and outbox event. Return 202 only after commit.
  3. Outbox relay publishes committed events to the ingress queue, marking published afterward. A crash can duplicate publication.
  4. Orchestrator applies preferences, quiet hours, template version and channel selection. Persist deterministic delivery rows plus dispatch outbox in one transaction.
  5. Dispatch relay routes to queues per channel and priority. Messages contain IDs and small metadata; large payloads stay in DB/object storage.
  6. Workers obtain durable leases, recheck consent/suppression/expiry, apply provider and tenant rate caps, persist attempt intent, then call provider adapters.
  7. Persist outcomes before acknowledging queue messages. Capability-specific callbacks enter a verified durable webhook inbox and update delivery status through a reconciler. Scheduled requests stay in durable storage until due. Scheduler claims due rows using bounded leases/skip-locked transactions and creates outbox events atomically; it does not rely on memory timers or arbitrary long queue delays. Quiet-hour deferrals must not exceed expiry.

For campaigns, store an audience snapshot/reference, then fan out in bounded pages with checkpoints, tenant budgets and deterministic recipient IDs. A retry of a page must not recreate deliveries.

Database boxes on the canvas are logical table groups, not a requirement for separate clusters. Cross-table outbox transactions must stay within the same database transaction boundary. All outbound channels use the shared reliability controls even where arrows are omitted for readability. Email/SMS callbacks pass through the verified webhook inbox. Push feedback depends on provider capabilities; no universal delivered callback is assumed.

The transactional outbox avoids a database/queue dual-write gap; consumers still require idempotency. AWS outbox guidance

3. Delivery correctness

Internal processing is at least once. External exactly-once delivery is not guaranteed.

Enforce unique (tenant_id, idempotency_key) in PostgreSQL and compare a canonical request hash. Same key and payload returns the original ID; different payload returns 409. Retain dedupe records for at least the published retry/replay window. Redis is only a cache.

Create one delivery per notification, recipient, channel and endpoint where relevant. Include endpoint_id for multiple push devices; use a stable non-null logical endpoint for other channels. A durable unique constraint prevents concurrent duplicate fanout.

Delivery states: SCHEDULED → READY → PROCESSING → PROVIDER_ACCEPTED → DELIVERED when supported. Additional states: RETRY_WAIT, UNKNOWN, FAILED, SUPPRESSED, EXPIRED and CANCELLED. Notification-level status aggregates its deliveries. READ is a separate inbox attribute.

Acquire a lease only for eligible READY jobs. Persist attempt intent before external I/O; update outcomes with attempt ID/version fencing. Keep lease/queue visibility longer than the provider timeout and renew during work. Recovery of expired PROCESSING attempts must check whether provider acceptance is uncertain, then reconcile UNKNOWN before resending. A stale worker must not overwrite a newer result. Fencing cannot retract a provider request already in flight.

Use a stable provider idempotency key where supported. Timeout after sending may mean the provider accepted the message: query status or await evidence before a bounded product-specific retry decision. Do not blindly switch providers on ambiguous timeouts.

Callbacks are deduplicated by provider/event ID, can arrive before synchronous responses, and must never regress DELIVERED to PROVIDER_ACCEPTED. Preserve raw normalized events and use provider-specific transition rules. Provider acceptance alone never proves receipt by a person/device.

4. Retries, scheduling and overload

Condition Action
Invalid address/token or permanent payload error Fail permanently; invalidate endpoint or suppress confirmed bounce
429 Honor Retry-After; reduce sending rate
Transient 5xx/network failure with definite non-acceptance Exponential backoff with full jitter, provider-specific minimums
Ambiguous acceptance UNKNOWN reconciliation before retry/failover
Exhausted attempts/poison job Durable DLQ record and alert
Expired/opted-out job EXPIRED/SUPPRESSED; no send or replay
Bound retries by attempt count and expiry. Persist next_attempt_at before ACK; scheduler publishes due retries through an outbox with the original delivery identity. Audit DLQ replay and recheck consent, TTL and current terminal state. Confirmed terminal deliveries must not be resent.

Use circuit breakers by provider/channel. Route to an approved alternative on definite failures or reconciled outcomes, subject to cost and policy. Re-check consent immediately before dispatch, while documenting that a concurrent opt-out cannot retract a send already accepted by the provider.

Redis token buckets enforce tenant, provider and channel limits. During Redis failure, use conservative bounded local capacity or pause bulk; never silently dispatch without limits. Autoscale on queue age and throughput within provider caps. Sustained quota overload requires backpressure, bulk throttling and admission control; queues alone cannot fix it.

FCM recommends avoiding traffic spikes and respecting retry/backoff signals. Do not assume a fixed quota without checking the actual provider account. FCM scaling guidance

5. Data model

All tenant-owned records and queries enforce tenant scope.

Table Key fields and constraints
tenants id, policy, quotas, budget
notification_requests id, tenant_id, idempotency_key, request_hash, recipient_ref, template_version, category, priority, schedule_at, expires_at, status; unique tenant/key
deliveries id, tenant_id, notification_id, recipient_id, channel, endpoint_id, status, provider, provider_message_id, attempt_count, next_attempt_at, lease_until, current_attempt_id, version; unique notification/recipient/channel/endpoint
delivery_attempts delivery_id, attempt_no, provider_request_key, intent_at, result, error, completed_at; unique delivery/attempt
outbox id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload_ref, available_at, published_at; index pending/due
webhook_events provider, event_id, payload_hash, received_at, processed_at; unique provider/event
preferences tenant_id, user_id, category, channel, opt_in, timezone, quiet_hours, version
endpoints tenant_id, user_id, endpoint_id, encrypted_destination, valid, updated_at
templates tenant_id, template_id, version, locale, channel, content; immutable versions
inbox_items delivery_id unique, tenant_id, user_id, created_at, read_at; cursor index on tenant/user/created_at/id
Index delivery scheduler queries by status/next_attempt_at and expired leases separately. Use immutable template versions and timezone-aware schedules with an explicit daylight-saving ambiguity policy.

At 1KB per delivery, 15M/day means 15GB/day raw or 450GB/30 days before indexes, replicas and attempts. Suggested starting retention: 7-day hot attempt details, 30-day delivery summaries, configurable encrypted S3 archives. Retention must match business requirements. Prune outbox rows only after safe publication and audit retention; keep dedupe keys long enough.

Partition hot data and benchmark maintenance/write amplification. If write latency/storage headroom fails targets, shard by tenant with outbox transactions local to each shard; alternatively redesign the delivery store around DynamoDB with its own transactional/stream publishing boundary. Do not introduce a new DB/queue dual-write gap during migration.

6. API contract

Tenant identity comes from credentials, never a trusted body field.

POST /v1/notifications Headers: Authorization, Idempotency-Key

{
  "recipient_id": "user_123",
  "template_id": "order_shipped",
  "template_version": 3,
  "channels": ["email", "push"],
  "category": "transactional",
  "priority": "transactional",
  "variables": {"order_id": "ord_456"},
  "schedule_at": null,
  "expires_at": "2026-10-01T12:00:00Z"
}

202 response: notification_id, status="ACCEPTED", status_url. Expiry shown is illustrative; clients must supply a valid future timestamp.

Endpoint Behavior
GET /v1/notifications/{id} Authorized per-delivery status, timestamps and evidence
POST /v1/notifications/{id}/cancel Best effort; cannot unsend accepted/in-flight messages
PUT /v1/users/{id}/preferences Validated channel/category preferences
GET /v1/inbox?cursor=... User-scoped stable cursor pagination
POST /v1/inbox/{id}/read Idempotent mark read
POST /v1/campaigns Durable campaign acceptance; async paged fanout
400 validation, 401/403 auth, 409 idempotency mismatch, 429 rate limit with retry guidance. Authenticate admin/template/campaign endpoints separately. Enforce payload size, variable schema and channel allowlists.

7. In-app and mobile delivery

Inbox worker commits inbox item and realtime outbox together. Relay notifies SSE/WebSocket gateways; pub/sub is an optimization. Clients reconnect and fetch the durable inbox using a cursor. Track read state per user; authorize every subscription. No message is lost merely because a socket disconnects.

Push endpoint fanout is deterministic per device. Remove invalid device tokens and account for multiple devices in capacity estimates. Device OS policies and user permissions influence notification visibility independently of backend acceptance.

8. Capacity and scaling

Average deliveries: 15,000,000 / 86,400 ≈174/s; 20× burst ≈3,500/s excluding retries. At a hypothetical 200ms average provider request time, concurrency = 3,500 ×0.2 =700 in-flight calls; provision roughly 1,400 for 2× headroom only if quotas and load tests support it. Size each channel separately.

Backlog drain time = backlog / (service rate − incoming rate). A 1M backlog with 5,000/s service and 3,500/s incoming drains in about 667s, assuming quotas permit that service rate. If service rate is not greater than arrival rate, backlog never drains.

Keep autoscaling bounded by provider quota and spend caps. Reserve critical worker pools, fairly schedule tenants, smooth campaigns and expire obsolete OTPs. Measure database IOPS, connection pools, queue lag, retry amplification and gateway connection counts before scaling.

9. Deployment, security and disaster recovery

Run API, relay, scheduler and workers across availability zones; use managed database failover and durable queues. Start with one active sending region. Warm standby needs an ownership epoch/fencing mechanism and a verified old-region shutdown before promotion to avoid split-brain sends.

Proposed DR targets: RPO ≤5min and RTO ≤30min, conditional on replication and restore drills. Asynchronous regional replication can lose acknowledged notifications during a regional disaster; document that tradeoff and reconcile uncertain provider attempts after failover.

Use TLS, encryption at rest, secret manager and rotated provider credentials; restrict network and IAM permissions. Encrypt addresses/tokens, redact PII/OTP/payloads from logs, escape templates, validate webhook signatures/timestamps and prevent replay. Apply tenant RBAC, audit admin/replay actions and spend caps. Opt-out/transactional exceptions require explicit category policy; no blanket consent bypass.

10. Observability

Track API availability/acceptance latency; oldest unpublished outbox age; queue age per channel/priority; scheduler lateness; worker saturation; provider 429/error/success; UNKNOWN age; retry/DLQ rates; suppressions/bounces; delivery evidence latency; tenant fairness and spend.

Trace notification_id → delivery_id → attempt_id. Avoid user IDs as metric labels. Alert on critical queue age, stuck outbox, prolonged UNKNOWN, quota saturation, DLQ growth, high bounce rates and database capacity. Dashboards distinguish provider acceptance from confirmed delivery.

11. Failure recovery matrix

Failure Recovery
DB unavailable Do not return 202; bounded retry/backpressure
Relay crashes after publish Republish possible; durable consumer dedupe
Worker crashes before external request Recover intent/lease; establish safe resend
Worker crashes after possible acceptance UNKNOWN; reconcile before retry
Provider outage Circuit breaker, persistent retry, eligible failover
Duplicate/out-of-order webhook Durable dedupe and non-regressing transitions
Scheduler restarts Reclaim due durable jobs through leases/outbox
Redis unavailable Conservative cap/pause bulk
Socket disconnect Durable inbox catch-up
Region failure Fence previous owner; promote; reconcile uncertain sends

12. Validation plan

Test concurrent identical idempotency requests and mismatched payloads; deterministic paged fanout; tenant isolation; consent/cancel/expiry races; duplicate and out-of-order callbacks; stale leases; ambiguous provider acceptance; safe DLQ replay.

Inject crashes at DB commit, outbox publish, provider call and ACK boundaries. Run 20× burst and soak tests with provider stubs, then validate actual provider quotas with controlled integration tests. Test backlog recovery, Redis failure, database restore and regional fencing. Verify neither generated diagrams nor capacity formulas are treated as production test results.

13. Implementation roadmap and open decisions

  1. Build API, PostgreSQL schema/outbox, SQS ingress, email worker, durable idempotency, preferences and inbox.
  2. Add SMS/push, scheduler, retry/DLQ, provider feedback, cancellation and UNKNOWN reconciliation.
  3. Add campaigns, tenant fairness, reserved critical capacity, dashboards, rate caps and load-driven autoscaling.
  4. Validate partitioning/sharding and warm-standby DR through measured capacity and recovery drills. Confirm actual volume and burst shape, channel mix/device fanout, providers, cloud, budget, regions, retention, tenant isolation requirements and critical delivery SLOs before production sizing.

Originally published at yasiramin.dev.

title: Parallel coding agents in separate git worktrees
description:
A worktree gives each coding agent its own checkout, yet branches, ports, secret files and output folders can still collide. Here is what to check.

Running several coding agents at once is easy to start and surprisingly easy to get wrong. The usual first step is to give each agent a separate worktree, so that one agent editing files does not disturb another. That step really does solve the file-editing problem. It does not solve the rest of the shared machine: the branch each agent commits to, the network port its dev server opens, the untracked files it needs, and every path outside the checkout that more than one process writes to. This guide explains what a worktree isolates, then goes through the five places where parallel agents still collide, and closes with a pre-launch comparison for your own launcher.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/git-worktrees-parallel-agents?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social

title: Your Users Don’t Care About Your Design System
description:
Your UI can look consistent and still leave users guessing where to click next.

I’ve worked on SaaS products where the design system was already in good shape. The team had reusable components, defined design tokens, and clear rules for building new screens. Everyone used the same UI patterns, and the interface looked consistent across the product. Still, users struggled to find what they needed.

They couldn't figure out where certain features lived. Some tasks took too many steps. Support kept getting questions about things that seemed obvious to the team.

So, what was going on?

I've noticed this pattern in products that have been growing for years. Teams add features, adjust workflows for enterprise clients, and respond to new customer requests. Eventually, the product becomes harder to navigate, even when the UI looks perfectly fine.

The first instinct is often to clean up the interface or build a new design system. Sometimes, that helps. But I'd first want to know what's actually making the product difficult to use. A consistent UI doesn't automatically make a product easy to understand.

A design system helps teams build interfaces faster and keep things consistent. Information architecture helps users find what they need and understand how the product works. Both matter, but they solve different problems.

A consistent UI doesn't guarantee a good user experience

A design system gives designers and developers a shared set of components, design tokens, and rules. Instead of building every button, form, or table from scratch, the team can reuse existing elements.

This saves time, reduces visual errors, and makes new features easier to build. For a growing B2B SaaS product with dozens of screens and different user roles, that's a big advantage. But consistent components don't tell you if users can find a feature or understand what to do next.

Imagine a CRM where every button looks the same, all tables follow the same layout, and forms work consistently across modules. The UI looks great. Yet users might have to open three sections to find one setting. Two pages might contain similar information, with no clear explanation of how they differ. The same action might appear in several places, while another is buried deep in the navigation. The interface may look consistent to the team, while for users getting things done is still harder than it should be.

I've seen teams improve their design systems and speed up development without reducing the number of support tickets about navigation. The new components worked well, but nobody had revisited how the product was organized. That's an important distinction to make before investing time and money in a redesign.

I usually look at three areas:

  • UI consistency - do elements look and behave the same way across the product?
  • Design system - does the team have shared components and clear rules for using them?
  • Information architecture - are features and information organized in a way that makes sense to users?

These areas are connected, but each needs a different kind of attention.

Sometimes, the problem is bigger than the UI change

I remember a project where a client asked us to remove the dividers between sections on a screen. It was a very specific request about one visual element. We removed them, but the client still wasn't happy with the result.

After looking at the screen again, we could see the bigger issue. There was too much information competing for attention. Everything seemed equally important, and users had to figure out where to look first. The dividers were just the thing the client had noticed.

This happens quite often. People who work with a product every day know it inside out. They know where the features are, how the workflows work, and which details matter. But knowing the product so well can make it hard to see it through a new user's eyes.

A client might ask to change a color, move a button, or remove a visual element. Those requests are worth considering, but they don't always explain what's causing the problem.

When I look at a screen like this, I want to understand what the user is trying to do. Is all this information necessary at this point? Which details help users make a decision? Are several actions competing for attention? Could we simplify the workflow or move some information elsewhere?

Sometimes, a small visual change is enough. Other times, we need to rethink the screen's structure. The important part is understanding what the change should achieve before deciding how to make it.

Information architecture becomes harder to manage as a product grows

Early versions of a SaaS product are usually easier to use. There are fewer features, fewer user roles, and fewer workflows to think about. Then the product grows.

Sales asks for features that enterprise customers need. Product teams introduce new workflows. Different teams build separate modules. Permissions become more complex, and older features stay because customers still rely on them.

Each change may make sense on its own. Over time, though, the product can become a collection of features that don't fit together as well as they should.

Users may find the same information in several places. Related features can sit in separate sections. Even a simple task can require switching between screens and remembering details along the way.
Information architecture helps solve these problems by organizing features and pages in a clear way. It shows how different parts of the product fit together and helps users find what they need and know where to go next.

This gets especially tricky in enterprise UX. An administrator, a manager, and an employee might all use the same platform, but their responsibilities and permissions are different. They may need different views of the same information and different ways to complete related tasks. The challenge is to support those needs without making the entire product harder to understand.

A design system helps the team build these screens consistently. Information architecture helps the team decide how the screens should fit together.

A clean interface can still feel complicated

Notion is a good example of this. Its interface has a recognizable visual style, and its building blocks give users plenty of ways to organize their work.

At the same time, the number of features and customization options can feel overwhelming, especially for people who are still figuring out how to use the product.

A clean UI makes individual elements easier to scan. It doesn't necessarily make the whole product easier to understand.

The same thing happens in SaaS products. A dashboard can look polished but leave users unsure which metrics matter most. A CRM can offer several ways to reach the same customer record. An ERP can have all the right settings, but finding the one you need takes too long.

When I see these problems, I look at how users move through the product. If people keep opening the wrong section, I'd check the navigation labels and how features are grouped. If they switch between two pages over and over, I'd look at why the information is split between them. If they complete the same task through several different routes, I'd want to understand whether those routes serve different needs.

An information architecture audit can help answer these questions. It looks at how the product is organized and whether that structure works for the people using it. The outcome might be simpler navigation, a better grouping of features, a different page structure, or fewer steps in a common workflow.

These changes can make a real difference to SaaS UX, even when the existing UI components are already well designed.

A component library is a starting point

Tools like shadcn/ui and Radix UI make building interfaces much easier. They give teams reusable components and established interaction patterns, so developers don't have to start from the very beginning.

I think they're great foundations for many products. But having a library of components doesn't answer every design question.

  • When should you use a particular component?
  • Does the interaction make sense for the task?
  • How should different patterns work together?
  • What happens when a new feature introduces another user role or a more complicated workflow?

These decisions need their own rules.

For example, a team might use the same dropdown component across the entire product. That keeps the UI consistent. But if a dropdown contains dozens of options, finding the right one can still be frustrating. The component works as expected. The design decision might need another look.

A design system should give the team guidance on when and how to use its components. It should help designers and developers make decisions that work across the product, rather than just giving them a set of ready-made elements.

The same issue comes up with AI-generated UI. AI coding tools can produce polished screens surprisingly quickly. You can get buttons, tables, cards, and forms that look consistent enough to demonstrate a product idea.

The problems often show up when the team starts building on that work. Developers might find duplicated code, components that are difficult to reuse, or patterns that don't fit the existing product architecture. Some of the interface may need to be rebuilt before the team can maintain it properly.

Even when the code is reusable, the team still needs clear rules for how components should work together and how new features should fit into existing user flows.

A collection of components is useful. A system also needs decisions about how those components should be used.

How I decide where to start

When a client comes to us with a UI problem, I want to understand what they're trying to improve. Are developers spending too much time rebuilding similar elements? Are users struggling to find features? Are new screens becoming harder to fit into the existing product? The answers help us decide what to look at first.

A design system audit makes sense when components look or behave differently across screens, developers keep rebuilding the same elements, or the team lacks clear rules for using UI patterns.

An information architecture audit is worth considering when users struggle with navigation, related features are scattered across the product, similar pages have unclear purposes, or common tasks involve too many steps.

Sometimes, both are necessary. For example, inconsistent navigation labels might come from missing design standards. But they might also reflect a deeper problem with how the product groups its features. Standardizing the labels can help, but it won't solve the problem if the overall structure still confuses users.

I'd also look at what users are actually experiencing. Support tickets, onboarding questions, product analytics, and user interviews can help identify where people get stuck. A UX audit can bring these findings together and help the team decide which changes deserve attention first.

The idea is simple, understand the problem before choosing the solution.

Build a system that works for the whole product

At UITOP, we work with complex SaaS products, dashboards, CRM systems, and internal tools. These products often have multiple user roles, detailed workflows, and years of features behind them.

When working on these products, I look at how the interface is built, what users need to do, how the screens connect, and which parts of the structure make everyday tasks harder. Visual consistency matters, but so do component architecture, navigation, information hierarchy, and interaction patterns.

A good design system gives the team a shared foundation. It makes development more predictable and helps keep the UI consistent as the product grows. Good information architecture helps users find what they need and understand how to get things done. When both work well together, the team can add new features without making the product harder to use.

So, before deciding to rebuild your design system, take a closer look at the problems users are facing. If the issue is slow development and duplicated UI work, the design system may need attention. If people can't find features or keep getting lost in workflows, start by looking at the product structure. And if you're seeing both, it's worth addressing them together.

Your users experience the product as a whole. They want to find what they need, understand their options, and get their work done. Good product design should make that easier.

title: An Effective Spoken Language Understanding Approach Leveraging Query-Adaptive Intent Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.09491v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models enable fine-tuning-free spoken language understanding (SLU) through in-context learning, but direct query-based retrieval may select semantically similar yet intent irrelevant demonstrations. This paper presents Query-Adaptive Intent Detection via Prototype Extraction (APEX), a two-stage retrieval framework that first selects candidate intents using intent-level prototypes and then retrieves contextual exemplars within the selected intent space. Experiments on the SLURP dataset evaluate joint SLU performance using Exact Match Accuracy (EMA) under full-transcript and perplexity-stratified conditions, with additional retrieval analysis on ASR-generated transcripts. Compared with query-based retrieval, APEX improves EMA by 4.34 and 3.97 percentage points with Qwen3 4B and Gemma-3-4B, respectively, on full transcripts. Under high-perplexity inputs, APEX also yields EMA gains of 7.66 and 2.13 percentage points. Retrieval analysis further indicates that prototype-guided candidate selection achieves higher ground truth intent coverage across multiple input conditions.

title: Invisible characters that break your code (and how to find them)
description:
You copy a value from a web page, a PDF or a chat message. It looks correct. But the password fails, JSON.parse throws, or two strings that look identical are not equal.

Often the cause is a character you cannot see. This post covers the usual suspects, why normal cleanup misses them, and how to find them in JavaScript, Python and the terminal.

The usual suspects

Character Code Where it tends to come from
Zero Width Space U+200B Web pages, chat apps, rich text editors
Byte Order Mark (Zero Width No-Break Space) U+FEFF Files saved as "UTF-8 with BOM", some CSV exports
No-Break Space U+00A0 Word processors, HTML  , PDFs
Narrow No-Break Space U+202F Formatted numbers and dates in some locales
Soft Hyphen U+00AD Text copied from typeset documents
Word Joiner U+2060 Rich text and some keyboards
Direction marks and overrides U+200E, U+200F, U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069 Mixed left-to-right and right-to-left text
Zero Width Joiner / Non-Joiner U+200D / U+200C Emoji sequences, Persian and Indic scripts

Most of these are in the Unicode "Cf" (format) category. They have no width, so editors and browsers show nothing.

Why trim() and \s don't catch them

This surprises people, so here it is in code:

/\s/.test('​');   // false: a zero width space is not whitespace
/\s/.test('﻿');   // true
/\s/.test(' ');   // true

JSON.stringify('  a​﻿'.trim());
// "a​"  <- the zero width space is still there

Python behaves similarly:

'​'.isspace()   # False
'﻿'.isspace()   # False
' '.isspace()   # True

'  a​ ﻿'.strip()
# 'a​ ﻿'  <- both survive

So a value can pass your "trim and compare" step and still not match.

Three bugs they cause

1. String comparison fails

'abc' === 'a​bc';   // false, though both print as abc

This is the classic "the password is correct but login fails" bug, and the reason a spreadsheet lookup won't match a value that looks identical.

2. JSON won't parse

A BOM at the start of a file breaks JSON.parse:

JSON.parse('﻿{"a":1}');
// SyntaxError: Unexpected token '﻿', "﻿{"a":1}" is not valid JSON

The error message even contains the character, which is why it looks like there's nothing wrong. In Python, open such files with encoding='utf-8-sig' and the BOM is dropped for you.

3. Code that "looks fine" doesn't run

A zero width space pasted into an identifier or a config key gives you an undefined variable or a missing setting, on a line that looks perfect.

Finding them in JavaScript

List each hidden character with its code and position:

const hidden = /[­​-‏‪-‮⁠-⁤⁦-⁩﻿]/g;

function findHidden(text) {
  return [...text.matchAll(hidden)].map(m =>
    'U+' + m[0].codePointAt(0).toString(16).toUpperCase().padStart(4, '0') +
    ' at ' + m.index
  );
}

findHidden('pass​word and ﻿end');
// [ 'U+200B at 4', 'U+FEFF at 14' ]

No-break spaces are not in that pattern on purpose. They are visible as a gap, so it's usually better to turn them into normal spaces than to delete them:

const cleaned = text
  .replace(/[­​‎‏‪-‮⁠-⁤⁦-⁩﻿]/g, '')
  .replace(/[  ]/g, ' ');

Finding them in Python

The unicodedata module names every character, which makes the output readable:

import unicodedata

def find_hidden(text):
    for i, ch in enumerate(text):
        if unicodedata.category(ch) == 'Cf' or ch in '  ':
            print(i, f'U+{ord(ch):04X}', unicodedata.name(ch, '?'))

find_hidden('pass​word and ﻿end')
# 4 U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE
# 9 U+00A0 NO-BREAK SPACE
# 14 U+FEFF ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE

Finding them in files

With GNU grep and a UTF-8 locale:

grep -nP '[\x{200B}-\x{200F}\x{2060}\x{FEFF}]' file.txt

cat -A file.txt also shows them as byte sequences. A zero width space appears as M-bM-^@M-^K.

Recent versions of VS Code highlight many invisible and confusable characters by default, so it's worth checking that the Unicode highlighting settings are on in your editor.

Don't delete ZWJ and ZWNJ blindly

The zero width joiner (U+200D) is what turns three separate emoji into one family emoji. Strip it and 👨‍👩‍👧 falls apart into 👨👩👧. The zero width non-joiner (U+200C) is a normal part of written Persian and several Indian scripts.

That's why the cleanup pattern above leaves U+200C and U+200D alone. Remove them only when you're cleaning code, passwords, IDs or spreadsheet keys, where they never belong.

A quick way to check by hand

If you just want to paste a piece of text and see what's hiding in it, I built a free hidden character checker. It marks each character with its name and code and can remove them, with an option to keep emoji joiners. It runs in the browser, so the text isn't uploaded.

Have you been bitten by one of these? I'd like to hear which character it was and where it came from.

title: OpenCode for older CPUs: a Node.js build for Windows
description:
If you tried to run OpenCode on an older Windows machine, you may have hit this:

this CPU is missing SSE4.2 support, which Bun requires

The standard Windows binary is compiled with Bun, and Bun won't start on CPUs without SSE4.2. Nothing is wrong with your computer. The runtime just refuses to launch.

So We made a build of OpenCode v2.2.6 packaged as a Node.js executable. The Bun CPU check never runs.

Repo: (https://github.com/foxauraai/opencode-node/)

What you get

  • A ready-to-use zip for Windows x64 (OpenCode v2.2.6)
  • No installation. Node.js is already inside the package
  • Setup with Command Prompt only

Install and run

  1. Download the zip from the Releases page and extract it, for example to C:\opencode.
  2. Open Command Prompt and run: 
cd /d C:\opencode\cli-node-windows-x64
OpenCode.bat

Any arguments you add after OpenCode.bat are passed to the program.

What's in the folder 

cli-node-windows-x64/
├─ OpenCode.bat              <- launcher, run this
├─ package.json
└─ bin/
   ├─ opencode2-node.exe     <- the app (Node executable, ~187 MB)
   └─ photon_rs_bg.wasm      <- needed by the app

OpenCode.bat is a one-line launcher that starts bin\opencode2-node.exe. Keep both files in bin\ together.

Run it from any folder

To run it as just OpenCode.bat from anywhere, add C:\opencode\cli-node-windows-x64 to your user PATH in Edit the system environment variables, then open a new Command Prompt.

Limits

  • This removes the Bun CPU requirement, not every requirement. Windows and your CPU still need to meet the basic requirements for modern 64-bit programs, and I haven't tested every older processor.
  • It's an unofficial build, not affiliated with the OpenCode project.

If it doesn't start on your machine, open an issue with your CPU model, Windows version, and the full error text.

Apigee X

Announcement

On October 22, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-7).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
573663408 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the ingress gateway to patch security vulnerabilities.
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.
