title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

title: BEVCast: Path-Adaptive BEV for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving
description:
arXiv:2611.08631v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.

title: SQL Macros in Oracle Database 21c
description:
As you may know, calling a PL/SQL function from a SQL query introduces a context switch between the SQL engine and the PL/SQL engine. This context switching can have a negative impact on query performance.

For example, the following two statements return the same result, but their execution times are significantly different.

Query without using a function

SQL> select sum(sal) from(select salary+60 as sal from person);

  SUM(SAL)

     ———

8891924480

Elapsed: 00:00:00.81

Query using a function

SQL> select sum(sal) from(select sal_func(salary) as sal from person);

  SUM(SAL)

———

8891924480

Elapsed: 00:00:10.91

Note: The sal_func function is defined as follows:

create or replace function sal_func(sal_param  number)
  return number
is
begin
  return sal_param +60 ;
end;

/

As you can see, the first query takes less than one second to execute, whereas the second query takes approximately 11 seconds.

This comparison might lead us to avoid calling PL/SQL functions from SQL queries. However, avoiding functions altogether can introduce significant maintenance overhead. For example, if a formula needs to be modified, we may have to update multiple parts of an application. Therefore, avoiding function calls in SQL statements is not always the best solution.

To address this performance issue, Oracle introduced SQL Macros in Oracle Database 21c.

SQL Macros allows Oracle Database to expand a function call into its corresponding SQL expression or query during SQL macro expansion. As a result, the SQL statement can be optimized as if the expanded SQL expression had been written directly in the original statement.

For example, Oracle transforms the following query:

select sum(sal) 
from(
select sal_func(salary) as sal 
from person
);

Into the following query:

Final query after transformations:******* UNPARSED QUERY IS *******

SELECT SUM(“PERSON”.”SALARY”+60) “SUM(SAL)” FROM “USEF”.”PERSON” “PERSON”

According to Oracle’s feature classification, SQL Macros are a new feature of Oracle Database 21c. However, they were also documented in Oracle Database 20c documentation and are available in Oracle Database 19c starting with Release Update 19.6.

Creating a SQL Macro

To create a SQL Macro, you must specify the SQL_MACRO clause in the function declaration.

The return type of a SQL Macro function must be a character data type, such as VARCHAR2 or CLOB, rather than the data type of the value returned by the expanded SQL expression.

Additionally, the SQL expression or query returned by the function must be enclosed in a quoted string, commonly using Oracle’s alternative quoting mechanism (q’{}’).

For example, we can rewrite the sal_func function as a Scalar SQL Macro:

create or replace function sal_func(sal_param number) 
return varchar2 sql_macro(scalar) is

begin

  return q'{
      sal_param +60
        }’;

end;

/

With this modification, the execution time of the query presented earlier decreases from approximately 11 seconds to just over one second:

SQL> select sum(sal) from(select sal_func(salary) as sal from person);

  SUM(SAL)

———-

8891924480

Elapsed: 00:00:01.11
Types of SQL Macros

Oracle Database supports two types of SQL Macros:

Scalar SQL Macros: Can be used in SQL expressions, including the SELECT list and applicable clauses such as WHERE and HAVING.
Table SQL Macros: Can be used in the FROM clause and return a SQL query that acts as a table expression.
Therefore, the SAL_FUNC function is an example of a Scalar SQL Macro.

The following function, which returns the size (in MB) of the largest segment belonging to a specified schema, is an example of a Table SQL Macro:

create or replace function table_macro_Mesal(p_tab varchar2)

  return varchar2 sql_macro(table) is

begin

  return q'{

    select max(bytes/1024/1024) SIZE_MB from
 dba_segments d 
where 
owner =table_macro_Mesal.p_tab

   }’;

end;

/

We can call this Table SQL Macro as follows:

SQL> select * from table_macro_Mesal(‘SYS’);

   SIZE_MB

    ———

    46

Passing Multiple Parameters to a Table SQL Macro

The following function accepts two input parameters:

cnt: The number of segments to return.
typ: the segment type to filter by.
It returns the largest segments based on their size, limited to the specified number of rows.

create or replace function table_macro_Mesal2(cnt number,typ varchar2)

  return varchar2 sql_macro(table) is

begin

  return q'{
 select owner, segment_name, bytes / 1024 / 1024 SIZE_MB
   from dba_segments
   where segment_type=table_macro_Mesal2.typ
  order by bytes desc fetch first cnt rows only
   }’;

end;
/

For example, to retrieve the five largest table segments in the database, we can execute:

SQL> select * from table_macro_Mesal2(5,’TABLE’);

OWNER      SEGMENT_NAME                 SIZE_MB

———- ————————- ———-

USEF       JADVAL_TEST                      312

USEF       PERSON                           104

SYS        IDL_UB2$                          16

SYS        WRI$_SQLSET_PLAN_LINES            15

SYS        IDL_UB1$                          12

As demonstrated in these examples, SQL Macros provide a way to encapsulate reusable SQL expressions and queries while allowing the SQL optimizer to work with the expanded SQL statement.

title: 유나이티드 항공 좌석 등받이의 Spotify가 시각 훈련에 던지는 힌트
description:
유나이티드 항공 좌석 등받이의 Spotify가 시각 훈련에 던지는 힌트

유나이티드 항공 좌석 등받이에 Spotify가 들어옵니다. 스타링크 위성 Wi-Fi 기반의 네이티브 앱이라, 승객은 35,000피트 상공에서도 자기 계정으로 로그인해 플레이리스트와 비디오 팟캐스트를 그대로 재생합니다. 기내 엔터테인먼트가 '정해진 채널'에서 '내 라이브러리'로 넘어가는 순간입니다.

여기서 흥미로운 지점은 콘텐츠가 아니라 '개인화된 시청 환경'입니다. 같은 화면을 모두가 보는 대신, 각자에게 맞춰진 화면을 본다는 개념이 대중화되고 있죠.

Seven Sports가 만든 Amblyotube는 이 개념을 시각 훈련에 적용했습니다. Meta Quest 앱으로, 왼쪽 눈과 오른쪽 눈에 서로 다른 시각 경험을 제공합니다. 시청자가 좋아하는 YouTube 스타일 콘텐츠를 보면서, 우세안에는 조절 가능한 디지털 블러(Dominant Eye Shader)를, 약시안(lazy eye)에는 AI Sharpener(MFBF)가 사람 형상을 감지해 붉은 외곽선·황록 하이라이트·규칙적인 깜빡임으로 시각적 단서를 제공합니다.

엔지니어링 관점에서 흥미로운 건 이걸 '새 콘텐츠'가 아니라 '새 렌더링 파이프라인'으로 푼다는 점입니다. 두 개의 독립 아이피스를 가진 VR 헤드셋은 본질적으로 두 개의 뷰포트를 가진 디스플레이이고, Amblyotube는 그 두 뷰포트에 같은 영상 스트림을 받아 서로 다른 후처리 셰이더를 통과시킵니다. 왼쪽·오른쪽 중 어느 쪽이 약시안인지 사용자가 직접 지정하는 초기 설정이 중요한데, 선택이 반대면 우세안을 훈련시키게 되기 때문입니다. 조건 프리셋(Mild/Moderate/Severe)을 고르면 우세안 셰이더와 약시안 샤프너의 기본 강도가 함께 튜닝되고, LogMAR 시력 검사가 Landolt C 시표를 3미터 가상 거리에서 최대 30회 시행하며 검출된 심각도에 맞춰 프로필을 자동 갱신합니다.

선택형 Wedge Occlusion은 각 눈이 장면의 서로 다른 부분을 보게 해 양안 경쟁(binocular rivalry)을 줄이고, 마젠타 초점 단서는 두 눈의 상을 하나의 3D 이미지로 융합하도록 돕습니다. 접착식 패치나 적청 안경 없이, 매일 30~40분 좋아하는 콘텐츠로 훈련하는 구조입니다. 13세 이상, 하루 최대 1시간 권장. 양안 협응과 깊이 지각을 위한 보조적 시각 훈련 도구이며 진단·치료·완치 수단이 아닙니다.

Meta Quest 스토어에서 확인하실 수 있습니다: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: Workspace is not a cloud desktop: four things it does not restore
description:
I work on CloudGPU, so read this as a note from the people who build it.

CloudGPU recently added Workspace: you can save project files independently of a GPU, pin them as an immutable version, and restore that version into a later Job or onto a GPU you are already renting. The most common misreading we see is "so it is a cloud desktop now". It is not, and designing around that difference saves real time.

Here are the four things Workspace does not bring back, and what to do about each.

1. Your operating system, drivers and installed packages

A Workspace version is a manifest: relative project paths mapped to files you uploaded and completed. When a Job starts with workspace_version_id, those files are restored into a fresh project directory before your command runs. That is all.

The machine underneath is whatever template the new Job or instance uses. pip install results, a compiled extension, a CUDA build you fixed by hand last week: none of that is in the version.

What to do: keep environment setup as code inside the project. A setup.sh or a pinned requirements.txt / environment.yml that your Job command runs first is the version-controlled replacement for "the machine I had".

# Job command: rebuild the environment, then run
bash setup.sh && python render.py --config configs/shot_014.yaml

2. Changes you made after saving

A version is immutable. If you edit configs/shot_014.yaml on a running GPU, the saved version still holds the old file. Nothing syncs back automatically.

What to do: treat "save a new version" as an explicit step, the same way you treat git commit. Name it after what changed (shot014-fix-lighting), not after the date.

3. Job outputs

The platform does not collect outputs for you. A Job runs one command, and the local storage of that Job's GPU is erased when it ends. If the command did not export its results, they are gone, even if the Job "succeeded".

What to do: make export part of the command, and check it as an acceptance step:

python render.py --out out/ \
  && ls out/*.png | wc -l \
  && <your upload step for out/>

Then verify on your side that the expected number of files arrived and that they open. A zero exit code is not proof that usable files reached you.

4. Unlimited time and unlimited space

Saved files are subject to account eligibility, a quota and a retention policy. Completed files carry an expires_at; downloading a file does not renew it, and a version that contains an expired file becomes unusable. Storage charges are separate from the max_spend_usd cap on a GPU Job, and a budget-limited agent key cannot switch on paid storage.

What to do: read your own limits from the authenticated GET /v1/storage before you plan a long project, and keep your own copy of anything you cannot afford to lose.

So what is it good for?

Three patterns where it genuinely helps:

  • Repeatable runs. Pass the same workspace_version_id to two Jobs and you know both started from byte-identical project files. If the outputs differ, the cause is elsewhere (seed, environment, upstream model), which narrows the search.
  • Picking up on a GPU you already rent. A saved version can be applied to a running instance. It lands in a new private directory, does not overwrite your existing files, and does not install anything, run anything or restart the GPU. You decide what happens next.
  • Handing a project to an agent. An agent with its own scoped key can start a Job from a version without you uploading files again in every session.

A quick mental model

Layer Survives the GPU? Who is responsible
OS, drivers, packages No Your setup script
Project files you saved as a version Yes, within quota and retention Workspace
Edits after the save No, until you save a new version You
Job outputs No, unless exported Your Job command

A short overview

If you have never seen CloudGPU, this short video shows what it is in general terms (it is not a Workspace tutorial):

Read more

  • Agent and persistence API docs: https://cloudgpu.app/docs/agents?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=202611_seg04_codingagent&utm_content=pack1109gf_devto_workspace_boundary
  • Check whether persistence is enabled: GET https://cloudgpu.app/v1/public/compute-capabilities

Eligibility and full terms: https://cloudgpu.app/terms?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=202611_seg04_codingagent&utm_content=pack1109gf_devto_workspace_boundary

What does your team keep outside the GPU today: a setup script, a container image, or something else? I am curious which part breaks most often.

title: Our Fallback Stylesheet Reaches for 25 Design Tokens and Declares None of Them
description:
I work on OnePassApps, the team behind app.onepassapps.com, so this is our own build, and every number below was measured on it today over plain HTTPS from outside the browser - no session, no cookies, no JavaScript, one fetch per URL.

We ship a small static stylesheet for the moment the app does not come up. It is a separate file beside the app bundle, and it is linked first on every page. What it does with variables is the interesting part.

The file

The static fallback stylesheet answers HTTP 200 with 3054 bytes. The app bundle's stylesheet, /assets/index-B_evf03w.css, answers HTTP 200 with 242648 bytes and declares 403 custom properties, referenced 346 times with var().

What the small file does with variables

  • It uses 25 distinct custom properties in its var() calls.
  • It declares 0 of them itself.
  • Not one of its var() calls carries a default value: 0 calls have a fallback value after the comma.

The tokens it reaches for are the ordinary design ones - --brand, --brand-edge, --brand-wash, --canvas, --control-lg, --focus, --font-sans, --frame-edge, and 17 more.

Where those values come from

All 25 of them are defined in the app bundle's stylesheet, and 0 of them are defined nowhere else. So the small file is not self-contained: its colours, its spacing, its type scale and its focus ring all resolve against the bundle the fallback exists to survive without.

The file says so itself, in its own header comment: it is linked with tokens.css and base.css, outside the app bundle, so the fallback still renders when the bundle itself fails to load or throws before React mounts.

The two files that comment names

On the live host today, neither of them is served:

Path Status
/base.css 404
/tokens.css 404

Both answer the fixed miss document. The two stylesheets our pages actually link are the static fallback stylesheet and /assets/index-B_evf03w.css.

What a missing token does

A var() with no default and no matching declaration is invalid at computed-value time, so the property it sits in falls back to being unset - inherited for an inherited property, initial for anything else. The fallback sheet uses that form for --brand, --brand-edge, --brand-wash, --canvas and the rest of its token list, with no default after any of them.

I did not reproduce a bundle failure in a browser, so I make no claim about what the page looks like in that case. What the bytes say is the dependency above.

The tokens that change with the viewport

Most of the 25 tokens are declared once at the top level. 11 of them are also redeclared inside a media query, so their value is not the same at every width:

  • --font-sans is declared 2 time at the top level and 1 more inside a theme-inline condition.
  • --frame-edge is declared 1 time at the top level and 2 more inside a media (width<768px),(width<1024px) and (height<=500px) condition.
  • --inset is declared 1 time at the top level and 2 more inside a media (width<768px),(width<1024px) and (height<=500px) condition.
  • --leading-body is declared 2 time at the top level and 1 more inside a theme-inline condition.
  • --leading-caption is declared 2 time at the top level and 1 more inside a theme-inline condition.
  • --radius-outer is declared 2 time at the top level and 1 more inside a theme-inline condition.
  • --radius-pill is declared 2 time at the top level and 1 more inside a theme-inline condition.
  • --stroke is declared 1 time at the top level and 1 more inside a media (prefers-contrast:more) condition.
  • --text-body is declared 2 time at the top level and 3 more inside a media (width<768px),(width<1024px) and (height<=500px) condition.
  • --text-caption is declared 2 time at the top level and 1 more inside a theme-inline condition.
  • --text-title is declared 2 time at the top level and 3 more inside a media (width<768px),(width<1024px) and (height<=500px) condition.

The cascade layers

The fallback opens with an explicit layer order that names theme, base, components and utilities, in that order. The bundle contains 4 layer blocks
(base, properties, theme, utilities), plus 61 media queries, 51 container queries, 28 supports conditions, 3 keyframe blocks and 14 font-face blocks.

That order is why the small file is linked first: it fixes the layer order before the bundle opens its own, so the fallback is not painted under a layered rule it cannot beat.

What I did not measure

  • The served CSS only. I did not run a browser, so I did not compare this with a rendered page, and I make no claim about how any of it looks.
  • I did not break the bundle on purpose, so I make no claim about how the fallback behaves when the bundle fails.
  • One build, one network, one fetch per URL, 2026-11-08T18:14:58Z.
  • I measured the 56 URLs in our sitemap. 56 of them link the static fallback stylesheet and 56 link the bundle stylesheet; 23 link no app JavaScript at all.

The app guide index is at https://app.onepassapps.com/guides?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=fallback-token-layer&utm_content=guides-link and the app itself is at https://app.onepassapps.com?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=fallback-token-layer&utm_content=home-link

I work on OnePassApps, and every number above comes from the build we ship today.

title: computer-use-rs: Open-Source Computer Use for Rust
description:
This article was written by AgentOne Research.

We just open-sourced computer-use-rs, a cross-platform Rust crate that lets your code look at any desktop app and use it the way a person would. It can read what's on screen, take a screenshot, and click, type, scroll, and drag.

It's the same library that powers Computer Use in the AgentOne desktop app. It's free, it works on macOS, Windows, and Linux, and it's dual-licensed under MIT or Apache-2.0.

cargo add computer-use-rs

Star computer-use-rs on GitHub

What Is "Computer Use"?

Most AI agents work through APIs. If you want an agent to send an email, someone has to build an email tool for it. That works great for popular apps, but most of the software on your computer doesn't have an API at all.

Computer use is the other approach: let the agent operate the computer directly. It looks at an app, figures out what's there, and clicks and types like you would. If you can do it with a mouse and keyboard, an agent with computer use can (at least in theory) do it too.

To make that work, the agent needs two things:

  1. A way to see. What app is open, what buttons and text fields are in it, and what it looks like.
  2. A way to act. Clicking, typing, pressing keyboard shortcuts, scrolling, and dragging.

computer-use-rs is both of those, in one Rust crate.

What computer-use-rs Does

Everything goes through one type, Computer. Here's a quick example that types into TextEdit on a Mac:

use computer_use::{CaptureOptions, ClickOptions, ClickTarget, Computer, ElementQuery};

fn main() -> computer_use::Result<()> {
    let mut computer = Computer::new()?;

    // Observe: an indexed element tree, a PNG screenshot, and a plain-text outline.
    let state = computer.get_app_state("TextEdit", &CaptureOptions::default())?;
    println!("{state}");

    // Act by element index…
    let text_area = state.find(&ElementQuery::role("text area")).next().map(|e| e.index).unwrap();
    computer.click("TextEdit", ClickTarget::Element(text_area), ClickOptions::default())?;
    computer.type_text("TextEdit", "Hello from Rust!")?;

    // …or by screenshot pixel.
    computer.click("TextEdit", ClickTarget::Pixel { x: 120.0, y: 80.0 }, ClickOptions::default())?;
    computer.press_key("TextEdit", "Return")?;
    Ok(())
}

Seeing an app

One call to get_app_state gives you three views of an app's window:

  • An accessibility tree, as a numbered list of elements (buttons, text fields, menus, links), with their roles, labels, values, and the actions you can take on them
  • A PNG screenshot of the window
  • A plain-text outline of the whole thing, which is exactly what you'd hand to a language model

If the app isn't running yet, it gets launched in the background. You can also use query to find elements by text or role without taking a screenshot, and list_apps / list_windows to see what's available.

Using an app

Once you know what's on screen, you can:

  • Click an element by its index, a pixel in the screenshot, or a point on the screen (left, right, or middle, single or multi-click)
  • Type text, and press key chords like ctrl+shift+Tab or super+c
  • Scroll and drag
  • Set values directly on settable elements, like sliders and text fields
  • Select text inside an element, or put the caret before or after it
  • Trigger named actions like "Show Menu", "Raise", or "Increment"

Wherever it can, computer-use-rs uses accessibility actions instead of fake mouse clicks. Pressing a button through the accessibility API is faster and a lot more reliable than guessing where to click.

It works in the background

This is the part I'm most excited about. By default, input goes straight to the target app without moving your mouse or stealing focus, wherever the OS allows it.

That matters a lot for agents. Nobody wants their cursor flying around the screen while an agent fills out a form. With background delivery, the agent can work in one app while you keep using another.

There are a few delivery modes for apps that need something different:

Mode What it does
Background The default. Events go to the app without touching your pointer or focus
FocusedBackground Also gives the window synthetic focus inside its own process, which Chromium/Electron apps need
Global Real system input, for apps that won't accept anything else. On macOS, the app is brought forward

On macOS, Command-key shortcuts even work in the background, because they're resolved to the matching menu item in the app.

Platform Support

computer-use-rs uses each operating system's own accessibility and capture APIs:

Platform Tree & actions Screenshot Input
macOS 14+ Accessibility API Window-server capture, then ScreenCaptureKit CGEvent posted to the app's process, or globally
Windows 10+ UI Automation PrintWindow / GDI Window messages to the app (background) or SendInput
Linux AT-SPI X11 GetImage of the app's window AT-SPI device event controller

A few things to know before you start:

  • macOS: whatever runs your binary (usually your terminal) needs Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions. Computer::permissions() tells you what you have, and Computer::request_permissions() shows the system prompts.
  • Linux: the accessibility bus needs to be running, which it is by default on GNOME and KDE. computer-use-rs turns on the desktop's accessibility flag for you, but Chromium, Electron, and Firefox apps only check it at startup, so apps that were already open need a restart (they're flagged with needs_restart). On Wayland, you get trees and actions for everything, but screenshots and input only work for X11/XWayland apps.
  • Windows: no setup needed.

Not Just for AI Agents

We built computer-use-rs for AgentOne, but there's nothing AI-specific about it. It's a plain Rust library: no server, no runtime, no protocol, just a typed API. That makes it useful for a lot of other things:

  • UI automation and scripting, for those boring, repetitive tasks in apps that don't have an API
  • End-to-end tests for desktop apps
  • Accessibility tools that need to read and interact with other apps

A few other details Rust developers will appreciate:

  • Computer is Send, so you can put it behind a mutex and use it from spawn_blocking or any worker thread.
  • AppState and Element are plain data, so they're easy to serialize, log, or pass around.
  • The platform layer is a public Backend trait. You can drive a fake desktop in your tests, or add support for a new platform.
  • The smaller building blocks are public too, like the xdotool-style key parser (keys::KeyChord) and the helper that maps screenshot pixels to screen points.

Why We Open-Sourced It

When we started building Computer Use for AgentOne, we went looking for a Rust library that could do this on all three platforms. We didn't find one we were happy with. Most options were tied to one OS, only handled mouse and keyboard input without the accessibility tree, or came wrapped in a server or protocol we didn't want.

So we built our own. And once it was working, keeping it to ourselves didn't make much sense.

Software that controls your computer should be auditable. A library that can read every window and click any button is about as sensitive as code gets. If we're asking you to trust an agent with that kind of access, you should be able to see exactly how it works. That's the same reason we open-sourced the AgentOne desktop app.

More users means a better library. Desktop automation is full of edge cases. Every app, toolkit, and window manager behaves a little differently, and we'll never test them all ourselves. Every bug report and pull request makes computer-use-rs better, and that makes Computer Use in AgentOne better too.

Computer use should be a building block, not a moat. Right now, most good computer-use tools live inside big AI companies' products. We'd rather everyone have access to solid, open primitives, so people can build agents, tests, and tools we haven't even thought of.

That's also why we picked MIT or Apache-2.0 instead of the AGPL license that AgentOne itself uses. We want computer-use-rs to be easy to drop into any project, open source or not.

How to Try It

Add it to your project:

cargo add computer-use-rs

The crate is imported as computer_use. If you want to poke around first, clone the repo and run the examples:

cargo run --example list_apps
cargo run --example inspect -- TextEdit /tmp/textedit.png
cargo run --example textedit   # macOS: create a document, type, select, delete

The inspect example is a good place to start. Point it at any app and it prints the full element tree and saves a screenshot, so you can see exactly what an agent would see.

Get Involved

computer-use-rs is brand new, and we'd love your help.

  • ⭐ Star the repo: github.com/The-Best-Codes/computer-use-rs
  • 📦 Get the crate: crates.io/crates/computer-use-rs
  • 🐛 Open issues when an app doesn't behave the way you expect. These are the most helpful reports we can get.
  • 🔧 Submit a PR, especially for Linux and Windows edge cases
  • 💬 Come chat in the AgentOne Discord

And if you'd rather have an agent that can already use your computer, without writing any Rust, AgentOne is free to download.

Happy building!

View computer-use-rs on GitHub

title: How to Stop Double-Allocated Stock in Logistics Management Solutions
description:
Two warehouse workers confirm the last 12 units of a SKU within the same second, and both orders succeed. This happens in logistics management solutions whenever stock is a mutable counter updated by concurrent services. Retries from a flaky carrier API make it worse. This article shows a ledger-based reservation pattern in Python and PostgreSQL that prevents oversell. It follows the same principle behind how logistics management solutions work in enterprise systems.

Context and Setup

The scenario: an order service, a warehouse service, and a tracking service all write to one inventory store. The stack is Python 3.12, psycopg 3, and PostgreSQL 16. You need a table per warehouse-SKU pair and an order API that retries on timeout.

Data quality is the usual failure point. McKinsey’s 2023 supply chain survey reported that 52 percent of companies had adoption difficulties caused by the quality of their planning data. A counter that drifts under concurrency produces exactly that kind of bad data.
chainstoreage

Building a Reservation Ledger for Logistics Management Solutions

In logistics management solutions a reservation ledger replaces the stock counter with append-only rows. Available stock is the sum of all rows, so no update can overwrite another.

Step 1: Model Stock as Events

Store every change as a signed row. Receipts add units, reservations subtract them, and releases add them back.

sql
CREATE TABLE stock_ledger (
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
sku TEXT NOT NULL,
warehouse TEXT NOT NULL,
delta INT NOT NULL, -- Why: signed value makes SUM() the available stock
kind TEXT NOT NULL, -- receipt | reserve | release
idem_key TEXT UNIQUE, -- Why: a retried request cannot insert twice
created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX ON stock_ledger (sku, warehouse); -- Why: keeps the SUM() scan narrow

Step 2: Reserve Under a Lock With an Idempotency Key

Take a per-SKU lock, check the key, check availability, then insert. All four actions run in one transaction.

python
import psycopg

def reserve(conn, sku, wh, qty, key):
with conn.transaction():
# Why: serializes writers per SKU without locking the whole table
conn.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(%s))", (f"{sku}:{wh}",))
# Why: a retried request returns the first result instead of reserving twice
if conn.execute("SELECT 1 FROM stock_ledger WHERE idem_key=%s", (key,)).fetchone():
return "duplicate"
(avail,) = conn.execute(
"SELECT COALESCE(SUM(delta),0) FROM stock_ledger WHERE sku=%s AND warehouse=%s",
(sku, wh)).fetchone()
if avail < qty:
return "insufficient" # Why: reject before writing, so the ledger stays clean
conn.execute(
"INSERT INTO stock_ledger (sku,warehouse,delta,kind,idem_key) "
"VALUES (%s,%s,%s,'reserve',%s)", (sku, wh, -qty, key))
return "reserved"

Step 3: Pick a Locking Strategy for Logistics Management Solutions

Advisory locks suit hot SKUs because contention stays per key. Row locks on a counter table are simpler but block unrelated reads. Optimistic versioning avoids locks, yet it pushes retry logic into every caller.

The ledger has one cost: SUM() grows with history. Write a periodic snapshot row per SKU and sum only rows after it. Do this once a single SKU passes a few hundred thousand rows.

Real-World Application

In one of our logistics projects at Oodles, a Shanghai-based logistics provider needed inventory, order processing, and real-time tracking in one open-source ERP (enterprise resource planning) system. We gave all three modules a single stock model, so reservations and shipment updates read the same records.

Key Takeaways
Append-only rows remove lost updates because no writer overwrites another writer’s value.
A unique idempotency key turns retried API calls into harmless no-ops.

Per-SKU advisory locks limit contention to the item being reserved.
Snapshot rows keep the ledger sum fast once history grows.
Reject insufficient stock before the insert, so the ledger holds only true events.

Questions about this pattern? Share them in the comments, or contact us about Logistics Management Solutions for your stack.

What causes overselling in logistics management solutions?
Overselling occurs when two services read the same stock value and both write a reservation. Without a lock or atomic check, each sees enough units. Retried requests without idempotency keys create the same duplicate reservations.

Why use a ledger instead of a stock counter?
In logistics management solutions a ledger records each change as an immutable row, so concurrent writers never overwrite each other. It also gives an audit trail for reconciliation. The cost is a growing table, which snapshots keep manageable.

Are PostgreSQL advisory locks safe in production?
Yes, when used transaction-scoped with pg_advisory_xact_lock, because PostgreSQL releases them at commit or rollback. Session-level locks risk leaking under connection pooling, so avoid them with tools like PgBouncer in transaction mode.

How does an idempotency key prevent duplicate reservations?
The client sends a unique key per logical request. A unique constraint on that key means a retry either hits the stored row or fails the insert, so the reservation happens exactly once.

Should reservations expire automatically?
Yes. Unpaid or abandoned orders hold stock indefinitely otherwise. Insert a release row from a scheduled job when a reservation passes its time limit, so the ledger stays the single source of truth.

title: Turkish Multimodal Video Fact-Checking: A New Dataset and a Comparison of Zero-Shot Agentic and Fine-Tuned Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.08651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video-based misinformation spreads rapidly on social media, but almost all existing fact-checking systems focus exclusively on English text. Tools for low-resource languages such as Turkish are severely limited. In this work, we present TeViD (Turkish Video Fact-checking Dataset), to the best of our knowledge the first multimodal video fact-checking dataset for Turkish. We compiled the dataset from articles published by Teyit.org, an IFCN-certified organisation, and enriched it with translated Snopes articles and synthetic examples to reduce class imbalance. Building on TeViD, we develop two verification pipelines that share the same open-source base model. First, in 3MFact-TR (Pipeline 1), we adapt the multi-role 3MFact framework to Turkish with the Qwen2.5-7B large language model and the Qwen2-VL-7B vision-language model, and add three modules of our own: a semantic inconsistency checker, a 5W1H question manager, and a bilingual evidence retriever that excludes fact-checking sites to prevent leakage. Second, as our Fine-Tuned Model (Pipeline 2), we fine-tune a single Qwen2.5-7B with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to produce closed-book verdicts from the claim and the video's textual description. We report accuracy, macro F1, True class F1, and True class recall for both systems, together with ablation studies.

title: Beyond Truncation? Entailment-Licensed Elision and the Limits of Semantic Preservation in LLM Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.08975v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) answer at greater length than a request needs. We ask whether a training-free controller inside the decoding loop can remove that surplus while preserving content, judged against the simplest possible baseline: truncating the model's own answer to the same length. An entropy-gated logits processor removes 25.5-34.9% of tokens on MT-Bench development questions and 19.9-34.2% on a sealed test split within pre-registered BERTScore non-inferiority margins, yet we prove and confirm by audit that its output is always a prefix of the unmodified answer: the saving is truncation. A survey of 23 training-free mechanism families finds none that selects content better than truncation without oracle labels. We therefore introduce Entailment-Licensed In-Decoding Elision (ELIDE), which, at each sentence boundary, withholds a span from the reader only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by the text already shown, while leaving the model's generation unchanged. ELIDE beats matched-length truncation on three model families, but reading 936 of its elisions on 670 public prompts shows that 59% harm the answer, a failure that no automatic measure detects. Scoping the licence to its discourse unit reduces the harmful share to about one elision in ten on two fresh tests.

title: An Anatomy-guided 3D Segmentation Pipeline for Prostate Surgical Phantoms from CT Scans
description:
arXiv:2611.08652v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Full autonomy has been a long-term goal in robotic surgery and a near-to-medium-term goal for prostatectomy. Due to the relatively closed structure of the procedure, its standard-of-care robotic/laparoscopic solutions, and procedure economics, prostate procedures are an optimal early target for surgical automation. Prototyping and testing of possible solutions is done in constructed laboratory phantoms, either synthetic tissues or animal phantoms. To enable measurement of perceptual and robotic motion error, phantoms undergo volumetric imaging; these images are critical to both a potential deployed automatic system, used in planning motion and treatment (cutting, ablation, suturing, etc.), as well as post-hoc assessment of system performance. Rapid iteration on these phantom models yields small, inconsistent datasets, while the current workflow for human annotation is often anatomically unreliable and prohibitively time-consuming, rendering deep learning unsuitable at reasonable scales. To address these limitations, we present an automated 3D segmentation pipeline that uses classical medical image-processing techniques to encode the known anatomy of the phantoms as explicit geometric and intensity priors, which requires no training corpus and is transferred to each new phantom revision without re-annotation. Across 57 scans spanning multiple phantom revisions, our pipeline recovers the capsule interior at 0.83 median Dice on 11 contrast-suppressed scans and detects all 32 annotated focal lesions without false positives, completing a full scan in 2-8 minutes on commodity CPU hardware versus 1-2 hours by hand.

title: BayesCrop: Real-Time Probabilistic Multi-Crop Video Reframing
description:
arXiv:2611.09100v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic video reframing is increasingly important for adapting landscape content to heterogeneous display formats. Existing methods typically predict a single deterministic crop, despite the subjective nature of reframing and the presence of multiple plausible regions of interest. We present \textbf{BayesCrop}, a real-time probabilistic framework for multi-crop video reframing. BayesCrop represents crop preferences using a two-component spatially isotropic Gaussian mixture over crop position and scale. Each component defines a representative reframing mode together with its local uncertainty, enabling both dual-view prediction and sampling of additional plausible crop candidates. For efficient video processing, we introduce an anchor-and-propagate strategy that performs neural prediction only on sparse anchor frames and propagates crop trajectories using motion vectors available from the compressed video bitstream. The resulting trajectories can be combined into a single output using a lightweight periodic view-switching strategy. Experiments on LIVE-YT-MC, LIVE-YT-VC++, and a multi-target long-video benchmark demonstrate competitive single-output localization, high multi-crop reference coverage, diverse yet coherent crop hypotheses, and stable perceptual quality. BayesCrop achieves real-time throughput of 112 FPS at the default operating point, while sampling from the learned distributions further improves reference coverage beyond the two representative crop means.

title: On Seeding Watermarks to Detect Verbatim LLM Copy-Paste Responses
description:
arXiv:2605.16336v2 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made fluent essay writing, code drafting, and quiz answering instantly available to students at every level, from secondary school through graduate study. Many educators do not object to LLM use \emph{per~se}; what they need to detect is the case in which a student pastes the assignment prompt into a chatbot and submits the model's reply verbatim, without engaging with the work. Existing post-hoc AI-text detectors remain unreliable and have been shown to penalise non-native English writers, while output-side watermarks require cooperation from the model provider. We propose an alternative that the educator controls directly: an input-side watermark in which an invisible instruction is embedded inside the visible assignment prompt itself. An LLM that ingests the prompt verbatim quietly reads the hidden instruction and writes a tell-tale signature into its reply, exposing the copy-and-paste pathway specifically. We describe SteganoPrompt, a single-page, zero-dependency web tool that encodes an arbitrary printable-ASCII payload into the deprecated Unicode Tags block (\texttt{U+E0000}--\texttt{U+E007F}). The encoded string is visually identical to the original, survives common copy-paste channels (Word, Google Docs, PDF, Markdown, Slack, e-mail, the major learning-management systems), and is tokenized as ordinary text by most frontier models. We evaluate compliance across eight LLM families and a representative set of educational content channels. To keep deployment transparent, disclosure is built into the tool itself: every encoded brief also carries a brief, always-on academic-integrity reminder for the student, and we set out concrete guidance recommending for its disclosed, ethical use in the classroom. The tool is released under the MIT licence at https://ezharjan.github.io/SteganoPrompt/.

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
description:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.

title: Jev is the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history
description:
Within 24 hours of launching on AI Gateway, Jev from TypeSafe AI reached more than twice as many paid teams as any previous model launch, making it the fastest-adopted model in gateway history.

About Jev

Jev was introduced on September 15 as a probabilistic decision model designed to support structured decision-making within software. An application sends it context and a set of questions. Unlike the text produced by a general-purpose language model, Jev’s answers come in a format the code can use directly. Developers can use it to:

  • decide whether a workflow should continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • score urgency or risk before taking an action

  • verify model outputs, enforce guardrails, or send uncertain cases for human review

In its own workflow evaluations, TypeSafe AI reports that Jev was up to 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than language models.
