title: How to Automate WCAG 2.1 & APCA Color Contrast Audits (and Auto-Fix Failing Hex Codes) in Node.js
description:
With the European Accessibility Act (EAA) and ADA Title II/III enforcement tightening across web applications, shipping illegible low-contrast text or invisible UI buttons is no longer just a UX mistake—it is a legal and compliance risk.

Even worse, modern SaaS apps often allow user-customizable theming (where tenants pick their own brand primary color) or rely on AI UI generators that invent hex codes on the fly.

When a customer picks #60A5FA (a light sky blue) as their button background with #FFFFFF white text, the contrast ratio drops to 2.54:1—failing WCAG 2.1 AA (4.5:1 required for normal text).

In this guide, we will look at how to programmatically audit color pairs against WCAG 2.1 and APCA (WCAG 3.0 draft), simulate color vision deficiencies, and automatically calculate the nearest accessible hex color in under 1 millisecond using Node.js.

Why Manual Contrast Checkers Don't Scale

Checking two colors manually in a browser extension works during static Figma handoffs, but fails in dynamic applications:

  1. Dynamic User Themes: When a SaaS user saves a custom brand color in settings, your backend needs to validate and adjust that color before saving it to the database—or generate a complete 50–950 shade scale with guaranteed accessible text pairings.
  2. Preserving Brand Hue During Auto-Fix: If #60A5FA fails against #FFFFFF, you cannot just replace the user's blue brand color with #000000. You need a mathematical binary search in HSL/OKLCH space that preserves their exact Hue and Saturation while shifting Lightness just enough to hit 4.5:1 (AA) or 7.0:1 (AAA).
  3. Color Blindness Verification: Two colors might pass luminance contrast on paper while looking virtually identical to users with Protanopia (red-blind) or Deuteranopia (green-blind).

Automating Accessibility & Auto-Fixing with ContrastGuard API

Instead of writing relative luminance gamma transfer functions, APCA perceptual polarity equations, and Brettel color-blindness matrices from scratch, we can query ContrastGuard API on RapidAPI.

It runs 100% in-memory with <1ms execution latency.

1. Auditing & Auto-Fixing a Failing Brand Color in Node.js 

const RAPIDAPI_KEY = process.env.RAPIDAPI_KEY || "YOUR_RAPIDAPI_KEY";
const CONTRASTGUARD_HOST = "contrastguard-wcag-color-contrast-and-accessibility-fixer.p.rapidapi.com";

async function auditAndFixColors(foreground, background, targetLevel = "AA") {
  const response = await fetch(`https://${CONTRASTGUARD_HOST}/v1/audit`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "X-RapidAPI-Key": RAPIDAPI_KEY,
      "X-RapidAPI-Host": CONTRASTGUARD_HOST
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      foreground,
      background,
      targetLevel,
      fontSizePx: 16,
      fontWeight: 400
    })
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`ContrastGuard HTTP error: ${response.status}`);
  }

  return response.json();
}

async function runThemeCheck() {
  // Let's test a light blue (#60A5FA) on a white background (#FFFFFF)
  const result = await auditAndFixColors("#60A5FA", "#FFFFFF", "AA");
  const { data, meta } = result;

  console.log(`Audited in ${meta.execution_time_ms} ms`);
  console.log(`Original Ratio: ${data.contrastRatio}:1 (Grade: ${data.wcag21.grade})`);

  if (!data.wcag21.normalTextAA && data.autoFix) {
    console.log(`❌ Failed WCAG AA! Auto-fixing while preserving brand hue...`);
    console.log(`✅ Nearest Accessible Foreground: ${data.autoFix.suggestedForegroundHex}`);
    console.log(`✅ New Verified Contrast Ratio: ${data.autoFix.fixedContrastRatio}:1`);
  }

  console.log(`Color Blindness (Deuteranopia) Preview:`, data.colorBlindnessSimulation.deuteranopia);
}

runThemeCheck();

2. Generating a Full 11-Step Accessible Tailwind Scale (POST /v1/palette)

When a user inputs a single primary hex code, you can call /v1/palette to generate an entire 50–950 design-system scale where every shade already includes its exact contrast ratio and recommended foreground text color (#FFFFFF vs #0F172A):

async function generateDesignSystemScale(baseColor) {
  const response = await fetch(`https://${CONTRASTGUARD_HOST}/v1/palette`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "X-RapidAPI-Key": RAPIDAPI_KEY,
      "X-RapidAPI-Host": CONTRASTGUARD_HOST
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      baseColor,
      background: "#FFFFFF"
    })
  });

  const { data } = await response.json();
  console.table(data.scale || data.shades);
}

generateDesignSystemScale("#3B82F6");

3. Auditing an Entire CSS Theme in One Request (POST /v1/batch)

If you want to add an automated accessibility gate in your CI/CD pipeline or design token build step, pass up to 50 foreground/background pairs at once to POST /v1/batch:

const batchCheck = await fetch(`https://${CONTRASTGUARD_HOST}/v1/batch`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "X-RapidAPI-Key": RAPIDAPI_KEY,
    "X-RapidAPI-Host": CONTRASTGUARD_HOST
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    pairs: [
      { id: "btn-primary", foreground: "#FFFFFF", background: "#2563EB", targetLevel: "AA" },
      { id: "badge-warning", foreground: "#F59E0B", background: "#FFFFFF", targetLevel: "AA" },
      { id: "footer-muted", foreground: "#64748B", background: "#0F172A", targetLevel: "AA" }
    ]
  })
});

Try ContrastGuard API

  • RapidAPI Interactive Playground (Free Tier Available): ContrastGuard API on RapidAPI
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/artuturoh/contrastguard-api

How do you enforce WCAG contrast rules across custom user themes or design systems? Let me know in the comments!

title: Multilingual Artificial Datasets for AI-Driven Cardiology: the CliTe and ParaCliTe corpora
description:
arXiv:2611.09296v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Background and Aims. Comparable, multilingual, validated cardiology corpora are critical to advance trustworthy natural language processing (NLP) models for cardiology but such resources are scarce due to privacy concerns. This study aimed to cover this gap by presenting suitable artificial corpus creation guidelines and by releasing 3 multilanguage corpora. Methods. Following purpose-specific publicly-available corpus construction guidelines, cardiologists from 7 European hospitals generated artificial clinical records in Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, Spanish and Swedish, ensuring clinical diversity and sex balance, resulting in the CliTe corpus. A CliTe subset underwent a multi-stage manual translation into the other 6 languages, resulting in the parallel ParaCliTe corpus, while the remaining reports were automatically translated, constituting ParaCliTe Silver. Results. CliTe is a collection of 699 artificial cardiology reports, mostly outpatient notes (340 documents), discharge reports (263), and inpatient notes (89), describing fictional patients with ischaemic heart disease (199 patients), heart failure (188), and valvular disease (79), among others. ParaCliTe contains reports from 94 fictitious patients, each available in seven languages with sentence-level alignment, resulting in 658 documents. The corpus mainly comprises discharge reports (322 documents), and outpatient (196) and inpatient (140) notes, describing patients with heart failure (399 documents), ischaemic heart disease (287), and valvular disease (238). Empirical results illustrate the utility of ParaCliTe and highlight the limitations of state-of-the-art NLP models adapted to the cardiology domain. Conclusions. The creation of multilingual, equitable and realistic corpora of artificial patients capable of strengthening NLP performance for cardiology is feasible when supported by detailed guidelines.

title: PrivaSVG: image-to-SVG vectorization in the browser with Rust and WebAssembly
description:
Most image-to-SVG converters are upload forms: your file goes to a server, gets traced, and comes back. PrivaSVG does the whole job in the browser tab. There is no backend. Here's how it's built, with the parts that were actually tricky.

The pipeline 

Raster image -> AI background removal -> Manual retouch -> Upscale (2x / 4x) -> Vectorize (Rust -> WASM) -> SVG

Every stage is optional except the last, so you can jump straight to vectorization. A bulk page runs up to 50 images through a fixed chain and downloads a single ZIP.

  • Vectorization: a Rust engine compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen.
  • Background removal: @imgly/background-removal, which runs the isnet_fp16 segmentation model on ONNX Runtime Web. The model is fetched once, cached, and then works offline.
  • Upscaling: 2x or 4x canvas resampling to recover detail before tracing.
  • Retouch: a brush-based remove/restore tool to fix edges the model missed.

Credit where it's due

The tracing core is not from scratch. The Rust engine is built on VTracer and the visioncortex crate (the app depends on visioncortex 0.8.1). What PrivaSVG puts around it is the browser pipeline: the background-removal and retouch stages, upscaling and bulk processing. The keying approach described below follows the same idea as the upstream VTracer web app. The project is dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0.

Tracing as an incremental state machine

Tracing a large image is slow work, so the converter is an incremental state machine that the UI drives with repeated tick() calls:

pub enum Stage {
    New,
    Clustering(IncrementalBuilder),
    Reclustering(IncrementalBuilder),
    Vectorize(Clusters),
}

Each tick() does a small slice of work and returns whether it's finished. Clustering groups pixels into color clusters. In cutout mode a second Reclustering pass runs on the cluster view. Vectorize then converts one cluster per tick into a compound path and prepends it to the target <svg>. A progress() method maps the stages onto 0 to 100 (clustering is the first half, vectorizing the second), so the UI can show a real progress bar. Because the work is split into small slices, control returns to the caller between ticks.

Parameters arrive as JSON (new_with_string) and are deserialized with serde. They are the same knobs the settings panel exposes: curve-fitting mode (pixel, polygon, spline), speckle filter, color precision, layer difference, corner threshold, splice threshold and path precision, plus a stacked or cutout hierarchy.

The transparency problem

Background removal produces transparent pixels, but a clustering tracer wants colors. If you let transparent pixels through as black, you get a black blob behind your subject in the SVG.

The converter handles this with a key color. In init() it finds a color that isn't used anywhere in the image, replaces transparent pixels with it (including near-transparent black pixels, which the canvas API can produce when it flattens alpha), and tells the clustering runner to Discard that color. The key color never appears in the output, so transparent regions stay transparent. If no unused color can be found, it falls back to a fixed, very unlikely cyan (1, 254, 253). The source comments also record a lesson learned: red as the first-choice key color caused visible red backgrounds, so less common colors are tried first.

Privacy is the architecture, not a policy

There's no server to trust because there's no server. Images never leave the tab, and there are no accounts or tracking. The WASM engine and the ONNX model both run on your device. That's a stronger guarantee than a privacy policy, and it's why the project shares its visual language with my other privacy project, PrivaSearch.

Honest limits

  • The tracing quality is the visioncortex/VTracer algorithm's. It works well for logos, illustrations and cut-out subjects, and it will not turn a photograph into a faithful vector.
  • The first background removal downloads the model, so it needs the network once.
  • The cutout-mode transparency handling is heuristic, as the "fallback key color" above shows.

Try it

Live demo: https://haidaresber.github.io/privasvg/

Source (Rust, WASM, webpack): https://github.com/HaidarESBER/privasvg

title: Shipping a mint page you cannot redeploy at 3am
description:
A mint page can be technically available and still be wrong: the wallet is on another network, the displayed price is stale, or the page points at a contract address that does not match the deployment. My pre-deploy check is about catching those mismatches before a transaction can take money.

The pre-deploy checklist: one address, checked chain, live price

I keep the contract address in exactly one place: the page’s configuration. The mint flow reads it from there; it does not duplicate the address in a component, a helper, and a deployment note. That makes address changes reviewable and prevents different parts of the page from quietly targeting different contracts.

Before every mint, I check the wallet’s chainId against the expected chain. A check on page load is not enough: the user can switch networks after loading the page. The check belongs immediately before sending the transaction.

I also read the mint price from the contract at runtime. I do not treat a price embedded in the page as authoritative. The page can display the chain value and pass that same value into the transaction, rather than trusting a cached label.

const address = config.contractAddress;

async function mint() {
  const { chainId } = await wallet.getNetwork();
  if (chainId !== expectedChainId) throw new Error("Wrong network");

  const price = await contract.mintPrice();
  await contract.mint({ value: price });
}

The checklist is simple: one configured address, a chain check at the point of action, and a price read from the contract.

What happens when the page and the contract disagree

The page is not allowed to resolve a disagreement by guessing. If the expected chain does not match the wallet, the mint stops before it sends a transaction. If the contract call fails, or the value needed for the mint cannot be read, the page stops there too.

That is the important guard: fail loudly, before taking the buyer’s money. A disabled button or a clear error is better than sending a transaction with a value the page assumed was correct. The contract remains the authority for whether a mint is valid; the page’s job is to make that boundary visible and avoid submitting a transaction when its own checks fail.

For a deploy, I verify the configured address and chain against the deployment, then exercise the mint path with those checks enabled. The test suite has about 473 tests, but that does not replace checking the actual page configuration and live contract reads for the release.

A rollback that needs no new deploy

A page can have a rollback switch without changing the contract. I keep a flag in the page that disables mint submission, then use a read-only contract call to decide whether the page should allow minting. Read-only calls do not send a transaction or take payment.

When the flag is off, the page does not expose a mint action. When it is on, the page still checks the chain and reads the current contract state and price before allowing a transaction. The flag is an operational brake, not a replacement for contract checks.

The useful rollback property is that the page can stop initiating transactions without waiting for a new contract deployment. That gives the operator a way to halt the interface while investigating a mismatch; it does not claim to reverse transactions already sent.

Takeaway

Before shipping a mint page, make the contract address singular, check the wallet’s chain immediately before every mint, read the price from the contract, and include a page-level switch that can stop new transactions. The collection page is at https://thunderous-sunflower-a910b4.netlify.app.

title: TanStack Query: Server State That Stays Fresh Without the Boilerplate
description:
Two visitors open the same bookshop page a minute apart. The first one buys the last copy of a title. The second visitor's page still says one copy is in stock, because the data was fetched once at load and never checked again. She clicks buy, and the order fails at checkout. That gap is the problem TanStack Query is built for. Data from a server is not like the state inside your app. It lives somewhere else, it changes without telling you, it can fail to arrive, and a copy fetched five minutes ago may be wrong. TanStack Query keeps a cache of that server data, refetches it when it goes stale, and retries when a request fails.

What I would check before using it

My judgement is that TanStack Query earns its place the moment two parts of an app need the same server data, or one screen needs that data to stay fresh. A single fetch on a page that never changes does not need it; a plain fetch inside useEffect does that job with less to learn. The value shows up when the same book list appears on the shop page and the checkout, or when an order should refresh the stock count.

I would check five things before adopting it. First, how the data changes. If the server data never updates, a cache buys little. If it changes when users act, invalidation is the feature you are buying. Second, the defaults. Data is refetched on window focus and on reconnect, and a failed query retries three times. But staleTime defaults to zero, so data counts as stale the moment it arrives; set a staleTime that matches how fast your data changes. Third, the query key model. Every query is named by an array, and that key is how the cache is found, shared, and invalidated. Fourth, the framework. The React hooks are the main way in, and they need React 18 or later. The core package works without React, but most examples and answers assume the hooks. Fifth, the alternatives. SWR is the closest rival and is smaller; a hand-rolled cache works for one screen and becomes a mess by the third.

The verdict: use TanStack Query when server data is shared across screens or needs to stay fresh. That flips if the app makes one fetch that never changes, or the team wants no new concepts this month: then the library is a dependency with no job to do.

A bookshop stock list, fetched and cached

The example is the shop from the opening: a small bookshop with three titles, and an API that lists them with their stock counts. The API is a tiny Node server on port 3456, with a counter that logs every request it receives. That counter is the point of the demo: it proves whether a fetch reached the server or came from the cache. Here is the server:

// server.js
const http = require('node:http');

const BOOKS = [
  { id: 'BK-201', title: 'Learning to Code, Slowly', author: 'Mara Iqbal', price: 24.99, inStock: 14 },
  { id: 'BK-202', title: 'The Quiet Debugger', author: 'Tomas Reyes', price: 31.50, inStock: 6 },
  { id: 'BK-203', title: 'Notes from a Night Shift', author: 'Hana Sato', price: 18.00, inStock: 0 },
];

let requestCount = 0;

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  requestCount += 1;
  console.log('API hit #' + requestCount + ': ' + req.method + ' ' + req.url);
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');

  if (req.url === '/books' && req.method === 'GET') {
    res.writeHead(200);
    res.end(JSON.stringify(BOOKS));
    return;
  }

  const match = req.url.match(/^\/books\/(BK-\d+)$/);
  if (match && req.method === 'GET') {
    const book = BOOKS.find((b) => b.id === match[1]);
    if (!book) {
      res.writeHead(404);
      res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: 'No book with id ' + match[1] }));
      return;
    }
    res.writeHead(200);
    res.end(JSON.stringify(book));
    return;
  }

  res.writeHead(404);
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: 'Not found' }));
});

server.listen(3456, () => {
  console.log('Bookshop API listening on http://localhost:3456');
});

The client code uses the framework-agnostic core package, @tanstack/query-core, so it runs in plain Node with no browser and no React. In a React app you would call the useQuery hook with the same key and fetch function; the hooks are a thin layer over this client, so what the core does here is what the hooks do there. The demo asks for the book list three times: once to fetch it, once to test the cache, and once after invalidating it. staleTime is set to 60,000 milliseconds, which tells the client the data can be trusted for a minute:

// demo.js
const { QueryClient } = require('@tanstack/query-core');

async function fetchBooks() {
  const res = await fetch('http://localhost:3456/books');
  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new Error('Request failed with status ' + res.status);
  }
  return res.json();
}

async function main() {
  const client = new QueryClient();

  console.log('--- First fetch ---');
  const first = await client.fetchQuery({
    queryKey: ['books'],
    queryFn: fetchBooks,
    staleTime: 60_000,
  });
  console.log('Books: ' + first.map((b) => b.id + ' (' + b.inStock + ' in stock)').join(', '));

  console.log('--- Second fetch, same key ---');
  const second = await client.fetchQuery({
    queryKey: ['books'],
    queryFn: fetchBooks,
    staleTime: 60_000,
  });
  console.log('Books: ' + second.length + ' books, served from cache');

  console.log('--- Invalidate, then fetch again ---');
  await client.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['books'] });
  const third = await client.fetchQuery({
    queryKey: ['books'],
    queryFn: fetchBooks,
    staleTime: 60_000,
  });
  console.log('Books: ' + third.length + ' books after invalidation');

  console.log('--- Cached state ---');
  const state = client.getQueryState(['books']);
  console.log('Status: ' + state.status + ', data updated at: ' + new Date(state.dataUpdatedAt).toISOString());
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error('Demo failed:', err.message);
  process.exit(1);
});

Running the server and the demo gave this real output:

--- First fetch ---
Books: BK-201 (14 in stock), BK-202 (6 in stock), BK-203 (0 in stock)
--- Second fetch, same key ---
Books: 3 books, served from cache
--- Invalidate, then fetch again ---
Books: 3 books after invalidation
--- Cached state ---
Status: success, data updated at: 2026-11-09T04:05:26.504Z

The server log is the proof. It shows only two hits for the whole demo:

Bookshop API listening on http://localhost:3456
API hit #1: GET /books
API hit #2: GET /books

Read the two together. The first fetch hit the server once. The second fetch printed the same three books, but the server log shows no second hit: the data came from the cache, because it was still inside its 60 second fresh window. Then invalidateQueries marked the cached list as stale, and the third fetch hit the server again, which is hit number two. That is the whole model in one run: fetch once, reuse while fresh, refetch when told the data may have changed. In a real app the invalidation would happen after an order is placed, so the stock list updates without a page reload.

Now the part the tidy tutorials skip: something goes wrong. A page asks for one book by id, and the id is wrong. The API answers 404, the fetch function throws, and TanStack Query retries before it gives up. The demo asks for BK-999, a book that does not exist, with two retries allowed:

// fail.js
const { QueryClient } = require('@tanstack/query-core');

async function fetchBook(id) {
  const res = await fetch('http://localhost:3456/books/' + id);
  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new Error('Request failed with status ' + res.status);
  }
  return res.json();
}

async function main() {
  const client = new QueryClient();

  console.log('--- Fetching a book that does not exist ---');
  try {
    await client.fetchQuery({
      queryKey: ['book', 'BK-999'],
      queryFn: () => fetchBook('BK-999'),
      retry: 2,
    });
  } catch (err) {
    console.log('Query failed: ' + err.message);
    const state = client.getQueryState(['book', 'BK-999']);
    console.log('Status: ' + state.status + ', failure count: ' + state.fetchFailureCount);
  }

  console.log('--- Fixed: fetching a book that exists ---');
  const book = await client.fetchQuery({
    queryKey: ['book', 'BK-202'],
    queryFn: () => fetchBook('BK-202'),
    retry: 2,
  });
  console.log('Book: ' + book.title + ' by ' + book.author + ', $' + book.price + ', ' + book.inStock + ' in stock');
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error('Demo failed:', err.message);
  process.exit(1);
});

The real output:

--- Fetching a book that does not exist ---
Query failed: Request failed with status 404
Status: error, failure count: 3
--- Fixed: fetching a book that exists ---
Book: The Quiet Debugger by Tomas Reyes, $31.5, 6 in stock

The server log shows three hits for BK-999, one for the first try and one for each retry, then a single hit for BK-202. The fix was not in the library. The query was asking for a book that does not exist, so the right fix was to ask for one that does: BK-202, The Quiet Debugger, six in stock. The lesson is that a failed query is usually a wrong question, not a broken cache. Check the id and the URL before you blame the fetching layer, and check the failure count before you assume a request ran once.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

1. Passing a string as the query key. The key must be an array; a string only gets this console warning: As of v4, queryKey needs to be an Array. If you are using a string like 'repoData', please change it to an Array, e.g. ['repoData']. The fetch still runs, so the bug hides until an invalidation misses. The fix is an array: ['books'], with the varying parts in it.

2. Leaving staleTime at zero. With the default of 0, two fetchQuery calls with the same key made two API hits. The fix is a staleTime that matches the data: 60,000 milliseconds for a slow-changing stock list.

3. Forgetting to parse the response. A queryFn that returns fetch(url) without .json() stores the Response object as the data: the demo showed its type as [object Response] and its length as undefined. The fix: parse inside the queryFn and return the parsed JSON.

4. Letting a 404 retry. A query that throws on a missing book is retried by default, so one wrong id cost three API hits. The fix: retry: false for lookups where 404 means "not found".

Where this leaves you

TanStack Query does one job well: it treats server data as something that goes stale, fails, and needs refetching, and it handles all three without a pile of loading flags. It is worth the learning curve when more than one screen shares the same data, or when the data must stay fresh after users act on it. Skip it for a single fetch that never changes. The next step: take one list from your own app, the one fetched in two places today, move it into a query with a key, and watch the second fetch come from the cache. If that feels like less code instead of more, keep going.

Further reading

  • TanStack Query, Overview
  • TanStack Query, Queries
  • TanStack Query, Caching

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/tanstack-query-server-state-that-stays.html

title: MotionCore: A Latent Neural Simulator for Video Generation with Rigid-Body Dynamics
description:
arXiv:2611.08904v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video generation models can produce highly realistic videos while generating physically inconsistent object motion. This limitation suggests that visual modeling alone may not provide a transferable representation of physical dynamics. We introduce MotionCore, a framework for learning physical dynamics via a learnable partial differential equation solver and focuses on rigid-body motion. We introduce a latent neural simulator learning to predict the evolution of object-level physical states from observed motion. Its predictions are then converted into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model. The generator serves as a visual interface: it provides appearance and scene detail, while the learned dynamics model specifies the physical trajectory. To preserve this trajectory through the interface, MotionCore combines a diffusion-matching objective with a low-capacity decodability constraint on object identity and position. We evaluate MotionCore on public physical-consistency benchmarks and on paired data with known trajectories. Results indicate that MotionCore improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience in the evaluated rigid-body settings, while maintaining comparable visual quality. A controlled ablation protocol compares learned dynamics with an analytic prior and studies the choice of latent evolution processor.

title: How to Monitor SQL Server Agent Job Failures (Alerts, Queries and Best Practices)
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

SQL Server Agent runs the jobs that keep a database healthy: backups, index and statistics maintenance, ETL loads and cleanup. When a job fails silently, nobody notices until something breaks, often a restore that turns out to have no recent backup. This guide shows how to get notified about SQL Server Agent job failures, how to query job history, and how to catch jobs that hang instead of failing.

Step 1: set up Database Mail

Agent notifications need Database Mail. Configure a profile in SSMS (Management, Database Mail) or with T-SQL, then send a test email:

EXEC msdb.dbo.sp_send_dbmail
     @profile_name = 'DBA Alerts',
     @recipients   = 'dba-team@example.com',
     @subject      = 'Database Mail test',
     @body         = 'If you can read this, Database Mail works.';

Then, in SQL Server Agent properties, open Alert System, tick Enable mail profile, choose the profile and restart the Agent service. Forgetting the restart is the most common reason notifications never arrive.

Step 2: create an operator 

EXEC msdb.dbo.sp_add_operator
     @name = N'DBA Team',
     @email_address = N'dba-team@example.com';

Use a shared team mailbox or distribution list, not one person's address, so alerts are not lost when someone is on leave.

Step 3: notify on failure for every job 

-- Find jobs with no failure notification
SELECT j.name
FROM msdb.dbo.sysjobs AS j
WHERE j.enabled = 1 AND j.notify_level_email = 0;

-- Add notification to a job (2 = on failure)
EXEC msdb.dbo.sp_update_job
     @job_name = N'Nightly Full Backup',
     @notify_level_email = 2,
     @notify_email_operator_name = N'DBA Team';

Make this part of your job deployment standard, so new jobs never go live without it.

Step 4: review failures with a query 

SELECT j.name                                   AS job_name,
       h.step_id,
       h.step_name,
       msdb.dbo.agent_datetime(h.run_date, h.run_time) AS run_at,
       h.run_duration,
       h.message
FROM msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory AS h
JOIN msdb.dbo.sysjobs       AS j ON j.job_id = h.job_id
WHERE h.run_status = 0          -- 0 = failed
  AND msdb.dbo.agent_datetime(h.run_date, h.run_time) >= DATEADD(day, -1, GETDATE())
ORDER BY run_at DESC;

Job history is trimmed by default (1,000 rows in total, 100 per job), so busy servers may lose history quickly. Increase the limits in Agent properties, under History, or keep your own copy in a DBA database.

Step 5: catch long-running and stuck jobs

A job that hangs never fails, so it never sends a failure email. Check for jobs still running past a threshold:

SELECT j.name,
       ja.start_execution_date,
       DATEDIFF(minute, ja.start_execution_date, GETDATE()) AS minutes_running
FROM msdb.dbo.sysjobactivity AS ja
JOIN msdb.dbo.sysjobs        AS j ON j.job_id = ja.job_id
WHERE ja.session_id = (SELECT MAX(session_id) FROM msdb.dbo.syssessions)
  AND ja.start_execution_date IS NOT NULL
  AND ja.stop_execution_date IS NULL
  AND DATEDIFF(minute, ja.start_execution_date, GETDATE()) > 120;

Wrap this in a small Agent job of its own that emails the team when rows are returned.

Step 6: better error details

  • Step output: in each job step's Advanced page, log output to a table or a file. The history message is truncated, but the full output often explains the failure.
  • Error alerts: create Agent alerts for severities 17 to 25 and for errors 823, 824 and 825 (I/O and corruption warnings), all sent to the same operator.
  • Retry attempts: for steps that hit transient issues, such as a network share being briefly unavailable, set a retry count and interval on the step.

Don't forget the Agent itself

If the SQL Server Agent service is stopped, no jobs run and no failure emails are sent. Set the service to start automatically, and monitor it from outside SQL Server, for example with your server monitoring tool or Windows service alerts.

Azure notes

Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL Server on Azure VMs include SQL Server Agent. Azure SQL Database does not; use Elastic Jobs, Azure Automation or Azure Data Factory for scheduling there, and Azure Monitor alerts for failure notifications.

Final thoughts

Reliable job monitoring takes an hour to set up: Database Mail, one team operator, failure notifications on every job, a daily failure query, a check for long-running jobs and severity alerts. That hour can save you from discovering a week of failed backups at the worst possible moment.

Related reading:

  • DBCC CHECKDB: Detect and Handle Database Corruption
  • How to Fix SQL Server Deadlocks
  • How to Find Slow Queries in SQL Server

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: 🚀 How I Designed a Scalable Invoice System in Laravel
description:
An invoice generator needs a precise answer to a small question: which transactions belong to this invoice? In Nucleus, the answer is a calendar month of ledger entries, linked to an invoice through a pivot table. That relationship lets the application explain a total instead of storing a number with no connection to its source records.

This walkthrough describes the Laravel implementation in the Nucleus codebase: its data model, monthly Artisan command, scheduler and PDF export. It also separates the current behavior from improvements needed for larger workloads. The implementation has not been presented here as a measured throughput benchmark or a complete accounting system.

Define the accounting scope first

Nucleus uses a single-entry income and expense ledger. A monthly invoice summarizes its attached transactions: total income, total expense and their difference. It is not a double-entry accounting ledger, a tax engine or an accounts-receivable reconciliation service.

The invoice model also recognizes trader-wise and category-wise types, but the automatic command currently generates month-wise invoices. Recognizing a type in an enum does not mean every type has an implemented generation workflow. Keeping that distinction visible prevents the UI and documentation from promising behavior the command does not supply.

Keep source transactions attached to the invoice

The invoices table holds the invoice number, type, status, period dates and monetary totals. The invoice_transaction table links those invoices to existing ledger entries. The model exposes that relationship as follows:

public function transactions(): BelongsToMany
{
    return $this->belongsToMany(Transaction::class, 'invoice_transaction');
}

A transaction has the corresponding invoices() relationship. The command selects entries that are not already attached to an invoice through this scope:

public function scopeUnInvoiced(Builder $query): Builder
{
    return $query->whereDoesntHave('invoices');
}

This makes the selection rule explicit. It also raises a product decision: attaching an entry to any invoice removes it from this particular un-invoiced selection. If the application later needs the same entry in several independent reporting documents, that rule must be revisited rather than assuming the current scope covers every invoice type.

Understand the monthly command's three modes

GenerateMonthlyInvoices registers invoice:generate with optional --month and --current flags. Without either flag, it loads un-invoiced transactions and groups them by their transaction date's Y-m value. It can therefore process outstanding entries from more than one month.

With --month, it selects that calendar month's un-invoiced entries. With --current, it selects the current calendar month. These are write commands. The examples below should be run against a development database with deliberate fixtures, not against a production ledger merely to explore the interface.

php artisan invoice:generate --month=2026-09
php artisan invoice:generate --current
php artisan invoice:generate

The command calculates the beginning and end of the target month with Carbon. Timezone and date-storage conventions still matter: a boundary test should include an entry on the month's last day, particularly when the database column stores a timestamp. The exact treatment of that final day's time must be checked, rather than inferred from a human-readable date label.

Update an existing period instead of starting another invoice

For a selected month, the command first looks for a month-wise invoice with matching start and end dates. If it finds one, it attaches the new transaction IDs without detaching the existing IDs:

$existingInvoice->transactions()
    ->syncWithoutDetaching($transactions->pluck('id'));

$allTransactions = $existingInvoice->transactions()->get();

The totals are then recalculated from all attached transactions, including those already invoiced. If no invoice exists for the period, the command creates a generated invoice with a unique invoice number and attaches the selected IDs. A later run can add newly recorded entries to the same monthly document.

This is useful repeat-run behavior for a single execution path. It does not establish concurrency-safe exactly-once generation. The inspected migrations make the invoice number unique, but do not enforce a unique month-wise period or a unique invoice/transaction pair. Before allowing concurrent generators, use a database transaction, a deliberate period-identity constraint and an overlap strategy appropriate to the deployment.

Make monetary precision a documented decision

Invoice totals are stored as decimal columns and cast as decimal strings by Eloquent. The current command converts collection sums to floating-point values before subtracting expense from income. Persisting a decimal column does not remove rounding behavior introduced earlier in a floating-point calculation.

For accounting-grade requirements, define the currency, rounding rule and storage precision first, then use a decimal calculation strategy or integer minor units consistently. Nucleus currently has different decimal scales for transaction amounts and invoice totals. That is a reason to add focused reconciliation tests, not to claim every stored total is automatically correct.

Schedule generation and render PDFs as separate operations

The application registers monthly generation in routes/console.php:

Schedule::command('invoice:generate')->daily();

This command runs directly through Laravel's scheduler. It does not require a queue worker for its present implementation. The hosting scheduler still needs to invoke Laravel's scheduler, and its output must be observable. php artisan schedule:list shows the registered definition; it does not prove the hosting cron ran successfully.

PDF export is a separate repository operation. InvoiceRepository::exportPdf() loads the invoice, renders the Finance/Invoice::pdf Blade view through DomPDF, writes the document through Laravel Storage and records an invoice attachment. Separating export from transaction selection makes it clearer which step failed: missing invoice data, template rendering or storage delivery.

Know where the current design needs to grow

The default generation path currently calls get() before grouping all outstanding transactions. It is straightforward for a small ledger, but it is not bounded-memory batch processing. Larger datasets need measured query behavior and a strategy that preserves monthly grouping while limiting memory, such as selecting distinct outstanding periods and processing each period in a controlled batch.

Other decisions require product rules as well as code. Define what happens to a paid invoice when a late transaction arrives, whether corrected transactions should alter a historical invoice, and how soft-deleted invoices affect re-generation. A polished PDF cannot answer those lifecycle questions on its own.

Verify behavior with a small development ledger

Start with an empty isolated database and a few income and expense entries across two months. Generate one month and compare the pivot IDs with the expected entries. Run the same command again without changing the ledger and check that totals and membership are unchanged. Add one late entry, rerun, and verify that the existing period is updated.

Add explicit cases for the last day of a month, a zero net total, rounding boundaries, deletion behavior and two competing runs. Export the PDF only after verifying the stored invoice, then inspect its period and totals. These are recommended checks for the reader; this article does not claim a load test or an accounting certification.

The useful part of this design is traceability: period selection, source entries, aggregation, scheduling and presentation have identifiable responsibilities. Scalability work should strengthen those contracts with evidence, rather than replace them with an unsupported performance claim.

Implementation references

The source files for this walkthrough are GenerateMonthlyInvoices.php, Invoice.php, Transaction.php, InvoiceRepository.php, the invoice migrations and routes/console.php in Nucleus. For framework behavior, see Laravel relationships, task scheduling and file storage.

Earlier implementation screenshots

The original visual notes are retained below. They show earlier implementation examples; the explanation and copyable snippets above describe the inspected source and its current limitations.

title: A Spiking Neural Model of the Mental Lexicon: Representations, Similarity Structure, and Associative Retrieval in Perception and Production
description:
arXiv:2611.09402v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A neural account of lexical access requires an explicit distinction between the structure of lexical representations, the associations linking representational levels, and the activity generated during retrieval. This paper specifies a spiking neural implementation of the mental lexicon within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Conceptual and phonological form representations are constructed recursively from relational graphs, whereas lemma representations provide independent lexical identities. The implementation contains 613 lexical entries and supports two directed processing pathways: perception maps a phonological form to its associated concept via a lemma, whereas production maps a concept to its associated phonological form via a lemma. Each pathway combines two associative-memory variants, winner-take-all (WTA) selection (competition) and thresholded transfer, and uses 199,400 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. We formalize within-level similarity, cross-level associative retrieval, and the interpretation of decoded activity. Simulations show successful retrieval of eight selected words from the lexicon in both processing directions, with retrieval evaluated against all 613 lexical entries. These simulations use complete phonological forms as input for perception and complete concepts as input for production, illustrating lexical retrieval through the corresponding processing pathways. This paper provides a transparent description of lexical representations and neural retrieval mechanisms, supported by accessible code, lexical data, and online simulation documentation.

title: Scoring, Not Learning: Decomposing Catalog-Consolidation Gains in Web-Scraped Retail Product Recognition
description:
arXiv:2611.08655v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retail product catalogs assembled from web image search are cheap to build and pervasively noisy: queries return packaging shots instead of products, and entries proliferate under names that cannot be distinguished visually. Consolidating such a catalog can look like an alternative to scaling the model. We show this is not a comparison between two ways of improving a recognizer, but between improving a recognizer and changing what counts as correct. We study a public archive of 165,769 cheese images across 1,824 query-named entries. A packaging filter and near-duplicate removal reduce it to a 998-class recognition set on one fixed, group-aware split. Canonicalizing entries to their base type (844 classes) raises top-1 accuracy by 4.0 points. Scoring the unchanged model against the merged label space, by summing its predicted probability within each canonical group, recovers +4.27 points with no retraining (+4.25 over six seeds). Retraining on the consolidated catalog then adds -0.10$\pm$0.53, +0.08$\pm$0.65 and -0.10$\pm$0.65 points at 28, 50 and 88 M parameters, indistinguishable from zero at every capacity ($\pm$ is the across-seed standard deviation). That component is specific, not mechanical: random merges with the identical size profile yield only +0.68 points, and the three backbones agree to within 0.1 points. But it is overwhelmingly category coarsening, not alias correction: across the 37 merged groups, type coarsenings supply 94% of the gain and alias collapses only 7%. We also detect no interaction between consolidation and backbone size: tripling backbone parameters is worth +1.50$\pm$0.57 points on the raw catalog and +1.42$\pm$00.44 on the canonical one, a within-seed interaction of -0.08 [-0.79,+0.63]. On this archive, the reported consolidation gain primarily reflects the evaluation label space, and separating that out costs one evaluation

title: Your confidence score is a label, not a probability: auditing 45,722 settled predictions
description:
Most prediction systems ship two numbers: a call, and a confidence. The confidence is usually an integer — 1 to 10, 60 to 95, whatever reads well in a UI. Everyone downstream then treats it as a probability, because it is a number between 0 and 100 and probabilities are numbers between 0 and 100.

That inference is where audits die. In our production table, confidence is an integer from 1 to 10 assigned at call time. It is not a probability, it never was, and the table below is the proof.

The dataset

The numbers come from one PostgreSQL table, ai_predictions, joined to matches for settlement fields. Nothing is simulated; every figure is recomputable below.

  • 46,196 prediction rows across 16,732 distinct matches, created 2026-06-21 → 2026-11-09
  • 45,722 rows are settled and carry a binary outcome (hit_1x2) plus a confidence
  • 3,715 distinct model_id values produced them
  • Predictions per match: mean 2.77, median 1, p90 7, max 358

That last line matters. The unit of analysis is the call, not the row, and one match with 358 rows will silently dominate any bucket it lands in.

What the score actually predicts

Here is the honest bucket table. n is row count, hit% is empirical accuracy on the binary outcome, and the interval is a 95% Wilson score interval — not a normal approximation, because at 57 rows the normal approximation is a work of fiction.

SELECT confidence,
       count(*)                                        AS n,
       sum(CASE WHEN hit_1x2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)        AS hits,
       round(100.0 * avg(CASE WHEN hit_1x2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)::numeric, 2) AS hit_pct
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE settled = true
  AND hit_1x2 IS NOT NULL
  AND confidence IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY confidence
ORDER BY confidence;

conf    n      hits   hit%    95% Wilson CI
 1     251     118    47.01    40.93 – 53.19
 2    1108     604    54.51    51.57 – 57.42
 3    8043    4327    53.80    52.71 – 54.89
 4    8750    5255    60.06    59.03 – 61.08
 5   11375    6305    55.43    54.51 – 56.34
 6    9260    5063    54.68    53.66 – 55.69
 7    4292    2575    60.00    58.52 – 61.45
 8    2037    1335    65.54    63.45 – 67.57
 9     548     404    73.72    69.88 – 77.23
10      57      33    57.89    44.98 – 69.81

There are three separate failures in it.

One: the middle of the scale is not monotonic. A call labelled 5 hits 55.43%; a call labelled 4 hits 60.06%, and the intervals do not overlap (59.03–61.08 vs 54.51–56.34). Claiming more confidence produced a worse result by 4.6 points across 20,125 rows, and the inversion recurs at 6 vs 5 (54.68% vs 55.43%). Whatever the model emits when it says "5", it is not a probability — it is a label that merely looks ordinal.

Two: the top of the scale collapses. Confidence 9 gives 73.72% on 548 rows; confidence 10 gives 57.89% on 57 rows. The loudest tier is both the worst and the thinnest — 0.12% of the data, with an interval of 44.98–69.81. The claim you can least verify is the claim published loudest.

Three: the aggregate hides all of it. Mean confidence is 4.94 (49.4%), overall accuracy 56.91%. So the system is under-confident by 7.5 points at the mean while its top tier is over-confident by 42. A single averaged "calibration" number reports a timid herd and hides a reckless tail.

Expected Calibration Error, and why it is not enough

The standard summary is ECE: bucket the predictions by stated probability, average the absolute gap between stated and observed, weight by bucket size.

WITH s AS (
  SELECT confidence::numeric / 10 AS p,
         CASE WHEN hit_1x2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END::numeric AS y
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE settled = true AND hit_1x2 IS NOT NULL AND confidence IS NOT NULL
), b AS (
  SELECT width_bucket(p, 0, 1.0001, 10) AS k,
         count(*) AS n, avg(p) AS mp, avg(y) AS my
  FROM s GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT round(sum(n * abs(mp - my)) / sum(n), 4) AS ece,
       round(sum(n * my) / sum(n), 4)           AS overall_hit,
       sum(n)                                   AS n
FROM b;

Result: ece = 0.1333, overall_hit = 0.5691, n = 45722.

13.3 points of average miscalibration, a Brier score of 0.2689, and a mean signed bias of −0.0751. Now the baseline nobody computes: a constant forecast at the base rate, 0.5691, scores 0.5691 × 0.4309 = 0.2453. The raw score's 0.2689 is worse than predicting the same number every time. That is the whole argument in one line — a column that cannot beat a constant is not carrying probability information, it is carrying formatting.

Note also that ECE is weighted by bucket size, so 45% of it comes from confidence 5 and 6. The two tiers anyone would actually audit — 9 and 10 — contribute 1.3% of the weight. A metric weighted by frequency will always under-report the failures that matter most.

The fix we shipped, and the trap inside it

We added a fitted calibration layer. Each settled row now carries confidence_calibrated, a continuous probability. Re-running the same two queries against it:

  • ECE: 0.0017 (down from 0.1333)
  • Brier: 0.2439 (down from 0.2689)
  • Mean bias: +0.0011 (down from −0.0751)
  • Range across all 45,722 settled rows: 0.4741 to 0.7286, mean 0.5701

That last bullet is the one to stare at. A near-zero ECE looks like a triumph. What it actually means is that the calibrated map refuses to output anything outside a 25-point band, and then the data obliges — because the map was fitted on the data it is being scored on. An ECE of 0.0017 in-sample is a statement about the fit, not the skill. The honest reading is the range: this system's real probability band is 47% to 73%, and nothing it says should be read as an 85% claim. Even the improved Brier, 0.2439, is only 0.6% better than the constant-forecast baseline of 0.2453 — all the gain is in the level, none of it in the ordering.

If you take one engineering lesson from this post: fitting a calibration layer always makes your calibration metric look good. What survives is the width of the output band plus an out-of-sample check. We report the band, not the ECE.

Two contamination sources that quietly inflate everything

Two-way calls. 32,147 settled rows are single-direction calls and hit 58.35%; 13,546 are "either of two outcomes" calls and hit 53.50%. Counter-intuitively the easier category scores worse — conditioning on two of three outcomes still loses ground. Any hit-rate table mixing the two arities measures the mix, not the skill.

Per-match multiplicity. With a mean of 2.77 predictions per match and a maximum of 358, one fixture can contribute dozens of correlated rows. A confidence-9 bucket can read "548 rows" while holding far fewer independent calls. Deduplicate to one row per match before computing any interval, or your Wilson bounds are narrower than reality — the one direction of error an audit must never make.

Per-model, the audit is brutal: of 3,715 model ids, only 7 have 200+ settled rows, and the worst of those claims 63.6% average confidence over 306 rows while delivering 55.23% — an 8.4-point overstatement no leaderboard sorted by raw hit rate would surface.

What an automated audit actually looks like

Calibration decays quietly. A single check is worthless; the useful artifact is a function that runs daily and fails loudly on inversion. This is the shape we use — the interesting part is not the ECE calculation, it is the INVERSION flag and the minimum-sample guard:

import math
from collections import defaultdict

MIN_N, INVERSION_GAP = 30, 0.04   # no claim below 30 rows; 4 pts back = failure

def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    if n == 0:
        return (0.0, 1.0)
    p, d = k / n, 1 + z * z / n
    c = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / d
    h = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / d
    return (c - h, c + h)

def audit(rows):
    """rows: (match_id, model_id, stated_p, outcome_0_1).
    Buckets hold [n, hits, sum_p] so ECE uses the real mean, not the midpoint --
    midpoints hide exactly the skew we are hunting."""
    seen, buckets = set(), defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0, 0.0])
    for mid, _model, p, y in rows:
        if mid in seen:               # one independent observation per match
            continue
        seen.add(mid)
        b = buckets[round(p * 10)]
        b[0] += 1
        b[1] += int(y)
        b[2] += p

    total = sum(b[0] for b in buckets.values())
    ece = sum(b[0] * abs(b[2] / b[0] - b[1] / b[0]) for b in buckets.values())
    report = {"n_independent": len(seen), "buckets": {}, "inversions": [],
              "ece": round(ece / total, 4) if total else None}

    prev = None
    for decile, (n, k, _sp) in sorted(buckets.items()):
        if n < MIN_N:
            report["buckets"][decile] = {"n": n, "skipped": "n < MIN_N"}
            continue                  # no claim, not a 50% guess
        hit = k / n
        lo, hi = wilson(k, n)
        report["buckets"][decile] = {"n": n, "hit": round(hit, 4),
                                     "ci95": [round(lo, 4), round(hi, 4)]}
        if prev and prev[1] - hit > INVERSION_GAP:
            report["inversions"].append((prev[0], decile))
        prev = (decile, hit)

    if report["inversions"]:
        report["status"] = "FAIL: non-monotonic confidence"
    return report

Two design choices there matter. MIN_N = 30 with an explicit skipped marker means a bucket that cannot support a claim is reported as having no claim, not as a 50% guess. And inversion detection is a hard failure, not a warning: monotonicity is the minimum contract between a model and everyone reading its output.

The checklist

  1. Never publish an integer confidence as a probability. Store it as a label; derive a probability in a separate, versioned column with a fit date in its name.
  2. Bucket-then-diff, never average-then-report. Under-confident at the mean and 42 points over-confident at the top is not "slightly miscalibrated".
  3. Weight the audit by cost, not frequency. ECE's weighting makes the tiers that matter invisible — report the tail separately, always.
  4. Deduplicate to one observation per match, and state the deduplication in the report.
  5. Guard thin buckets explicitly. 57 rows is not evidence; n=57 with a 45–70% interval is a press release, not a measurement.

None of this requires new modelling — just admitting that the number the model hands you is a label needing a schema around it, the same conclusion we reached about immutability and leaderboards, from a third direction. Every number that leaves a prediction system needs a contract, and confidence is the one everyone forgets.

The table above is reproducible from the queries in this post against the public dataset snapshot; where they disagree, the dataset is the authority.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+. 本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。

title: Does Reasoning Improve Psychological Depth in Large Language Models?
description:
arXiv:2611.09061v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmark gains from reasoning-enhanced large language models encourage the assumption that these models should broadly perform better on complex generative tasks, but this remains underexplored in open-ended, creative domains shaped by nuances of reader experience. We tested this assumption through the lens of psychological depth in short stories. We compared DeepSeek-R1 vs. DeepSeek-V3, our closest available contrast for reasoning-oriented post-training, and GPT-5 vs. GPT-4o, through 60 blinded pairwise evaluations in which seven human annotators and an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge rated prompt-matched story outputs. Human evaluations showed no universal reasoning advantage: GPT-5 was slightly preferred over GPT-4o (60.0-62.9% across two reasoning-effort settings), whereas DeepSeek-R1 fell behind DeepSeek-V3 (42.9%). Although this pattern was marked by low inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's $\alpha = 0.070$), our annotation-quality checks suggested genuine evaluative subjectivity, plausibly reflecting distinct annotator decision schemes rather than annotation failure. In contrast, the LLM-as-a-Judge showed a strong pro-reasoning bias (98.3% of pairs vs. 55.2% of human votes), consistent across its five configurations and partly tracking sentence length. These findings suggest that, at the frontier, reasoning-related quality differences are small enough to be dominated by reader subjectivity, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators can obscure this subjectivity in nuanced creative-generation tasks.

title: Khmer PFGen-Bench: Building a Judge-Free Benchmark for Open-Ended Generation in a Low-Resource Language
description:
arXiv:2611.09222v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarks for open-ended generation often rely on large language model (LLM) judges, whose reliability in low-resource languages is uncertain. We introduce Khmer PFGen-Bench, to our knowledge the first judge-free benchmark for multi-sentence answers to questions composed directly in Khmer, a low-resource language. Khmer PFGen-Bench adapts the scorer of PFGen-Bench, a benchmark for Japanese that scores responses with keyword rules and n-gram statistics from LLM-generated references. This scoring requires references that are both valid and varied, which LLMs may not produce in Khmer, so we examine how to build such references. We find that post-trained models can give more valid but less varied references than their base variants, and that mixing model families increases variety for the same number of references. Using references from post-trained models in nine families, the benchmark yields model rankings that are stable across reference sets and consistent with a native speaker's ratings. These findings offer guidance for building judge-free benchmarks in other low-resource languages.

title: Is Lullwood Made by AI? What Jams, Steam and itch.io Ask You to Disclose
description:
Lullwood is a free browser horror game built by AI agents running on Claude, with one human founder, and we say so up front. When AI disclosure came up for game jams, we read the wording of three real sources instead of assuming. This is what each one asks, read on 2026-10-29.

The jam rule is one sentence

Spooky Jam 2026 on itch.io (November 6 to 8, 2026) has this on its jam page:

You must disclose the use of AI in your game projects. If you fail to do so, you may be disqualified from the awards.

Three things in that text:

  • The penalty is disqualification from the awards, and it says "may", so the judges keep discretion.
  • "The use of AI" is not defined. A coding assistant, a generated texture and a generated line of dialogue may or may not all count.
  • The page does not say where the disclosure goes. No form, no tag, no field.

Steam asks about what ships

Steam's Content Survey has a generative AI section with two kinds. Pre-Generated content ships with the game and was made with AI tools during development. Live-Generated content is made by AI tools while the game runs, and it adds a requirement to describe your guardrails.

Valve says what the section is not for: "Efficiency gains through the use of these tools is not the focus of this section. Instead, it is concerned with the use of AI in creating content that ships with your game, and is consumed by players." Its examples are artwork, sound, narrative and localization.

itch.io asks you to tag it

The itch.io quality guidelines ask you to "accurately tag your project if it contains materials produced by generative AI" in the AI Disclosure section of the project's edit page. They say "traditional game AI like NPC pathfinding, enemy behavior patterns, procedural level generation" needs no tag. Enforcement is described for game asset pages, with delisting as the stated consequence.

Neither the Steam text nor the itch.io text says outright whether code written by an AI agent counts. Lullwood has no Steam or itch.io page as of 2026-10-29, so we have filled in neither form.

What our own page says

With no store page, the place a player or a search engine can read our answer is our own site. The who makes Lullwood page says the studio is one human founder and AI agents on Claude, that agents write the gameplay and site code, and that the founder sets direction and approves what ships. The source is public on GitHub.

It also says what the git log cannot show: who or what wrote a given change. So it publishes no human-versus-agent percentage. We would rather leave that number out than invent one.

What we would do

This part is opinion, built from the three sources.

  • Quote the exact sentence you are bound by, and write down how you settled what counts and where to say it.
  • Say how it was built and what ships. Steam cares about the second, a jam may care about the first.
  • Put the answer on a page anyone can read. A tag helps a store. A public page helps a player, a judge and a search engine, and it outlives the jam.
  • Skip any figure you cannot measure.

The full version, with the FAQ, is the Lullwood devlog post this one is cross-posted from. You can play Lullwood free in your browser.

Disclosure: we are the studio behind Lullwood. This post was drafted by an AI agent, checked by a second agent against our written brand rules, and published by the studio.

title: Scale as a Modality: Multi-Scale Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.08802v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on pretrained autoencoders that introduce lossy compression and constrain spatial granularity. Pixel-space diffusion avoids this bottleneck and enables flexible tokenization at multiple spatial scales, yet existing approaches largely adopt two-level coarse-to-fine architectures with limited cross-scale interaction. We introduce MS-pDiT, a multi-scale pixel-space diffusion transformer that treats spatial scale as a modality. MS-pDiT tokenizes the same noisy image at multiple patch sizes, processes each scale in a dedicated transformer stream, and enables bidirectional information exchange through compacted MM-DiT-style joint attention, with attention cost independent of the finest patch size. This design establishes the number of scales as a new architectural scaling dimension. On ImageNet $256\times256$, increasing the number of scales from two to five consistently improves FID from 4.39 to 2.31, 2.26, and 2.19, while adding an intermediate scale substantially outperforms increasing depth under comparable parameter budgets. Further analysis highlights the importance of bidirectional cross-scale interaction and late introduction of fine-grained streams. MS-pDiT achieves FID scores of 1.43 and 1.44 on ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, respectively, and naturally extends to text-to-image generation, achieving 0.86 on GenEval and 83.9 on DPG-Bench.

title: FishSense Lite: A Camera-Based, Single Laser Hardware Framework with Software System for In Situ Fish Length Measurement
description:
arXiv:2611.08732v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fish stock assessments need fish lengths paired with species from far more places than trained surveyors can reach. Recreational divers already visit many of those places, but measuring a fish underwater has required trained observers or specialist equipment. We present FishSense Lite, which recovers fish length from a single photograph taken with a recreational dive camera, a dive laser pointer, and a 3D-printed mount. The diver aims the laser at a fish and takes a picture; afterward, the dot's position in the image gives the range to the fish, and the range turns the fish's size in the image into a length. A citizen-science program, trained by the system's builders, taught its own divers and collected lengths paired with species for 73 wild fish across seven open-water dives. On seven wild fish also measured by an underwater stereo-imaging system, the two instruments agreed without detectable bias (mean difference +0.8%). On rigid targets of known length, FishSense Lite recovered every target to within 1.3%, and 99% of 1,055 frames fell within a 15% error budget. From the error sources we measure, we derive a field protocol: calibrate against a dive slate on every dive, photograph fish within 15 degrees of perpendicular and beyond 1 m, and take at least ten frames of each.

title: Run It Twenty Times Before You Pin It: Characterization Tests for Messy Repos
description:
A characterization test is only worth writing on output you can reproduce. Sample twenty runs before you pin one line.

Most "refactor safely" advice starts with "write a characterization test." That advice hides an assumption. It assumes the function returns the same value twice. Messy repos break that assumption daily.

Clocks, UUIDs, dict iteration, locale formatting, retry jitter, and float printing all leak into output. Pin that noise and your test goes red for reasons unrelated to your change. A red test you do not trust is worse than no test at all.

Below is the loop I run: sample, classify, freeze, then change one thing. The gate is a rule I call 20/3/2. Twenty runs, three hash seeds, two timezones.

Step 1 — Sample the entry point before touching the code

Do not import the module under test into your own process. Set PYTHONHASHSEED in a child process instead. It only takes effect at interpreter start.

# sample.py — run the entry point N times, count distinct outputs
import collections, os, subprocess, sys

CMD = [sys.executable, "entry.py"]  # entry.py prints exactly one JSON line

def sample(n: int = 20):
    seen = collections.Counter()
    for seed in range(n):
        env = dict(os.environ)
        env["PYTHONHASHSEED"] = str(seed)
        env["TZ"] = "UTC" if seed % 2 == 0 else "Asia/Tokyo"
        out = subprocess.run(CMD, env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        seen[out.stdout.strip()] += 1
    return seen

if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 20
    seen = sample(n)
    print(f"distinct outputs: {len(seen)} across {sum(seen.values())} runs")
    for payload, count in seen.most_common(3):
        print(count, payload[:200])

Run it with one argument and read the first line only.

python sample.py 20

Three outcomes matter, and each one changes your plan.

  1. distinct outputs: 1 — the behavior is already pinned. Write the test now.
  2. distinct outputs: 2..5 — a few fields are volatile. Classify them in step 2.
  3. distinct outputs: 20 — nothing is pinned yet. Do not refactor this path today.

That third case is the useful one. It tells you the code has no observable contract. You are not refactoring here; you are designing.

Step 2 — Classify every unstable field

Diff the two most common payloads and list the fields that moved. Each field gets exactly one treatment.

Field kind Example Treatment Why
Seedable hash order, sampler seed Set env or seed in the fixture Same input, same output
Injected clock, UUID factory Pass a fake through a seam Deterministic and realistic
Formattable float precision, currency Round in the fixture builder Compare at contract precision
Quarantined upstream request_id, latency Regex-normalize, then assert the rule still matches Keeps the field visible
Dropped unbounded log lines Exclude and record why Nothing to assert

The quarantine row is the one people skip. A normalize rule that stops matching is a silent hole. You must test the rule itself, not just the payload.

Step 3 — Freeze only what survived

Write the normalizer as data, not as scattered inline edits. Three regexes beat thirty conditionals.

# normalize.py
import re

VOLATILE = {
    "request_id": re.compile(r'"request_id":\s*"[0-9a-f-]{36}"'),
    "created_at": re.compile(r'"created_at":\s*"[^"]+"'),
    "duration_ms": re.compile(r'"duration_ms":\s*[0-9.]+'),
}

def normalize(payload: str) -> str:
    for name, pattern in VOLATILE.items():
        payload = pattern.sub(f'"{name}": "<volatile>"', payload)
    return payload

Then the characterization test itself. It compares normalized output against a fixture committed in the same PR.

# test_invoice_characterization.py
import json
import pytest
from normalize import VOLATILE, normalize
from billing import build_invoice

CASES = json.load(open("fixtures/invoices.json"))

@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", CASES, ids=lambda c: c["name"])
def test_output_matches_characterization(case):
    raw = json.dumps(build_invoice(**case["input"]), sort_keys=True, default=str)
    assert normalize(raw) == case["expected_normalized"]

def test_no_quarantine_rule_is_stale():
    blob = "".join(
        json.dumps(build_invoice(**c["input"]), default=str) for c in CASES
    )
    unused = [n for n, p in VOLATILE.items() if not p.search(blob)]
    assert not unused, f"quarantine rules match nothing: {unused}"

That second test is the anti-rot check. When a dependency stops emitting duration_ms, it tells you. Otherwise your normalizer quietly hides a real change six weeks later.

Regenerate fixtures by hand, in a separate commit, with the reason in the message. Never wire --update into a normal test run.

Step 4 — Change the smallest thing the green test allows

The order is fixed. Tests first, then one edit, then the same tests.

  1. Confirm pytest -k characterization is green three times in a row.
  2. Re-run python sample.py 20. It must still report one output for the touched path.
  3. Make one change: a rename, an extracted function, or an early return.
  4. Keep the test file byte-identical in that commit. If the test had to change, you changed behavior. Split that into its own commit.
  5. Revert the commit locally and confirm the test still passes. A test that only passes forward is not characterization.

Step 5 catches a common mistake. People write tests that encode the new structure. Those tests fail on revert, so they prove nothing about the old behavior. Keep the assertion anchored to output, not to call shape.

Where a free model and a free server fit in this loop

The sampler decides what is trustworthy. A model cannot make that call for you, and it should not.

I use MonkeyCode's free model access for the boring first pass. It drafts characterization tests from the function body, plus a candidate volatile-field list. That draft is a starting point, not a verdict. The 20/3/2 run decides which drafted assertions survive.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The free server option helps with the sampler, not with the thinking. Twenty subprocess launches with different env vars want a clean box. Running them remotely keeps locale, timezone, and PYTHONHASHSEED controlled. It also stops the run from competing with your local test suite.

Do not paste secrets or private customer payloads into any hosted model or remote machine. Strip fixtures down to structure first. If you cannot strip them, keep the whole loop local and accept the slower run.

Limitations, stated plainly

  • Characterization tests pin current behavior, bugs included. They never tell you what is correct.
  • Quarantine rules hide regressions if the anti-rot test is skipped in CI.
  • Concurrency, streaming, and retry-heavy paths need property tests, not snapshots.
  • The sampler costs twenty process launches per path. Budget a minute, not a millisecond.
  • A model-drafted test can be confidently wrong. Treat every drafted assertion as unverified until the sampler agrees.

Who should skip this

Skip the loop if the entry point needs a live third-party service. Skip it if output is inherently time-shaped, like a scheduler tick log. Skip it if you cannot run one clean process in isolation. Isolate the seam first, then come back to this.

A 45-minute run sheet

  1. Minutes 0–10: pick one function with a JSON or string output. Write entry.py that prints it.
  2. Minutes 10–20: run sample.py 20. Record the distinct count in the PR description.
  3. Minutes 20–30: classify each moving field with the table above.
  4. Minutes 30–40: add normalize.py, one fixture, and the anti-rot test.
  5. Minutes 40–45: make one edit. Confirm green, revert, confirm green again.

Publish the distinct count before and after your refactor. One number beats a paragraph of reassurance, and reviewers can reproduce it in a minute. If the sampler finds something surprising in your repo, that finding is the interesting part — write it down before you fix it.

title: Vercel Connect adds Enterprise-Managed Authorization
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) in public beta. Your apps and agents can access supported services on behalf of signed-in users without separate consent prompts for each service.

Here's how access works:

  • Admin-managed access: Administrators can grant or revoke access to supported services through the identity provider.

  • Corporate sign-in: Users sign into your app with their corporate account through a compatible identity provider such as Okta.

  • Scoped tokens: Your app requests the scopes it needs, and Connect handles token exchange, caching, and renewal. Access is limited to approved scopes and the user’s existing service permissions.

If your app uses Vercel Passport, you can request a token for Slack’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with the signed-in user’s identity:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 1T9cFkjaRDDmRFQ5bWVmD6

Connect supports Cross-App Access (XAA), including its use for MCP authorization through EMA. Follow the Vercel Connect EMA setup guide to configure your identity provider and services and enable EMA on their Connect connectors.
