description:
This is a Spring Boot lesson from open source: a small bug, a small fix, and a mistake of my own that taught me something about Git.

The bug

Logbook has a Spring Boot starter that sets everything up automatically. One of the things it registered was a LogbookClientHttpRequestInterceptor bean, every time.

That interceptor depends on a class from spring-web. So if your app used logbook-spring-boot-starter with another HTTP client (OkHttp or Apache HttpClient, for example) and did not have spring-web on the classpath, the app crashed at startup:

title: YouTube's Quest Redesign Quietly Changes What a Headset Screen Is For — And Why My Amblyopia Finally Has a Training Partner
description:
YouTube's Quest Redesign Quietly Changes What a Headset Screen Is For — And Why My Amblyopia Finally Has a Training Partner

UploadVR's report that Google is rebuilding YouTube's immersive view on Quest — closer to Android XR and visionOS — sounds like a UI story. To me, it's something else entirely.

I'm a developer. I think in frames, pipelines, latency budgets. I've spent my career optimizing render loops I'd never personally feel — shaving milliseconds off compositors, arguing about reprojection, treating the display stack as an abstraction layer you tune and forget. Then I got diagnosed with amblyopia as an adult, and the abstraction became the whole point.

My left eye never learned to team up with my right. It was a lazy eye that nobody caught in time, which is the boring, common story. The standard toolkit is a graveyard of childhood compliance: adhesive patches that itch and peel, red-blue glasses that turn the world into a headache, atropine drops that blur everything into soup. All of it designed for a kid I stopped being decades ago. The honest truth clinicians tell you: adult neuroplasticity exists, but the compliance cliff is real. You quit because it's boring, not because it doesn't work.

So I did what any engineer does when the off-the-shelf tooling fails — I started reading papers. And what I found is that the treatment has always been a rendering problem. You want two eyes to fuse, you have to give them different images. The brain, faced with a mismatch, learns to reconcile. That's the entire mechanism behind dichoptic therapy. It's been known for years. The delivery vehicle was always the bottleneck.

Then the headset arrived.

Two Eyes, Two Feeds: The Technical Insight

The Quest's architecture has always had this hiding in plain sight: two independent eyepieces, two render targets, one compositor. Most apps just mirror the same frame. It's the path of least resistance, and it's fine — nobody notices the redundancy.

But if you don't mirror — if you send a slightly blurred frame to the dominant eye and a selectively sharpened frame to the lazy eye — you've built a dichoptic training system inside a consumer device. The binocular rivalry the hardware fights to eliminate becomes the therapeutic signal. No specialized hardware. Just software, and a render loop that treats the two eyes as two clients instead of one.

That's Amblyotube's entire premise. Seven Sports built it.

I want to be precise about what this is and isn't, because I'm a developer and I've been burned by magic. This is not a clinical trial in your living room. It's a tool that applies a well-understood optical principle using hardware you already own. The product page is explicit that it's a training aid, not a replacement for a clinician. I'll hold that line honestly.

The Pipeline, Step by Step

What sold me was the pipeline. It's clean, and it's tunable, and as an engineer that matters more than any marketing claim.

Setup (takes two minutes in-headset): You pick Left or Right lazy eye — critical, wrong choice trains the wrong eye. You choose a severity preset (Mild/Moderate/Severe) or run the integrated LogMAR check: Landolt C optotypes at virtual 3m, staircase algorithm, up to 30 trials per eye, outputs logMAR acuity and can auto-tune your profile. I ran it. It matched my last clinic visit within 0.1 logMAR. That number is the reason I kept going — it told me the virtual display was faithful enough to trust.

The render loop:

  • Dominant Eye Shader: adjustable blur, contrast, brightness, gamma, opacity. At 100% opacity it's digital patching. I run ~40% — enough to disadvantage the strong eye without killing immersion.
  • Lazy Eye Sharpener (MFBF mode): on-device AI detects human figures (faces/bodies) in the video stream and applies selective sharpening only to the lazy eye's view.
  • Visual Accents: fluorescent yellow-green highlight + red outline on detected humans. Pulse controls let you set Hz and depth — a breathing rhythm that keeps visual cortex engaged.
  • Controlled Flicker Stimulation: a subtle temporal modulation. This is the part I understand least from the outside and respect most from the inside — it's clearly the product of people who read the plasticity literature.

The sharpener is the clever bit. Instead of sharpening the whole frame — which just makes a sharper confusing image — it uses object detection to find the one thing your brain is already wired to look at: other humans. Attention is the gate for plasticity. So the app pays attention to what you pay attention to.

Why This Maps to the YouTube News

Here's where the UploadVR story snaps into focus. If YouTube's immersive view is being rebuilt on Quest closer to Android XR and visionOS, that's not just a player refresh. It's a statement that the headset's screen is becoming a general-purpose stereo surface — a place where two feeds can legitimately diverge. That's the platform-level precondition for what Amblyotube does.

For years, dichoptic tools lived on bespoke rigs or lab hardware. The thing that made them impractical was never the science — it was the delivery. A general stereo surface on the world's biggest video platform means the delivery layer is quietly becoming commodity infrastructure. The interesting work moves up the stack.

I've watched enough platform shifts to be wary of over-reading one announcement. But the direction is unmistakable: the eyes are becoming two addressable endpoints, and once that's true, a whole category of software that was previously gated behind hardware becomes just... an app.

What It's Actually Like

I won't pretend it's fun the way a game is fun. It's training. Some sessions my lazy eye aches in a way that's hard to describe — not pain, more like a muscle you forgot you had. Other sessions nothing happens and I close the headset convinced I've wasted twenty minutes.

But I log them. And the log has a slope.

Three months in, I can hold a page of text with both eyes without the letters swimming. That's not a miracle. That's just what happens when you remove the boring from a boring treatment. The headset doesn't care that I'm an adult. The compliance cliff was always about friction, not biology — and friction is a software problem.

A Builder's Note

If you're a developer reading this on HN, the takeaway isn't "buy this app." It's that the most interesting thing about the Quest platform was never the games. It's that you get two synchronized, independently-addressable render targets for the price of a console. Almost nobody is using them as two.

Amblyotube uses them as two. If you or someone you love has a lazy eye and you've already written off the patches and the drops, that's worth knowing.

Train gently. Log everything. The slope is the point.

Amblyotube

title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
description:
Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

Read more

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability was discovered in the SubWorkflow task in Application Integration versions prior to September 11, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-074 security bulletin.

Feature

Application Integration agent skills

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/DiscoveryClient
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Group
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ImportJob
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/PreferenceSet
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ReportConfig
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Settings
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Source

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (261001) is available. This image removes compromised CA certificates from the OS trust store. See the security bulletin for more details.

This image also adds support for running workload containers as a non-root user. Workload authors can require non-root execution with the tee.launch_policy.nonroot_container launch policy, and workload operators can enable it with the tee-nonroot-container metadata variable. For more information, see Non-root container execution.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Support for Brazil (br) region (GA with allowlist)

You can use the Gemini Enterprise app in the Brazil (br) in-country region with at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP) in region.

This location is available in GA with allowlist. To get access to this location for use with Gemini Enterprise, contact your Google account team.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Change

Use a single regional Agent Registry instance for Gemini Enterprise apps

For Gemini Enterprise apps, we recommend associating each Agent Gateway with a single regional Agent Registry instance in the same project and region as the gateway. Use the us-central1 registry for global and us apps, and the europe-west1 registry for eu apps.

This note updates the September 9, 2026 entry. For more information, see Register your agents and destination resources.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

title: Backends on Vercel: Python, containers, and Daemons
description:
Last year, we expanded zero-config support for Python and TypeScript backend frameworks. By this summer, developers could deploy their frontend and backend together with Vercel Services and coordinate background work with queues and durable workflows.

Today at Vercel Ship in San Francisco, we are expanding the backend workloads you can run on Vercel. Python on Vercel is now generally available, container support in Vercel Functions enables custom runtimes and system libraries, and we are introducing Vercel Daemons in Public Beta for background workers that pull work and stay running between jobs.

Python is now generally available

You can build your backend in Python with the Vercel infrastructure and development experience you know from your frontend, including local development, previews, and production deployments. Frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, and Django run on standard CPython with your PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling.

Already, 150,000 teams run Python backends on Vercel, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa.

SDKs for Python let you use Vercel products from your application, whether you’re storing files in Vercel Blob, sending background jobs to Vercel Queues, coordinating durable steps with Vercel Workflows, running untrusted code in Vercel Sandbox, or streaming model responses and handling tool calls with the AI SDK for Python.

Delphi, which builds AI digital minds from books and talks, moved its Python backend from AWS ECS to Vercel. With ten engineers and no dedicated infrastructure role, the team ships to production more than 100 times a day and uses Queues to handle background jobs.

Visit the Python knowledge base for framework details and examples.

Applications in any language with containers

The Vercel container runtime lets you deploy applications written in any language, packaged with the OS libraries and executables they need. Since container support entered Public Beta, 5,000 teams have shipped 150,000 container deployments on Vercel.

Containers deploy as Vercel Functions on Fluid compute, scaling with traffic and using Active CPU pricing, which doesn’t charge for idle time spent waiting for API responses, database queries, or LLM inferencing. Vercel Services lets you develop and deploy your backend alongside your frontend, while Vercel CDN serves traffic on your domains, Vercel WAF protects it, logs help you investigate issues, and rollbacks restore earlier deployments.

For example, take a video app that uses a container for background processing, preparing a playback copy and thumbnail for each uploaded clip. This Dockerfile packages the Python processor, its dependencies, and ffmpeg to run with Daemons:

When you deploy through Git or the Vercel CLI, Vercel builds the image and stores it in your Vercel Container Registry. Read our containerized Functions deployment guide to get started.

Background workers with Vercel Daemons

Vercel Daemons lets you deploy containers as continuously running background workers on Fluid compute. You choose the number of instances in each region, and Vercel maintains that capacity by restarting processes when they exit or crash.

Daemons launches with support for pull-based workloads, where your code requests work from another system and processes it as it becomes available. That could mean consuming queue messages or fetching pending jobs from a database.

In our example, Daemons runs the video processor continuously as it pulls jobs from Vercel Queues. In vercel.toml, define the Next.js frontend, route requests to it, and add the processor using Dockerfile:

Follow the Daemons deployment guide to add a background worker to your Vercel project.

Run your backends on Vercel

We’re continuing to invest in backend support so more of your existing application can run on Vercel, using the languages, dependencies, and execution patterns it needs.

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Cron Job Was Idempotent Until the Container Got Replaced
description:
I spent two days building a small daily reporting job, and the code was correct the whole time; the deployment was not. The job ran fine in my terminal, ran fine in a loop, and then ran twice in one day on a host I had rebuilt between runs. Why? Because I had put the thing that made it idempotent on the same disk as the thing that was disposable.

This is not a post about a platform deleting my data, and I want to be precise about that up front. I never verified any persistence guarantee for the free server option I was using, so I had no right to assume one. What I actually had was a mental model where "the file is still there" and "the process restarted" were independent facts, and in a throwaway host they are not.

What the job was supposed to do

The task itself is boring on purpose: once per UTC day, aggregate yesterday's rows, post one summary, write one receipt. The only interesting requirement is that a retry, a redeploy, or a double-scheduled tick must not produce a second summary. That requirement lives or dies on one question: where does the "I already did this" bit live?

My first answer was embarrassingly casual. I used a ./state/seen.json file next to the script, loaded it at start, appended the day key, and wrote it back. It passed every test I ran, because every test I ran happened to reuse the same working directory.

The assumption hiding in that file

Look at what that design quietly requires: the filesystem must outlive the process, the working directory must be the same on every start, and nothing else may write that path. In a long-lived VM all three are usually true, which is exactly why the bug never shows up in staging. In a host that gets replaced, the first one is false and the other two become irrelevant.

The reproduction: wipe the state, watch the duplicate

I replaced the JSON file with a SQLite store behind a tiny interface, so I could swap the "durable" location without touching job logic. SQLite is not magic either, but it gives me an atomic INSERT ... PRIMARY KEY claim, which is the primitive I actually wanted all along.

# job/store.py
from __future__ import annotations

import sqlite3
from contextlib import contextmanager
from pathlib import Path


class Store:
    """Dedupe store. The path must point somewhere the process does not own."""

    def __init__(self, path: str | Path) -> None:
        self.path = Path(path)
        self.path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with self._conn() as conn:
            conn.execute(
                "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS receipts ("
                " key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,"
                " claimed_at TEXT NOT NULL)"
            )

    @contextmanager
    def _conn(self):
        conn = sqlite3.connect(self.path, timeout=5, isolation_level=None)
        try:
            yield conn
        finally:
            conn.close()

    def claim(self, key: str, now: str) -> bool:
        """True exactly once per key, even across process restarts."""
        with self._conn() as conn:
            try:
                conn.execute(
                    "INSERT INTO receipts (key, claimed_at) VALUES (?, ?)",
                    (key, now),
                )
                return True
            except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
                return False

The runner stays deliberately small, and the clock is an argument rather than a global. That single choice turned a vague "sometimes it double-posts" complaint into a test I can rerun in two seconds.

# job/run_once.py
import argparse
import datetime as dt
import json
import os
import sys

from job.store import Store


def window_key(now: dt.datetime, window: str = "day") -> str:
    if now.tzinfo is None:
        raise SystemExit("refusing to schedule on a naive timestamp")
    if window != "day":
        raise SystemExit(f"unknown window: {window}")
    utc = now.astimezone(dt.timezone.utc)
    return "daily-report:" + utc.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--now", default=None, help="ISO-8601 with offset; tests inject this")
    p.add_argument("--store", default=os.environ.get("JOB_STORE", "./state/receipts.db"))
    args = p.parse_args(argv)

    now = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(args.now) if args.now else dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc)
    key = window_key(now)

    if not Store(args.store).claim(key, now.isoformat()):
        print(json.dumps({"event": "skipped", "key": key, "reason": "already claimed"}))
        return 0

    print(json.dumps({"event": "ran", "key": key}))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Now the tests. The third one is the important one, because it asserts the failure instead of the fix, and a test that documents the bug is worth more than a comment that apologizes for it.

# tests/test_idempotency.py
import shutil

import pytest

from job.run_once import main


def run(store, now):
    return main(["--store", str(store), "--now", now])


def test_second_tick_same_utc_day_is_a_no_op(tmp_path, capsys):
    store = tmp_path / "state" / "receipts.db"
    run(store, "2026-11-09T00:05:00+00:00")
    run(store, "2026-11-09T23:55:00+00:00")
    lines = capsys.readouterr().out.strip().splitlines()
    assert '"skipped"' in lines[1]


def test_tokyo_midnight_is_still_the_same_utc_day(tmp_path, capsys):
    store = tmp_path / "state" / "receipts.db"
    run(store, "2026-11-09T00:30:00+09:00")  # 2026-11-08T15:30Z
    run(store, "2026-11-09T10:00:00+00:00")
    lines = capsys.readouterr().out.strip().splitlines()
    assert '"ran"' in lines[1]


def test_replaced_host_replays_the_job(tmp_path, capsys):
    store = tmp_path / "state" / "receipts.db"
    run(store, "2026-11-09T00:05:00+00:00")
    shutil.rmtree(store.parent)  # simulate a fresh container with the same key
    run(store, "2026-11-09T00:05:00+00:00")
    lines = capsys.readouterr().out.strip().splitlines()
    assert '"ran"' in lines[1]  # the failure, made visible and repeatable


def test_naive_timestamp_is_rejected(tmp_path):
    with pytest.raises(SystemExit):
        run(tmp_path / "r.db", "2026-11-09T00:05:00")

python -m pytest -q tests/test_idempotency.py
JOB_STORE=/data/state/receipts.db python -m job.run_once --now "$(date -u +%FT%T+00:00)"

All three tests passed on the second run of the suite, which tells you nothing about the host and everything about the clock handling. That is the sobering part: my timezone bug and my durability bug looked identical from the outside, and only one of them was in the code.

Three rules I would keep from this exercise

  1. Put the dedupe key somewhere the process cannot delete. A local file is fine for a scratch script, but treat any host-local path as cache, never as memory. If you cannot name the volume's lifetime, you cannot name the job's.
  2. Inject the clock, and reject naive timestamps at the boundary. datetime.utcnow() in a scheduler is a bug with a delay fuse, and the fuse burns fastest for anyone running near midnight UTC.
  3. Log a receipt per run, not a log line per step. I print one JSON object per invocation, ran or skipped, with the key included, so a duplicate is a one-line grep instead of an archaeology project.

A decision table for the state file

State Keep on host disk? Where it belongs
Dedupe key / run receipt No Durable store you can name
Last-seen cursor No Durable store, written after the side effect
Parsed config Yes, rebuildable Baked in or fetched at start
Model response cache Yes, if loss is cheap Local disk with a TTL
Credentials Never Environment or secret store

That table is the whole post in six rows. Everything I got wrong sat in the first two lines, and everything I got right sat in the middle two.

Where the free model actually fit

There is a second half to this job: after a successful run it writes a short human-readable digest of what changed overnight. I send the raw diff to a free model tier for that summary, then store the summary next to the receipt. Two things matter here, and both are boring on purpose.

  • The model never decides whether the job runs; it only describes a run that already happened.
  • The summary is regenerable, so it is cache, not state, and losing it costs one extra call.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. I used the free server option as the throwaway host for exactly this kind of experiment, and the free model access for the digest step, because both are things I am willing to lose mid-run while I watch what happens.

Limitations and who should skip this

This workflow will not save you if your side effect is not idempotent downstream, because a perfect dedupe key in front of a non-idempotent POST just moves the duplicate. It also assumes you have somewhere durable to put a row, and if you are running with zero external storage, your honest options are a single scheduled trigger or an at-least-once design with a visible duplicate. Finally, if your job must survive a hard kill mid-write, none of this replaces a real transaction boundary in the system that owns the data.

If you are running a one-shot script that nobody depends on, skip the receipt table and go outside instead. If anything downstream pages a human, the receipt is cheaper than the apology.

What I would repeat in the next 48 hours

The habit I am keeping is writing the failing test before the fix, and specifically a test that deletes the state directory to prove the duplicate exists. It takes eight lines, it fails for the right reason, and it converts a vague worry about hosts into a check I can run on every change. What would your version of that test delete, and would your job still be able to tell you it had already run?

title: UAV-Based Computer Vision for Cattle Detection and Feed Bunk Spatial Analysis
description:
arXiv:2611.08928v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Beef cattle production is central to Brazilian agribusiness and faces growing demands for efficiency, sustainability, and animal welfare. Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) offers tools to address these challenges, particularly through monitoring feeding-related spatial patterns in confined systems. Feeding management plays a decisive role in animal performance, yet its evaluation still relies largely on subjective, labor-intensive visual inspections that are hard to scale and prone to bias. This work proposes a computer vision framework based on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to quantify cattle alignment and spatial dispersion at the feed bunk under real-world feedlot conditions. A UAV dataset was collected during flight campaigns at a commercial feedlot in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil. Images were manually annotated into cattle head and cattle back classes to support object detection and image-level spatial analysis of cattle distribution. You Only Look Once (YOLO) models, namely YOLOv8 and YOLOv11, were evaluated, with YOLOv8 small used for the downstream spatial analysis. The feed bunk region was segmented using the Segment Anything Model (SAM), and geometric metrics based on detected head positions were developed to characterize alignment, spacing regularity, and clustering. The selected detector achieved 84.30% mAP50 and 35.50% mAP50-95, with an inference time of approximately 2.7 ms per image on an NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti GPU. The resulting metrics distinguished representative regular and irregular spatial distributions by Root Mean Square Deviation - RMSD (1.06 m and 4.26 m), Coefficient of Variation - CV (42.70% and 96.31%), and clustering (0 and 2 clusters), respectively. These findings indicate that the proposed approach can provide indicators for assessing feed bunk spatial patterns in PLF.

title: HackerTV Dropped. My Lazy Eye Finally Has a Reason to Watch Again.
description:
HackerTV Dropped. My Lazy Eye Finally Has a Reason to Watch Again.

I opened the terminal at 2 a.m., the glow of the monitor the only light in the room. The new HackerTV binary had just landed on GitHub Releases, and the changelog promised a WebRTC‑based player with a built‑in high‑contrast theme and per‑stream subtitle scaling. My left eye has never tracked fast motion well — the “lazy eye” diagnosis from childhood still shows up every time I binge a 60 fps stream. I cloned the repo, ran cargo build --release, and pointed the player at a test H.264 feed.

The first frame rendered clean, no tearing, and the contrast slider responded instantly. I cranked the UI to “high contrast,” enlarged subtitles to 150 %, and enabled the experimental “eye‑comfort” mode that reduces blue‑light peaks above 460 nm. Within seconds the jitter that usually forces me to pause disappeared. I watched a 20‑minute tech talk without once reaching for the remote to rewind.

What surprised me most was the architecture: a thin Rust front‑end talking to a Go‑written media pipeline over gRPC, both exposing Prometheus metrics. I could see the buffer health, decode latency, and frame‑drop count in Grafana while the video played. That observability let me tweak the max_buffer_ms flag from 500 to 300 and shave another 12 ms off end‑to‑end latency — something I never could do with the old Electron wrapper.

After the stream ended I sat back, eyes relaxed, and realized I’d just spent an entire evening coding and watching without the usual strain. If you’ve been looking for a player that treats accessibility as a first‑class citizen, give HackerTV a try — you might find your own reason to watch again.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.107.0 is available. This release adds the random_name_suffix variable to the resource-policy module so that you can optionally omit the random hexadecimal suffix from the names of resource policies.

This release also upgrades Slurm to version 26.05.4 and updates image families to include CUDA 13.2.2 and NVIDIA driver version 595 for H4D, A3 Ultra, A4, and A4X blueprints.

Additionally, this release enforces context timeouts to prevent unresponsive commands in the gcluster CLI, and pins kubectl calls and the dynamic client to the configured kubeconfig context for operations on GKE.

This update also resolves slice shorthands for Cloud TPU, unifies placement policies across GPU and TPU machine types when you submit jobs, and waits for Pods to start before the gcluster job logs command fetches logs.

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.22

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

  • Fixed an issue where ending a chat session in one browser tab didn't automatically close the chat widget in other open tabs.
